text: To address this inquiry, let's revisit the '90s era. Serious computing tasks were predominantly executed through the command line interface, commonly known as the terminal or shell. Networking began gaining significant traction during this time, necessitizing remote access capabilities for users working on specific machines while away from them. A longstanding protocol named Telnet existed since the late '60s, facilitating remote login and command execution over networks. However, its lack of security hindered its adoption in the mid-'90s, exposing sensitive information such as usernames, passwords, and commands to potential eavesdroppers within the network. The rise of the Internet during the '90s prompted demand for secure remote access beyond corporate boundaries, leading to the creation of Secure Shell (SSH). This technology employs robust encryption techniques to safeguard data exchange exclusively between the involved computers. Concerning practical effects of Windows omitting SSH support, they are minimal. Given that Windows isn't typically managed via its command line, SSH is largely unnecessary. Instead, Microsoft's Remote Desktop Connection tool provides a comparable level of security and ease of use. Moreover, users requiring SSH connectivity from Windows devices can utilize available open-source alternatives.

Higher-order Fourier analysis, developed over prime fields, has been recently used in different areas of computer science, including list decoding, algorithmic decomposition and testing. We extend the tools of higher-order Fourier analysis to analyze functions over general fields. Using these new tools, we revisit the results in the above areas. {enumerate} For any fixed finite field K , we show that the list decoding radius of the generalized Reed Muller code over K equals the minimum distance of the code. Previously, this had been proved over prime fields and for the case when - K 1 divides the order of the code . For any fixed finite field K , we give a polynomial time algorithm to decide whether a given polynomial: P K n K can be decomposed as a particular composition of lesser degree polynomials. This had been previously established over prime fields . For any fixed finite field K , we prove that all locally characterized affine-invariant properties of functions: f K n K are testable with one-sided error. The same result was known when K is prime and when the property is linear . Moreover, we show that for any fixed finite field F , an affine-invariant property of functions: f K n F , where K is a growing field extension over F , is testable if it is locally characterized by constraints of bounded weight.

The military (and military personnel) have another set of laws that they have to follow in addition to all the regular laws. This set of laws is called the Uniform Code of Military Justice or UCMJ for short. Here's a sample: Article 92 - Lying A person may not intentionally, voluntarily and wilfully make any false oral statement or written declaration which he knows to be materially untrue with an intent thereby to deceive any Department of Defense personnel as to a material fact concerning information affecting his eligibility for appointment, promotion or other formal action involving such appointment; employment by the United States Government; assignment or transfer; retention of grade; advancement; selection; training; pay, salary or allowance; reimbursement, reward, benefit, privilege or gratuity including all benefits incident thereto; or discharge from service; provided, however,nothing herein shall preclude prosecution under this subchapter if there was corrupt influence on the part of any officer authorized to investigate alleged violations hereof who failed either expressly or impliedly while conducting any investigation of such violation to disclose fully the truth as known to him thereof. It shall also be unlawful for any member of the Armed Forces to knowingly aid or abet any person violating any provision of this Article nor shall it prevent investigations into whether members of specified organizations acting within their scope of authority violated provisions of this article. Penalties: For each offense pursuant to paragraph 1 of this Article, a court-martial composed only of officers commissioned through cadre will be convened at the earliest practicable date to adjudicate guilt or innocence after opportunity has been given to present evidence, sworn statements are taken, and a transcript of testimony admitted. The accused shall receive due process afforded by law. In cases where the element of knowledge does not exist but the elements otherwise do apply, offenses committed willfully and without lawful justification shall be punished as dereliction of duty, desertion, absence without leave, conduct unbecoming an officer and gentleman, making a false official report, mutiny, seditious conspiracy or other misdemeanor punishable as prescribed by regulation. If death resulted from commission of an act described in paragraphs 2 through 6, 7, 8 (a), 9, 11., 12, 13, 14 or 15 of this section, proceedings preceding sentence conviction notwithstanding punishment of life imprisonment, confinement in prison for life or death penalty, as well as execution itself, must conform to applicable procedures established by Army Regulation 601-10, "Military Deportation" unless waived by the Secretary concerned, excepting when ordered under United States Code 10 USC 287g or Executive Order No. 12425 (1962). A nonjudicial proceeding before a general court martial during peacetime may include findings of facts and imposition of penalties similar to those provided in chapter 47, title 37, United States Code, insofar as appropriate; cf. Art 47 U.S.C. 2361-2365. Judicial review of findings and sentences following sentencing trial held by a court-martial in accordance with regulations governing courts-martials subject to these Articles cannot be granted. Life or death sentences imposed upon appeal can only be reviewed by the convening authority until final disposition of appeals according to procedure outlined below. Service connection may not be denied merely because prisoner received satisfactory administrative or disciplinary action prior to entry into active status. Such administrative or disciplinary actions shall be disregarded unless they were used specifically to evade service obligation resulting from disability incurred during period covered by this case. Any references contained in Regulations regarding time periods subsequent to completion of basic training, initial qualification and subsequent advanced individual training (including Advanced Individual Training Phase V) shall read 36 months instead of 90 days excepting those instances mentioned above. This work develops techniques for the sequential detection and location estimation of transient changes in the volatility (standard deviation) of time series data. In particular, we introduce a class of Sequential Probability Ratio Test (SPRT) procedures that are well suited for the purpose of detecting changes in the variance of a stationary univariate time series. Asymptotic bounds on the probability of detection and the average delay are derived and analytical formulas are obtained for these performance measures. When the time series is nonstationary, we extend the SPRT procedure by incorporating a cumulative sum (CUSUM) test, a well known methodology for detecting the trend in a nonstationary time series. The performance of the methodology is demonstrated through extensive Monte Carlo simulation, and the procedure is applied to a data set of daily trading volume on the Australian Stock Exchange (ASX).

The growth of the Bronx owes much to its advantageous position nestled between New England and Manhattan. During Britain'pta colonization, authority over the spans crossing the Harlem River caused significant turmoil. Established in 169pta, Kingsbridge emerged at the juncture where Broadway intersected with Spuyten Duyvil Creek, under the domain of Frederick Philipse as part of Philipse Manor. Local agriculturists from either side of the creek found the levies imposed burdensome. Consequently, in 1759, figures such as Jacobus Dyckman and Benjamin Palmer orchestrated the creation of an untaxed passageway over the Harlem River, leading to the complete cessation of toll collection.

Once upon a time, there was a small village surrounded by dense forests and snow-capped mountains. The village was known for its freezing winters, where the temperature would often drop to the point where it would be too cold to sleep. One such winter, a young girl named Emily was struggling to keep warm in her small hut. She had covered herself with layers of fur blankets, yet she shivered uncontrollably. Meanwhile, the howling winds outside only intensified, making her feel even colder. Just then, Emily heard a faint knock on her door. She opened it to find her elderly neighbor, Mrs. Jenkins, standing outside. Mrs. Jenkins had been living in the village for decades and had experienced many harsh winters. Seeing Emily's plight, Mrs. Jenkins offered to share her firewood and blankets to help the little girl stay warm. Emily gratefully accepted the offer and moved into Mrs. Jenkins' hut. As soon as she entered, Emily felt the comforting warmth of the roaring fire. Mrs. Jenkins had also lined the walls with thick blankets, ensuring that no cold air could seep in. Emily felt a sense of relief that she no longer had to bear the biting cold by herself. The two spent the night talking and singing songs to distract themselves from the frigid weather outside. As the hours passed, Emily felt her eyes getting heavier until she finally drifted off to sleep. The next morning, as the sun rose over the mountains, Emily woke up feeling refreshed and warm. She thanked Mrs. Jenkins for her kindness and vowed to return the favor. From that day on, Emily and Mrs. Jenkins became close friends, sharing many more cold winter nights together. They were grateful for each other's company and warmth, understanding that in the freezing cold, it takes a village to keep warm.

In this article, we propose a model-driven deep learning (DL) approach that combines DL with the expert knowledge to replace the existing orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) receiver in wireless communications. Different from the data-driven fully connected deep neural network (FC-DNN) method, we adopt the block-by-block signal processing method that divides the receiver into channel estimation subnet and signal detection subnet. Each subnet is constructed by a DNN and uses the existing simple and traditional solution as initialization. The proposed model-driven DL receiver offers more accurate channel estimation comparing with the linear minimum mean-squared error (LMMSE) method and exhibits higher data recovery accuracy comparing with the existing methods and FC-DNN. Simulation results further demonstrate the robustness of the proposed approach in terms of signal-to-noise ratio and its superiority to the FC-DNN approach in the computational complexities or the memory usage.

Geologists use a number of field, laboratory, and numerical modeling methods to decipher Earth history and understand the processes that occur on and inside the Earth. In typical geological investigations, geoscientists formulate hypotheses to explain observed phenomena, test them with new observations or experimentation, and develop scientific theories to explain the observations and test results. Geologists who work for oil companies look for oil and natural gas. They examine rock cores and use seismic and magnetic information to find oil and gas deposits. Geologists for mining companies look for metals, minerals, and coal. Geologists use their knowledge of map reading, mathematics, chemistry, and physics to solve problems in their fields of research. Geologists held about 11,000 jobs in 2002. About 32 percent were employed by oil and gas extraction companies, and 30 percent by consulting firms. Geology is one of the oldest scientific disciplines. It deals with the physical materials of Earth, the rocks of which it is composed, and the processes acting upon them. It embraces three major subdivisions: (1) historical geology, which includes the study of past geologic events, (2) descriptive geology, which includes the study of the present features of the Earth's surface, and (3) economic geology, which includes the study of rocks as a source of mineral wealth. Geology also encompasses geophysics and the related sciences of physical geography, cartography, and geodesy. Geologists study how the Earth works. Geologists are employed by oil companies to help find oil and gas deposits. They examine rock cores and use seismic and magnetic information to find oil and gas deposits. Geologists for mining companies look for metals, minerals, and coal. They examine rock samples and test how rocks react with acid to determine which minerals they contain. Mining companies also employ geologists to monitor the ground above mines to check for surface movements that might indicate a cave-in. Geologists in government work for the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) and the U.S. Bureau of Mines. The USGS is the largest nonmilitary user of helicopters in the world. Geologists also work for consulting firms, or as independent consultants. Most geologists work for oil companies or mining companies. In 2002, about 60 percent worked in oil and gas extraction, and 30 percent in mining. The remainder worked in consulting firms, government, or educational institutions. About 16 percent of geologists worked for the government. Most geologists work full time, and about 20 percent worked more than 50 hours per week in 2002. They may be required to work in the field for extended periods. As with most jobs in the sciences, most geologists are employed by private industry. The number of jobs in government, colleges, and universities is much smaller. The best opportunities for geologists are in the petroleum and mining industries. Jobs in the geoscience industry as a whole are expected to grow about as fast as the average for all occupations. Oil and gas exploration and production are expected to continue, and so will exploration for other resources. The largest employers of geologists are oil and gas extraction companies. Jobs with these firms are expected to grow as fast as the average for all jobs, as oil and gas reserves are still being found. Mining companies are also expected to grow at about the average rate for all jobs. Jobs with consulting firms are also expected to grow at about the average rate for all jobs. There are a number of reasons for the expected job growth of geologists. The need for energy and mineral resources is expected to grow. In addition, there are concerns about the possibility of oil and gas depletion. The need to increase exploration and production to ensure that the resources will be available in the future is expected to increase demand for geologists. As big data becomes increasingly prevalent, attention shifts towards ensuring the quality and completeness rather than just focusing on its volume. Data gathered from diverse sources often lead to the creation of multi-view or multi-modal databases. Addressing the issue of incomplete data within these complex structures poses significant difficulties. Particularly troublesome is the scenario where some instances lack an entire perspective of data, leading to what is known as the "missing view" dilemma. Traditional techniques like multiple imputations or matrix completion prove largely ineffective under such circumstances since they rely on available data within the omitted view, which isn't present. Moreover, discarding all cases with a missing perspective drastically reduces the dataset size, thereby weakening the impact of any ensuing analytical efforts. Our research introduces a pioneering technique named VIGAN, utilizing generative adversarial networks (GANs) for filling in missing perspectives. Initially, each perspective is treated independently, mapping domains through a GAN that uses random samples drawn from every aspect. Subsequently, a multi-modal denoising autoencoder (DAE) leverages paired data between perspectives to restore the absent one, guided by the GAN outcomes. By fine-tuning both the GAN and DAE concurrently, our methodology facilitates the seamless blending of domain insights and inter-perspective connections necessary for successful reconstruction of lost viewpoints. Experimental findings on standardized datasets corroborate the superiority of the VIGAN strategy over current best practices. Furthermore, the application of VIGAN in analyzing genetic factors linked to substance abuse disorders underscores its practical relevance and adaptability within the realm of biological sciences.

The BERT language model's exceptional outcomes on conventional benchmarks like Named Entity Recognition (NER) and Semantic Textual Similarity (STS) have marked considerable advancements in Natural Language Processing (NLP). Nevertheless, the effectiveness of these systems in essential areas, including law and medicine, remains uncertain. To address this concern, we introduce a novel adversarial assessment approach utilizing two prominent medical NER and STS datasets. Our proposed method includes three distinct kinds of perturbations mimicking human error, such as misspellings, typographical mistakes, and alternative medical term synonyms. These adversarial conditions cause notable declines in model performance, which we measure accurately. Furthermore, we demonstrate enhanced resistance against such adversarial inputs through retraining using perturbed samples. Through our research, we aim to encourage the adoption of adversarial testing to bolster the resilience of models dedicated to medical applications.

The International Football Association Board (IFAB), the body which oversees the rules of the game, passed the law at a meeting in Zurich. It will come in to force on 1 June, in time for the World Cup in Brazil. The new law was proposed by the Football Association and will apply to domestic and international football. FA general secretary Alex Horne said: "The idea is to get some consistency. The simplest rule for the image of the game is to start from the basis that slogans will not be allowed." From the time the new rule comes in to place, incidents such as Mario Balotelli's infamous "Why Always Me?" message, which he revealed after scoring against Manchester United in 2011, will be banned and subject to a sanction. Fifa general secretary Jerome Valcke said: "It is definitely decided that players must not have any slogan or statement, and we are making the decision that it will apply to the World Cup." Law 4 of the game, which relates to players' equipment, will be amended. It states: "Players must not reveal undergarments that show political, religious, personal slogans, statements or images, or advertising other than the manufacturer logo. "A playerteam of a player that reveals an undergarment that shows political, religious, personal slogans, statements or images, or advertising other than the manufacturers' logo will be sanctioned by the competition organiser or by Fifa." Meanwhile, the IFAB rejected a proposal from Uefa to amend the so-called "triple punishment" which occurs when a penalty kick is given within a game, warranting a player being sent off and a possible goal being scored. It was agreed that a pilot project carried out by the FA and Scottish Football Association relating to revolving substitutes in amateur football will continue, as will a Uefa experiment into the use of a sin bin in recreational football. The IFAB also discussed the potential use of video replays for match officials but remains of the view that technology should be allowed only for goal-line incidents because "it is a clear yes or no decision." An IFAB statement read: "Concerns were raised about video replays slowing the game down and increasing the number of stoppages."

A BBC analysis suggests 195 out of 402 official bathing waters are patrolled between July and September. The National Water Safety Forum said it was "impractical" for every beach to be covered. There is no formal list of which beaches have lifeguards as the Royal National Lifeboat Institute (RNLI) only publishes details of the ones it patrols. Local councils and private land owners provide others. Seven people died in two incidents at Camber Sands in East Sussex in summer 2016. The families of five men, who died in the second incident in August, described the victims as physically fit and competent swimmers. An inquest into the deaths, which concluded in June 2017, heard the RNLI had recommended that Rother District Council employ lifeguards after a risk assessment in 2013. The inquest was also told the RNLI then rejected a request to put lifeguards on Camber Sands 16 days before the August deaths, citing a lack of resources. Lifeguards now patrol the beach. However, the inquest concluded that the men may still have drowned even if there had been lifeguards. 490 in 2016 215 suspected accidents or natural causes, almost half of which were between June and September 163 males died in accidents or by natural causes 32 females 67 by a coast, shore or beach RNLI lifeguards rescued 2,082 people across the UK and Jersey, and saved 127 lives, in 2016. The charity, which lists the beaches it patrols on its website, said it worked with councils and other beach owners to determine lifeguard cover. "There may be times when we will approach a local authority or beach owner if there has been something that has happened on that beach, but the majority of times it will be due to the local authority or beach owner coming to us," a spokeswoman said. The RNLI said it would not be possible to put lifeguards on to all bathing waters and services "need to be judged on a needs basis as opposed to a cost implication." The cost to train a RNLI lifeguard is PS712 plus a further PS812 for equipment. The water safety forum said some of the beaches not covered by lifeguards may not attract significant numbers of people or pose a significant risk. Recently, advanced Fourier analysis techniques applied to prime fields have gained traction across various domains within computer science such as list decoding, algorithmic decomposition, and verification processes. In our study, we broaden these methods to encompass analyses conducted on general fields. Utilizing these updated analytical instruments, we reevaluate outcomes related to the mentioned sectors. Specifically: (1) Over a predetermined finite field K, we demonstrate that the list decoding range for the extended Reed-Muller code aligns with the minimal separation between codewords; prior evidence supported this only over prime fields or when the ratio of the code's size minus one to its order equaled K. (2) We also propose a polynomial time algorithm capable of determining if a specific polynomial P(K^n), defined over the finite field K, can undergo decomposition into lower-degree constituent polynomials. Earlier research validated this concept solely over prime fields. Lastly, (3) we establish that every functionally unique attribute identified through affine-invariance within functions f(K^n), operating within finite field K, can be assessed accurately using a single-error evaluation methodology. This finding corroborates existing knowledge regarding prime number fields and linear characteristics. Furthermore, we reveal that any characteristic defining affine-invariance within functions f(K^n), where K represents a progressively expanding extension from base field F, remains assessable provided it conforms to local constraints with capped magnitude.

My points are as follows: 1. No rational justification exists for treating CP ownership dissimilarly compared to possessing other types of crime videos 2. Subjecting the viewer to punishment due to the victim's revictimization isn't sufficient grounds for imprisonment 3. Legalizing CP may not increase demands for such content or could potentially yield positive outcomes If we consider the perspective commonly held today, people believe that watching distressing images which represent crimes should remain within legal boundaries and that individuals viewing them aren't committing criminal acts. There appears to be no discernible difference between CP materials and those related to other criminal activities. What makes viewing certain crime footage illegal while others are permitted and even monetized? Is there truly a valid argument supporting the idea that witnesses of non-CP crimes cannot advocate for the prosecution of those who have seen their trauma? This appears inconsistent. In each situation, victims endure lasting emotional harm and humiliation yet receive varying levels of support. Thirdly, if one believes that CP victims deserve particular attention, then addressing the psychological pain inflicted upon them must also have limitations. Taking this further, if a CP victim demanded the perpetrator's torture and execution, the government wouldn't comply. Similarly, if the victim insisted that mere imprisonment wasn't adequate until the viewer experienced prolonged torment, authorities would still resist. Ultimately, the person viewing the material retains specific rights that can't be relinquished solely based on the victim's wishes. Therefore, what level of physical and emotional hardship (through incarceration) is expected from someone who views CP versus someone who watches another type of crime? Shouldn't the compensation required from these two scenarios be equal with regard to the victims involved? Finally, some argue that consuming CP increases the likelihood of future abuses by boosting demand. However, few make similar claims about viewership leading to escalated rates of murder, robbery, or violence. People generally reject the notion that watching footage of various crimes contributes to higher occurrences of those offenses.

Consequently, these atoms combine to create an ozone molecule comprised of three oxygen atoms.

The root cause lies in the tendency for people to mostly engage with the early comments and their inclination towards upvoting much more frequently than downvoting. To elucilibate further, consider a scenario involving a six-hour-old discussion with 100 comments. Suppose the first five comments garnered 50 upvotes each despite being average, while a superior comment later added received upvotes from approximately 90% of its audience but started at a lower rank. Given that fewer individuals viewed this excellent contribution initially, its visibility remains limited compared to earlier, yet inferior entries. By encouraging equal usage of upvotes and downvotes, such imbalances could be rectified, ensuring that valuable insights aren't obscured simply because they were introduced later.

With the rapid advancement of mobile devices and crowdsourcing platforms, spatial crowdsourcing has attracted much attention from various research communities. A spatial crowdsourcing system periodically matches a number of location-based tasks with a pool of available workers who are located in the same or nearby area as the task. This way, the tasks can be completed quickly and efficiently while minimizing travel costs and time. The tasks can range from simple tasks such as taking a photo of a certain location to more complex ones such as analyzing traffic patterns or detecting and reporting environmental issues. Spatial crowdsourcing has a wide range of applications, including urban planning, disaster response, environmental monitoring, and tourism.

Nevertheless, these methods encounter issues when attempting to accurately reproduce structures and hues over larger occluded areas. These limitations stem from instabilities encountered during the model's training phase. Our research proposes a novel incremental learning strategy tailored specifically for image inpainting. Throughout the training process, we gradually expand the extent of the obscured regions; during testing, users can specify varying sizes and multiple irregularly placed gaps. Lake Constance consists of three bodies of water: the Obersee upper lake, the Untersee lower lake, and a connecting stretch of the Rhine, called the Seerhein Lake Rhine. The lake has a surface area of 144.6 km2 (55.7 sq mi), and a total volume of 4,400 km3 (1,620 cu mi). In the middle of the lake, at an altitude of 1,520 m (4,900 ft), is the Wetterhorn, a famous mountain in the Alps. The mountains and the lake are popular with hikers, but there are few places for camping or accommodation. The area around the lake is also popular with tourists, especially in summer. It is possible to walk from one side of the lake to the other. The northern side of the lake is occupied by Germany and the south by Switzerland. The boundary between the two countries is roughly along the shore. The island of Rugen, part of Germany, lies to the south. The Swiss lake shore is the main tourist attraction of the lake, with hotels, restaurants, shops and small settlements. The most famous of these is the town of Constance. The lake is also an important fishery, especially for trout and carp. The islands of Rugen, Kyffhauser and Lowen are important bird colonies.

The Restore Justice campaign, spearheaded by Paul Staines who writes the Guido Fawkes political blog, calls for the death penalty to be brought back for child and police officer murderers. He cites opinion polls which suggest about half the population would like it re-introduced for murderers. This rises to 60 when it comes to child or police officer killers. Mr Staines needs 100,000 people to support his e-petition on the government website to prompt a possible parliamentary debate on the issue. The last executions in the UK took place in 1964. The death penalty was formally abolished in Britain in 1965 and in Northern Ireland in 1973. Despite it rating high on public opinion polls, it was last debated in Parliament in 1998 during the passage of the Human Rights Act. It was rejected by 158 votes. "The majority are in favour for bringing back the death penalty everywhere except in Parliament," said Mr Staines. "Politicians are complaining that there's a disconnect and that the public aren't engaged with them - maybe if they represented the views and the will of the voters, there wouldn't be such a big disconnect." He added: "The people want the death penalty, and politicians aren't prepared to vote for it. That's not right. "What I'm trying to do is get Parliament to discuss this issue between what Parliament wants and what the people want." House of Commons leader Sir George Young has warned that it would damage democracy to ignore strong opinions among members of the public "or pretend that their views do not exist." Douglas Carswell MP agreed, saying, although he was firmly against the death penalty, he was in favour of Parliament debating it and would support a referendum on whether it should be brought back. "I'm convinced that if there was a referendum on capital punishment we could win it; we could get most people to say'no' to the death penalty. "We need to treat people as grown-ups and have the debate and not do what we have done for half a century which is to ignore the public's concern and treat them with contempt. "The important thing is we have this debate." Mr Carswell added that the reason why Parliament had not debated this topic in recent years was because it was "out of touch with the public." "The mistake MPs have made is to not trust the people and to try and ignore their concerns. We can disagree with it but we have to trust it." But Neil Durkin from Amnesty International said it was a "waste of time and money that we as a nation cannot afford." In September 2010, YouGov conducted the last opinion poll to ask directly if people want the death penalty re-instated. It suggested that 51 did. And a Mori poll in July 2010 asked people which of a list of crimes they thought should have the death penalty. For child murder, 62 supported it while a YouGov poll in November 2010 found 74 of people supported the death penalty for murder in some circumstances, though only 16 supported it for all murders. However, when similar polls were carried out in the 1970s, support for it was far higher with 70 in favour. Anthony Wells, associate director of YouGov, says polls which ask about the death penalty are straightforward: "Do you support it or not?" "When people already know about it and have established views then it is quite simple. The hard ones [opinion polls] are when people need to have an issue explained to them." He said historically opinion polls on capital punishment have been commissioned by newspapers when there has been a heinous crime such as after the Soham murders. Mr Wells added that such polls are not often commissioned in times when a high-profile murder is not in the news. However, the last two polls on the subject were not about a specific case, being conducted for a story about sentencing for murder and for a Channel 4 programme. Polls are quite accurate, plus or minus 3, said Mr Wells, and their accuracy can be checked against real life events such as who is going to win the election or X Factor. "All the polls about the death penalty show similar patterns so even if it was worded differently it would still get the same result," he added. "You can only tell what people think at the moment, but if it follows current trends then yes, I'd expect it to go down." Mr Durkin from Amnesty International said it was important to have an informed debate, rather than a simple "yes or no" question. "Public opinion polls are usually conducted after a particularly horrible murder that's had lots of publicity so you do tend to get that outcry. "On top of that, when we have looked at opinion polls in the US, most people tend to think that the US is firmly in terms of public opinion pro death penalty. "If you offer in those questions to the public alternatives to capital punishment - the lethal injections, the electrocutions, whatever it is - and talk about longer sentences then support drops away."

Her cold wet nose nuzzled it's way into my clasped hands. As I reached out, wrapping my arms around her thick fur coat, the wet tissue fell from my hand and onto the muddy ground. I'm not crying, I thought. I'm just a little choked up, that's all. I'm sure that's what others have said as they've stood over the grave of their beloved companion. But I'm also sure that like me, they were lying to themselves. I cried as I stood at the grave of my pet dog, the family pet, the friend who'd been with me for fifteen years. He was my first pet and I'm not sure if I'm ready for another one. He was a rescue dog, a Basset Hound, given to me by my grandparents. When I was a teenager I'd said to them that I wanted a dog. They said, 'If you want a dog, you'll have to look after it.' So I'd looked after the dog, a beautiful, gentle natured dog. I'd had to look after him when I went to university. I'd had to look after him when I'd moved out of the family home. I'd had to look after him when I'd moved to Cornwall. And finally I'd had to look after him when I'd made the hardest decision of all - to have him put down. The decision wasn't easy. He'd developed a tumour in his mouth. His jaw was swollen and he could barely eat. He'd lost half of his body weight in three months. But still, he'd tried to make me happy. As he lay on the floor, unable to stand up, he'd still greet me with that wagging tail. I'd still felt him lick my hand as I'd bent down to stroke his head. But there were good times, too. The walks in the park. The nights where he'd sit with me on the sofa as I read a book, or watched TV. The days when we'd go to the beach, or take a road trip. I don't know what I'll do without him. I'm not sure what to do with all of the dog toys he's left behind. I'm not sure what to do with his lead, his collar, his harness. It's all just too much. But I know that he's in a better place. I know that he's in doggy heaven, chasing rabbits and playing with his friends. I know that I'll see him again. Goodbye my friend. I miss you. I love you. He just wanted to sit outside one last time. When I touched him, he spoke to me, as if he knew I was coming. Not once in my many decades of existence has anyone ever spoken to me, but his voice was clear, and frail. "Can I sit outside, with the birds, one last time?" He asked me like he was a child asking for permission. I couldn't bear to tell him that technically, I wasn't allowed to let a soul live past its expiration date, but the way he spoke to me..... it was without fear. It made me wonder how many nights he had laid in that bed, closed his eyes, and reached out to me, trying to let me know that he was at peace with his fate. How long had he awaited death? I knew the answer, I could see his whole life displayed right before my very eyes, and still the question pulled on me in ways I couldn't describe. His childhood was filled with happy memories, but overflowing with bad ones. Loud arguments muffled by doors and pillows flooded my ears, and strategically placed bruises lined his arms and legs. Some of his teeth were missing, and the kids at school called him Checkerboard. Then the scenes changed. He was an adult now, strolling down the street of a big city, the scent of morning coffee and fresh gasoline in the air. A woman with her head down rushed by, slamming into his side, sending his coffee splashing onto the parked car next to him, and the only good suit he owned. She apologized profusely, handed him a twenty-dollar bill, and stormed off in the other direction. Another scene change. The man and the coffee-spiller had somehow ended up together, their love as bright as it was during their first kiss. But then the arguments began, and the familiar feeling of dread returned. It was little things at first, but it only grew from there. Soon they were locked in a shouting competition, and in tears, she dashed from the apartment, and his life, leaving him wondering just where he went wrong. Weren't arguments healthy? He thought, prayed that she would come back. She didn't. And he knew she would never when he saw her two years later at that same coffee shop, a diamond ring on her finger and a million-dollar man wrapped around her waist. She had moved on, why couldn't he? Dropped into a world of depression, confusion, and alcoholism, he wandered aimlessly, looking for a light that was only ever advertised, never sold. Deeper and deeper he sank into his own mind until one day, he found himself under a light. The light of a doctor's flashlight. It was bright, and annoying, and a man was asking him if he was okay. He didn't know. He couldn't remember. Decades passed in between empty cans and hospital rooms, until one word stuck in his mind: Dementia. It was like a big fat F, like the ones he used to get on his report cards from school. He hid the word just as he did with the grades, and continued on with his life. He was given medications, but they didn't help with the pit he was in, and eventually he was admitted to some kind of psychiatric ward. He wasn't crazy. He was depressed, though he couldn't remember why. There, he spent many years, where he made some of the best memories of his life. Like the one where he went outside to feed the birds just as the sun was waking up, and one of them hopped into his hand to eat the seeds. Or the one where he got to visit with some animals from the local shelter, while other patients visited their family. It would've made him sad to think he had no family to visit with, if not for the memory of his childhood nickname. The animals were kind, and gentle, they were better than his parents, and the coffee-spiller. They understood him, and listened to him. I had to pull away from his relaxed form. His closed eyes and rickety breathing was too much for me, where normally, I'd have no qualms about taking his life. His eyes opened slowly, and searching through the darkness of the room, they found mine. "Please," he whispered, "just one more sunrise." Thinking of the birds he had held, I nodded. "One more sunrise." With a gentle exhale of breath, he smiled softly, and in what little light there was, I could see he was missing a few teeth. So this was longer than I intended, but it was fun to write!

Billy went to the mall with his father. He really wanted a new pair of shoes. His father told him if he was good, he would buy him the shoes. Billy and his friend Cole decided to play hide-and-seek in the shopping center. Once they were all hiding their place on the ground floor from each other, Little Red Riding Hood came along. She heard the children playing outside the store window. They started laughing at her when she called out for help. The next thing she knew, her brothers had gotten so scared that they ran away. Billy's young brother and one more boy got caught up in the car the minute they found out what happened. Their parents were ashamed and angry because they didn't want them near the boys who did it. When they asked Billy about it, he said he thought it would be funny to play this game and scare off the kids by pretending to do something terrible like they'd seen TV shows do before. This is how I first learned about "playing bad" or even worse, getting into trouble. Of course my siblings - who watched television much less than me - didn't understand why maybe there might have been some sort of reason behind these violent games we played as kids. I don't remember ever being punished but it's clear today that most of us will avoid dealing with real consequences until after our teenage years are over. This means many adults think and act similar to kids: "Stick around long enough and eventually you'll get your way." Instead, celebrate successes together as families now! Many times they take advantage of situations where teens can cause a lot of damage without facing any consequence: school events, holiday parties, sports activities... Give them credit instead! Recognize that once again they're trying very hard to please others; let them know that family support always counts (and let's face it: nothing makes someone happier inside than knowing they've done well).

Religious and political connections played an essential role in shaping Rome's domestic administration, international relations, and growth across different phases such as the Kingdom, Republic, and Empire stages. After the fall of the monarchical rule, the civil and sacred responsibilities formerly held by the king were distributed fairly among the aristocratic class through the creation of two consul positions that were filled on an annual basis. During the initial period of the Republic, similar to possibly during the reign of kings, commoners (plebeians) were barred from holding influential roles in both religion and government and faced penalties for violating unfamiliar legal codes. To challenge the oppressive grip of patricians over crucial positions, religious duties, and access to legal information, plebeians engaged in protests and violent actions. As a response to this crisis, the Senate chose Camillus as dictator who resolved the issue through negotiation and consecrated the agreement with the inauguration of a temple dedicated to Concordia. Eventually, religious timetables and statutes became accessible to all citizens. Positions like plebeian tribunes, possessing inviolable standing and the power to obstruct legislative discussions, were established. While theoretically, membership in the augural and pontifical organizations was opened up to plebeians, practically speaking, these posts remained under the control of the noble patrician families and to some degree, their plebeian counterparts throughout the entirety of the Roman Republic and even afterward.

In binary jumbled pattern matching we wish to preprocess a binary string S in order to answer queries (i , j) which ask for a substring of S that is of size i and has exactly j 1-bits. The problem naturally generalizes to node-labeled trees and graphs by replacing "substring" with "connected subgraph." In this paper, we give n 2 2 (log n log log n) 1 2 time solutions for both strings and trees. This odd-looking time complexity improves the state of the art O ( n 2 log 2 n) solutions by more than any poly-logarithmic factor. It originates from the recent seminal algorithm of Williams for min-plus matrix multiplication. We obtain the result by giving a black-box reduction from trees to strings. This is then combined with a reduction from strings to min-plus matrix multiplications.

Increased adoption and deployment of machine learning (ML) models into business, healthcare and other organisational processes, will result in a growing disconnect between the engineers and researchers who developed the models and the model's users and other stakeholders, such as regulators or auditors. This disconnect is inevitable, as models begin to be used over a number of years or are shared among third parties through user communities or via commercial marketplaces, and it will become increasingly difficult for users to maintain ongoing insight into the suitability of the parties who created the model, or the data that was used to train it. This could become problematic, particularly where regulations change and once-acceptable standards become outdated, or where data sources are discredited, perhaps judged to be biased or corrupted, either deliberately or unwittingly. In this paper we present a method for arriving at a quantifiable metric capable of ranking the transparency of the process pipelines used to generate ML models and other data assets, such that users, auditors and other stakeholders can gain confidence that they will be able to validate and trust the data sources and human contributors in the systems that they rely on for their business operations. The methodology for calculating the transparency metric, and the type of criteria that could be used to make judgements on the visibility of contributions to systems are explained and illustrated through an example scenario.

The nucleus of an atom consists of protons and neutrons. When additional neutrons bombard the atom, its weight increases significantly, causing it to collapse and release energy in the form of heat due to the strong forces within the nucleus. This process also emits various electromagnetic waves. Consider uranium-235, an inherently unstable element; when struck by neutrons, it undergoes fission, breaking apart into smaller fragments while simultaneously releasing energy. This reaction produces more neutrons, triggering further fission events in nearby uranium-2EE nuclei. Consequently, a chain reaction occurs, resulting in substantial energy output after splitting large quantities of uranium-235.

Atomic structure comprises protons, neutrons, and electrons. A single hydrogen atom, the lightest element, contains one proton, one electron, and zero neutrons. Neutrons determine atomic isotopes, such as protium (hydrogen), deuterium, and tritium. Protium and deuterium remain stable throughout time unless altered externally. In contrast, tritium is unstable and eventually transforms into helium-3 through radioactive decay, generating radiation and neutrinos during the process. Each decay event differs based on the original atom involved, but the primary outcome involves the production of new particles and the release of energy.

In this position paper we present a novel approach to neurobiologically plausible implementation of emotional reactions and behaviors for real-time autonomous robotic systems. The working metaphor we use is the Affective Neuronal Network (ANN), a connectionist model of the emotional response systems in the brain. In the ANN the emotional response is computed by the total activity of a subset of neurons (emotional neurons), which are in turn influenced by the neural activations that represent the inputs to the brain (perceptual neurons). This organization of the emotional system implies that, when it comes to designing a robotic implementation of the ANN, the perceptual neurons must be placed in the low-level sensory-motor processing modules of the robotic system, and the emotional neurons must be placed in the high-level behavior control modules.

Nonlocal operators of fractional type are a popular modeling choice for applications that do not adhere to classical diffusive behavior; however, one major challenge in nonlocal simulations is the selection of an appropriate spatial kernel function for the nonlocal operator. The kernel function describes the long-range interactions between particles and influences the type of behavior that the nonlocal operator exhibits. Different applications may require different kernel functions depending on the underlying physics. Some commonly used kernel functions include the Gaussian kernel, power-law kernel, and exponential kernel. Each kernel function has its unique properties and can be chosen based on the specific application. For example, the Gaussian kernel is often used for diffusion processes, while the power-law kernel is relevant for scale-free systems that exhibit power-law behavior. In addition to the choice of kernel function, the choice of the domain over which the nonlocal operator is defined and its associated boundary conditions can also affect the behavior of the simulations. The choice of domain and boundary conditions can vary depending on the specific problem being modeled. Overall, selecting an appropriate kernel function and domain for nonlocal simulations is crucial for accurately modeling the underlying physics of a system.

Hinchingbrooke Hospital in Cambridgeshire, run by Circle, was branded "inadequate" by the Care Quality Commission (CQC) last month. However, its chief executive, Hisham Abdel-Rahman, said the report was "problematic" and full of errors. The CQC accepted some mistakes but said it stood by the report. Mr Abdel-Rahman was giving evidence to the House of Commons Public Accounts Committee on Monday. Circle announced on 9 January that it was in talks to ensure an "orderly withdrawal" from its contract to run the hospital, near Huntingdon, citing "unprecedented" increases in AE attendances and funding cuts. The CQC released its report hours later, raising "a number of serious concerns" about staffing, risks to patient safety and medical care. Mr Abdel-Rahman told the committee he was disappointed the inadequate rating had not been changed, even though the CQC had acknowledged 65 of the 300 errors. In one example, he told the committee a member of staff was criticised for shouting at a patient, who later turned out to be profoundly deaf. Stewart Jackson, committee member and Conservative MP for Peterborough, told David Behan, the head of the CQC, that the report was based on "anecdote - some might say tittle-tattle." "You have traduced the reputation of a popular hospital," Mr Jackson said. "You should be ashamed of yourself." But Mr Behan said he stood by the report and many of the changes pointed out by the hospital had been based on its presentation and spelling. "I am not ashamed of myself," he said. "We did find good care at Hinchingbrooke but we also found care that needs to improve and needs to improve quickly." A spokeswoman for the CQC said the "exact number of changes" made to the report, which she said was at a draft stage, was not known. "None of the changes that were highlighted during the factual accuracy process would have been about the overall rating of the provider," she said. "Our judgments are based on what our inspection team saw and heard on their visits." The hospital, which was taken over in 2012 when it faced closure with debts of PS40m, is to be returned to the NHS in March. A follow up report by the CQC, due to be published in the next few weeks, is expected to say improvements have been made.

Sheriff Alastair Brown sentenced him to two years in prison, to be served consecutively to the four-year sentence he is already serving. The man will also be subject to an order banning him from entering any mosque in Scotland for 10 years.

The field of bio-inspired robotics seeks to create mechanical systems that mimic the designs and concepts used by biological systems. One of the more challenging biological concepts to imitate in mechanical systems is the ability to create an internal environment that can foster homeostasis through the use of a membrane similar to skin. A robot with this ability would be able to regulate internal parameters, repair itself using the internal sub-environment, and defend its internal parts from the surrounding environment. This paper presents the internal structure of a non-holonomic wheeled system that enables homeostasis via a fully connected interior, protected from the outside environment by a flexible membrane. The three objectives of this paper are to: 1) Explore the idea of nature creating higher-order life forms with wheeled limbs given the correct intermediate steps. 2) Characterize a robot that uses a homeostasis enabling wheel. 3) Determine the feasibility of using a homeostasis enabling wheel as a mode of locomotion.

The first visible institution to run into trouble in the United States was the Southern California-based IndyMac, a spin-off of Countrywide Financial. Before its failure, IndyMac Bank was the largest savings and loan association in the Los Angeles market and the seventh largest mortgage originator in the United States. The failure of IndyMac Bank on July 11, 2008, was the fourth largest bank failure in United States history up until the crisis precipitated even larger failures, and the second largest failure of a regulated thrift. IndyMac Bank's parent corporation was IndyMac Bancorp until the FDIC seized IndyMac Bank. IndyMac Bancorp filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy in July 2008.

The sun rose as I logged in to my avatar on planet B-73932 and set off for the mountain. It's the only mountain around, but still, I suppose I should name it. Seeing as I discovered it and all. Avatars, by the way, are bio-organic constructs humans use to interact with the world around them. They can vary in size and shape to fill any number of roles, from tiny spider-like bodies for maintenance and repair to gigantic starships. We can transfer between them simply by logging out of one and logging into another, switching back and forth between any number of bodies. The avatar I was currently inhabiting was a Rezenic TrHu-87 model with some modifications I've made myself. The Tr stands for tracked because it has several large tank treads it maneuvers with, and Hu stands for humanoid, because the upper body is shaped like a human's. Not that most people have ever seen a human body. It's just a designation left over from Rezenic's founding. The TrHu-87 is designed for long distance autonomous operations, equipped with built in solar energy collectors and charging ports for other avatars to plug in. I have two other bodies with me, a Rezenic ArRe-41 (Arthropod -Repair) and a Gresson Skywatch for scouting. The ArRe (or Ari as I call it) is for fixing up the TrHu if it breaks. It's about 2 feet long with six legs and a stunning array of repair tools in its carapace. The Skywatch has four wings like a dragonfly and many sensors. This planet was a waste of time. It has no organic compounds, hardly any atmosphere, and worst of all, hardly any metals deposits. Beyond the occasional iron meteorite or tiny vein of copper, there is almost no concentrated resources of any kind. It's not even a nice planet to look at. The soil and the sky and the blinding dust storms are all greyish-beige. But still, prospecting beats running the reproduction farms on Varia 5. I knew I wouldn't make the mountain today, so I set the TrHu on autopilot and logged into the Skywatch. I unclasped the handles on the back of my former body and launched myself into the sky. With such a thin atmosphere I mostly have to use compressed gas to keep myself aloft, but the gravity's fairly low anyways so it's not a big difference. I had been flying for an hour, circling out from my TrHu wider and wider, when an FTL communication lit up a notification on the screen in front of my eyes. The software that interfaces our minds with the machines is designed not to interface with us directly except through neuron mimicking devices, so all other input has to be done with a second screen in front of my normal visual input sensors. That way, no electronic beepers or radios can directly interact with our minds. It's a safety precaution. The communication notified me that a mandatory software update was scheduled for today. I was mildly perturbed that this was the first time I had heard of this update, so I started back to the TrHu immediately. I don't even remember blacking out. I woke up crashed head first into the grainy, rocky soil near a dry riverbed. I crawled out of my own impact crater and looked around. There was the TrHu only a few hundred feet away. I set out as soon as I had cleared my gas vents of debris Something was wrong. Software updates were supposed to be seamless, and they certainly never caused syncope (loss of consciousness). I had to check and make sure nothing was wrong with the TrHu or ArRe. I made the mental effort to leave my body that let me log out, but nothing happened. I tried harder, still nothing. I reached to my underside for the manual override switch. My vision faded to black, but I could tell I was not in the ether between bodies. I pushed myself back to where I came from, and found myself staring once again at the TrHu through the eyes of the Skywatch. I was trapped. I could no longer log out of my body. Throughout the Middle Ages, Newcastle was England's northern fortress. Incorporated first by Henry II, the city had a new charter granted by Elizabeth in 1589. A 25-foot (7.6 m) high defensive wall was erected, surrounded by a ditch and earthen mound. Gateways and towers provided passage for the King's men through the walls. The townsfolk were restricted to a smaller area within the walls. They were allowed to leave the city only after they had paid a heavy tax, and their gates were closed each evening. The "Lovelace Tower" of 1473 was one of the city's four original towers. The "Beswick Tower" was built in 1380 and a third, the "Blaydon Tower" in 1404. The remains of these towers and the city walls can still be seen in the Garden of Remembrance. The "Cowgate" was a second city gate; the "Rose-gate" was a third; and "Barrack-gate" was the only post-medieval entrance. In 1548, Newcastle was awarded a Royal Charter by Henry VIII, which allowed the town to administer its own affairs and to hold an annual fair, but the city retained its strong links with the Crown. In 1600, James I's son, Henry, Earl of Newcastle, rebuilt the "Beswick Tower." This replaced the previous tower in the same location, which was demolished to accommodate the new fortifications. A 25 feet (7.6 m) high wall was built with a moat and two drawbridges. The town was a garrison town, housing soldiers to guard against Scottish attacks. Another 16th-century garrison building was the Royal Gunsite. In 1616, James I granted the Duke of Buckingham the right to build a fort on Tyneside. In 1642, the Parliamentarians used the fort to mount their successful siege of Newcastle. The English Civil War ended in 1648 with the victory of the Parliamentarians at the Battle of Dunbar, and Newcastle surrendered to the Scots. After the Restoration in 1660, Charles II raised the Royalists to power. The Newcastle garrison was raised again and a new fortress was built in the High Level area. In 1674, Charles II granted a charter to Newcastle, which allowed it to hold its own fairs, manage its affairs, and elect its own mayor and aldermen. During the 17th and 18th centuries, Newcastle was a major centre of shipbuilding. The port and town became prosperous from its shipbuilding and export of coal. This was a time of rapid development. By the 18th century, the town had a population of about 12,000. In 1706, the first corn exchange in England was built in the town. In 1776, the town's population was 23,000. In 1796, the town had 31,000 inhabitants. The population was growing rapidly because of its strong commercial links with the cotton industry in Manchester and the coal mining industry in Northumberland and County Durham. By the 1830s, the population of Newcastle was around 80,000. The first passenger railway service, on the Stockton and Darlington Railway, began in 1825. By the 1840s, passenger and goods railways had spread throughout the region. In 1847, the Great North of England Railway (GNER) was formed, linking Newcastle and York. By 1850, the population of Newcastle had increased to 100,000. During the 19th century, Newcastle became a major centre of heavy industry. Coal was dug from pits in the Northumberland and County Durham coalfields. Iron ore and coal were transported to the blast furnaces in the area for the production of steel, and ships were constructed in the town's shipyards. The population reached a peak of 214,000 in 1911. During the Victorian era, Newcastle became a major centre of the Arts. The Theatre Royal and the Literary and Philosophical Society were built in 1837. A Free Library opened in 1857. Artificial sweeteners mimic the sweetness of sugar without adding calories because they metabolize differently, making them suitable for individuals with diabetes as they don't affect blood sugar levels. However, despite their intense sweetness, there may be concerns regarding their usage. Recent research suggests that our bodies might possess internal taste receptors throughout the digestive system. We prove a quantum information-theoretic conjecture due to Ji, Liu and Song (CRYPTO 2018) which suggested that a uniform superposition with random binary phase is statistically indistinguishable from a Haar -random state with high probability. The conjecture can be stated formally as follows: Let psi be a uniform superposition of n qubits with random binary phases such that: psi 1sqrt (2n) (0 e (itheta1) 1) (0 e (itheta2) 1) ... (0 e (ithetan) 1) where each thetai is chosen uniformly at random from {0,pi}. Then, for any efficient Boolean function f on n bits, the statistical distance between the distribution of f (psi) and the corresponding distribution for a Haar-random state phi is at most epsilon, for some small constant epsilon. In their original paper, Ji et al. provided a heuristic argument suggesting that the conjecture should hold true, and also provided some numerical evidence supporting their conjecture. However, they did not provide a rigorous proof. Recently, however, Aaronson et al. (2020) managed to prove this conjecture in a strong sense. Specifically, they showed that the conjecture holds true for any polynomial-time computable function f, with probability 1-o (1) over the choice of phases in the uniform superposition. Moreover, they showed that this result can be extended to hold for functions that are computable by quantum circuits of bounded depth and size. The proof relies on a combination of tools from quantum information theory and probability theory. In particular, it uses the technique of matrix concentration inequalities to bound the second moments of the output distribution of the function f on the uniform superposition, and then applies the so-called "quantum de Finetti theorem" to show that the distribution is close to the corresponding distribution for a Haar-random state. Overall, the result has important implications for quantum cryptography and quantum algorithms, as it provides a new way of generating highly entangled states that are statistically indistinguishable from random states, but can be generated efficiently using quantum circuits.

On one hand he was cleaning up after pigs, but on the other hand, he finally could feel what it was like to be seen as one of the normies, someone who doesn't carry the responsibility that comes with being the most powerful, only remaining wizard. He sighed and felt real relief. Then his boss walked in. He watched his boss in slow motion, labeling every aspect of him the second time that day. Pig-like. Dim-witted. He understood the blokes life at a glance. Merlin knew this was normal behavior of himself, the kind he was trying to avoid, so he let it go. He watched as the man's mouth opened. Flecks of saliva fell loosely into the air. A moment of self consciousness spread across his expression for a moment, then it was stifled by the discipline of a hateful character, leaving only worry and hate. " THIS..." He watched the hatred spread across the mans face. He wondered if this man had ever had a moment of empathy in his entire existence. It made him reflect on his own life when it was puny and mortal. He overcame that stuff. He was much different from this man. " FLOOR..." This man clearly wanted to hurt him. He had no respect for him, and he barely knew him. Why? What did this person think of him? " IS..." A man who walked through the door, seeming slightly unhinged, occasionally referencing something beyond his conceptions. His boss disrespected him because he thought Merlin was a loser worse than himself! Well Merlin could hardly blame him. A creature longing for love, but unwilling or unable to put himself out there, to find others who could love the good in him. " STILL..." Merlin wondered if he should set this man up on a date, or put him out of his misery. Date, misery, date, misery...... Misery. Fire boiled up from his eyes. Quantum computers would be used to solve a very narrow specific set of problems. It is not likely they would be used for most computer problems. Transistor based computers will likely still do those things faster. Here's an example of this narrow focus. Integer factorization. For example, take two very large prime numbers (dozens and dozens of digits each). Now multiply them together. Now throw away the original primes. The question becomes, can you figure out what those two original primes were? For humans, this would take universe lifetimes. For current transistor based computers, this would also take universe lifetimes (well, this hasn't been proved, but it's likely to be the case). For quantum computers, they could produce a result in minutes. However, there are only a handful of important problems that quantum computers could solve which regular transistor computers could not. This part is hard to describe, but I'll try to simplify it. You can think of all types of problems to be solved with algorithmscomputers into four categories. P, NP, NP-Complete, and NP-Hard. Current computers are meant to solve the first category, the P problems. Sometimes we need to have more computers or faster computers to solve more of these P problems, but the idea is that P problems are the kinds of problems we can conceivably do. The others, NP, NP-Complete, NP-Hard aren't really computable in universe lifetimes when the problems get bigger. Here's where quantum computers come in. They can solve some NP problems. Not all NP problems, but some. Unfortunately they can't help us with the NP-Complete or NP-Hard problems. And P problems are still best done with current computers. So quantum computers will be best used only for a few problems.," "There's actually a very good video series by veratisium explaining it all. The British Army's Royal Welsh regiment has recently announced the arrival of its new mascot, after the beloved predecessor sheep, Private Derby XXXI, passed away earlier this year. The mascot holds significant importance to the military regiment and has been an important part of its traditions since the 1700s, providing a sense of identity and camaraderie to the soldiers serving within it. The new mascot, known as Fusilier Shenkin IV, is a five-month-old goat born and bred in Wales. He was selected from a flock of goats in the Brecon Beacons due to his friendly and adventurous nature, making him the perfect fit for the regiment. The tradition of a regiment mascot goes back centuries, with soldiers taking their own animals with them to war as companions and protection. Over time, these animals became a symbol of the regiment, representing the core values and identity of the troops who serve within it. The Royal Welsh regiment, in particular, has had a long history with its mascot sheep. The first one joined the regiment in 1844 and was presented to the troops during the Crimean War. Since then, a succession of 30 Derby sheep have served as the regiment's mascot, including the most recent sheep who passed away earlier this year. The selection of a new mascot may seem like a small tradition, but it holds significant importance to the soldiers within the regiment. The mascot represents the sense of community and identity that is so deeply cherished by the troops, helping to build morale and camaraderie among them. The arrival of Fusilier Shenkin IV marks the continuation of a long-standing tradition and will no doubt be welcomed by the soldiers of the Royal Welsh regiment. The goat's arrival is a symbol of new beginnings and a testament to the enduring traditions and bonds within the military community.

One issue limiting the adaption of large-scale multi-region segmentation is the sometimes prohibitive memory requirements. This is especially troubling considering advances in massively parallel computing and commercial graphics processing units (GPUs) have improved the speed and efficiency of image processing. The most effective way to reduce memory requirements for large-scale multi-region segmentation is to use data partitioning and parallelization techniques. Data partitioning involves dividing the data into smaller chunks, which can then be processed in parallel using distributed computing or GPUs. This allows for faster segmentation times and reduces the amount of memory needed to store the data. Additionally, algorithms can be optimized to reduce their memory footprint, as well as lower their computational complexity. This can be done by taking advantage of symmetry in the data, reducing the number of parameters used, and utilizing efficient data structures.

We investigate the problem of cost-optimal planning in ASP. Current ASP planners can be trivially extended to a cost-optimal one by adding weak constraints, but only for a given makespan . This approach is not suitable for on-line planning where the makespan is defined by the planner. We propose a novel cost-optimal planner based on the Dijkstra's algorithm. Our experiments show that our planner outperforms the existing one in terms of cost and runtime. The proposed cost-optimal ASP planner extends the existing ASP planners by adding weak constraints, but with the added flexibility of being able to adjust the makespan as needed. The planner leverages the Dijkstra's algorithm to find a path from the initial state to the goal state that minimizes the cost while ensuring the makespan is within the specified constraints. Experiments were conducted to compare the performance of our cost-optimal planner against the existing planners. The results showed that our planner was able to achieve higher cost savings and better runtime performance than the other planners.

I don't engage in video gaming, haven't ever acquired a pre-owned game, and disapprove of copyright infringement. Additionally, I reject the notion that illegal actions are inherently immoral. From what I gather, retail stores such as GAME purchase secondhand games from consumers and resell them at a higher price without sharing profits with the original creators. Game producers are resorting to strategies like downloadable content (DLC) and online passes to address this issue; however, let's set aside scenarios wherein the user subsequently purchases additional content or contributes financially through alternative methods. Regardless of whether a game is obtained brand new or through secondhand channels, the publisher does not benefit financially. This leads me to consider both options equally ethical. This study introduces a novel beam training method designed specifically for millimeter-wave communication systems involving highly mobile users. Frequent adjustments in beam alignment are necessary to accurately determine the channel state information for such users. To minimize the excessive use of resources typically associated with continuous beam training, our approach features a specialized strategy that directs training beams exclusively toward a selected high mobility user (referred to as the target user), while preserving the regular timing of standard beam training procedures. This tailored training process consumes fewer resources because it allows for the optimization of training beams aimed at the target user. We further recommend an ideal training beam selection tactic that identifies the most effective beamforming vectors to achieve minimal channel estimation errors using the probable channel data related to the target user. By integrating this customized beam training with a savvy channel estimation algorithm that takes into account both the sparsity and time-varying nature of the target user's channel, our research shows that our suggested framework delivers satisfactory channel estimation results while considerably reducing the training load when compared to traditional beam training methods.

I believe that the sorting of comments is improved when people downvote almost as frequently as they upvote. We are all familiar with the phenomenon of late posts getting buried and early posts remaining at the top of the thread. This phenomenon is the direct result of the fact that most people only read the first few comments in a thread combined with the fact that people tend to upvote significantly more than they downvote. Let me use a hypothetical example to explain my point. Imagine there is a 5 hour old thread with 100 comments in it and the top five comments are all mediocre comments that 50 of people who read them upvote. Then someone posts an extremely high quality comment that over 90 of people who read it upvote. This comment starts with 1 upvote so it is at position 70 or so out of the 100 comments. So after a couple hours 1000 people view the comments, 100 of them view the first five comments and only about 2 of them view the 70th comment. So the top five mediocre comments would get upvotes from 50 of the 1000 people (500 upvotes) and the amazing post at position 70 would get upvotes form 90 of the people who read it (18 upvotes). I hope this illustrates how, in a world where people only use upvotes and not downvotes, top posts will tend to remain at the top even if they are only moderately good comments while great comments that are posted late will tend to remain near the middle or bottom (unless they are linked to by rbestof or something). I think we can all agree that it is more desirable to have comments sorted by perceived quality than by some other arbitrary method (how early you posted). If instead of only using upvotes, people used downvotes just as frequently, this problem is greatly improved. In the same example as before let's assume that everyone votes, up or down, on every post they read. So instead of just not upvoting the posts that they feel don't deserve an upvote, they downvote it. In this situation, 50 of people would upvote the top five posts and 50 of people would downvote them, so even though only 2 of people actually go down the list to read the high quality 70th post, its upvote count will still rise faster than the top five mediocre posts. I believe that in a subreddit such as rCMV you should not downvote opinions just because you disagree with them, but I also think that you shouldn't upvote comments just because you agree with them for the same reason. You should upvote comments that you feel are of high quality and downvote comments you feel are of low quality. We want the comments to be sorted from best to worst so that when someone visits a thread they will be confronted with the most compelling arguments first. So that is why I think it is misguided for the mods of rCMV to encourage people to not downvote posts in general. I totally support them asking people to not vote just based on whether they agree or disagree with someone, but I think people should vote both up and down based on how compelling they feel the argument is. I'm going to preempt a few concerns here: 1) Downvoting discourages people from voicing unpopular opinions. First off, I don't think you should downvote an opinion for being unpopular, but only if you think it is a bad argument (i.e. it is a logical fallacy or it makes some assertions that are objectively wrong, like if they claimed that we shouldn't invade Iran because it's in South America). Secondly, I think it's more important to sort comments properly than to worry about people's feelings getting hurt from negative karma. I think if you are avoiding posting things because you are worried about a negative karma score, that is pretty ridiculous. 2) Even if most people think a comment is low quality, that doesn't mean everyone will think so. By downvoting comments that the majority of people find low quality, you are making it less likely that someone who might find it compelling will see it. You could make the same argument against sorting it by upvotes only. "Just because the majority of people consider a post to be high quality doesn't mean everyone will and by allowing the highest upvoted comments to rise to the top you are pushing the less popular posts to the bottom making them less likely to be seen by someone who isn't convinced by the popular arguments." I think if you want to make this argument, you can't just make it against downvotes, but against sorting by perceived quality in general. 3) If people downvote OP's comments, heshe won't get as many responses so it will be harder to change their view. I agree 100 with this and you should never downvote OP's comments in their own thread. But if you aren't the OP, then I think it is better to address the most compelling arguments. 4) It is better to report arguments that break the rules than to downvote them. I am not talking about comments that violate the rules. I am talking about totally legitimate comments that address the topic with real questions and concerns. But if there are a lot of really great comments, they should be sorted in a logical way with the best comments first and the worst comments last. Yes, you should report any comments that violate the rules. Other than that, you should upvote comments you find especially good and downvote comments you find especially bad. Maybe there are two comments making the same point but one does so with referenced sources and the other does so without sources and in a confusing or arrogant way. So upvote the better one and downvote the worse one even though neither of them needs to be reported. EDIT: I'd also like to add that I don't think there is really any value in downvoting people into the negatives unless they are trolling. I can see how that would be disheartening to people trying to contribute while not really adding anything to the sorting.
