Reflections generally affect polarization. For radio waves, one important reflector is the ionosphere which can change the wave's polarization. Thus for signals received following reflection by the ionosphere (a skywave), a consistent polarization cannot be expected. For line-of-sight communications or ground wave propagation, horizontally or vertically polarized transmissions generally remain in about the same polarization state at the receiving location. Matching the receiving antenna's polarization to that of the transmitter can make a very substantial difference in received signal strength.

In mathematics, a group is an algebraic structure consisting of a set of elements equipped with an operation that combines any two elements to form a third element. The operation satisfies four conditions called the group axioms, namely closure, associativity, identity and invertibility. One of the most familiar examples of a group is the set of integers together with the addition operation, but the abstract formalization of the group axioms, detached as it is from the concrete nature of any particular group and its operation, applies much more widely. It allows entities with highly diverse mathematical origins in abstract algebra and beyond to be handled in a flexible way while retaining their essential structural aspects. The ubiquity of groups in numerous areas within and outside mathematics makes them a central organizing principle of contemporary mathematics.

The model could also benefit those who do not have access to insulin due to geopolitical or financial reasons. Neutrophils and macrophages are phagocytes that travel throughout the body in pursuit of invading pathogens. Neutrophils are normally found in the bloodstream and are the most abundant type of phagocyte, normally representing 50 to 60 of the total circulating leukocytes. During the acute phase of inflammation, particularly as a result of bacterial infection, neutrophils migrate toward the site of inflammation in a process called chemotaxis, and are usually the first cells to arrive at the scene of infection. Macrophages are versatile cells that reside within tissues and produce a wide array of chemicals including enzymes, complement proteins, and regulatory factors such as interleukin 1. Macrophages also act as scavengers, ridding the body of worn-out cells and other debris, and as antigen-presenting cells that activate the adaptive immune system.

The discipline of ecology typically traces its origin to the synthesis of Darwinian evolution and Humboldtian biogeography, in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Equally important in the rise of ecology, however, were microbiology and soil science - particularly the cycle of life concept, prominent in the work Louis Pasteur and Ferdinand Cohn. The word ecology was coined by Ernst Haeckel, whose particularly holistic view of nature in general (and Darwin's theory in particular) was important in the spread of ecological thinking. In the 1930s, Arthur Tansley and others began developing the field of ecosystem ecology, which combined experimental soil science with physiological concepts of energy and the techniques of field biology. The history of ecology in the 20th century is closely tied to that of environmentalism; the Gaia hypothesis, first formulated in the 1960s, and spreading in the 1970s, and more recently the scientific-religious movement of Deep Ecology have brought the two closer together.

In this study, we propose a novel method named A ttention M odel E nhanced N etwork (AMEN), which is formulated in a multi-branch fashion with pixel-wised attention model and classification submodular. Specifically, the feature learning part in AMEN can generate pixel-wised attention map, while the classification submodular are utilized to classify the samples. To focus more on subtle detail information, the sample image is enhanced by the pixel-wised attention map generated from former branch. Experiments conducted on three benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method under various scenarios.

That fluid accepts heat from the outside air, and is then compressed, which raises the temperature, higher than that of the indoor area. How can I mark this "explained"?','No matter how cold it is outside, the air is still above absolute 0, which means there is always heat to extract from it. In a heat pump or air conditioner, there are two coils, one inside, and one outside. Between these coils moves a refrigerant. At room temperature, under normal pressures, the refrigerant is a gas. When the compressor compresses the refrigerant going into your house, the refrigerant turns into a liquid. The molecules in a liquid move slower than in a gas, which means they have less energy. So the excess energy is given off as heat (the liquid gets really hot. The hot liquid heats a coil in your house, and a fan blows that heat into the home, cooling the liquid in the process. When it goes outside, it is allowed to decompress, which turns it back into a gas. The opposite happens, and it gets really cold, colder than the outside air,. The air can then heat this gas up a bit, and this heat will be recovered in the house when the refrigerant is compressed back into a liquid. The same process happens in reverse for air conditioners.

Deep residual networks (ResNets) outperform traditional deep feedforward networks (FFNets) in terms of generalization capabilities. The underlying reasons for this superiority remain somewhat elusive. Through examining deep learning via the lens of 'neural tangent kernels,' this study delves into this essential issue. Initially, it is established that when network width approaches infinity, training ResNets effectively becomes an exercise in mastering reproducing kernel functions using specific kernel functions. Subsequently, a comparative analysis between the kernels of ResNets and FFNets reveals that while FFNet's kernel induces a set of functions which become unlearnable as depth increases infinitely, ResNet's kernel avoids this limitation. These findings offer partial explanations for why ResNets surpass FFNets in their ability to generalize, corroborated by numerical evidence presented herein.

The nurse pulled out the needle and stuck band aid on the small hole. "There you go Mr. Olson. You are all set. Make sure to set up an appointment with the cancer specialist here at the hospital." He sat up in the bed, wondering what was going to happen next. "Now we just have to wait for the results to come back." He sighed and rubbed his head. He hated hospitals. He hated sitting in one place for hours on end. He hated the way the nurses talked to him like he was a child. He hated the fact that he wasn't in control of his own health. He hated being here at all. He hated this hospital with a passion. The nurse walked back over to him, her expression sympathetic. "I know it is hard to deal with, but you just have to have faith that everything is going to turn out fine." "And if it doesn't?" "Then you fight it. You go and beat it into submission. You don't let it win." She patted him on the back and walked out of the room. He was alone now. He sighed and took out his phone, texting his girlfriend to let her know that the test was over. A few minutes later, she texted him back, asking him to come over to her house so they could talk about it in private. He sent a response and then looked back over at the door. A doctor walked into the room and then handed him a card. "This is your appointment card. You need to schedule an appointment with Dr. Lee within the next week. She will be the one who reads the results and decides what you need to do from there." He nodded and took the card. "Thank you. I will." "If you have any questions, call the reception desk." He nodded again and the doctor left. He looked at the card. He had another week to sit around and think about what was going on. What if he was going to die? What if he only had a few months left? Would he even survive long enough to see the results? He got up and pulled his clothes on. He was going to see his girlfriend. He didn't know if it would help, but he wanted to be with her. He wanted to feel her warmth and reassurance. He wanted to know that she would be there for him. He walked out of the hospital and got into his car. He drove to her house and pulled into the driveway. He walked up the stairs and knocked on her front door. A few minutes later, she opened the door and then she pulled him into her arms. He wrapped his arms around her and held her tightly. He didn't want to let go. He didn't want to ever let go. He didn't want to ever have to leave her. He pulled away from her and then looked at her. "I'm scared." "I know. I'm scared too. I love you too much to lose you." He held her again. He didn't want to lose her either. He didn't want to have to go through this alone. He couldn't do this alone. She would have to stay with him through this. She would have to be there to help him. He needed her, no matter what happened. Labels: hospital, short story, story, writing

With the recent outbreak of COVID-19, creating a means to stop it's spread and eventually develop a vaccine are the most important and challenging tasks that the scientific community is facing right now. The first step towards these goals is to correctly identify a patient that is infected with the virus. Our group applied an unsupervised machine learning technique to identify COVID-19 cases. This is an important topic as COVID-19 is a novel disease currently being studied in detail and our methodology has the potential to reveal important differences between it and other viral pneumonia. This could then, in turn, enable doctors to more confidently help each patient. Our experiments utilize Principal Component Analysis (PCA), t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE), and the recently developed Robust Continuous Clustering algorithm (RCC). We display the performance of RCC in identifying COVID-19 patients and its ability to compete with other unsupervised algorithms, namely K-Means (KM). Using a COVID-19 Radiography dataset, we found that RCC outperformed KM; we used the Adjusted Mutual Information Score (AMI) in order to measure the effectiveness of both algorithms. The AMI for the two and three class cases of KM were 0.0250 and 0.054, respectively. In comparison, RCC scored 0.5044 in the two class case and 0.267 in the three class case, clearly showing RCC as the superior algorithm. This not only opens new possible applications of RCC, but it could potentially aid in the creation of a new tool for COVID-19 identification.

A recent line of research has developed around logics of belief based on information confirmed by a reliable source. In this paper, we provide a finer analysis and extension of this framework, where the confirmation comes from multiple possibly conflicting sources and is of a probabilistic nature. We combine Belnap-Dunn logic and non-standard probabilities to account for potentially contradictory information within a two-layer modal logical framework to account for belief. The bottom layer is to be that of evidence represented by probabilistic information provided by sources available to an agent. The modalities connecting the bottom layer to the top layer, are that of belief of the agent based on the information from the sources in terms of (various kinds of) aggregation. The top layer is to be the logic of thus formed beliefs.

Characters with diacritical marks can generally be represented either as a single precomposed character or as a decomposed sequence of a base letter plus one or more non-spacing marks. For example, e (precomposed e with macron and acute above) and e (e followed by the combining macron above and combining acute above) should be rendered identically, both appearing as an e with a macron and acute accent, but in practice, their appearance may vary depending upon what rendering engine and fonts are being used to display the characters. Similarly, underdots, as needed in the romanization of Indic, will often be placed incorrectly[citation needed]. Unicode characters that map to precomposed glyphs can be used in many cases, thus avoiding the problem, but where no precomposed character has been encoded the problem can often be solved by using a specialist Unicode font such as Charis SIL that uses Graphite, OpenType, or AAT technologies for advanced rendering features.

Hardcoding simplifies programming tasks by reducing potential errors since fewer variables need consideration. However, it also limits flexibility, particularly relevant in gaming scenarios where modifications ('mods') might be desired. When certain parameters are firmly integrated into the game code rather than extracted from external sources, modifying them becomes exceedingly challenging. As a general rule, modders lack direct access to comprehensive game source codes, relying solely on scripts or additional data files to adjust functionality. Game creators must deliberately design accessible interfaces for script-based changes; otherwise, specific attributes remain inflexible due to their hardcoded nature. A best practice suggests eschewing hardcoded constants whenever feasible, opting instead for components amenable to future adaptations.

In this paper, the authors aim to combine the latest state of the art models in image recognition with the best publicly available satellite images to create a system for landslide risk mitigation. We focus first on landslide detection and further propose a similar system to be used for prediction. Such models are valuable as they could easily be scaled up to provide data for hazard evaluation, as satellite imagery becomes increasingly available. The goal is to use satellite images and correlated data to enrich the public repository of data and guide disaster relief efforts for locating precise areas where landslides have occurred. Different image augmentation methods are used to increase diversity in the chosen dataset and create more robust classification. The resulting outputs are then fed into variants of 3-D convolutional neural networks. A review of the current literature indicates there is no research using CNNs (Convolutional Neural Networks) and freely available satellite imagery for classifying landslide risk. The model has shown to be ultimately able to achieve a significantly better than baseline accuracy.

The goal of categorizing medical images and diagrams within scholarly texts involves assigning labels based on the technique employed for creating them. This task is crucial yet difficult in the realm of automatic literature analysis, extraction, and evaluation. Challenges arise due to substantial variations within categories and similarities across different ones, stemming from numerous imaging techniques and diagram styles. To tackle this issue, we introduce a cooperative deep learning (CDL) framework in this study. We have devised a dual deep convolutional neural network architecture enhanced with a cooperative signal mechanism, which allows simultaneous learning of visual representations. The cooperative signal verifies if a pair of images belong to the same group and provides adjustments when necessary. Our CDL approach can be fully integrated ('end to end'). During testing, the probability scores generated by both parts of the network are combined to predict the category of a given image. Results from the ImageCLEF2pta Subfigure Classification Challenge indicate that our suggested CDL method outperforms other approaches in this field, surpassing even the top-ranked solution on the competition's scoreboard thus far.

It was a red day meaning service day. The men in uniforms pushed us along the cells, those neat lines of indiscriminate hate and metal. The bars that secured us in our homes were the same that kept us alive. Service day, a red day. A nothing day. A day that comes and goes, like the ashes of our fallen. We pay homage to the service of our fellow man, be he in uniform toiling the farms, the land, the sea. Be it a woman making way for life, tending the children or healing the discarded. Be it the machines that protect us, to the bolts that hold us in our homes, we pay service to those around us. Please report to your designated stations. Shuffled again through more doors, past more windows, we reached the main auditorium. A drab, solemn room, devoid of emotion. A condescending room, filled with the imagination of a coffin. I hacked up a chunk of my lung as I found my allotted seat, trying to hold my cough down before the service began. Service will begin soon, please be mindful of those around you. It always began with the achieved quotas, production estimated and yielded results. Nothing of importance gained or lost as I drifted slowly into a grey abyss of thoughtless state of mind. "And now, a moment of silence for those lost." Suddenly, the purring of the projector was the only audible noise. Breathing became a chore, as not to disturb the service, everyone temporarily held their breathe. No one coughed, no one sneezed. No one dared breathe. "We thank you for showing respect." I thought of the possibilities as more rations would stream in. It was a red day. It was a good day. A doing day. A day to celebrate. It was service day.

In the Cambrian era, Gondwana experienced a temperate weather pattern. Parts of West Antarctica resided in the Northern Hemisphere, leading to extensive accumulation of sedimentary rocks like sandstones, limestones, and shales. Conversely, East Antarctica sat along the equatorial region where marine creatures like sea floor dwellers and trilobites thrived amidst warm oceanic conditions. As we transition into the Devonian epoch around 416 million years ago, Gondwana shifted towards higher southern latitudes resulting in a colder climate, yet evidence suggests existence of terrestrial plant life during that span. Depositional processes resulted in formations of sands and silts within the present-day Ellsworth, Horlick, and Pensacola mountain ranges. The advent of glacial activity occurred nearing the conclusion of the Devonian period when Gondwana gravitated toward the polar south axis, causing further temperature decline while still sustaining vegetative growth. Throughout the Permian age, seed-bearing plants, particularly Glossopteris—a type of pteridosperm found in wetland environments—grew prevalently. These marshy regions eventually transformed into coal beds situated within the Transantarctic Mountain range. Eventually, approaching the terminal phase of the Permian timeline, an escalating thermal trend fostered arid and scorching climatic conditions across most parts of Gondwana.

It may be their signature pose, but how and why the birds perch on one limb has been a longstanding puzzle. Now, a team from the US has shown that flamingos employ no active muscular effort when they're unipedal, meaning they are also expending less energy. A passive mechanism is engaged in the one-legged position, allowing flamingos to stand proud while having a doze. Previously, researchers had wondered whether the one-legged position might help reduce muscle fatigue, as the birds alternated from standing on one leg to the other. Other teams have proposed that this behaviour helps regulate body temperature. Now, Prof Young-Hui Chang, from the Georgia Institute of Technology (Georgia Tech) in Atlanta, and Lena H Ting, of Atlanta's Emory University, have uncovered the mechanical secrets behind this impressive trick. The researchers conducted several experiments with both live and dead birds. Amazingly, they found that flamingo cadavers could be made to stand one-legged without any external support. In a paper published in the Royal Society journal Biology Letters, they describe this phenomenon as a "passive gravitational stay mechanism." "If you look at the bird from the front, while they're standing on one leg, the foot is directly beneath the body which means that their leg is angled inward. That's the pose you have to strike in order to engage the stay mechanism," Prof Chang told BBC News. However, dead birds cannot stand unsupported on two legs, suggesting a greater role for active muscle force in this posture: "If you tilt it to the vertical, like you would if you were standing on two legs, the whole thing disengages," said the director of the Comparative Neuromechanics Laboratory at Georgia Tech. The researchers also studied live birds, and showed that when they were standing one-legged and resting, they hardly moved at all - underlining the stability of this passive position. However, the birds did sway somewhat when the one-legged posture was combined with an activity, such as grooming or calling out. Prof Chang said the underlying anatomical apparatus that enables the passive posture was not yet understood - this is the next step in the team's research. But he explained that the phenomenon did not involve the limb joints locking. "A lock would imply that it's fixed in both directions. What we found is that it's fixed in one direction, but flexible in the other direction, so we call it a'stay' rather than a'lock'. It's more akin to a doorstop," he told me. Dr Matthew Anderson, an experimental psychologist who specialises in animal behaviour at St Joseph's University in Philadelphia, described the team's results as a "significant step forward." The researcher, who was not involved with the latest study, added: "They begin to answer the question of how flamingos are able to rest on one leg. Importantly, these authors do not examine when and where flamingos actually utilise the behaviour in question, and thus this paper does not really address the issue of why flamingos rest while on one leg." Dr Anderson's own research suggests that the birds adopt the unusual posture in order to conserve heat. Among other things, his team found that the number of birds resting on one leg falls as temperatures rise. "Providing evidence of the mechanism that supportsallows for the behaviour to occur does not necessarily provide insight into why it happens in the first place." Follow Paul on Twitter.

Machine learning over graphs have been emerging as powerful learning tools for graph data. However, it is challenging for industrial communities to leverage the techniques, such as graph neural networks (GNNs), and solve real-world problems at scale because of inherent data dependency in the graphs. As such, we cannot simply train a GNN with classic learning systems, for instance parameter server that assumes data parallel. Existing systems store the graph data in-memory for fast accesses either in a single machine or graph stores from remote. The major drawbacks are in three-fold. First, they cannot scale because of the limitations on the volume of the memory, or the bandwidth between graph stores and workers. Second, they require extra development of graph stores without well exploiting mature infrastructures such as MapReduce that guarantee good system properties. Third, they focus on training but ignore the optimization of inference over graphs, thus makes them an unintegrated system. In this paper, we design AGL, a scalable, fault-tolerance and integrated system, with fully-functional training and inference for GNNs. Our system design follows the message passing scheme underlying the computations of GNNs. We design to generate the k -hop neighborhood, an information-complete subgraph for each node, as well as do the inference simply by merging values from in-edge neighbors and propagating values to out-edge neighbors via MapReduce. In addition, the k -hop neighborhood contains information-complete subgraphs for each node, thus we simply do the training on parameter servers due to data independency. Our system AGL, implemented on mature infrastructures, can finish the training of a 2-layer graph attention network on a graph with billions of nodes and hundred billions of edges in 14 hours, and complete the inference in 1.2 hour.

The major literary product of this cultural syncretism is the Septuagint translation of the Hebrew Bible from Biblical Hebrew and Biblical Aramaic to Koine Greek. Simultaneous inference after model selection is of critical importance to address scientific hypotheses involving a set of parameters. In this paper, we consider high-dimensional linear regression model in which a regularization procedure such as LASSO is applied to yield a sparse model. To establish a simultaneous post-model selection inference, we propose a method of contraction and expansion (MOCE) along the line of debiasing estimation that enables us to balance the bias-and-variance trade-off so that the super-sparsity assumption may be relaxed. We establish key theoretical results for the proposed MOCE procedure from which the expanded model can be selected with theoretical guarantees and simultaneous confidence regions can be constructed by the joint asymptotic normal distribution. In comparison with existing methods, our proposed method exhibits stable and reliable coverage at a nominal significance level with substantially less computational burden, and thus it is trustworthy for its application in solving real-world problems.

Inference on a large-scale knowledge graph (KG) is of great importance for KG applications like question answering. The path-based reasoning models can leverage much information over paths other than pure vertices in KG, and have been demonstrated to be effective at inferring new entities associated with specified queries [5, 13]. However, existing methods are usually unable to solve these tasks when the training data size is insufficient, especially if there exists an unknown entity. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach named Spectral Pseudo-Entity Refinement (SPER). SPER incorporates a spectral algorithm into the traditional pseudo-entity refinement model [13], so that it learns the weights of edges from related pairs with respect to the existing references. In particular, given some test query, SPER first generates its candidate set through top-k nearest neighbors search using cosine similarity as well as its reference list generated simultaneously based on state-of-the-art approaches [23, 10]; then by employing two modalities such as pairwise relationships and local structure information represented by paths, SPER serves to refine those candidates while alleviating the sparse problem. To evaluate our proposed method, we conduct extensive experiments on five real-world tasks including entity disambiguation task, entity subgraph detection task, entiy-mention number prediction task, relation extraction task, and ontology completion task. Experimental results show that SPER outperforms the most competitive methods both statistically and practically. Related work Path-reasoning models: There has recently received increasing attention about pathbased reasoning techniques which take advantage of more structural clues compared to vertex-based ones [8]. For example, [5] proposes a framework called Path-Based Reasoner (PbR), where PbR uses shortest-path induced matching algorithms to construct node-link matrices, and employs further modifications to generate high-quality relationship scores between nodes. Recently, [13, 14] propose a simple yet efficient solution to reconstruct epistemic graphs under a probabilistic matrix factorization setting, which shows good performance on many complex logic reasoning problems e.g., fact checking [1, 24]. Pseudo-entities: Given a large scale KB like Freebase or Wikipedia, learning pseudo-entities provides a better approximation of original objects via mapping them onto concepts found in such resource [15, 16, 17]. These works suffer from limited resources due to their assumptions, i.e., only one entity may correspond to several different pseudonyms. Inspired by such assumption, [15] introduces a non-parametric variant of concept embedding, which could help us obtain embeddings of any object that might lie around, regardless of whether they exist in DBpedia or not. [18] augments SemEval-2007 Task 7 dataset by adding correct answers retrieved from Semantic Web services; [19] creates a very comprehensive online repository containing formal definitions of terms taken directly from Wikipedia articles, thus enriches wordnet glossaries with semantic annotations. [20] pre-trains various neural network architectures with labeled sentences extracted from linked triples stored in a knowledge base to predict coreference links among noun phrases within each sentence. The potassium and sodium ion concentrations are what cause the neuron to fire. Or actually they allow the action potential to propagate along the nerve. A nerve cell starts off by firing an electrical impulse that sends a signal out of its cell into the surrounding tissue, then it continues with another one releasing more information about itself to the rest of the neurons of the body. When the ion concentration is too high (negative ions) or too low (positive ions), neurons can't communicate properly anymore. Neurons are connected together through long slender fibers called axons. Acupuncture works in much the same way as acupuncture needles: tiny electric currents pass through your body from point A to B while other points on the spinal cord receive impulses and send them back down towards the head. Depending on how you hold the needle, different parts of the body will receive specific amounts of current which stimulate nerves in particular areas. For instance, if you're going to be touching any part of your legs, it might make sense to do so before starting to touch your feet because those touchpoints have been linked with many different nerve pathways.

Many sciences have made significant breakthroughs by adopting online tools that help organize, structure and mine information that is too detailed to be printed in journals. In this paper, we describe how a community of biomedical researchers, using our web-based Knowledge Management tool, BioKnowledge, organized their knowledge to help combat the worldwide threat of malaria. We show how this software enables scientists to share information, collaborate with colleagues, and ultimately improve the quality of their work. Knowledge is a complex concept, and as such it has generated many definitions. In the context of this paper, we understand knowledge as information that is communicated to and shared between individuals. Knowledge is a cornerstone of all sciences and is especially important in biomedical research, where scientists are tackling complex challenges such as the biology and treatment of malaria. In the last 30 years, medicine has made enormous progress in understanding diseases such as cancer and AIDS, which are mainly caused by abnormal genetic changes, but much less progress has been made in understanding and treating diseases caused by parasites such as malaria. This is because, at a genetic level, these parasites are extremely similar. To increase our understanding of these parasites, biomedical scientists must work together to share knowledge, but this is difficult because most labs do not have the resources to maintain the equipment and personnel needed to generate and store large amounts of information. To address this problem, we developed BioKnowledge, a web-based tool that allows biomedical scientists to share information with each other and with their colleagues anywhere in the world. BioKnowledge is freely available to scientists all over the world and currently includes more than 350,000 records. To illustrate the use of BioKnowledge, we have analyzed information from a project to characterize the parasite Plasmodium berghei, the major cause of malaria in rodents in sub-Saharan Africa. Scientists in this project use BioKnowledge to organize and share information in a way that is useful to their work. We show how BioKnowledge facilitates the generation and exchange of knowledge, and how it encourages the members of this community to work together to solve common problems. Knowledge Management is an area of growing interest in research labs, because it offers the potential to improve the quality of research. Knowledge Management (KM) is the process of capturing, storing, sharing and using knowledge to increase the productivity of a team [1, 2]. Biomedical research is increasingly dependent on information technology, and the biomedical sciences are no exception. The growth in the use of web-based tools has led to the emergence of "Web 2.0," a term used to describe the new generation of Internet applications that encourage communication, collaboration, and sharing of information. In the last 10 years, the proliferation of these Web 2.0 tools has changed the way biomedical researchers work. In the US, when a defendant is charged with a "capital offense" it means there is the possibility that they will be sentenced to execution. In order for this to happen, the jury must vote (normally unanimously) in favor of execution after first voting that the defendant is guilty. Many US citizens believe that executions should be banned, and would never vote in favor of executing a defendant if they were on a jury in a capital case. Because of this, such candidates are generally excluded from being on the jury in a trial for a capital offense. My view is that this is a problem because it creates a selection bias among juries. I believe that there is a correlation between people who support death sentencing and people who are predisposed against people accused of crimes. I'm not claiming that death sentence supporters on juries don't consider the evidence and reach a sincere conclusion. But in my experience, people have different expectations when it comes to the burden of proof and aggravating and mitigating circumstances. And I believe that people who favor executing convicts are also more inclined to vote guilty given the same evidence compared to the average juror, and are more likely to feel that a crime meets the conditions that make a defendant eligible for execution compared to the average juror. I believe that the aggregate bias introduced in this way will be strong because only about half of the population believes in the death sentence, so half of all jurors will be turned away - overall, the half that is statistically more likely to vote not guilty given the same evidence. The ideal jury would not have this statistical bias. Obviously, if jurors who were completely opposed to executions were allowed to participate in sentencing, they would probably never vote in favor of it, so I don't have a solution (other than banning executions). Maybe there could be two sets of jurors, and those who would be excluded based on their objection to executions would still vote on whether to convict, but that is imperfect because death sentence supporters would still be the only ones evaluating the mitigating and aggravating factors, and because those who object to death sentencing might potentially vote against convicting someone they think is guilty if they know it will allow others to sentence the defendant to execution. I found [one article] that discusses the bias I describe here. In order to change my view, I expect you would probably need evidence that jurors who support death sentencing are not statistically more likely to vote guilty compared to the average juror. Yes, I am placing the burden of proof on you instead of myself. If no such evidence exists, I think a study should be done.

Police hope the scheme will help reduce financial crime by spotting scams before money has been handed over. The plan is to train every single front-facing employee of banks, building societies and Post Offices. Cash payments to fraudsters are typically much harder to trace than online payments with the vast majority of cases going unsolved. Typical frauds of this kind include paying rogue builders, romance scams and elderly abuse. 'It just didn't add up' Staff at one bank which has trialled the scheme helped stop a customer being swindled out of PS13,000. Ray, who is in his 60s, was approached by a builder at his home in London about some work on his house. He had withdrawn PS6,000 from his local branch after explaining to staff what it was going to be used for. But when he returned a week later to take out another PS13,000 he was recognised by staff member Ann-Marie. She asked him questions about his cash withdrawal which raised suspicions. Ray handed over the flier he had been given with the builder's contact details and staff gave him a call. Ann-Marie added: "The person that answered wasn't very professional and the alarm bells started to ring. Plus the amount he [Ray] wanted to cash and the work he needed done just didn't add up." Staff contacted the police who visited Ray the next day when the builder was at his property. Officers did a background check on the builder and which uncovered suspicious activity and he was arrested. The new scheme, known as the Banking Protocol, is aimed at ensuring banks and police are more active in protecting customers. It is being run as a joint venture between the police, Financial Fraud Action - which represents banks - and Trading Standards. All customer-facing bank staff will be told to look out for specific signs that a client may be the victim of ongoing fraud. If they have suspicions, they are encouraged to call the police and give a special password. Police trained under the protocol will also commit to investigating the fraud as a priority - often visiting the bank branch, or the customer's home, immediately. In some cases, they may be able to catch the criminal waiting outside the bank or the victim's home to collect the cash. Bank staff taking part in the trial scheme in London made 178 calls to police which resulted in 16 arrests. Banks say PS1.4m has already been stopped from leaving customer accounts. Police, Financial Fraud Action and Trading Standards have hailed the trial a success. The scheme is expected to begin in the next few weeks with the first 16 police forces trained by the end of June.

Because video isn't generally a small thing to carry, whereas 3D data can be. Video is just being read and played back, all the data you're seeing has to be written somewhere. The video is being written to a video buffer somewhere, and then that buffer is being written to RAM somewhere else. All that data has to be there. 3D data can be used to generate that same video output, it's just that the data is read and written in memory at a much faster rate. So you don't need a big buffer for it. A: When you write to a video file, you're writing to a memory buffer that's already been allocated. Video files are just giant chunks of raw data. When you read from a video file, you're reading from a memory buffer that's already been allocated. The video file is just giant chunks of raw data. This is where the two become confused. If you want to read a video file, you need to read the entire file into memory first, and then use it to generate the frame. If you want to generate a video from data, you need to generate the frame first, and then use it to generate the video. For the latter, it's easier to generate a video from a bunch of images and then write that file to disk. For the former, it's easier to generate a video from a bunch of raw data, and then write that file to disk.

Flights heading east operate at odd thousands while those going west function at even thousands. This occurs because jet engines perform better in cooler conditions, and the aircraft encounters reduced resistance since air molecules are more spaced out. For wings to generate sufficient lift, they require a specific rate of airflow. Air density at sea level is nearly double compared to higher elevations. Consequently, if an aircraft travels at 250 mph through the air, its ground speed will also be 250 mph (presuming no wind). However, when flying at 35,000 feet where air molecules are further apart, the aircraft must move at double the velocity for the wings to remain effective, resulting in a doubling of ground speed. It's essential to note that when someone mentions an airliner cruising at 500 mph, this refers to its ground speed. Additionally, turbulence tends to decrease with altitude, leading to smoother flights; however, wind speeds can be higher aloft. Depending on the direction of the wind, pilots might choose to ascend or descend accordingly.

Our study introduces an efficient Markov Chain Monte Carlo approach based on fast potential partitioning, requiring constant time per iteration for extracting samples from equilibrium distributions related to particle models with unique interaction mechanisms. In this technique, the complex interaction potential is divided into two components; one has a long reach yet remains continuous, while the other possesses limited scope but could exhibit singular behavior. When moving a particle, we initially apply a stochastic differential equation (SDE) influenced by the smoother component, utilizing the concept of random batches similar to those found in stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics. Subsequently, we employ the closer-range component via a Metropolis acceptance/rejection process. Unlike traditional Langevin dynamics, here the SDE governed by random batches operates briefly, yielding a linear time complexity relative to the batch size 'p'. The short-range component's accept-or-reject phase maintains constant time expense due to its restricted nature. Through theoretical justification and practical simulations, we validate our hybridized random-batch Monte Carlo strategy that merges random batch and division tactics. This method delivers outcomes comparable to conventional algorithms like Metropolis-EE, such as Dyson Brownian motion and Lennard-Jones fluids, while offering enhanced computational efficiency.

Your body temperature (which is closer to 37degC IIRC) is the result of an equilibrium. The stuff you do to keep alive generates heat. You also lose heat to the environment. These have to be in a balance to maintain a constant body temperature. The difference between your internal temperature and the external air temperature is vital in determining how fast heat is lost. When the external temperature is too close to your internal temperature, you can't lose heat fast enough without sweating. If you didn't start sweating, the very act of staying alive would raise your temperature and kill you. Hence your body has to sweat well before the air temperature reaches 37degC Also, when it gets too cold, you stop sweating, but your body also has to do extra things to keep your heat generation higher than the rate you lose heat. That is why you shiver.

He'll throw my favorite toy, the one he dug out of the junkyard for me, with this hand. He'll splash water from the park lake at me with this hand. Ever since that first day that Master found me, almost frozen to death in a cardboard box, and took me into his coat, I knew this human was different. No one shared anything with me. But, he shared his warmth. He shared his smile. He had nothing, but gave me everything. His smile saved me. But, Master isn't smiling anymore. This always makes him laugh, even when he was just frowning a minute ago. Master isn't laughing. Suddenly, I feel something go up and over my neck. A hard tug sends me backwards. It is nothing in comparison to the unbearable pain located under my fur in my chest. I try to lunge at the human controlling this device, but it is tightened and I am forced back. A memory of the warmth of Master hugging me close flashes in my mind as my sight begins to dim. You said wherever you go, I go, Master. A whimper escapes my throat. So, why are you leaving me behind now? My legs give out and I hit the ground hard. Every part of my body is numb. Please take me with you. Japan's terrain doesn't allow for forests of wind turbines or fields of solar panels, so Japanese engineers are looking to ocean currents for renewable energy. The IHI Corporation has completed a demonstration project in the coastal city of Iwakuni that uses tidal flow and wave power from waves hitting the shoreline from the Pacific Ocean. The company is working on a plan to build a total of 60 gigawatts of offshore wind generation by 2050; part of this will come via tidal power plants like the one at Iwakuni. And because it's not as expensive to transport power as traditional fuel-based renewables, tidal-generated electricity could be cheaper than other forms of energy such as coal. "Wind energy is uneconomic," said Tomoko Terayama, an engineer with IHI who helped design the system. "But wave energy can generate enough power to run our industrial machines." IHI will keep its focus on wind and wave power until it commits to a bigger investment in gas turbines, which are more efficient before they need expensive maintenance.

Sound quality has already hit a maximum with the equipment that most people use. No sense in upgrading video quality when everyone is watching your video in an old CRT TV. To really get the detail of quality sound you need quality equipment, and most people don't notice the difference enough to drop 800 on a preamp and speaker cabinets.," "We've had great sound quality for a long time, and that's mainly because sound is a lot simpler to capture and reproduce. Sound is essentially just variations in air pressure, all you have to do is convert the changes into an electrical signal, and then send them to a speaker to convert back into air pressure. People can only hear up to 20 000 Hz, so we don't need to bother with anything higher than that. It's a low enough bandwidth that we can easily fit 50 minutes of high quality sound onto a vinyl record, and digitally, it doesn't take a lot of space to store, even uncompressed. Video is a lot more complicated. One way to record video is to use film, so essentially taking a picture for each frame. This can give you quite good quality (which is why old movies can be released in HD on BluRay), but it's quite expensive to do. To convert video into an electrical signal, it's quite a bit more complex. Analog cameras would capture the video line by line (top to bottom), and send that information to the TV. They need to be synchronized, otherwise the camera might be sending the middle of the picture and the TV could be putting it on the top of the screen. And if you want color, that means you have to do the process 3 times (for reds, blues and greens). And the real hurdle is bandwidth - the more lines and resolution you do, the more space it takes up on the airwaves (which meant fewer TV stations back in the day before cable), and it's harder to store, so you wouldn't be able to record as much on tape. It also takes up much more space than music digitally. For comparison, a TV station in North America gets 6 MHz (6 million hertz) of bandwidth. An FM radio station gets 200 kHz (200 thousand hertz) of bandwidth. Quality because we're figuring out how to compress digital videos better (finding ways to remove information without noticing it), and storageinternet speeds are faster than they used to be.," "I won't say it's at it's maximum, but it's a very close asymptote, meaning you can try and pour a ton of money to get minimal benefit. We already have better than 96kHz24-bit and better. The main area of improvement is in speakers and headphones, making the audio quality of those better for lower retail prices. Assessing uncertainty can serve as a useful method for identifying adversarial samples—inputs that are intentionally designed to mislead a model into confidently making wrong predictions. Various approaches have been developed to measure this uncertainty, such as predictive entropy and mutual information, each reflecting distinct aspects of it. Our research examines these techniques and clarifies the reasons behind the effectiveness of mutualinfo in spotting adversarial instances. Additionally, we pinpoint limitations associated with MC dropout, a prevalent strategy for gauging uncertainty within neural networks. By doing so, our work enhances comprehension regarding the shortcomings of existing practices and suggests improvements through the use of probabilistic ensemble models to refine uncertainty evaluations. To illustrate our points, we conduct experiments with both synthetic data from the MNIST set and genuine images from the challenging Kaggle competition's dog versus cat classification dataset.

The 4.4-metre-long (14-ft) cloth is on show until 24 June. Viewings are free but must be booked. One million people have already signed up. Some devotees believe the shroud is the burial cloth of Jesus Christ. Sceptics point to carbon dating that suggests it is a medieval forgery from the 1300s. Scientists have not agreed on how the image of a man was imprinted on the cloth. Turin Shroud: See it in detail Pope Francis will be among those to view the shroud, during a visit to the northern Italian city on 21 June. The last public viewings were in 2010, when 2.5 million people came to see it. The Church has not officially claimed that Christ's body was wrapped in the shroud, preferring instead to focus on what it means to those who see it. "Whether you believe or don't believe, there is no doubt it is something special," an Italian man who was among the first visitors on Sunday told the AFP news agency. Earlier this week, Archbishop of Turin Cesare Nosiglia said: "What counts the most is that this shroud.... reflects in a clear and precise manner how the gospels describe the passion and death of Jesus. "It is not a profession of faith because it is not an object of faith, nor of devotion, but it can help faith." Archbishop Nosiglia said that many of those coming to see the shroud would be returnees. "That means there is a fundamental need in people's hearts to renew this incredible experience that they had the first time they saw it," he said. "Even non-believers will come. It's an occasion that brings everybody together." The shroud is displayed in a climate-controlled case for 12 hours a day in Turin's Cathedral of St John the Baptist.

It took me a while to figure out what my nose is capable of. Growing up, I remember people telling me that I had the worst sense of smell. Sometimes I would be so grossed out by a smell that I had to leave the room while other people doesn't even appear to be noticing it, let alone bothered; other times I would easily overdose on perfume and turn myself into a human car freshener, or stick my nose so close into the flowering shrubs that my friend felt " obliged " to nudge my ass into it. Anyways, growing up, all of my families and close friends have established that my nose is not to be trusted. It either understates the situation to my brain, or gives it false alarms. No doctor could figure out what was wrong with me, not even psychologists. I think it makes food less agreeable too, but over the year I've long made peace with it. After I hit 20 years old, my crazy nose got even worse. The first time I realized I had an ability was in college. My roommate was a Chinese dude who dedicated much of his time to our kitchen. Apparently, legit Sichuan cuisine involves a lot of oil and stir-frying, and gives out a strong although mouthwatering smell that at times confused our fire alarm, to the point we had to take the batteries out. But everything smelled muffled to me anyways, so I didn't really mind. One day, I was woken up from a nap by the sharp smell of smoke and burnt fabric. I jumped up and dashed out to grab the fire distinguisher, only to find my roommate staring at me in shock, apron around the waist, looking as in control as always. While I tried to explain to him how I thought I smelled fire, I could barely focus on the conversation because the smell was only getting stronger and stronger. All of a sudden, his wok caught fire, and before he could react, his apron lit up like Katy Perry's Super Bowl outfit. All the splashed oil on it made it extra combustible and my poor roommate was already rolling on the ground screaming out of panic. It took me one second to react to what I already have imagined happening. I grabbed the apron, and with a swift kick in his stomach, tore it away from his neck. I never put down the fire distinguisher, so although I was scrambling a bit, it didn't take me long to put out the small patch of fire that already melted his sweater. Then we just sort of froze there, shaking, and watched the burning apron and his dinner run their natural course of carbonization. " Fuck. I think I'll never grow chest hair again, " he said. He got several burn wounds and had to wear sharpie eyebrows for a long time, while I got blisters all over my right arm and peed a little in my pants. But I was ecstatic. It all made sense now! The wok caught fire in front of my eyes, but I was able to smell it minutes before it happened. After some experiment and practice, I realized that I could detect two kinds of smells: the kind that I share with everyone else, which appears distant and dull to me; and the kind that only I can detect, which I am very sensitive to. The more fresh it smells, the closer it is to happening. I became the legend of our college. Well, not really. But I put my ability to good use and sometimes it made me feel like a secret superhero. Besides saving my roommate from his suicidal cooking skill, I also always knew when to drag my drunken friends out of a party right before they could throw up on their date. Sometimes I could even predict the weather. My ability isn't a great one, but I love it, and I genuinely enjoyed deducing the future based on what I can discreetly pick up in the air to protect my friends and I from undesirable situations. So I started paying more attention to the second kind of smell; it made me feel like a secret hero on the move, only instead of a miserably crappy childhood and all the moral burdens, I get the adoration from my families and friends. Last week, I caught the most disturbing scent when I got out of the coffee shop. It took me a while to find the spot where the smell is the strongest, and it was in the middle of the street. A trace of smoke, some hint of burnt rubber, and the fragrance of roasted meat - it finally hit me that there was going to be an accident! For the second time, life is on the line, and I can use my ability to prevent it. I started hanging out at this crossing when I don't have classes, screening for safety hazards. I forced the air deep into my lung to try and figure out the details, the time. Today. It is going to happen today. The ensanguined sweetness is in the air, so dense and vivid that I feel like I can taste it in my pores. Shit's going down any minute now. I take out my phone and dial 911: " Hello, I would like to report an acciden... " I see a little girl on her tricycle crossing the street, while an oil truck is taking a turn onto the same road. Fuck! Like every superhero story, of course there is going to be a little fucking innocent girl! There's still time, she's not at the spot where the smell is the strongest yet, maybe I can push her out of the way. I launched for the other side of the street, at the same time, the truck driver sees me and makes a sharp turn to come to a stop. Did..... did the smell just disappear? It, totally, did! There I find myself standing triumphantly in the middle of the street, smiling with tears rolling down my cheeks, while raising my arms up high to chant " GOOO MEEEEE! " like an idiot..... And that's when two things hit me. One was the SUV that knocks me from my back and wedges me directly into the oil tank; the other is the realization that the disappearing scent doesn't necessarily mean that I stopped the accident - it could have just been me stopping to breathe, in a split of a second's future.

Private schooling in the United States has been debated by educators, lawmakers and parents, since the beginnings of compulsory education in Massachusetts in 1852. The court will hear oral arguments Tuesday morning on whether California can deny more than 500 million annually from its public elementary and secondary schools budgets to students attending "nonpublic" (i.e., mostly Catholic) K-12 institutions under Proposition 98. About 70 percent of these funds go directly to faith-based nonpublic schools. Since vast sums of money have gone into building new campuses at such places as Notre Dame High School in San Jose, St. Mary's College Preparatory Academy in Oakland, Nativity Prep in Marin County, and others like them all over the state each year without any financial help coming back to support neighborhood public programs, it would seem advisable for Catholics and other believers who hold their own children sacrosanct above government spending sprees to respond with overwhelming force when called upon this time around too.

During the rule of the Fatimid and Mamluk dynasties and their successor states in the medieval Middle East, many of the ruling elite founded madaris through a religious endowment known as the waqf. Not only was the madrasa a potent symbol of status but it was an effective means of transmitting wealth and status to their descendants. Especially during the Mamluk period, when only former slaves could assume power, the sons of the ruling Mamluk elite were unable to inherit. Guaranteed positions within the new madaris thus allowed them to maintain status. Madaris built in this period include the Mosque-Madrasah of Sultan Hasan in Cairo.

The Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B) system is a key component of the Next Generation Air Transportation System (NextGen) that manages the increasingly congested airspace. It provides accurate aircraft localization and efficient air traffic management and also improves the safety of billions of current and future passengers. While the benefits of ADS-B are well known, the lack of basic security measures like encryption and authentication introduces various exploitable security vulnerabilities. One practical threat is the ADS-B spoofing attack that targets the ADS-B ground station, in which the ground-based or aircraft-based attacker manipulates the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) address (a unique identifier for each aircraft) in the ADS-B messages to fake the appearance of non-existent aircraft or masquerade as a trusted aircraft. As a result, this attack can confuse the pilots or the air traffic control personnel and cause dangerous maneuvers. In this paper, we introduce SODA - a two-stage Deep Neural Network (DNN) -based s p o ofing d etector for A DS-B that consists of a message classifier and an aircraft classifier. It allows a ground station to examine each incoming message based on the PHY-layer features (e.g., IQ samples and phases) and flag suspicious messages. Our experimental results show that SODA detects ground-based spoofing attacks with a probability of 99.34, while having a very small false alarm rate (i.e., 0.43). It outperforms other machine learning techniques such as XGBoost, Logistic Regression, and Support Vector Machine. It further identifies individual aircraft with an average F-score of 96.68 and an accuracy of 96.66, with a significant improvement over the state-of-the-art detector.

The Crimean War represented a protracted struggle among Europe's great powers vying for dominance over regions within the weakening Ottoman Empire. As a result of the conflict, the Ottoman government found itself compelled to secure external financing through loans totaling 5 million British pounds on August 4th, 1854. This tumultuous period also saw significant displacement of populations; notably, approximately 200,000 Crimean Tatars sought refuge in the Ottoman Empire due to successive migration movements. Concurrently, towards the conclusion of the Caucasian Wars, around 90,000 Circassians faced forced expulsion from their ancestral lands in the Caucasus region and subsequently settled in Turkey, with estimates ranging from 500,000 to 700,000 individuals relocating there. Various Circassian groups assert even more substantial figures, suggesting that upwards of 1-1.5 million may have been either deported or perished during this time.

The agricultural sector primarily revolves around growing and marketing staple foods like cassava, peanuts, maize, sorghum, millet, sesame, and plantains. The average yearly increase in actual GDP hovers slightly above 3 percent. Food crops take precedence over cash crops intended for export, which can be seen through the fact that each year's cassava yield—the primary sustenance source for many residents of Central Africa—ranges from 200,000 to 300,000 tons, whereas cotton output (the main cash crop sold internationally) falls within 25,000 to 45,000 tons annually. Although these food products aren't widely traded abroad, they remain the top revenue generators due to the sporadic sales of excess produce bringing in higher earnings compared to exported commodities like cotton or coffee. Most areas manage their own food supply needs, yet animal husbandry progress faces obstacles stemming from the prevalence of the tsetse fly.

Sleep procrastination, also known as bedtime procrastination, is an emerging trend that involves delaying sleep despite having the intention to do so earlier. This behavior often stems from prioritizing current activities over going to bed at the appropriate time. For example, one may continue gaming or binge-watching TV shows instead of heading to bed, losing track of time and eventually staying awake well into the night.

On average, it usually takes around 10-15 minutes to drift off to sleep, during which many individuals opt to engage with their devices like laptops, tablets, or phones rather than reading books. However, the artificial light emitted by such electronic screens can disrupt our natural sleep cycle by signaling to our bodies that it's daytime. As a result, this habit intended to pass the time ultimately contributes to prolonged periods of wakefulness.

According to Professor Charles Czeisler from Harvard University, exposure to blue-hued light during evenings delays the release of the sleep-inducing hormone melatonin and pushes back our body's circadian rhythm, leading to difficulty falling asleep and waking up early. He suggests avoiding screen usage if feeling unready for sleep since it would only exacerbate feelings of tiredness. A developing frontal lobe, responsible for evaluating pros and cons and resisting temptations, could play a part in contributing to this issue among young people.

Other than oxygen, carbon is the dominant element making up life forms as we know them. We refer to this as carbon-based life. It's very possible (and a scientific theory) that other life forms could exist based on different elements. However, all life that we know of today is carbon-based. The first five periods of the periodic table of elements are known as the s-block (Group 1 and 2), the p-block (Group 13-18) and the d-block (Groups 3-12). The atoms in these elements have full valence shells. Carbon is in the p-block. In the p-block, the electrons in the valence shell are in the p orbital, a dumbbell-shaped orbital in which the electrons can only occupy the middle area. Carbon forms four covalent bonds with other carbon atoms. This is what allows for the large variety of carbon compounds. Carbon can also form covalent bonds with atoms of other elements. Carbon forms covalent bonds with the elements hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and halogens (fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine and astatine). Carbon can be found in a variety of compounds. Carbon dioxide is a gas. Carbon monoxide is a gas. Carbonates are salts of carbonic acid. Carbonates are usually solids. Carbonates include limestone (calcium carbonate), soda (sodium carbonate) and baking soda (sodium bicarbonate). Coal and charcoal are also carbon compounds.

Architectural description languages are a useful tool for modeling complex software systems at a high level of abstraction. If based on formal methods, they can also serve for enabling the development and verification of software by providing more effective means to address programming errors before reaching the implementation stage. In this paper we describe some of our research in this area: The abstract architectural design language REX (Recursive Equational Expressions) is a general-purpose software architecture modeler that supports both object oriented software architectures as well as non object oriented ones such as functional models. It has been used in organizations like NASA, Microsoft Research, HP Labs, IBM Research and several other companies. Our first emphasis was to integrate it with compilers for higher level languages. This resulted in the compiler integration product called YARN - an acronym standing for "Yield Analysis Reconstruction Notation." Later we developed a set of tools for data modeling using REX which includes: 1. A visual editor where you write your program's source code; 2. An expressible subset of C that enables users to use their favorite text editors or Integrated Development Environments (IDEs); 3. A command line interface that allows programmers working offline to interactively create their programs from scratch! We have extended this approach to verify the correctness of computer programs written in high level languages including Java and Python. We will discuss our current efforts to extend REX towards higher levels of abstraction for increasing its usability.

It was shown before that the NP-hard problem of deterministic finite automata (DFA) identification can be effectively translated to Boolean satisfiability (SAT). Modern SAT-solvers can tackle hard DFA identification instances efficiently. We present a technique to reduce the problem search space by enforcing an enumeration of DFA states in depth-first search (DFS) or breadth-first search (BFS) order. We propose symmetry breaking predicates, which can be added to Boolean formulae representing various DFA identification problems. We show how to apply this technique to DFA identification from both noiseless and noisy data. Also we propose a method to identify all automata of the desired size. The proposed approach outperforms the current state-of-the-art DFASAT method for DFA identification from noiseless data. A big advantage of the proposed approach is that it allows to determine exactly the existence or non-existence of a solution of the noisy DFA identification problem unlike metaheuristic approaches such as genetic algorithms.

If there is any graffiti, it's almost certainly going to be in perfectly punctuated English. But what it also has is hundreds of students from the UK - and the number is rising. This is the university application season for UK students - and open day visits now include trips to Dutch universities, which are pitching themselves as if they were offshore Russell Group institutions. Since tuition fees rose to PS9,000 in England there have been repeated forecasts that students would head for cheaper European universities. Now it seems to be actually happening. Across the Netherlands, there are 2,600 UK students in universities this term - up by a third in a year. And independent school head teachers want Dutch universities to be included in the Ucas application form. The University of Groningen is a microcosm of this - up by 33 to around 300 UK students, for whom it has had to put on special open days. This 400 year-old university, second oldest in the Netherlands and in the top 100 of international rankings, now designates itself as an English-speaking institution. It is running more degree courses taught in English than in Dutch, with students from Germany, China, the UK and the Netherlands itself, all learning in English. For families from England attending the open day in Groningen, the question of tuition fees is never far from the surface. Phoebe Watkinson and her father Phil had travelled from Wirral. Phoebe said that as well as being less expensive, going to a European university would give her an "edge" in the jobs market. "It shows a certain quality, it shows bravery to go to another country and it's not that far from home," she said. The distance does not seem daunting, she says, as it is as quick to get home from the Netherlands as from some other parts of the UK. Her father says he is from a generation when higher education was free - and he finds it "difficult to fathom" the level of debt being piled up. "I would be extremely pleased if she came here," said Mr Watkinson. He says it would benefit her academically and socially as well as financially. "If you ask most people what their primary driver was for looking at foreign universities, probably most of them would say straight off 'lower fees'," he says. "But I think there's a lot more to it than that. If people look further than just the cost and see the other advantages, a lot more people will start to look at it seriously." Saskia Dutton from Sheffield said her concern about studying at home is that she might "end up with PS40,000 of debt" for a university in England, regardless of its quality. "I thought do I want to settle for paying PS9,000 to go to a university that is not going to give me the same quality of education as somewhere that costs 2,000 euros (PS1,400)? "The hesitation would be that I would be far away from my family.... University can be quite a lonely experience," she said. More stories from the BBC's Knowledge economy series looking at education from a global perspective and how to get in touch Nick Verspeak from Wiltshire says the attraction is learning in an international environment, as a step towards working in a globalised jobs market. But what's it like to be an English student at Groningen? Gemma Scott from Newcastle says the initial draw was the cost, but it's been a different experience than she expected. "It's made me a different person, made me much more confident in my own abilities, because I moved country when I was 18," she says. She adds that her friends leaving universities in England will face immediate pressure to find work and begin paying off debts, while she will leave debt-free. "I think I'm the only student to come out with savings." Gemma is studying English literature, in a Dutch English-speaking university, and admits to having learnt almost no Dutch while studying there. She says that the distance from family is a real factor - "you can't just hop on a train." But she says social media and video links like Facetime can fill the gap. "I'm physically separated, but I talk to my mum every day and I say good night to my sister." Holly Jane Shaddock from Shrewsbury, who is studying languages, says she is "embarrassed" telling other European students how much fees cost in England. "They find it incredible, they are shocked. It's similar to my reaction when my American friends tell me how much their tuition costs. It's the same:'How can you pay that much?' But you realise people don't have a choice." But she says even though the fees are lower: "Financially it can still be a bit of a struggle." It's a misunderstanding to think that studying in the Netherlands is free. There are tuition fees of 2,000 euros (around PS1,400) per year and students from the UK can apply for support for this. But they cannot get financial support for living costs, so parents will have to pay for accommodation or students need to get part-time jobs. The typical room cost is about 360 euro (PS254) per month, says the university. But why would Dutch universities want to attract so many more UK students? Groningen's rector, Elmer Sterken, says being an international institution improves the quality of teaching and research. But there's also a practical motivation. "The number of Dutch students will drop, so we're interested in attracting more international students," he says. Adopting English as the first language - apart from subjects such as Dutch literature or Dutch law - is now accepted, says the rector, after "some resistance at the beginning from some of the staff." "The lingua franca of universities and research is English and maybe 90 of Dutch people speak English to some extent," he says. So is studying abroad going to become more mainstream? Chris King, chairman of the Headmasters and Headmistresses Conference, in a report from Maastricht University, said the big change was that it was no longer just about a year abroad. "Heads are emphasising to more students the benefit of enrolling for a complete degree programme abroad," he said. The government has signalled that fees are going to rise again above PS9,000. An unintended consequence could be rising numbers of English students cycling around Dutch cities.

First and foremost, let's clarify that this discussion pertains solely to tertiary education institutions. It's reasonable to utilize basic assessment criteria for primary level students due to their early stages in mastering fundamental writing abilities, where evaluation tends to follow a straightforward correct/incorrect approach. However, when it comes to university studies, especially within fields like mine—Physics at an engineering college in Colorado—the situation changes significantly. As someone who considers themselves proficient in written communication, recognizes its significance across various disciplines, appreciates the value of well-crafted argumentation comparable to mathematical analysis, and acknowledges the importance of writing as a means of expression, I must express strong reservations regarding the effectiveness of quantitative grading systems and related mechanisms such as GPAs, scoring guidelelles, and bonus credits. These methods seem counterproductive to my educational growth, often fostering skepticism instead.

For instance, during my experience with a history course at another institution, our essay evaluations included a section for grammatical accuracy which assigned scores ranging from 8 to 10 points for 'flawless' grammar without clarifying the distinction between these levels. More recently, in a current class, I received remarkably close scores of 2125 and 2225 for separate short assignments devoid of personalized comments or guidance. While I recognize my own imperfections as a writer and accept the necessity for improvement, the lack of clear feedback makes it challenging to comprehend how my performance aligns with the given scores. This scenario exemplifies my belief that the current system leaves room for confusion rather than providing constructive insights for enhancement.

Furthermore, I perceive an evident trend towards grade inflation. Ideally, an average GPA should hover around 2.0, serving as a realistic benchmark for both academic progress and potential employers. The discrepancies observed suggest a dilution of standards and may potentially diminish the overall quality and relevance of degrees earned by graduating students. Therefore, it becomes increasingly crucial to reassess existing grading practices and implement more meaningful approaches that genuinely contribute to learners' development and better prepare them for future endeavors beyond academia.

There is no "degree" in front of "kelvin," by the way - the SI unit is the "kelvin," not the "degree kelvin" (although it was called that formerly). As a unit, the symbol K stands only for kelvin in scientific usage, and so does not need a degree symbol in front of it.', "A degree can be defined as an arbitrary measurement. Why do we have 360o in a circle? Because we decided to, arbitrarily. 360 is a convenient number to work with because it can be divided in many different ways.
