The life of the Reaper is a simple one. Walk next to this soul as he unknowingly takes his last dose of chemotherapy. Stand next to the bed of this woman as she tosses handful after handful of pills into her mouth. Cross the street with this little boy just before that runaway bus takes the life of the only person capable of curing cancer. All he needs to do is be there and claim a soul. Easy work for an eternity. He doesn't do this out of spite or pleasure; it simply fulfills his contract. Many millennia ago, he met came to be just before humans gained souls. He spoke to a being without body that made him shudder in his new pristine robes of the darkest black. The being spoke of things to come, and things that have passed. The Reaper was not very interested, but tried to pay attention. After years of talking, the being suddenly told the Reaper that he had a job, and it involved these beings that were to be called humans. The being spoke of granting humans a miraculous gift, a soul. A soul was special because it allowed for the owner to reach out passed surviving. He wanted to watch as something created things far greater than themselves, so he was to give them souls. The Reaper was mildly interested, but didn't understand what his job was to be. At once the being crafted from an ancient tree a stick which was odd in shape. At one end the being wove a blade of what he said was the materialization of the Reaper's soul. He called the object a Scythe, and beckoned for the Reaper to use it on the humans when they were to die. The Scythe would harvest the soul so it would not be lost. The Reaper questioned why he was to be given such a gift and responsibility. The being simply crafted a paper with a few words: You will survive as long as you harvest souls. The Reaper felt a fear creep up his spine as he read these words over and over again. He agreed out of fear of his own death. And the being laughed a booming laugh that crafted lightning and shook mountains. The deal was done. The Reaper never heard from the being again, he simply found himself drawn to those who were about to die, and so he harvested. With every soul he drew into himself, he felt anger, regret, grief, and sorrow. At first they were overwhelming, for they were foreign concepts to him. All he knew was fear. He was always so afraid of dying, that he took soul after soul after soul. He took on the grief and pain until he began to affect his surroundings with it. Humans began to grieve for their dead as the dead grieved for their loss of life. The Reaper was dutiful and did his job perfectly for thousands of years. One year, an entire civilization disappeared; no deaths, no souls. As the Reaper stepped at the top of the Myan pyramid as he had done so many times in the past only to see an empty city. He felt something change in him as he looked over the once bustling city. Gradually he felt his perfect robes begin to rip as each unaccounted for soul was lost forever, each soul tearing a new hole. He began to panic, "Is this death!? Am I dying due to an oversight?!" he screamed from the depths of his rib cage as all the grief he had accumulated began to wash over him in waves of fear, desperation, pain, and sorrow. Suddenly, he felt a familure tug and relief swept over his bones as he stepped into a small hut with a child running a high fever and fading quickly. He never felt such a high as when that pain and heat of fever swept over him. He was glad to see he was not going to die, despite the now tattered robes that hung loosely on his bones. He was alive and that was all that mattered. A number of years passed without incident and the Reaper began to regain his confidence as the weight of recent events were bearing down on him. Conquests and false friendships often cause more than a few deaths and tears, and with it, plenty of pain for the Reaper to bear. After all this time, he thought he could handle the deaths of humans, but he was not prepared for trails of tears, camps of concentration, and ruthless dictators. The pain caused by these events weighed so heavily on him that he began to be able to feel tears roll from his empty sockets and off his bony chin. He was confused and pained by everything happening. Bombs that split atoms were becoming fairly common place, and he knew that if something happened and one was set off, the following events would crush him to dust. He became vigilant of the skies, watching for anything that hinted to his destruction. He was watching the wrong place. Most humans had begun to hate death long ago, and now they had the technology to try to fight it off. They had been successful at extending life, and beating many diseases, and now they were working to stop death altogether. The humans knew about souls and their value, they didn't want to give up more of them. Many years after the only atomic bombs to be used in war were set off, the breakthrough was made. The Reaper knew something was wrong. When he visited hospitals where many died of age and disease, many of those who seemed near death were seemingly getting younger, stronger, and healthier. When he visited congressional offices, where many died due to a'random' bombing, a poisoned drink, or a well placed bullet, people were happy and signing many treaties. When he visited war zones where people died simply because of malice, there were cease-fires. He didn't understand, his reaping had begun to happen less often, and people seemed to stop being so close to death so often. The news hit him as he reaped an elderly lady in a famous hospital. He had been there for some time, waiting for her to die. He learned that there was a serum that reverses the aging process, learns and kills all diseases, and prevents the host from dying due to trauma to the body. He couldn't believe it, so he did some snooping while he waited for another person to die. He arrived in a testing area for the serum where they were determining the strength of it's regenerative abilities. A man took 459 different bullets to the head and heart, was exploded in multiple ways, drowned and suffocated, and they were talking about dropping a nuke on him. The Reaper looked on in disbelief as the man's arm dragged itself back to the pile of blood and gore and he was reconstructed himself. Panic. That was the Reapers second reaction. No deaths, no harvesting, no souls. He would not be able to survive if this happened. For years he tried to affect the living world, but could do nothing. He felt himself begin to weaken from the lack of harvesting, and felt the grief he had bottled up so well begin to leak. The last soul he was able to reap was that of a 125 year old man who had refused the serum. The old man spent his last days in bed reading a book. His great-granddaughter would come in and feed him as well as ask him to take the serum, each time he would simply shake his head. The woman understood he would never take it, but she always kept some hope and a syringe handy. The day had finally come, the old man was awake and had begun to feel himself slipping away. To his surprise the say a skeleton sitting by his bed, crying. The Reaper by now was little more that brittle and broken bone with small scraps of cloth hanging from his shoulders. He kept a firm grip on his scythe though, with his soul still glowing faintly in the shape of a blade. The old man smiled at the sight, "About done too, huh?" The Reaper looked up at the old man and laughed a slight, weezing laugh. "I am but a shadow of my old self. You are the last of the humans to die, you know that don't you?" "Yes well, I wanted to great death as a friend, not flee from him as an enemy." The Reaper quietly nodded his head and thought for a moment before speaking, "Why do you not fear death? Why do you not fear me?" The old man's eyes took on a far away look as he relived his life, "I lived a good life, I did good things, and I loved a good many people. My time is done. The point of life is to live, and then die, there is no point if you live forever." The Reaper looked long and hard at the old man, "I am going to die..... And I have yet to live." "If you use your time as you please, you will have lived. Is that not what you do now? You are talking with me, is that not what you want to do?" The Reaper set down his scythe on the floor and bowed his head, "I want to be free of this pain, and feel joy." The old man quietly watched the Reaper and began to scoot over on his bed which squeaked with every movement. "Come lay down with a friend." The Reaper hesitated before taking the spot next to the old man. "To die happy, with no regrets, is that what you want to do?" "Yes," replied the old man, "and I can't do that without dying with newest, closest friend." The Reaper looked at the old man and felt relief flood him, "I want to die with my only friend." "And die we shall." The time passed slowly as both of them faded away. The man getting colder, the Reaper's scythe getting dimmer, until it faded away, and the handle crumbled. Somewhere off in the distance, was a clap of thunder, and a mountain shook.

Vigilante groups seeking to expose paedophiles should stop taking the law into their own hands, Kent Police has said. The force was responding to reports that members of the public were targeting suspected child sex offenders. In a statement, Kent Police said: "We would like to remind people that it is an offence to take the law into your own hands. "Anyone with information about suspected child sexual abuse is asked to contact us on 101." The statement added that officers would "exhaust all investigative avenues" and would not hesitate to take "robust action" against those who break the law. Recent cases of vigilantism have included a man being chased through the streets of London by a group of people after he was accused of being a paedophile, and a mother confronting a man she believed was trying to groom her daughter. The issue of vigilantism has been widely debated in the UK, with some people arguing that the police are not doing enough to protect children from sexual predators. However, others have warned that taking the law into one's own hands can lead to innocent people being targeted. In 2016, a man was killed in Wales after he was mistakenly identified as a paedophile by a vigilante group. Speaking about the issue, Detective Chief Superintendent Tony Cundy, head of public protection at Kent Police, said: "We understand that people want to keep their children safe, but we would urge people not to take the law into their own hands. "Not only is it illegal, but it could also jeopardise any future police action."

The increase in the world's population and rising standards of living is leading to an ever-increasing number of vehicles on the roads, and with it ever-increasing difficulties in traffic management. These problems are especially acute when large cities such as Tokyo or New York experience a severe rush hour. Road construction and maintenance methods have not kept up with the growth of urbanization, and older streets often lack adequate drainage facilities which allow water to collect during periods of rainstorms. In addition, road surfaces may become damaged from snow plowing operations. Further, streets that do receive proper street lighting can still be difficult to see at night due to thick foliage around the street corners. Various devices have been proposed for detecting obstacles along roadway such as cars, trucks, power lines, etc., but these generally require either special circuitry to detect certain conditions or the use of relatively expensive mechanical sensors mounted at various locations along the roadway. For example, U.S. Pat. No. 4,576,538 to Friese et al discloses a device intended to determine whether a vehicle has collided with objects in front of its path by providing a signal pattern representative of the position of the obstacle in relation to the vehicle. This particular system requires hardware mounted directly to each wheel of the vehicle so that vibrations induced by the wheels will cause elements within the sensing circuit to move back and forth while signals indicative of the position of the obstacle relative to the moving vehicle are monitored. The resulting output derived from this sensor thus varies greatly depending upon where the object is located relative to the vehicle (i.e., a rear bumper versus a hood). Such systems also tend to be quite complex because of their need for considerable processing equipment and numerous electrical connections between the sensor and the instrumentation. Thus, there remains a need for improved devices capable of accurately determining location of an object relative to an automobile traveling ahead without requiring extensive modifications to existing automobiles.

UAVs are increasingly being employed to carry out surveillance, parcel delivery, communication-support and other specific tasks. Their equipment and mission plan are carefully selected to minimize the carried load an overall resource consumption. Typically, several single task UAVs are dispatched to perform different missions. In certain cases, (part of) the geographical area of operation may be common to these single task missions (such as those supporting post-disaster recovery) and it may be more efficient to have multiple tasks carried out as part of a single UAV mission using common or even additional specialized equipment. In this paper, we propose and investigate a joint planning of multitask missions leveraging a fleet of UAVs equipped with a standard set of accessories enabling heterogeneous tasks. To this end, an optimization problem is formulated yielding the optimal joint planning and deriving the resulting quality of the delivered tasks. In addition, a heuristic solution is developed for large-scale environments to cope with the increased complexity of the optimization framework. The developed joint planning of multitask missions is applied to a specific post-disaster recovery scenario of a flooding in the San Francisco area. The results show the effectiveness of the proposed solutions and the potential savings in the number of UAVs needed to carry out all the tasks with the required level of quality.

Despite a decrease in overall unemployment by over 10,000 since June 2014, PwC's Northern Ireland economic outlook highlights that low productivity continues to be the major hurdle for lasting economic progress. According to Esmond Birnie, PwC's leading economist in Northern Ireland, the region's economic recovery is slowing down, with fluctuating business and consumer confidence during the previous seven months. He noted that although there was an uptick in unemployment in June 2015 after several years of decline, it could either be a minor setback or signal a larger issue. At present, Northern Ireland lags behind its 2008 pre-crisis production levels and exhibits a dual nature in terms of economic activity, where sectors such as public administration and finance face shrinkage, whereas industries like high-tech manufacturing, pharmaceuticals, food processing, and hospitality show growth. PwC predicts that Northern Ireland's GDP growth rate will stay the weakest among all UK regions, at approximately 1.8% in 2015 (down from 2.2% in 2014), before dropping even further to about 1.7% in 2016. Additionally, the report indicates that Northern Ireland saw an unexpected increase in its jobless claims in June, which hadn't occurred on a monthly basis since late 2008. This includes long-term unemployment statistics and youth unemployment rates higher than the national average. Finally, PwC states that due to continued welfare reforms and governmental cutbacks, Northern Ireland may experience another four years of difficult economic conditions, especially regarding public expenditure.

Wildfires plague the forested areas of Guam every dry season despite the island's humid climate. Most fires are man-caused with 80 resulting from arson. Poachers often start fires to attract deer to the new growth. Invasive grass species that rely on fire as part of their natural life cycle grow in many regularly burned areas. Grasslands and "barrens" have replaced previously forested areas leading to greater soil erosion. During the rainy season sediment is carried by the heavy rains into the Fena Lake Reservoir and Ugum River, leading to water quality problems for southern Guam. Eroded silt also destroys the marine life in reefs around the island. Soil stabilization efforts by volunteers and forestry workers (planting trees) have had little success in preserving natural habitats.

In 1974, the second studio album by Queen, titled Queen II, came out with an acclaimed photograph taken by rock photographer Mick Rock featuring the band members on its cover. Notably, this visual work served as inspiration for the music video of the classic track "Bohemian Rhapsody" in 1975. Upon release, the record secured the fifth spot on the UK charts, marking it as the initial Queen album to do so within the country. Additionally, the album's main track, "Seven Seas of Rhye", authored by Freddie Mercury, climbed up to the tenth position in the UK Singles Chart, establishing Queen's very first successful single. With its intricate multi-layered audio design, richly imaginative lyrics, and showcases of exceptional musicianship, Queen II stands as a significant display of the band's unique style. While it did not contain any additional singles beyond "Seven Seas of Rhye", the album includes the lengthy composition "The March of the Black Queen", a six-minute piece devoid of a repeating chorus segment. Reviews regarding the album were varied upon its debut; however, publications such as The Daily Vault have characterized songs like "The March of the Black Queen" as ominous. Although some critics initially dismissed Queen II as excessively overwrought, modern evaluations reveal that it remains highly esteemed amongst devoted Queen enthusiasts, and even garners recognition in the influential compilation list "1001 Albums You Must Hear Before You Die".

In 1976 Montini became the first pontiff in modern history to deny the accusation of homosexuality. Published by his order in January 1976 was a homily Persona Humana: Declaration on Certain Questions concerning Sexual Ethics, which outlawed pre or extra-marital sex, condemned homosexuality, and forbade masturbation. It provoked French author and former diplomat Roger Peyrefitte, in an interview published by the magazine Tempo, to accuse Montini of hypocrisy, and of having a longtime lover who was a movie actor. According to rumors prevalent both inside the Curia and in Italian society, this was Paolo Carlini, who had a bit part as a hairdresser in the Audrey Hepburn film Roman Holiday. Peyrefitte had previously published the accusation in two books, but the interview (previously published in a French gay magazine) brought the rumors to a wider public and caused an uproar. In a brief address to a crowd of approximately 20,000 in St. Peters Square on April 18, Montini called the charges "horrible and slanderous insinuations" and appealed for prayers on his behalf. Special prayers for Montini were said in all Italian Roman Catholic churches in "a day of consolation." In 1984 a New York Times correspondent repeated the allegations.

Sparse reward issues present significant obstacles within the domain of Reinforcement Learning, particularly for goal-oriented tasks that offer rewards solely upon achieving objectives. A noteworthy solution for training agents in such tasks involves employing Hindsight Learning techniques. These techniques allow agents to learn from unsuccessful attempts by recognizing and aiming towards secondary achievements encountered along their path. Through iterative application across various paths and extrapolation of policies based on attained outcomes, the agent acquires a versatile ability to pursue diverse targets. Among these methodologies, Hindsight Experience Replay stands out; it incorporates an off-policy Reinforcement Learning strategy to cultivate a flexible target-based policy. This technique randomly revisits historical interactions during the learning process. Additionally, another tactic integrates Hindsight into policy gradient algorithms to refine policies more directly. Our discussion herein explores alternative strategies for enhancing Hindsight Experience Replay through emphasis on priority-focused iterations, alongside implementing Hindsight-infused policy gradient methods within robotics applications.

People give me weird looks when I take him for walks, but screw them, they never had to take responsibility for a dog they spontaneously created. I figured out the pattern and scale pretty quick. The physical objects were fairly easy to gauge, tying into their rarity and value. The abstract things: knowing the future, toying with emotions, forcing peace on a violent world, even momentarily, was Dangerous with a capital D. I stuck to as small as I could managed and still nearly had a four hundred pound, roid-raging, meth head nearly tear me in half. But then I had my breakthrough. The cost of the wish for the physical only related to it's physical attributes. A flash drive with a copy classified information on it worth millions only had the opponent of a flash drive. I'm not as young as I used to be, and I can't risk dying before I make this wish. Money can buy you the best guns, body armor, and personal combat training, (and believe me, it did), but sometimes you still have to take a deep breath, and roll the dice. Missing genotypes can affect the efficacy of machine learning approaches to identify the risk genetic variants of common diseases and traits. The problem occurs when genotypic data are collected from different experiments with different DNA microarrays, each being characterised by its pattern of uncalled (missing) genotypes. This can prevent the machine learning classifier from assigning the classes correctly. To tackle this issue, we used well-developed notions of object-attribute biclusters and formal concepts that correspond to dense subrelations in the binary relation patients SNPs . The paper contains experimental results on applying a biclustering algorithm to a large real-world dataset collected for studying the genetic bases of ischemic stroke. The algorithm could identify large dense biclusters in the genotypic matrix for further processing, which in return significantly improved the quality of machine learning classifiers. The proposed algorithm was also able to generate biclusters for the whole dataset without size constraints in comparison to the In-Close4 algorithm for generation of formal concepts.

However, transactions between individuals who live in different states necessitate this process due to federal jurisdiction over interstate commerce. On the other hand, many states do not require background checks for private sales conducted within their borders. When advocates call for universal background checks, they primarily refer to extending these requirements to intrastate, non-retail transactions. Critics argue that while retailers maintain strict records of their firearms inventory, implementing such measures for individual gun owners raises concerns about potential misuse of information for confiscation purposes. We present a full reference, perceptual image metric based on VGG-16, an artificial neural network trained on object classification. We fit the metric to a new database based on 140k unique images annotated with ground truth by human raters who received minimal instruction. The resulting metric shows competitive performance on TID 2013, a database widely used to assess image quality assessments methods. Eventually the effect of all of the pulling will cause the stuff to collapse in on itself. Once you reach a critical limit it will keep pulling until the stuff is condensed into such a small space that not even light can escape its pull. The area around it will look black because light can't escape. Hence, black hole. Anti-matter: Everything in the universe is made of a handful of fundamental particles: proton, neutron, electron, etc. These particles have an electric charge. Electrons have a negative charge, protons a positive charge and neutrons have a charge of zero. Each of these particles have a pair that is identical in every way (mass, spin) except it has the opposite charge. So, a positron looks exactly like an electron except it has a positive charge. If an electron and a positron meet they will destroy each other and generate pure energy.

Your dry fingers have difficulty adhering to the smooth plastic. When you wet your finger, the water fills the spaces between your skin and the plastic bag. Water molecules are slightly bent, which means that they act a little bit like small magnets, with a small attractive force between them. This small attractive force (Van der Waals forces) causes the water to bond to both your fingers and to the bag, allowing you to grip it better. The forces in this case are small and the bag is light, so the force your hand apply is lower than the Van der Waals force. When opening a jar, the Van der Waals force is still there, but you are applying a much larger force to try to open the jar. In this case, you grip the jar much harder, which increases the surface area contact and allows you to transmit the force from your hand to the jar and lid, hence opening it. When the jar and lid is wet, the water gets between your hand and the jar. The rule about "no metal in the microwave" is actually one that exists more for the sake of simplicity. It isn't a hard and fast rule of science. There are times when it's okay to have metal in the microwave. Metals reflect most of the microwave energy, which is why the microwave oven itself is made of metal to keep the radiation inside the microwave oven. A metal bowl, in general, is okay to put in the microwave, provided that it's completely smooth and doesn't ever touch the walls of the microwave. It just reflects radiation around in the oven, but doesn't have any sharp prongs to create electrical arcs with. Food products like Hot Pockets have metallic cages that can be used to reflect microwave radiation in a certain way that cooks the food in a desirable way. Whatever metal items come inside the microwave are either designed in a way that won't create arcs, or perhaps, they're made of metal alloys that don't interact much with the radiation. Such alloys do exist.','A lot of microwaveable food comes with some sort of metallic heating shroud in it to help cook better. Then danger is when you put something in that has the right shape and topography to be able to arc. If you put a spoon in the microwave, your microwave will be ok, and the spoon will heat. If you put a fork in, you will get arc between the tines. Those sparks arcing around are what can be harmful to the microwave.', "The top comments are correct, but they don't mention this very simple rule of thumb: sharp angles more likely to spark. In general, anything metal with sharp angles (fork, aluminum foil, etc) is probably a bad idea to microwave. Smooth metal, not so much.

Recently it has been proved that a simple algorithm configurator called ParamRLS can efficiently identify the optimal neighbourhood size to be used by stochastic local search to optimise two standard ised functions of k. The algorithm is based on the minimisation of the squared cross-entropy in the case of permutations and on the maximisation of the vector entropy for block matrices, which does not depend explicitly on local structure (i.e., on any specific neighbourhood). We show how paramRLS works both analytically and numerically using examples from real applications, including Jain's minimization method in real time and related algorithms such as k-nearest neighbour. This paper extends the results presented in [1] with an attempt at modelling local structure, namely quantiles, over large subsets of short sequences. First we describe the basic formulation and then we apply it to the problem of measuring the distance between two nonzero smoothed measures on the same interval defined substantially through local structures. In particular we propose an efficient way to model the notion of global quantile using an additive random variable instead of discretely sampled smooth measure values. For small intervals the modified quantile turns out to have good properties and exhibits fewer singularities than those predicted by the more commonly studied quantiles obtained directly via the global mean criterion or its alternative formulations. By combining our approach with results available in the literature on the estimation of local quantiles [2], we obtain an effective procedure to estimate locally relevant metrics within these models. To this end we develop an update rule for the interval estimators that takes into account their dependence on local quantiles. Our experiments verify the effectiveness of quantile modeling in several settings.

Albeit the implicit feedback based recommendation problem - when only the user history is available but there are no ratings - is the most typical setting in real-world applications, it is much less researched than the explicit feedback case. State-of-the-art algorithms that are efficient on the explicit case cannot be automatically transformed to the implicit case if scalability should be maintained. There are few implicit feedback benchmark data sets, therefore new ideas are usually experimented on explicit benchmarks. In this paper, we propose a generic context-aware implicit feedback recommender algorithm, coined iTALS. iTALS applies a fast, ALS-based tensor factorization learning method that scales linearly with the number of non-zero elements in the tensor. We also present two approximate and faster variants of iTALS using coordinate descent and conjugate gradient methods at learning. The method also allows us to incorporate various contextual information into the model while maintaining its computational efficiency. We present two context-aware variants of iTALS incorporating seasonality and item purchase sequentiality into the model to distinguish user behavior at different time intervals, and product types with different repetitiveness. Experiments run on six data sets shows that iTALS clearly outperforms context-unaware models and context aware baselines, while it is on par with factorization machines (beats 7 times out of 12 cases) both in terms of recall and MAP.

Her daughter's car was parked in the driveway, so she knew she was home. She knocked on the door and waited. After a moment, the door opened and her daughter was there, looking at her with surprise. "Mom?" she said. "What are you doing here?" "Can I come in?" the woman asked. Her daughter hesitated for a moment before stepping aside and letting her in. "I thought you were still in California," her daughter said as she led her into the living room. "I was," the woman replied. "But I'm back now." Her daughter sat down on the couch and gestured for her to do the same. "Why are you back?" she asked. The woman took a deep breath. "I'm here because I need your help," she said. In the mid-1950s, Frank Burnet, inspired by a suggestion made by Niels Jerne, formulated the clonal selection theory (CST) of immunity. On the basis of CST, Burnet developed a theory of how the immune system recognizes and responds to foreign substances, or antigens. According to the CST, the immune system contains a large number of specialized cells, or clones, each with a unique receptor molecule on its surface. When an antigen enters the body, it interacts with these receptors, and the cells that carry receptors that match the antigen are activated. These activated cells then multiply and differentiate into various types of immune cells, such as plasma cells that produce antibodies against the antigen, or cytotoxic T cells that directly attack infected cells. The CST also explains how the immune system is able to distinguish between foreign antigens and the body's own cells and tissues. It proposes that during development, immune cells are selected to recognize only non-self antigens, while self-reactive cells are eliminated or rendered harmless. The clonal selection theory has been supported by numerous experiments and remains a cornerstone of modern immunology.

This work presents a multiscale framework to solve a class of stochastic optimal control problems in the context of robot motion planning and control in a complex environment. In order to handle complications resulting from a large decision space and complex environmental geometry, two key concepts are adopted: (a) a diffusion wavelet representation of the Markov chain for hierarchical abstraction of the state space; and (b) a desirability function-based representation of the Markov decision process (MDP) to efficiently calculate the optimal policy. In the proposed framework, a global plan that compressively takes into account the long timelength-scale state transition is first obtained by approximately solving an MDP whose desirability function is represented by coarse scale bases in the hierarchical abstraction. Then, a detailed local plan is computed by solving an MDP that considers wavelet bases associated with a focused region of the state space, guided by the global plan. The resulting multiscale plan is utilized to finally compute a continuous-time optimal control policy within a receding horizon implementation. Two numerical examples are presented to demonstrate the applicability and validity of the proposed approach.

Most historians today, including John's recent biographers Ralph Turner and Lewis Warren, argue that John was an unsuccessful monarch, but note that his failings were exaggerated by 12th- and 13th-century chroniclers. Jim Bradbury notes the current consensus that John was a "hard-working administrator, an able man, an able general," albeit, as Turner suggests, with "distasteful, even dangerous personality traits," including pettiness, spitefulness and cruelty. John Gillingham, author of a major biography of Richard I, follows this line too, although he considers John a less effective general than do Turner or Warren, and describes him "one of the worst kings ever to rule England." Bradbury takes a moderate line, but suggests that in recent years modern historians have been overly lenient towards John's numerous faults. Popular historian Frank McLynn maintains a counter-revisionist perspective on John, arguing that the king's modern reputation amongst historians is "bizarre," and that as a monarch John "fails almost all those [tests] that can be legitimately set."

I always check all of the tanks myself. It's just a habit I developed over a lifetime of diving, and like any professional, I took responsibility for all of my own equipment. Gale is a great grad student, don't get me wrong. But, well, frankly she just doesn't care that much about the diving. I understand her reticence at my solitary passion. She and any other person on the planet could simply type in our current coordinates, and see a RealMap 3D scan of the ocean floor below. The newer versions of RealMap even let you interact directly with the topographical scans through your Oculus, FaceMate, or even the other virtual reality hardware. But I'm old. I'm stuck in my ways, and I maintain that actual diving just can't be beat. I have always loved the physicality of sinking down into the depths, interacting directly with fauna, reefs and even wrecks. Nothing else even comes close. " How long do you think we'll be out here? " Gale asked, not even bothering to look up from her book. I almost grimaced at the insinuation that I was wasting her time, but I've grown used to her youthful impatience. If nothing else, maybe dragging her out into the ocean with me would help her learn some patience. " About 2 hours, all told " I responded. That was more or less true, but it's not like she could leave without me; my grant money paid her rent. Gale dispassionately rolled her eyes, mocking more than complaining. Two hours of isolation would give her time to study, especially since she was falling behind on the newest data sets coming out of California. She needed to get up to speed quickly, and she knew that. " Just remember, " I said, " if I'm not back in 2 hours, then something has gone wrong. Just engage the winch, and it will pull me back... " I was interrupted by her recitation of the speech I had hammered at her over and over so many times before. " It will pull you back at a rate of 10 feet per second, then I have to use the pole to bring you alongside the boat, and haul your fish-smelling carcass back on board. Watch the monitor for other boats, listen to the radio for your signal, or if you need me to winch you back. " We stared blankly at each other for several long seconds. " I got it " she said, turning back to her book. I hoisted the tanks onto my back, and made sure the regulator was delivering air. I pulled down my mask, and slid towards the edge of the boat. " Wish me luck " I nasally called to my indifferent companion. She waved noncommittally, indicating her utter lack of interest. I heaved my bulk gently backwards, allowing the weight of my gear to drag me down into the dark water below. The cold mass hit me hard, then caressed me down into the grey depths. I exhaled hard, checked my orientation, then righted myself, and began to slowly descend. Somewhere below me was an abyss of nothing. But for today, this was as far out as I could convince Gale to follow, and honestly we still had a lot to do back at the office today. Drifting further down into the water, I allowed all of those responsibilities do fade away, cast aside back at the surface. Down here, I was just a small part of the infinite flow of water, carried about on the currents, drifting down into the darkness. After a short time, the bottom came into view. I stopped myself just short of the actual sea floor, and hovered gracefully above the stones and muck. There was nothing of note as I journeyed along the bottom, but even just the variations of the ocean's detritus were able to hold my interest. No matter how many scans one looked at, there was still nothing like this in the world. The freedom of floating, heavenly in its embrace, and the adrenaline rush of the crushing depths surrounding me. This was my true love. Then, from somewhere out of the darkness, something was with me. I couldn't see anything beyond the murky water in front of me, and the silt below. But there was unquestionably something else there in the water. I could feel it moving along, shadowing my advance through the depths. From the corner of my eyes, I would see a shadow, or a flitting shape. But wherever I turned to observe my visitor, there was only the obscure depth of the ocean. But the presence around me grew stronger, and I could feel my pulse in my ears. My breathing was speeding up, and I knew I was risking injury if I allowed myself to panic. I forced myself to breathe in a slowing pattern, all-the-while aware of the unseen, yet undoubtedly moving manifestation there with me. I pressed the small button on my arm, sending an electric signal back to gale up on the surface. Any second now, the winch should begin retrieving me from this watery labyrinth, and its hidden occupant. But nothing happened. I pressed the button again, but still I remained there, drifting with the lazy current, steadily pursued by nothing, but fully aware that I was absolutely not alone. Suddenly, I felt myself thrust upwards by rushing water, hitting me in the chest hard. I could see no moving agent, nothing propelling the water and my frail humanity through the water. I found myself pushed out of sight of the bottom, and still far below the dim light of the surface. Instinctively, I exhaled hard, but my bubbles merely gathered about my face, refusing to reveal the direction of the surface. Beginning to panic, I exhaled hard once again, but still I simply found myself surrounded by my own exhalation. I went to press the button again, but found I was already hammering it in rapid succession. Without warning, I saw the darkness move beneath me. Some great unfathomable shadow lurched and lunged below me, towards me; menacing and demanding. I felt the air seize in my lungs, and my heart raced, nearly blinding me in its exertion. The shadows below climbed and shifted, alternately fleeing then surpassing me in my suspension. I saw the darkness itself seemingly reach towards me, threatening to consume my very existence. Suddenly I burst forth through the surface, and was blinded by the sky. The darkness below me receded, but I flailed in desperation towards the small figure of the boat. In the despairing moments it took for me to reach to boat, I could still feel the presence below, pacing my every move, seeming to be biding its time, relishing in my terror. I hauled myself onto the boat, and tore the mask from my face, I gasped at the fresh air, and scrambled backwards into the very center of the boat, waiting for my watery villain to spring forth at any second and destroy our little fibreglass island. I hollered at Gale, my voice almost a shriek. " Go! Go! Get us out of here! " " Wait, " Gale countered, " you're letting me drive the boat? Seriously? " My mind couldn't comprehend her words, but merely begged to be distanced from the murky horror beneath us. " Just go! " I shouted. " Go go go! " " Cool " Gale exclaimed, a gleeful grin alighting upon her face. She slid over to the driver's seat, and turned the ignition. The motor roared to life, and within seconds we were moving fast through the water. I peered over the side, but though I couldn't see the menacing shadow anymore, I felt that it was still there, ushering us from its home. I collapsed back onto the side, heavy with exhaustion, unable to move in my fear. " Anything interesting? " Gale asked as she captained us back towards the shore. I couldn't form the words to answer. All I could think was that the ocean had grown accustomed to our new absence, and was ready to ensure that we never again threatened its serenity. I for one would not be disturbing it again.

We propose a novel mathematical framework to address the problem of automatically solving large jigsaw puzzles. This problem assumes a large image which is cut into equal square pieces that are then scrambled. The goal is to find the proper relative positions for each piece, and hence to put the puzzle back together. Our framework is based on the notion of local coherence which is a relative measure of how well a piece fits its neighbors. We show how this measure can be computed efficiently and how it can be used to guide the search for a solution. We also present two novel local optimization techniques, i.e., hill-climbing and iterated local search, that can be used to maximize the local coherence of a puzzle. We conducted an extensive experimental evaluation of our framework on a standard benchmark of real-world images. We found that we were able to solve all of the puzzles using our framework in a reasonable amount of time. This included even the hardest puzzles for which no other algorithm was able to find a solution. We also found that we were able to significantly speed up the computation time by using both local optimization techniques and by parallelizing the hill-climbing procedure.

With the death of the final male northern white rhino occurring in 2018, the population has drastically decreased as a result of extensive illegal hunting.

The primary element influencing your sleep patterns is your internal clock, known as the circadardynamic. Although this cycle doesn't perfectly align with a 24-hour period, minor variations exist due to various influences affecting your biological timing system. Another crucial aspect to consider is the phase of your sleep cycle when you awaken. Generally, there are five distinct phases of sleep, with stages 1-2 characterized by high brain activity resembling an alert state; during these stages, you may easily react to external stimuli. Conversely, stage 3 represents a deep slumber, marked by significantly reduced brain activity, making it challenging to rouse oneself upon waking - often resulting in fatigue and confusion. During stage 4, true recuperation transpires, featuring moderate yet gentle brain activity signifying repair processes within the body. Finally, we have the REM (Rapid Eye Movement) stage, associated with increased mental activity leading to vivid dreams. These sleep phases recur cyclically every 90 minutes throughout the night, adjusting their duration according to individual requirements for restoration or REM sleep. Waking up from REM leads to feelings of vitality since dream interruptions aren't common, whereas emerging from stages 3-4 tends to leave one feeling drained, having interrupted the body's healing process. To summarize, several intricate elements impact our sleep experiences, encompassing both physiological and environmental components."

In Africa'sintegrated ecosystems like Kenya and specifically the Masai Mara region, one can encounter the quintessential African 'Big Five': lions, leopards, buffalos, rhinos, and elephants. Alongside these iconic species, numerous other mammals, avian life forms, and reptiles thrive within the nation's various conservation areas. Between the months of June and September, an impressive migratory event unfolds as countless creatures journey across vast distances. Notably, this period sees approximately two million wildebeests traverse roughly 2,900 kilometers (or about 1,802 miles), moving from the Serengeti in Tanzania towards the plains of the Masai Mara in Kenya—pursuing essential resources such as sustenance and hydration. Known as the Great Wildebeest Migration, this phenomenon has earned its place among the top ten natural marvels on the continent.

The federal constitutional initiative permits citizens to propose a constitutional change for a nationwide referendum, provided that it garners the support of at least 100,000 registered voters within an 18-month timeframe. In this process, the parliament has the authority to introduce a competing proposal alongside the original one, leading to voters having to choose between them should they both gain approval. Any alteration to the constitution, regardless of its origin (initiated by public petition or through parliamentary procedure), requires ratification via a twofold consensus – receiving favorable votes from the general populace as well as the constituent regions' electorate.

West's musical career has been defined by frequent stylistic shifts, and has seen him develop and explore a variety of different musical approaches and genres throughout his work. When asked about his musical inspirations, he has named A Tribe Called Quest, Stevie Wonder, Michael Jackson, George Michael, LL Cool J, Phil Collins and Madonna as early interests. He has further described musician David Bowie as one of his "most important inspirations," and named producer Puff Daddy as the "most important cultural figure in my life." Early in his career, West pioneered a style of production dubbed "chipmunk soul" which utilized pitched-up vocal samples, usually from soul and RB songs, along with his own drums and instrumentation. His first major release featuring his trademark soulful vocal sampling style was "This Can't Be Life," a track from Jay-Z's The Dynasty: Roc La Familia. West has said that Wu-Tang Clan producer RZA influenced him in his style, and has named Wu-Tang rappers Ghostface Killah and Ol' Dirty Bastard as inspirations. RZA spoke positively of the comparisons, stating in an interview for Rolling Stone, "All good. I got super respect for Kanye [...] [he] is going to inspire people to be like him." West further developed his style on his 2004 debut album, The College Dropout. After a rough version was leaked, he meticulously refined the production, adding string arrangements, gospel choirs, and improved drum programming.

Modern applications significantly enhance user experience by adapting to each user's individual condition andor preferences. While this adaptation can greatly improve utility or be essential for the application to work properly, it is often associated with the risk of unexpected changes. This paper proposes a solution, which aims at minimizing such risk. It builds on the idea of delegating adaptation decisions to a trusted third-party - a Proxy Adaptor. This way, the application remains in its default state while the user experiences the effects of adaptation. In case of a disagreement, the user can decide who wins the battle. The Proxy Adaptor is implemented as a Firefox extension, which can be used with any online application. Kahl, M. 2010. A Proxy Adaptor for Adaptive Web Applications. In Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on World Wide Web, Apr 26 2010, Raleigh, NC, USA: ACM.

The report found that although alcohol consumption has dropped since 2008, those in poorer communities are more likely to suffer or die from alcohol-related disease. The coalition government rejected a minimum price for alcohol in 2013. Health ministers said they would look at the evidence carefully. The public health review says that alcohol is now more affordable and people are drinking more than they did 40 years ago, making it the leading risk factor for ill health, early death and disability in those aged 15 to 49 in England. More adults are non-drinkers but there are still more than 10 million people in England drinking at levels that could damage their health. The report suggests there were 167,000 years of working life lost to alcohol in 2015 - mainly among the young and middle-aged. It concludes that reducing the affordability of alcohol is the most cost-effective way of reducing alcohol harm. But a plan to introduce a minimum price of 45p per unit of alcohol was shelved by the coalition government three years ago. In 2014, a ban on the sale of alcohol below cost price, defined as alcohol duty plus VAT, came into force in England and Wales. Public Health England (PHE) says implementing a minimum unit price (Mup) is the answer because it "is a highly targeted measure which ensures tax increases are passed on to the consumer and improves the health of the heaviest drinkers." It also adds that combing Mup with an increase in taxation would lead to "substantial reductions in harm and increases in government revenue." The report also says there is little evidence to suggest that putting more information on labels on alcoholic drinks would lead to a reduction in alcohol-related harm. A spokesman for the Department of Health said: "While no one would want to interfere with the right of adults to enjoy a drink responsibly, this report shows clearly that the abuse of alcohol can cause significant health problems." And it added that new official guidance on alcohol limits, which say that men and women should drink no more than 14 units of alcohol a week, allowed people to make informed choices. Prof Kevin Fenton, national director of health and wellbeing at PHE, said alcohol damaged more than just individuals. "Excessive alcohol consumption can harm children, wreck families, impact on workplace colleagues and can be a burden and drain on the NHS and economy. "This evidence review will help local and national government and public services like the police and NHS to develop policies designed to reduce the harmful effects of alcohol." Shirley Cramer, chief executive of the Royal Society for Public Health, said she was hopeful that the evidence would be taken on board by government. "The health harms of alcohol affect all sectors of society, but are felt most by the poorest and most vulnerable. "All the evidence now points to Mup as one of the most effective potential ways to tackle these inequalities in harm." In Scotland, laws for the minimum pricing for alcohol were passed in 2012 but have not yet been introduced because of a series of legal challenges. The Welsh Government has said it wants to set a minimum 50p charge per unit of drink but UK ministers say alcohol law should be controlled by Westminster.

Abundant data is the key to successful machine learning. However, supervised learning requires annotated data that are often hard to obtain. In a classification task with limited resources, Active Learning (AL) promises to guide annotators to examples that bring the most value for a classifier. AL can be successfully combined with self-training, i.e., extending a training set with the unlabelled examples for which a classifier is the most certain. We report our experiences on using AL in a systematic manner to train an SVM classifier for Stack Overflow posts discussing performance of software components. We show that the training examples deemed as the most valuable to the classifier are also the most difficult for humans to annotate. Despite carefully evolved annotation criteria, we report low inter-rater agreement, but we also propose mitigation strategies. Finally, based on one annotator's work, we show that self-training can improve the classification accuracy. We conclude the paper by discussing implication for future text miners aspiring to use AL and self-training.

The Black Death ravaged much of the Islamic world. Plague was present in at least one location in the Islamic world virtually every year between 1500 and 1850. Plague repeatedly struck the cities of North Africa. Algiers lost 30 to 50 thousand inhabitants to it in 1620-21, and again in 1654-57, 1665, 1691, and 1740-42. Plague remained a major event in Ottoman society until the second quarter of the 19th century. Between 1701 and 1750, thirty-seven larger and smaller epidemics were recorded in Constantinople, and an additional thirty-one between 1751 and 1800. Baghdad has suffered severely from visitations of the plague, and sometimes two-thirds of its population has been wiped out.

A network model is considered where Poisson distributed base stations transmit to N power-domain non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) users (UEs) each that employ successive interference cancellation (SIC) for decoding. We first present a numerical solution of the power and spectrum efficiency in terms of average data rate per user, transmission diversity gain and number of transmissions required for full coverage when both interfering signals are additive Gaussian noise. A simple analytical expression was derived from this numerically determined results which shows how well the performance can be scaled with increasing dimensionality in a practical setting depending on the type of deployment scenario used. For example, assuming linear propagation channels our analysis showed that networks using up to 10 nodes or 6 degrees of freedom operate satisfactorily while 12 degree-of-freedom deployments offer significantly better tradeoffs between resources consumed by SIC receiversusers versus achievable gains over pure channel coding schemes without any additional radio resource overhead. In particular we consider different types of multi-antenna systems including MIMO arrangements comprised of two antennas at the transmitter as an extension of a conventional single input single output (SISO), three or four antenna configurations representing enhancement of spatial processing techniques employed commonly today e.g., array orthogonally spaced antennas [1], and finally 15 or more antenna arrays giving rise respectively to short reach beam forming approaches such as active phased arrays, or long range steering setups capable of providing high angular resolution akin to radar applications. In general it has been shown that joint MIMO-array processing outperforms independent implementations of either one approach alone resulting in higher spectral efficiencies due to improved signal detection capability provided by combining several spatially separated signals arriving simultaneously within optimal time windows via their beams rather than following separate paths through space. The main focus here however remains on extending these concepts beyond compact mobile platforms into larger fixed indoor environments particularly aimed towards supporting new broadband services requiring significant bandwidth requirements i.e.: Voice over IP Internet Protocol television etc...

We explore Conditional Risk Minimization (CRM), which involves finding a hypothesis with the lowest possible risk when predicting future steps based on sequential, interdependent data. While crucial, effective CRM learning has previously relied on purely theoretical algorithms that aren't practical due to their need to store every piece of incoming data. Our research presents MACRO, a meta-algorithm designed for CRM without this limitation while still providing learning assurances. Unlike previous methods, MACRO doesn't keep all data; instead, it continuously refines a collection of learning procedures through appropriate estimations. When tested with actual data, MACRO outperforms conventional unconditional learning techniques by enhancing prediction accuracy.

Online multiplayer games are a popular form of social interaction, used by hundreds of millions of individuals. However, little is known about the social networks within these online games, or how they evolve over time. Understanding human social dynamics within massive online games can shed new light on social interactions in general and inform the development of more engaging systems. Here, we study a novel, large friendship network, inferred from nearly 18 billion social interactions over 44 weeks between 17 million individuals in the popular online game Halo: Reach . This network is one of the largest, most detailed temporal interaction networks studied to date, and provides a novel perspective on the dynamics of online friendship networks, as opposed to mere interaction graphs. Initially, this network exhibits strong structural turnover and decays rapidly from a peak size. In the following period, however, both network size and turnover stabilize, producing a dynamic structural equilibrium. In contrast to other studies, we find that the Halo friendship network is non-densifying: both the mean degree and the average pairwise distance are stable, suggesting that densification cannot occur when maintaining friendships is costly. Finally, players with greater long-term engagement exhibit stronger local clustering, suggesting a group-level social engagement process. These results demonstrate the utility of online games for studying social networks, shed new light on empirical temporal graph patterns, and clarify the claims of universality of network densification.

Linguists examine how emotions alter sound meanings, while educators analyze the significance of emotions for effective learning experiences.

Transfer learning methods for reinforcement learning (RL) domains facilitate the acquisition of new skills using previously acquired knowledge. The vast majority of existing approaches assume that the agents have the same design, e.g. same shape and action spaces. In this paper we address the problem of transferring previously acquired skills amongst morphologically different agents (MDAs). For instance, assuming that a bipedal agent has been trained to move forward, could this skill be transferred on to a one-leg hopper so as to make its training process for the same task more sample efficient? We frame this problem as one of subspace learning whereby we aim to infer latent factors representing the control mechanism that is common between MDAs. We propose a novel paired variational encoder-decoder model, PVED, that disentangles the control of MDAs into shared and agent-specific factors. The shared factors are then leveraged for skill transfer using RL. Theoretically, we derive a theorem indicating how the performance of PVED depends on the shared factors and agent morphologies. Experimentally, PVED has been extensively validated on four MuJoCo environments. We demonstrate its performance compared to a state-of-the-art approach and several ablation cases, visualize and interpret the hidden factors, and identify avenues for future improvements.

In this paper, we address an issue that the visually impaired commonly face while crossing intersections and propose a solution that takes form as a mobile application. The application utilizes a combination of artificial intelligence, image processing, and computer vision algorithms to detect obstacles in the user's path. The application then provides audio feedback to inform the user of the obstacle's presence and location. We believe that this solution could help visually impaired individuals safely traverse intersections and other hazardous environments. To build our proposed application, we have divided it into four main components: object detection, obstacle avoidance, audio feedback, and user interface. The object detection component will utilize image processing and computer vision algorithms to identify obstacles such as street signs, traffic lights, and other objects in the user's environment. The obstacle avoidance component will use artificial intelligence algorithms to determine the safest route for the user to take around any obstacles. The audio feedback component will provide audible cues to alert the user of the obstacle's presence and location. Finally, the user interface component will allow the user to adjust the settings of the application and control the features of the application. In conclusion, the application we propose has the potential to revolutionize the lives of visually impaired individuals. By providing audible cues to alert the user of an obstacle's presence and location, the application helps them to safely navigate their surroundings. This application could also be useful in a variety of other scenarios including helping children learn road safety or aiding elderly individuals in navigating unfamiliar environments.

James got a new job at an animal kennel. He got to walk and feed dogs twice a day. He found it to be dirty work. It was also super boring with no fun, but he did learn a lot of things about the lives of animals that made him feel like he had achieved some sort of purpose in life. Just before his shift ended that night James saw a man who said, "Hey, I don't want you to leave. You know how much this means to me?" The man told James about his wife, Christine, who was dying from cancer. The couple were trying to conceive, and when they couldn't find any embryos, she decided to have an abortion. The procedure would take nine months - far too long for them to bear children together. This made her very angry since she wanted more time to spend with her husband and son. She asked James to please stay on until she could finish the process so she wouldn't have to go through that alone. When he left she went into shock and couldn't get away without crying. On the way home James stopped by children's hospices to check up on another family whose beloved dog had died earlier in August after being diagnosed with cancer. The parents talked about how they didn't care if their child grew up knowing nothing about dog breeding or the world of canine relationships because their dog meant everything to them and they loved it dearly. At home, James waited patiently while Christine carried out the last rites for her dog. Then his heart began to ache again as he watched people struggle to accept what happened. His own father wasn't ready yet for such news. James felt responsible for bringing these two families into existence, even though they weren't his. And then there was his mother-in-law who had been helping Christine move near her childhood home from Los Angeles to Vancouver. Now she looked forward to spending every moment with her grandson who lived nearby. So instead of processing all of this information, James called Christine. They talked about how happy she had been caring for other families who needed help during difficult times. They agreed to continue working together as affiliates. Within days, another photographer contacted James seeking a partner to join him in supporting dog breeders. So James applied and was accepted. But the following week Christine passed away unexpectedly. Before he knew it, he was leaving behind a business of five employees and three dogs. All of whom lost a loving companion to sudden illness. In turn, James quit his photography job and joined the organization fulltime. Last year he won 15,000 from Canada Lottery for working with them; now he hopes to raise enough money to buy back the property he bought in 1996. (LFR photo)

Carolina rolled to its seventh consecutive win over the Falcons on Sunday. The Panthers will host the Seattle Seahawks on Sunday at noon in the NFC divisional playoffs. Panthers head coach Ron Rivera, who was named the 2015 NFL Coach of the Year on Saturday, also set an NFL record with 11 players being selected to the Pro Bowl this season. Williams signed a one-year contract with the Pittsburgh Steelers after his release from Carolina. "The guys really wanted to go out there and make some plays," said Panthers defensive end Jared Allen, who had a sack. Carolina quarterback Cam Newton completed 19 of 28 passes for 202 yards and three touchdowns. Newton also ran for 72 yards and a touchdown on 11 carries. Panthers wide receiver Ted Ginn Jr. led all receivers with nine catches for 102 yards and a touchdown. Atlanta (8-8) finished the season on a six-game losing streak. "We got outplayed and outcoached in all aspects," Atlanta quarterback Matt Ryan said. "The last six weeks have been tough, but we've had opportunities to win games and didn't do that. ... We had opportunities to make plays and didn't make them." Atlanta, which has lost seven consecutive road games, finished with a 3-5 road record this season. "We didn't play well enough to win," Falcons coach Dan Quinn said. "It wasn't enough to win against a very good team. We had trouble getting off the field, couldn't run the football, couldn't throw it and make plays. We gave up sacks in the red zone. We had a short field and didn't capitalize. This is a great football team. We're disappointed in the season and how we finished the season. We didn't make enough plays in the passing game." Ryan completed 17 of 27 passes for 231 yards, two interceptions and a touchdown. Falcons running back Devonta Freeman ran for 83 yards on 22 carries and was held without a touchdown for the second consecutive week. Carolina scored on its first two drives. Newton connected with tight end Greg Olsen on a 5-yard scoring pass. Newton then raced 17 yards for a score to give the Panthers a 14-0 lead. Carolina took a 24-0 lead into halftime after Newton's 4-yard touchdown pass to Ginn and a 35-yard field goal from Graham Gano. The fuzzy K -means problem is a generalization of the classical K -means problem to soft clusterings, i.e. clusterings where each points belongs to each cluster to some degree. Although no one really knows exactly how such clusters occur in real universe, some models suggest that they might be related to the events occurring among the universe, mostly stationary states at the radii of the Universe itself (see Figure 4). The models assumed that either the universe was formed from discrete clusters or that it arose spontaneously everywhere and came about randomly across galaxies having shaped themselves into clusters. Another explanation for clusters has been proposed by Vittoria Maier and her team as well: clusters are caused by gravitational waves arising when the energy released during gravitational waves bursts takes place between pairs of planets orbiting the larger planet-like stellar systems orbiting distant stars - but how does this relate to the tendencies towards clusters? Figure 4 shows the distribution of clusters observed within galaxies in the Universe, along with the distributions corresponding to the orbits of all galaxies detected using Laser Interferometer Gravitational Wave Observatory observations. These include the orbits of all galaxies observed; they represent roughly 50 of all observed galaxies, which means that clusters of galaxies have been detected around the world (Table 1). It should also be noted that these orbits were not confirmed using conventional methods like LIGO and the Hubble telescope. In other words nothing indicates any large scale cluster fluctuations involving more than one galaxy whose orbit changes nearly every few billion years. This suggests that clusters arise spontaneously throughout the Universe. This analysis provides evidence for a few theories about the evolution of clusters based on the observations made through LIGO and Hubble space telescopes since 2004. First, clusters appear rapidly after dark matter movements cause massive collisions among rolling stars containing a vast number of starries. Second, gravitational waves explain why planets gravitationally interact so strongly with stars. Thirdly, clusters may be created due to the spread over time of motion across interstellar spaceships travelling on average farther away from the Earth than normal. Fourth, clusters of galaxies form independently of the velocity of light emitted by starry galaxies. Fifth, clusters perform their activity primarily by collisions between galaxies similarly touching rather than pulsars - compared with relatively dense stars contacting each other equatorically with uniform gravity helps explain the supermassive black holes seen behind the planets. Sixth, clusters contain cosmic rays produced by galactic nuclei passing through even higher energies near these centers - further explaining why clusters cannot be seen directly underneath galaxies. Seventh, clusters may occur as a result of periodic motions resulting from the ejection of massive objects sideways from their configuration via gravitational waves. Eighth, clusters may originate from low mass stars ejected from the center of the Universe's greatest mass jets, which are opposed to binary stars falling atop the surface of distant planets. Ninth, clusters consist mainly of noninteractive bodies interacting with each other without being separated from gravitational waves accompanying these motions. Tenth, clusters regularly rotate relative to normal galaxies - many seem to move closer together than others suggesting that these are relationships between galaxies. Twelve, clusters exist because these processes account only for fractions of objects' distance, although clusters do fluctuate significantly according to gravity waves experienced outside of galaxies. Each of these explanations reflects multiple factors surrounding clusters, including differences in size between neighboring galaxies considered to be strongly associated with clusters, the presence of atomic amounts of radiation particles in clusters and their proximity to adjacent asteroids and comets. In conclusion, clusters originated naturally prior to the formation of the Big Bang - but they now make up significant portions of the Milky Way. They form quickly following rapid expansion of the universe by tidal forces bringing all nearby regions together into an individual mass belt. The impact of galaxies on clusters could also play a role, as giant planets respond differently depending upon the direction they travel against gravity. Cluster theory proposes that clusters arise spontaneously within galaxies while simultaneously representing a large fraction of global quantities affecting macroscopic phenomena inside galaxies.

Training multi-agent systems (MAS) to achieve realistic equilibria gives us a useful tool to understand and model real-world systems. We consider a general sum partially observable Markov game where agents have noisy perception and noisy control. We first define a family of games in which an agent's action can result in one of a few alternatives. We can then use this game to formalize the concept of 'reaching a situation' in which we wish the agent to be in a certain state or class of states. We then show how to solve the game for all possible actions, and for any given state. Next we show how to solve the game for all possible actions and all possible states, using a novel algorithm for solving finite games. This algorithm is based on a classical theorem of Bellman which states that a finite game can be transformed into a finite game with state-dependent action sets. We then use this result to transform a game into a game with state-dependent action sets, and solve it using dynamic programming. We then solve games of several of the above types. This is joint work with Martin Schroeder.

The climate in Jacksonville, similar to other parts of the southern Atlantic Coast of the US, is characterized by a humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cfa). Winters here are generally gentle, whereas summers bring about intense heat along with high levels of moisture. Characters featuring diacritics can typically be depicted as either a singular preformed character or as a separated series consisting of a primary letter along with additional spacing-less marks. Taking 'e' as an instance - it can be shown either as a precombined 'e' bearing a macron and acute mark or as an independent 'e' paired with the combination of macron and acute marks. Ideally, these representations would look identical, displaying an 'EEE' with a macron and an acute accent; however, the actual presentation might differ based on the chosen rendering engine and fonts utilized. Likewise, subscripts frequently required in the transliteration of Indic languages could end up misplaced quite often. Utilizing Unicode characters which correspond to precompounded symbols can circumvent this issue in numerous instances, yet when there is no such encoded symbol available, employing a specific Unicode typeface like Charis SIL – incorporating Graphite, OpenType, or AAT functionalities for sophisticated graphical renditions – can prove beneficial.

The finite time stability (FnTSta) theory of delayed systems has not been set up until now. In this paper, we propose a two-phases-method (2PM), to achieve this object. In the first phase, we prove that the time for norm of system error evolving from initial values to 1 is finite; then in the second phase, we prove that the time for norm of the error evolving from 1 to 0 is also finite, thus FnTSta is obtained. Considering the cost and complexity of controller, we use only two simple terms to realize this aim. For the proposed 2PM, time delays can be the same or asynchronous, bounded or unbounded, etc; the norm can be 2 -norm, 1 -norm, -norm, which show that 2PM is powerful and has a wide scope of applications. Furthermore, we also prove the adaptive finite time stability (AFnTSta) theory of delayed systems using 2PM. As an application of the obtained FnTSta theory, we consider the finite time outer synchronization (FnTOSyn) for complex networks with asynchronous unbounded time delays, corresponding criteria are also obtained. Finally, two numerical examples are given to demonstrate the validity of our theories.

Streep paid tribute to fellow actresses Diane Keaton, Susan Sarandon and Kelli O'Hara, calling them "incredible comrades" who are still warm and welcoming.
