From Mike Rowe's recent AMA to posts on rpersonalfinance, I see more and more redditors advising their peers to forego college and pursue a certification in a trade. I think this is generally bad advice: not because I think that no one should go into the skilled trades, but because 1.) I think most people aren't cut out for a trade career, and 2.) the stable income one can earn as a skilled tradesman is maintained by the scarcity of skilled tradesmen. To expand: Skilled trade jobs are hard, physical work: I come from a family of roofers, and live in an area that has been experiencing constant new home construction since the early '90s. My father was a satellite TV installer back when a satellite dish would take up most of your back yard, and a TVtelephone installer after that. Most of my (older) family members have had major knee, back, and hip surgeries in their 40s and 50s, and many have sustained life-altering or career-ending injuries. Physically, I would never have been able to pursue a career in the 'family business' (I'm a skinny dude), and I think it's better to work 40 years and retire with your body mostly intact than work 25-30 years and retire because you've destroyed your body and physically can't work any more. It's going to be a long time (possibly never) until skilled trades are 'respected'. I'm sure many people don't care how society views their career, and would laugh in the face of someone who denigrates their job while making substantially less money. That said: there will always be some people who look down on the 'dirty jobs', and some people who avoid those jobs because of it. I don't think income level alone will be enough to legitimize certain careers at certain levels of society. I'm not saying it's right: I'm saying it's a reality. Some people will always balk at marrying a sewage technician, even if that sewage technician is making 100k. (The Big One) The only reason the skilled trades are well-paid is because they are scarce. We will always need contractors, plumbers, electricians, and welders; but we only need so many. In the '70s, everyone was advising young people to go into medicine. In the '80s, everyone was advising young people to go into law. In the '90s, everyone was advising young people to go into technology and computers. Look at the job prospects of those fields today. Medicine is still well-paid, but only because it takes a decade (and hundreds of thousands of dollars) to become a doctor. Starting lawyers are earning 40k, after accruing 100k in law school debt. Information Technology grads have a higher unemployment rate than Theater or English majors. Any field that experiences a rapid influx of credentialed professionals suffers from depressed wages and high unemployment. If young people take the oft-proffered advice and enter the skilled trades: their experience is going to be worse. It takes much less time, money, and (please don't be mad at me for saying so) intellectual rigor to become certified as a skilled tradesman than it does to become a doctor, lawyer, or computer scientist. By the same token ... Wages and working conditions in the skilled trades have been protected by unionization, which is ever-diminishing. The trajectory of unions in the US has been sad and getting sadder for decades. Unions are the weakest today that they've been since before the Gilded Age. An influx of newly credentialed tradesmen, desperate for work in an increasingly saturated market, will lead to fewer union-affiliated workers. As union membership decreases, wages will fall. With Right-to-Work laws in a majority of US states, unions will lose power and skilled trade jobs will go to the lowest bidders - skilled trades will no longer provide a middle-class income. A college degree is still a worthwhile investment. Statistically, a college degree is worth somewhere between 800k to 1.2m over the course of a working career. Even if a student takes out 32k in loans (the average for a college graduate), that investment returns many, many times over the course of a career. An investment that provides a very real monetary return while affording the graduate a less physically-demanding career with greater social recognition seems like a good investment to me. Today, as it stands, few people enter the skilled trades because they are physically difficult and because they don't garner the level of social respect that the so-called 'white collar' careers attain. For the people who still choose the skilled trades - this is good news. It means that their wages are better and they can use their scarcity of labor to control their pay and working conditions. Further, it means that young people who are inherently suited for the skilled trades (because of family background, physical prowess, andor difficulty with traditional education) have the opportunity to earn a comfortable living in a skilled trade. Encouraging many people who wouldn't have considered entering the skilled trades on their own volition to make that choice will depress wages and discourage those who could have earned a university degree (which would have been a better investment) to enter a lower-paying and more physically-destructive career. Skilled tradesmen are benefitting from the scarcity of employees in their fields. Let's allow them to keep that scarcity, encourage those who can excel in college to pursue a degree, and encourage everyone to pursue the field that best suits their abilities: not the one that will earn the most money. The most familiar, and historically the oldest, types of glass are "silicate glasses" based on the chemical compound silica (silicon dioxide, or quartz), the primary constituent of sand. The term glass, in popular usage, is often used to refer only to this type of material, which is familiar from use as window glass and in glass bottles. Of the many silica-based glasses that exist, ordinary glazing and container glass is formed from a specific type called soda-lime glass, composed of approximately 75 silicon dioxide (SiO2), sodium oxide (Na2O) from sodium carbonate (Na2CO3), calcium oxide, also called lime (CaO), and several minor additives. A very clear and durable quartz glass can be made from pure silica, but the high melting point and very narrow glass transition of quartz make glassblowing and hot working difficult. In glasses like soda lime, the compounds added to quartz are used to lower the melting temperature and improve workability, at a cost in the toughness, thermal stability, and optical transmittance.

For this purpose, we framed it as a contest wherein contenders aimed to devise a controller allowing a biological human model to swiftly maneuver through an elaborate maze devoid of empirical data input. Contestants received access to a human skeletal blueprint and a simulation tool based on physical principles. Herein, we delve into the contest's setup, encountered challenges, findings, and evaluation of superior controllers. Deep residual networks (ResNets) have demonstrated better generalization performance than deep feedforward networks (FFNets). However, the theory behind such a phenomenon is still largely unknown. This paper studies this fundamental problem in deep learning from a so-called "neural tangent kernel" perspective. Specifically, we first show that under proper conditions, as the width goes to infinity, training deep ResNets can be viewed as learning reproducing kernel functions with some kernel function. We then compare the kernel of deep ResNets with that of deep FFNets and discover that the class of functions induced by the kernel of FFNets is asymptotically not learnable, as the depth goes to infinity. In contrast, the class of functions induced by the kernel of ResNets does not exhibit such degeneracy. Our discovery partially justifies the advantages of deep ResNets over deep FFNets in generalization abilities. Numerical results are provided to support our claim.

Monet's later years saw him obsessively paint the lilies in his garden at Giverny, in northern France. But his artistic legacy could have looked very different had Monet's rural neighbours had their way. Local farmers wrote to the town hall to object to his plans to extend his garden in 1893. The original documents about the case were unearthed by Ann Dumas, co-curator of the Royal Academy's Painting the Modern Garden: Monet to Matisse exhibition. "There was a protest from local farmers who were very suspicious of these strange aquatic plants that Monet wanted to plant because they they would poison their water and kill their cattle," she said. Monet, who moved to Giverny in 1883, had been able to buy land on the other side of a railway line that bordered his house. It was here he wanted to create his water garden by diverting the river Epte, a tributary of the Seine. Dumas said Monet acquired planning permission for his garden "after a lot of difficulty." "The farmers were suspicious of Monet anyway," she added. "He kept himself to himself so they saw him as an outsider. When they got wind that he wanted to make a water garden they complained." The Royal Academy show, which opens next year, looks at the role of gardens in the paintings of Monet and his contemporaries. Its 120 works span the early 1860s to the 1920s. Alongside 35 paintings by Monet will be works by Paul Klee, Emil Nolde, Gustav Klimt and Wassily Kandinsky. "It will be a show that will be both popular and scholarly," said Tim Marlow, the RA's artistic director. "It isn't just a Monet show - though he is a central figure - and it isn't just an Impressionist show. It involves a whole range of late 19th Century and early 20th-Century artists." One of the highlights will be Monet's water lily Agapanthus Triptych of 1916 - 1919 - the first time the monumental triptych has been seen in the UK. "Monet thought of himself as a better gardener then he was a painter," said Dumas. "Not everybody knows what a serious and knowledgeable gardener and horticulturalist Monet was." Painting the Modern Garden: Monet to Matisse will run at the Cleveland Museum of Art, Ohio, US from 11 October 2015 - 5 January 2016 and then at the Royal Academy of Arts, London 30 January - 20 April 2016.

Or much about it, in fact; it was still reliant on many of the same old-school methods of construction and growth as she'd used for most of her history. This was... different. It was much bigger, too. At least, that's what it seemed like to Iki. The first time she'd seen the city, a week ago, she'd been surprised by its size, its immensity. The planet was huge, but the city was enormous. It's true, Iki's experience of the Earth was very limited, but it had been enough to show her that she was on a planet that was far larger than any she'd seen before. And the city, she thought, was very much larger than the world itself. She'd taken a few days to get used to her new surroundings. After landing, she'd immediately sent out her 'augmentations to scan the surrounding area. The raw data was astonishing. There were millions of people in the city, spread out over millions of square kilometres. The buildings were tall, many of them very tall. There were parks, too, and vast open areas that Iki could only assume were for sporting or entertainment purposes. There were lakes and rivers, but also... canals? It was hard to tell what they were, given how crowded the city was. She'd seen people sailing on them, riding the currents, sailing upriver and then waiting for a barge to pass, so they could sail downriver and out of the city. Iki didn't know what she was supposed to do, so she'd stayed in the docks for a few days, waiting for someone to show her around. Eventually, a small group of 'augmentation-augmented scientists had appeared and given her some rudimentary instructions. Iki had taken them very seriously. The scientists had wanted her to study the city, and the surrounding area, to learn about its history and the processes that were keeping it alive. But there were many things that Iki couldn't see, that the scientists couldn't tell her about. The city was so vast, and it was growing so fast. Iki couldn't see all of it, not from where she was. But she knew that there were plenty of people out there, far away from the docks, that were much further away than she was. Iki was only aware of the surface of the planet, but there was another world beneath her feet. And the people of that world were still just as scared of her as she was of them. They'd been warned, of course. It had been easy enough to find out about the mission, even with the artificial intelligences having gone offline. Iki had managed to get into the feeds, which were only just starting to come back online. And there she'd found the scientists and the administrators. She'd found out that they were only beginning to find out what had happened to the artificial intelligences. But Iki didn't know what to make of that. Somebody had hacked the artificial intelligences, and it was now just a matter of time before they found out who it was. And, given how long it had taken to hack them, that person must have been very powerful indeed. Iki was no power user, but she was pretty sure she could have done it. And that was why she was here. It was because she was a power user that the scientists were sending her out into the world, where they couldn't keep an eye on her. They'd given her a list of questions to ask, but they'd been vague about what they wanted her to do with the answers. She was expected to find the people who'd attacked the artificial intelligences, and she was expected to do it as soon as possible. Iki didn't know if that was a good idea. There were many people in the city who'd been working on the AIs. It was entirely possible that some of them had turned against their creators. Iki had been instructed to stay away from them, but that was a problem, too. They might not want her to know about them, but they'd want her to know about the other AIs. And she wasn't allowed to look for them, either. That was one of the rules of the mission. Iki was supposed to be exploring the planet, learning about its history and the processes that were keeping it alive. But the rules were made for her benefit, not the planet's. If she found a way to look for the other AIs, and if she found them, they might find a way to sabotage her mission. That was a very bad thing.

I enjoy watching old and low-quality skifee movies just like many others. When I discovered "Attack of the Galactic Slime," I found a combination of ridiculousness and fond memories that exceeded my expectations. This movie from the 1960s, which was made inexpensively but has a high level of exaggerated humor, is the perfect example of sci-fi films that are hilariously bad but still entertaining. We could begin with the story, or rather the absence of it. A harmless-appearing extraterrestrial substance arrives on Earth and immediately starts eating and replicating any material in its way, resulting in the event referred to in the title. The dialogue is overdone, the props are unrealistic, and the scientific accuracy is questionable, as is typical of skifee productions. However, it is unexpected that the feeling of amazement and fascination that characterized films of that era still manages to come across. Even though the acting lacks refinement, it actually increases the level of enjoyment. Although the lead actor's portrayal of a heroic, stoic scientist is unintentionally comical, it still manages to receive a few cheers when he eventually saves the day. Similarly, the other acts invoke a feeling of joyful nostalgia, where characters oscillate between formal behavioral patterns from the 1960s and exaggerated, melodramatic expressions. However, what is the most significant accomplishment of this movie? The special effects used to create creatures. The green gelatin that has been given life by invisible forces is what is referred to as "galactic slime." It's fun to watch a cheap monster devour miniature cars and dolls with ease, and its ultimate defeat at the hands of cleaning soap is a thrilling finale that will be remembered for a long time. To summarize, "Attack of the Galactic Slime" cannot be categorized as a good movie by traditional criteria, but as a low-rated, vintage skifee film, it holds a valuable, undiscovered quality. Although it falls short in terms of storyline, character development, and visual effects, it compensates for those shortcomings by fully embracing its ridiculous concept and being delightfully campy. If you are a fan of this type of entertainment, it is worth looking for and enjoying with friends, some popcorn, and a willingness to believe in things that may not be entirely realistic.

In response to the early-to-mid-17th century "continental rationalism" John Locke proposed in An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689) a very influential view wherein the only knowledge humans can have is a posteriori, i.e., based upon experience. Locke is famously attributed with holding the proposition that the human mind is a tabula rasa, a "blank tablet," in Locke's words "white paper," on which the experiences derived from sense impressions as a person's life proceeds are written. There are two sources of our ideas: sensation and reflection. In both cases, a distinction is made between simple and complex ideas. The former are unanalysable, and are broken down into primary and secondary qualities. Primary qualities are essential for the object in question to be what it is. Without specific primary qualities, an object would not be what it is. For example, an apple is an apple because of the arrangement of its atomic structure. If an apple was structured differently, it would cease to be an apple. Secondary qualities are the sensory information we can perceive from its primary qualities. For example, an apple can be perceived in various colours, sizes, and textures but it is still identified as an apple. Therefore, its primary qualities dictate what the object essentially is, while its secondary qualities define its attributes. Complex ideas combine simple ones, and divide into substances, modes, and relations. According to Locke, our knowledge of things is a perception of ideas that are in accordance or discordance with each other, which is very different from the quest for certainty of Descartes.

Well, have you ever mixed red and blue paint to make purple? That works with paint because when you mix two colors together, they absorb certain colors of light and reflect others. But when we use lights or screens, the way we make colors is a little different. RGB stands for red, green, and blue. So if you combine those three colors of light, your eyes will see white light. That's why computer and TV screens use RGB. On the other hand, CMYK stands for cyan, magenta, yellow, and black. These colors are used in printing. When you mix these colors, the ink absorbs some light and reflects others. That's why printed materials look a little different than things on a screen. So even though mixing colors can make all the colors we need, different ways of using light and pigment will make them look different to our eyes.

After reflecting on my experiences within the American education system and workforce, I've concluded that certain groups possess inherently greater qualities compared to others. These distinrights aren't necessarily tied to religion, race, or visible characteristics. Over time, these dominant traits evolved - from physical prowess and assertiveness two millennia ago, to intellectual capacity and creativity today. Consequently, individuals deemed less capable in these areas might belong to what could be considered a 'lesser class.'

Society often favors the intellectually adept, yet many less astute individuals still wield influence due to their wealth and popularity. Instead of attempting to eliminate such disparities, I propose identifying these differences via assessments, subsequently offering tailored opportunities. While acknowledging everyone deserves respect and life, providing equal chances may hinder societal progress. In summary, some people naturally excel above others for various reasons, and while it's unjust to marginalize anyone completely, equitable access to resources isn't always beneficial for all parties involved. Would you consider changing my viewpoint?

MIC KEY EMMO YOU ESS EE....... The chanting of the marine corps filled my head. We had been brought up on a diet of violence, death and torture for the last 18 months. We were the toughest guys around, probably the toughest ever. We were barely human, most of us would later go on to describe ourselves as extreme killing machines dressed in fatigues. Indeed, that was the supposed aim when we were first created. But that doesn't mean we didn't scare. Put yourself in a field of fire long enough, and the fear of death begins to leave you. That's good, but you don't want to go as far as I've gone. Me and my friends, we've been fearing for our lives everyday for so long. The calendar tells us it's been a few months. It feels more like a decade. These men standing beside me. They're my brothers, but they aren't me. And as much as I fear for their lives, I fear for mine even more. We aren't scared of gunfire any longer. We aren't scared of grenades. We aren't scared of barbed wire and we aren't scared of wounds. But we still want to be alive, oh so badly. Perhaps more than most of the people sitting comfortably in air conditioned buildings. And I never believed in angels, until I saw one with my own eyes. Except that this one didn't have wings and had assumed the guise of a small boy. He was around 10 years old, the same age as my son. At close to 5 feet tall, he had wavy brown hair and even browner eyes. He wore plain white clothes, a ridiculous contrast to the crimson mixture of blood, mud and gravel that surrounded us. Looking back, I wonder how I managed not to wonder what he was doing here, and why nobody else had noticed him but at the time it seemed perfectly natural. "Uncle Dave." The little pipsqueak knew my name. And it still didn't ring any alarm bells. "Uncle Dave, you need to listen to me. Don't try to get to higher ground. It's too predictable." Marines don't do well taking orders from strange folk. We were killing machines yes. We took orders from our platoon commanders, damn straight. We would throw ourselves right in the line of enemy fire if that was what was called for. But make a stranger, an outsider say the same things and we didn't listen. We then possessed the skepticism of a full blown atheist and we took time. "Listen to me Dave. The corps tactics have been in use since the last fifteen years. It was a great plot and the corps has had a great run. But you need to wisen up. Do you have to lose your life to this battle? Does the military only change their tactics every time they lose a few thousand lives?" I was listening now. Gunfire sounded all around me. I could see the rest of my brothers make their way up the hill. A higher vantage point meant a number of things to us. Well over half our training was spent on exercises designed to reward the individuals and teams who found their way to the vantage points. So it did sound weird when there was this little boy, dressed in clothing so white that it reeked of symbolism telling you not to do the one thing the bloody drill sergeant had spent months training you to do. Yet, the pipsqueak had a point. You only heard the voices in your head when they were telling you something important. "Who the fuck are you?" I managed, though what I really should have asked was'what should I do instead?' "I'm Butters. I'm Timmy's friend." Holy crap. The whole thing came flooding back to me. My wife and I for the short time we were together had fought often about how to raise Timmy. My wife always thought I was naive. I usually gave in to the bitch. Domestic peace and all, right? But not when it came to Timmy. He was the only son I had at the time and he meant the world to me. I would rip her heart out, before I let her corrupt a single thought my boy might have. But Bebe didn't see things my way. She had changed Bebe had. She was no longer the caring girl I had caressed and made love to when we were teenagers. It must have been her sister. Or her parents. Or all of em. Didn't fucking matter to me. Bebe was always telling Timmy to sit straight, or comb his hair or put away his things. She was killing the one thing that Timmy had. The one thing I was risking my life for on the battlefield. She was killing freedom. It wasn't just about the country. It wasn't just about the red, white and blue and the right to press your thumb against a person's name. It was about the right to think for yourself. Timmy didn't have too many friends. He even had a habit of talking to himself. It drove Bebe up the wall. One day I saw her smacking my little boy across the face for'talking to Butters'. I pulled the boy out of her reach and put him on my shoulder, my freshly washed shirt absorbing the moisture that had gathered across his face. That was the last time I ever saw Bebe outside of a courtroom. Bebe won custody back and I only got to visit when I wasn't on tour. Butters had all but slipped out of my mind. Until he showed up and I could see him right before my eyes. The mud, the blood, the gravel, the bullets, the screams, the silence that followed a round of gunfire - it was all insignificant to the incarnation of Timmy's best and perhaps only friend. I still hadn't digested his entry. Clearly, this vision or ghost or whatever he was knew a thing or two about what was going to happen, and was in fact trying his best to get it across. Instead, the next words out of my mouth were "Please don't tell Timmy I used the F-word" Butters nodded. "I try to be a good role model. I really do. I wish I could get to see him more often." 'If that's what you want, you'll do as I tell you." "I hear ya" I replied. "You'll take the third largest hill as your target. Same drill. Don't go for the highest ground. They've got a battalion of shooters, most of them snipers, sitting far away waiting for soldiers to cross the only path. They've got more firepower than you have soldiers. Do the math." I did. It wasn't particularly hard. "What you'll do is going to be hard. You'll have to make sacrifices and you'll have to make difficult ones. Kenny, Stan and Kyle will have to die." I nodded in profound dumbness. "As they make their way past the passing over there" he pointed as he spoke and I looked and understood well enough what he meant. I would have to look away as my friends died and make notes. I would have to let them be shot through their hearts while I looked out for myself. Not surprisingly, I was okay with that. I moved out of my position. No one noticed I was missing as I slithered away, moving only on my elbows and knees, my chest flat and facing the ground. Once I was further away, I knew by instinct when the rest of the contingent realized that something was amiss. And sure enough a few moments later, I heard Kyle and Stan exclaim in sequence..... "Oh My God! They killed Kenny!" "You Bastards!!!" I knew them so well I was visualizing their dialogue right before my eyes. I turned towards Butters. "I always thought you'd have blond hair." Not my brightest day. But then I wasn't sure whether I'd ever see the kid again. I watched the gunshots come flying out of the darkness. I saw where they came from. I saw how many they were. And then I fired. I killed them all one by one.

The aim is to motivate individuals to engage in recycling practices. This may have been more effective in the past when a five-cent return offered a higher proportion of the original purchase cost. Currently, only certain states have implemented such initiatives due to specific legislation enacted by their lawmakers, which incurs associated expenses. For instance, Michigan enforces a ten-cent rebate on non-water bottles and cans to foster recycling habits among residents. Consequently, littering is less prevalent, as locals often collect these items for monetary compensation. Previously, soft drink producers distributed products in glass containers that could be returned and either reused or recycled at designated facilities. Some areas even provided collection services for convenience. However, with the advent of plastic packaging, the impetus to reclaim and reuse these materials diminished, resulting in increased environmental degradation. Consumers struggled with proper disposal methods, leading to escalating pollution levels. As criticism mounted against soft drink makers for contributing to this problem, they defended their position through extensive lobbying efforts and emotionally charged advertising campaigns, shifting focus onto individual accountability rather than corporate responsibility. To address this issue, numerous states introduced soda levies to financially incentivize the retrieval and recycling of empty bottles, effectively promoting sustainable behavior.

This study introduces a hands-on methodology for granular information extraction. Drawing from numerous examples of implementing information extraction techniques within business process automation, two primary technical issues arise: (i) access to sufficient labeled datasets is typically restricted, and (ii) intricate categorization is necessary. Our suggested solution involves employing transfer learning principles by utilizing pre-existing models derived from deep neural networks, paired with standard statistical classifiers to assign categories to individual terms. Initially, we apply BERT to overcome the challenge of insufficient training data in realistic situations, followed by integrating BERT with Convolutional Neural Networks to discern concealed patterns for classification purposes. To assess the effectiveness of our strategy, we tested it on a genuine instance involving the examination of official documentation related to competitive bids for government contracts in Japan. Utilizing a dataset comprising 100 documents for both training and evaluation, we verified that our model proficiently extracts precise fine-grained named entities, including specific details like department names associated with applicants.

A [private copying levy] is a levy or tax that is charged on purchases of recordable media. Such levies have been instituted in several countries to compensate content producers for the inevitable private copying of their product enabled by consumer recordable media. Notice, in particular, that the levy is collected on the assumption that the media will be used to privately copy copyrighted content, regardless of whether it happens or not. The levy exists as a compensation scheme for copyright holders for alleged losses incurred from lost sales. I argue that this scheme provides fair compensation to the copyright holders as negotiated between their representatives and the government which, barring commercial use, provides end users with a moral (if not legal) license to copy and distribute as much content as they want. Notice that this reasoning excludes content for which no private copying levy exists, countries where it doesn't exist and commercial use of private copying (e.g. re-selling of private copies for profit).

The explosion in workload complexity and the recent slow-down in Moore's law scaling call for new approaches towards efficient computing. Researchers are now beginning to use recent advances in machine learning, artificial intelligence and laser-based computing in order to optimize performance of cores and memory while lowering power consumption by creating more efficiently embedded video processors or memory modules. In a paper published on Oct. 5 in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, researchers at the University of Washington are working with AI and ML experts from the RAND Corporation and IBM Research Lab in Southern California to assess the impact of "computational efficiency" (CEO) on performance and efficiency of core cores. The researchers analyze the efficiency of CEO using multiple different methods: First, they used a two-dimensional approach that uses several processor cycles to compute and store data. They then simulated how much CPU time it would take to process common code. They found that the overall CEO cost was less than 8 per CPU chip for the average CPU cycle, compared with about one per CPU set. Second, they performed simulations based on CPU scheduling patterns. In this case, they measured the central clock speed in both CPU cycles and averaged that across the five CPU cycles before determining whether there is an appropriate number of CPUs to run. After this benchmarking process, they determined that the remaining CPUs needed to be optimized for the current target memory latency when the network expected to last longer. This was achieved through tryout scenarios where the user might need to have three or four CPU cycles to make sure all cores were running in peak performance even though they had no hardware or programming experience. Finally, when they analyzed the performance of individual cores that were having trouble processing the same amount of data per second, they found that their performance did not depend on their device usage. For example, a smartphone can consume 12.5GB of data per second if its desktop computer consumes 14GB. When these numbers went into account, a typical mobile phone would look possible only one week after installing the operating system. QoS-aware networking applications such as real-time streaming and video surveillance systems require nearly fixed average end-to-end delay over long periods to communicate efficiently, although may tolerate some delay variations in their packet transmission. In a typical QoS application for high speed network communications the data flow is mapped into control packets that carry priority information about packet quality of service (PQOS) requirements at each node along the path from sender to receiver. The router or other device which receives this PQOS information can look up the destination address contained in these control packets within its memory or map them directly on their way according to predetermined rules based upon the selected priority level and outgoing port type. When a single link fails there is no guarantee that all the packets destined for any given IP address will be dropped by the new link. Hence one approach to addressing this problem has been to construct flexible servers capable of using alternate links when available without having to drop any incoming connection. Such an arrangement would allow both local and remote services to continue with little loss to performance even if only one of two links were working. Unfortunately it requires special hardware and software dedicated to managing bandwidth availability across multiple links simultaneously and without manager intervention. Another solution to this problem involves upgrading existing equipment so that it supports links of varying quality but not including any features intended to automatically route connections through alternative paths where possible.

The interior of Galicia is characterized by its hilly landscape, although mountain ranges rise to 2,000 m (6,600 ft) in the east and south. The climate of Galicia is temperate and rainy, but it is also markedly drier in the summer, being usually classified as Oceanic in the west and north, and Mediterranean in the southeast. Its topographic and climatic conditions have made animal husbandry and farming the primary source of Galicia's wealth for most of its history. With the exception of shipbuilding and food processing, Galicia was largely a semi-subsistence farming and fishing economy and did not experience significant industrialization until after the mid-20th century. In 2012, the gross domestic product at purchasing power parity was 56,000 million, with a nominal GDP per capita of 20,700. The population is largely concentrated in two coastal areas: from Ferrol to A Coruna in the northwest and from Pontevedra to Vigo in the southwest. To a lesser extent, there are smaller populations around the interior cities of Lugo, Ourense and Santiago de Compostela. The political capital is Santiago de Compostela, in the province of A Coruna. In this paper we present a generic framework for the asymptotic performance analysis of subspace-based parameter estimation schemes. It is based on earlier results on an explicit first-order expansion of the estimation error in the signal subspace obtained via an SVD of the noisy observation matrix. We extend these results in a number of aspects. Firstly, we demonstrate that an explicit first-order expansion of the Higher-Order SVD (HOSVD) -based subspace estimate can be derived. Secondly, we show how to obtain explicit first-order expansions of the estimation error of arbitrary ESPRIT-type algorithms and provide the expressions for R -D matrix-based and tensor-based Standard ESPRIT as well as Unitary ESPRIT. Thirdly, we derive closed-form expressions for the mean square error (MSE) and show that they only depend on the second-order moments of the noise. Hence, we only need the noise to be zero mean and possess finite second order moments. Additional assumptions such as Gaussianity or circular symmetry are not needed. Fourthly, we investigate the effect of using Structured Least Squares (SLS) to solve the overdetermined shift invariance equations in ESPRIT and provide an explicit first-order expansion as well as a closed-form MSE expression. Finally, we simplify the MSE for the special case of a single source and compute the asymptotic efficiency of the investigated ESPRIT-type algorithms in compact closed-form expressions which only depend on the array size and the effective SNR. Our results are more general than existing results on the performance analysis of ESPRIT-type algorithms since (a) we do not need any assumptions about the noise except for the mean to be zero and the second-order moments to be finite (in contrast to earlier results that require Gaussianity andor second-order circular symmetry); (b) our results are asymptotic in the effective SNR, i.e., we do not require the number of samples to be large (in fact we can analyze even the single-snapshot case); (c) we present a framework that incorporates the SVD-based and the HOSVD-based subspace estimates as well as Structured Least Squares in one unified manner.

These changes aimed at boosting reserve forces, thus expanding the overall force size to an intended total of 800,000 upon activation. The seahorse placenta is a fascinating example of convergent evolution. Male seahorses' brood pouches develop and function like human placentas. During pregnancy, the males provide embryos with everything they need. As the embryos grow, the brood pouch becomes thinner and sprouts more blood vessels, much like a mammalian placenta. This allows the baby seahorses to breathe inside the pouch. The pouch reverts to its prepregnancy form 24 hours after giving birth.

Severe storms in December 2013 caused damage to an existing dune system to the east of Barkby Beach in Prestatyn. A report, to be considered by Denbighshire councillors, says there is a "significant risk of flooding" to properties at Barkby Beach if the dunes are not restored. The report says a loss of dunes is a "significant risk" to the properties at Barkby Beach and it recommends that a one metre sand dune be restored, at a cost of 250,000. The report says that a loss of the dunes would also be a risk to the sewerage works in Prestatyn, which serves the whole of the North Wales coast. The dune system is to be restored to a design which includes sedge grass and dune shrubbery, and the dunes will be topped with sand fencing. The work is expected to start in the summer. A spokesman for Denbighshire council said: "The dunes at Barkby Beach have been severely eroded following a number of severe weather events and the loss of the dune system is putting properties at risk of flooding. Many cultures define the transition into adultlike sexuality by specific biological or social milestones in an adolescent's life. For example, menarche (the first menstrual period of a female), or semenarche (the first ejaculation of a male) are frequent sexual defining points for many cultures. In addition to biological factors, an adolescent's sexual socialization is highly dependent upon whether their culture takes a restrictive or permissive attitude toward teen or premarital sexual activity. Restrictive cultures overtly discourage sexual activity in unmarried adolescents or until an adolescent undergoes a formal rite of passage. These cultures may attempt to restrict sexual activity by separating males and females throughout their development, or through public shaming and physical punishment when sexual activity does occur. In less restrictive cultures, there is more tolerance for displays of adolescent sexuality, or of the interaction between males and females in public and private spaces. Less restrictive cultures may tolerate some aspects of adolescent sexuality, while objecting to other aspects. For instance, some cultures find teenage sexual activity acceptable but teenage pregnancy highly undesirable. Other cultures do not object to teenage sexual activity or teenage pregnancy, as long as they occur after marriage. In permissive societies, overt sexual behavior among unmarried teens is perceived as acceptable, and is sometimes even encouraged. Regardless of whether a culture is restrictive or permissive, there are likely to be discrepancies in how females versus males are expected to express their sexuality. Cultures vary in how overt this double standard is - in some it is legally inscribed, while in others it is communicated through social convention. Lesbian, gay, bi-sexual and transsexual youth face much discrimination through bullying from those unlike them and may find telling others that they are gay to be a traumatic experience. The range of sexual attitudes that a culture embraces could thus be seen to affect the beliefs, lifestyles, and societal perceptions of its adolescents.

Edit: I think I may have overestimated the problem, due in part to my sources, and in part to my zealousness. Many comments so far have pointed out that even if this was not a system bug, it is still a design flaw - which is exactly what we all expected. However, when the entire company seems to be working on a new version of Windows Phone 7, we were foolish to put our hopes so high for an OS upgrade. The thing with "official" software updates is this; they don't happen fast enough. Microsoft can't afford to take its time fixing bugs or getting things right, as much as it would like to do otherwise. They need to make sure the hardware and operating systems are ready for whatever new features are added down the road. It has been six months since KitKat came out (Android 4.2) and people have gotten used to it being slow, buggy, etc... not only will users expect the same from the next update, but companies are looking forward to it too because of their own marketing campaigns. So why is there such a big deal about WP7? Well, while Android and iOS often receive two major OS versions every year, most other platforms get one or sometimes none at all. And many of us, myself included, want more than just a single update during our lifetimes! We're a technology-obsessed generation who demand newer and better products faster than any demographic ever before. That's where the bigger issue lies here. The reality is that most other platforms see no reason to wait until the last minute to add additional features. Plus, they already know how well the product works; they probably won't change anything unless it actually breaks something important. This means that many developers focus their resources on making the best possible experience rather than having to worry about updating outdated codebases. This brings me to the biggest problem now facing WP7. To handle increased consumer expectations, Microsoft had to develop an OS that could keep up with them. With C and the.NET Framework behind it, it should be able to achieve a good balance between overall performance and security. But once again, this is proving to be extremely difficult given the amount of pressure Microsoft faces these days. For example, the current release of.Net 1.0.1 isn't quite finished yet, and Microsoft used to talk about a more stable build by Spring 2012. Is this really realistic anymore? Do you seriously believe that Microsoft needs Spring 2012 ready to go in October 2011? If Microsoft does decide to push back the release dates of future releases, it will likely cause an uproar among the community. Not only will this upset consumers and programmers alike, but it also puts Microsoft in bad light as a responsible developer. That said, let's look at the positive side of this situation. One of the biggest problems with previous generations of mobile devices was the fact that older phones and tablets couldn't run modern apps. The main reason being that the mobile processor wasn't powerful enough. While doing away with that restriction was a smart move from a business standpoint, that didn't sit well with many customers. Luckily, the upcoming Windows 8 platform promises better technology for Android and iOS. Windows Phone 7, therefore, is going to suffer less from this problem. By switching to ARM processors instead of x86 ones, many hardware manufacturers are finally starting to offer updated phones equipped with Mali GPUs and Qualcomm chipsets. These technologies aren't compatible with old handsets, but they are designed to help OSes perform better regardless of whether they are running the latest app. Perhaps that's why Nokia decided to drop support for Symbian after a few years. In addition to these improvements, the upcoming Windows 8 Operating System will bring a number of new features that will benefit both phone makers and end-users alike. All together then, the two issues above present some interesting challenges for Microsoft. Will it truly improve its development process to produce timely, quality software? Or will it continue to rely solely on Microsoft programming frameworks and antiquated coding techniques? Either way, the prospects are mixed.

A suitable state representation is a fundamental part of the learning process in Reinforcement Learning. In various tasks, the state can either be described by natural language or be natural language itself. It is, however, not straightforward how to find the most useful linguistic features in a sentence. Recently, different methods were proposed to extract linguistic features from natural language, including static ones such as word counts, or more complex ones such as syntactic trees. In this paper, we present an alternative approach where we extract a state representation from natural language based on a topic model. This representation is more compact than the original text and shows how well it is suited as input to a Reinforcement Learning agent. We show that in the case of natural language, a simpler, less interpretable, representation can be a better choice for a Reinforcement Learning agent. A few glaciers have periods of very rapid advancement called surges. These glaciers exhibit normal movement until suddenly they accelerate, then return to their previous state. During these surges, the glacier may reach velocities far greater than normal speed. These surges may be caused by failure of the underlying bedrock, the pooling of meltwater at the base of the glacier - perhaps delivered from a supraglacial lake - or the simple accumulation of mass beyond a critical "tipping point." Temporary rates up to 90 m (300 ft) per day have occurred when increased temperature or overlying pressure caused bottom ice to melt and water to accumulate beneath a glacier.

In the helical thylakoid model, grana consist of a stack of flattened circular granal thylakoids that resemble pancakes. Each granum can contain anywhere from two to a hundred thylakoids, though in some species up to one thousand may be present (Sato and Fujita 1973, Porter et al. 2008. The stromal space between adjacent cells within each single layer is filled with water. The number of layers forming the stacked array has been estimated at approximately 10 for spinach and up to 100 for blue-green algae such as Scenedesmus obliquus (Burba 1991). In order to maintain consistent dimensions throughout their length, arrays have been shown experimentally to adopt an almost uniform profile thickness regardless of individual cell size or chloroplast dimensions (Tigges 2002a). An important feature seen in many photosynthetic organisms when examined by transmission electron microscopy (TEM) is the so-called'mother-daughter' arrangement where a central protuberance known as the 'thylakoid' mother centrum emerge from the center of each large granular membrane called a 'grana lumen'. These membranes are generally attached together via intermediate filaments forming super-wrapped bundles. Two-dimensional images created using TEM reveal how this structure forms (Figure 1): A continuous sheet of stacked lamellae develop through correct folding and interdigitation in both directions; these become entangled on the outer surface which results in the formation of spirals that eventually encompass the entire granum. As additional lamellar sheets fold into place, older ones fall away leaving only those directly underneath them. TEM images do not show exactly what happens during stepwise condensation but would suggest that it involves bending rather than stretching (Porter et al. 2008). A modification of the idea proposed above was suggested by Hueth (1982) based upon the observation made by Bullough (1966), showing close resemblance between chlamydomonas mitochondria and inner mitochondrial membrane sheets. It assumed that if the stalk form of the thylakoid were similar then there should also exist flagellated structures allowing movement along the cytoplasmic face. This suggestion was supported by observations of Lorentz and colleagues who described thin tubular structures termed 'caulonemes' connecting proximal and distal regions of Chlamydomonas blades. Similar structures have since then generated considerable interest due to their similarity to models describing the origin of animal cilia (Dailey 1993, Roos 1995. All chlorophyll-containing eukaryotic organisms possess characteristic plant-specific plastoglobuli distributed randomly over all areas of the organelle including whole frond cross-sections and even inside light-harvesting complexes (LHCs) (reviewed by Chen and Specht 2016). All LHCs observed under fluorescence microscope showed radially arranged particles located around starch grains and ribosomes (Figure 2). This pattern appears different from bacterial systems based on reports suggesting that they lack ordered particle distribution along the periphery of red edge emitting phycobilisomes (Roosen-Jansen 1987). Chloroplast Development Many physiological properties seem to change dramatically after fertilization because of changes in gene expression. Such events include re-programming of metabolism and increase in respiration rate associated with oxygen production. However, most developmental processes occur either before or immediately after mating while the embryo is still enclosed in maternal envelope. During early embryogenesis, genes involved in primary metabolic pathways seem to be down regulated. Their transcripts begin accumulating in late zygotesearly embryos in correlation with major accumulation of carbohydrates and storage proteins. For example, nitrate reductase activity increases during early development whereas rates of glutamine synthetase, argininosuccinate synthase and ATP-synthesis decrease accompanied by increased levels of mRNA encoding enzymes controlling nitrogen assimilation (Moller 1992). Protein synthesis decreases markedly before the onset of embryogeny (Bessman 1990). During the first few hours following fertilisation, transcript abundance of several Calvin cycle-related enzymes shows drastic reduction followed by rapid recovery of enzyme activities indicating activation of alternative carbon fixation routes (Keller et al. 2010). Throughout its life span, plants constantly experience environmental changes affecting cellular homeostasis. To survive harsh conditions, plants need mechanisms enabling adaptation to new environments andor repair damaged macromolecules as well as maintaining normal intracellular ion concentrations, pH value and turgor pressure (Hanson 2012). Changes in stress response repertoire vary considerably depending on particular organism ranging from active sensing of signals triggering immediate responses until adaptive acclimation leading to long-term modifications of growth habits. Since physiological reactions occurring during stressful periods cause permanent damage to DNA, RNA, protein biosynthesis machinery, ionic balance and osmotolerance, any attempt to understand genetic control of stresses must take into account pleiotropic effects caused by mutations causing stress-responsive phenotypes. Although some general principles could be applied across kingdoms, among other reasons, regulation of transcriptional networks differs substantially in chloroplast genomes of cyanobacteria and land plants. Despite numerous attempts efforts to identify transcription factors involved in regulating key steps of chloroplast biogenesis, no specific regulators with homology to commonly accepted TF families have so far been identified. The Border Patrol serves solerightly as a law enforcement body responsible for upholding U.S. legislation within its borders. Conversely, the Coast Guard functions dually as both a policing organization and possesses an extended range of responsibilities, including activities conducted beyond national boundaries. It holds legal authorization to participate in and assist military actions unlike civilian-based agencies such as the Border Patrol. Legally speaking, this stems from Title 14 Section 1 of the United States Code which designates the Coast Guard as a component of the nation's military framework. Logically, as one of the country's five military divisions, the Coast Guard operates under the Navy's command during wartime. However, unlike the other branches, it falls under the Department of Homeland Security rather than the Department of Defense. Federal statutes and guidelines grant the Coast Guard authority over federal and global maritime territories, allowing them exclusive power in enforcing these regulations. On the other hand, the Border Patrol, though housed within the Department of Homeland Security, has a unique function centered around implementing customs and immigration policies alongside additional duties. In summary, while the Coast Guard can align with naval operations in times of conflict, it primarily concentrates on its designated tasks such as search and rescue, maritime law enforcement, and navigational assistance. Meanwhile, the Border Patrol lacks the legal capacity to collaborate militarily.

As we fly off I once again try to count the nicks on his scythe, but it's impossible to keep score. The little lines are like a pointillist painting, nearly impossible to discern because they all blend in together to make a much bigger picture. The scratches from an endless voyage through time and space. The slightest jostle from his bony elbows and I lose my place. He breaks the perfect silence. It has been millions of cycles since someone made it this long. Deadpan though Death can be, I can tell he's impressed. "I can't imagine why. There's so much to see every time!" I feel almost giddy at the prospect of a whole new universe about to be born, like a present waiting to be unwrapped. I've lived through over two universes now, and have lived so much, even eons of waiting fly by as I relive all the unique experiences I've encountered. Your love of life will be the Death of you, one day. "Hold on," I exclaim, "When we began this bet you told me your spare cloak would make me immortal!" Yes, even through the rebirth of the universe itself. But eventually you will tire of this life. They all do. And I will reclaim my cloak and usher your soul out of this realm. "I'm not even close to tapping out yet!" I say, smirking at his confidence. We arrive at where it will all begin again. He turns to me as I get off the scooter. Your enthusiasm still astounds me. I grin, then wave as the new universe explodes into being, sending me careening away through space to a new unknown destination. The next adventure awaits. Jaded? Death thinks, Maybe. But not tired. He looks at the churning universe around him, and scratches a new mark onto his ancient weapon. Maybe this time, when I show up..... I'll be riding a couch. He grins to himself. Or a mermaid. The military (and military personnel) have another set of laws that they have to follow in addition to all the regular laws. This set of laws is called the Uniform Code of Military Justice (UCMJ). One of the most serious crimes is called an Article 120 offense, which is a sexual offense. If you are found guilty of a sexual offense under the UCMJ, you may lose all your benefits, be separated from the military dishonorably, and be sentenced to prison. For military members, a sexual assault is defined as: An intentional touching, not through the clothing, of the genitalia, anus, groin, breast, inner thigh, or buttocks of another person with an intent to abuse, humiliate, or degrade any person An intentional and unlawful sexual act with another person by force or threat of force A sexual act against another person's will by threatening or placing the person in fear that any person will be subjected to death, grievous bodily harm, or kidnapping An act of rape An act of aggravated sexual contact An act of abusive sexual contact An act of sexual harassment If you are facing an Article 120 offense, you need an experienced attorney who can help you fight the charges and who can help you get the best possible outcome for your case. Charges of Article 120 Offenses If you are charged with an Article 120 offense, you may have to face charges for the sexual offense itself as well as charges for "compelling another person to commit a sexual act." When you are charged with "compelling another person to commit a sexual act," you are being charged with using your superior rank or authority to coerce or manipulate another person to commit a sexual act. You may also be charged with "consent of the victim" if you are accused of committing a sexual act and the prosecutor claims that the victim consented. To be guilty of this offense, the prosecutor must prove that the victim consented under force, threat, or fear. Article 120 Offenses: Defenses There are two possible defenses to an Article 120 offense: consent or mistake of fact. To use consent as a defense, you would have to prove that the sexual act was consensual. To use mistake of fact, you would have to prove that you did not know that the act was not consensual, or you did not know that the victim did not consent to the act. This article presents essential techniques for handling network data and introduces a user-friendly visual data manipulation tool called Origraph, facilitating the application of these methods without extensive coding knowledge. Important functions include generating networks from sources like tables, modifying networks by adding new elements, refining networks by removing specific components, and calculating additional characteristics. Origraph simplifies executing these tasks while providing immediate visual feedback. It offers different perspectives, including examining the overall network structure, viewing samples, and exploring attributes. Furthermore, we propose specialized interfaces to assist users in selecting appropriate parameters for effective network manipulation. To showcase its practicality, we present two case studies using Origraph; one investigates gender disparities in Hollywood, and the other examines how financial interests affect political backing for military involvement in Yemen.

We study the problem of Robust Outlier Arm Identification (ROAI), where the goal is to identify arms whose expected rewards deviate substantially from the majority, by adaptively sampling from their reward distributions. We compute the outlier threshold using the median and median absolute deviation of the expected rewards. This is a robust choice for the threshold compared to using the mean and standard deviation, since it can identify outlier arms even in the presence of extreme outlier values. Our setting is different from existing pure exploration problems where the threshold is pre-specified as a given value or rank. This is useful in applications where the goal is to identify the set of promising items but the cardinality of this set is unknown, such as finding promising drugs for a new disease or identifying items favored by a population. We propose two -PAC algorithms for ROAI, which includes the first UCB-style algorithm for outlier detection, and derive upper bounds on their sample complexity. We also prove a matching, up to logarithmic factors, worst case lower bound for the problem, indicating that our upper bounds are generally unimprovable. Experimental results show that our algorithms are both robust and about 5 x sample efficient compared to state-of-the-art.

The day before I took the test my family threw a huge party. We lived in a nice neighborhood in the 130 district, and life had been pretty good. My friends from school were there, friends of my parents and everyone was looking forward to me staying pretty close by. Everyone within a score of 3 points up or down lived within driving distance and since the airports were only for government officials from 200 and visas for anywhere of more than 5 points were expensive, they were all hoping that life I'd lived would mean I wouldn't be far. I had had a good life, school was pretty normal from what I could gather from stories my grandfather had told. He had lived before the tests came in and said that in this neighborhood hadn't really changed since then. I was excited but had grown weary of the chirpiness of everyone I met. I figured life wasn't meant to be like this and it all seemed fake. On the day of the test there was only 3 other people there but we had to sit in silence until the test took place. I watched the first girl go into the machine and saw her smile while the doors closed. It seemed to be over pretty quickly and the doors opened again, I was surprised there was no one in there now so the other girl went in. Smiled at me again while the doors closed. Why was she smiling at me? She probably wouldn't see me again. "Ugh" I thought to myself and the idea of being near these people started to really get my back up. The doors opened and I was ushered in by some unknown force, I just got up and in the machine. The door closed and the last guy was still sitting there. I forced a smile at him as the doors closed and he actually waved! What the hell was that I thought. Then the voice hit me like a tonne of bricks falling in and around my head. At first there was just hints of language then suddenly it started talking clearly to me. "I can see your entire essence young man" "You can? What does it look like?" "Look like? A life lived in lies! A life of fakery and betrayal!" "Betrayal? What?! I've not betrayed anyone!" "Every single person who was genuine in their feelings towards you and you scorn each and every single one with a mirror of those feelings rather than how you actually feel!" "Well yeah, I mean, everyone was chirpy all the time it felt completely fake, how could they act like that all the time? It exhausted me every...." I was cut off at that last one "I know and I have a place for you. You're not violent in your acts but the evil of disdaining everyone around you has sent you further..." Then everything is back to normal, my head no longer feels like a closed vice trying to keep squeezing and I can tastes orange. I exit out the other side of the machine a little unsteady and start walking down the corridor. I keep walking past other corridors leading off of this one until I get a door, I walk through it and to my amazement I am stood to the side of an airplane. I am ushered to move quickly up the steps and into the plane. There's nobody else there and as I am shown to a seat I am handed a pill and a cup of water by the attendant. We'll get you up when you get there he says as I swallow the pill and his face melts into black and I am out cold.

I wake up in a bed of grass and leaves. Hard roots discomfort the left side of my right arm and the bottom of the back of my head. My feet hurt, my legs itch, my chest is bare. I am a man. I feel that I am a man. My eyes are closed. I open them. White light fills my vision. It fades into a clouded ceiling of branches and more leaves and rays of sunshine peeking in between them. I feel hair on the sides of my cheeks. I have hair, a lot of hair. And a full beard. It is scruffy and hot. I am sweating. The grass pricks my bare skin. I press my palms down onto the ground. A stick pokes my left hand. I wince. I look to the left. A tree. A tree is behind me. I am laying underneath it, feeding like one of its many roots. I sit up and scoot back, scratching my right leg on another stick in the process. The bark is course but steady. I have created a makeshift seat. I look down. My legs are bare too. I am wholly bare save for a protective layer of cloth covering my midsection. I wiggle my toes. Everything works, prim and proper. My vision completely clears, no foggy peripherals, and I start to hear. Bugs, insects, crickets. They chirp all around me. It is an equally beautiful and intolerable sound. A pain shoots through the back of my head and the top of my nose. It pulses. I have a headache, a migraine, an even more intolerable migraine. I close my eyes in pain. I hear more. The whistle of the wind, the shuffle of the trees, the chirps of the birds. I hear everything around me. My migraine subsides. I open my eyes again. I see more trees. To the left and to the right, as far as my vision takes me. I am in a forest. I see no movement. No animals, no dramatic shifts of light. I see the changing of the light from the ever-swaying tops of the trees, but no movement on the ground. I am alone. I carefully stand up, bracing my weight on the side of the trunk as I shuffle my sensitive feet closer and closer to its large base. I am stiff. My muscles ache. I stretch my arms in an effort to relief some of their discomfort. It works. I do the same for my legs, repeating the process after thirty seconds. I am now limber, ready to take on the world. But what is the world? I do not know. I do not know anything. I am alone, alone in a forest in a place I do not know, wholly bare save for a protective layer of cloth covering my midsection. This is no way to be. I am a man, I feel it. And I live in the world. I do not know what the world is, whatever the world means, or what kind of a man I am, whatever that means. I do not know my name, where I'm from, who I'm from, or whatever kind of place they live in. I do not know who I love. I do not know who I hate. I just do not know. Something whistles in from behind my head and goes screaming past me, landing several feet in front of the tree. It startles me. I look at what it is. A stick. Someone threw a stick at me. Someone else is here. I am not alone. I hear footsteps running towards my general direction. They get closer, louder. I look to my right, the side of the tree where the stick came from. A person comes running across my field of vision. A smaller person. A boy. He is like a little me. He wears the same fabric as me. He has the same hair as me. Long, brown. He has the same skin as me. He turns around. He has the same face as me, or what I imagine my face would look like. He looks at me. He picks up the stick and we look at each other. " Father? " he says in a language I do not understand. We continue to look at each other. He stares into my eyes, heavily. He walks toward me. I stay against the tree, confused by his actions and worried about my safety. He stands beneath me, looking at my face. " You are not my father. " He taps me in my side with his stick. It was not painful. I look at him curiously. " Who are you? " he says, still in a language I do not understand. I move my hand to touch his cheek. I poke him. He is warm, fleshy. He is a little version of me. " I do not know, " I say in a language I do not understand. He smiles. " Well, I do not know either. " He pauses. " But you are funny. Here, come with me. " He walks off. I take a step away from the tree. It is slightly... sad. This place is all I have ever known. This tree, this house that I have awoken to, is all I have to my name. But I have no name. It is a perplexing feeling. The boy has not stopped to allow me to contemplate my existence. He has scurried off. I am forced to say goodbye. " Goodbye, " I whisper. I take step after step away from this place. I walk. He walks in front of me. I walk faster to catch up to him. We settle into a steady rhythm. My feet hurt from the leaves and sticks we walk over, each bump in our invisible path causing a pinpoint of discomfort in my course but sensitive heels. He turns back to look at me. A smile is plastered across his tiny face. I smile back at him. It is funny, the way I feel about him. We have no relation. I have just met him. But the warmth that resonates between us, the warmth that keeps me on this track behind him, is special. More special than the warmth I felt from the tree. He begins laughing and picks up speed. He starts to run. I am still walking. The distance between us grows. He is leaving my field of vision. I decide to start running too. It is fun. Despite the inconvenient pains from the terrain beneath my feet, I am having fun. I run faster, catching up to the little me. He laughs some more. I laugh too. We continue this way for several hundred yards. The trees start to get thinner. The sticks and rocks disappear. We run into a field, a grassy field. The terrain gets steeper. My legs are starting to get tired. "Where are we running?" I say loudly. I still do not know what I speak, but I speak it. He does not answer. He keeps running. I realize that we are running on a hill. He slows down to a stop at the top. I slow down too, and walk carefully up behind him. "This is home," he says. I look across the landscape. It is so beautiful. The hill we are standing on is the largest I can see. Beyond it lies a sea of grass and trees and a small river running across the middle. There are houses, people, living there. In between the trees and the smaller hills, straddling the river on its far side, is a village. Other people are there, living like me. I must meet them. I must see who they are. "Come," the boy says. This is a project I canned a long time ago. It was pretty inspired by Rip Van Winkle, which is why I posted it here after making a couple changes. I stopped writing it because I lost the taste for the first personpresent tense and the weird simple language to complicated thought transition. It freaked me out reading this guy's basic, basic mind. For real though, it's just freaky.

Using concise sentences efficiently conveys information in natural language. Nevertheless, texts made entirely of brief sentences can seem dull and mechanical. Conversely, longer sentences require substantial mental exertion to understand. Research into sentence length variations across a vast collection of renowned literary works reveals that an engaging balance lies midway, featuring a mix of different-length sentences arranged in a patterned manner. This balance exhibits a consistent mathematical relationship in its structure, similar to patterns found in music or brain activity. Most examined texts display these intricate qualities, particularly those resembling stream-of-consciousness narratives which showcase complex multi-layered patterns known as multifractals. The presence of full stops plays a significant part in creating connections within the text; their occurrence affects the flow of ideas throughout the work. Full stops also follow a specific frequency pattern when viewed as individual elements. On the other hand, common words do not influence these patterns as much, and removing them eliminates any irregularity observed in the text's structure.

Advertising drugs on television is not suitable due to the complexity involved, making it challenging for consumers to make educated decisions based solely on commercials. Unlike tangible goods such as cars or paper towels, whose features can be easily explained through advertisements, medications cannot be effectively promoted by comparing their ingredients to competitors'. Instead, drug ads often depict happy individuals alongside numerous severe side effects. 

While some products may utilize misleading imagery unrelated to their function, prescription medications carry greater risks when bought impulsively, unlike less significant purchases like chewing gum or appliances. Since physicians ultimately decide whether to recommend these treatments, questioning the necessity of direct-to-consumer advertising becomes relevant. Perhaps providing medical professionals with promotional materials would suffice. Moreover, the idea that consumers could choose between options based on preference doesn't apply here; non-medical experts aren't equipped to determine superior medications. Additionally, people generally don't experiment with various medications to find a preferred option. In conclusion, I believe pharmaceutical commercials primarily serve as a means for corporations to promote their products for financial gain, rather than focusing on patient outcomes. The legality of such advertisements reflects concerning priorities within the healthcare industry, where profits take precedence over individual wellbeing. Change My View (CMV)! Our research focuses on examining the difficulty level associated with two specific issues related to graphs. The first issue involves identifying the biggest possible subgraph within a given graph G where each vertex has an odd degree; this subgraph is termed as an "odd subgraph." The second problem requires determining the minimum count of such odd subgraphs needed to cover all vertices of G. These aspects are denoted by the variables mos(G) and odd(G), respectively.

Through our investigation, we have established that evaluating whether odd(G) equals q can be resolved through polynomial-time computations when q is less than or equal to 2. However, the process becomes NP-hard when q exceeds 2. To address these challenges, we've developed algorithms capable of computing mos(G) and verifying odd(G) = q with complexities expressed as O(n^O(rw)) and O(q*n^O(rw)), respectively, specifically designed for graphs comprising n vertices and possessing rank-width no greater than rw. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that the reliance on rank-width remains optimally stringent even considering the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH). In addition, we present several precise upper and lower bounds for these measures based on particular types of graphs or their connection to different parameters.
