Video moment retrieval is to search the moment that is most relevant to the given natural language query. Existing methods are mostly trained in a fully-supervised setting, which requires the full annotations of temporal boundary for each query. However, manually labeling the annotations is actually time-consuming and expensive. In this paper, we propose a novel weakly-supervised moment retrieval framework requiring only coarse video-level annotations for training. Specifically, we devise a proposal generation module that aggregates the context information to generate and score all candidate proposals in one single pass. We then devise an algorithm that considers both exploitation and exploration to select top-K proposals. Next, we build a semantic completion module to measure the semantic similarity between the selected proposals and query, compute reward and provide feedbacks to the proposal generation module for scoring refinement. Experiments on the ActivityCaptions and Charades-STA demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.

Text-to-image synthesis aims to automatically generate images according to text descriptions given by users, which is a highly challenging task. The main issues of text-to-image synthesis lie in two gaps: the heterogeneous and homogeneous gaps. The heterogeneous gap is between the high-level concepts of text descriptions and the pixel-level contents of images, while the homogeneous gap exists between synthetic image distributions and real image distributions. For addressing these problems, we exploit the excellent capability of generic discriminative models (e.g. VGG19), which can guide the training process of a new generative model on multiple levels to bridge the two gaps. The high-level representations can teach the generative model to extract necessary visual information from text descriptions, which can bridge the heterogeneous gap . The mid-level and low-level representations can lead it to learn structures and details of images respectively, which relieves the homogeneous gap . Therefore, we propose Symmetrical Distillation Networks (SDN) composed of a source discriminative model as "teacher" and a target generative model as "student." The target generative model has a symmetrical structure with the source discriminative model, in order to transfer hierarchical knowledge accessibly. Moreover, we decompose the training process into two stages with different distillation paradigms for promoting the performance of the target generative model. Experiments on two widely-used datasets are conducted to verify the effectiveness of our proposed SDN.

I can remember everything about her. Her face, the length of her average laugh, her shoe size, what clothes she wore, what movies she liked, how I used to kiss the back of her hand and how much she loved it, but none of my memories compare to her. As a person. As a real life, human being. Someone I could hold and kiss and tell stories to. Someone I would die for. I looked everywhere for her. First place I checked was her work because that's where she was when shit hit the fan, but that's not where she stayed. I tried calling her, but she didn't pick up. I asked everyone I could, I put up fliers, I fired flares into the sky, but nothing. I haven't stopped looking for her, but I'm out of ideas, so now I just kind of wander around the city, looking for anything that might bring me to her. I've been searching for her so long, it's taken its toll. My eyes are sunken, I can barely feel my heart beat and the soles of my feet are worn out because they never leave the ground when I walk. Call it a bad habit. The apocalypse forces you into a lot of those. It also forces you to get focused. Normally I was focused on her and how much I was still in love with her, but at this particular moment, my attention was drawn to something else. A noise. Far off. Down the road. It grew louder. I hadn't heard a noise like that in months. Soon, a car came swerving around the corner and rocketed down the street. Not a sedan, or a minivan, but a mish-mash of random metal bits with four, rouge wheels sticking out of the bottom. It roared down the asphalt, coming towards me. This started to agitate the crowd. Oh yeah, the crowd. They're the one's responsible for ending the world in the first place and they've gotten a lot of hostility these days for that, but they're not to be hated. They're just searching for something too. We all are. We just couldn't tell you what it was. And holy fuck there was a lot of them. Like a parade times twelve of them, they clogged up the road like a fur-ball clogs your shower drain. The car tried to drive straight through them, but was diverted almost immediately into a street pole. Whoever was driving must not have been paying much attention. The door flew open, knocking some of the crowd onto their feet and the old, familiar sound of a shotgun blast reverberated around the corridor that was the street. A man jumped out, a real action hero looking guy complete with scars, bandanna and a sneer. And from the passenger side rose the most beautiful girl I've ever seen in my life. It was her. With her perfectly straight hair, freckled cheeks and high-powered assault rifle, it was her! It had to be! The woman I'd been searching for since I could remember. What was she doing with this bandanna-wearing jerk? My legs were moving before I could even put a thought together, slapping against the pavement as I sprinted for her. I had so many questions. "Get to the alley! Go!" The action hero roared, signaling my sweetheart to retreat into the alleyway behind them, but I couldn't let her get away. I tried yelling to get her attention, but my mind just wouldn't put words together. I was overwhelmed by desire. I needed her. The crowd was making it difficult to maneuver and I know it's not dignified, but I had to start climbing on people just to give chase. My foot on someone's head, hand clutching a collar, until finally I climbed over the tsunami of bodies and fell, face first into the alleyway. Picking myself up wasn't difficult, it almost felt automatic and once I was on my feet, I saw her. Her gorgeous figure hoisting herself up a fire escape. I knew she was scared, but I also knew that if I could just talk to her, I could make this all make sense. A group of five people made it to the fire escape before me and had the beefcake on his ass before he could say a word. Grateful as I was, he wasn't a concern of mine. Instead, I leaped at the fire escape and pulled myself up, booking it to the roof like the Flash. With each step, I had a new idea of what I should say, but I didn't settle on anything. Nothing was good enough. It's a good thing my muscles were still forcing me up the stairs, otherwise I might have just frozen there in shock or nervousness. I reached the roof and there she was, standing at the other end, wind blowing her hair around, hands wrapped around her gun. When I appeared, she spun in place and took aim. Then she stopped. The barrel of her gun lowered to the ground. Even at this distance, I could see her eyes swell with tears. "Oh my god," she whimpered. I tried to smile. I think it worked. At least it felt like it did. Still no words though. This is exactly what I was afraid of. "Michael?" She had a hard time saying that name. It was my name. She's said it before a hundred times. I wonder why it was hard for her. I had just started noticing that I was standing completely still. This was odd because usually I'd be in constant motion. It felt like a struggle to keep myself in one place, like I was fighting my own desire, but for some reason, I knew it was the right thing to do. Until I just couldn't take it anymore. I wanted her. I wanted her so bad, and my body did too, so it took charge. We bolted at her, arms outstretched, I just wanted to hold her again. She raised her gun and threw a bullet into my shoulder. The shot knocked me to the ground. It didn't hurt, it just confused me. Why did she want to kill me? I haven't seen her so long! God damnit, if only I could find the right words..... Another gunshot went off. I looked up just as she pulled the trigger for a third time. Then a fourth. Behind me, I could hear the pattering feet slap against the concrete. The crowd was on their way. They were going to ruin everything. And they did. She lowered her gun again, her whole body deflated, then she looked into my eyes one last time before stepping up onto the edge of the building and throwing herself off. If I could have screamed, I would, but I couldn't. Instead, I just started running. Straight towards the edge of the building, chasing the girl I'd been chasing since as long as I could remember. Then I jumped. Half of me wished I wouldn't survive the fall. The other half knew I would. I remember him. Michael. His short crop of brown hair and his heart bigger than the universe. I knew he loved me, but I never knew how much. He was no Austin Leblanc who taught me how to use a gun, modify a car and generally survive. Look how well that turned out. I woke up. That's a weird thing to say after you've just tried to kill yourself, but I did. I woke up lying on the sidewalk, feeling less than okay, but I wasn't in pain. I sat bolt upright thinking I was dead. This couldn't be death. It looked exactly like life. In fact, this was the same city street I thought I died on. Was this death? I wanted to use words, but I couldn't. I tried, but it just didn't happen. Besides that, the only other feeling I could focus on, truly, was the burning desire I had to see Michael again. I couldn't tell you why, but I knew Michael was out there somewhere and something inside of me just wanted to see him again, to tell him I'm sorry. I felt something on my hand and looked at it. There was Michael, on his knees, his lips pressed against the back of my hand. When he removed them, he left a bite mark. He stared at me and I stared at him. Without any words we read each other's minds. Yes, he still loved me. Yes, I still loved him. Yes, we were both unimaginably hungry.

This paper presents a novel neural network design that learns the heuristic for Large Neighborhood Search (LNS). LNS consists of a destroy operator and a repair operator that specify a way to carry out the neighborhood search to solve the Combinatorial Optimization problems. The proposed approach in this paper applies a Hierarchical Recurrent Graph Convolutional Network (HRGCN) as a LNS heuristic, namely Dynamic Partial Removal, with the advantage of adaptive destruction and the potential to search across a large scale, as well as the context-awareness in both spatial and temporal perspective. This model is generalized as an efficient heuristic approach to different combinatorial optimization problems, especially to the problems with relatively tight constraints. We apply this model to vehicle routing problem (VRP) in this paper as an example. The experimental results show that this approach outperforms the traditional LNS heuristics on the same problem as well. The source code is available at .

Researchers from Facebook AI have created a model for robotic locomotion that adapts in real-time to any terrain it encounters. Rapid Motor Adaptation was developed from the idea that humans can move efficiently in different types of terrain without any real training or practice. The new model allows the robot to learn how to move in a variety of terrains, such as hard, slippery and soft surfaces. "For example, if a robot is trying to navigate a slippery hill, it's relatively easy for it to learn how to navigate that particular hill," said Joelle Pineau, Head of Facebook AI Research. "But, it's very hard to generalize that to other hills it hasn't seen before. That's where Rapid Adaptation comes in. It generalizes to a range of different slippery hills, without being exposed to each one individually." According to my recollection, equilibrium is detected through the presence of fluid in the inner ear. As you revolve in circles, this fluid begins to rotate as well, similar to a whirlpool effect; once you cease spinning, the fluid remains in motion. Consequently, even though you've halted your movement, there still exists an illusion of continued rotation. Balance is managed by minute hair strands within the inner ear, surrounded by liquid. It's the interaction between the fluid's motion and these tiny hairs that allows us to perceive acceleration. While spinning, the fluid experiences constant acceleration, and upon abruptly stopping, one may experience the impression of the surroundings rotating in the reverse direction due to the deceleration of the fluid. 

Alternative explanations fall short of being entirely accurate. Indeed, there are fluid-filled cavities in the inner ear; nevertheless, the fluid itself does not directly induce vertigo, albeit its role is supportive. Nevertheless, our equilibrium depends on calcium carbonate crystals situated within these fluid compartments. These crystals connect with sensory hair cells present in the related structures. They enable us to identify the position of our heads, particularly identifying 'downward.' During rapid spins, the force generated causes the calcium carbonate particles to redistribute across the chamber walls instead of remaining concentrated at their base. This results in mixed signals sent to our brain about our body's alignment, creating discordant visual inputs and ultimately leading to feelings of disorientation or dizziness.

In essence, Occam's razor is a philosophical guideline suggesting that among multiple potential solutions for a problem, the simplest one tends to be the most accurate. This notion originated from a 14th-century English monk called William of Ockham. For instance, imagine arriving home to find garbage strewn across the floor. A complex scenario might involve a burglar using treats to distract your pet, committing petty theft, tidying up, accidentally discarding the loot, realizing their mistake, tearing up the trash again, but failing to recover the object before escaping. Alternatively, your own dog could have simply torn open the trash bin due to enticing odors. The less complicated explanation usually prevails. However, please note that my illustration represents a fanciful speculation, often referred to as an ad hoc hypothesis, which contradicts the very purpose of Occam's razor - promoting simplicity rather than complexity. In scientific circles, Occam's razor advises favoring the straightforward theory devoid of unnecessary intricacies or dependencies. Essentially, it suggests opting for the less elaborate hypothesis amongst equally plausible alternatives. Although it does not guarantee accuracy based soleright on simplicity alone, it serves as a valuable tool during theoretical comparisons by endorsing the option with minimal presumptions. Originating from a British philosopher, Occam's razor has gained widespread acceptance, particularly within psychology, where researchers employ it to develop grounded theories while reducing unwarranted assumptions and basing conclusions on empirical evidence."

The problem of mesh matching is addressed in this work. For a given n -sided planar region bounded by one loop of n polylines we are selecting optimal quadrilateral mesh of the region using multilevel quadrilateral mesh. We generate a mesh by inserting a few vertices at each level. The mesh obtained at each level is used to refine the mesh at next level. We establish the relation between the number of vertices of the boundary of the region and the mesh size at each level of the multilevel mesh. Our experimental results show that the method proposed gives a very good approximation to the optimal quadrilateral mesh for a given planar region. The term "Seattle" is documented on official records from the Washington Territory as early as May 23, 1853, marking the filing of initial village plans. By 1855, some form of land claims had been made. Subsequently, on January 14, 1865, the legislative body of Territorial Washington officially formed the Town of Seattle, which was governed by a group of trustees. However, this township was dissolved on January 18, 1867, reverting back to just another district within King County. It wasn't until the end of 1869 that a fresh request was submitted, leading to the reestablishment of Seattle as a city on December 2, 1869, now under a Mayor-Council system of governance. Interestingly, the emblem representing the City of Seattle bears the year "1869" along with an image depicting Chief Sealth from a side view.

Like most things to do with wine, it's a fiddly sort of thing that isn't easy to pin down exactly. What it boils down to is finding flavours that work well together, and that's a matter of taste. It's not difficult to imagine the problem: your seafood main course is looking fantastic, but it's hard to find a wine that won't overwhelm it. The same goes for steak: you want to pick something that will hold its own against the meat, but you don't want it to be too heavy. Fortunately, there are plenty of white wines that will suit the task. Sauvignon Blanc is a good bet - especially if you're serving a zippy white fish such as scallops. It's one of the few whites that can be eaten with a creamy sauce. Chardonnay is another good bet. It's one of the most versatile white grapes, and can go from unoaked to fully oaked. It's also quite refreshing, and you should be able to find a bottle that's not too expensive. It's pretty difficult to go wrong with a New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc, or a Chablis. They're two of the best whites in the world. But that's only half the story: it's just as important to find a red that will work with the food. In the past, this could have been a challenge, but fortunately there's been a revolution in the way wines are made, especially in New World countries such as Australia and New Zealand. Most modern wines will work well with food. The most important thing to remember is that a wine doesn't necessarily have to match the meat. A light red wine will work equally well with pork, beef or lamb. It's also worth knowing that the strongest-tasting red wines, such as Cabernet Sauvignon, are often the best for pairing with food, especially red meat. Merlot is another good choice - it's a much softer and more approachable style of wine than Cabernet Sauvignon. So with all that in mind, here are five of the best wines for serving with steak, lamb, chicken and pork. New Zealand is one of the best places to look for a red wine to go with lamb - and this bottle from Hawkes Bay is the perfect example. It's not too heavy, but it's full of juicy, ripe flavours. It's a blend of Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon, and is just the right style for lamb. The smooth tannins make it an excellent match for the meat. This one from Argentina is an outstanding value for money, and it's a great wine for pairing with steak. It's a Malbec, which is one of the country's most popular grapes. The tannins in this wine are a little too strong for eating on their own, but with food they work brilliantly. It's an exceptionally well-made wine, with lots of dark, ripe fruit. This one from Chile is another Malbec that is bound to go down a treat with steak. This wine has a little more finesse than the Argentinian bottle, with less of the power and more of the fruit. The tannins in the wine aren't as strong, but they still work well with the meat. It's a wine with a smooth finish, and plenty of character. This Australian red wine is another of the country's great reds. It's made from Shiraz, and is a good example of the style. It has a smooth, silky texture that makes it perfect for eating with lamb, and it's full of juicy, spicy flavours. This is a very good wine that's reasonably easy to find. And finally, for the meat-lovers, here's an Italian red wine that's bound to work well with a steak. It's a Barolo, made from the Nebbiolo grape, and is one of the best wines in Italy. There's no better way to end a meal than with a Barolo, and this one is an exceptional example of the style. It's a wine that will work well with a steak, but it's also one of those wines that can age for decades. It's a real investment, and one you won't regret.

Advertising is a primary means for revenue generation for millions of websites and smartphone apps. Naturally, a fraction abuse ad networks to systematically defraud advertisers of their money. Modern defences have matured to overcome some forms of click fraud but measurement studies have reported that a third of clicks supplied by ad networks could be clickspam. Our work develops novel inference techniques which can isolate click fraud attacks using their fundamental properties. We propose two defences, mimicry and bait-click , which provide clickspam detection with substantially improved results over current approaches. Mimicry leverages the observation that organic clickfraud involves the reuse of legitimate click traffic, and thus isolates clickspam by detecting patterns of click reuse within ad network clickstreams. The bait-click defence leverages the vantage point of an ad network to inject a pattern of bait clicks into a user's device. Any organic clickspam generated involving the bait clicks will be subsequently recognisable by the ad network. Our experiments show that the mimicry defence detects around 81 of fake clicks in stealthy (low rate) attacks, with a false-positive rate of 110 per hundred thousand clicks. Similarly, the bait-click defence enables further improvements in detection, with rates of 95 and a reduction in false-positive rates of between 0 and 30 clicks per million - a substantial improvement over current approaches.

My argument is mainly based on the arguments used for maintaining the status of the British royal family, but I think it applies to any country. I've heard many arguments for continuing the practice, from tourism money to engaging in charitable causes and diplomacy to preservation of cultural memory, but I just don't see any of those things as compelling arguments. Tourism will likely not be very affected since the things people come to see (palaces, crown jewels, etc) will still be around even if the royals have been stripped of their status. Their 'celebrity' influence can still remain without acknowledging that they are born with some kind of intrinsic merit that is greater than ordinary citizens. To me, royals traditionally taking on the role of a diplomat or cultural ambassador is not as worthwhile as someone attaining that role through merit and effort and ability. As far as keeping this tradition because it is part of a cultural legacy: that point makes the least sense to me. There are many cultural practices that are considered oppressive or at least unsavory to modern sensibilities. Why preserve relics of a time in history when people were at the whim of powerful, autocratic rulers who believed they had a mandate from God? This has no place in the modern world. The status and state-sanctioned privilege of any royal family sends a message to the non-royals about how the government perceives its own people, namely that they are not all equal in the eyes of the state. I think that stripping royalty of their status, not their possessions, would be a very powerful, symbolic statement that affirms the belief that all citizens are all born equal in both status and potential. I don't think that would be a waste of the time or money it would cost to implement. I should caveat that I'm talking about these terms as applied to humans not plants, nonhuman animals, or electronic devices. And by "socially-sanctioned," I mean a definition broadly acceptable to all parties, not just a narrowly-construed legal definition. The core of the problem is that there are many ways to categorize people, and few of them are universally accepted. As an extreme example, we could use hair color to divide people into two categories: those with red hair, and those without red hair. This would work fine for most of us, but it's going to cause problems when you try to apply it to albinos or bald people. We could try to come up with a better system, one which accounts for albinos and bald people. But then we run into the issue that there are other ways to categorize people, each with their own advantages and disadvantages. Gender is a particularly thorny case. Is a person born with a penis male? Well, sort of. Is a person born with a vagina female? Well, sort of. What about someone born with both a penis and a vagina? What about someone born with neither? What about people who change their genitals through surgery? What about people who identify as a gender which doesn't correspond to the sex they were assigned at birth? And so on. The point is that there is no "correct" way to categorize people, because there is no property of people that is universally recognized and universally agreed as a good basis for dividing people into categories. There is no single "true definition" of sex or gender. So we end up categorizing people in arbitrary ways, and then arguing over what those categories mean. It's a mess. And then there's race. Here's where things get really messy. First, let's start with the fact that race isn't real. That is, there is no meaningful scientific basis for dividing people into racial categories. The concept of "race" is a socially constructed one, not a biologically meaningful one. Second, let's consider the fact that different cultures have different ideas about what races exist. For example, in the United States we traditionally divide people into four racial categories: White, Black, Asian, and HispanicLatino. But in Brazil, people are divided into five categories: White, Pardo (mixed race), Black, Asian, and Amerindian. In South Africa, people are divided into three categories: Black, Colored, and White. Third, let's consider the fact that people often self-identify as belonging to multiple racial categories. In the United States, this is typically expressed as "multiracial." But in Brazil, people self-identify as "Pardo" even if they only have one ancestor who was Pardo. Fourth, let's consider the fact that the boundaries between racial categories are often fuzzy and contested. For example, in the United States, there has been a long-standing debate over whether Jews should be considered a separate race or not. In Brazil, there has been a long-standing debate over whether Japanese Brazilians should be considered a separate race or not. All of this leads to a lot of confusion and disagreement over what "race" means. And it gets even more complicated when you try to apply it to nonhuman animals or electronic devices. So, to answer your question: There is no single, universally accepted definition of "race," "sex," or "gender." These terms are used in different ways by different cultures, and there is no single, universally agreed upon way to categorize people.

Classifying breast cancer poses difficulties because of similarities within classes and differences between them. Current approaches using deep learning create complicated mappings but often rely on global characteristics derived from whole images, overlooking the importance of minute details for identifying distinctive traits. Our research introduces an innovative framework called Attention Model Enhanced Network (AMEN), designed as a multi-path structure incorporating both a pixel-level attention mechanism and a categorization submodular component. The AMEN's feature extraction segment produces a detailed attention map at the pixel level, whereas the classification submodules use it to sort the samples accordingly. Additionally, our approach emphasizes fine details through enhancement of the input image via the previously created attention map. We also apply a strengthening technique to merge outcomes from diverse pathways, thereby improuming overall effectiveness. Testing on multiple standard datasets has shown our method surpasses others across different conditions.

House music is a genre of electronic dance music that originated in Chicago in the early 1980s. It was initially popularized in Chicago, circa 1984. House music quickly spread to other American cities such as Detroit, New York City, and Newark - all of which developed their own regional scenes. In the mid-to-late 1980s, house music became popular in Europe as well as major cities in South America, and Australia. Early house music commercial success in Europe saw songs such as "Pump Up The Volume" by MARRS (1987), "House Nation" by House Master Boyz and the Rude Boy of House (1987), "Theme from S'Express" by S'Express (1988) and "Doctorin' the House" by Coldcut (1988) in the pop charts. Since the early to mid-1990s, house music has been infused in mainstream pop and dance music worldwide.

There exists a passageway called the Eustachsin tube that links the interior of your ear with your nasal cavity. This tube serves to eliminate surplus liquid and balance the pressure within the ear. Under normal circumstances, this tube remains shut tightly. However, actions such as swallowing, yawning, or stretching can momentarily open the tube, enabling pressure equilibrium. For instance, during flights, when one experiences ear popping due to altitude-induced pressure changes, swallowing or chewing gum may alleviate discomfort. Typically, external sounds reach our ears via air vibrations impacting the eardrum. Yet, when the tube is open, additional sounds entering through the nose can interfere with regular auditory perception and affect eardrum movements. Consequently, discerning surrounding noises becomes challenging. Nonetheless, internal sounds like one's own speech or respiration remain unaffected since they directly transmit vibrations through bones to the inner ear, resulting in amplified hearing compared to usual conditions. It's likely that this phenomenon involves specific muscle activity.

While theoretically possible, humans solving complex problems at the same rate as quantum computers isn't feasible due to their vastly superior speed. A quantum machine could potentially resolve intricate issues within seconds, whereas humans might require thousands of years for the same task. Nonetheless, computers, including quantum ones, rely on preprogrammed algorithms created by individuals. Their potential lies in processing inputs swiftly and analyzing massive datasets that may remain unexplored by humans.

Quantum computers excel in addressing highly specialized tasks rather than general computing challenges. They aren't expected to replace traditional computers in terms of speed for everyday computations. Take integer factorization as an illustration. Determining two extremely large prime factors from their product poses an immense challenge for both humans and conventional computers, possibly taking longer than the age of the universe. Yet, quantum machines could achieve results in mere minutes.

However, only a limited number of significant problems exist wherein quantum computers hold an advantage over classical counterparts. Problem-solving can broadly fall under four algorithmic categories – P, NP, NP-Complete, and NP-Hard. Presently, digital devices tackle P problems efficiently, though increased computational power sometimes becomes necessary to handle more complicated instances. Overall, quantum computers offer unique capabilities but primarily target niche applications.

The transition of an athlete from being 'naturally talented' in a sport to becoming 'capable of winning an Olympic medal' often hinges on the supporting sports infrastructure and backing provided to semi-professional athletes. Countries like the US, China, and Russia invest billions of dollars into ensuring that youth have access to top-notch training and organized activities, which is not prioritized similarly in India, resulting in fewer medals. For instance, despite excelling in field hockey until 1972, India struggles to secure medals after the switch to artificial turf in 1976 due to lack of funding for equipment. Additionally, two main factors contribute to this issue - limited financial support for budding athletes' training and the absence of sports like cricket in the Olympics. Furthermore, Indian society tends to undervalue sports and focus more on academia, leading to untapped potential among naturally gifted individuals. Lastly, as a developing nation ranking low in terms of per capita income, creating world-class athletes demands significant resources. Moreover, there isn't a strong cultural inclination towards Olympic sports or sports overall, unlike in some other nations.

New remote sensing sensors now acquire high spatial and spectral Satellite Image Time Series (SITS) of the world. These series of images are a key component of classification systems that aim at obtaining up-to-date and accurate land cover maps of the Earth's surfaces. More specifically, the combination of the temporal, spectral and spatial resolutions of new SITS makes possible to monitor vegetation dynamics. Although traditional classification algorithms, such as Random Forest (RF), have been successfully applied for SITS classification, these algorithms do not make the most of the temporal domain. Conversely, some approaches that take into account the temporal dimension have recently been tested, especially Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs). This paper proposes an exhaustive study of another deep learning approaches, namely Temporal Convolutional Neural Networks (TempCNNs) where convolutions are applied in the temporal dimension. The goal is to quantitatively and qualitatively evaluate the contribution of TempCNNs for SITS classification. This paper proposes a set of experiments performed on one million time series extracted from 46 Formosat-2 images. The experimental results show that TempCNNs are more accurate than RF and RNNs, that are the current state of the art for SITS classification. We also highlight some differences with results obtained in computer vision, e.g. about pooling layers. Moreover, we provide some general guidelines on the network architecture, common regularization mechanisms, and hyper-parameter values such as batch size. Finally, we assess the visual quality of the land cover maps produced by TempCNNs.

We show that it can be suboptimal for Bayesian decision-making agents employing social learning to use correct prior probabilities as their initial beliefs. We consider sequential Bayesian binary hypothesis testing where each individual agent makes a binary decision based on an initial belief, a private signal, and the decisions of all earlier-acting agents - with the actions of precedent agents causing updates of the initial belief. Each agent acts to minimize Bayes risk, with all agents sharing the same Bayes costs for Type I (false alarm) and Type II (missed detection) errors. The effect of the set of initial beliefs on the decision-making performance of the last agent is studied. The last agent makes the best decision when the initial beliefs are inaccurate. When the private signals are described by Gaussian likelihoods, the optimal initial beliefs are not haphazard but rather follow a systematic pattern: the earlier-acting agents should act as if the prior probability is larger than it is in reality when the true prior probability is small, and vice versa. We interpret this as being open minded toward the unlikely hypothesis. The early-acting agents face a trade-off between making a correct decision and being maximally informative to the later-acting agents.

In recent years, deep learning has made tremendous progress in a number of fields that were previously out of reach for artificial intelligence. The successes in these problems has led to deep neural networks being used across many disciplines such as speech recognition (deep voice), computer vision and natural language processing[b1b2]. However, the biggest limitation currently is that deep network architectures require large amount of computational resources; it also takes substantial time to train them because they are not only data-hungry but also prone to overfitting due to their high connectivity among neurons in various layers[b3]. These factors have seen major roadblocks faced by researchers working on complex biological tasks, which typically involve training datasets with more than 105 examples[b4] or even larger ones found in some areas like genomics[b5], miRNA prediction[b6], liver disease diagnosis[b7], brain disease study and protein mutation detection[b8]. To address this challenge, an unprecedented level of parallelism enabled through GPUs has been harnessed successfully. For example, using GPU accelerated machine learning techniques for genetic association mapping analysis can speed up the process of associating variants with diseases by more than 50 times compared to CPU implementation[b9]. Recently, we reported our work towards accelerating deep learning via distributed computing through Spark framework[b10]. In particular, our approach demonstrated promising results in terms of scaling up deep learning models from hundreds to thousands of nodes surprisingly fast without sacrificing accuracy. Building such scalable deep learning frameworks requires incorporating novel algorithms, new execution models, efficient use of memory management etc., all together while keeping track of several challenges inherent to hardware infrastructure. We present here ScaDeepNet: Scalable Deep Learning Framework built upon top of Hadoop MapReduce architecture for handling massive volumes of genomic information. We introduce two key elements a Spark based shuffle operator named HDDT (Hierarchical Data Distribution Tree) and its associated algorithm called HIERDISC (HIerarchical Discretization scheme for clustering). Our experimental studies show that when applied to highly skewed data distribution patterns within input dataset, HDDT can significantly improve performance of both supervised and unsupervised classification models under different computation budgets. Moreover, our findings suggest that with appropriate tuning parameters, HDDT can be effectively employed to accelerate other forms of hierarchical structure including neighbor search, kNNkMapper, nearest neighbors graph construction etc. Therefore, building scalable deep learning framework may become possible through exploiting HDDT's ability to distribute workloads between clusters in addition to providing support for realtime workload generation. As the first attempt at designing a hybrid model for global genome scale bioinformatics problem, we believe that this new tool will enable research communities dealing with huge amounts of genomic data to adopt new approaches much faster. Results Background Motivation Over a decade ago, there was no doubt about the success story of parallel programming paradigm introduced by GPGPUgraphical processing unitbased systems. This technology allowed scientists to perform strong acceleration on complex computations, leading to breakthrough discoveries in molecular biology research[b11]. While GPU based solutions continue to enjoy popularity today, the major drawback of such platforms is that they primarily target single task applications, i.e. each vertex represents specific optimization criteria defined during application design phase and any change in the underlying code would result in rework of entire program. In contrast, traditional multi-threading paradigms allow users flexibility to modify individual threads of programs independently, but lack scalability; hence, requiring considerable effort to construct software environment capable of supporting such complexities. With advances in modern computing technologies, programmers now focus on creating specialized libraries dedicated mainly to preparing and transferring data into main memory to make better utilization of available compute power thereby improving overall system efficiency[b12]. Free movement of goods within the European Union is achieved by a customs union, and the principle of non-discrimination. The EU manages imports from non-member states, duties between member states as well as non-pricing barriers on trade (such as licensing requirements). However, it can only regulate tariffs applied to imported products in order for free movement to take place. The Treaty Establishing the European Community has laid down that more restrictions may be imposed if there are reasons such as security or national economic interests. According to WTO law: "All tariff rates shall be eliminated through liberalization of all markets except those designated solely for safeguard purposes. All non-tariff measures must also lose their protectionist features if they do not meet specific conditions set out under Article XX." (WTO Agreement) In addition, WTO agreements require governments to: "Avoid by any means whatsoever discrimination among countries which have agreed to abide by these rules... [and] eliminate discriminatory policies affecting international trade.... If one country adopts any restrictive measure regardless of whether this measure was justified; then other members will no longer adhere to the previous agreement. This serves to prevent further distortions of competition at world level." (WTO Agreement) Based on these legal provisions, import taxes should compete with cross-border prices without additional fees or charges -in particular when they disproportionately affect small producers andor impoverish consumers over large regions like Europe. It seems obvious that similar tax schemes would not be allowed, given the strict geographic scope as highlighted above. Criminal law deals with wrongs against society the social order. It can get you sent to jail or forced to pay fines to the state. Civil law is when you wrong somebody else and they deserve to be compensated. There's no jail time involved any restitution goes directly to the victim. Many things have both a criminal and a civil element. Let's say there's a car accident. The civil law side of things has the at-fault party pay for repairs to the victim's car. If it's just a random accident, there's no criminal charges involved however, if there's excessive speeding, drunk driving, etc, there can be an additional criminal aspect of it on top of the civil issue.,In addition to other comments there is a difference of burden of proof in the two. In the United States, civil courts use a lower standard of "preponderance of evidence," while criminal courts use a higher standard of "beyond a reasonable doubt" when deciding a case.','Philosophically, criminal law is the idea that you have harmed all of society and the full weight of society itself is punishing you. Civil actions are private disputes between two people which the court system (the state society) will judge over using the law. Technically, a civil action could potentially involve questions of society as a whole but the dispute itself is not considered a harm against all of society. This is usually because of the scale and severity of the conduct. For example, if there is a consumer fraud claim (a company defrauds you), that does affect society as a whole in the sense that if there are a lot of companies defrauding consumers, then society as a whole is affected. However, if it's one isolated instance, we don't consider that criminal and it's a civil wrong (against one person). There are things which are both civil and criminal. For example, if that company defrauded every customer, then you could sue them and the state could bring a criminal action against them (if the state has passed a relevant law saying it would be criminal for companies to engage in a pattern of consumer fraud). So, I guess the line between criminal and civil (philosophically) is a question of gravity and what we as a society consider to be Bad Things. For example, take homosexuality being legal or not. If a state passed a law allowing you to have gay sex, it's not like gay people suddenly become "good people" when they were "bad people" prior to the law changing. But we as a society have changed and determined having gay sex isn't a Bad Thing that we should punish. (N.B. I just chose this example because it's a nice bright line example. No political statement is being made here.) Practically speaking, civil lawsuits result in money damages. Very rarely, a court may grant other things, such as injunctions or specific performance (forcing someone to do a specific thing). But money is the baseline consequence. In a criminal suit, there could be money damages (fines), but the main power of a criminal suit is the threat of imprisonment, beating (where corporal punishment is allowed), death (where capital punishment is allowed), and a loss of civil liberties (public humiliation). Loss of civil liberties includes things like not being able to vote, registering as a sex offender, having a criminal record (the adult version of a "permanent record, and a loss of standing in society. The punishments are much more severe because it's not one person punishing you, it's every person punishing you. (As an aside, it also relates to the fact that only the state has a monopoly on violence, and therefore is the only entity authorized to do those punishments against you.) Procedurally, a civil lawsuit begins when one person decides someone has wronged them and hires his own attorney to sue the other person. In America, each person bears the cost of hiring their own attorney; in other countries, the winner pays for both attorneys. Either way, the attorneys are paid privately between the two parties. In a criminal suit, the state brings the suit through its prosecutors. The prosecutors are attorneys with special powers who are paid by the taxpayers. No individual person pays to prosecute (sue) an alleged criminal and, most importantly, no individual person gets to decide if they are prosecuted. Put another way: if you are murdered, you (obviously) don't get to decide if your murderer should be punished or not, but neither does your family. Society itself (the state) will automatically punish him, and no one can stop it because the conduct that occurred is so appalling that it's not up to individual people to decide whether to punish (sue) them or not. Different places have different names for prosecutors, but their names are usually something like district attorney, county attorney, city attorney, city counsel, United States attorney, state's attorney, or the crown prosecutor. You'll notice that the official title for a prosecutor usually is related to the government. This is reflected in the case name of the lawsuit as well. A civil suit would be called John Smith v. Joe Blogg. A criminal suit is called the United States v. John Smith, the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania v. John Smith, or the Crown v. Joe Blogg. This is another reflection that it's all of society punishing one person.

Most generative models of audio directly generate samples in one of two domains: time or frequency. While sufficient to express any signal, these representations are inefficient, as they do not map well between the real world (i.e., temporal responses) and mathematical space (i.e., frequencies). To address this problem, L2S has introduced a generic domain-specific representation called the Classic Model which maps both the temporal and frequency information into a single vector representing an audio signal that is free from some aliasing artifacts at the boundaries between multiple spectral components across the signal spectrum. The Classical Model can be seen as a generalization of the regularized harmonic regression technique described by Coyle et al [1]. These authors present a variety of examples illustrating how their approach provides additional precision and detail over traditional linear methods, including near-infinite types of spectral envelopes, noise suppression approaches, nonlinear analysis techniques such as multidimensional Fourier transforms, harmonics-based filters, etc. The most important difference between classical modeling algorithms like those presented above and "generic" ones proposed herein lies in they require close synchronization with an actual sound source - in contrast to our methodology where we access pre-existing data sets when designing model parameters and feedback control loops for continuous monitoring. Given recent technological advances in computer memory capacity, it may soon become feasible to store hundreds or thousands of input signals without significant bandwidth consumption; however, there currently exists no practical way to retrieveprocess them quickly enough for use in practice. It would thus be highly advantageous if more powerful spectral estimation methodologies could be developed using already available large amounts of audio inputs in order to achieve faster convergence times while retaining robustness and accuracy features essential to good performance in real-time applications. This would make L2S's tools even more attractive to researchers working on acoustic systems design and optimization problems involving complex parametric functions, since the time saved implementing new models will allow for improved refinement at finer levels while still performing computationally efficiently.

Search engine users rarely express an information need using the same query, and small differences in queries can lead to very different result sets. These user query variations have been exploited in past TREC CORE tracks to contribute diverse, highly-effective runs in offline evaluation campaigns with the goal of producing reusable test collections. In this paper, we document the query fusion runs submitted to the first and second round of TREC COVID, using ten queries per topic created by the first author. In our analysis, we focus primarily on the effects of having our second priority run omitted from the judgment pool. This run is of particular interest, as it surfaced a number of relevant documents that were not judged until later rounds of the task. If the additional judgments were included in the first round, the performance of this run increased by 35 rank positions when using RBP 0.5 , highlighting the importance of judgment depth and coverage in assessment tasks.

Forecasting stock market direction is always an amazing but challenging problem in finance. Although many popular shallow computational methods (such as Backpropagation Network and Support Vector Machine) have extensively been used to analyze the market behavior, accurate forecasts are still elusive. This book presents a new approach that utilizes the recently demonstrated success of artificial intelligence techniques for stock price prediction. First, it shows how large scale random walk statistics can be used to construct a probabilistic model with appropriate weights to predict the future price of any given security, then it demonstrates its performance on a simulated trading system based upon the same random walk distribution framework as previously discussed. Finally, results from empirical studies and simulations are discussed and examined.

As a biologist, let me explain: Your muscles require significant amounts of energy. They obtain this energy via a molecule known as ATP (Adenosine Triphosphate), which acts as the primary source of power within cells. Energy extraction occurs when one phosphate group is removed from the molecule, transforming ATP into ADP (Adenosine Diphosphate). While ADP holds less potential energy due to having only two phosphate groups, its conversion back into ATP is crucial for sustained muscle function. This process involves cellular respiration, whereby additional nutrients are utilized to restore ADP levels. Creatine enters this scenario by storing unused phosphates during periods of rest. During high-intensity activities, such as weightlifting, these stored phosphates can then be transferred from creatine to ADP, regenerating ATP and extending short bursts of performance. However, the benefits provided by creatine typically last for roughly 2-10 seconds, potentially enabling individuals to accomplish an additional repetition or two before exhaustion sets in.

Your body is really just a bunch of tiny molecular machines and building blocks (like lego bricks) that either hold things in place, create tiny structures, change molecules into other molecules, make large molecules by stringing small molecules together, or do a whole range of other things. But none of these machines can think and act for themselves - they need to be 'activated' by something. Sometimes that something is heat, sometimes it is electricity, and sometimes it is when it 'sees' and 'locks on' to another molecule that it recognises. Think about if you are blindfolded, then someone puts something in your hands, your hands close around the object and feel out what it is. If you recognise it as, say, an apple, by the weight of it, the shape of it and the texture of it, the nerves in your hands send a signal to your brain that says "APPLE." Biosensors are just like your hands but they are (mostly) designed to only recognise one particular type of object. They can interact with lots of objects, but only when they encounter a particular one, will they send out a signal that says 'I found my object'. We use that ability of these tiny, very specific, 'biosensing' machines that nature has created, to send us signals when they encounter the things we are looking for. The signal can be either a mechanical (pushing or pulling) force, a flash of light (photon), an electrical signal (electron), or change in mass (because they held onto something, just like you gain the mass of an apple when you hold one), or one of many other even more strange signals!

Conducting a safety risk assessment is crucial in creating a reliable Cyber-Physical System (CPS). While traditional risk assessments consider solely physical breakdowns, contemporary CPS face increasing threats due to cyber attacks. Current research efforts aim at merging safety and security throughout their lifecycles while also broadening the scope of formal models used in risk evaluation to account for security breaches. However, the effects of this interplay on overall system design and how disregarding security failures could result in decreased reliability have been largely unexplored. In response to these gaps, we introduce a novel safety planning technique called Cyber Layer Of Protection Analysis (CLOPA), which augments the established LOPA structure with potential cyber attack-induced faults. Our suggested strategy presents a precise mathematical representation illustrating the compromise involved in crafting either a supremely trustworthy or exceptionally secure CPS. Additionally, we suggest a combined life cycle procedure that synergizes safety and security hazard evaluations. To gauge our CLOPA concept and the integrated life cycle's effectiveness, we apply them to a realistic scenario involving a process reactor managed through an industrial control simulator. A comparative analysis against conventional LOPA risk appraisal methods is also provided.

Feature selection (FS) is now crucial when addressing intricate pattern recognition issues characterized by a vast array of features. Herein, we introduce a novel wrapper-based FS technique utilizing binary simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation (BSPSA), which operates through iterative enhancements starting from an initial feature set towards achieving the ideal one. During these cycles, each component within the existing feature vector undergoes concurrent adjustments via randomly determined deviations derived from a specific probability distribution. Through extensive computational trials involving various datasets featuring hundreds to several thousand attributes, we employed popular classifiers - namely nearest neighbor, decision tree, and linear support vector machines - to evaluate our proposed strategy. Comparisons were drawn between our method and exhaustive feature usage, alongside a binary genetic algorithm and traditional FS techniques, measuring effectiveness through cross-validation accuracy rates and AUC metrics. The findings reveal that BSPSA outperforms conventional approaches across most scenarios, especially excelling in handling enormous datasets comprising countless features while scrutinizing only a minuscule portion of potential solutions. To our knowledge, there exists no comparable wrapper FS process capable of efficiently managing such voluminous data collections with robust converging characteristics. Key terms include: Classification, feature selection, stochastic approximation, genetic algorithm.

Abstract: We present a novel classification approach based on multiple stacked features for the purpose of object detection. This technique utilizes stacked images captured from different cameras equipped with filters or lenses to achieve high resolution. The proposed method combines multi-view stereo depth information of two cameras along with edge orientation data extracted from individual views. As a result, our system extracts both 3D point clouds and 2D human body silhouette contours from each image. A person can then be detected automatically by matching the contour map of their head shape in a particular view with the corresponding feature maps from other views. Compared to existing systems, our approach achieves significantly higher accuracy, especially in low light conditions due to its inherent parallelism. We also provide experimental results comparing the performance of our method with those of the conventional convolutional neural network and depth from defocus methods. In this talk I will describe how deep learning has been used to train generative models for the generation of realistic facial expressions. Specifically, Three-Body Generation (3BG), a popular generative model for producing faces, was applied using Deep Neural Networks (DL) trained on a dataset consisting of 678 videos. DL worked well to generate synthetic faces but did not have enough power to fully capture subtle nuances of the real thing. To address these problems, we specifically designed the training process so that the DNNs were built up over time from subsets of short preprocessed frames while keeping track of every pixel in the video. While doing this, we provided feedback allowing the DNNs to self-learn complex relationships between certain parameters like skin color and expression type. At the end of the training cycle, 300 new faces were generated from 12 million video samples. With this face generator, users could create any kind of facial configuration imaginable - from simple smiles and smirks to full blown smiling or crying expressions. Abstract: With the recent advances in computer vision technology, computer scientists have struggled with creating robust automated solutions for a wide variety of tasks. For example, many action recognition tasks such as tracking humans' gestures fail despite achieving good accuracy in laboratory settings [1], [2]. One reason for these failures may stem from poorly designed rule networks or biased decision rules. Rule networks consist of predefined concept representations and associated decision rules that define what actions to take given each input. Although useful tools, they suffer from several limitations including being unable to generalize to unseen examples, resulting in false positives; requiring enormous amounts of training data to improve performance; and having poor runtime efficiency, i.e., computation costs increase exponentially with the number of inputs. Decision trees are similar to rule networks in terms of structure and decisions made, except instead of defining concepts, they specify output probabilities for each possible outcome. However, unlike rule networks, decision tree structures do not scale well to large datasets because of the resource requirements involved in generating trial distributions for every branch and node of the tree. Recently, Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) techniques have shown promise in addressing these drawbacks. GANs consist of two layers of agents, called generator and discriminator, working together to solve a mathematical optimization problem. Each agent attempts to learn a digital representation of the solution space (i.e., an abstract probability distribution) that maximizes a reward function. By alternating between training and testing sequences, both agents gradually converge towards a global optimum. Given enough training data and iterations, GANs appear to be able to produce convincing images and videos [37]. Therefore, they offer the potential to revolutionize computer vision research and stand poised to become key components of future AI applications. Advances in hardware capabilities and democratization of GPU computing via cloud infrastructure make practical implementation of GANs easier than ever before. In this presentation, the team behind the newly released Google Visual Recognition library will discuss our experiences building a suite of image processing functions leveraging GANs and share preliminary insights into the benefits and challenges encountered during this project. Finally, the team plans to demonstrate some of the promising combined visual and pattern recognition use cases emerging from these experiments.

Debtor person who owes money. Creditor person who claims money. Bankruptcy is a legal process where the government protects a debtor from his overwhelming debts. The whole point is to protect debtors from being thrown on the street. Bankruptcy is VERY different by country, but the US is an example of a generally debtor-friendly country. In the United States, bankruptcy is a federal law the [US Bankruptcy Code] (URL0). It's about 500 pages long in most printings, and most of the text makes no sense unless studied with care. For normal persons, bankruptcy comes in two flavors: Chapter 7 and Chapter 13. The law now favors putting debtors into Chapter 13 high-income debtors are required to use it. Under Chapter 13, the court puts you on a payment plan. You get a court-ordered budget, and have to pay your debts according to the plan. If you fall off the plan, the court may switch over to Chapter 7. Chapter 7 is the traditional bankruptcy method. The court piles up all your assets, counts up all your debts, and sells things to pay your debts. After that, the creditors are done they can't go after the debtor any more. Even better for the debtor, there's a list of exempt property that the creditors can't touch no matter what. This lets you keep your near-worthless but sentimental personal property, your basic means of transportation, and possibly your house (depends, oddly enough, on your state the Bankruptcy Code borrows state law). A bankruptcy is definitely a black mark on a credit rating, but it isn't forever. Credit ratings are done by private companies, so they choose what they think predicts a person's credit risk. Mostly, bankruptcy falls off their radar screen after about 5 years. Corporations aren't treated sympathetically. They can go through Chapter 7, but basically it kills the company. Everything gets sold off, the company ceases to exist. Much more common is the special Chapter 11. This is "Reorganization" the idea is that the company was mismanaged or hit tough times, but it can be turned around. There's a complex process for planning this turn-around, but the gist of it is the shareholders get wiped out (their stock certificates turn into monopoly money) and the creditors take over as the new owners. Municipalities and other sub-units of states are treated separately, under their own special Chapter 9 of the Bankruptcy Code. We can't kill a city, and we can't hand the keys to the city over to the creditors, so it's kind of like Chapter 13 in its spirit it puts the city on a payment plan, which will eventually pay off the debts. States can't go bankrupt. The US states have virtually unlimited taxing power, so their solution to high debt is to raise taxes. A state can default on its debt by not repaying it when it's due. Usually what happens is the state will do an emergency shutdown of non-essential agencies to save money, and get back to paying its bills on time. Countries can't go bankrupt either. What court would control them? Countries basically can do whatever they want. Countries don't invade each other on behalf of banks (at least, not since the 1920s, when it used to happen occasionally). Instead the real discipline is that lenders won't lend to your country anymore, and the national economy will basically shut down. The bad part is, lenders start doing this before your country defaults see Greece.', "So I'm a bit late to the game on this, but wanted to add on to uPLJVYF's explanation a bit. I'm going to focus on US personal bankruptcy here, as I'm most familiar with Chapter 7 and 13 cases. I'll leave all the theorycraft on Detroit's Chapter 9 to the uber thread of doom. Source: I've worked in default services for over 6 years. One of the most important bankruptcy concepts that's similar through all Chapters is something called the automatic stay - it's used in the same context as "stay of execution." Once the bankruptcy petition is filed, a stay goes into place as to all of your creditors preventing any collection activity from that point forward. This applies to all collection methods - with the automatic stay in place, a creditor can't call, write, e-mail, foreclose on your house or even send a carrier pigeon to try to collect on the debt. There are ways for a creditor to get around that, but that's maybe another comment if there's interest. Chapter 7 At a very basic level, uPLJVYF is pretty close to the mark on Chapter 7 cases. However, it's a little more complicated than this. In Chapter 7 cases, the court appoints a trustee whose role is to administer the bankruptcy estate. The estate is, simply put, all of your assets - car, house, checking account, 401k - everything. That's not to say the trustee writes checks and pays your bills. Their primary role is to determine if there are assets that can be distributed to creditors and then make that happen as needed. Trustees get some percentage cut of all assets administered as well, which is how they pay themselves, their staff, etc. So, back to the trustee - in a Chapter 7, the trustee looks over all of the documentation you're required to file and basically compares assets to liabilities. As uPLJVYF mentioned, there are exemptions you can take which will protect most assets for the average middle class person on down (ie: you are just below your state's median income level). Exemptions used appropriately, for example, will protect your 401k in its entirety, potentially your home, cash on hand and various other things. This scenario is typically referred to as a no asset case. Anything above that, however, is fair game for the trustee to sell for the benefit of your creditors - an asset case. If you've filed bankruptcy and own 3 BMWs free and clear, for example, you're likely to own only 1 by the end of the case. Typically, this results in a very small return to unsecured creditors (credit cards, medical bills and the like); if an unsecured creditor gets more than 25, they're doing amazingly well. Once a Chapter 7 discharge is entered, all of your unsecured debt is wiped clean. Secured debt is a different story and again, I'll leave that for another comment if there's feedback because it gets a bit wibbly wobbly. For the average person with no appreciable assets, a Chapter 7 case only lasts 6-8 months. The individual files, attends a meeting of creditors which is normally attended only by the trustee, who asks a few confirmatory questions about information already in the bankruptcy petition and a couple months later, the discharge is entered and the case is closed. If there are assets, the process can take significantly longer, but typically not more than 2-3 years. Chapter 13 Fundamentally, the documentation required for a Chapter 13 is similar to Chapter 7, with a couple important additions. First, the Chapter 13 plan is a summary of how all outstanding pre-petition (outstanding at the time BK was filed) debt will be paid over a 3-5 year period. For example, let's say a debtor is significantly behind on a mortgage and at the time of filing, owes 6,000. Over a 60-month plan, they will pay 100month plus some amount of attorney fees plus some percentage to the trustee. For easy math, assume this is 125.00month. This means that monthly, the debtor will pay their regular mortgage payment plus any normal household expenses, plus 125 to the bankruptcy trustee. This sounds kind of bad until you remember that during the case, normal household expenses would exclude any amount due to an unsecured creditor (ie: credit cards). A Chapter 13 trustee is quite different from those in Chapter 7 cases. In a 7, the trustee administers the estate. In a 13, the trustee's role is more like an accountant. They take in plan payments from the debtor (the 125month mentioned above) then divide it up and make monthly disbursements to the creditors who should be getting them. In order to receive disbursement from the trustee, all creditors (including unsecured) must file a proof of claim. The proof of claim provides identifying information about the debt such as what type of debt, who the creditor is, amounts owed, any arrears (typically missed payments, but any outstanding amount beyond the unpaid principal) and such. Secured debt generally must have backup attached to the claim - taking the form of loan documents such as a mortgage and promissory note. If everything goes well, the debtor will make all of their plan payments on time for 5 years and at the end of it, receive a discharge which, like in a Chapter 7 case, wipes out all unsecured debt. Because the trustee is also an officer of the court, they have some oversight responsibilities in a Chapter 13 case as well - if the debtor fails to make payments as scheduled, the trustee may file a motion to dismiss the case. If the case is dismissed, it's as if it never happened for all intents and purposes. Any debts owed remain in place and creditors can resume normal collection activity. I'll freely admit there are a lot of little nuances here that I'm leaving out; it's mostly because bankruptcy can get awfully complicated awfully quickly when things don't go perfectly. If you have more specific questions about any part of the process, feel free to ask and I'll answer as best I can. Edit: Formatting.

In this scenario, it's essential to consider the meaning of "observe." While we may presume that the minimal energy contained within light cannot significantly modify an object's behavior on a larger scale (e.g., the sun's location doesn't greatly affect a baseball's path), this notion does not hold true at the atomic level. A solitary photon has enough power to change a molecule's state. Consequently, observing objects at such a tiny scale inherently involves interaction. Photons, magnetic fields, and other particles passing near the subject of observation will all influence the observed entity. Thus, at the quantum level, observation and interaction become indistinguishable.

Furthermore, measuring any quantity necessitates interacting with the system being measured. Taking a bathwater's temperature reading using a thermometer, for instance, results in slight fluctuations due to the thermometer's own temperature. God maths was the worst, especially first thing on a Monday. I laid my head on the desk and huffed. "Jason," Dave hissed, knocking my leg suddenly, "Sir's looking at you." I sat up quickly and looked over to where a glowering Mr. Johnson stood, arms folded against his crisp shirt. He looked angry enough to beat me with the metal ruler that was clenched so tightly in his fist, it may well have cut into his hands. "Do I really need to dish out a supervised study session this early in the day, Mr. Woodward?" he spat, brandishing the ruler in my direction. "Um, no Sir," I mumbled, "I'm sorry." Mr Johnson inhaled sharply, pushing his thickly rimmed glasses back up his beak-like nose. Dave sniggered once Sir had turned his back, and only stopped when I elbowed him, hard. He let out a yelp that caused Mr Johnson to whip around and furrow his brow, eyeing us warily. He sighed deeply and resumed writing out the quadratic equation we were meant to be working on. Dave grabbed my arm and yanked my sleeves up, giving me the worst chinese burn I'd ever received. I let out a silent scream as he twisted the life out of my wrist. But then as suddenly as it had happened, the pain stopped. "What's that," Dave whispered, his face a pale grey. He jabbed at my stinging arm, where there was a black smudge. "Ink I guess," I replied behind my hand, licking my finger to wipe it off. Except it didn't come off. Dave's chair fell to floor with a loud clatter. He was barely stood, shaking terribly and staring at my arm with apparent terror. The class turned to stare as Dave ran into the hall, the door slamming behind him. My classmates began to talk amongst themselves, to Sir's frustration, glancing every so often at me and the empty seat next to me. Eyes fell upon the mark on my arm. I tugged my sleeve down and kept my arm off the table for the rest of the lesson. When the bell finally rang, I practically ran to Dave and I's usual break spot. My arm felt like it was burning. That mark. It resembled the letter v, with a small loop where the two lines met. I'd seen it before. Little kids often showed each other their birth tattoos, so I had seen Dave's when we met on the first day of Middle School. He told me the v stood for his name, and then cried when I pointed out that for his birth tattoo to stand for his name, he'd have to be called Vave, or the tattoo would have to look more like a d. I thought it was a bit silly to cry over that, but I felt bad and gave him the chocolate bar my mum had packed in my lunch. We'd been friends since. I didn't expect Dave to be in our spot when I got there, but he was. He didn't look up until I sat next to him on the wall. "Are you ok?" I asked. When he didn't answer, I nudged him. He leapt off the wall and glared at me. "Don't touch me!" he snapped. He rubbed his ankle with his foot. "That's my birth tattoo on your arm." "I know, but it's not real. It can't be. It's probably just permanent marker or something," I reasoned, "maybe someone did it for a joke." "Maybe," he mumbled, but took a small step backwards. I frowned at the movement. Did he actually think it was real? "It's not real," I hissed, "it can't be, because I'd have had to have killed you already for your mark to appear." "Not necessarily." "Look, come with me, I'll try and wash it off with soap and you'll see. I bet someone drew it on earlier or something." As the words came out my mouth, I realised there wasn't any time for someone to have drawn it on without me noticing. Dave knew that too, because a look of anger overcame him. He charged at me, knocking me backwards off the wall. I landed heavily on my back, and lay there winded as he walked around to stand by my head. "It's real. It's real and you know it," he shouted furiously, raising his foot above my head. I rolled over just before his foot made contact with the concrete. "Dave," I wheezed, struggling to my feet, holding my hands out in front of me, "I wouldn't hurt you, I wouldn't do that." But he wouldn't listen. He came at me his fist raised above his head, and I did what I needed to do. I shoved him hard, sending him staggering backwards, hitting his head hard on the corner of the brick wall as he fell. A trickle of red turned to a lake. If only he had listened.

Sociologist Jake Rosenfield of the University of Washington asserts that the decline of organized labor in the United States has played a more significant role in expanding the income gap than previously realized. Rosenfield, a professor in the College of Arts and Sciences, believes the Great Recession, which began in December 2007, and subsequent wage stagnation are worsening this long-term trend, as evidenced by a 2016 analysis of income tax returns by the Congressional Budget Office. The CBO study found that the share of total income earned by the bottom 20 percent of U.S. households fell from about 5 percent in 1979 to 3.5 percent in 2014. The consequences of this trend are far-reaching, with implications for social mobility, inequality and economic growth, according to Rosenfield. "Economic growth has slowed, and the economy is more dependent on consumption and household borrowing," said Rosenfield. "This has worsened the inequality problem because most households are dependent on low-paying jobs and borrowing to make ends meet." The percentage of the workforce that belongs to labor unions has dropped dramatically from 20 percent in 1979 to 11 percent in 2015. "Between 1979 and 2007, the number of union members grew by about 20 percent," said Rosenfield. "But then, in the early years of the Great Recession, the number of union members fell by nearly 20 percent." At the same time, employers have become more aggressive in managing labor costs, including by suppressing wages, outsourcing work, eliminating benefits and refusing to bargain with unions. These trends have contributed to the rise in the income share of the top 1 percent and the bottom 50 percent of the U.S. population, Rosenfield said. The top 1 percent's income share rose from 12.4 percent in 1979 to 21.2 percent in 2015. The bottom 50 percent's share dropped from 15.5 percent to 13.4 percent over the same period. The impact of these trends on economic growth is less clear, Rosenfield said. A study by economist Mark Cullen, professor of economics and political science at the University of Minnesota, found that declines in labor union membership are associated with slower economic growth. A study by economist Lawrence Katz, a professor of economics at Harvard University, found that the decline of organized labor may be responsible for as much as 10 percent of the income gap between high-wage and low-wage workers. "In 1979, the income share of the bottom 50 percent of workers was 15.5 percent and the income share of the top 1 percent was 12.4 percent," said Rosenfield. "In 2015, the income share of the bottom 50 percent of workers was 13.4 percent and the income share of the top 1 percent was 21.2 percent." Rosenfield said the decline in union membership has also made it more difficult to raise the minimum wage, since the average union worker earns more than the minimum wage. "Without unions, raising the minimum wage can hurt workers who are not unionized," he said. "The labor market has become more and more polarized," said Rosenfield. "But that is not necessarily a bad thing. The problem is that economic growth has slowed, and the economy is more dependent on consumption and household borrowing. This has worsened the inequality problem because most households are dependent on low-paying jobs and borrowing to make ends meet." Rosenfield's research on inequality is funded by the National Institute on Aging, the National Institute on Child Health and Human Development, and the National Science Foundation.
