As air rises in elevation the air becomes less dense allowing the molecules to spread out and cool down. The higher you go the more room they have to spread out and cool. This process is called adiabatic cooling. The colder air is then able to hold less moisture. As the air cools, it is able to hold less water vapor. This causes the air to become drier. Adiabatic cooling is one of the ways to get orographic precipitation. The other way is called orographic lift. The wind coming off of the cold ocean at the coast is moving very fast. As it climbs over the hill and starts to warm up, it also starts to rise up into the air. The faster the wind is moving, the faster the air will rise. As the wind starts to rise, it creates an area of low pressure. As the air in the low pressure area rises, the air molecules spread out. This allows the air to cool down. The cooler air holds less water vapor and is able to hold less moisture. This is called saturation. When the air is no longer saturated, it can't hold all the water vapor it has. This means that some of the water vapor will start to fall out as rain or snow. The rain and snow that forms at the top of the hill falls as it comes down. As it does, the air temperature gets warmer. Since the air is warmer, the air can hold more water vapor. This means that the air is saturated again and can hold all the water vapor it has. The air is no longer able to hold water vapor. This means that any more water vapor that is still in the air will fall out as rain or snow. This is how orographic lift works to make it rain and snow more at the coast. The coastal mountains of Washington get the most precipitation out of all the places in Washington. This is due to the warm air coming off the coast, the cold ocean water and the air rising up over the coastal mountains. The areas of Washington with the least amount of precipitation are the eastern regions of the state and the Columbia River Plateau. These areas of Washington are very flat and have no mountains. The cold air coming off of the mountains can't rise over the flat land, so the air remains close to the surface. This means that the air doesn't get as warm and doesn't rise up as much. This means that the air doesn't cool down as much. This means that the air doesn't saturate and start to rain out. Washington's climate is caused by the mountains and ocean water. The mountains cause orographic precipitation. They also keep Washington from getting hotter in the summer and colder in the winter. They also stop the hot and dry air from coming in during the summer. The ocean keeps the temperature cooler in the summer and warmer in the winter. It also provides water for the plants and animals to live.

We propose novel real-time algorithm to localize hands and find their associations with multiple people in the cluttered 4D volumetric data (dynamic 3D volumes). Different from the traditional multiple view approaches, which find key points in 2D and then triangulate to recover the 3D locations, our method directly processes the dynamic 3D data that involve both clutter and crowd. The volumetric representation is more desirable than the partial observations from different view points and enables more robust and accurate results. However, due to the large amount of data in the volumetric representation brute force 3D schemes are slow. In this paper, we propose novel real-time methods to tackle the problem to achieve both higher accuracy and faster speed than previous approaches. Our method detects the 3D bounding box of each subject and localizes the hands of each person. We develop new 2D features for fast candidate proposals and optimize the trajectory linking using a new max-covering bipartite matching formulation, which is critical for robust performance. We propose a novel decomposition method to reduce the key point localization in each person 3D volume to a sequence of efficient 2D problems. Our experiments show that the proposed method is faster than different competing methods and it gives almost half the localization error.

Scientists have successfully 3D printed ears inside living mice using light for the first time. The achievement, which was led by researchers at the University of Minnesota, could have major implications for the treatment of human patients with congenital defects or injuries. In the study, which was published in the journal Nature Biomedical Engineering, the team used a process called two-photon lithography to create precise 3D structures from hydrogel, a water-based material. They then embedded these structures inside the mice, where they were exposed to near-infrared light. This exposure caused the hydrogel to solidify and form the shape of an ear. Over the course of several weeks, the ear grew and developed blood vessels, just like a normal ear. "This is the first time that anyone has been able to 3D print complex tissues with such high fidelity," said lead author Dr. Yang Yu. "Our technique could someday be used to create other complex tissues and organs for medical therapies." The potential applications of this technology are vast. In addition to treating congenital defects, the team believes that their technique could be used to repair damage from injuries or diseases. "This discovery opens up a new avenue for regenerative medicine," said co-author Professor Juan Carlos Izpisua Belmonte. "We are now one step closer to being able to generate complex tissues and organs to treat a variety of diseases."

Amidst the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic, one of the primary concerns for the scientific community is halting the virus's transmission while simultaneously developing a vaccine. To achieve this, accurptaive diagnosis of those infected by the virus remains critical. Our team employed an unsupervised machine learning strategy to detect COVID-19 instances among patients. Given that COVID-19 represents a newly emerging illness under extensive investigation, such techniques may elucidate distinctions from other types of viral pneumonia, thereby empowering medical professionals to provide better treatment options. By employing various methods like Principal Component Analysis (PCA), t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE), and the innovative Robust Continuous Clustering algorithm (RCC), we demonstrated that RCC surpasses traditional clustering approaches like K-Means (KM) when analyzing a radiographic dataset related to COVID-19. Utilizing the Adjusted Mutual Information Score (AMI) metric for evaluation, RCC achieved significantly higher scores than KM across different classification scenarios, suggesting its greater efficacy in distinguishing COVID-19 cases. These findings underscore the value of RCC in advancing diagnostic capabilities during the COVID-19 crisis and point toward future research directions involving this promising algorithmic approach.

A report commissioned by Food Standards Scotland found that in-store promotions were heavily weighted in favour of food with high levels of salt or sugar. "The findings are particularly concerning given the growing evidence linking high sugar diets to the development of chronic disease and an increased risk of premature death. It is crucial for consumers to know where their food comes from - whether it has been produced using healthy farming methods that protect animal welfare or not." Some examples they gave as examples included over 50 sales of large-sized cakes, mince pies, quiches and pastries compared to just 2 of sales of smaller portions; 11 times more sweets were sold per unit area than cheese sticks; 26 more confectionery products per square metre versus fruit juices and milk alternatives. Items such as crisps, savoury snacks, biscuits and chocolate bars had double the average number of stickers per product than fresh meat and fish products. Calum Campbell, national co-ordinator at Environmental Health Foundation (EHF), said: "More than half of shoppers who buy packaged foods have a diet higher in fat, salt or sugar. Digitisation of fruit trees using LiDAR enables analysis which can be used to better growing practices to improve yield. Sophisticated analysis requires geometric and semantic understanding of the data, including semi-automation for key tasks such as tree delineation or segmentation. Tree delineation: A 3D digital model is required that shows all individual stems in a given area - thus we must first create an accurate digital elevation map (DEM). We use this to detect individual trees; then identify stem boundaries by detecting changes in slope between each segmented stem and its surrounding environment; finally remove erroneous points within these segments from our initial point cloud dataset. The resulting data is easy to visualise with a variety of editing tools enabling us to easily modify any areas present on the scene. Segmenting: Segmenting plant tissue into different objects helps analyse important physiological parameters, through segmenting leaf area index (LAI), crown volume density (CVD) and foliage height distributions over several years etc., all aspects which are essential for guiding management decisions. Delineating fruit trees located at varying distances: Our projects have been conducted across various geographical locations ranging upto 1500m apart but also involved sharing information offsite via remote access, where transmission errors may occur due to unstable internet connections. In order to achieve reliable results while maintaining accuracy a significant challenge was finding ways of delineating trees without needing user interaction. This problem has now become solved thanks to a patent-pending algorithm based on deep learning called 'DeepShot'. The DeepShot image processing algorithm allows distant orchards to be analyzed reliably even when there may be large gaps in connectivity. A key advantage of the Deep Shot technology is it does not require expert knowledge about how to extract useful features from images.

Being engaging, knowledgeable, and empathetic are all desirable general qualities in a conversational agent. Previous work has introduced tasks and datasets that aim to help agents to learn those qualities in isolation and gauge how well they can express them. But rather than being specialized in one single quality, a good open-domain conversational agent should be able to seamlessly blend them all into one cohesive conversational flow. In this work, we investigate several ways to combine models trained towards isolated capabilities, ranging from simple model aggregation schemes that require minimal additional training, to various forms of multi-task training that encompass several skills at all training stages. We further propose a new dataset, BlendedSkillTalk, to analyze how these capabilities would mesh together in a natural conversation, and compare the performance of different architectures and training schemes. Our experiments show that multi-tasking over several tasks that focus on particular capabilities results in better blended conversation performance compared to models trained on a single skill, and that both unified or two-stage approaches perform well if they are constructed to avoid unwanted bias in skill selection or are fine-tuned on our new task.

In the latter part of the Middle Ages, English Dominican mysticism diverged from its European counterparts by emphasizing not just ecstatic encounters with the divine but also prioritizing the significant aspect of individual relationships with God. The core of this form of mysticism lay in morally mirroring Jesus Christ as a model for transformative religion, aiming to reform humankind into reflections of the divine. It comprised four main components: firstly, reflecting the virtuous character of Christ's existence; secondly, correlating the moral replication of Christ's life with humans being depictions of the divine; thirdly, centering around a corporeal spirituality driven by organized compassion towards others; and finally, striving for either ethical or tangible unification with God as its highest goal.

Literature reviews allow scientists to stand on the shoulders of giants, showing promising directions, summarizing progress, and pointing out existing challenges in research. At the same time conducting a systematic literature review is a laborious and consequently expensive process. In the last decade, there have a few studies on crowdsourcing in literature reviews. This paper explores the feasibility of crowdsourcing for facilitating the literature review process in terms of results, time and effort, as well as to identify which crowdsourcing strategies provide the best results based on the budget available. In particular we focus on the screening phase of the literature review process and we contribute and assess methods for identifying the size of tests, labels required per paper, and classification functions as well as methods to split the crowdsourcing process in phases to improve results. Finally, we present our findings based on experiments run on Crowdflower.

The increasing stress on the power grid system arises from the integration of new significant loads such as Electric Vehicles (EVs) and the variable nature of power supply resulting from renewable energy sources inclusion. Consequently, managing and regulating anticipated EV demand within an extensive network of high-speed charging stations emerges as a vital and intricate issue. This study presents a decentralized control strategy rooted in game theory designed to mitigate adverse effects associated with EV consumption. Our approach considers the irregular geographical dispersion of EVs causing disparities in power demands across different charging stations, striving to: (i) prevent overburdening of grid capabilities through providing cost reductions, encouraging users to utilize underutilized stations; (ii) enhance overall income generation by accommodating more clients using identical grid capacities; and (iii) ensure a satisfactory level of Quality-of-Service (QoS), which signifies the reduced likelihood of customer denial in the long run. We investigate progressively complex situations mirroring actual conditions. Findings demonstrate notable advancements concerning our objectives, relative to existing practices.

The term "imperialism" is often conflated with "colonialism," however many scholars have argued that each have their own distinct definition. Imperialism and colonialism have been used in order to describe the process by which the dominant countries in the world control the less powerful ones. Imperialism has been defined as "the economic, military, and cultural domination of lesser developed nations by more powerful ones" whereas colonialism can be defined as a "form of economic and political exploitation carried out by one nation over another one or more." This "hegemony" was used to refer to "the political and economic control of one nation over another." In the 19th century, Britain's domination of the British Empire was a good example of imperialism, while the "United States' political and economic domination of the Western Hemisphere during the 19th century is a good example of colonialism." The French and British were both imperialists in the late 19th century. Both of them were seeking resources such as timber, rubber, and ivory. Britain was involved in a civil war in Afghanistan and India. The French in the same period of time, were engaged in a conflict with the Russians in Egypt and in China.

Instead, your progress will almost always appear smooth without any pauses whatsoever. Another thing that's worth noting here is that swiping up now brings you home as opposed to tapping the top notification shade region as it did previously on KitKat and below. Just as David Letterman had his painfully awkward "Uma, Oprah" routine and Seth Macfarlane his catastrophically misjudged song We Saw Your Boobs, Harris will be recalled mostly as the guy who presented in his pants. It was certainly an arresting image, the How I Met Your Mother star clad only in socks, shoes and what are referred to in America as "tighty whiteys." It was a reference to a scene from Birdman, and - like any time Johnny Depp sings - you had to admire the courage, if not the execution. And at least it was memorable, unlike almost anything Harris actually said. Bafflingly, given the amount of potential material to work with - the Sony hack; the Interview row; the OscarsSoWhite Twitter campaign - the script saw Harris referring to Reese Witherspoon as someone he could eat "with a spoon." The actor was one of a team of 12 Oscar writers. Just think - one of them worked on that humdinger. The other 11 approved it. Even more puzzling, things had started brilliantly. The first line was by far the best - "tonight we honour Hollywood's best and whitest - sorry, brightest" - a reference to the OscarsSoWhite debate that followed the nominations. Then there was the opening song, about the wonder of "moving pictures," featuring Harris, Anna Kendrick and Jack Black - and dancing Stormtroopers. Harris, a Tony Award-winner on Broadway, pulled it off like Steve Martin or Billy Crystal at their best, putting himself into classic movie scenes while pulling off clever rhymes like "Argo And Fargo Or when Marty made his car go." Having nailed it, he turned to the camera and smiled. "That whole thing? Completely improvised." It was pretty much the last big laugh he achieved. From there on, flat setups began crashing into flubbed punchlines with the alacrity of a drunk sailor inviting the entire pub to have a go if they think they're hard enough. There was a predictable joke about Harvey Weinstein (there always is); a bit where he started to talk to the seat fillers and then seemed to immediately lose heart; a routine about his Oscar predictions so laboured it was on the verge of setting up its own union. By halfway through there was terror in Harris' eyes whenever the camera came to him. A part where he asked David Oyelowo to read an insult about the remake of Annie - which had recast the lead with a black actress - was fist-gnawingly uncomfortable. It's worth noting, however, that it was this undercurrent of racial politics that gave the night its most memorable moments. Oyelowo was in tears as he listened to the performance of Glory by John Legend and Common from Selma. It was an intense, powerful performance which had the entire audience on their feet as it finished. When Glory shortly afterwards gained Legend and Common (under their real names of John Stephens and Lonnie Lynn) the best song trophy, they electrified with a passionate joint speech. "Nina Simone said it was an artist's duty to reflect the times we live. Selma may be 50 years ago, but it is now, because the struggle for justice is right now," they insisted, and the music that normally strikes up to urge the winners off the stage stayed silent. Indeed it was a night for politics. Best Actress Patricia Arquette called for equality for women; Best Adapted Screenplay winner Graham Moore urged young people confused about their sexuality to "stay weird"; Best Director Alejandro Gonzalez Inarritu spoke about the Mexicans "who came before and built this incredible immigrant nation." Meanwhile, at the end - in every sense - Harris fluffed a gag about mispronouncing Chiwetel Ejiofor's name. In the context of what had preceded it, it struck a particularly flat note. The Oscars aren't going to stop being seen as white and elitist if every year the writers insist on mining this seam of "exotic names are weird and hard to say." That is hardly Harris' fault. Nevertheless, it really did highlight the contrast of the night: That between black politics and white pants.

Console producers typically decide on the internal components of the gaming machine well over a year prior to its market launch. Subsequently, they distribute 'development kits', which are essentially computers mirroring the console's hardware, albeit slightly enhanced (to support debugging and development utilities), allowing creators to evaluate their games before fine-tuning them for optimal performance. Development kits rarely resemble the actual console due to incomplete designs and lack of necessity for portability or attractiveness. Examples include the bulkier PlayStation 2 dev kit compared to standard desktop cases used by other consoles like the Xbox, GameCube, and Dreamcast. Regarding the programming aspect, modern games primarily share identical codes across platforms because they are constructed using specialized software known as engines. To illustrate, consider creating a first-person shooter; you would begin by coding three-dimensional space representation, followed by movement mechanics within that environment, collision detection between objects, alterations in viewpoint based on elevation, gravity effects, character mobility, non-playable characters navigating predefined paths, light emission from particular objects, shadow casting influenced by object form and proximity to light sources, among many others. Upon completing your initial project, you may realize that subsequent games necessitate only minor adjustments rather than entirely new codes. This contrasts sharply with older practices where distinct codebases were developed specifically for each platform, such as the divergent source codes observed between Nintendo Entertainment System (NES) and Sega Master System versions during earlier generations.

After a death sentence is affirmed in state collateral review, the prisoner may file for federal habeas corpus, which is a unique type of lawsuit that can be brought in federal courts. Federal habeas corpus is a species of collateral review, and it is the only way that state prisoners may attack a death sentence in federal court (other than petitions for certiorari to the United States Supreme Court after both direct review and state collateral review). The scope of federal habeas corpus is governed by the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996, which restricted significantly its previous scope. The purpose of federal habeas corpus is to ensure that state courts, through the process of direct review and state collateral review, have done at least a reasonable job in protecting the prisoner's federal constitutional rights. Prisoners may also use federal habeas corpus suits to bring forth new evidence that they are innocent of the crime, though to be a valid defense at this late stage in the process, evidence of innocence must be truly compelling.

Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have provably enhanced the state-of-the-art Neural Machine Translation (NMT) with their capability in modeling complex functions and capturing complex linguistic structures. However NMT systems with deep architecture in their encoder or decoder RNNs often suffer from severe gradient diffusion due to the non-linear recurrent activations, which often make the optimization much more difficult. To address this problem we propose novel linear associative units (LAU) to reduce the gradient propagation length inside the recurrent unit. Different from conventional approaches (LSTM unit and GRU), LAUs utilizes linear associative connections between input and output of the recurrent unit, which allows unimpeded information flow through both space and time direction. The model is quite simple, but it is surprisingly effective. Our empirical study on Chinese-English translation shows that our model with proper configuration can improve by 11.7 BLEU upon Groundhog and the best reported results in the same setting. On WMT14 English-German task and a larger WMT14 English-French task, our model achieves comparable results with the state-of-the-art.

In this study, we explore reinforcement learning (RL) within an unbounded state space context, drawing inspiration from classic queueing network scheduling problems. Existing policies and error metrics tailored for finite or bounded state spaces necessitate infinite data collection to offer substantial performance guarantees when dealing with unbounded states. Consequently, we introduce a novel performance evaluation approach centered around the concept of 'stability'. Our proposed idea suggests that a good policy ensures the state dynamics stay confined within a certain range most of the time. 

To validate our hypothesis, we develop an RL policy leveraging a Sparse-Sampling-based Monte Carlo Oracle. We contend that this policy maintains the desired stability characteristic provided that the system's underlying dynamics align with a Lyapunov function - a condition that applies whenever the system is positively recurrent or stable. Notably, our policy operates without requiring explicit knowledge about the specific Lyapunov function involved. Additionally, we enhance the efficiency of our method through an optimized version of the Sparse-Sampling-based Monte Carlo Oracle equipped with a Lipschitz value function. Finally, we present an adaptable variant of the algorithm, incorporating meticulously devised statistical tests, enabling automatic adjustment of the relevant tuning parameters.

Restricting computational time to a specific function f(n) frequently results in complexity classes being influenced by the selected computing model. As an example, the language consisting of all strings with repeated prefixes {xx x}, where x represents any binary string, can be resolved using linear time on a multitape Turing machine. However, it necessitates quadratic time when utilizing a singletape Turturing machine. According to the Cobham-Edmonds thesis, as stated by Goldreich (2008), Chapter 1.2, there exists a polynomial relationship between time complexities across any two sensible and widespread computational models if we permit polynomial fluctuations in processing duration. This concept serves as the foundation for the complexity class P, comprising decision issues resolvable through a deterministic Turing machine within a polynomial timeframe. Similarly, the associated collection of functional challenges constitutes FP.

Bayesian optimization (BO), an effective technique for identifying the optimal value of complex functions that do not reveal their internal workings, excels in adjusting the settings of machine learning algorithms. The typical procedure includes constructing a predictive model of the objective function and selecting the next sampling point using an acquisition function. However, these operations struggle when dealing with problems involving more than 10-20 variables due to the curse of dimensionality. Our study introduces a novel BO strategy capable of handling higher-dimensional spaces by discovering a simplified, lower-dimensional representation of the parameter space through a deep learning architecture incorporated within the kernel of a Gaussian process. By integrating unsupervised feature extraction into a supervised learning context, our method leverages the inherent strengths of Gaussian processes while simultaneously reducing computational complexity. Furthermore, we enhance our model's ability to map back to the original high-dimensional space utilizing multi-task Gaussian processes, which we optimize collectively by maximizing the log probability of observed data. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that our proposed low-dimensional BO surpasses existing methods across various challenging 60-dimensional test cases.

The classical constant-sum 'silent duel' game had two antagonistic marksmen walking towards each other. A more friendly formulation has two equally skilled marksmen approaching targets at which they may silently exchange arrows, without pistols, shotguns or any of the weapons with which modern warfare is based. The first markman to reach the target will be declared winner and receive a prize. The game was popularised in England by Sir Thomas Gresham (born c. 1777) who devised it as a means for children to learn how to shoot accurately while having fun. His book, "A Book on Shooting," published in 1821, contains instructions for various games among its many references to shooting sports. The current format involves two coaches: one coach supplies the ball and the other coach provides ammunition. Each player then starts by holding his weapon horizontally above the ground. The opponent's gun is placed over this, facing him or her. Each player must aim and fire in exactly the same direction, using only their eyesight. If he successfully hits his target, then the receiver wins; otherwise their scores are counted accordingly but add up to zero. In case both players miss, neither can claim victory until the next turn, when the receiver gets another shot at the target. The tray book from which the balls are distributed have been made into trading cards that were sold worldwide under the name of "Silent Duel Game."

Traditional finance methodologies may struggle to address the intricate relationships present in extensive financial forecasting challenges; however, deep learning presents a potential solution for identifying connections within intricate market structures. This study employs deep learning techniques on econometric gradient constructions to identify and utilize delayed correlations between S&P 500 stocks, evaluating model responses during both steady and tumultuous market conditions without relying on data from the predicted stock itself. To assess the impact of different time frames, we make predictions about intra-day and day-to-day fluctuations in stock prices across various intervals and adjust our model design accordingly to reflect the complexity involved. Results indicate that despite decreasing accuracy as prediction windows shorten, there remains considerable value in leveraging lagged correlations within the stock market. These outcomes have notable consequences for contemporary financial theories and could serve as a useful analytical instrument for fund managers. Furthermore, we validate our model's robustness amidst market instability by testing it against the economic downturn experienced during the 2007-2008 financial crisis.

A lot of color blind people are red-green color blind and many of those cases are due to the fact that the red cones and the green cones in the eyes (the color sensors) have too much overlap in the colors they respond to. Because there is so much overlap the brain cannot decide if the light that is causing the response is red or green.... that results in red-green color blindness.... the brain not being able to tell the difference between red and green light. The Enchroma lenses heavily filter out much of the over lap region, enough so that the red cones are stimulated with only very red light and the green cones are stimulated only with very green light (since much of the over lapping light is blocked). This lets finally lets the brain tell the difference between red and green. This only works for people whose color blindness is the result of the red-green response having a large over lap region that is then filtered out by the glasses.

It is recognised that an epidemiological account of the plague is as important as an identification of symptoms, but researchers are hampered by the lack of reliable statistics from this period. The obvious problem with this approach is that if the plague did not exist in 19th-century China, the numbers are either entirely fictitious or inaccurate. The paucity of data makes it difficult to work out whether the deaths in China were due to the plague or other diseases, such as cholera, typhoid or malaria. At present, however, it is thought that bubonic plague was the main cause of death, although in the 19th century it was rare to see the symptoms of the disease, and the population was mostly in denial of the possibility of the plague. Dr Coghill, the deputy director of the Wellcome Library, said: 'Our discovery shows that the plague had a much longer history in China than was previously known, and was probably not as well-known as the common belief in Europe at the time.' The researcher added that the impact of the disease was probably underestimated in Europe. He said: 'We know that the plague is responsible for a great number of deaths and there is evidence of it killing a large proportion of the population of China, so it is likely that there were many more deaths than have been recorded.' The library is working with experts at the Pasteur Institute in Paris to investigate the 19th-century accounts to see if they can find the actual numbers of people who died from the disease. We transform reinforcement learning (RL) into a form of supervised learning (SL) by turning traditional RL on its head, calling this RL or Upside Down RL (UDRL). Standard RL predicts the outcome and makes decisions based upon that prediction. But UDRL uses information from past experiences to predict future outcomes without using predictions. To demonstrate how our approach works we show how an algorithm called Deep Reinforcement Learning can be used in a vehicle self-driving system. In our paper, we present two challenges for autonomous vehicles: detecting obstacles nearby and removing objects within them so as not to collide with parked cars waiting at traffic lights. Unfortunately these tasks are very difficult due to many variables like pedestrians crossing unexpectedly; light changes, unexpected road closures, etc. Despite their complexity, they would benefit greatly if learned through reinforcement learning. We use UDRL to teach Deep Reinforcement Learning algorithms how to handle such situations. The proof of concept video shows us driving an automated car over three scenarios both in real time - when no one is around -and during a pre-recorded training set where someone stops at every red signal along a street. For each scenario, we look at how well the AI learns by observing the output after applying different policies. Both videos feature the same performance test which measures how good the AI is at finding the safest path between sets of checkpoints. The first demonstration has been done before but it's interesting to see just how much better the AI was given a new tool for solving problems! Our lab recently launched udrl.ai, aimed at helping people learn deep reinforcement learning techniques online. Deep reinforcement learning is currently being used for various machine vision applications including image classification and object detection. It also powers some popular speech recognition systems right now, such as Google's NN-trained Gboard (see below), which transcribes your voice onto text more accurately than any other app out there. Employers aim to spend as little as possible when offering positions, so they commonly request your previous earnings details and provide a marginally higher or comparable compensation proposal. They avoid setting their initial salary offer too high to prevent attracting candidates seeking the highest available wages. This strategy also helps them maintain flexibility during negotiations, which generally favors the company, although outcomes can vary. Companies usually establish a salary range for each role, preferring not to advertise the upper limit to discourage applicants from expecting top-end offers. Conversely, listing the lower boundary could deter highly qualified individuals who refuse to settle below a certain threshold. In cases where exceptional talent emerges, exceptions can be made to exceed the predetermined maximum salary. By providing limited information, employers reduce the employee's ability to negotiate effectively, thus keeping labor costs down by starting with conservative figures. However, this approach can lead to missed opportunities for securing a more lucrative offer elsewhere since potential employees remain unaware of better options available locally. Salaries ultimately depend on factors such as skills, experience, expertise, and negotiation abilities, and employers frequently present a range rather than a fixed figure, encouraging candidates to begin at the lower end to allow room for future raises.

The Principle of Unforeseen Outcomes is frequently cited by Libertarians (and others) as evidence of the pitfalls associated with advocating for societal manipulation or regulatory measures. They argue that actions such as raising the minimum wage or enforcing healthcare requirements may ultimately lead to job losses and negatively impact those they were meant to assist. Similarly, they question environmentalist opposition to nuclear energy, resulting in increased reliance on coal-burning, and criticize educational reforms that unintentionally diminish academic standards. While I am a proponent of taking action to address issues within society, recognizing the intricate nature of our world means acknowledging the potential for exacerbating problems rather than improving them. Therefore, I seek compelling reasons to challenge the notion that this principle holds excessive weight and rely primarily on weak examples, suggesting that well-meaning efforts tend to produce more negative consequences than positive ones. For most of US history, party nominees have been decided by political power brokers and deal-makers behind closed doors. Parties operate like private clubs - they make their own rules and are suspicious of outsiders. Only in recent history has a more open system of primaries and caucuses been grafted onto the process to give the average American a say in who appears on the general election ballot. In a close, contentious primary season, however, the veneer of accountability can rub off, exposing the sometimes unsightly gears that still power the US political system. This has prompted objection from the supporters of two candidates in particular - Donald Trump and Bernie Sanders - who feel that the party establishments are arrayed against their presidential quests. But are their concerns valid? Here are answers to four pertinent questions as the nomination battles approach its final months. 34 Number of delegates Ted Cruz received in Colorado, which held conventions to pick delegates 759 Trump total delegate count 529 Cruz total delegate count Mr Trump is leading the race for the Republican nomination, but it's starting to feel like he's not winning. While he's comfortably ahead, with 757 delegates to 529 for second-place Ted Cruz, there's mounting evidence that he's being outmanoeuvred in the behind-the-scenes political process that could come into play if he doesn't reach the magic 1,237 delegate number necessary to secure the nomination outright. In Colorado - which selected its delegates at party gatherings last week and not through primaries or caucuses - Mr Cruz walked away with all 34 delegates. Even in states that have held contests won by Mr Trump, Mr Cruz's team has been working doggedly to ensure that their people become delegates. While Mr Trump swept South Carolina's 50 delegates, for instance, the state's convention delegation will be riddled with Cruz supporters who, while bound to Mr Trump on the first few ballots, can switch to the Texas senator if there is a protracted convention battle. It has Mr Trump and his people crying foul. "This is happening all over our country - great people being disenfranchised by politicians," Mr Trump tweeted on Monday. "Repub party is in trouble!" Paul Manafort, Mr Trump's new aide in charge of managing the delegate-selection process, accused the Cruz campaign of using "Gestapo tactics, scorched-earth tactics" in Colorado. If, as Mr Trump asserted on Monday, the system is "rigged" and "crooked," however, it isn't always tilted in favour of Mr Trump's opponents. Thanks to the Republican Party's delegate-apportioning system, including Florida's winner-take-all primary, Mr Trump has secured a larger share of the delegates so far (45) than he has of the raw primary vote (37). If Mr Cruz manages to win the nomination at the Republican convention despite trailing Mr Trump in total delegates and share of the popular vote, Mr Trump may have reason to feel aggrieved. But before he complains too loudly, he might want to heed some sage advice attributed (incorrectly) to Albert Einstein: "You have to learn the rules of the game. And then you have to play better than anyone else." Mr Trump should be familiar with the quote, since he tweeted it in October 2014. 17 States Bernie Sanders has won 18 States Hillary Clinton has won Mr Sanders has won five state contests in a row and seven of the last eight. If he were an American football team he'd be poised for the playoffs. If he were prize fighter, he'd be tuning up for a title bout. Instead his pledged-delegate deficit to Mrs Clinton has gone from daunting to only fractionally less daunting. Over the course of his recent run, the Vermont Senator has picked up a net of just 91 delegates, despite winning Wisconsin 56 to 43, Utah 79 to 20 and Washington 72 to 27. According to a New York Times calculation, the former secretary of state currently has 1,305 pledged delegates, while Sanders stands at 1,086. Add in the non-binding support of "super-delegates" - Democratic officeholders and party functionaries who also cast ballots for the nominee at the convention - and Mrs Clinton's lead balloons to 1,774 to 1,117. To secure the Democratic nomination without drama at the convention a candidate needs the backing of 2,383 delegates The problem for Mr Sanders is that while he's been posting sizeable wins over the past month, they've largely been in delegate-poor states, like Wyoming (14 delegates), Idaho (23) and Alaska (16). His successes pale when compared to Mrs Clinton's massive earlier wins in populous southern states like Texas, Florida and Georgia, which alone netted her 184 delegates over Mr Sanders. If Mrs Clinton performs as expected in the coming contests in New York (291 delegates), Maryland (118) and Pennsylvania (210), she'll largely erase all the modest ground Mr Sanders made up over the past three weeks. 9,412,426 Votes for Hillary Clinton during primary season so far 7,034,997 Votes for Bernie Sanders during primary season so far If delegate maths and selection rules make your head hurt, at least we can rely on the raw vote totals to get a feel for how popular the remaining candidates are, right? Wrong. According to current tabulations Hillary Clinton has received 9,412,426 votes during the primary season so far. Bernie Sanders has received 7,034,997. That 2.4m vote lead has been relentlessly touted by the former secretary of state and her supporters to counter the claims of Sanders faithful that their man is more popular than the delegate tallies indicate. Some states that hold caucuses - like Iowa and Washington - aren't included in that number, however, because they don't report vote totals. The Washington Post's Glenn Kessler tried to extrapolate numbers for the remaining states based on their total voter turnout and concluded that Hillary Clinton leads Bernie Sanders by 2.3m votes - still a significant margin. Among the Republicans, who are better about providing full vote totals, Mr Trump leads with 8,256,309 votes. Mr Cruz is second (6,319,244), former candidate Marco Rubio is third (3,482,129), followed by Mr Kasich (2,979,379). In the end the popular vote may give the leading candidates a claim of legitimacy as the people's choice - but appearances can be deceiving. "The media has created the perception that the voters choose the nomination. That's the conflict here," North Dakota delegate Curly Haugland told a television interviewer. "The rules are still designed to have a political party choose its nominee at a convention. That's just the way it is." "Well, there's the law, and then there's ethics, and then there's getting votes. I'm not going to get into what tactics are used." If, as appears to be increasingly likely, the Republican primary season ends without Donald Trump securing the 1,237 delegates needed to secure the nomination, the Republican National Convention could turn into a political free-for-all unrivalled in modern US political history. After several rounds of deadlocked balloting, most convention delegates would be free to vote their conscience. But could that conscience be nudged by, say, a free weekend at a Donald Trump golf resort, a nice dinner with the Cruz family or even a choice spot in a John Kasich administration? Maybe! While there are detailed anti-corruption laws governing the behaviour of public officeholders, convention delegates are private citizens. While government regulations prohibit them from taking money from corporations, labour unions, government contractors or foreign nationals, the law beyond that is much murkier. Campaigns and their wealth donors could likely cover delegate travel expenses, no matter how lavish. Gold watches? Bags of small, unmarked bills? Who knows? State anti-bribery laws may apply, but there's scant legal precedent. Perhaps the greatest deterrent to untoward action by campaigns is the negative publicity such naked attempts at influence could have if they're documented. But public perceptions and attitudes this political season has been difficult to predict, to say the least. Although the national convention is still months away, accusations of dirty tricks have already started flying. On Sunday Mr Trump took to Twitter to accuse the Cruz campaign of misdeeds during the South Carolina state party convention - a charge Mr Cruz vehemently denied. "I win a state in votes and then get non-representative delegates because they are offered all sorts of goodies by Cruz campaign," Mr Trump wrote. "Bad system!" During a television interview that same morning, however, Trump adviser Paul Manafort appeared to acknowledge that his campaign won't be shy in wooing delegates at the national convention, however. "Well, there's the law, and then there's ethics, and then there's getting votes," he said. "I'm not going to get into what tactics are used. I happen to think the best way we're going to get delegates is to have Donald Trump be exposed to delegates, let the delegates hear what he says." Another Trump adviser, Barry Bennett, said they wouldn't be offering "seats on the Trump airplane or anything like that." "There's obviously a big line - we're not going to do anything immoral, illegal or unethical," he said. But when a presidential nomination is at stake, and it comes down to just a handful of delegates, that "big line" may end up looking awfully fuzzy.

Sad to see no one grabbed this one, but here's an overview. The actual technique are rather varied and I don't really know too much about them but they all follow a similar pattern. DDoS Attack A Distributed Denial of Service attack is where you have a lot of computers all sending requests to a server. An easy way to think of this is like a pharmacy. You walk in, ask for something (Service Request) and the pharmacist verifys your information (Request Parsing) then goes to get your medicine (Data Retrieval). A DDoS attack would be like getting a huge group of people to all go to the pharmacy at the same time and demand things all at once and over and over that may or may not be something they actually have (Junk Data). Eventually the pharmacy gets overwhelmed and they have to stop all incoming requests meaning that it shuts down. This is usually accomplished through things called "Botnets" which are vast non-centralized computer networks, most of which have no idea that they're being used as such, they're hijacked for this purpose through spyware and viruses. To control all of these computers you have "Herders" or people that control the "Herd" of "Zombies" or "Bots," they pick where to direct the attack and all the "Zombies" start sending as many requests to a website that they can. The power of a given botnet can be measured in PPS or RPS, pings per second or requests per second respectively. A DoS attack or Denial of Service attack usually originates from a small group of computers or an individual computer, these don't work as well as it's rather trivial to block all requests from a single or small group of IPs but can take down lesser site with hosting that's either not ready for an attack or don't really care enough to protect a tiny domain. It should be added that not all DDoS scenarios are malicious or intentional. You may have heard of reddit "hugging" sites to death and that happens because reddit is so huge that they can unintentionally take down a site in the exact same manner as a DDoS attack but completely on accident by diverting such a huge amount of traffic to smaller sites. Also, as a personal note, no hacking knowledge is illegal to know or research. As long as you don't use anything you learn maliciously, you should never be afraid to research any topic relating to hacking or "cyber-terrorism." In fact, knowing about this sort of thing can stop it from happening to you so learn all you can. The concept is extremely simple, and the reason it is so effective. Have you ever been on Reddit and you come to a screen that say's "Reddit is under heavy load right now."? That's because there is too much data going in and out of Reddit's servers for them to properly handle. This data is called traffic. Servers can only handle X amount of traffic (bandwidth); depending on how they are set up and how large they are. DDoS works by having a program effectively refresh a page on a website many times per second (hundreds or thousands), creating an immense amount of traffic for the severs to handle. Predicting a binary sequence serves as a quintessential illustration of real-time machine learning, which we refer to as the "stock forecast issue." Here, the sequence represents the fluctuating value of a stock, increasing or decreasing by one unit per time interval. The goal in this scenario is for an investor to utilize the insights provided by multiple "specialists" and aim to reduce their ultimate regret concerning the top performer among them. Unlike traditional approaches, probability does not factor into this situation, as the market behaves antagonistically. Our focus lies on the circumstance where two experts provide input based on the four preceding stock movements. By applying techniques derived from optimal control, graph theory, and partial differential equations, we explore potential tactics for both the investor and the hostile market. Furthermore, we establish the corresponding upper and lower boundaries for the investor's end-of-game regret. As 'd' surpasses 4, these upper and lower limits merge, rendering the suggested methods asymptotically ideal. Notably, unlike prior studies involving partial differential equations for prediction, our approach introduces a novel aspect: dual timescales - while the stock history updates after each step, regret accrual occurs at a slower pace.

The Intensive Care Unit (ICU) is a hospital department where machine learning has the potential to provide valuable assistance in clinical decision making. Classical machine learning models usually only provide limited information and are not able to predict individual patient outcomes; instead they tend to focus on predicting risks of severe events for entire groups or populations, often with high false positive rates CR1. One reason why classical machine learning algorithms perform poorly when applied to ICUs is that patients spend many hours each day without any input being received from clinicians - this time period corresponds roughly to nadir physiological stability whilst a patient is sedated but still receiving mechanical ventilation support. In recent years, however, there have been an increasing number of studies using wireless sensors and smart-watches which can collect large amounts of data continuously during this low intensity activity phase CR12], [CR17CR19], [CR22; these increasingly ubiquitous technologies will be discussed further below. Several neural network models have also recently shown some success in modelling short periods of time within intensive care admission episodes CR2], [CR8], [CR9], [CR16, raising hope that such methods could potentially help improve long term prediction accuracy for longer durations than their current ability covers. While it may seem difficult to model time series regression problems over several weeks at once due to memory limitations, kernel techniques like Gaussian Processes (GPs), as well as Online Linear Regression Models (OLRMs) CR10, allow us to train our systems incrementally based on the most up-to-date data available while maintaining full generalisation capabilities by providing samples from future predictions. This approach allows users to make progress towards training more accurate models despite having poor initial calibration leading to higher quality final predictions. Furthermore, extending these methods into multiple hospitals CR6 allows the scaling ability of GPs to exceed human capacity limits. To achieve all this requires certain conditions to hold: A clear understanding of the underlying correlation structure between inputs and outputs. An appropriately small amount of historical data, ideally collected under tightly controlled conditions and free of confounding factors (e.g. other drugs administered). If spurious correlations do exist amongst variables then we must understand what causes them so that we can remove them before fitting our model. The use of proper validation procedures ensuring that the trained model does indeed behave correctly on unseen test datasets. This paper provides details of how GP-based approaches might work for data obtained from critically ill ward patients who require constant monitoring through support provided via ventilator interfaces. We show results demonstrating that GP performs worse than OLRM. However, even though its predictive performance across different internal validations was not particularly good, it performed much better than random guessing, showing that sufficient regularity exists among the patients' dependence on respiratory system measurements for clinically relevant predictions. When I say this the thought might come to mind "well wait, I thought you could say that either twin has turned around - you just change your reference frame" but that's not true. The theory of relativity simply says that all inertial reference frames are equivalent (if you're not accelerating, you're in an inertial reference frame). Notice the distance from the origin for each. What's the difference there? Perhaps, ohhh.... 0.9? The difference between the two experiences in the twin paradox is that one experiences some non-inertial action. Something pushes him (notice that one of them needs to feel a push to get back - in our case, that's Bob). It's also interesting to note at this point that we can feel acceleration but not velocity - more precisely, no object "experiences" velocity as every object can say it's at rest in inertial reference frames; every object experiences acceleration. This acceleration warps Bob's coordinate system, causing his "plane of simultaneity" to go sweeping across alice's time axis. Many individuals do not possess a clear-cut dominant eye; however, in general, the stronger eye takes precedence. Although prescription glasses bring visual clarity, they reduce the size of the perceived images slightly—by approximately 1 mm for the weaker eye and 3 mm for the stronger one. This disparity might seem minor, yet it is significant enough for the brain to notice. Additionally, having both eyes perform optimally offers advantages such as improved depth perception. The dominant eye typically exhibits more neural connections to the brain, leading individuals to depend primarily on its input while using the secondary eye mainly for gauging distances accurptaions.

Achieving transparency in black-box deep learning algorithms is still an open challenge. High dimensional features and decisions given by deep neural networks (NN) require new algorithms and methods to expose the internal workings of the decision-making process. In this paper we apply a recent breakthrough method, called LRP (Layer-wise Relevance Propagation), to explain the decisions of deep neural networks. LRP is a local algorithm that propagates relevance scores from the output layer backward to the input layer. The relevance score of a given input variable is the sum of relevance scores that are propagated back from all output units. LRP is efficient as it requires to run the NN only once from the input to the output layer. The relevance of input features, which are present in the first layer, can be interpreted as how relevant they are to the output decision. We evaluate the explanatory power of LRP on a number of benchmark datasets from the MNIST and CIFAR-10 domains. Our experimental results show that LRP is well-suited for explaining the decisions of NNs.

Indoor localization for autonomous micro aerial vehicles (MAVs) requires specific localization techniques, since the Global Positioning System (GPS) is usually not available. We present an efficient onboard computer vision approach for indoor localization and mapping, which is based on the combination of a monocular camera and an Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU). This system is able to provide accurate and reliable position estimates of the MAV even in GPS-denied environments. Our method consists of two main components: a visual-inertial odometry module that uses a monocular camera and IMU data to estimate the MAV's trajectory, and a place recognition module that uses image features to match keyframes and map the environment. We validate our system on a dataset of real flight trajectories and show that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy, robustness, and computational efficiency.

Recently, collaborative robots have begun to train humans to achieve complex tasks, and the mutual information exchange between them can lead to successful robot-human collaborations. In this paper we demonstrate the application and effectiveness of a new approach called mutual reinforcement learning (MRL), where both humans and autonomous agents act as reinforcement learners in a skill transfer scenario over continuous communication and feedback. An autonomous agent initially acts as an instructor who can teach a novice human participant complex skills using the MRL strategy. While teaching skills in a physical (block-building) ( n 34) or simulated (Tetris) environment ( n 31), the expert tries to identify appropriate reward channels preferred by each individual and adapts itself accordingly using an exploration-exploitation strategy. These reward channel preferences can identify important behaviors of the human participants, because they may well exercise the same behaviors in similar situations later. In this way, skill transfer takes place between an expert system and a novice human operator. We divided the subject population into three groups and observed the skill transfer phenomenon, analyzing it with Simpson"s psychometric model. 5-point Likert scales were also used to identify the cognitive models of the human participants. We obtained a shared cognitive model which not only improves human cognition but enhances the robot's cognitive strategy to understand the mental model of its human partners while building a successful robot-human collaborative framework.

A joint UK and US team utilizing data from an infrared telescope in Hawaii has identified extremely high temperatures reaching up to 1,500°C within Jupiter's upper atmosphere. These findings indicate significantly warmer conditions compared to other areas on the planet. The researchers propose that intense sound waves, similar to sonic booms, might generate these elevated temperatures in the sparse layers of the outermost atmosphere. Published in Nature, this study addresses the longstanding scientific puzzle regarding excessive heat levels observed in the upper atmospheres of gas giant planets like Jupiter, despite their considerable distance from the sun. If the origin of this thermal phenomenon lies locally—possibly linked with Jupiter's renowned tempestuous storm system—the mystery could potentially be resolved. This groundbreaking discovery provides the initial concrete proof supporting such theories. Co-author Dr. Tom Stallard from the University of Leicester remarked that understanding heat distribution on Jupiter has been a challenging endeavor spanning two decades. According to him, prior explorations only indicated uniformly high temperatures throughout Jupiter's entirety, particularly near the poles. While the extraordinary displays of light known as Jupiter's auroras account for the extreme cold in polar regions, explaining how this chill propagates towards the equatorial zone remains elusive due to insufficient modeling. Conversely, Dr. James O'Donoghue of Boston University, who spearheaded the recent investigation, pointed out that there seems to be no justifiable reason behind the exceptionally high temperatures recorded. By employing a specialized instrument located at the Nasa Infrared Telescope Facility situated in Mauna Kea, Hawaii, the team uncovered a significant temperature anomaly situated approximately several hundred kilometers above the cloud formations of Jupiter's iconic Great Red Spot. This observation hints at an underlying tumultuous environment contributing to the generation of immense heat. Although some experts previously postulated that heat may emanate from deeper within the planet, empirical evidence had not yet substantiated those claims until now.

Paul likes to collect comic books. One of his favorites is Batman. Paul has over 500 Batman comic books. He keeps his books inside of plastic bags with cardboard backs. "The problem with this is that the outside material gets damaged, and then it's a lot harder to read," said Paul about keeping them safe from rain and snow. "I've been looking for something else." For years he has wished there was a way to protect his collection without messing up their value. That wish came true recently when Brian and Erin Ferreira created the Batcave Boxes. They are insulated boxes made especially for comic book collections. The boxes come in four different sizes and each one can hold anywhere between 10-100 comics. Each box costs 69.95 Erin says the idea behind the company started after they had trouble finding a solution to storing their own comics safely. After brainstorming some ideas on how to make an affordable storage unit, she brought Paul into the project. Since starting, they have sold nearly 2,000 boxes around the country. Their product line consists mainly out of two colors: black or white. Some people may think these color choices were made by accident but Erin says both options look good together. She also says the color choice allows customers to match their Comic Cave with other items such as furniture, artwork, etc. When asked what makes their product so special, Erin explained that most companies use foam or bubble wrap when creating their products. However, they chose to use a patented fabric called ThermaShield which protects the outside of the bag while still allowing moisture vapors through and protecting the interior. They say they chose to go with this patent because it would last longer than typical consumer grade materials and could be cleaned easier. In addition, no foam adhesive will ever dry out due to the fact the board absorbs all the water leaving nothing for any glue to dry on. This means that your entire collection will not deteriorate if exposed to water. For those who love action figures or statues - most known for being brittle - the new invention has become a perfect partner for display purposes. As far as durability goes, after testing various thicknesses of ThermaShield, they decided 4 mils would be best. This ensures that the cover won't tear unless you try to rip your collection apart and that the inner lining will keep your possessions fresh for decades. And with thousands of reviews online, the boxes seem to live up to every promise. To top things off, Brian and Erin believe that their customer service plays just as large a role as the quality of construction of their product. As soon as someone places an order (whether its free or paid), they are given a name tag and put at the head of the customer queue. If there is anything wrong with the product, Brian says they want a chance to fix it right away rather than waiting until months later. According to Erin, they even send people personalized thank you notes! It seems like only time will tell how well the business grows since they don't yet advertise extensively. The appetite for Chinese commodities like silk, porcelain, and tea in Europe hinged on converting scarce silver reserves into transactions with China. By the latter half of the 18th century, British and French authorities became increasingly alarmed by this skewed trading dynamic and the consequent depletion of silver. Consequently, the British East India Company ramped up opium cultivation in Bengal to cater to the escalating demand in China. Given that China largely relied on internal production, it rarely required imports from Europe, resulting in payments typically made via silver. Worried about both the diminishing silver supply and the harmful effects of opium use among his people, the Daoguang Emperor instructed Lin Zexu to halt the opium commerce. Lin seized opium inventories uncompensated in 183EE, prompting Britain to retaliate militarily the subsequent year.

Grounding occurs when a vessel strikes the bottom of a body of water or encounters an obstruction beneath the surface. Essentially, this refers to the ship colliding with the seafloor below it. The risks associated with grounding are significant because it may cause harm to the hull or create openings within it. This could result in the release of cargo, potentially leading to complete loss of the ship and, in severe instances, human fatalities. Spills involving hazardous substances, such as chemicals or oil, have particularly devastating consequences. A notable example is the incident where the Exxon Valdez ran aground, releasing almost 11 million gallons of oil which led to an ecological disaster. In simple terms, the ship impacts the base of the water body it is navigating through, causing undue stress on its structure due to being supported at a specific concentrated point.

Hi CMV! I'm out to genuinely seek to understand this perspective, because I confess it rubs me the wrong way when I hear it discussed in media, here on reddit or anywhere - "America is the land of the free" is a slogan we all know and lovehate in this world. I believe that it is clearly propaganda, as is all discussion of one's nation's supremacy over others - and that individuals who buy into this rhetoric are sorely lacking reasonable thinkig on the matter. Firstly - the word "free" has no specific meaning in the social context that is implied in these kind of statements. The freedom to shout and the freedom to sit in silence are mutually exclusive from the perspective of two individuals sitting in a room - one denies the other. Further, all civilised society is based around limiting freedoms - as a race we have typically clustered into social groups and nations and elected (in developed nations) representatives to govern our societies. That government imposes rules on those groups, as well as collecting taxes and all sorts of other sensible things which let nations work. What rules and restrictions are laid down vary very little between developed nations. Comparing the US and Canada [from what I know of both] you have your basic: - No murder - No rape - No theft That kind of things. However you frame a discussion, these are restrictions on "freedom" - they are'nt bad IMO, but they clearly restrcit people in a nation doing those things. So America is not "perfectly" free. Fine - so what is this claim meaning? That the list of things American's are not able to do is the smallest in the world? I don't know if that's true but it doesn't feel like it - America has quite an active government style - for example it's very restrictive about alcohol: - No drinking under 21 (that's pretty harsh where I grew up - the UK is 18) - No drinking in the street (as far as I can tell) That last one is a pretty big restriction of my own decisions, and again to cite the UK because it's what I know, we are free to drink almost anywhere, we can stroll down the street with a beer. Some big ones that are often mentioned in this discussion: The freedom to own firearms For one thing, this isn't just the US, though many developed nations do restrict them, Switzerland for example has no restrictions on personal fire arm ownership (well they have restrictions but you know what I mean). For another, yes the US have a list of weapons you are allowed to use, but they have lists you aren't allowed to use as well: isn't this just arbitrary line drawing: In the UK I'm allowed to own a knife, not a gun or a grenade or a nuke. In the US you are allowed to own a knife, a gun, not a grenade (I presume) and not a nuke (I presume). Both populations are free to own weapons, the line where the US says it's illegal is higher than the UK but that's surely not in and of itself an argument that there is more freedom occuring? This also relates to my point about mutually exclusive freedoms: in the UK you are free to walk down the street knowing that no one will have a gun and is able to shoot you, in the US you do not have this freedom (just an illustration of how this word doesn't really mean anything). Freedom of speech In the US this is a big deal, and often the corner stone of arguments about freedom. But most (can't say all, but I feel like almost all) have extremely high freedoms of speech, and further the US does not have perfect freedom of speech as far as I can tell. The UK (again, apologies, it's what I know) restricts speech around "inciting racial hatred" - that's it! I am free to criticse the government, I am free to tell someone they smell - whatever, I'm not going to be arrested, but I am not allowed to encourage people to commit acts of violence racially (I feel pretty good about this rule, but that's a side point). The US you are allowed to do this, but you aren't allowed to divulge government secrets, even if you are morally obliged to - Edward Snowden was not free to do what he did, somethings: you cannot say. (The same is true for most developed nations I believe). Even if the entire "most free country in the world" premise comes down to that thin line in freedom of speech between total freedom and the freedom except in very specific circumstances, what kind of calculus can we use that weighs that priviledge against other freedoms other nations have Scandinavian countries have the right to free university education! UK has the right to drink beer outside and free healthcare! The Netherlands has the freedom to smoke weed! Canada allows gay marriage! (though the US is catching up) We each as national groups choose our laws, and in the developed world they are all basically the same - and nothing about what I see of the US suggests life there is any more "free" (whatever that means) than other developed nations. As far as I can see - with the cost of healthcare, lack of gay marriage, no drinking under 21, heavy handed policing, anti drug laws and massive prison populations is a candidate for being one of the less free of the developed nations. As it stands, there are many topics of opinion which are taboo to discuss. Many of these topics have to do with sex and sexual behavior, and especially unconventional forms of sexual activity or orientations, such as ZoophiliaBestiality, Incest, Necrophilia, Pedophilia, and so on, though other restrictions exist. I think taboos exist to suppress unpopular viewpoints. No one wants to hear from someone who thinks that, say, necrophilia is okay. But people still hold those unpopular viewpoints, and, without discussion, who is to say they are not right? I freely admit, there are some topics that I am squeamish about (corophagia, for example). But I shouldn't feel that way, and I wouldn't stop such discussion. And, I do admit that some topics need to be discussed carefully (such as letting young children know about death). But though care may be necessary, an outright taboo is completely overkill. Edit: There seems to be a common misconception here. A taboo is a prevailing societal attitude which discourages someone from bringing up a subject, enforced through societal pressures. Whether you have the right to bring up those topics is an entirely different subject, falling under freedom of speech. Whether anyone listens to you or not is also an entirely different subject, and no one here (not me, certainly, and no one else I've seen) is suggesting that people should be forced to listen. Note: I used "topic of opinion" to avoid issues about discussion of, say, military troop positions and so on, which are not matters of opinion but of information - and such information is important to be kept secret. I do not believe this applies to any matter of opinion.

Object recognition continues to be a vibrant domain within computer vision, witnessing significant progress and accomplishments due to the development of sophisticated deep convolutional neural networks aimed at addressing object identification tasks. However, despite these achievements, deploying such advanced object detection frameworks widely across edge devices and mobile platforms poses substantial obstacles because of their extensive computational demands and memory footprints. Consequently, recent scholarly endeavors have concentrated on crafting more streamlined deep learning models optimized for use in resource-constrained environments like edge computing and mobile applications. This paper introduces YOLO Nano, an exceptionally lightweight deep convolutional neural network engineered for object detection duties. Our innovative approach employs a cooperative human-AI systematic design process to devise YOLO Nano, integrating fundamental design methodologies derived from the YOLO series' single-shot object detection architecture blueprints with algorithmic automation to engineer a remarkably condensed network featuring meticulously designed modules specifically adapted for performing object detection in embedded systems. Remarkably, our newly developed YOLO Nano boasts a mere 4.0MB in terms of model size—a reduction by 15.1% compared to Tiny YOLOv2 and 8.3% relative to Tiny YOLOvEE—and necessitates only 4.57 billion calculations during its inferencing phase, which represents a decrease of 34% vis-à-vis Tiny YOLOv2 and 17% against Tiny YOLOv3. Furthermore, it secures an impressive mean average precision (mAP) score of 69.1% when evaluated using the VOC 2007 dataset, surpassing both Tiny YOLOv2 and Tiny YOLOv3 by 12% and 10.7%, respectively. Empirical trials assessing processing velocity and energy efficiency under varying power constraints conducted on a Jetson AGX Xavier embedded processor corroborate the suitability and effectiveness of YOLO Nano in embedded contexts.

Users have little control of what information is processed and are often left with an all-or-nothing decision between receiving free services or refusing to be profiled. This paper explores an alternative approach where users only disclose an aggregate model - the "gist" - of their data. We aim to preserve data utility and simultaneously provide user privacy. We show that this approach can be efficiently supported by letting users contribute encrypted and differentially-private data to an aggregator. The aggregator combines encrypted contributions and can only extract an aggregate model of the underlying data. We evaluate our framework on a dataset of 100,000 U.S. users obtained from the U.S. Census Bureau and show that (i) it provides accurate aggregates with as little as 100 users, (ii) it generates revenue for both users and data brokers, and (iii) its overhead is appreciably low.

The prediction of a binary sequence is a classic example of online machine learning. We like to call it the "stock prediction problem," viewing the sequence as the price history of a stock that goes up or down one unit at each time step. In this problem, an investor has access to the predictions of two or more "experts," and strives to minimize her final-time regret with respect to the best-performing expert. Probability plays no role; rather, the market is assumed to be adversarial. We consider the case when there are two history-dependent experts, whose predictions are determined by the d most recent stock moves. Focusing on an appropriate continuum limit and using methods from optimal control, graph theory, and partial differential equations, we discuss strategies for the investor and the adversarial market, and we determine associated upper and lower bounds for the investor's final-time regret. When d 4 our upper and lower bounds coalesce, so the proposed strategies are asymptotically optimal. Compared to other recent applications of partial differential equations to prediction, ours has a new element: there are two timescales, since the recent history changes at every step whereas regret accumulates more slowly.
