Imperialism is defined as "A policy of extending a country's power and influence through diplomacy or military force." Imperialism is particularly focused on the control that one group, often a state, has over another. One example would be if America were to become more powerful than any other nation in the world because they have an ideology called capitalism. The primary function of imperialism was to extend the economic dominance of European nations throughout much of Asia and Africa by forcing them to trade with those countries. While there are many reasons for wanting to take advantage of others economically, there are also cultural issues involved. The roots of modern-day colonialism can be found in the desire to learn about the cultures of distant lands, especially Islam and its surrounding culture known as the Middle East. This was done partly due to the large amount of wealth which could be gained from trade with these regions and their unique religious beliefs. Eventually, however, this practice turned into colonizing the lands to make use of the natural resources at hand. Colonists began demanding that people convert to Christianity, which did not reflect the customs of most native cultures. In response, natives attacked colonists out of fear of losing themselves and what only represented a small part of who they truly were. There are many stories regarding conflicts between native populations and colonial powers such as France and Britain during the time period when these countries had colonies around the globe (such as South American Borneo). Europeans felt they needed to protect themselves against the native population since they were used to being able to fight larger armies alone compared to Native Americans who considered themselves "friendly" towards outsiders. The type of weaponry introduced into warfare changed with the introduction of gunpowder weapons, which allowed for firearms to kill even greater numbers of opponents at once. This led to vastly superior forces being fielded whenever the two sides met, leading to bloodshed. Another important factor which influenced colonization was religion. Before Western involvement, Native Americans and Latin Americans lived peaceful lives full of hunting, fishing, farming, trading, and local government. After contact with European settlers, conflict arose among indigenous groups as well as between individual tribes within different territories. For instance, Native Americans believed that it was the duty of Christians to spread Christian doctrine to nonbelievers. However, because of differences in belief systems between different groups of Catholics, Protestants, Jews, etc., there developed an antagonistic relationship where each group viewed itself as superior. Consequently, some Native peoples resisted colonization while others accepted it willingly. It was difficult for a single group to colonize the whole continent; therefore, several groups formed alliances to conquer territory and allow for easier distribution of goods obtained from conquests. When Catholicism became the official state religion for Spain in 1492, its missionaries traveled throughout Central and South America under the guise of bringing the New World to Christ. They massacred native people along the way and took their land so that millions of acres of crops could be grown and exported back to Europe. As stated before, warring between European powers occurred after contact with the New World increased. Trade routes, agricultural technology, and social structures created animosity between the various European states. Once romanticized folklore that portrayed Europeans in heroic light faded away (the fairy tale 'Little Red Riding Hood' depicts wolves as kidnappers) and replaced with harsh reality, hostility between European imperial powers intensified. Their conflict resulted in brutal wars, including the Thirty Years War, that brought devastation upon both Catholic and Protestant areas alike.

We prove the completeness of an axiomatization for differential equation invariants. First, we show that the differential equation axioms in differential dynamic logic are complete for all algebraic invariants. Our proof includes two novel methods: We provide a new definition and interpretation of the generalized principle of equivalence; we recover under this definition how to determine if a representation is commutative from any set C for which F is a subset of all sets, by the usual way (meaning either C or C for every vector space). Next, we use these same definitions to prove that there exists an "incomplete" version of the basic differential equations covering F (an axiomatized version), drawing on recent results about partial order-theorem properties. Finally, using the derivation of fully enumerated Euler-Schmidt identities, we prove that there exist inverse and nonnegative complex conjugate relationships between elements, without that too being incomplete! How do you define what it means to guarantee a certain class of objects? I would say that is this question related to one of the main aims in computational physics - to obtain more accurate descriptions of physical phenomena. The most important goal has been achieved with strongly coupled theories. But even theoretical physicists often need an upper bound on some objective measure of the calculations. So I think it must be clear now that if we want to give such higher bounds, then it makes sense to model them explicitly. And a better understanding of how high values can arise means we will have to extend our models dynamically as well.

The concept of uplink downlink (ULDL) decoupling offers greater flexibility in cell association and improved throughput within heterogeneous networks (HetNets). However, it poses challenges in obtaining downlink channel state information (CSI) in TDD systems because different base stations (BSs) are involved in ULDL. To overcome this issue, our study introduces a new data-assisted (DA) channel estimation technique leveraging decoded uplink (UL) data for extracting CSI from the received UL data signal in separated HetNets featuring numerous MIMO macro cells alongside densely situated micro cells. By calculating the Bit Error Rate (BER) performance of the decoded UL data, we have formulated an approximate Normalized Mean Square Error (NMSE) equation for the DA Minimum Mean Square Error (MMSE) estimator. Our findings indicate that the NMSE effectiveness of various estimators correlates with their Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR)-like factors, revealing that the DA approach surpasses traditional methods under all conditions. This superiority is attributed to its dependence on variables such as increased UL data strength, extended UL data duration, and enhanced BER metrics, resulting in more precise channel estimates using the DA strategy. Validation via numerical simulations confirms the closeness of our theoretical BER and NMSE calculations to actual results, demonstrating significant improvements in both NMSE accuracy and downlink rates across diverse scenarios and modulation types when employing the DA methodology.

We present a dictionary-based approach to racism detection in Dutch social media comments, which were retrieved from two public Belgian social media sites likely to attract racist reactions. These comments are also linked with people's identities via unique Twitter IDs. We construct an automatic algorithm that uses the content of these comments and their sentiment analysis as context features for identifying potentially negative online racial attitudes. The algorithm outputs a list of potentially derogatory terms or other indicators of racism. This is done by first clustering similar comments within each user based on those feature vectors and then applying a Poisson regression model to identify terms that deviate significantly from expected values due to being associated with term clusters. By using this method we identified 1595 potentially negative Dutch expressions about race per 100000 words; of them 930 (60) could be considered as racist depending on existing definitions used elsewhere.

The displays on clocks are made up of seven segment displays. There are seven lines that form the boxed-up figure 8. If we provide power to just one segment, it appears very bright. But powering multiple segments makes the brightness go down. This would cause different numbers to have different brightnesses (eg 8 would be very dim while 1 would be very bright). So, to counteract this, power is provided to only one segment at a time. Now if we had the number 7 on the screen, first the top line would be powered, then the top right and then the bottom right. Then it goes back to the top line. This happens in a matter of milliseconds. Due to persistence of vision, we don't notice that the segments are constantly going on and off. This is the same principle used behind CRT TVs, where the picture is drawn one line at a time from top to bottom but since it happens so fast, you don't notice. When you're eating, the vibrations in your head causes this refreshing to be thrown off, since your head is moving relative to the display. This causes the segments to move apart and the on-off pattern is a lot more apparent. You can try this with a TV too - go in front of a CRT TV and start vibrating your lips (like you're imitating a motorbike) - the whole screen will start going crazy till you stop.

Quantization plays a crucial role in simplifying Deep Neural Network (DNN) inference within edge computing environments. However, conventional uniform and non-uniform quantization techniques face challenges due to the trade-off between representation range and resolution, leading to wasted bits or substantial declines in accuracy. Additionally, they suffer from several limitations, including the lack of a measurable metric for analyzing quantization error sources, their narrow scope focused solely on convolutional neural network (CNN)-based image classification tasks, and ignorance towards actual hardware and energy savings achieved through decreased bit-width usage. This study introduces two quantitative measures—the Clipping Error and Rounding Error—to assess the distribution of quantization errors. These errors are observed to fluctuate notably across layers, models, and tasks. To address this issue, we introduce a groundbreaking quantization approach that optimizes both weights and activations. Our innovative technique, Adaptive Superposed Non-Uniform Quantization (AUSN), comprises a unique encoding mechanism devoid of additional hardware requirements, an adjustable quantization algorithm capable of catering to diverse DNN architectures, tasks, and layers, as well as a rounding strategy designed to prevent common bit-width overflow and re-quantization problems. Extensive theoretical analyses (refer to Appendix A) and performance evaluations on various DNN models demonstrate AUSN's efficacy and broad applicability. Furthermore, our experimental findings reveal that implementing AUSN on Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) yields up to a 50% reduction in energy consumption and 25% to 50% decrease in hardware resources required.

This transformation can be computed from the spectrum of the network Hessian. We argue that the similarity of networks trained on the same dataset arises from their shared expressivity. We conclude by examining some implications for the interpretation of neural networks. In this paper, we provide a comparative study of different methods for making a deep neural network robust to adversarial attacks. We examine the effects of adversarial training, input transformations, and two-stage training in the context of the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets. We conclude that adversarial training is the most effective approach, but also the most computationally expensive. Two-stage training methods are effective, but require additional data. We begin by making a simple modification to the cross-entropy loss function that allows us to learn the transformation parameters simultaneously with the network weights. Our analysis indicates that while the EU has played a significant role in shaping laws promoting fairness, withdrawing from it wouldn't automatically lead to losing these advantages. According to the Treaty of Rome, all participating nations must guarantee "equal compensation for equal labor" between genders. This mandate became even stronger with the introduction of the 1975 Equal Pay Directive, alongside additional judgments made by the European Court of Justice (ECJ) defining equitable employment conditions. Moreover, decisions by the ECJ also established part-time workers' eligibility for joining company retirement plans, declaring their exclusion as gender-based unfair treatment. Should the UK depart from the EU, these regulations might potentially be abolished or altered. Nevertheless, it is worth mentioning that the UK has implemented stricter policies in some instances beyond the minimum requirements dictated by the EU. For instance, the UK offers 52 weeks of paid maternity leave compared to the EU standard of 14 weeks. Proponents of Brexit argue that there's no justification to assume that any forthcoming British administration would compromise female rights. Nonetheless, critics like Ms. Harman contend that leaders advocating for separation – such as Boris Johnson, Nigel Farage, and Iain Duncan Smith – lack credibility when it comes to safeguarding women's interests. Though acknowledging that this aspect of her argument relies partly on conjecture, she cautions that potential rollbacks on women's rights might occur disguised as efforts toward deregulation and bureaucratic simplification.

Search engines utilize an automated tool known as a crawler to record the presence of websites and associated data. These crawlers traverse the web, attempting to reach all available websites and pages. When encountering a hyperlink, the crawler adds it to its list of sites to explore. Ethical programmers instruct their crawlers to look for a "robots.txt" file prior to scanning a website. This file communicates to the crawler whether the site should be excluded from indexing or certain content should not be accessed. Website owners opting for non-indexation risk having their site completely overlooked by compliant crawlers, while those preferring limited visibility will be indexed without revealing specific details about their site, resulting in messages like "This site's robots.txt file prevents further exploration." There are various reasons behind these decisions; privacy concerns, avoidance of additional web traffic, or preference for indexing only primary URLs instead of numerous subsidiary ones.

Although dissertations on clothing and its function appear from the 19th century as colonising countries dealt with new environments, concerted scientific research into psycho-social, physiological and other functions of clothing (e.g. protective, cartage) occurred in the first half of the 20th century, with publications such as J. C. Flugel's Psychology of Clothes in 1930, and Newburgh's seminal Physiology of Heat Regulation and The Science of Clothing in 1949. By 1968, the field of environmental physiology had advanced and expanded significantly, but the science of clothing in relation to environmental physiology had changed little. While considerable research has since occurred and the knowledge-base has grown significantly, the main concepts remain unchanged, and indeed Newburgh's book is still cited by contemporary authors, including those attempting to develop thermoregulatory models of clothing development.

Tracking down every single individual involved in unauthorized downloading proves to be an arduous task, as their actions often don't warrant pursuing legal action due to minimal impact. Targeting bigger entities responsible for multiple infractions is not only easier but also results in higher penalties, which effectively reduces piracy rates more significantly compared to prosecuting lesser-scale offenders. Consequently, lawsuits against numerous individuals aren't practical.

The music industry attempted this approach by selectively targeting certain individuals engaged in file sharing, leading to negative publicity, including cases involving vulnerable parties such as children being unjustly sued. These incidents portrayed the industry as oppressive, utilizing its power against defenseless individuals. As a result, the practice ceased.

In the realm of jurisprudence, there exist civil and criminal courts. Civil disputes typically involve private litigation, similar to those seen on television programs like Judge Judy, through which copyright holders sought compensation from individuals sharing copyrighted materials online. Those accused were never criminally charged nor faced imprisonment. Moreover, while illegally downloading content remains legally questionable without substantial court precedents, authorities tend to focus primarily on those distributing the material.

As such practices became ubiquitous, ceasing to pursue individual downloaders became commonplace. However, prominent figures associated with piracy sites, like The Pirate Bay founders, faced both types of charges - civil and criminal. Their deliberate, extensive violations differ markedly from casually sharing files with friends versus commercial distribution. Additionally, for heinous content available soleptailed activities on the dark web, authorities continue to take action against individual perpetrators.

The first buildings of the University of Chicago campus, which make up what is now known as the Main Quadrangles, were part of a "master plan" conceived by two University of Chicago trustees and plotted by Chicago architect Henry Ives Cobb. The Main Quadrangles consist of six quadrangles, each surrounded by buildings, bordering one larger quadrangle. The buildings of the Main Quadrangles were designed by Cobb, Shepley, Rutan and Coolidge, Holabird Roche, and other architectural firms in a mixture of the Victorian Gothic and Collegiate Gothic styles, patterned on the colleges of the University of Oxford. (Mitchell Tower, for example, is modeled after Oxford's Magdalen Tower, and the university Commons, Hutchinson Hall, replicates Christ Church Hall.)

Warsaw was occupied by Germany from 4 August 1915 until November 1918. The Allied Armistice terms required in Article 12 that Germany withdraw from areas controlled by Russia in 1914, which included Warsaw. Germany did not comply with this, however, not only refusing to withdraw its troops but also incorporating the area into the German Empire as Wartheland. The collapse of Germany in November 1918 saw Poland regain its independence. This was formalised in the Treaty of Versailles in 1919. Germany was forced to relinquish control of Warsaw and the surrounding area, and Poland once again became an independent country.

Initially, let's clarify our understanding of 'dimension' within this framework. We aren't discussing fictional realms where everyone possesses malicious intentions and sport facial hair; that notion belongs solely to the realm of science fiction. Instead, we refer to the quantity of data needed to pinpoint a location. For instance, identifying a residence requires knowledge of its crossroads—Main Street intersecting with Peterson Street serves as an illustration. Consequently, a city map operates on a two-dimensional plane. Yet, should we factor in the building level (e.g., sixth story), we introduce a third dimension. Expanding further, incorporating a scheduled meeting time (say, 4 PM) adds a fourth dimension. Thus, four parameters are necessary to precisely determine one's position in both space and time. This process isn't limited by constraints; we can continue adding details such as a particular room number (like Room 4). Essentially, dimensions represent methods for quantifying the requisite information to identify a given subject. Naturally, they manifest in various scenarios. Often mathematicians employ numerous dimensions while examining their subjects, including concepts applicable beyond traditional spatial limits. These abstract ideas prompt intriguing questions regarding the composition of physical reality. While familiar directions like verticality, lateral movement, and forward/backward motion exist, it remains uncertain whether additional unperceived paths are viable. Focusing exclusively on spatial elements, current evidence suggests only three dimensions exist. Why so? Consider wrapping a uniform layer of clay around a spherical object like a baseball, measuring its thickness. Repeat this experiment with a larger sphere using identical clay mass, resulting in decreased surface coverage due to increased size. Hence, the existence of extra dimensions appears unlikely based on these observations.

The links between religious and political life were vital to Rome's internal governance, diplomacy and development from kingdom, to Republic and to Empire. Post-regal politics dispersed the civil and religious authority of the kings more or less equitably among the patrician elite: kingship was replaced by two annually elected consular offices. In the early Republic, as presumably in the regal era, plebeians were excluded from high religious and civil office, and could be punished for offenses against laws of which they had no knowledge. They resorted to strikes and violence to break the oppressive patrician monopolies of high office, public priesthood, and knowledge of civil and religious law. The senate appointed Camillus as dictator to handle the emergency; he negotiated a settlement, and sanctified it by the dedication of a temple to Concordia. The religious calendars and laws were eventually made public. Plebeian tribunes were appointed, with sacrosanct status and the right of veto in legislative debate. In principle, the augural and pontifical colleges were now open to plebeians. In reality, the patrician and to a lesser extent, plebeian nobility dominated religious and civil office throughout the Republican era and beyond.

Between Bingen and Bonn, the Middle Rhine flows through the Rhine Gorge, a formation which was created by erosion. The rate of erosion equaled the uplift in the region, such that the rocks were pushed down into the river valley as the water flowed over them.ref"The Rhine River Gorge" (1906). Google Books.ref Bingen's first inhabitants lived on both banks; they were farmers who had their fields along the middle bank. These people would often burn wood near the steep cliffs to keep it from falling off to the ravines below. As the Middle Rhine carved away at the natural terrain surrounding Bingen, these hills became increasingly eroded until there remained only about above sea level today. Over this time, the soil was replaced with sand and silt brought downstream by rivers. This process continued for several thousand years before the current summit plateau formed. A broader rock outcrop called Warzburggraben formed just south of the city later during the Neolithic era, and was covered by gravel-rich alluvium deposits when the area began its retreat toward floodplains. Later, the dry land expanded eastward under the influence of glaciers melting elsewhere in Europe. In response, the Rhine gorge gradually grew wider so that more sediment could be deposited onto the incoming stream flow. Eventually, this increased pace of deposition resulted in an overhanging cliff nicknamed "the Spiegelberg," thus giving rise to the name Gebirgsgebiet mountain country. By 7500 BC, the river channel narrowed considerably but retained much of the original form. It widened again between 6300 and 5200BC due to organic materials washed downriver from Melk Abbey. Because the current is not strong enough to push such material back upstream, it was carried instead downhill to form a wetland area known as Langsee Creek, which has played an important part in the history of Bingen ever since. The story involves floods, smallpox epidemics, water control measures, Germanic settlers, Romans, Vikings, Austrians, British, Americans, Japanese, French Canadians, Peruvian Indians, Spanish conquistadors, Russian engineers and miners digging up ore in the 1850s, and finally Nazi scientists using nuclear weapons tests conducted underground in the nearby Gebirgschenke Ptychosolare Chain Area. The resulting radioactive fallout caused cancers among local residents and affected crops, livestock and fish in the upper reaches of the river basin. Harmonic sequences involve sound waves which occasionally intersect in a synchronized manner, producing a pleasing auditory experience. Imagine having two distinct tones; if one tone possesses half the duration of the other, it aligns seamlessly within the latter twice, resulting in an octave interval where the shorter wave appears at a higher pitch. Similarly, if the waves of one sound match thrice those of another, their difference yields a perfect fifth, while a 3:4 relationship forms a perfect fourth. Although these combinations may not resonate as strongly as octaves, they remain melodic due to their mathematical proportions, earning titles like 'perfect fifths' and 'perfect fourths.' For instance, a 4:5 ratio creates a major third, whereas a 5:6 ratio produces a minor third. As we progress towards less harmonious intervals—such as 6:7, approximated to a minor third, or 7:8, approximated to a major second—the resultant sounds become increasingly discordant.

The harmonic sequence also refers to a collection of musical notes attainable through successive overblowing on a wind instrument, enabling musicians to reach exceptionally high frequencies despite their instruments' physical size. To illustrate, let's select a fundamental frequency—a single wavelight—and ascend through subsequent octaves via specific ratios: first doubling to form an octave, followed by steps representing a fifth, a fourth, a major third, a minor third, another minor third, and finally a major second. Commencing with a C note, you would sequentially play its corresponding octave, a G note forming a fifth interval, another octave leading to a higher C note, an E note constituting a major third, a G note creating a minor third, a B-flat note representing another minor third, and ultimately reaching a final C note equivalent to a major second. Consequently, this progression culminates in an eightfold increase in frequency compared to the initial tone.

In essence, major chords comprise a combination of a major third and a minor third, which contributes to their characteristic sonority.

Gene Levoff, the previous senior director of law and corporate security at Apple until September last year, has been charged with securities fraud and is set to appear in court on 16 October. Levoff is accused of trading on inside information, receiving confidential corporate documents from former employee and consultant Robert Scoble, and then selling shares he owned in companies Apple was considering making acquisitions of, according to court documents seen by Reuters. Scoble was a Silicon Valley tech journalist who moved to tech startup UploadVR as a marketing director in 2015 and was eventually fired for allegedly leaking confidential information to Levoff, who was then the executive in charge of corporate security at Apple. According to a complaint filed by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Levoff used a private email account to get information about companies Apple was considering buying, including AMD and Dialog Semiconductor. Scoble told Levoff about Apple's plans to buy Dialog in August 2017 and Levoff sold all his stock in the semiconductor firm a few weeks later, making a profit of about 38,000. Levoff then allegedly received documents from Scoble with financial forecasts and other non-public information about AMD and sold his shares in that company too, before the acquisition was publicly announced in July last year. Levoff used the private email account to contact Scoble because he knew that Scoble had received confidential information in the past from Apple employees and that such information was privileged, the complaint reads. The US Department of Justice also filed a criminal charge against Levoff of one count of securities fraud and he is scheduled to appear in court on 16 October. Levoff said he would plead not guilty to the charges.

Researchers have found that both humans and animals frequently opt for choices that are not strictly aligned with maximizing their anticipated benefits; instead, they tend to select among potential results based on probabilities that correspond proportionally to these expected advantages. This approach, known as "probability matching," aligns closely with what is termed maximum entropy reinforcement learning (MaxEnt RL), although it doesn't necessarily yield optimal utility maximization. Our study demonstrates analytically that MaxEnt RL effectively addresses specific categories of control challenges characterized by fluctuating rewards. We establish that MaxEnt RL can tackle a subset of partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) and equate it to a dualistic competition wherein an opponent determines the reward structure. The implications point towards a more intricate relationship between MaxEnt RL, resilient control strategies, and POMDPs. Furthermore, our findings indicate that environments marked by uncertain objectives could potentially benefit greatly from the application of MaxEnt RL techniques.

We propose Cluster Pruning (CUP) for compressing and accelerating deep neural networks. Our approach prunes similar filters by clustering them based on features derived from both the incoming and outgoing weight connections. With CUP , we overcome two limitations of prior work - (1) non-uniform pruning: CUP can efficiently determine the ideal number of filters to prune in each layer of a neural network. This is in contrast to prior methods that either prune all layers uniformly or otherwise use resource-intensive methods such as manual sensitivity analysis or reinforcement learning to determine the ideal number. (2) Single-shot operation: We extend CUP to CUP-SS (for CUP single shot) whereby pruning is integrated into the initial training phase itself. This leads to large savings in training time compared to traditional pruning pipelines. Through extensive evaluation on multiple datasets (MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Imagenet) and models (VGG-16, Resnets-183456) we show that CUP outperforms recent state of the art. Specifically, CUP-SS achieves 2.2 flops reduction for a Resnet-50 model trained on Imagenet while staying within 0.9 top-5 accuracy. It saves over 14 hours in training time with respect to the original Resnet-50. Code to reproduce results is available here 1 1 footnote 1 .

Considering current understanding of gene mutation rates, it appears highly improbable that every person on Earth could trace their heritage back to just these two individuals within a relatively brief period suggested by traditional narratives. Furthermore, this notion extends beyond mere physical variations like eye color, stature, and complexion; it includes susceptibility to certain illnesses and conditions.

To better comprehend this concept, imagine observing a series of family portraits spanning multiple generations. As we analyze pictures from various points along this timeline - starting from yourself at age 10 and moving backwards through each preceding generation - similarities will likely emerge, indicating familial resemblance. However, as we continue tracing back even further into the past, eventually encountering images depicting non-human predecessors becomes plausible. This illustrates how incremental transformations occur throughout successive generations. Ultimately, finding a representation of a distant ancestor who no longer falls under the classification of Homo sapiens showcases the slow yet constant process of biological adaptation that has shaped our existence.

Jack Ma has been absent from public view for the past two months. His last public appearance was in late October, where he blasted China's regulatory system. This resulted in a massive sell-off on Chinese tech stocks: Alibaba (BABA), Tencent (TCEHY) and Meituan Dianping (3690). Since then, the shares of these three companies have tumbled over 20, and many others such as JD (JD) and Pinduoduo (PDD) are down by even more than that. (Source: Bloomberg) The chart above shows how much all FAANG names underperformed the SP 500 since September 30th when Jack Ma's comments were made public to November 12th. As you can see, it is an ugly picture indeed. Alibaba, which just recently reported record quarterly revenue, saw its stock drop 22 during this time period while Tencent fell 21. The sharp decline in Alibaba caused its market capitalization to fall below 700 billion whereas it had previously reached almost 1 trillion. In the third quarter, Alibaba generated 66 of total revenues from retail sales, with the rest coming from cloud computing services. Looking at online shopping, Taobao Mall continued to lead in terms of sales volume, generating 17.5 billion yuan (2.6 billion) gross merchandise value compared to 16.7 billion yuan in the second quarter. However, as we've seen in our analysis here, mobile commerce still outpaced desktop, with a YoY increase of 48; hence, it would be interesting to closely monitor how Alibaba performs going forward. Tencent also witnessed significant declines in recent weeks following the announcement of new regulations regarding streaming games. We will discuss Tencent further later in this report, but let us focus now on why Jack Ma's decision to criticize the regulators may not impact other businesses like Alibaba or JD.com too significantly. We believe that Jack Ma's criticisms against the current state of China's financial regulation did little to hurt his own business and long term prospects. Taking into account that Jack Ma actually owns 40 of Alibaba along with 39 owned by Yahoo!, the impact on Alibaba appears limited. In fact, it can add fuel to the fire if anything. With the Alibaba share price already suffering due to the crackdowns, there could well be some bargain hunting opportunities available among shareholders who want to take advantage of the "sell first ask questions later" mentality prevalent today. On December 9th alone, Alibaba's stock traded down 10 and only recovered after CEO Daniel Zhang said that the company intends to use its cash reserves to buy back up to 100 million American Depositary Shares worth up to 10 billion. It should also be mentioned that Jack Ma stepped down from the board of directors of Alibaba in August 2019; however, he remains its biggest shareholder. Due to this, it makes sense that any action taken against him would probably be taken through the Alibaba board rather than being directed directly at him personally. Just look at the reaction to the Larry Ellison scandal last year, or the allegations against Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg earlier this year - both cases show that companies tend to respond better if they know that their top executives are standing behind them and supporting whatever actions they decide upon. Therefore, given Jack Ma's status as the largest individual investor in Alibaba alongside co-founder Joe Tsai, it is highly unlikely that his criticism would be reflected throughout the entire business. Although Alibaba is growing strongly, the regulatory scrutiny placed on it in the recent months could actually help accelerate growth among smaller competitors. From a macro perspective, however, this does not seem likely in the near future. While China is set to achieve its goal of becoming the world leader in 5G technology within the next few years, the country seems reluctant to open itself fully to foreign firms offering internet services. Many Chinese consumers simply don't trust Western brands anymore; therefore, it is difficult to imagine them switching away completely. Furthermore, while the current powerplay between the government and private sector could cause problems for entrepreneurs, one thing is certain; if the ruling party wishes to maintain its absolute control over society, it needs to keep economic growth strong enough so that people continue blaming someone else instead of questioning the political direction of the country. Even though, as we discussed in a previous article, excessive censorship and consolidation of wealth amongst the Communist Party elite might eventually come back to bite the economy, the risk of doing nothing far outweighs the potential benefits of cracking down harder on private enterprise. As always, readers should do additional research before making investment decisions. I took out my phone to show them an episode where my character Hunson Abadeer turns into a horrific monster with a frightening visage complete with tentacles and horns and a gaping mouth resembling a toothed vagina. I murmured under my breath. I must have had too much to drink. I loosened my tie and carefully walked back downstairs to go home. Bio-inspired robotics endeavors to develop mechanical constructs that emulate the mechanisms and principles observed in living organisms. Replicating certain intricate biological processes such as maintaining equilibrium within an internal setting via a skin-like barrier poses significant difficulties for these mechanical systems. Such a robot could control its inner workings, heal itself utilizing its internal ecosystem, and shield its components against external factors. In this study, we introduce a non-holonomic wheeled framework that achieves stability through a completely interconnected interior safeguarded by a pliable covering. Our goals include investigating how natural selection may have led to advanced lifeforms with wheeled appendages under specific evolutionary stages; defining characteristics of a robot equipped with a self-regulating wheel mechanism; and assessing whether employing a self-maintaining wheel as a means of movement holds potential.

There are two ways to think of light when looking at something. It either generates light itself, like a light bulb or the sun, or it's showing reflected light, like an image on a mirror. The amount of energy needed for creating light depends on what kind of material you're using and how much mass is in that object too. Light can be made from hydrogen atoms bouncing off each other, but this process produces heat instead of light. In comparison, ice creates heat as opposed to light-emitting photons. Ice reflects sunlight more than water does; basically, materials reflect different wavelengths of light depending on their density, which explains why they warm up if we leave them outside in direct sunshine. These differences allow us to tell certain objects apart based on where they were created - so rocks are easier to spot because they've been heated by volcanic eruptions while sand might have originated near a riverbed. We also know about stars with planets orbiting around them via variations in temperature and brightness caused mainly by the star's particles reflecting some part of its light back into space (known as gravitational lensing). This provides information not just about the star itself, but also about any exoplanets passing through or even surrounding it. And telescopic observations could help discover new types of gases in the atmosphere of rocky planets. Even though we will never travel to another system and see all these things directly ourselves, there may still be clues available within our own solar system. Astronomers use tools similar to those used earlier to detect possible moons orbiting Jupiter: for example photometry is measuring the variation between different parts of a planet. If a moon passes across one side of the planet during a transits would scientists notice? Light Doppler shifts indicate changes in distance to celestial bodies and thus reveal the presence of exoplanets and distant galaxies. So far, astronomers haven't found many exo-planets beyond Earth, but maybe revisiting old data stored away under dusty shelves or buried in archives will yield useful clues. What else do astronomers need to uncover hidden worlds?

The World Economic Forum's'Future of Jobs Report' surveys corporate executives in 35 countries around the world about how they think the workforce will change in the next five years. Its findings are sobering: The rapid pace of technological advance is going to have a big impact on jobs and skills, possibly upending entire industries from one Day 1. For example, nearly three-quarters (73) believe that artificial intelligence, advanced robotics, 3D printing, virtual reality or other new technologies have "strong potential" for reducing human labor needs over the next decade - while only 14 say these advances have no such effect nor do any harm at all. And almost half (47, compared with 11 who don't) predict that technology - rather than unemployment itself - will be responsible for most net job losses during this period; just 4 expect it to create most new opportunities. This means we may soon see an even greater divergence between winners like tech titans Google and Amazon, which can enjoy low cost-per-employee because their staffs consist mainly of robots and software engineers as opposed to fleshy humans, and losers like Boeing, whose planes require lots of skilled manual workers but face increasing competition from cheaper self-driving cars and drone delivery services. As a society, it's important not simply to figure out whether people actually lose jobs due to automation but also what kinds of careers need protection and where we might use the newly freed up time more productively, argues Thrun. The precise details vary from state to state, but here's the basics. You need to occupy and use a piece of land for a set term of years (usually 20). During that time, you need to fence it off, mow it regularly and, if there's anyone else with an equally legitimate claim to the land, give them a notice to quit. At the end of the time, you file a claim with the county, and that's it: You own it. You may be thinking, "Cool! I've got a swath of land that I've been looking at for years. Let me get started!" Before you get too excited, remember: The land in question needs to be completely abandoned. No one can claim it, no one has claimed it and no one has used it for years. And it needs to be unoccupied. You can't just go out and claim a piece of land because you want it. There has to be no one else in the world who can claim that same piece of land. So, who is this land for? It's for the person who can find an unclaimed piece of land and then go through all the legal steps to claim it. This is most likely to be the owner of a property that adjoins the abandoned land, or a local government. For the average person, the process is impractical, and often impossible. But let's say you've found a piece of land that you believe is unclaimed and abandoned. What then? Well, you're going to need to consult a real estate attorney. There are a lot of legalities and a lot of paperwork involved. You'll need to file notices, you'll need to make your claim with the county, and you'll need to defend your claim against anyone else who might try to stake a claim. You'll need to make sure you understand the law of the state where the land is located. In short, claiming land can be legally difficult and confusing. Most people who do it are lawyers themselves, or have the money to pay one. But the upside is, you can make money. If you manage to claim a piece of land, you can sell it for quite a bit more than you paid. If you're really clever, you might even start your own business by buying abandoned land and reselling it, or you might buy a chunk of land and use it for yourself. Due to these advantages, the 4-cylinder triple-expansion engine gained significant traction within the maritime industry, particularly amongst grand oceanic vessels like those belonging to the Olympic class. Bathroom scales come in two types: analog mechanical, such as those found online ([URL1](https://www.example.com)), or digital. Regardless of their design, both varieties function based on the principle of measuring weight through the compression of a spring or similar device, which responds to the pressure exerted by an individual's body weight above it. As weight constitutes a force capable of causing movement, applying this force to a spring under specific conditions allows us to express the relationship between the applied force (F) and the spring's compression (x) using the formula F = kx, where 'k' represents the spring constant. By incorporating the gravitational acceleration ('g', approximately equal to 9.81 ms^2), the equation transforms into mgkx. Consequently, with the knowledge of values 'k' and 'g', determining an object's mass ('m') becomes possible by simply observing the extent of the spring's compression ('x'). This explains why many bathroom scales struggle to detect minimal weight variations; if an individual's mass is relatively low, the resulting spring compression will also be slight, rendering the scale unable to accurately gauge such minute differences. Although bathroom scales primarily aim to display weight, individuals often seek noticeable fluctuations rather than minuscule alterations, such as three pounds instead of fractions thereof. For instance, our school possesses a highly precise wrestling scale that registers weight down to the nearest hundredth of a pound. Hence, manufacturers tend to opt for less precision in order to cut costs.

He scooted cautiously closer to the arch and came face-to-face with a dead body floating headless above the water. The family of the late former Australian cricket captain and legendary cricket commentator Richie Benaud has rejected an offer from Prime Minister Tony Abbott for a state funeral. "Our father was a very private person and while he had great respect for the office of Prime Minister, he would have been uncomfortable with the attention that a state funeral would bring," the family said. Instead, they asked that any public tribute be "in keeping with the style and dignity which he brought to every part of his life." Mr Abbott said he respected the family's decision, saying "Richie Benaud was a great man and a great Australian. I understand and accept the decision of the Benaud family." Benaud, who captained Australia in 28 Test matches between 1958 and 1964, is widely regarded as one of the greatest cricketers of all time. He believes there is a strong possibility that a vote in the assembly will take place due to its potential implications on Welsh laws. Although the court determined that Prime Minister Theresa May couldn't activate Article right away without approval from MPs and Lords, they acknowledged that UK ministers aren't mandated by law to confer with the devolved governments. The potassium and sodium ion concentrations are what cause the neuron to fire. Or actually they allow the action potential to propagate along the nerve. A nerve cell starts off with a hyperpolarized membrane, which is then depolarizes through Ca2 influx from an external source (usually calcium ions). In turn this causes the proton and electron "anions" in the cell's inner workings (phosphorylation) to be swept out of equilibrium by the influx of negative charge coming into contact with its negatively charged neighbors. This process goes on until you have reached a point where electrical conduction across the cell becomes impossible due to the high voltage applied. At that time there will no longer be any net flow of protons or electrons between neighboring cells - any more positive charges would attract their oppositely charged neighbor (s), while negative charges repel each other. This can't last forever as it gives way to a breakdown state called conductance loss. In short we're dealing with continuous decay at some level (even if we don't know how much yet; we just need to figure it out someday!).

Mahmoud Amir Alagha is working in four dimensions to capture digitally the way partial paralysis affects people's expressions. His research is supported by the university which awarded him a scholarship and supported him when, as a refugee from the conflict in Syria, he applied for permission to stay in the UK. Mahmoud began studying in Glasgow in 2014 but was only able to complete his postgraduate course because he received a fee-waiver scholarship from the university. The 28-year-old graduated with distinction in his Masters degree and hopes to take his research to a higher level. He is currently applying to do his PhD and the UK government has given him leave to remain for five years. Mahmoud has been using technology developed in Scotland to capture 3D images of moving faces. "This is stepping into the fourth dimension," he says. "Capturing 3D images over time." After capturing the images he superimposes a digital mask. "This mask is composed of points, could be thousands," Mahmoud says. "It is a mathematical construction so you can do decimation to make more points or reduce the number of points. "It depends how much is really clinically significant." Those thousands of reference points highlight how our faces move, or fail to move, because of injury, conditions such as Bell's Palsy or the aftermath of surgery, which can cause facial paralysis. Mahmoud say this technique could provide pointers to the correct treatment. He says: "Muscles move the face. There are a very big number of muscles. "Being able to decode the face by region, for example, you can know that this muscle that is being supplied by that branch of the nerve is being affected because it is paralysed or is weak. "Being able to study the region rather than the whole face, or both of them, gives us a new dimension into the management of these cases." Mahmoud, who is from war-torn Aleppo, was half way through his masters degree when he became a refugee. He says: "By the end of the first year, the situation in Syria got mad. I had driven past the decrepit, shitty building at least a thousand times since moving into the apartment complex it sat next to, constantly polluting the space in which I lived. I had always assumed it was abandoned, as the windows were boarded up and there was no sign of life inside. But one day, I noticed a small flicker of light coming from inside. Curiosity getting the better of me, I parked my car and approached the building. As I got closer, I could see that there was indeed someone inside, moving around with a flashlight. Fighting the urge to turn away and forget about what I had seen, I knocked on the door. After a few moments of silence, the door creaked open, revealing a man in his 50s with a wild beard and unkempt hair. "What do you want?" he growled. "I just wanted to make sure everything was okay," I replied, trying to sound as friendly as possible. "I've never seen anyone in here before." The man eyed me suspiciously for a moment, then shrugged. "I'm just fixing some stuff up," he said gruffly. "Nothing to worry about." I nodded, feeling relieved but still uneasy. "Well, if you need any help or anything, just let me know. I live right over there," I gestured towards my apartment complex. As I turned to leave, the man called after me. "Hey, kid... thanks." I smiled and waved, feeling like I had made a small difference in someone's day. From then on, I often left a friendly note or a plate of food by the building, just to let the man know that someone cared.

Kate was out for a jog. On the way back it started to rain. She ran faster to make it home sooner. She still got soaked. Kate figured the intense heat and humidity in Miami made her sweat more than normal. She didn't tell anyone, just kept on running until she reached her apartment building. The weather wasn't too hot when they were finally home; however, despite wearing long sleeves and linen pants with leggings underneath, the temperature felt like it could have been much warmer by now. KATE walks into her bedroom where there is a picture of herself from this summer hanging on the wall, but no shirt or shorts. Her mom walked in immediately after seeing that and said "you look totally different!" KATE then turned around and looked at herself in the mirror; she had gotten rid of most of her clothes except for one pair of boxers she wore every day. Her face was very pale and her lips were puffy. The skin under her eyes looked really old as well. Kate began to feel miserable while thinking about how cold she must be. "I wish I could get off work today and go back to school. Please Mom, don't take away my credits again...please don't do that..." Her mother came inside so quickly that she couldn't even say anything before Kate saw the look of horror on her daughter's face. The doorbell rang, and Kate rushed outside to answer it while her mom went back upstairs. In spite of feeling shy once she arrived home, Kate emerged while her mom was putting things away to see who it was. As soon as she opened up the front door, Kate recognized the person looking at her. For the first time in almost two years, she noticed him without his glasses - he was perfectly clean-shaven. He had his own car parked right next to hers with only a few signs showing his name written on the bumper. His black hair was cut short, and Kate thought he might have gotten a little cold since he left his jacket on the seat in front of their house. But at least he hadn't stolen any packages yet. It kind of made sense though because he wouldn't be able to leave his car unlocked all the time anyway. "Hey Kate, why are you here? Why isn't your dad coming over tonight?" "Hi Paulie, I guess we should go tell him what happened." Paul stepped forward and took Kate's hands. His arms felt warm against them, and he was also tight against her body. While they stood there on the stoop, his gaze never wavered towards Kate's feet. Instead, he seemed completely focused on looking through the open window of their neighbor's house. Instead of saying something, Kate simply let Paul hug her tightly. Then she kissed his cheek getting ready to run inside to call an Uber. When she turned around she realized that Paul had stopped walking and just sat down beside her on the step. "You didn't sign up for this, did you? Don't worry, I won't give up anytime soon" "We can always find someone else" After hearing those words, Kate realized that Paul has already fallen asleep. Letting go of Kate's hand, she decided not to wake him up.

Google's DeepMind AI team has successfully trained its software to control a tokamak. Small reactors like tokamaks use software to monitor the state of the plasma they contain and respond accordingly when needed. A group of researchers have successfully developed an artificial intelligence algorithm that can, for the first time in history, be used to control a tokamak reactor. The tokamak is a small reactor with a magnetic field inside which electrons are trapped, causing them to move around, creating atomic nuclei. The research was carried out by the Artificial Intelligence Research Group (AIRG) at Google-backed DeepMind Technologies. It has been presented at this year's Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR). The paper itself describes the controlled reaction as "a simple, nonpointed coating method for making fluorescent materials glow under ultraviolet light." In fact, it would have been easier just to model the chemical reactions occurring inside the tokamak - but the researchers only need to address one problem: how do you steer the robot towards the desired object? To solve this, they use deep learning techniques that allow the computer to process large amounts of data very quickly. They then apply these skills to a standard programming language called Python. They create a neural network suitable for controlling the tokamak using the information stored from previous experiments with fireflies. The system responds instantly to changes in the environment and makes decisions based on what the machine knows about the environment and its data. In other words, it learns over time without needing to look up complex equations or formulas. It could also be a game changer. For example, if we want our robots to navigate through tunnels or water, all we need to do is write down how long each path takes and how much power the robot needs to travel in order to reach the end point. This could make things far more efficient than using an extremely complicated equation. I'm assuming you have some knowledge of programming, judging from your question, so I'll try to pitch my answer at the right level, and not at a 5-year-old! The concept behind functional programming is that each time you call a function with the same parameters, it returns the same result. In order to accomplish this, functional programming languages must not hold any kind of state. For example, a function add (a, b) which adds a to b and returns the sum is fine. A function addtoaccount (a, accountno), which gets the balance of an account then adds a to it is not, because it returns different values depending on the current balance of the account. The advantage of this is that it makes code easier to test, more predictable, and therefore, in theory, more reliable. Functional programming can indeed use objects, but only immutable objects, that is to say the objects can not store or maintain any kind of state. Now, on to object oriented programming, which is all about encapsulation - creating objects and classes that encapsulate real-world concepts, and keep all the functionality of that concept together. Object oriented programming is a type of imperative programming, meaning that it stores state - in the case of object oriented programming, state is saved in the objects' member variables. Object oriented code can use functions. They can even be "pure" functions in a functional programming sense - but they don't have to be. Let's imagine that we have an account object. We can create a function to return the balance of our account. This function could return a different value each time we call it, depending on what the balance is. This would not be allowed in a functional language. Hope that's broken down enough for you! The light detection and ranging (LiDAR) technology allows to sense surrounding objects with fine-grained resolution in a large areas. Their data (aka point clouds), generated continuously at very high rates, can provide information to support automated functionality in cyberphysical systems. Clustering of point clouds is a key problem to extract this type of information. Methods for solving the problem in a continuous fashion can facilitate improved processing in e.g. fog architectures, allowing continuous, streaming processing of data close to the sources. We propose Lisco , a single-pass continuous Euclidean-distance-based clustering of LiDAR point clouds, that maximizes the granularity of the data processing pipeline. Besides its algorithmic analysis, we provide a thorough experimental evaluation and highlight its up to 3x improvements and its scalability benefits compared to the baseline, using both real-world datasets as well as synthetic ones to fully explore the worst-cases.

A recent study released by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has revealed a remarkable decline in birth rates in the United States over the past decade. According to the report, the U.S. birth rate has dropped 12 percent since 2007, with the nation's total fertility rate falling to its lowest level since 1978. The fertility rate measures the estimated number of children a woman will have during her lifetime. The study also found that the average age of first-time mothers has increased from 25.1 years old in 2007 to 26.3 years old in 2018. This is the oldest median age at which women gave birth since the CDC began tracking this data in 1940. The sharp decline in birth rates is likely due to a combination of factors, such as an aging population, rising costs of living, and changing social norms about having children. In addition, the Great Recession of 2008 may have played a role in dissuading people from starting families. Experts say the declining birth rate could have far-reaching economic implications, as it could lead to slower economic growth and labor shortages in the future. It could also put pressure on the government to provide more support for aging populations, including those relying on Social Security and Medicare benefits. Despite the decline in births, the U.S. still has one of the highest fertility rates among developed countries. The report also noted that the drop in births was not seen across every demographic group. Women ages 30-34 and 35-39 saw increases in their birth rates, while all other age groups experienced a decrease. Overall, the study underscores the importance of understanding why the U.S. birth rate is declining, and how this trend is likely to affect the country in the coming years.

I'm not here to say that this is completely true and that if you 're well versed in something, do it instead; but rather I want to talk about specialization: The more specialized you are at one thing or another, the less likely you'll be able to understand other things as deeply. If your only skill is programming, for example (or just coding), then you will lack experience with things ranging from system administration to web design. You have no idea what's going on behind the scenes because you don't know how the pieces fit together. On top of this, unless you get really good at everything else, you won't make much money doing generalist work anyway. It may seem like an easier decision when you think "I could make 150hr working as a programmer," but after taxes and business expenses you should realistically expect to never make over 60k for any real time period - even higher-paying specialties such as finance still pay poorly relative to their supply demand. This doesn't mean we should avoid specializing! There are many situations where specialization can (and does) work out very nicely. Just keep these things in mind...

We consider the problem of automated assignment of papers to reviewers in conference peer review, with a focus on fairness and statistical accuracy. Our fairness objective is to maximize the review quality of the most disadvantaged paper, in contrast to the commonly used objective of maximizing the total quality over all papers. We design an assignment algorithm based on an incremental max-flow procedure that we prove is near-optimally fair. Our statistical accuracy objective is to ensure correct recovery of the papers that should be accepted. We provide a sharp minimax analysis of the accuracy of the peer-review process for a popular objective-score model as well as for a novel subjective-score model that we propose in the paper. Our analysis proves that our proposed assignment algorithm also leads to a near-optimal statistical accuracy. Finally, we design a novel experiment that allows for an objective comparison of various assignment algorithms, and overcomes the inherent difficulty posed by the absence of a ground truth in experiments on peer-review. The results of this experiment corroborate the theoretical guarantees of our algorithm.

People frequently refer to "the dark side" instead of "the far side" of the moon due to our planet's gravitational lock with Earth, resulting in the same duration for both a lunar day and a lunar orbit. This causes us to observe only one hemisphere of the moon. The other portion, known as the far side, remained unseen until spacecraft could enter lunar orbits. Conversely, the term 'dark side' signifies the region not receiving direct light or experiencing nighttime at any given moment, constituting roughly half the moon's surface minus a small fraction. These two sides coincide solely during a full moon phase. Some believe the term 'dark side' stems from this alignment; however, the correct reason lies in the moon's synchronous rotation, revealing only one face towards us while concealing the opposite side. Although the hidden side experiences darkness periodically, it receives equal amounts of sunlight compared to the visible side. Therefore, saying the 'dark side' refers to perpetual darkness would be incorrect. Additionally, when observing a quarter illuminated moon, approximately three-quarters of the far side would actually be bathed in sunlight."

China blocked Wikipedia in April, using DNS injections to prevent its citizens from accessing the encyclopedia. There has been no official statement as to why the website was blocked. In August 2011, 440,000 users in China were affected by a DDoS attack that originated from China. The attack lasted for over 24 hours. In January 2012, The Register reported that in order to circumvent censorship in China, users were using VPNs. It was also reported that several VPN providers were operating in China, in violation of local law. The government's censorship of Wikipedia has been criticized by other websites, such as Google. In April 2011, Google's then-President Eric Schmidt expressed concern about the block on Wikipedia. Schmidt said, "If you're a user in China and you want to look up some information on the Web, the Wikipedia entry for, say, a human rights lawyer in China is blocked. That's something we think is wrong." In August 2011, Google launched a project called "We the Internet" to encourage Chinese people to "provide, share, and organize information about their lives." Organizers hoped that the initiative would "create a more open, more transparent, and more accountable China." However, the project was reportedly canceled in September 2011. In October 2011, a statement was released by the Wikipedia Foundation, calling for a "Chinese Wikipedia" to be established. The statement said, "We understand the concerns about the censorship of the Chinese Wikipedia and understand that China does not allow open, uncensored discussion on its Internet." In November 2011, China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said, "The Chinese government never interferes in other countries' Internet governance, and does not control their domestic Internet." In February 2012, Google announced it was suspending operations in China, in part due to pressure from the Chinese government. The Chinese government has been accused of censoring news, including censoring Wikipedia. In September 2012, Google shut down its Chinese search engine, Google.cn. On November 1, 2012, Google removed Google.cn from its list of search engines, citing "technical problems." Google was not permitted to make a statement about the removal, and the official explanation for the removal was that "the Chinese government is concerned about the company's ties to the Communist Party." Google.cn was replaced by a link to Google's global search engine. On February 1, 2013, Google resumed censored searches in China, this time by setting up a censorship circumvention tool, known as the "tor" system, which allows users to bypass the site's ban on certain keywords. In May 2013, the China Internet Network Information Center (CNNIC) reported that Chinese users had accessed more than 100 million Wikipedia articles. On May 23, 2013, a Wikipedia article about a popular Chinese singer was removed from the Chinese version of Wikipedia. The article, which was about the singer and her performance at the 2013 Cannes Film Festival, was removed for a reason that has not been made public. On July 21, 2013, the Wikipedia website was banned in China. The site's operator, the Wikimedia Foundation, announced that the site had been blocked in China, with no explanation. The Chinese government denied the claim. On July 22, 2013, the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced that the Chinese government was in the process of developing a "Chinese Wikipedia." The announcement stated that the project was in its early stages and that "the Chinese government does not control the domestic Internet in China, and does not censor Internet information." However, the announcement did not clarify whether the project would be an independent encyclopedia or a "Chinese version" of Wikipedia. The government also stated that the government did not ban Wikipedia, and that "China does not interfere in other countries' Internet governance." The Ministry of Foreign Affairs later clarified that the Chinese government was not blocking Wikipedia. The project has been criticized by human rights groups and the European Union. In November 2013, the European Union requested that the Chinese government provide more information about the project. In April 2014, the project was suspended, and it was unclear whether it would resume. In October 2014, the project was revived. In July 2015, the Chinese government reportedly removed some pages about Chinese celebrities from Wikipedia. In February 2016, the Chinese government reported that it had blocked Wikipedia for 336,906 times in 2015, with 96 percent of the blockings occurring in China.

Current 6D object pose estimation methods usually require a 3D model for each object. These methods also require additional training in order to incorporate new objects. As a result, they are not easily applicable to new object categories. In this paper, we present a novel approach to pose estimation using monocular depth images. We first learn a mapping between a 3D model and a 2D image, and then regress the camera pose. Our method is able to estimate the pose of an object from an image without having to use a 3D model. This paper investigates the opportunities and limitations of adaptive virtual machine (VM) migration to reduce communication costs in a virtualized environment. We introduce a new formal model for the problem called Network VM Migration, which allows us to study related problems such as cooperation between multiple VMs on different physical hosts or mutual resource sharing among more than one host simultaneously. Two techniques are presented that allow users to migrate individual VM instances from one host to another without losing any state information about them: 1 - A port-based technique is used to apply an IP address change operation at each physical host level; 2 - An ActivePassive mechanism based upon specific ports is applied when moving entire VM instance groups. The results show that these two approaches have their own advantages while also showing some important tradeoffs. Existing attempts to efficiently move large numbers of VMs seek ways to preserve VM states during the process. However, this approach has several drawbacks, including making cost calculations difficult because it is not possible to accurately estimate the number of copies needed to run all the applications on a given system before migrating its resources. In addition, existing methods often require end users to modify network traffic topology configurations manually even though they can be automated by using techniques such as virtual router forwarding [22]. This work addresses these challenges through a novel set of protocols, the Application Signal Protocol (ASP), designed specifically for moving data streams across many hosts within a virtualized network. ASP then enables application designers to specify how exactly they want to distribute their workloads to avoid bottlenecks caused by unbalanced load and inefficient utilization of available links. In our experiments we found that the use of ASP was successful with respect to both latency violations and overall CPU usage, improving efficiency just enough so that VM migrations could still meet SLAs and throughput targets under heavy loads.

During the 78 rpm era, several companies experimented with creating breakable or non-standard records using unique materials. For instance, Nicole records composed of celluloid coated on a cardboard core began being produced in the UK starting in 1904; however, they had excessive surface noise levels. Around the same time, in 190right, Columbia Records launched flexible, fiber-core "Marconi Velvet Tone Record" pressings in the USA, offering quieter playback if maintained properly with specialized equipment. Nevertheless, this venture didn't succeed. By the 1930s, Germany’s Phonycord and Britain's Filmophone and Goodson records emerged, utilizing slender, pliable plastic—but these too quickly disappeared. Similarly, the French Pathe Cellodiscs crafted from thin, dark plastic closely mirroring the vinyl "sound sheet" magazines prevalent at that period met the same fate. Meanwhile, in America, Hit of the Week records - transparent plastic known as Durium applied over a robust brown paper base - hit the market in early 1930. These weekly releases, comparable to magazines in distribution, initially thrived due to low prices, only to succumb to the economic downturn and cease production by 1932. Durium records persisted slightly longer in other countries, including until 1950 in Italy when it still served as a brand identifier on conventional vinyl records. Nonetheless, despite these inventive endeavors, traditional shellac mixtures remained the primary material choice for most 78 rpm record production throughout its lifespan.

A new approach for robust H filtering for a class of Lipschitz nonlinear systems with time-varying uncertainties both in the linear and nonlinear parts of the system is proposed in an LMI framework. The admissible Lipschitz constant of the system and the disturbance attenuation level are maximized simultaneously through convex multiobjective optimization. The resulting H filter guarantees asymptotic stability of the estimation error dynamics with exponential convergence and is robust against nonlinear additive uncertainty and time-varying parametric uncertainties. Explicit bounds on the nonlinear uncertainty are derived based on norm-wise and element-wise robustness analysis.

"I am saying the investigation team into the murder of Jock Davison would remain open minded as to who is responsible," he told a news conference. The detective also appealed for "those with influence in the community to use all their efforts to reduce tension and appeal for calm and restraint at this very difficult time." I don't often remember my dreams, and even when I do they don't make much sense. This dream was no different - there was a beautiful woman in my dream, and I saw several stages of her life. I had never seen her before, but after dreaming of her I could tell you her whole life story. There was a connection between the woman and myself, even though all I had done was watch her. I regretted letting it go as I drifted awake..... Wait, drifted? Is that sunlight? Why don't I hear my alarm? I'm going to be late for school! I sat up quickly, blankets falling around my waist, but stopped moving when I noticed my surroundings. I was naked. I never slept naked. Quickly, I pulled the sheets back up to cover my chest. The bed I was in was huge. I slept in a twin, why was I naked in a queen size bed in a room I didn't recognize? As I looked around, I saw little things that proved I was supposed to be there. A picture of my parents on the dresser. My brother's photo right next to it. Wait, why is he so old? The strangest thing was the woman who had been in my dreams sitting at the foot of the bed, buttoning her shirt. She must have noticed that I was awake, because she looked back at me and smiled. "Good morning, Claire," she said. "Who are you? Where am I? Why am I here? I'm missing school!" Just for a second, a crestfallen expression crossed her face. She quickly smiled again, though. "Claire, you're not in school anymore. You're 38 years old. I'm Teresa, and this is the house we live in now." She handed me a book, and I opened it to find an album. Starting with my high school graduation, there were pictures detailing my life up to, what I assumed to be, the current point. Memories came flooding back. I was 38. Teresa and I were married. We had a child. A child! "Aeru..... has Aeru left for school yet?" I asked. "It's Saturday, Claire, Aeru is downstairs watching cartoons." I sighed in relief. Plenty of time to spend with her while I was still here. "I dreamed about you last night," I said as I crawled out of the bed to find clothes. I had to open a few dresser drawers before finding what I wanted. "I didn't know who you were, but I loved you just the same."

Multilevel modeling extends traditional modeling techniques with a potentially unlimited number of abstraction levels. Multilevel models can be formally represented by multilevel typed graphs whose manipulation and transformation are carried out by multilevel typed graph transformation rules. These rules are cospans of three graphs and two inclusion graph homomorphisms where the three graphs are multilevel typed over a common typing chain. In this paper, we show that typed graph transformations can be appropriately generalized to multilevel typed graph transformations improving preciseness, flexibility and reusability of transformation rules. We identify type compatibility conditions, for rules and their matches, formulated as equations and inequations, respectively, between composed partial typing morphisms. These conditions are crucial presuppositions for the application of a rule for a match - based on a pushout and a final pullback complement construction for the underlying graphs in the category Graph - to always provide a well-defined canonical result in the multilevel typed setting. Moreover, to formalize and analyze multilevel typing as well as to prove the necessary results, in a systematic way, we introduce the category Chain of typing chains and typing chain morphisms.
