Oculus has announced business versions of their VR headsets, designed for enterprise use. The Oculus Go for business will start at 599 (64 GB) and the Oculus Quest for enterprise can be had in a 3-pack starting at 2,199 each. The new 'Go' is small enough to fit into any backpack or briefcase you don't mind leaving behind when travelling with it, but still powerful enough that users won't notice its lack of processing power compared to its more common consumer cousin. As well as having integrated LTE support, there's also a built-in battery pack so you'll never have to worry about recharging again while on the go - which should save you some precious time over your lunch break. It also supports USB Type C for charging too, making these headsets easily compatible across most laptops and tablets thanks to the standard used by both Apple and Android mobile devices today. Unlike previous generations though, all three models include full positional tracking, meaning you're able to move around freely inside virtual environments without getting dizzy like other VR solutions using cameras mounted above the headset itself. This means business users who want access to those high end experiences are no longer tied down to just sitting in front of a PC like they've done before. Also unlike other VR options currently available, it doesn't require an expensive gaming rig or massive setup space either: our tests showed the device running smoothly even on the lowest graphical settings; this only increases with higher resolutions. It comes complete with two controllers, enabling hands-free movement within games during gameplay whilst also letting developers integrate voice chat functions directly into game design via ambient audio technology called Solace Audio in order to improve immersion even further. Plus, because of the way the lenses themselves are positioned beneath the face instead of up top like older Rift and Vive technologies do, you won't need bulky goggles anymore if comfort is important. All the better, then, for office workers working away from home whose offices may not offer much room to play around in anyway! For now though we're limited to just one version of the Oculus Go - 4K at 60Hz resolution on Qualcomm Snapdragon 710 processor hardware paired with 2GB RAM and 32GB onboard storage - though Oculus plans to release additional chipset variants later on in 2019. While early reviews seem positive overall, UK customers looking forward to buying the headset online through Amazon haven't been given confirmation yet whether it'll launch here alongside the US launch on July 11th.

Bears experience something called "torpor," rather than true hibernation. During torpor, they periodically wake up and move around within their dens over the course of winter months. Despite being mostly immobile, bears manage to retain muscle mass to a greater extent compared to humans who remain inactive for extended periods. Some possible explanations could involve bear metabolism utilizing stored nitrogen to produce proteins or shivering-induced muscle contractions due to low temperatures inside the den.

True hibernators, such as certain amphibians, exhibit drastically reduced bodily functions, which includes preventing muscle degradation during their dormant state. Emerging from hibernation, these animals often display improved physical condition, particularly regarding muscle fiber composition. This phenomenon has sparked research interest among scientists, aiming to uncover the underlying mechanisms responsible for preserving muscle health during prolonged inactivity. While the specific factors contribright now causing this are not completely understood, investigations into animal hibernation offer valuable insights applicable to various fields, including medicine and space exploration.

However, he managed to get out and got into his car, driving off erratically. A short while later, he crashed into another car, injuring the driver. He then got out of his own car and began stabbing the other driver 39 times. The victim, a father-of-two in his 40s, died at the scene. Businessman Simon Wingett is trying to raise PS2.5m to build the bronze sculpture, cultural centre and park planned on land he owns at Ffordd Penygroes near Llanbedr-ym-Mochnant Published:08:30Tuesday 18 April 2012 Share this article Simon Wingett has been living with a dream for thirty years - to create an international reputation as one of Wales' leading sculptors after creating his first piece when he was 16. Despite being told it would never be finished due to lack of funds and support from local authority bosses 30 years later Mr Winget decided that enough was enough and resolved to wake up that dragon! He started lobbying councils with images of what could or should be built instead of remaining permanently asleep but had no success until recently where the opportunity arose for him and his wife Sarah to buy some very unkempt looking derelict woodland which sits between their two farms off Borth Road just outside Bangor. It stands alone without any trees excepting those planted decades ago so to use up any time before they fell down into ruin Simon agreed to have them removed...and then awoke the dragon once again! "This area used to be known as the 'Bog Wood' because there were bog holes everywhere," said Simon. "I saw these acres lying idle without anything growing in them when I came home from working abroad for a few months. My son Matthew arrived; we did a bit of gardening together and got talking about how many more hectares you need for a garden - can you imagine? We both work full-time jobs so now our weekends are scoured for every spare hour we can muster." The next day he commenced negotiations with landowners regarding the purchase of the site, eventually buying the entire plot from one owner with all three boundaries intact at 8500 each. And now here we are, almost ready to start building the largest bronze statue ever created in Northern Ireland...the Waking the Dragon project will take around six weeks to complete, beginning in May when scaffolding goes up and finishing mid August when the completed pieces will be unveiled to thousands who might otherwise forget its existence during the rest of summer. A legacy indeed! The family's plans include a "gardensculpture zone" (an Old Growth forest) comprising 10,000 sq metres along with picnic areas, playgrounds, dog walks and educational trails featuring public artworks. This will not only benefit children and adults alike but also help protect the environment through environmental education. An eclectic mix of native plants such as bluebells, primroses and wildflowers will cover vast swathes of grassland while even older redwoods will grow amongst beautiful mature oaks in the wooded part of the grounds. There will also be hedgerows along pathways, seating areas and lookout points across the whole estate. All new housing development will surround the statues making it totally invisible within ten minutes walk away. Two further sculptures are currently under construction, Rhapsody and Cwmllynfell. These will sit alongside each other and form another triangle pointing towards the Welsh mountains with windsweeping views over Anglesey and Holy Island. Work began last year and should be finished early September.

Researchers at Stanford University and the SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory have discovered a way to transform a substance found in fossil fuels into diamonds with pressure and low heat. Diamond is a gemstone prized for its beauty and hardness. It is also a material with many potential uses, from electrical insulation to transparent, flexible plastic. For decades, scientists have been trying to develop methods for transforming graphite - a type of carbon - into diamonds. But so far, they haven't found a method that is both efficient and inexpensive. "Our method for making diamonds from carbon is highly efficient and relatively inexpensive," said Fred Garcia, a materials scientist at SLAC and a member of the Stanford team. "We could be on the verge of making a new, inexpensive source of diamonds." The researchers report their findings in a paper published in the Jan. 24 issue of the journal Nature. SLAC is a multiprogram laboratory exploring frontier questions in photon science, astrophysics, particle physics and accelerator research. Located in Menlo Park, Calif., SLAC is operated by Stanford University for the U.S. Department of Energy's Office of Science.

Undergraduate admission to Harvard is characterized by the Carnegie Foundation as "more selective, lower transfer-in." Harvard College accepted 5.3 of applicants for the class of 2019, a record low and down from 6 in 2018; 31.7 percent were enrolled during their freshman year compared with 41.9 percent two years ago - but still an enviable level that compares favorably against other colleges' freshmen acceptance rates (The Carleton University School of Graduate Studies admitted 48 out of 82 applicants last fall). Harvard's cutthroat admissions standards have yielded another surprising result: Its first-year undergraduate population has become increasingly diverse racially and ethnically over time while maintaining its reputation as one of America's most elite institutions, despite historical claims about the racial makeup of HCo students being unrepresentative of American society at large. According to YDSA's statement on affirmative action, it seems many critics fail to recognize this progress because they are unaware of how much diversity there actually was among HCo students before 2003 or even 2000 when race became part of the conversation regarding campus life. As The Crimson reported shortly after Obergefell v Hodges legalized same-sex marriage nationwide, Harvard had already been working toward ending discrimination based on sexual orientation 28 years earlier! In 1986, all four Houses voted unanimously to adopt new policies offering equal rights regardless of gender identity or expression, along with domestic partnerships for gay couples across campus. That vote came just three months prior to Nixon signing into law POMS 2, which then went further than any US college policy in recognizing same sex relationships, including faculty members who formed civil unions with each other without benefit of state recognition such as children born through surrogacy arrangements (and parenthood) - though these benefits only applied to relationships between people having legal ties to Massachusetts. When I arrived on campus as a 1998 graduate, a senior member of one House recounted his experience coming out 10 days shy of completing high school. He said he felt not unwelcome nor overtly targeted, instead inspired by those around him whom he grew up admiring. Though perhaps no longer so uncommon today, back then, Boston offered few spaces where queer folks could congregate openly outside university grounds, making socializing difficult enough under the best circumstances. And yet my friend found himself surrounded by peers willing to accept him unconditionally as both human and classmate alike. There is nothing wrong with striving towards greater demographic representation amongst our student body, especially given Harvard will eventually be majority minority. But let us also remember history provides ample evidence suggesting change can occur incrementally rather quickly if we stay united behind shared values like tolerance and mutual respect.

While federated learning (FL) enables distributed agents to collaboratively train a centralized model without sharing data with each other, it fails to protect users against inference attacks that mine private information from the centralized model. Thus, facilitating federated learning methods with differential privacy (DPFL) becomes attractive. Existing algorithms based on privately aggregating clipped gradients require many rounds of communication, which may not converge, and cannot scale up to large-capacity models due to explicit dimension-dependence in its added noise. In this paper, we adopt the knowledge transfer model of private learning pioneered by and extend their algorithm PATE , as well as the recent alternative PrivateKNN (,) to the federated learning setting. The key difference is that our method privately aggregates the labels from the agents in a voting scheme , instead of aggregating the gradients , hence avoiding the dimension dependence and achieving significant savings in communication cost. Theoretically, we show that when the margins of the voting scores are large, the agents enjoy exponentially higher accuracy and stronger (data-dependent) differential privacy guarantees on both agent-level and instance-level. Extensive experiments show that our approach significantly improves the privacy-utility trade-off over the current state-of-the-art in DPFL.

The immune system protects organisms from infection with layered defenses of increasing specificity. In simple terms, physical barriers prevent pathogens such as bacteria and viruses from entering the organism. If a pathogen breaches these barriers, the innate immune system provides an immediate, but non-specific response. Innate immune systems are found in all plants and animals. If pathogens successfully evade the innate response, vertebrates possess a second layer of protection, the adaptive immune system, which is activated by the innate response. Here, the immune system adapts its response during an infection to improve its recognition of the pathogen. This improved response is then retained after the pathogen has been eliminated, in the form of an immunological memory, and allows the adaptive immune system to mount faster and stronger attacks each time this pathogen is encountered.

Recently, there has been significant progress in developing various regularization techniques for deep learning architectures like dense deep neural networks (DNNs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). Traditional approaches primarily focus on eliminating elements from input data and internal network layers through strategies like Dropout, Cutout, and DropBlocks, while DropConnect targets the removal of connections within fully connected layers. These methods mitigate overfitting and enhance model accuracy by randomly omitting certain features or connections. This study introduces two innovative regularization strategies called DropFilter and DropFilter-PLUS tailored for training CNNs. Unlike earlier methods, these new approaches alter the convolution filters instead. Additionally, DropFilter-PLUS incorporates an optimized methodology derived from theoretical insights to expedite the learning curve. Experiments conducted on the MNIST dataset demonstrate that employing DropFilter and DropFilter-PLUS can lead to better outcomes in image recognition tasks.

Dow Jones Industrial Average is a stock market index created by Wall Street Journal editor and Dow Jones Company co-founder Charles Dow. The industrial average was first calculated on May 26, 1896. The Industrial portion of the name is largely historical, as many of the modern 30 components have little or nothing to do with traditional heavy industry. The average is price-weighted, and to compensate for the effects of stock splits and other adjustments, it is currently a scaled average. The value of the Dow is not the actual average of the prices of its component stocks, but rather the sum of the component prices divided by a divisor, which changes whenever one of the component stocks has a stock split or stock dividend, so as to generate a consistent value for the index. Since the divisor is currently less than one, the value of the index is larger than the sum of the component prices. The Dow Divisor is currently 0.15571590501117 as of September 27, 2013. Presently, every 1 change in price in a particular stock within the average, equates to a 6.42 (10.15571590501117) point movement. The NASDAQ Composite is a stock market index of the common stocks and similar securities (e.g. ADRs, tracking stocks, limited partnership interests) listed on the NASDAQ stock market, meaning that it has over 3,000 components. It is highly followed in the U.S. as an indicator of the performance of stocks of technology companies and growth companies. Since both U.S. and non-U.S. companies are listed on the NASDAQ stock market, the index is not exclusively a U.S. index. The S P 500, or the Standard Poor's 500, is a stock market index based on the market capitalizations of 500 large companies having common stock listed on the NYSE or NASDAQ. The S P 500 index components and their weightings are determined by S P Dow Jones Indices. It differs from other U.S. stock market indices such as the Dow Jones Industrial Average and the Nasdaq Composite due to its diverse constituency and weighting methodology. It is a capitalization-weighted index, which means, movements in the prices of stocks with higher market capitalizations (the share price times the number of shares outstanding) have a greater impact on the value of the index than do companies with smaller market caps. To calculate the value of the S P 500 Index, the sum of the adjusted market capitalization of all 500 stocks is divided by a factor, usually referred to as the Divisor. For example, if the total adjusted market cap of the 500 component stocks is US13 trillion and the Divisor is set at 8.933 billion, then the S P 500 Index value would be 1,455.28. Although the adjusted market capitalization of the entire index can be accessed from Standard Poor's website, the Divisor is considered to be proprietary to the firm. However, the Divisor's value is approximately 8.9 billion

The root system and the shoot system are interdependent - the usually nonphotosynthetic root system depends on the shoot system for food, and the usually photosynthetic shoot system depends on water and minerals from the root system. Cells in each system are capable of creating cells of the other and producing adventitious shoots or roots. Stolons and tubers are examples of shoots that can grow roots. Roots that spread out close to the surface, such as those of willows, can produce shoots and ultimately new plants. In the event that one of the systems is lost, the other can often regrow it. In fact it is possible to grow an entire plant from a single leaf, as is the case with Saintpaulia, or even a single cell - which can dedifferentiate into a callus (a mass of unspecialised cells) that can grow into a new plant. In vascular plants, the xylem and phloem are the conductive tissues that transport resources between shoots and roots. Roots are often adapted to store food such as sugars or starch, as in sugar beets and carrots.

In his Science of Logic Hegel argues that finite qualities are not fully "real" because they depend on other finite qualities to determine them. Qualitative infinity, on the other hand, would be more self-determining and hence more fully real. Similarly finite natural things are less "real" - because they are less self-determining - than spiritual things like morally responsible people, ethical communities and God. So any doctrine, such as materialism, that asserts that finite qualities or natural objects are fully real is mistaken.

Ask questions about your grandparent's life, especially if you did not know her well. Focus on addressing her death with others in your family as a way to cope together. If possible, have someone within the family photograph or document all of their lives and deaths so that it will be easy for future generations to remember what happened when they were young. If there is an obituary or memorial service available online that can help, contact the funeral home directly or look at local newspapers for information from other families who are going through similar experiences. Regardless how much time passes after the loss, grieving takes time to heal. It may take months, years or even forever. The good news is it does get better, but the healing process requires active participation and dialogue throughout the entire grieving process. Asking respectful and kind questions during this phase of grief is important because these open-ended conversations provide insight into parts of your deceased loved one's personality and daily activities that often went unnoticed by others. Grieving is an opportunity to grow personally as well as professionally, which will benefit you both long term. There is no right or wrong approach to dealing with loss; only personal comfort levels will dictate whether coping strategies work best for you. If you feel uncomfortable discussing things related to your Grandmothers' death with those around you due to fear or embarrassment, consider bringing up topics such as this article whenever appropriate (e.g., if you see another picture of Grandma in your grandma's old photo album). This encourages people around you to talk about different aspects of her life without judgment. In addition, try inviting friends over or taking small groups with you to events where you can meet new people. These activities allow you to share more openly about your experience since you won't feel like you're alone trying to grieve. Try sharing stories also. Laughter heals the wounds faster than tears. The key to effectively grieving is to make room for yourself while mourning. While spending some quality time with close friends and family members helps tremendously, this doesn't mean shutting out everyone else entirely. Be mindful of being too hard on yourself for suffering immensely during this difficult period. Accepting responsibility for your emotions is vital to healing. Reminiscing about the person she was before losing her battle against cancer will help you. Taking care of yourself physically, mentally and emotionally during the grieving process will ensure you don't lose focus during this tough time. Remember: everything happens for a reason!

The resting membrane potential refers to the voltage difference between the inside and outside of a cell. The reason it hyperpolarizes is because there is a higher concentration of negative ions on the inside of the cell, and a higher concentration of positive ions on the outside of the cell. This creates a voltage gradient across the cell membrane, which the cell uses to generate energy. When the cell is at rest, this voltage gradient is maintained by the cell's ion pumps.

We consider the problem of reinforcement learning (RL) with unbounded state space motivated by the classical problem of scheduling in a queueing network. Traditional policies as well as error metric that are designed for finite, bounded or compact state space, require infinite samples for providing any meaningful performance guarantee (e.g. error) for unbounded state space. That is, we need a new notion of performance metric. As the main contribution of this work, inspired by the literature in queuing systems and control theory, we propose stability as the notion of "goodness": the state dynamics under the policy should remain in a bounded region with high probability. As a proof of concept, we propose an RL policy using Sparse-Sampling-based Monte Carlo Oracle and argue that it satisfies the stability property as long as the system dynamics under the optimal policy respects a Lyapunov function. The assumption of existence of a Lyapunov function is not restrictive as it is equivalent to the positive recurrence or stability property of any Markov chain, i.e., if there is any policy that can stabilize the system then it must posses a Lyapunov function. And, our policy does not utilize the knowledge of the specific Lyapunov function. To make our method sample efficient, we provide an improved, sample efficient Sparse-Sampling-based Monte Carlo Oracle with Lipschitz value function that may be of interest in its own right. Furthermore, we design an adaptive version of the algorithm, based on carefully constructed statistical tests, which finds the correct tuning parameter automatically.

ELI 13: Computer programs are formulas. If a computer program is'8x 4 y', then the code is'8x 4' and'y' is what you see happen. The' 4' part is hard coded you cannot change it, however you can influence the final output by changing the x that part isn't hard coded. You're stuck with'8x 4 y', but you can influence what'y' is by changing'x'.,Program parts that can be changed by users read those parts from configuration files. Imagine a program "multiply.exe" that multiplies its input by three. So if you call "multiply.exe 5," it outputs 15. The factor 3 is "hardcoded." Now you can make it more flexible by reading in a file called "multiplier.txt" which contains the other factor. So if "multiplier.txt" contains "5," a call to "multiply.exe 5" will output 25; if it contains "120," the output will be 600. Hardcoding has the advantage that you have to account for much less error conditions. For example, what's supposed to happen if "multiplier.txt" contains "R" instead of a number.', "It means something is embedded in the game code itself instead of being read from a separate file. For example if someone hardcoded the strength of gravity, it's difficult to change. But if they put it in some kind of config file, or allow it to be edited in a level editor, then it's relatively easy to change. So in a modding context, if something is hardcoded, it means you can't use a mod to change it. Generally speaking, mod developers don't have access to the whole game source code. They can only modify the game behaviour through scripts (i.e. code typically written in a different language that the game engine loads and runs) or some data files. The game developers have to explicitly expose methods to change the game through scripts, so if there's something that for some reason they didn't expose, a modder can't change it and you'd say it's hardcoded. It's generally good practice to avoid hardcoding specific values. Anything that can be tweaked should be something you can edit without changing the game's source code. However that doesn't necessarily mean the ability to edit them is something the end user can do. In most cases it's a development only feature.

While representatives are indeed supposed to consider the opinions of their constituents, they must also exercise sound judgment. For instance, imagine a scenario where a congressperson represents a district where the majority opposes same-sex marriage, yet the official supports its legality and views prohibition as detrimental to the nation. In such cases, if there were a vote regarding this issue in Congress, would the congressperson adhere strictly to the wishes of their electorate or uphold their conviction even if it contradicts popular sentiment? This predicament emphasizes that while public opinion serves as a valuable reference point and plays a role during elections, maintaining some degree of independence from these perspectives can lead to better decision-making within a representative democracy. Nevertheless, this approach may sometimes result in policies that don't necessarily align with public consensus.

Regarding listening to their constituents, members of Congress do take into account both voter preferences and financial contributions. A major concern arises due to gerrymandering, resulting in safe seats where elected officials needn'sin order to win re-election. Consequently, their focus shifts towards pleasing those whose votes and funds directly impact their political future rather than considering broader societal interests.

In terms of allocating resources toward causes like Alzheimer's research, basing decisions solely on heartfelt appeals – such as one made by actor Seth Rogen – might lack substantial justification. Although the seriousness of the disease is well-known, utilizing celebrity influence to dictate policy choices raises questions about the criteria used for determining funding levels. Ultimately, striking a balance between heeding constituent voices and employing independent critical thinking remains crucial for effective governance.

Storage allocation affects important performance measures of distributed storage systems. Most previous studies on the storage allocation consider its effect separately either on the success of the data recovery or on the service rate (time) where it is assumed that no access failure happens in the system. In this paper, we go one step further and incorporate the access model and the success of data recovery into the service rate analysis. In particular, we focus on quasi-uniform storage allocation and provide a service rate analysis for both fixed-size and probabilistic access models at the nodes. Using this analysis, we then show that for the case of exponential waiting time distribution at individuals storage nodes, minimal spreading allocation results in the highest system service rate for both access models. This means that for a given storage budget, replication provides a better service rate than a coded storage solution.

Led by the Hun military leader Toramana, they overran the northern region of Pakistan and North India. Toramana's son Mihirakula, a Saivite Hindu, moved up to near Pataliputra to the east and Gwalior to the central India. Hiuen Tsiang narrates Mihirakula's merciless persecution of Buddhists and destruction of monasteries, though the description is disputed as far as the authenticity is concerned. The Huns were defeated by the Indian kings Yasodharman of Malwa and Narasimhagupta in the 6th century. Some of them were driven out of India and others were assimilated in the Indian society.

Optical communication achieves high fanout and short delay advantageous for information integration in neural systems. Superconducting detectors enable signaling with single photons for maximal energy efficiency. We present designs of superconducting optoelectronic neurons based on superconducting single-photon detectors, Josephson junctions, semiconductor light sources, and multi-planar dielectric waveguides. These circuits achieve complex synaptic and neuronal functions with high energy efficiency, leveraging the strengths of light for communication and superconducting electronics for computation. The neurons send few-photon signals to synaptic connections. These signals communicate neuronal firing events as well as update synaptic weights. Spike-timing-dependent plasticity is implemented with a single photon triggering each step of the process. Microscale light-emitting diodes and waveguide networks enable connectivity from a neuron to thousands of synaptic connections, and the use of light for communication enables synchronization of neurons across an area limited only by the distance light can travel within the period of a network oscillation. Experimentally, each of the requisite circuit elements has been demonstrated, yet a hardware platform combining them all has not been attempted. Compared to digital logic or quantum computing, device tolerances are relaxed. For this neural application, optical sources providing incoherent pulses with 10,000 photons produced with efficiency of 10 - 3 operating at 20MHz at 4.2K are sufficient to enable a massively scalable neural computing platform with connectivity comparable to the brain and thirty thousand times higher speed.

The typewriter made it possible to write a large amount very quickly, with very little expense, as long as you only needed a single copy. Before the invention of the typewriter, the choice was between writing by hand, which was slow, and printing, which required setting up a printing press, and so was also slow. The typewriter was easy to use, and could easily fit on a desk. It was much faster and less effort than writing by hand, and didn't need a lot of setting up. It produced type that was almost as good as printing, with regular, even letters that were easy to read (not everybody's handwriting is very legible), and this made it the perfect technology for writing business letters, official reports, and manuscripts for novels and the like. The most successful typewriters used a keyboard, which quickly became refined into the familar "QWERTY" keyboards we still use today. When computers first came into the office, and typewriters started to be replaced by word processors, they simply adopted the typewriter-style keyboard, so for most people the transition was very easy: early word processers were essentially high-tech typewriters, but you could make corrections and even perfect the layout before printing your document; you could also print several copies without having to go to the photocopier or messing about with carbon paper, and you could save digital copies on tape or floppy disk.

Batch Normalization (BN) is capable of accelerating the training of deep models by centering and scaling activations within mini-batches. In this work, we propose Decorrelated Batch Normalization (DBN), which not only captures the statistical structure in our data but also swaps out a pre-specified convolutional layer with an unsupervised learning one while preserving the original feature vector. We then apply DBN to superimpose two images, where the left image features corresponding to the training set are centered on the network inputs and those corresponding to the test set are centered on their outputs. This shift results in greater similarity between the two sets when they are compared for classification purposes, increasing the resilience against outliers and mitigating their impact on classifying object detection tasks such as face estimation or text classification.

Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) and its variants are popular few-shot classification methods. They train an initializer across a variety of sampled learning tasks (also known as episodes) such that the initialized model can adapt quickly to new ones. However, current MAML-based algorithms have limitations in forming generalizable decision boundaries. In this paper, we propose an approach called MetaMix. It generates virtual feature-target pairs within each episode to regularize the backbone models. MetaMix can be integrated with any of the MAML-based algorithms and learn the decision boundaries generalizing better to new tasks. Experiments on the mini -ImageNet, CUB, and FC100 datasets show that MetaMix improves the performance of MAML-based algorithms and achieves state-of-the-art result when integrated with Meta-Transfer Learning.

He never tried to mask it either, even when Riley was sleeping. The creaking was slow and painful as if her father was slowly crushing a baby bird with each step. He wasn't rushing, bad sign. She only had a few seconds. Riley's fingers flew across the keyboard. "Riley!" Her father's voice boomed through the door as if it was made of paper. She didn't even have to smell her father's breath to know that the alcohol was there. When she didn't answer a huge hand slammed into Riley's door. "RILEY! Get yer ass out here." "You..." her father's voice sounded confused at first, "YOU B DO N'T YOU EVER DARE TO LOCK YOUR DOOR ON ME." Tears were streaming down Riley's face as she typed the last couple words into the prompt. "A period. You need a period, stupid." She was talking to herself again. She didn't care. A colossal crack shook the air and Riley's door flew off its hinges. Splinters flew everywhere falling like sharp needles against Riley's back. Her father's hulking figure stood silhouetted in the wan light of the hallway. Riley's hand flew to the mouse as he stalked toward her. The alcohol that she knew would be there permeated the air with his every breath. His hand enclosed her wrist like a vice. The historical dispute between Northern and Southern Ireland dates back centuries. In 1801, Ireland joined the United Kingdom under the Acts of Union 1800, although British influence extended well before that point. At its core, the disagreement is about those advocating for self-governance or an independent Irish Republic (Republicans), versus those wishing to maintain ties with the UK (Unionists). Religious differences further complicate matters, with Catholics generally supporting the Republicans and Protestants favoring the Unionists; however, there are exceptions within each group. A pivotal moment in deepening divisions was the devastating Potato Famine when the British response was largely seen as indifferent, while some landowners evicted tenants unable to meet rental demands, leading to violent acts like property destruction. This tragedy catalyzed the ongoing strife, which persisted throughout the subsequent decades marked by numerous rebellions, including the Easter Rising of 191EE. Prompted by these events, Irish nationalist leader Éamon de Valera persuaded British Parliament members to temporarily divide the country, hoping to placate both factions through a referendum known as the "Ulster Month." However, this plan failed because Ulster voted against joining the proposed Irish Republic, remaining part of the UK ever since. Even though the partition didn't resolve the issues, it led to more bloodshed, culminating in a civil war in 1922. Intermittent violence between the Irish Republican Army and the Ulster Volunteer Force, representing Nationalists and Unionists respectively, prompted Britain to deploy troops once again from the 1960s to the 1980s.

Refinement in Event-B supports the development of systems via proof based step-wise refinement of events. This refinement approach ensures safety properties are preserved, but additional reasoning is required in order to establish liveness and fairness properties. In this paper we present results which allow a closer integration of two formal methods, Event-B and linear temporal logic. In particular we show how a class of temporal logic properties can carry through a refinement chain of machines. Refinement steps can include introduction of new events, event renaming and event splitting. We also identify a general liveness property that holds for the events of the initial system of a refinement chain. The approach will aid developers in enabling them to verify linear temporal logic properties at early stages of a development, knowing they will be preserved at later stages. We illustrate the results via a simple case study.

The ELI15 answer is that buying the exact same basket of things you consumed in 1971 would probably cost more than 5 times as much in 2015-dollars, and the exact same basket of things you consumed in 2015 would have cost more than 15 as much 1971-dollars. This is because people substitute from less efficient to more efficient goods over time. I think Agatha Christie's biography illustrates this best: "I never thought I would ever be wealthy enough to own a car - nor so poor that I wouldn't have servants." In her childhood, even a wealthy family might not be able to afford a car and even a middling family might be able to afford a servant. Likewise for the 1970s - there were millionaires who couldn't afford a desktop computer, but other things that were much cheaper, like education, secretarial help, housing, etc. Edit: I forgot to add the final point, that inflation rates aren't calculated to directly calculate cost of living increases, but to measure "core inflation," the increase in the price level that is purely driven by supply and demand for money rather than the efficiency of production, scarcity of different natural resources, and so on. That is why inflation isn't always the same as the change in the foreign exchange rate or in the cost of living, and why we go to the trouble to calculate inflation rates even when direct comparisons between baskets of goods 40 years apart don't make much sense in principle.', "You've correctly understood inflation, yep. However, that salary information seems unlikely. Household median income in the US has increased at slightly above inflation between 1971 to 2015 (going from 7,713 to 53,657). Knowing isn't everything. I'm living proof of that statement. I don't know how I'm going to die, but I am the least paranoid person that you will ever meet. It started a few years ago. One day, everyone on the planet woke up to discover that they have a tattoo of..... something. No one knew for sure what it meant, until people started dying. I don't mean that there was a jump in the number of deaths or some sudden plague or something. I just mean that people died, and their tattoos, without a single error, showed a depiction of how they had died. I'm sure the government tried to keep this discovery from spreading, but once the internet discovered the truth, there was no stopping it. All of a sudden, everyone was paranoid. They went to great lengths to avoid the types of situations that their tattoos depicted. Then, the tattoos started to change. I had a buddy whose original tattoo showed him dead from a motorcycle accident, so he sold his bike and vowed never to ride again. The next day, his tattoo showed him at the bottom of a lake, so he avoided all bodies of water. A few weeks later, it still showed him drowned, so he bought a new motorcycle. The very next day, he died in a crash, and his family discovered that his tattoo had reverted to its original form. He wasn't the only one. This new information transformed the world from a bunch of mildly paranoid, but still bearable, people to a bunch of full-blown nutjobs that avoided every single item on the ever-growing list of possible ways to die. There were, of course, those lucky few who got old age or already knew that they were dying from whatever form of cancer, but they were the minority. And then, there's me. I woke up with a tattoo, same as everyone else. I think it showed some sort of explosion, or something, but a few days later, it was gone. It didn't move to a different spot on my body, it just vanished. My buddys joke that I'll die in a transporter accident and just be converted to energy or something. My girlfriend thinks that it means I'm immortal. I personally am not convinced. I think that I will die when I will die, and there is nothing that will change it. I am one of a small group of people that can still find happiness in the mundane and the everyday, without worrying about how it could kill me. I believe that I am one of the few people that passed the test. Check out rElementalHominid for more awesome stuff that I've written.

A single memory of a single object. Or sound. Or smell. Or place. Can tell you a whole story with almost limitless descriptive details and nuances that are the living poetry of life. Like how a waterfall can make me think of a scared but love-bearing red headed girl from Alabama. Or how a once empty bottle of Hubert's Lemonade, now filled with cigarette ash and smoke, reminds me of a blonde hairedblue-eyed heart breaker from Sweden. Or even how a shelf of liquor can make me reminisce of these lovely ladies individually or both simultaneously. I remembered all these things, not just the women, although they were my favorite to run through my mind, and it was equally reliving and intimidating. It was a power people take for granted so easily. To retain a moment in time, that will last forever as long as someone is around to still remember it actually happened. In this sense, nothing ever actually dies, it moves onto some other realm of existence. It is the most powerful force in the universe, and when someone loses that power, you can feel them lose themselves too. Because what are we without the memories we hold? Empty sea shells drifting onto the beach shores of eternal limbo. This was my great grandmother. A lost sea shell. And where I once saw bright shining lights in her eyes, were now dead stars in the night sky. She lost her power, but I still had mine. And I would see her each and every day while she lost her way. I'd reinvigorate her with that power she once had. I'd tell her those stories I still held dearly in my heart. She relived moments she thought she had lost forever, or didn't know existed to begin with. This was my one super power, and I cherish it for each moment I still have it, to help the living remember what was forgotten, and to help the forgotten dead that they can be remembered.

Glory and grounding. Fight for medals, learn your craft. The stage marries pressure of the here and now with a gateway to a professional future. British fighters know the pathway only too well - consider 2008 Olympians James DeGale and Billy Joe Saunders, both now professional world champions. The latest off that conveyor belt, IBF heavyweight champion Anthony Joshua, thinks Britain has a "unique" fighter waiting to make the transition to the pro ranks. Here, with the help of Joshua, former Olympic bronze medallist and WBC super-middleweight champion Richie Woodhall, and BBC Radio 5 live pundit Steve Bunce, we take a look at the decisions facing Great Britain's 2016 Olympians. Super-heavyweight Joe Joyce will leave the comforts of the state-of-the-art British Boxing training base in Sheffield as an Olympic silver medallist, braced for life as a pro, dreaming of emulating the success of previous gold medal winners in his weight class Wladimir Klitschko, Lennox Lewis and Joshua himself. "Joe Joyce is unique," says Joshua of the fighter who holds a degree in fine arts. "He's very intelligent, he's experienced different things, you can see he is a really solid athlete. He has got people eating out of his hand. He has so much energy." Joyce, 30, is quietly spoken to the cameras but ultra-confident in the ring. A competitive swagger perhaps supported by 2014 Commonwealth Games gold and European Games gold in 2015. He didn't start boxing until he was 22, following a chance introduction to the sport while at university. He is also a part-time model and unsuccessfully auditioned for a role in the James Bond film, Spectre. "He is most suited to turn pro out of the 12 in the GB squad at this time," says Woodhall, who turned pro after the Commonwealth Games in 1990. "At his age, his engine is more developed. I say that from my own experience as I recall how I felt at say 22 compared to when I was Joe's age. My fitness was more developed for the 12 rounds." 'Adams could set the pro game alight and get it to the same level as the men's' - 5 Live In Short Joyce is the oldest male fighter in the British squad. Time is of the essence if he is to attain the Las Vegas dreams those in the fight game seem to universally harbour. The pro move fascinates, we seem to obsess over it. At virtually every news conference in Rio came the question "will you now turn pro?" In June, the contentious decision was made to allow professionals to compete. However, it is not as simple as it may seem with the IBF stating in advance of the Rio Games that any boxer competing in Brazil would be stripped of their title. The IBF claimed it was a safety risk for professionals to face amateurs. "If I'm to be perfectly honest, I don't think there's anyone apart from Joyce that's ready for the pro game because they are all very young," added Woodhall, who works with GB's amateurs twice a week. "The more international experience you have in amateur or Olympic boxing, the better you are prepared for the pro game because you are experiencing so many styles of fighter. Too many of our amateurs turn pro far too soon." Six of the seven male British fighters from London 2012 have now had a pro bout. Britain's Rio 2016 elite were a fresh crop, delivering three medals as a squad, while Cuba led the way in the ring with six. "The Cubans, the Kazakhs, the Russians, the Ukrainians, they all keep their guys from four years ago," said Bunce. "It's quite absurd. If only we could keep ours, persuade them not to go chasing the money, the money will be there [in the future]." Promoters may promise big fights, big cheques, progression to domestic and world titles, yada, yada. The amateur game can sometimes be painted as a poor relation, not the sacred test many would argue it is. A Team GB fighter can earn up to PS28,000 a year in basic funding. They can have food, physio and costs of living four days a week in camp covered, while training at a centre often visited by rival nations on research missions, such is its standing. "When you turn pro you're funding yourself, you become your own boss," added Joshua, gold medallist at London 2012. "You have to find a nutritionist, a physio, training grounds and it all comes at a cost. You have to look at the whole idea of being left to your own devices and finding good people to work with. "You have to look at the system that made you successful and try to use it as a professional." Life on the other side offers an allure often too strong to resist, but there can be struggles. Audley Harrison - Olympic super heavyweight champion in 2000 - found pro life tough, Luke Campbell has tasted defeat in the paid ranks. Gold medals do not stop punches. But Joshua's 30-month march from pro debut to heavyweight champion provides hope of glorious transition. He remains the only class of 2012 fighter to even contest a world title. Will the bright lights among which he now lives come calling for the 2016 team? "He's made for the pro game," says Bunce of Joshua Buatsi, a bronze medallist at light heavyweight in Rio. Buatsi - still only 23 - displayed knockout power in Brazil. The St Mary's University student showed desire for a finish rather that the point-snatching style which historically shines in Olympic boxing. "He fights like a pro," Bunce added. "These Olympics have been more pro minded than any Olympics since 1980. These guys are having rows. The new scoring system means a return to old style blood, guts and thunder Olympic boxing which anyone above the age of 35 will remember falling in love with when they were younger." Buatsi could fall in love with offers from promoters post-Rio, although Joyce is still the only GB fighter to state he will certainly go over. Woodhall hopes for an amateur stay for the Ghana-born fighter, who claims Floyd Mayweather said he was "a future world champion" during a chance meeting in Rio. "To win bronze here with the international experience he has had which is very little, then another four years into Joshua Buatsi and you'd probably see him winning gold," added Woodhall. So have we seen our Anthony Joshua moment at Rio 2016? Have we seen a star born? The desire is there but how greedy are we? Great Britain is home to 14 world champions. British Boxing did not choose 12 fighters to go to Rio, they delivered 12 for a maximum of 13 spaces in tough qualifying. These are heady times. Nicola Adams did what Nicola Adams does to take gold and eight of the 10 male fighters in Brazil were under the age of 25. "We hit our medal target and should retain our funding," added Woodhall. "There's more to come from this team. I'm pretty sure we will win more than three medals in Tokyo." Joshua added: "I think the guys that didn't manage to medal gained valuable experience and if they stay on until Tokyo we will see these guys shine." It may hurt British Boxing bosses a little to see only Adams, Buatsi, Joyce and Savannah Marshall progress past the last-16 stage, but young fighters will "develop power and learn from mistakes" as their journey progresses, according to Joshua. So switch now, or soak up more knowledge? Bunce added: "All 10 of the men will win British titles. As many as six or seven will end up winning a version of the world title." That's expectation and with it comes pressure. We wait to see if anyone can reach greatness from boxing's Olympic springboard.

The Royal Assent ceremony takes place in the Senate, as the sovereign is traditionally barred from the House of Commons. On the day of the event, the Speaker of the Senate will read to the chamber a notice from the secretary to the governor general indicating when the viceroy or a deputy thereof will arrive. The Senate thereafter cannot adjourn until after the ceremony. The speaker moves to sit beside the throne, the Mace Bearer, with mace in hand, stands adjacent to him or her, and the governor general enters to take the speaker's chair. The Usher of the Black Rod is then commanded by the speaker to summon the Members of Parliament, who follow Black Rod back to the Senate, the Sergeant-at-Arms carrying the mace of the House of Commons. In the Senate, those from the commons stand behind the bar, while Black Rod proceeds to stand next to the governor general, who then nods his or her head to signify Royal Assent to the presented bills (which do not include appropriations bills). Once the list of bills is complete, the Clerk of the Senate states: "in Her Majesty's name, His [or Her] Excellency the Governor General [or the deputy] doth assent to these bills." If there are any appropriation bills to receive Royal Assent, the Speaker of the House of Commons will read their titles and the Senate clerk repeats them to the governor general, who nods his or her head to communicate Royal Assent. When these bills have all been assented to, the Clerk of the Senate recites "in Her Majesty's name, His [or Her] Excellency the Governor General [or the deputy] thanks her loyal subjects, accepts their benevolence and assents to these bills. The governor general or his or her deputy then depart parliament.

Charles W. Eliot, president , eliminated the favored position of Christianity from the curriculum while opening it to student self-direction. While Eliot was the most crucial figure in the secularization of Christianity - especially the 19th century - scholars and students were able to get the message of "denunciation" through a variety of strategies that had little effect on religion itself. The idea behind the "feminist revolution," Paille said, is not to create new religions but to reclaim old ones through social interaction. As an example, he went so far as to say that the United States should prevent women from buying guns from their husbands because they could "deform society." In his brief introduction to Paille's book, Eliot wrote: "We must never forget that men have been men for over two centuries. The world today has become more like us, and we are no longer left alone with some unattainable goal. We are now free to do anything or anyone we wish... where our enmity does not harm others; except Allah." The premise seems right. But what about the rest? Does Kant support a worldview based on equality and kindness towards all who share one common humanity? What if people who belong to different groups of people shared the same values and beliefs - such as love, respect and compassion? Or would the concept of equality serve only to maintain diversity among those who are different than themselves? Such ideas seem counterintuitive, considering the challenges faced by many Christians. Is this the case when religion is used against the majority? Or even worse? For instance, in the 1930s, the British government allowed religious schools to discriminate against students living with mental illnesses. In 1986, a U.S. judge ruled that schools can discriminate against people with hearing loss, autism and other conditions without regard for race, ethnic origin or national origin. There's nothing wrong with celebrating differences, but I believe that what belongs here instead is placing faith into people whose lives may be affected by them (and who share similar values). If you cannot understand why we have to rely on stereotypes and assumptions to solve problems, think twice before attempting to give yourself the benefit of doubt. If you believe that there is something wrong with accepting certain opinions, try teaching your children about the things they know best - using examples from the Bible to confirm their own ideas. If you disagree, please conduct searches for "risks associated with pregnancy and childbirth" and "difficulties of childbirth" before presenting counterarguments. The former private, who is in her 20s, has accepted a conditional caution for misconduct in a public office. The woman has agreed to make a payment of PS40 to an armed forces charity. She was arrested at her Nottinghamshire home under the Metropolitan Police's Operation Elveden inquiry into alleged corrupt payments to public officials. In a statement, the CPS outlined details of the offence but did not name the newspaper or the barracks. CPS lawyer Gregor McGill said:"The evidence in this case was considered very carefully and although there was sufficient evidence to prosecute this offence, when considering the public interest it was decided that a conditional caution was an appropriate course of action. "In accepting a conditional caution, an individual accepts responsibility for the offending set out." The former soldier was arrested in September. Offline learning is a key part of making reinforcement learning (RL) useable in real systems. Offline RL looks at scenarios where there is data from a system's operation, but no direct access to the system when learning a policy. Recent work on training RL policies from offline data has shown results both with model-free policies learned directly from the data, or with planning on top of learnt models of the data. Model-free policies tend to be more performant, but are more opaque, harder to command externally, and less easy to integrate into larger systems. We propose an offline learner that generates a model that can be used to control the system directly through planning. This allows us to have easily controllable policies directly from data, without ever interacting with the system. We show the performance of our algorithm, Model-Based Offline Planning (MBOP) on a series of robotics-inspired tasks, and demonstrate its ability leverage planning to respect environmental constraints. Crude oil is just as it's name suggest, crude. It contains a wide variety of carbon molecules ranging from small light ones like butane and propane up to massive ones having upwards of dozens of carbon atoms. Each chain of carbon molecules has a certain amount of energy in it corresponding to its composition. We can burn crude oil to release this energy, but the varied mix of molecules will produce many byproducts from combustion that it will quickly foul any engine. Heavy petroleum waxes and oils will destroy the engine. It just wouldn't be practical and we would lose the extra things we gain from refining the crude oil into other products. In the oil refining industry, there is something called the "crack spread" which is a simple formula that tells you roughly how much gasoline and fuel oil can be made from barrels of crude. A common spread of 3,2,1 says that for every 3 barrels of crude you put in, 2 barrels of gasoline and one barrel of heavy fuel oil can be made. That's still a very simplified version of things since the industry can vary the methods dramatically and produce a much wider amount of oil based products from that same spread. The refining process is complex and uses a lot of energy. You must separate the oil from the impurities it naturally contains. Sulfur molecules, Nitrogen molecules and even salt and sediment are in there. After removing what you can, the oil gets boiled up in tall columns and separates into different substances. The lightest stuff rises to the top (gasoline is in there) and the heavy stuff stays at the bottom (heavy waxes and oils). Once you have everything separated, you have to further refine it to get the mix of carbon molecules you want. You even have to add various other chemicals to make the gasoline perform the way you want in an engine. Lots of testing and lab work is done to ensure this all stays on track. The whole process is complicated and uses lots of energy and resources. Gasoline is just a part of the game here. It's not always the key to why we use crude oil. Ultimately, the fact that we pay so little for gasoline considering we don't get 1 barrel of gasoline out of 1 barrel of crude oil is pretty damn amazing. It's based on the overall marketability of the total products that come from crude oil. A refiner has to follow the market and their goal is to make back the most money out of what they are spending. High crude prices tend to lead to higher gasoline prices, but it has many forces in the market driving it. Some byproducts can fetch more money than gasoline at times and throws this all off. Ultimately it generally works out in the consumer's favor and we manage to get a highly refined product that will not destroy our car's engines at a very reasonable price when considering the amount of money a refinery needs to put up in equipment, energy and resources to make it. Gasoline costs less per gallon than milk, blood and printer ink and arguably takes more effort to produce. We're getting a bargain, really. TL;DR - crude oil is dirty and will break your car. Computer operating system kernels serve as the fundamental security component of most computing systems by providing essential protective measures. These kernels bear the responsibility of safeguarding their integrity against unauthorized access attempts by untrusted processes seeking elevated privileges. Our research establishes that confirming the non-existence of privilege escalation scenarios is crucial before claiming absolute security assurances for the kernel. Previous formal validations of operating system kernels have been conducted through various approaches involving manual intervention, such as scrutinizing the source code or employing simplified versions of kernels. In contrast, we present a novel automated technique capable of analyzing executable code directly from a current microkernel without alterations, thereby ensuring robust defense against privilege escalation at minimal expense. This approach has been tested on two distinct embedded microkernels, one being the commercial AnonymOS—whose name has been concealed due to the nature of blind reviews. With just 58 lines of input and under ten minutes of processing time, our procedure successfully detects flaws in an initial (flawed) iteration of AnonymOS while affirming the secure state of its subsequent (secured) release.

In 1862, amidst the Civil War, the issuance of paper currency commenced without the support of valuable metals like gold or silver. Despite this change, silver and gold coins remained in circulation until 1878 when they were once again tied to the paper notes. A similar situation arose during the conflict of 1812 where there was a separation from these metal-backed currencies. Even earlier, during the period governed by the Articles of Confederation (1777-1788), unsecured paper money was utilized. However, because it lacked tangible backing and could be easily replicated, its worth plummeted rapidly, leading to the expression "not worth a continental." To prevent such occurrences, the U.S. Constitution included an amendment stating that no state should issue anything other than gold and silver as legal tender for settling obligations.

Courts have distinguished between two types of civil disobedience: "Indirect civil disobedience involves violating a law which is not, itself, the object of protest, whereas direct civil disobedience involves protesting the existence of a particular law by breaking that law." During the Vietnam War, courts typically refused to excuse the perpetrators of illegal protests from punishment on the basis of their challenging the legality of the Vietnam War; the courts ruled it was a political question. The necessity defense has sometimes been used as a shadow defense by civil disobedients to deny guilt without denouncing their politically motivated acts, and to present their political beliefs in the courtroom. However, court cases such as U.S. v. Schoon have greatly curtailed the availability of the political necessity defense. Likewise, when Carter Wentworth was charged for his role in the Clamshell Alliance's 1977 illegal occupation of the Seabrook Station Nuclear Power Plant, the judge instructed the jury to disregard his competing harms defense, and he was found guilty. Fully Informed Jury Association activists have sometimes handed out educational leaflets inside courthouses despite admonitions not to; according to FIJA, many of them have escaped prosecution because "prosecutors have reasoned (correctly) that if they arrest fully informed jury leafleters, the leaflets will have to be given to the leafleter's own jury as evidence."

But Reaction Time is a bit of an unusual commission that left me, as producer, staring at a half-hour gap in the schedule and wondering what would fill it. It is the network's first programme made entirely on smartphones. The premise was simple on paper. BBC Radio 4 put a prompt on social media ahead of Valentine's Day: "Tell us a story about love," inviting anyone in the world to make a two-minute voice recording of their relationship story, on their phone, and email it in as an attachment. Then, I would knit the contributions into a half-hour of online dates, first loves, and bitter break-ups. I will confess to some nerves. Until recently, the quality from mobile recordings would not be good enough - but, in my day job as a journalist, I have used the technique when we have not been able to get an interviewee to a studio. The technology has improved massively in recent years and is often comparable to a traditional recording. As the process started, there were anxious days when nothing arrived, and, then, suddenly - a brilliant anecdote. (Caroline's wedding gets derailed spectacularly...) I would refresh the inbox open-mouthed at relationship stories that could not be broadcast; weeding out information about people's exes that could get me sued, and in one instance, deciding against broadcasting an entertaining but detailed account of what happens when you get dysentery on honeymoon. The other factor that gave me a few worries was that people seemed particularly keen to share their disasters - marital break-up, hated exes, a ruined wedding, loneliness, a complete inability to pull - was there anyone with a nice, romantic story? It turned out there was, and it was from a woman called Samantha. Her tale finishes the programme, and it is a bit of a jaw-dropper. I knew I had something when I played it to a reasonably hard-bitten reporter at the next desk and she cried. One of the key decisions about the programme was that if we were handing over half an hour to Radio 4's listeners, we should go the whole hog and get one of them to present it. So a few weeks ago, I emailed Narelle Lancaster. The 39-year-old advertising lecturer had sent in one of my favourite stories about a catastrophic night out. Her date's opening gambit was: "Your breasts look fantastic in that dress." And then it got worse. When I contacted her about presenting the programme, Lancaster, who lives in the UK, had gone back to Australia for two months. After realising every one of my phone recording sessions with her would have to take place not far off 00:00 GMT, I banged my head on the desk a few times and got on with it. Soon enough, Lancaster was sitting on the other side of the world with two phones in her hands, one landline against her ear so I could coach her, and a smartphone to record the script with in the other hand. She told me: "It was not easy - we did spend hours working it out, so recording a script was much more complicated than I thought it would be - lots of techniques to make you sound natural. "It's been incredibly exciting. "I only submitted because saw it on Twitter, and I really didn't think anyone would be interested in my story - I was really surprised. "Now, I just want to hear it." And now, it is time for the listeners to decide if they like the sound of themselves. Reaction Time can be heard on Radio 4 at 1130 GMT on 11 February.

I'd be willing to bet there are significantly more businesses posting those "This business serves everyone" signs than there are businesses blocking gay people. I mean, when only one business announces that they won't serve gay people, it ends up being a huge story on Reddit and Facebook. That would seem to tell me it's an incredibly uncommon occurrence. Which brings me to another point: Banning gay people from your business is just bad, well, business. Even on the off chance that all businesses selling one particular service decide to ban gay people, wouldn't this just create a market for a business that doesn't discriminate against gays? Then everyone who opposes the other businesses' discrimination can patronize that business and, boom, they make a shitton of money. If a business wants to not serve a particular group, I say let them decide not to. And if someone doesn't want to support that business, then they don't have to. People act like the ruling automatically bans all gays from all businesses when that choice lies with the business owners. And making the choice to not serve gay people works almost entirely against them. One thing that does concern me is the possibility of businesses not hiring gays because of their sexuality, but I suspect the reaction to this would be the same as if businesses refused to serve gay customers. An entire group is alienated and refuses to do business with them, and another mass of people would refuse to do business with them solely on the basis that they're bigot assholes. Is there something I'm missing here? Am I missing the overall point of what's wrong with this law? To put it simply, there seem to be no legitimate arguments against wearing a helmet while cycling. There are numerous benefits to consider: helmets significantly minimize the severity of injuries sustained during a biking mishap, reducing them by 85-88%. Approximately 70-80% of bicycle incidents result in some form of head trauma. Mandatory helmet use for kids aged 5-15 could potentially circumvent around 39,000 - 45,000 instances of cranial harm, as well as between 18,000 - 55,000 facial and scalp wounds. These advantages are easily verifiable through an internet search under 'bicycle helmet statistics'. Furthermore, properly fitted helmets should not obstruct your ride; they may slightly alter air resistance, yet advanced streamlined designs exist to counteract such concerns. Addressing common reservations, issues related to hairstyle inconvenience, discomfort, or perceived lack of style are trivial compared to the risks associated with head injuries. Even if you have been fortunate enough to avoid accidents thus far, it doesn't guarantee future safety, particularly when sharing roads with motor vehicles. As for costs, an economical helmet typically falls within the $10 range, which is a negligible expense considering the potential medical fees resulting from head injuries. In summary, the evidence overwhelmingly supports the regular usage of bicycle helmets, rendering excuses for noncompliance relatively insignificant.

The changes in root morphology and physiology are linked to a fluctuation in the relative growth rate caused by a decrease in nitrogen availability. Plants demonstrate adaptability in their growth rates and root systems when they encounter a decrease in nitrogen availability. Changes in root morphology due to reduction in nitrogen levels may involve longer roots, more branching of roots, and the formation of root hairs that enable the plant to obtain more nutrients from soil, particularly nitrogen. When there is a deficiency in nitrogen, the enlargement of the roots leads to an increase in the surface area, allowing more absorption of nutrients, ultimately promoting plant growth. The roots' reaction to a limited level of nitrogen typically includes modifications in metabolic activities, nutrient carriers, and other mechanisms that encourage effective nitrogen absorption. The flexibility in the rate at which growth occurs involves improvements in the efficiency of nitrogen usage. This can be accomplished through adjustments to the expression of genes that transport nitrogen, as well as by enhancing the efficiency of metabolic processes in the roots and altering the pathways of nitrogen assimilation. To sum up, when there is less nitrogen available, plant growth rate can adapt due to changes in root morphology and physiology. This gives plants the ability to optimize nutrient uptake and continue growing as best as possible despite constrained nitrogen resources.

Communism gained significant traction in Korea during the Cold War era. Northern Korea aligned itself with both China and the USSR, while Southern Korea allied with the United States, receiving military aid and support to combat its northern counterpart. Initially, the northern region thrived due to substantial financial assistance from China and Russia; however, over time, economic struggles plagued the Soviet Union, leading to a decrease in funding for its allies. Concurrently, China distanced itself from Northern Korea following various natural disasters. As a result of these geopolitical shifts, Western nations refrained from engaging with North Korea, severing ties with its former communist comrades who realigned themselves closer to the West. This isolation has transformed North Korea into an impoverished and enigmatic entity unable to conduct international trade effectively. With no trading relationships established since the dissolution of the USSR two decades ago, North Korea remains a perplexing state steeped in poverty and seclusion, making it unwelcome for global commerce. The origins of North Korea trace back to Kim Il-Sung, whose collaboration with China and the Soviet Union aimed to establish a unified government on the Korean Peninsula. Despite efforts to replicate Stalin's "cult of personality," Kim's approach lacked authenticity, resulting in the title of "Glorious Leader" rather than simply a revered figurehead. Although technically, North and South Korea remain engaged in conflict, the armistice agreement created a buffer zone between them, marking the cessation of active hostilities.

Congratulations, you've just figured out by yourself the first lesson of Linguistics 101: Orthography (writing system) has absolutely nothing to do with language. Language is part of the human experience. It is not merely a bunch of letters and words strung together. Language is much more than that. Languages are all unique, but they have something in common. They have elements, each of which has a different function. The same goes for writing systems. You can have the same elements in different languages, but the functions of those elements are different. So what is a writing system? A writing system is a set of symbols or elements that represent the sounds of language. It is a code. That code can be a unique code for a particular language, or it can be a code for a set of languages (as is the case with the International Phonetic Alphabet). What is the connection between the written word and language? In the first place, language is written by means of the writing system. Language is not written in the air. Language is not written in the ether. Language is written on paper, on the screen, etc. Second, each language has its own writing system. The same language cannot be written with different writing systems. Third, each language is made up of sounds. It is the sounds that make up the words. However, sounds do not make up the written word. What is the relationship between writing system and spoken word? The relationship between the written word and the spoken word is one to many. There is only one spoken word, but there are many written words. This is because writing system is a code. Thus, the writing system represents a code. The written word represents the spoken word. Example of writing system and spoken word Let us use the example of the English language. The following shows the relationship between the written word and spoken word: Written word Spoken word Word Word Let's look at this example. A written word is made up of letters. There can be 26 letters or more. A spoken word is made up of sounds. There can be 40 sounds or more. A written word is also a word. It can be a noun, a verb, an adjective, or an adverb. The written word is also an element of the sentence. The spoken word is also a word. It can be a noun, a verb, an adjective, or an adverb. The spoken word is also an element of the sentence. So what is a written word? It is a code. It is a written symbol that represents a spoken sound. The written word is not a sound. It is merely a written symbol. How do we write words? There are basically three ways to write words. One, write the word using the sounds of the word. This is called transcription. Two, write the word using the letters of the word. This is called orthography. Three, write the word using the letters of the alphabet. This is called transliteration. Four, write the word using the letters of the alphabet using Roman characters. This is called romanization. Five, write the word using the letters of the alphabet using non-Roman characters. This is called non-romanization. What is a written word? If you think about it, what is a written word? It is a symbol, and the symbol can be made up of letters, sounds, or both. So what is a written word? It is a written symbol that represents a spoken sound. The written word is not a sound. It is merely a written symbol. For more information on written symbols, see What is a Written Symbol?

This study presents the novel concept of the Packing While Traveling dilemma, which can be described as a variant of the non-linear knapsack conundrum. A collection of cities each possess unique items characterized by individual profits and weights, along with a transport mechanism capable of retrieving these objects while traversing through the cities sequentially. Upon choosing an object, it adds value proportional to its worth yet incurs expenses depending on its mass. The objective here is identifying an optimal selection of items to enhance overall gains. In this research, we explore both restricted and free variations of the issue, demonstrating their inherent complexity via NP-hardness. "This is a key message, particularly when you consider that the UK - for the past five years or so - has imported more gas than it has produced domestically." She told BBC News that under a high gas scenario (gas power plants replacing end-of-life coal and nuclear plants) and a 40 increase in gas prices by 30, electricity prices would increase by 8. However, under a high wind scenario (wind farms replacing end-of-life coal and nuclear plants), electricity prices would still rise but by only 4. "For the wind scenario, you have higher upfront capital costs but fewer uncertain variable costs, leading to more price resilience," Ms Billington added. The report said that the UK electricity sector had undergone a substantial change in recent decades, shifting from a coal-based system to a more balanced mix "encompassing nuclear and gas-fired power stations, as well as emerging renewable energy technologies." It observed: "Over the next 10 to 20 years, the energy sector will need to be re-shaped again if the UK's targets to reduce CO2 emissions are to be met." Rob Norris, RenewableUK's head of communications, said that currently there were "not enough renewables in the system to meet those targets." "What you really need is a long-term vision out to 2030 so then you can plan, especially when it comes to things like large offshore developments." On my usual stop in the break room to pour myself a much-needed cup of the miracle of life, in walks in my unremarkable coworker Lettie.
