Simple. Because the President of the United States is elected by the States. He is not the President of the United People. The electoral college is a number of votes from each State that is equal to the number of Senators and Congressmen in each State. Nearly all of the States (with a few exceptions) will pledge ALL of their electoral college votes to the presidential candidate who wins in that State. So, you have a contest of "who can win in the most States" and not "who can convince the most people to vote for himher." If the popular vote was all that counted, then it would be theoretically possible that the president could be elected by 10 or 11 of the biggest States and the other 3940 would have no say in who gets elected. Plus, the candidates would be tempted to ONLY concentrate their campaigning in those large States and ignore the rest, thereby disenfranchising a huge geographic area. By forcing the candidates to win the most States (and hence electoral college votes), the candidates have to bring their message to the whole country. The electoral college, akin to the assurance of two Senators from each State regardless of population, is just one more way to ensure that the smaller States still have influence and are not dominated by the larger States. This is also why a president can be elected who did not win the popular vote. Win more States by a slim margin and get ALL of the electoral votes in those States, while your opponent beats you handily in the other States and gets more popular votes, and you will still win. Disenfranchising a large number of popular voters in a large States is far less important than disenfranchising entire States, right?

The methods of science should then be used to answer any empirical question about the natural world, and theology should be used to answer questions about ultimate meaning and moral value. In this view, the perceived lack of any empirical footprint from the magisterium of the supernatural onto natural events makes science the sole player in the natural world.

Overhead elements such as packet timestamps, checksums, acknowledgment packets, and other control messages occupy some of those bits. Ultimately, measuring data flows predominantly in bits aligns with the nature of the physical medium used, rendering the concept of 'bytes' less relevant at this level. Object detection remains an active area of research in the field of computer vision, and considerable advances and successes has been achieved in this area through the design of deep convolutional neural networks for tackling object detection. Despite these successes, one of the biggest challenges to widespread deployment of such object detection networks on edge and mobile scenarios is the high computational and memory requirements. As such, there has been growing research interest in the design of efficient deep neural network architectures catered for edge and mobile usage. In this study, we introduce YOLO Nano, a highly compact deep convolutional neural network for the task of object detection. A human-machine collaborative design strategy is leveraged to create YOLO Nano, where principled network design prototyping, based on design principles from the YOLO family of single-shot object detection network architectures, is coupled with machine-driven design exploration to create a compact network with highly customized module-level macroarchitecture and microarchitecture designs tailored for the task of embedded object detection. The proposed YOLO Nano possesses a model size of 4.0MB ( 15.1 and 8.3 smaller than Tiny YOLOv2 and Tiny YOLOv3, respectively) and requires 4.57B operations for inference (34 and 17 lower than Tiny YOLOv2 and Tiny YOLOv3, respectively) while still achieving an mAP of 69.1 on the VOC 2007 dataset ( 12 and 10.7 higher than Tiny YOLOv2 and Tiny YOLOv3, respectively). Experiments on inference speed and power efficiency on a Jetson AGX Xavier embedded module at different power budgets further demonstrate the efficacy of YOLO Nano for embedded scenarios.

During the time of King Henry VIII, an innovative mechanism for approval was developed. In 1542, Henry aimed to put his fifth spouse, Catherine Howard, to death on charges of infidelity; however, instead of conducting a formal trial, he intended to sanction her execution through a legislative act known as a bill of attainder. This required him to review and consent to the full document. To avoid reliving distressful details, Henry found it unbearable to hear about the betrayal again. Thus, Parliament included a provision within the Attainder Act stating that authorization given by appointed commissioners held equal validity to those granted directly by the ruler. Although this method saw limited use throughout the 16th century, its application increased significantly during the subsequent two centuries, particularly when George III's health declined. Finally, in 1854, Queen Victoria was the last queen to personally signify agreement before such practices evolved further.

Many industrial machine learning (ML) systems require frequent retraining to keep up-to-date with constantly changing data. This retraining exacerbates a large challenge facing ML systems today: model training is unstable, i.e., small changes in training data can cause significant changes in the model's predictions. In this paper, we work on developing a deeper understanding of this instability, with a focus on how a core building block of modern natural language processing (NLP) pipelines - pre-trained word embeddings - affects the instability of downstream NLP models. We first empirically reveal a tradeoff between stability and memory: increasing the embedding memory 2 x can reduce the disagreement in predictions due to small changes in training data by 5 to 37 (relative). To theoretically explain this tradeoff, we introduce a new measure of embedding instability - the eigenspace instability measure - which we prove bounds the disagreement in downstream predictions introduced by the change in word embeddings. Practically, we show that the eigenspace instability measure can be a cost-effective way to choose embedding parameters to minimize instability without training downstream models, outperforming other embedding distance measures and performing competitively with a nearest neighbor-based measure. Finally, we demonstrate that the observed stability-memory tradeoffs extend to other types of embeddings as well, including knowledge graph and contextual word embeddings.

A species of seahorse is possibly extinct after the last one on a Cornish beach was not seen for three years. Since 2008, about 40 spiny seahorses have been recorded on the seahorse study site at South Beach in the bay, but none have been spotted since 2014. The seahorse study site was set up by the Seahorse Trust as a result of research in the 1990s, which showed that spiny seahorses were extremely vulnerable to the changes in the ecosystem that are associated with sewage pollution. It is thought the extinction of spiny seahorses in the bay is a result of water quality improving in recent years, which has reduced the need for the seahorses to find food and breed in the bay. Water quality in the bay has improved significantly, said scientists at the Seahorse Trust. Hannah Dudley, the trust's programme manager, said: "Before, the bay was very polluted, and so seahorses were forced to come into the bay because of the lack of food sources in the surrounding area. She said seahorses had not been recorded on the site since October 2014, although there were signs they had been there. "We are still seeing spiny seahorses in the bay, we just don't see them on camera," said Ms Dudley. "We do see them around the Porthcurno site, but we haven't seen them around the South Beach site. She said the species was a native of the Mediterranean and parts of the Middle East, but was also found in the east of North America and Australia. It is listed as vulnerable by the International Union for Conservation of Nature. The researchers have used a camera trap to try to document the seahorse activity in the bay. The spiny seahorse has a scaly tail and a tail that is spiny rather than prehensile.

Predictors of unfavorable repeat biopsy results in men participating in a prospective active surveillance program can include several factors. Some common predictors are: 1. Age: Older men are at a higher risk of unfavorable repeat biopsy results compared to younger men. 2. Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level: Higher PSA levels are commonly associated with a higher probability of unfavorable biopsy results. 3. PSA density: Higher PSA density, which is the PSA level divided by prostate volume, is also a significant predictor of unfavorable repeat biopsy findings. 4. Prostate size: Larger prostate sizes can indicate an increased risk of unfavorable biopsy results. 5. Number of positive cores and core involvement: The higher the number of positive cores and greater percentage core involvement on the initial biopsy, the greater the likelihood of unfavorable findings on re-biopsy. 6. Gleason Score: Higher Gleason scores on the initial biopsy may predict unfavorable biopsy outcomes upon repeat assessment. 7. Clinical stage: Higher clinical stages indicate greater tumor involvement and may predict a higher likelihood of unfavorable repeat biopsy results. 8. Time between biopsies: Shorter intervals between biopsies might be associated with a higher likelihood of unfavorable results, especially if there was evidence of cancer progression. 9. Family history: A family history of prostate cancer may suggest an increased risk of unfavorable repeat biopsy results. It's important to note that each patient is different, and factors may have varying degrees of influence on individual outcomes. It is essential to discuss these factors with a healthcare professional to make informed decisions regarding active surveillance and prostate cancer management.

It was 1993 and Muhammad Ali was in Glasgow signing books with his friend, the photographer, Howard Bingham. We stood in that queue for three hours or more, people of all ages chatting about Ali and what he meant to them. There was an old man there - maybe 80. Twenty-three years later and his face is as clear in the mind's eye as it was then, when we inched our way forwards and listened to his stories. This was no braggadocio. As Ali once said,'It ain't bragging if you can back it up'. And that Glasgow man could definitely back it up. He spoke about being at Wembley when Clay beat Henry Cooper in 1963, about being at Earls Court when Ali took apart Brian London in 1966, about being in Dublin when Ali did Al'Blue' Lewis in 1972. He knew it all. He spoke - quietly and not at all boastfully - about attending Ali's fight with Karl Mildenberger in Germany. None of us so-called Ali aficionados in that slowly moving line had ever heard of Karl Mildenberger. So when Ali's people lowered the boom about his death at the weekend, one of the first thoughts was for that wee man in 1993 and what happened when we eventually got to the top of the queue and entered the bookshop, like children heading into Santa's Grotto. Media playback is not supported on this device He did not ask for Ali's autograph or take his picture, he just stood away at the side and watched Ali do his thing. Then he became emotional. And Ali noticed. Ali was exhausted - he should have been out of there hours before but he promised to stay until the last person left - and he did not have the strength to speak, but when he got up to leave he looked over at the old man, smiled as much as his illness would allow and then slowly put his up his fists, as if challenging him to a fight. The old man did the same - and smiled back. It is funny the things you remember, but that one tender and fleeting image is impossible to forget. No words were exchanged, but none were needed. Ali was the most eloquent man in the history of sport, but even when Parkinson's robbed him of his full voice he still moved people with the simplest gestures. Since his death, the eulogies have come thick and fast from all corners of the world and all spheres of society. There was not a nook or cranny on this planet that his legend did not reach. For the best part of half a century he has inspired not just great sports writing but great literature. Hugh McIlvanney, Tom Wolfe, Gay Talese, Norman Mailer, George Plimpton, Pete Hamill, Hunter S Thompson, Mark Kram, David Remnick, Thomas Hauser - all heavyweights in their own game, all with a body of work that will keep Ali's complexity and the epic sweep of his personality alive for eternity. In looking back on his life, you have to look at the whole life, not just the best of it. Hagiography has no place in the Ali story. To accentuate the greatness at the expense of the ugliness would actually diminish what he was. Ali was the most remarkable sportsman in history but he was also, at times, one of the most bigoted, one of the cruellest, one who preached love but delivered hate on to men like Joe Frazier, a man who tried to help Ali at his lowest ebb and got little back apart from racial hatred. Ali became world champion in 1964 when shaking up the world in victory over Sonny Liston. He defended his title against Liston in 1965, the same year he came to Scotland to fight exhibition bouts at the Paisley Ice Rink. Even by then he was in the grip of the Nation of Islam, a frightening mob made up, in part, of ex-cons who preached a doctrine of separation of black and white. The integration of the races was a sin and they used Ali for all he was worth to get their message out there. No better man, no bigger audience. This was one of the many contradictions of Ali. He was, as he said, free to be who he wanted to be, but he was not free at all in that period of his life, he was being manipulated remorselessly; ideologically and financially. The Nation got into Ali's head - and his bank account - to such a degree that he was, by the mid-1960s, espousing the view that any black person who had sexual relations with a white person should be killed. Media playback is not supported on this device He carried on that hateful mantra for years. You look at some of the television interviews he did with Michael Parkinson back then and you get chilled to the bone by Ali's thoughts. He came across as a Ku Klux Klan member in reverse. The complexity of the man was profound. In 1967 - when still world champion - he appeared in front of the US Armed Forces Examining and Entrance Station in Houston. The army wanted to enlist Ali for the war in Vietnam that day. If he had taken a step forward when his name was called out he would have been on the first bus out of Houston bound for Fort Polk, Louisiana and then onwards to Vietnam. Ali never took the step. Everybody knew he was not going to take it. The FBI had his every move under surveillance. They regarded him as a subversive. As soon as Ali conscientiously objected to the draft Man, I ain't got no quarrel with them Vietcong' - he was aware of what was coming. The backlash was seismic. His title was stripped, his reputation trashed by white America and his life put at risk. He was not allowed to leave the country. Red Smith, one of the most influential sports columnists of the age, took out a literary blow-torch and let Ali have it. "Squealing over the possibility that the military may call him up, Cassius makes himself as sorry a spectacle as those unwashed punks who picket and demonstrate against the war," he wrote. Ali was branded a coward and a phony. David Susskind, the famous American television presenter and political commentator, went on TV with Ali and branded him "a disgrace to his country, his race and what he laughably describes as his profession." Susskind called Ali a "simplistic fool" who ought to be jailed. Time proved Ali right, of course. It cost him almost four years of his career and an estimated 10m, but his principled stance became a hallmark of his greatness - or one of them. Ali said that he was prepared to die for what he believed in. Nobody doubted that there were people out there in 1960s America who would have wanted Ali dead. Ali was suspended from boxing on April 28, 1967 and returned with a fight against Jerry Quarry on October 26, 1970. Those around him said then, and they've been saying it ever since, that the three-and-a-half years he lost would have been his peak years. Ali knew it, too. Not that it stopped him marching onwards into boxing history. He now entered the Joe Frazier years - The Fight of the Century at Madison Square Garden in 1971, the Thrilla in Manila in 1975 and, in-between, the Rumble In The Jungle - the reclaiming of his world title against George Foreman. Ali versus Frazier - the blood feud trilogy - has spawned books and films and every new one that comes out adds another layer to what is surely the greatest rivalry in sporting history. What Ali did to Joe was shameful - and he was remorseful about it until the end. Joe lent Ali money and helped him get his boxing licence back. He went to the White House and asked president Richard Nixon to help Ali out. Joe did not agree with Ali's stance on Vietnam but he felt it wrong that he was banned because of it. "Not right to take away a man's pick and shovel," was his immortal line. Ali forgot all of that. When he fought Frazier first, in 1971, he belittled him in public. He called him dumb and ignorant and ugly. He called him ape man and the gorilla. Through the force of his oratory, Ali turned black America against Frazier. He said that anybody who supported Frazier was a traitor. "The only people rooting for Joe Frazier," said Ali, "are white people in suits, Alabama sheriffs and members of the Ku Klux Klan. I'm fighting for the little man in the ghetto." Frazier was presented as an Uncle Tom - a grotesque distortion of his life, which was entrenched in the kind of poverty that Ali never knew. Their three fights were savage. "The closest thing to dying," as Ali put it. Frazier was prepared to die, no doubt about it. Right to the end of his own life, in November 2011, Frazier held a grudge against Ali. He used to speak about Ali's Parkinson's and the fact that he could not talk much anymore and he would mock him. He would say that God sent him to fix Ali. "He sent me to get him. I don't think that, I know that." Ali said sorry to Joe many times over the years. He felt guilt and tried to make amends. It never quite worked out with Frazier, not in this world at least. As he got older Ali became all about tolerance and love. All the hard edges softened and then disappeared. He lived out his life as a fighter of another kind, not the Louisville Lip, but a crusader against racism, injustice, crime, illiteracy, poverty. Those things, you sense, were of far greater importance to him than anything he achieved in the ring, from his first professional fight against Tunney Hunsaker at the Freedom Hall in his hometown of Louisville to his last, against Trevor Berbick, 21 years later. "This life is nothing but a fraction of a second compared to eternity," Ali once said. "You give God one good second and God will give you heaven for eternity."

This leads to flatter, less full-bodied music. As part of the Welsh Government plans, councils will need to have a "public toilet strategy." Rob Poultney of Criccieth, Gwynedd who has Crohn's disease, said it was vital for people to be able to access adequate toilet facilities. And the British Toilet Association called for more clarity on the plans. But the Welsh Local Government Association (WLGA) said the plans placed an "unnecessary and disproportionate burden" on local authorities. Mr Poultney, 23, whose condition causes inflammation of the lining of the digestive system, said the disease and a lack of public toilets facilities made "it really difficult for him to leave home." "It causes bowel problems and and discomfort, and it could lead to an accident.... it would be very embarrassing for me." He said it was essential for him to be able to access disabled toilets which often have a sink in the cubicle and called for each Welsh council to be ordered to provide a set number of toilets per population area. "If this bill is legally binding, then councils haven't got a choice and it's a great thing," Mr Poultney added. Meanwhile Ray Martin, managing director of the British Toilet Association, called for "one strategy across all 22 councils." He said authorities should be legally obliged to provide toilets in truck stops, heritage sites, and major junctions, as well as in towns and villages. "It's great that the councils will have to have a strategy - but we don't know exactly what that will be yet," he said. "Going to the toilet is like eating and breathing. It's something we all do every day. It's vital we have the right facilities." Public toilets across Wales have been closing as councils face budget cuts. Merthyr Tydfil in south Wales has no council-run toilets at all. In March, seven public toilets closed in Cardiff, with costs estimated at PS16 per use. Earlier this year, Gwynedd council proposed shutting down two-thirds of all council-run toilet facilities to save PS244,000. But in June, the council's cabinet agreed to ask community and town councils to help fund public toilets in the county. Anglesey council took the same approach. Mr Poultney said handing toilet facilities over to community councils did not protect their future in the long term. Mr Martin agreed, and said: "What happens in five years time, or when councillors retire?" The WLGA said it was against the plans, unless they were accompanied by "adequate funding arrangements." It warned that the proposed new duty was "unrealistic," and fears it would force councils to move funds away from services that are "of equal or greater priority." More facilities could instead be provided through community toilet schemes; the community toilet grant scheme; more user charging and better planning. A spokesperson added: "No doubt such proposals would require local authorities to regularly review their strategy; put in place action plans to secure their delivery and allow the Welsh Government to monitor progress with their delivery. "This is clearly unrealistic in the current financial climate."

Scientists found a single dose of the protein Hi1a worked on lab rats. They said it showed "great promise as a future stroke treatment" but had not yet been tested in human trials. The Stroke Association said the research was at its early stages but it would "welcome any treatment that has the potential to reduce the damage caused by stroke." The researchers, from the University of Queensland and Monash University, travelled to Fraser Island in Australia to hunt for and capture three potentially deadly Australian funnel web spiders. "We regularly collect spiders from Fraser Island off the south coast of Queensland," explained lead researcher Prof Glenn King. "The reason for this is that funnel-web spiders dig burrows that can be as deep as 20-30 cm. Thus, digging them up from hard clay soils is very difficult. Fraser Island is a sand island which makes it easy for us to extract the spiders from their burrows." The team then took the spiders back to their laboratory "for milking." This involved coaxing the spider to release its venom, which could then be sucked up using pipettes. Next the scientists dissected the venom gland of the spiders and honed in on a protein in the venom to recreate a version of it in their lab. They then injected this Hi1a into the lab rats. A stroke is a brain attack that happens when the blood supply to part of the brain is cut off or there is bleeding on the brain Source: Stroke Association They found that the protein blocked acid-sensing ion channels in the brain - something the researchers say are key drivers of brain damage after stroke. Prof King said the protein showed "great promise as a future stroke treatment." "We believe that we have, for the first time, found a way to minimise the effects of brain damage after a stroke. "Hi1a even provides some protection to the core brain region most affected by oxygen deprivation, which is generally considered unrecoverable due to the rapid cell death caused by stroke." The research was published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. "My lab is interested in developing drugs for human nervous system disorders. Many of these disorders involve either dysfunctional ion channels (e.g. epilepsy) or over-active ion channels (chronic pain and stroke). Thus, we are typically looking for molecules that modulate the activity of ion channels. The venoms of small venomous invertebrates such as spiders, centipedes and scorpions have evolved to target the nervous system of insects, and consequently they are absolutely full of ion channel modulators. Because the human nervous system is more complex and wired differently to insects, ion channel modulators that kill or paralyse insects can actually be beneficial to humans. Thus, looking in venoms for ion channel drugs is not as weird as it seems." Dr Kate Holmes, deputy director for Research at the Stroke Association, said: "We do not have an accurate picture of what happens in human brains from this research, therefore, it is currently unknown if this could be a successful treatment option for humans in the future. "We welcome any treatment that has the potential to reduce the damage caused by stroke, particularly if this can benefit people who are unable to arrive at hospital quickly. "Current treatments must be given in half this time period, and it is too early for us to know if this research can offer an alternative for stroke patients. "We urge for stroke to be treated as an emergency - the sooner a person can get to hospital after a stroke, the sooner the right treatment can be received, which can improve survival and help recovery."

This paper shows connections between command injection attacks, continuations, and the Lambek calculus: certain command injections, such as the tautology attack on SQL, are shown to be a form of control effect that can be typed using the Lambek calculus, generalizing the double-negation typing of continuations. Lambek's syntactic calculus is a logic with two implicational connectives taking their arguments from the left and right, respectively. These connectives describe how strings interact with their left and right contexts when building up syntactic structures. The calculus is a form of propositional logic without structural rules, and so a forerunner of substructural logics like Linear Logic and Separation Logic.

Bangladesh had only beaten Zimbabwe and a weakened West Indies team in 95 previous Tests, but the 108-run win means the series finished 1-1. England needed their highest successful run chase in Asia and looked well set after a century opening partnership between Alastair Cook and Ben Duckett. But they lost all 10 wickets in 22.5 overs in the final session as Bangladesh secured the biggest win in their history. Bangladesh had lost 72 of their previous Tests and last played in August 2015 because of security concerns in the country. Duckett (56) scored his first Test half-century but was bowled by 19-year-old off-spinner Mehedi with the first ball after tea, prompting the stunning collapse - the third worst in history by a team who had been 100 without loss. Joe Root was lbw in the following over to Shakib, before Gary Ballance and Moeen Ali were dismissed in the same Mehedi over shortly afterwards. Cook made 59 but, despite successfully overturning one dismissal, the England captain was caught off Mehedi by Mominul Haque at silly point. Fittingly, Mehedi took the final wicket of Steven Finn to finish with six in the innings, 12 in the match and 19 in the series. Openers Cook and Duckett, who batted together for the first time in the first Test in Chittagong, had only managed a best partnership of 26 in their previous three innings. Climate change or global warming as it previously was known as is a hot potatoe and not a very clean cut science to predict. There are thousands of climate scientists and climate models that provide completely different results. There is absolutely no consensus in the scientific community about what the consequences of human-induced global warming will be. The UN's Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), which includes many of the world's leading climate scientists, acknowledge this uncertainty in its 2007 report. The IPCC said it is "very likely" that mankind has caused most of the global temperature rise since 1950 and warned that temperatures will continue to rise for decades. But the exact magnitude of the future warming and its effects are highly uncertain. The IPCC called for a wide range of possible emissions reductions to limit the temperature increase to between 1.1 and 2.9 degrees Celsius by 2100. In its subsequent 2014 report, the IPCC cut the likely temperature increase by the end of the century to between 0.3 and 1.7 degrees Celsius, while acknowledging even this was highly uncertain. The main cause of global warming is greenhouse gas emissions from human activity. The primary greenhouse gases are water vapor, carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, and ozone. Greenhouse gases trap heat in the atmosphere, causing the Earth's average temperature to rise. Over the past century, the burning of fossil fuels such as coal and oil has greatly increased the concentration of atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2). This is the most important greenhouse gas, and it contributes to global warming. Methane is another important greenhouse gas. It is produced by the decomposition of organic matter in landfills, animal agriculture, and leaky natural gas systems. Nitrous oxide comes from agricultural fertilizer, industrial activities, and vehicle exhaust. These greenhouse gases form a "blanket" around Earth that trap energy from the sun. This trapped energy makes the Earth's atmosphere warm, and disturbs the Earth's climate. It can cause more extreme weather conditions, like hurricanes, floods, and droughts. It can also cause long-term changes in climate patterns, like shifting rain belts and expanded deserts. Over the past century, the global average temperature has risen by about 1.4 degrees Fahrenheit. Most of this warming has occurred since 1970. The rate of warming has been even greater over the past few decades. Scientists expect the Earth to continue to warm in the coming years and decades, largely due to increasing levels of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere. If greenhouse gas emissions continue to rise at the current pace, global average temperatures could increase by as much as 8 degrees Fahrenheit by 2100. This would have major impacts on our environment, our economy, and our way of life. There is no single solution to the problem of climate change. Reducing greenhouse gas emissions will require a concerted effort from individuals, businesses, and governments around the world.

The internet operages by transmitting small units of information, typically around 1500 bytes, to specified computer addresses. Regardless of the volume of incoming data directed towards your designated address, as long as your network and device are sufficiently quick, your system will receive these messages and potentially respond in kind. This process is facilitated by 'ports', which function similarly to unique identifiers enabling access to specific services on a computer. Imagine ports as various service counters such as those found in an ice-cream truck or a drive-through, each assigned with distinct numerical values corresponding to particular tasks - retrieving a webpage (port 80), sending an email (port 25), fetching emails (port 110). In instances where a requested service isn't available, the port remains unattended or closed; otherwise, it is manned by a virtual attendant ready to assist. To optimize efficiency and prevent congestion, users may be redirected to alternative, randomly generated port numbers upon request initiation. Upon successful identity verification, the user receives their desired content before concluding the session when further requests cease. Contrary to popular belief, every computing device linked to the internet possesses interconnectivity via physical connections or wireless signals, rendering them theoretically traceable within the vast digital landscape. Information acquisition from the internet occurs via 'requests'; entering a URL initiates several stages, starting with querying a server for the precise location of the targeted resource.

The past few years have witnessed the fast development of different regularization methods for deep learning models such as fully-connected deep neural networks (DNNs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). Most of previous methods mainly consider to drop features from input data and hidden layers, such as Dropout, Cutout and DropBlocks. DropConnect select to drop connections between fully-connected layers. By randomly discard some features or connections, the above mentioned methods control the overfitting problem and improve the performance of neural networks. In this paper, we proposed two novel regularization methods, namely DropFilter and DropFilter-PLUS, for the learning of CNNs. Different from the previous methods, DropFilter and DropFilter-PLUS selects to modify the convolution filters. For DropFilter-PLUS, we find a suitable way to accelerate the learning process based on theoretical analysis. Experimental results on MNISTshow that using DropFilter and DropFilter-PLUS may improve performance on image classification tasks.

Evaluating conjunctive queries and solving constraint satisfaction problems are fundamental problems in database theory and artificial intelligence, respectively. These problems are NP-hard, so that several research efforts have been made in the literature for identifying tractable classes, known as islands of tractability, as well as for devising clever heuristics for solving efficiently real-world instances. Many heuristic approaches are based on enforcing on the given instance a property called local consistency, where (in database terms) each tuple in every query atom matches at least one tuple in every other query atom. Interestingly, it turns out that, for many well-known classes of queries, such as for the acyclic queries, enforcing local consistency is even sufficient to solve the given instance correctly. However, the precise power of such a procedure was unclear, but for some very restricted cases. The paper provides full answers to the long-standing questions about the precise power of algorithms based on enforcing local consistency. In particular, the paper deals with both the general framework of tree projections, where local consistency is enforced among arbitrary views defined over the given database instance, and the specific cases where such views are computed according to so-called structural decomposition methods, such as generalized hypertree width, component hypertree decompositions, and so on. The classes of instances where enforcing local consistency turns out to be a correct query-answering procedure are however not efficiently recognizable. In fact, the paper finally focuses on certain subclasses defined in terms of the novel notion of greedy tree projections. These latter classes are shown to be efficiently recognizable and strictly larger than most islands of tractability known so far, both in the general case of tree projections and for specific structural decomposition methods.

So let's say your body is a see-saw, but it likes to be level at all times with nothing weighing too much on either side. When you're inside, the temperature is regulated, and your body doesn't have to work to keep itself at it's core temperature, so there's nothing pushing on either side of the see-saw that your body has to work to balance out. Now when you work in the sun, your body has the heat of the sun pushing on one side of the see-saw, and your body has to work extra hard and exert more energy to keep the see-saw stable and balance out what the heat of the sun is pushing on one side. tl;dr When you're outside in the heat your body has to work harder to keep you cool.

The Intensive Care Unit (ICU) is a hospital department where machine learning has the potential to provide valuable assistance in clinical decision making. Classical machine learning models usually only provide pure predictions about future health outcomes, but can also be used as powerful tools for analyzing observational data and designing new experiments. In this paper we present an approach that combines supervised prediction with interpretable modeling of observed covariates using latent factor analysis. We illustrate how this model improves two classic application areas: early-warning identification of poor outcome and selection of optimal treatments in the ICU. The problem of avoiding adverse events in intensive care patients was first posed by Chen et al. cite13. They showed that blindly applying standard treatment regimens may not always produce favorable patient outcomes when applied on various groups within their study population; instead certain subgroups appeared at high risk of serious complications such as sepsis or bleeding episodes following arterial lines insertions. These observations were initially interpreted based on traditional risk factors like age, comorbidities etc., but eventually led to the development of predictive scoring systems to identify the most likely risky groups from prospective studies cite27 cite1. In follow up work these methods have been extended to include additional predictors like inflammatory biomarkers cite18, individualized treatment algorithms cite20 and more recently probabilistic classification techniques cite15. However, none of these approaches are feasible to use routinely due to lack of large scale trials which might justify their usage outside controlled settings. Recent developments however allow us to overcome some limitations associated with previously proposed solutions while improving our ability to deal with missing data through advances in deep neural networks. Deep learning has shown tremendous success in many computer vision nd medical applications including image recognition cite3, cancer detection cite33, natural language processing cite21, speech recognition cite43 among others. Instead of trying to directly incorporate these complex features into existing risk scorers we propose a simpler method to learn from available symptoms and diagnostic reports combined with generalized linear mixed effects regression. When no covariate values are known or if even the most reliable predictor variables cannot provide acceptable confidence intervals we use reinforcement learning to select realistic surrogate covariances to balance out observable correlations between symptom predicting markers and disease severity. Previously, math -policy reinforcement learning has demonstrated superior performance on 2D gridworlds simulating real world environments compared to other algorithm classes cite46; see e.g. cite25.

[ Part One ] I'm sick of it..... They say that some people are happy enough alone, and based on more than a few accounts it certainly seems true enough. Hermits, monks, nuns..... there are all sorts of people who'v managed to avoid all human contact and remain completely'there'. Men and women who haven't spoken a word to their fellow man in years, but still somehow manage to wear a smile on their face. It's some sort of sick insanity, I'm certain of it. That they can spend a lifetime along and still pretend that they're completely fulfilled thanks to simply not needing people, or worse, thanks to some divine power. Five years..... that's all that it'd taken me to realize that if I wanted to continue to be me that I ought to be alone. Sweet sixteen buddy, you're not normal. Oh, happy twenty-first birthday, in order to improve the world you'll kill everyone around you. Friends, family, lovers..... you're a parasite who drains them to fuel yourself in the most sickening of ways. At the very least, I'd been able to have a few drinks before I made my way out into the wilderness to try and emulate those crazy bastards who can stay away from humanity. The first few months hadn't been too hard. I was doing this to save the people that I loved, to keep away from everyone, to insulate myself from them. Then, the hunger set in..... I began to talk to the animals when I saw them. Birds, rabbits..... whatever was around. I needed something, some sort of communication. Food, water, shelter..... all that was easily enough taken care of. But hearing only my own voice and the chattering of squirrels, birdsongs, it was grating. But I endured, I knew that I had to. There were husks of people I'd left behind to attest for what I was. Wouldn't it be so much better for everyone if I remained hidden? Wouldn't it keep the world so much brighter if I were to stay so far away from it? But as months dragged into years, as my voice began to even fade as the conversations with the animals dwindled..... I think that I might have actually began to lose it. The world at large had to know that I was still alive, had to know that the damage I caused when I got angry wasn't natural. A forest didn't just suddenly have a massive clearing right in the middle of it, become pockmarked with craters. They started to search for something. It was..... almost reassuring sometimes, to be looked for. Scary, yes, I'd always known what the government might do with me if they found me and knew what I was. Experiments tantamount to torture, imprisonment I couldn't break out of..... all that fun. But having a helicopter fly overhead, having people walk past me knowing they were looking for something that I was. It'd become a game for me. It became my'escape' from my solitude, to destroy some portion of the forest, some outlying abandoned structure in order to get the search parties nearby. It was a sad, pathetic thing to do. But it sustained my need for hearing the voices of others for a while longer. Not nearly long enough though..... not nearly a lifetime before I finally broke and returned to civilization. Maybe, after several years of solitude I could learn to simply watch. To either abandon using my abilities for good or to never truly love another person again. After so many years alone, I doubted that I could even remember what love was. I'd found my way into a bit of a small town. Bought a razor, some new clothes, gotten a haircut with the money that'd still been in my bank account, accruing a whole dollar's interest. I looked half a wild man- was..... half a wild man when I first came back. The people in the town thought that I had been something of a hermit, lost to the world for so long. But none of them had seen me, had connected a mere human to the sporadic events on the outskirts of the community and deep in the nearby wilderness. In fact, they were somewhat saddened by the fact that the'anomalies' had stopped. It drove business in, from the paranormal'experts' who thought it was a haven for interesting events. From the various search parties who were searching so carefully for what'thing' might have been out there. But they took me in with no problem..... I found a job despite a true lack of a resume, had people more than willing to help me get back into the new subtle nuances of society. Food, shelter, water, the necessities were all so readily provided to me by good, honest people rather than the wilderness. It took effort, conscious effort on my part not to get close. Not to go beyond a simple thank you. Not to pursue any opportunities beyond being'strictly professional' in all manners. It hurt. A little less than simply being an outsider looking in, a little less than talking to merely animals in the wilderness, but it hurt all the same. But I'd settled in comfortably, I'd sat back and made myself a part of the town, if a somewhat eccentric part. I did my part for the town too, ensuring that the'anomalies' continued in the general area, driving the bit of tourism that we got. It was a way that I could be close without being close, my silent and thankless contribution to good people. Sighing, I set into my meal before me. Another shift at the yard, another day's pay earned, and another planned excursion for the evening. My life could be summed up so simply by variations in that sentence, occasionally interspersed with meals and the usual mundane bits of life. "Excuse me, sir?" I blink, the voice having a different'accent' than that of the locals. Around here, there's a bit of a drawl on everyone's speech besides my own..... save the tourists of course. Looking up, I see a gorgeous woman to my side, looking at me. Long dark brown hair, brown eyes, a pleasant face..... A body that the'business casual' suit simply didn't do justice for. The sort of'young professional' woman that you simply can't find in a place like this. I blink, realizing my rudeness as she looks a little uncomfortable as the silence drags on. "Yes?" "More than a few people in the town have told me that you might be someone who I could do an interview with on the recent...'events' around this town. They say that you actually lived out there while all sorts of things were happening." She says, looking just a little nervous as she states things fairly enthusiastically. "I'm trying to get a few freelance reports done, to make a bit of a name for myself. You've never done an interview, despite everyone saying that you might really have an interesting story to tell about things." She explains hastily, tripping over herself in her haste to explain things.

If they shift on these subjects in a single direction- say 'guns are bad and need to be banned', there's little point arguing. The anti-gunners will just shrug their shoulders and look away from the screen wondering what we're all talking about. The same applies with debates about environmentalism and sustainability. We know that making changes is going to have an impact; it doesn't make sense doing nothing. But when you try to argue the issue, the answer invariably appears as 'the laws aren't strict enough!' for many of our viewers. Consensus without facts isn't rational thinking - it's possibly dishonesty! It would help if politicians were more prepared to take some responsibility themselves, but so far this has been very rare among them. It's why 'climate change denialism' was called out by David Cameron as one of his five biggest political mistakes: he didn't want to admit failings on his watch. And it's also why I think most British voters would side with the government taking action against it even though they might not agree with every decision taken - after all, they do appear to believe that 'science' tells us that global warming poses serious threats to life on Earth. In fact, recent polls suggest that very few Britons actually believe that climate change exists at all. Just 26 said that they believed humans had caused global warming over the past 35 years; 33 said that human activity made up only part of the causes. 57 did not believe there was any connection between anthropogenic emissions and increased greenhouse gas concentrations. In other words, even assuming that this is entirely true, this means that around 55 million Brits won't accept the science behind climate change either because it contradicts what they believe or because they won't accept anything else. All those would probably vote Conservative anyway. The problem with the media I'm afraid there's no silver bullet here; commentators all have different areas where things could improve. For instance, whenever someone criticises me personally, my response is always 'well... wouldn't you wish your parents hadn't put you into such a difficult situation?' Well yes I would - and yet, I still feel like I've got quite a good record compared to most politicians. But I can understand how others may find it easier to brush off criticisms of politics than they'd expect. When they hear that Tony Blair proposed legislation which could protect children from online pornography, they assume that he must be something of a hypocrite. However, the reality is that when Blair was Prime Minister, he spent much time trying to tackle child abuse. He famously argued vehemently against plans to remove these images from the internet during the Digital Millennium Copyright Act negotiations (which eventually failed). This wasn't because he was concerned about paedophiles hanging around the parliament building I suspect...more likely he thought there was sufficient evidence already available to show that online pornography was harmful to kids. So while I think that we should get rid of any footage of naked young boys being abused online, it seems positively perverse to bring back censorship when faced with similar concerns elsewhere. But then again...somebody has to keep watching TV! Are we really suggesting introducing new age restrictions where children can watch adult content? Or perhaps we should simply ban social networking sites for kids altogether? Children would clearly be better served by avoiding them all together. Of course, political leaders don't live and breathe the lives of everyday citizens regularly. Yet they nevertheless represent them on the national stage. They do at least try to act responsibly towards society's most vulnerable people. Politicians who ignore both domestic and international climate change issues should resign immediately, along with those who deny its existence altogether.

We present a novel algorithm for instrumental variable (IV) regression, DualIV, which simplifies traditional two-stage methods via a dual formulation. Inspired by problems in stochastic programming, we show that the IV problem can be recast as a convex optimization problem over a dual variable. Our algorithm combines the dual formulation with a Newton-like method to obtain a two-step algorithm that can be used to efficiently estimate the conditional mean of a high-dimensional random vector, even when the number of independent variables is high. To demonstrate the power of our new approach, we compare our method to other dual-based methods for IV estimation, and to traditional IV estimation methods. We use simulated data to evaluate the properties of the IV estimator under a variety of settings, and apply the method to study the relation between maternal immigration and child behavior.

The reforms introduced by Emperor Augustus enhanced both the financial support and visibility of the Vestal Virgins. They were granted privileged seats during entertainment events such as games and plays. Later on, Emperor Claudius designated them as spiritual leaders for the worship of the deified Livia, who was Augustus’ spouse. These women maintained their unique religious roles and societal statuses until the late 3rd or early 4th century CE, even after the center of imperial authority transitioned towards the Christian faith. However, when Christian ruler Gratian declined the position of chief priest (pontifex maximus), he initiated a move that would lead to the disbandment of the Vestal tradition. Subsequently, his successor, Theodosius I, put out the holy flame of Vesta and abandoned her sanctuary.

Once upon a time, there was an old blind man who lived in a big house. He had been living in the house for many years and he was very content with his life. One day, the old blind man decided to take a walk around his big house. He used his cane as a guide and carefully navigated through the halls. As he walked around, he noticed a peculiar sound coming from one of the rooms. It sounded like someone crying. The old blind man cautiously opened the door and peered inside. To his surprise, he saw a young boy sitting on the floor, sobbing. The old blind man asked the boy what was wrong. The boy told him that he had been lost in the forest for days and he had no idea how to get home. The old blind man felt sorry for the boy and decided to help him. He took the boy back to his big house and gave him some food and a place to stay. The old blind man taught the young boy how to take care of himself and also showed him around the house. The boy quickly adapted to his new environment and soon enough he came to see the old blind man as a father figure. The old blind man and the young boy lived happily together in the big house for many years. They were both incredibly grateful for each other's company. The old blind man will always remember the young boy who found his way into the big house and became like a son to him.

Additionally, contractions aren't common at the start of sentences or within formal or legal texts. Ending a sentence with such a contraction is also incorrect. For instance, saying "He's superior to you're" is grammatically improper due to the separation of "you" and "are" into distinct components. A new report has revealed a dramatic decrease in investment in commercial property in Aberdeen over the last two years. The report, by consultancy JLL, shows that investment in office, retail and industrial property in the city fell from 257 million in 2015 to just 41 million last year. This is a massive drop of 84 and is the sharpest decline of any major city in the UK. The fall in investment is in line with a general decline in the Aberdeen economy since the oil price crash in 2014. The city has been hit hard by job losses in the oil and gas industry, and this has had a knock-on effect on the commercial property market. JLL's report highlights the need for urgent action to kick-start the Aberdeen economy and attract new investment into the city. Without this, the commercial property market is likely to continue to decline, putting even more jobs at risk.

We stood, shivering, huddled around the whiteboard. Our standup meetings were a huge risk, but what resistance could manage without them? Jim went around the circle, asking everyone what they'd like to do that day. "I think we should go for lunch," said one guy. "Nah - let's just work on this idea I have." He started sketching something out with his finger. The board was covered in scribbles and ideas; everything from ways of splitting up teams into smaller groups to better ways of tracking stuff during development. We'd run out of toothpicks. The room stank of coffee and cigarettes now, so people weren't really concentrating anymore: everyone had given up trying to write anything down. One person who didn't smoke wondered how much longer our frozen state would last: surely if it got any colder than today we wouldn't be able to continue working. It felt as though they hadn't even noticed when Matt spoke again: he thanked us all for coming out and hoped there wasn't too many more days where we needed to get together at six o'clock in the morning before jumping straight back to work afterwards. Everyone nodded politely, although no-one actually seemed happy about having missed their shifts back home or after school. Some of them looked dispirited by the whole thing altogether. Matt left, leaving behind some kind of draft plan which nobody read through properly because everybody turned their attention towards our next meeting, half an hour later, at nine. In fact, most people left completely shortly after eight. There was still an hour and a quarter until then, though, and while no-one wanted to waste any time (especially not when you're going away for four months), there wasn't enough space on the stands for everyone to sit down comfortably, so instead of sitting a few feet apart from each other talking amongst themselves, they gathered round in small knots outside the main conference area: smoking, using their phones, poking fun at someone else's drawing. They knew exactly how long they had left: they spent twenty minutes arguing over whether to eat first or drink tea first, knowing full well that they couldn't possibly start eating breakfast unless everyone sat down. Eventually, someone flicked on Twitter to see if anyone was reporting trouble across London. But besides those reports being mostly good news no big rush queues on bridgesroads" etc.) nothing major had happened yet: things were slowly getting underway, but not dangerously so. People carried on chatting quietly. At 8.30 sharp, two guys came running in looking stressed. Nobody quite believed how fast they arrived, despite only living ten minutes walk away: they must have skipped breakfast entirely. By way of apology, they handed out biscuits that had been brought along specially for the occasion. Soon everyone was tweeting about traffic jams and rail delays and tube evacuations. Meanwhile, inside the building, the team leader explained briefly why we were cancelling standing meetings for the rest of the week: one side effect of thousands of people jamming up the capital is that trains are delayed everywhere, meaning there aren't nearly enough buses available to transport us between offices quickly. With fewer opportunities to meet face to face, communication can break down easily within the team. Instead, we were encouraged to spend less time together and use Google Hangouts whenever possible. This meant that rather than hanging around the office all day, waiting for assignments, people could log off, come home and keep working. Then, once dinner finished, they'd check emails on their mobiles and respond whilst they cooked food. Repeat every night. There was no point worrying about tomorrow, anyway. Today was important enough. At 9 o'clock sharp, everyone filed downstairs ready to catch the bus to Liverpool Street station.

Between the 16th century and 19th century, the traditional Armenian homeland composed of Eastern Armenia and Western Armenia came under the rule of the Ottoman and successive Iranian empires, repeatedly ruled by either of the two over the centuries. By the 19th century, Eastern Armenia had been conquered by the Russian Empire, while most of the western parts of the traditional Armenian homeland remained under Ottoman rule. During World War I, Armenians living in their ancestral lands in the Ottoman Empire were systematically exterminated in the Armenian Genocide. In 1918, after the Russian Revolution, all non-Russian countries declared their independence from the Russian empire, leading to the establishment of the First Republic of Armenia. By 1920, the state was incorporated into the Transcaucasian Socialist Federative Soviet Republic, and in 1922 became a founding member of the Soviet Union. In 1936, the Transcaucasian state was dissolved, transforming its constituent states, including the Armenian Soviet Socialist Republic, into full Union republics. The modern Republic of Armenia became independent in 1991 during the dissolution of the Soviet Union.

Yes. "Reasonable person" is a hugely mutable definition. In most cases, what it means is "the reasonable person in a given set of circumstances." Obviously that "reasonable person" has changed over time, or the 18th Century "reasonable person" would proceed to freak the fuck out because wtf is this thing he's driving and oh god why are those people crying and standing near another one of the things he's driving but broken-looking? The best approximation of a non-legal way of saying "reasonable person" is "the average man on the bus." It's not got a fixed meaning; instead, it's mostly a thought-aid for jurors and fact-finders to use in assessing behavior, reactions, etc.','Yes. To be more direct. There's more context though, because there is a long history of legal jurisprudence that frames the "reasonable man" standard in a particular situation. "So..... you're a vampire. And I'm a vampire hunter." She sat primly on a boulder across him. The slope beyond led far down towards the dark castle and even from this distance it looked ominous, the cold light of the moon reflected on the surface of the lakes that surrounded it. In the air, so pure and fresh here, she could still taste the bitterness of her own blood, the dryness of her lips and the deep craving that had returned the moment she had walked outside. She had been eager to tell the other vampires about her mother, but she felt that she had to keep it to herself for a while. It was not the other vampires' business. "I'm not hunting you," he said. "I don't know who your mother is. I don't know what you are." She breathed in deeply, savouring the cold air, letting her senses soak it in. "I'm a vampire." "You're not," he said. "A vampire would be dead, at least, if not something else." "I'm different," she said. "I'm not like the other vampires. I'm stronger and...." She took in another breath. "Stronger?" He couldn't help but grin, looking down at her. She was too small to be a threat to him, but the look in her eyes was unnerving. "Yes," she said. "I'm stronger than any of them. I'm faster, I'm smarter, I can read people, I can sense emotions, I can learn languages, and...." "And?" he said, smiling. "And I can't be destroyed by a wooden stake to the heart, or sunlight, or any of the other things that supposedly kill vampires." "But why would you be stronger than them?" he said, confused. "How?" She shrugged. "I don't know. Maybe because my mother was a vampire hunter, but I can't be sure. I'm different. I can't explain it. It's just..... there's something different about me." "I can be sure of that," he said. "I've heard about vampire hunters. They're not myths, I've met one." "And what do you do?" she asked. "I kill vampires. I used to be human too." He held out his arm, and she gasped, shocked. In his arm was a large black mark, about three inches long, a dark spot that looked like a claw. "I was attacked by one, and I killed it." He pressed his forearm to his mouth, feeling the bite wound. He breathed out slowly. "That's what happened to me." She sat there, trying to grasp what he was telling her. "But how?" she said. "You don't look...." "You're so young," he said. "You don't have any memories of what happened to you. You're not a hunter. You don't know the difference between a vampire and a human." "How do you know I'm not?" "You smell," he said. "You smell of blood. Vampires don't smell of blood. They smell of death, of dirt, of leaves. They smell of rusty metal and old wood." "Well, that's not very nice," she said, looking down. "But what about you? Don't you smell of blood?" "I smell of anger, of hate, of...." he couldn't say it. "I smell like death. I'm not a vampire, but I've become one." "You're different," she said. "You're a vampire, like me." "No," he said. "I can't be. I can't smell of blood. I can't be like you." "You're a vampire," she said, raising her voice. "Look at yourself." "No," he said, shaking his head. "I'm not. I'm different. I don't want to be. I don't want to be like you. I don't want to be like them." "It's not my fault," she said. "It's not my fault that I was bitten. I was just an innocent human, like you."

I hold the view that life lacks a predetermined purpose. Rather, I consider life to be a random occurrence, with our existence happening by chance. Consequently, I reject the idea of absolute moral principles, particularly the concept of an intrinsic virtue that individuals should strive towards. Any perceived purpose must originate from within the individual since there seems to be no external reason for humanity's presence on Earth, other than serving natural processes, which humans often contradict, especially in contemporary society. Assuming a deity exists, one might suggest our existence serves its intentions, possibly for amusement, though this reasoning remains unclear to me. This perspective extends to the idea of a collective 'greater good', as well – it appears nonexistent outside of individual or social contexts. A hypothetical universal principle of goodness fails to explain the disparities in cultural norms regarding acceptable behavior across different societies. Nevertheless, I find this diversity empowering rather than disheartening. Unlike conventional forms of nihilism where purposelessness renders life worthless, I regard the absence of predefined objectives as liberating. Without an overarching sense of duty or morality, each person has the opportunity to create their own purpose based on personal experiences and fulfillment. One isn't bound by external expectations, but only by internal limitations imposed upon themselves. Therefore, my belief system aligns closely with ethical hedonism – embracing life's unpredictability and prioritizing enjoyable experiences above all else.

We address the problem of reasoning about interleavings in safety verification of concurrent programs. In the literature, there are two prominent techniques for pruning the search space. First, there are well-investigated trace-based methods, collectively known as "Partial Order Reduction (POR) ," which operate by weakening the concept of a trace by abstracting the total order of its transitions into a partial order. Second, there is state-based interpolation where a collection of formulas can be generalized by taking into account the property to be verified. Our main contribution is a framework that synergistically combines POR with state interpolation so that the sum is more than its parts.

He was never warm in his entire life. Not once. It was a fact that followed him around like a heavy cloud, an ever-present reminder of the void he felt inside. He had grown up in a small house with no insulation or heating system. His parents were too poor to afford much of anything and so he was forced to spend his days wrapped in blankets and sweaters, shivering against the cold. He had never really known what it was like to be warm. Whenever he closed his eyes, all he could feel was the chill air seeping through his clothes, chilling him to the bone. He would sit for hours, wrapped up in his blankets and sweaters, trying to will himself warm but nothing ever came. As he got older, he became more determined to find warmth. He read countless books on the subject and experimented with different techniques. He tried meditating and exercising, but nothing seemed to work. He searched endlessly for a way to make himself feel warm but to no avail. At long last, he stumbled upon something that worked. It wasn't a physical solution, but rather a mental one. He began to think of warmth not as a physical sensation, but as an emotion. He imagined what it might feel like to have a loving embrace or to experience the joy of accomplishment. He thought of all the things that made him happy and let those warm thoughts fill him up. For the first time in his life, he finally felt warmth inside.

Jay Leno was the host of the late night talk show Tonight Show after Johnny Carson (who had started hosting the show in 1962) retired in 1992. In 1993, Conan O'Brien (who had been a comedy writer and performer for everything from SNL to the Simpsons) took over the reigns of Late Night, the talk show that came after the Tonight Show. Late Night had been hosted by David Letterman, which had an unofficial tradition that the host of Late Night would take over the Tonight Show with some new talent taking over Late Night people assumed the Letterman would take over after spending so much time hosting Late Night. Instead, NBC decided to screw with things by giving the Tonight Show to Jay Leno, causing David Letterman to leave NBC entirely to move over to another channel (this will be a recurring theme). Anyway, in 2004 it was announced Leno would retire in 2009. That date came, Conan O'Brian took the reigns of the Tonight Show, and everyone thought that this transition would be the end of Leno's time. Then NBC decided to screw with things. NBC didn't want Jay Leno to follow David Letterman's example by jumping networks. So, they tried to get him to stay on NBC by offering some other non-Tonight Show position. Finally, they settled on creating "The Jay Leno Show," putting it before O'Brian's Tonight Show. It was basically Jay Leno's Tonight show skits. After the first few episodes the ratings went to the toilet. These ratings not only hurt the 10 o'clock timeslot, but also the Tonight Show and the various local late night news. Leno was under contract, so show couldn't be cancelled outright, so they shortened the show to 30 minutes and moved the Jay Leno show to 11:35, the timeslot the Tonight Show had occupied for 60 years. After more ratings wows, NBC decided the best solution was to just cut O'Brian and have Jay Leno host the Tonight Show again. O'Brian (and Leno for that matter) were not particularly pleased with this arrangement, but contract clauses were called upon. Jay Leno hosted the Tonight Show from 2010-2014. After less than a year on the Tonight Show, O'Brian left NBC for his own talk show (Conan) on TBS. Edit: Slight correction.', "Others have explained the situation really well, but I would add that the situation wasn't really Leno vs. O'Brien, it was NBC vs. O'Brien. Leno wasn't trying to get the Tonight Show back after he left, but he had the opportunity to try out a different show and give the headlining gig to Conan. He's not the bad guy, he was just performing according to his contract. NBC is who screwed Conan over by forcing him to air his show after midnight ET. There is a huge dropoff in viewers after the first half hour of late night television, because a lot of viewers just stay up for the monologue before going to sleep. If the show doesn't even begin until after that time, they lose those viewers. Basically, Conan was getting the tonight show, but they were sending all of the viewers to Leno's show.," "Jay Leno and the network promised the job to Conan years in advance. When it came for Leno to leave, the network still wanted him around for viewers so they gave him a new prime time show. Spinning wheels are more difficult to tip over than wheels at rest. It takes more energy to tip over a rotating wheel than a stationary one since you're working against its rotational inertia as well as its mass. It's the same effect that makes a spinning [gyroscope] (URL0) able to balance instead of falling over. The stability effect gets stronger the more momentum the wheel has, which is why balancing a bike is harder when you're barely moving but effortless when you're going fast.

The probability varies depending on whether it splits evenly at 50/50. Achieving ten consecutive heads with a coin toss has only one possibility, whereas numerous combinations exist for obtaining an equal number of heads and tails (e.g., alternating patterns, random sequences). Each unique sequence holds an equivalent likelihood due to their independence and identical probabilities per event. Regarding multiple coin flips, the chances of obtaining a balanced distribution (such as half heads and half tails) increase significantly compared to specific patterns like getting heads repeatedly throughout the entire series. In summary, while individual arrangements possess the same chance of occurrence, a near-even split becomes statistically more probable when considering larger sets of coin tosses.

For the salary year beginning April 2008, unpromoted teachers in Scotland earned from PS20,427 for a Probationer, up to PS32,583 after 6 years teaching, but could then go on to apply for promotion, or 'step'. They had to be relevant and "promote innovation and improvement of services." There appeared no limit to how far they might rise within their subject areas in terms of pay level. But in July 2009 in England it was announced that for the first time there would be an annual cap at 25,000 per annum (which was still not indexed), though this did not apply to new entrants who already qualified. The Office Professional Standards also put forward proposals about step increase bands which were not adopted by Ofsted. The government sought to reassure schools that the cap would be temporary and that all teachers will receive pay awards commensurate with inflation over the next four years as recommended by the independent Pay Review Body. At least until 2012 though, many believed the cap remained permanent. In 201011 the average starting teacher salary across Britain rose to about 24k. In some parts of London, such as Westminster, Holborn St Pancras, Kensington Chelsea, Camden Islington, Tower Hamlets Hackney, Lewisham Deptford, Haringey Newham and Redbridge, basic salaries started out at well above 30,000! By 2014, these had risen to between 40-45k where teachers earn salaries equivalent to those earning more than six times more than them. After the summer 2011 announcement that teacher pay would be frozen at its current level - resulting in a fall for all newly qualified teachers regardless of whether they took up the opportunity to move into leadership posts - momentum behind the profession began to wane further. It simply became harder to recruit. More recently in 2017, it was revealed that while the Chancellor Philip Hammond said he wanted to boost school budgets so that all children can have access to free education up to age 16, funding cuts meant only one million pupils would actually benefit. And when it comes to recruitment and retention, a 2016 survey carried out by Tes magazine found that while 48 of respondents thought teachers are paid too little, just 20 disagreed. Only 27 said they agreed that they were paid enough, compared with 42 in 2015. Another report published in 2018 by the National Education Union stated: "Teaching is one of the most undervalued professions." It seems clear that despite the claims made by politicians, the reality is quite different to what we see portrayed on TV screens nowadays.

Scientists from the University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences have developed a system that can accurately detect cancer cells in the bloodstream and destroy these cells in real time as they pass through the body. The machine could mean that doctors will eventually be able to destroy cancer cells in the bloodstream before they form new tumors in the body with a harmless, noninvasive, and thorough procedure. In the study, the machine was able to detect cancer cells in 27 out of the 28 patients, with a sensitivity that is about 1,000 times better than current technology. It works by aiming a laser at a vein, where it heats up circulating tumor cells faster than normal cells, causing them to expand quickly and die, a process which produces sound. The sound produced indicates how many cells have passed through the laser.

This isn't the best LI5, but it's my take on it.,The Paul McCartney "paradox" is a bit silly. It was proposed as a criticism of the Copenhagen Interpretation of Quantum Mechanics. The idea was that you put Paul McCartney in a box with a radioactively triggered vial of poison gas and then wait long enough such that there's a 50 chance for that vial to have been triggered (due to the half-life of the radioactive trigger). Our description of the trigger, since radiation is quantum mechanical, is that it is both simultaneously decayed and not decayed. This is a stronger statement than just saying that either it decayed or it didn't...until we measure it, the actual state of the system is a "superposition" of both decayed and not decayed. This isn't just a mathematical difference, this difference has real, observable effects and lies at the core of the "mysteries" of quantum mechanics. The "paradox" comes in by linking the microscopic system (the trigger) to the macroscopic system (Paul McCartney) and saying that if the trigger is both decayed and not decayed then Paul McCartney must be simultaneously alive and dead. Here's why that's nonsense. There's nothing special about our conscious observation of the Paul McCartney system. Because Paul McCartney is affected by the outcome of the quantum phenomenon, the whole system, in a mathematical sense, decays exponentially to a classical probability wherePaul McCartney is either alive or dead, but you don't know which. It's exactly the same as a coin flip that I can't see. I know it landed either heads or tails, I just don't know which. I don't think that it's both heads and tails until I look at it...it's not. Paul McCartney is really alive or really dead and it's no different than a coin flip. (For the experts, this is the decoherence of the density matrix of the system and the exponential suppression of the off-diagonal terms). There is a tendency in the popular press to conflate quantum observers with something far more grandiose, often giving special status to human, conscious observers. Even some very smart physicists do this, although I think it's wishful thinking. Psuedoscientific books and films like What the Bleep Do We Know? make precisely this misstep. You can think of an observer as simply something that interacts an isolated microscopic, quantum system with a complicated macroscopic system. This explanation of quantum mechanics doesn't explain why the Paul McCartney is alive or why its dead...the classical interpretation of quantum mechanics says that that question is without an answer and the fate of the cat is really, truly random...but it does tell you that Paul McCartney is actually alive or dead and not both. As a dragon of innumerable age, I had watched kingdoms rise and fall, seen many heroes come and go but none had ever managed to slay me. I had always guarded my vast horde of gold and treasure with the utmost vigilance, putting into use all my powers when necessary. But, a hero with a different approach came before me. He strolled up to me with a confident gait, his eyes sparkling despite the fear on his face. I flared open my nostrils, preparing to breathe out flames to incinerate him. But, before I did, he threw a single gold coin on my stash and kept walking calmly. I was astounded, it was something that had never happened before. Usually, the heroes would try to negotiate, give a long speech before they end up losing their life. This one, however, was different, his approach was unique. His eyes bore into mine, and for the first time in hundreds of years, I was tempted. A trade in exchange for the knowledge of the world, new cultures, and civilizations - that was something I couldn't resist. I looked at the gold coin that he had thrown, wondering what it held for me, whether it was a trap - but I decided to take a risk. I accepted his proposal and let him into my lair. In return, I let him take just enough gold to return home and keep his family comfortable for the rest of their lives. And so, the hero left, not with a sword or a shield, but with the memories and knowledge that would last him a lifetime.
