In this paper, we propose an efficient beam training technique for millimeter-wave (mmWave) communications. When some mobile users are under high mobility, the beam training should be performed frequently to ensure the accurate acquisition of the channel state information. In order to reduce the resource overhead caused by frequent beam training, we introduce a dedicated beam training strategy which sends the training beams separately to a specific high mobility user (called a target user) without changing the periodicity of the conventional beam training. The dedicated beam training requires small amount of resources since the training beams can be optimized for the target user. In order to satisfy the performance requirement with low training overhead, we propose the optimal training beam selection strategy which finds the best beamforming vectors yielding the lowest channel estimation error based on the target user's probabilistic channel information. Such dedicated beam training is combined with the greedy channel estimation algorithm that accounts for sparse characteristics and temporal dynamics of the target user's channel. Our numerical evaluation demonstrates that the proposed scheme can maintain good channel estimation performance with significantly less training overhead compared to the conventional beam training protocols.

Many individuals suffering from red-green color blindness experience this condition because their retinal cone cells responsible for detecting red and green hues exhibit an excessive degree of spectral overlap. Consequently, when exposed to certain wavelengths, the visual cortex struggles to distinguish whether the stimulus originates from a red or green source. This confusion manifests as red-incremental color deficiency. However, wearing Enchroma lenses can alleviate this issue for some affected individuals. These specialized eyeglasses effectively suppress a substantial portion of the overlapping spectrum, thereby isolating specific regions where red and green cones react distinctly to pure red and green lights respectively. As a result, these patients' brains are now capable of discerning between the two colors accurperceiving them separately. It should be noted though, that this solution proves effective solely for those whose form of color blindness stems from an extensive spectral overlap which can subsequently be mitigated through the use of such corrective eyewear.

The team set up a makeshift clinic in John's home, and soon people from all over the city were coming to him for help. There were many challenges along the way - trying to navigate the streets without being able to see, finding ways to communicate with people who had suddenly been rendered silent by the shock of their blindness, and figuring out how to treat the various ailments and injuries that had arisen in the darkness. They now communicated with their patients by touch and sound, inventing sound maps and new ways of using medical equipment. As word spread of their work, many volunteers came forward to help. Months turned into years, and the world started to slowly adapt to the new reality. People learned to rely on their other senses in ways they never thought possible. Technology adapted to assist those without sight, but it was never a replacement for vision itself. There were still many challenges that lay ahead, but John and his team continued to inspire hope in their community. They knew that humanity was far from perfect, but it was their ability to adapt and come together in the face of adversity that made them truly great.

As one of the largest social networks, Facebook receives a massive amount of content from users all over the world. While Facebook has rules regarding the type of content that can be posted, it has been known to take down photos of breastfeeding mothers, and other non-nude photos of women's breasts. Facebook has also been known to take down photos of women's nipples as well. These photos were taken down not because they were pornographic, but because they showed a woman's nipples. The American Civil Liberties Union is currently working on a case involving a transgender woman who posted photos of her transition on Facebook. Facebook took down the photos because she was born a man. Lila Perry, a transgender woman, posted a photo of her breasts on Facebook to celebrate her transition. Her mother, Jessica Perry, also posted a photo of Lila's breasts on her Facebook page. Facebook then removed both photos from their accounts. "My daughter had to go through this very traumatic experience and all she did was post a photo of herself on Facebook," Jessica Perry told Mashable. "I am her mom, and I'm here to support her. I can't even post a photo of my daughter on Facebook without it being removed." Perry then went on to say, "The fact that we even have to have this conversation is ridiculous." The Perrys reached out to the American Civil Liberties Union. The ACLU informed them that Facebook had discriminated against Perry. They also told them that Facebook had violated their First Amendment rights by taking down the photos. According to the ACLU, Facebook has a long history of discrimination against women and transgender people. "Lila Perry is not committing any crime by posting a picture of her chest on Facebook," said Galen Sherwin, a senior staff attorney for the ACLU Women's Rights Project. "Women have the right to live their lives online without being harassed or punished for their gender or sexual identity." The ACLU also sent a letter to Facebook, asking them to take action regarding the discrimination that takes place on their social media platform. "We have every right to use this platform to share our stories, as well as the right to use our chosen names and pronouns," the letter read. "We demand that Facebook remove its policy that requires users to use their legal name, a policy that is actively harming the most marginalized members of our community." Facebook then said that the content removal was a mistake. However, they refused to provide further comment. "We believe this was a mistake and we have already communicated with Jessica and Lila Perry to explain that this photo is allowed on Facebook," said spokesperson Fred Wolens. "We're sorry that this happened." The ACLU argues that, even if the content was removed by mistake, that does not change the fact that Facebook discriminates against certain types of people. "Facebook's actions were not a mistake. They are a direct result of Facebook's failure to recognize transgender women and people of all genders as who they are and the ongoing harassment and abuse that transgender people, particularly transgender women of color, face on the platform," the ACLU said in a statement. According to the ACLU, Facebook has no policies in place to protect transgender people from harassment and discrimination. "Women have the right to live their lives online without being harassed or punished for their gender or sexual identity," said the ACLU. "Facebook needs to take real and concrete steps to protect the safety of transgender people and all women on the platform." Archaeologists in Scotland have discovered the earliest dated evidence of human activity in the area - with the help of a herd of pigs. The discovery was made by experts from Historic Environment Scotland (HES), who used the animals to excavate the site near Biggar. The pigs, which are part of the Tamworth breed, were taken to the site where they were allowed to roam freely and root around for buried artefacts - uncovering 10,000 year-old flint tools. These tools, which included an arrowhead and a knife, are thought to be some of the oldest artefacts ever found in Scotland and are believed to date back to the Mesolithic period. Commenting on the find, HES archaeologist Dr Murray Cook said: "This is a really exciting find, not just because it's the earliest dated evidence of human activity in Scotland but also because it was found with the help of these remarkable pigs. "It's a great example of how modern technology and ancient techniques can be combined to uncover our past." The pigs will now be used at further archaeological sites across Scotland as part of HES' ongoing research into Scotland's history. The findings of the project have been published in a new report, which outlines the importance of the discovery and the use of pigs as a tool in archaeological excavation.

A cylindrical Service Module (SM) supported the Command Module, with a service propulsion engine and an RCS with propellants, and a fuel cell power generation system with liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen reactants. A high-gain parabolic antenna was used for long-distance communications on the lunar far side. An extending antenna was also used. The module also provided a base for the S-band antenna used for communication when the CSM was docked to the LM. One entire side of the module was covered by mylar multi-layer insulation which could be used as a radiation shied for the crew cabin and electronics. The Service Module was discarded just before re-entry. The Service Module engine, the Aerojet AJ10-137, used hypergolic propellants; Nitrogen Tetroxide and Aerozine 50. The propellants were pressurised by high-pressure helium, carried in tanks at 3900psi (265 bars). The SM engine was gimbal mounted so it could be used for pitch and yaw control as well as translation. It had a maximum thrust of 20,500 lbf (91 kN) and was used for major manoeuvres including lunar orbit insertion and Trans-Earth Injection. The Reaction Control System (RCS) on the SM allowed for translations and rotations in pitch, roll and yaw along and about the spacecraft axes. There were 16 x 440N thrusters and 4 x 990N thrusters; all used hypergolic propellants and were pressurised with helium. The fuel cells in the SM powered the spacecraft and the environmental control system. Each cell consisted of two stacks, one anode and one cathode, with hydrogen and oxygen flowing over a nickel catalyst. The main by-product of this reaction was water, which was used as a coolant and dumped overboard as a gas. The oxygen tanks were in the middle of the SM, with the hydrogen tanks wrapped around the outside. The two gases were mixed before entering the fuel cell. The cells were arranged into two banks, each with four cells. The cells were fed with gaseous oxygen and hydrogen at pressures of 800psi (55 bars) and 3900psi (265 bars) respectively. Each cell produced 31.3 kW of power. The CSM communicated with the Earth using the S-Band 2GHz system, with phased array antennas on the SM. The long-range antenna was 8ft (2.4m) in diameter and was used during translunar coast and transearth coast. The medium-range antenna was 3ft (91cm) in diameter and was used in the vicinity of Earth. Communications with the LM were carried out on UHF frequencies and used a steerable 3ft (91cm) high-gain antenna mounted on the SM and a fixed low-gain antenna.

If victory in the Ashes series down under a year earlier was the highlight of England's rise to the top, then one moment during that time stood out as a clear illustration of team spirit. The whole triumphant test team stood on the outfield performing the'sprinkler', a daft dance dreamt up in the dressing room. Fast forward three years and many of the same characters from that impromptu performance must be scratching their heads about went wrong following one of the most embarrassing weeks English cricket has ever gone through. Here are five things we've learnt about the sport this week. The image of a close knit collection of professionals pulling in the same direction is forever in tatters. The man at the centre of the storm is Kevin Pietersen, one of the most destructive batsman ever to have padded up for England. KP had a book to sell, and he's spared no effort in promoting his autobiography far and wide, making a number of damaging accusations in the process that talked of cliques in the dressing room. He said some bowlers were responsible for a culture of bullying that left junior team mates cold, and him in tears. Former Australian captain Ricky Ponting has backed Pietersen's claims saying some players abused each other for dropped catches. KP suggested the spoof Twitter account set up to parody him in 2012 was done with the full knowledge and approval of England's bowling clique. That claim appeared to have been lent credibility by former England captain Alec Stewart, who revealed the man behind that same Twitter account told him Stuart Broad, Graeme Swann and co were in on it. So far reaching were the shock waves of the accusations that even the BBC's cricket correspondent Jonathan Agnew felt compelled to quit Twitter after getting involved in the argument. There is no doubting KP's skill but he was criticised too many times for going all Hollywood on the pitch. He often went for the spectacular when safety was the better option. It seems off the field he's the same. The players on the receiving end of KP's cover drives have largely kept their council, although Tim Bresnan tweeted his disappointment at having been implicated, while Graeme Swann dismissed KP's ranting as "codswallop." Swann is now said to be consulting lawyers while Matt Prior has promised to have his say at some point. The group responsible for running English cricket, the ECB, has been forced to deny leaking a dossier on Pietersen's behaviour that led to his dismissal from the England set-up. They've also been forced to write press releases providing the official version of events in an ineffective attempt at damage limitation. KP always hoped there was still a chance he'd play for England again. Now though there isn't. There are even more people in the way of that happening. In cricket when you stop playing you often enter the stands. Power travels onwards and often upwards. When pushed too far, noughties pop stars fight back. Jessica Taylor was unhappy at commentator Jonathan Agnew challenging KP's character. He said the real KP is "an anxious, nervous character." She was also unhappy he had access to the parody Twitter account. They battled online. He later quit. Even Piers Morgan said he wouldn't mess with her. Neither would we. Thirty-nine Native American tribal governments are based in Oklahoma, each holding limited powers within designated areas. While Indian reservations typical in most of the United States are not present in Oklahoma, tribal governments hold land granted during the Indian Territory era, but with limited jurisdiction and no control over state governing bodies such as municipalities and counties. The tribal governments are required to submit a constitution and any subsequent amendments to the United States Congress for approval.

The main focus of Hayek's research in the field of economics revolved around issues related to capital, currency, and economic cycles. Building upon Mises' application of marginal utility theory to the worth of money in his seminal work 'Theory of Money and Credit', where he also presented an analysis of industrial oscillations inspired by British and Swedish economic theories, Hayek developed his unique perspective on the business cycle. This laid the groundwork for what would come to be recognized as the 'Austrian Theory of the Business Cycle'. He further expanded on this theory in his 1929 publication, which was translated into English as 'Monetary Theory and the Trade Cycle' in 1933, proposing a financial basis for understanding the cyclical nature of the economy. Moreover, in his 1931 work 'Prices and Production,' Hayek posited that the recurring instabilities within the free-market system were due to the central bank's tendency towards inflation through excessive credit creation, affecting interest rates and thus causing distortions in investment decisions. According to him, such volatility stemmed from not allowing the money supply to be governed by market forces.

To understand how an OS is built you first need to understand what an OS is and what composes it. An OS is simply an environment that allows one or multiple users to interact with a computer or other device. It is composed of the following elements: 1. Hardware: The physical components of the computer or device, including the processor, memory, storage, and inputoutput subsystems. 2. System Software: These are the low-level programs that control the hardware and provide basic functionality. Examples include device drivers, system utilities, and the boot loader. 3. User Interface: This is the layer that allows users to interact with the computer. This includes the graphical user interface (GUI) as well as command-line tools. 4. Application Software: This is the software that runs on top of the OS and is used by users to accomplish tasks. Examples include web browsers, word processors, and games. To build an OS, developers need to create all of these components and then integrate them together. This typically involves writing code in a variety of languages and technologies such as C, assembly language, and scripting languages. The code needs to be optimized for performance and reliability, and must also adhere to standards and conventions established by the OS's creators. Additionally, the developer needs to consider security and privacy when designing the OS. Finally, after completing the development phase, the OS is tested thoroughly to ensure it meets the criteria set out by the creator.

An elderly gentleman had a habit of gathering empty cans, with the intention of exchanging them for some extra cash. Eventually, on a particular occasion, he amassed numerous dozens of these cans. As Death drew near, Philip heard its voice offering solace amidst despair. Being the sole survivor of their kind, he faced an ultimatum: embrace oblivion alongside his peers or persist solo for centuries aiming to amend the planet. Could this proposition be a final mockery or a sincere opportunity to defy mortality temporarily? However, loneliness loomed large, questioning any potential impact on the world devoid of companionship. Contemplating both outcomes, Philip ultimately declined the offer, determined to confront his destiny head-on. Death acknowledged his decision with a subtle grin, gently releasing his spirit as Philip dissolved into thin air – a testament to the notion that our souls reside within our gaze.

Implementing weight and activation quantization within deep learning architectures enhances computational efficiency during inference phases, albeit sometimes at the expense of decreased precision. The disparity in performance between high-precision and low-precision (quantized) versions often stems from inherent quantization errors. This study concentrates specifically on binary quantization techniques wherein numerical values are constrained to either -1 or 1. By developing an integrated model for evaluating various scaling tactics, we draw inspiration from the Pareto optimality observed between 2-bit and 1-bit quantizations. Consequently, we propose an innovative method for 2-bit quantization characterized by minimal squared error characteristics. These quantization processes can be seamlessly executed on computer hardware through the use of bit manipulation techniques. Demonstrated theoretical justifications confirm the superior efficacy of our suggested approaches, supplemented by practical analyses examining error rates. Upon testing with the ImageNet dataset, our newly devised least squares quantization schemes significantly diminish the accuracy discrepancy typically associated with such procedures.

Classical matrix perturbation results, such as Weyl's theorem for eigenvalues and the Davis-Kahan theorem for eigenvectors, are general purpose. These classical bounds are tight in the worst case, but in many settings sub-optimal in the typical case. In this paper, we present perturbation bounds which consider the nature of the perturbation and its interaction with the unperturbed structure in order to obtain significant improvements over the classical theory in many scenarios, such as when the perturbation is random. We demonstrate the utility of these new results by analyzing perturbations in the stochastic blockmodel where we derive much tighter bounds than provided by the classical theory. We use our new perturbation theory to show that a very simple and natural clustering algorithm - whose analysis was difficult using the classical tools - nevertheless recovers the communities of the blockmodel exactly even in very sparse graphs.

When a data packet enters or exits your network interface card, it carries a specific port number. Every application running on your device utilizes its own unique port number, enabling multiple applications like Spotify, Steam, Firefox, Internet Explorer, etc., to simultaneously access the internet without confusion. Firewalls maintain a registry of these ports along with predetermined rules governing which data packets may pass through them. For instance, when a data packet attempts to enter via port 80, if the firewall rule allows traffic on port 80, it will permit passage; however, if the packet tries to enter through port 1712, where the rule denies entry, it will be discarded. In essence, firewalls act as non-flammable barriers, effectively containing any potential digital 'fire' within a designated area instead of letting it propagate across the system.

The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) outlines guidelines for determining maritime boundaries. Essentially, nations possess authority over bodies of water extending up to 12 nautical miles (approximately 14 miles or 22 kilometers) offshore, allowing them to implement and regulate laws within this area. Additionally, an adjacent 12-nautical-mile zone permits governance by individual states concerning specific matters such as customs, taxation, immigration, and environmental protection. Consequently, a nation may exert influence nearly up to 30 miles from its coastline. Beyond these zones lies what is commonly referred to as international waters. Furthermore, countries establish Exclusive Economic Zones reaching 200 nautical miles (roughly 230 miles or 370 kilometers) beyond their shores, granting exclusive resource extraction privileges. Isolated landmasses play a crucial role in expanding a country's EEZ significantly. In cases where territorial extents overlap, due to proximity limitations, nations typically divide the distance evenly. For instance, when neighboring countries share a 300-mile wide body of water, each state's EEZ would span 150 miles from their respective coasts before converging midway. However, numerous exceptions exist based on historical circumstances rather than logical reasoning. Regarding the situation in the South China Sea, it primarily concerns the actual possession of various islands rather than adherence to UNCLOS provisions. Multiple Southeast Asian nations claim ownership of these islands throughout history; however, the legitimacy of these assertions remains uncertain. It's interesting to note that disputes involving water boundaries have led to conflicts, like the Iraq-Iran War in 1980 sparked by disagreements over the Shatt al-Arab River border. Typically, river borders lie precisely along the center line, providing equal access to each side. Nevertheless, fluctuating agreements occasionally alter these arrangements.

Upon releasing the NES in the US market, Nintendo intentionally crafted it with a unique style compared to rival gaming systems. They aimed to differentiate their offering from others while evading the negative stigma attached to gaming consoles after the video game crash of 1983. This approach led to camouflaging the cartridge slot design within a front-loading zero insertion force (ZIF) cartridge socket, mimicking the look of a VCR. While this innovative connection performed adequately initially with clean components and fresh pins, the ZIF connector wasn't genuinely zero insertion force. As users placed the cartridge inside the NES, the act of pushing it in distorted the pin contacts and compressed the ROM board against the cartridge walls. Regularly inserting and removing cartridges resulted in pin degradation from constant use. Furthermore, the ZIF design was susceptible to contamination from grime and particles. Compounding these challenges was Nintendo’s selection of materials—the nickel connector springs wore down because of the design flaw, and the gold connections on the game cartridges experienced faster oxidation. In attempts to fix related game malfunctions, some individuals blew into the cartridges before reinserting them, unintentionally accelerating the copper connectors' corrosion process.

This research focuses on developing methods for sampling from evolving graphical models across different domains such as machine learning, computer vision, statistical physics, and theoretical computer science. Although significant progress has been made in sampling from fixed graphical models, similar advancements in dynamic versions are scarce. Herein, we introduce an innovative algorithm capable of generating samples from various classes of graphical models involving discrete random variables in real-time. Our method operates concurrently and emploers a 'Las Vegas' strategy—it determines the optimal stopping point and yields accurate distributions. Additionally, we outline necessary criteria ensuring the algorithm operates efficiently based on the model's size during modifications. Specifically, we present novel dynamic sampling techniques for the Ising and hardcore models, enabling them to manage updates effectively while remaining computationally feasible. These improvements stem from utilizing a localized resampling approach combined with a newly established 'equilibrium' characteristic that upholds the integrity of the algorithm through successive steps. Not only does this feature affirm the validity of our technique, but it also contributes to refining performance metrics for faster convergence rates on certain models, warranting further investigation due to its inherent value.

In this study, we address the challenge of automatically assigning research papers to appropriate reviewers during the conference peer review process, emphasizing both equity and precision. Rather than aiming solely to enhance overall review quality across all submissions, our approach prioritizes improving the evaluation of the least advantaged paper. To achieve this, we've developed an allocation method utilizing an iterative maximum flow technique, which has been demonstrated to closely approximate optimal fairness. Additionally, we have devised an innovative experimental framework allowing for unbiased comparisons between different assignment strategies despite the typical lack of definitive benchmarks in such settings. This setup validates the effectiveness of our algorithm not only in terms of fairness but also regarding its ability to accurptacially discern which papers warrant acceptance. Moreover, through rigorous analytical scrutiny, we assess the efficacy of two distinct scoring models—one established and one newly introduced within our work—and confirm that our algorithm excels in optimizing both the impartiality and reliability of the review outcome.

A new device for granting assent was created during the reign of King Henry VIII. In 1542, Henry sought to execute his fifth wife, Catherine Howard, whom he accused of committing adultery; the execution was to be authorised not after a trial but by a bill of attainder, to which he would have to personally assent after listening to the entire text. Henry decided that "the repetition of so grievous a Story and the recital of so infamous a crime" in his presence "might reopen a Wound already closing in the Royal Bosom." Therefore, parliament inserted a clause into the Act of Attainder, providing that assent granted by Commissioners "is and ever was and ever shall be, as good" as assent granted by the sovereign personally. The procedure was used only five times during the 16th century, but more often during the 17th and 18th centuries, especially when George III's health began to deteriorate. Queen Victoria became the last monarch to personally grant assent in 1854.

In reinforcement learning (RL), agents often operate in partially observed and uncertain environments. Model-based RL suggests that this is best achieved by learning and exploiting a probabilistic model of the environment, as opposed to directly modelled fitness functions for the agent.[1] The problem with this approach, however, is knowing how to select an appropriate data set from which to learn. For example: what parameters should we choose? Which features are important when training the model? What conditions should be included in the training data? A common solution consists of making assumptions about these properties during the design phase of the AI system. In many cases they can lead to inaccurate predictions or incomplete models. For instance, if you try to predict the temperature of a gas based on its density,[2] your prediction may only consider one dimension but not take into account other factors like pressure or molecules. This potentially leads to overfitting - a situation where the model is trained so well it predicts similar situations even when none actually exist. An alternative technique relies on supervised information transfer (SIT) to infer a distribution of unknown attributes. However, SIT techniques require explicit knowledge about the structure and contents of the original data, something not always available at the time of machine learning modelling. As such, there exists a need to incorporate nonhuman-related knowledge into modelling systems prior to training them.

Council hopefuls need to secure 200 contributions of $10 or more each, while mayoral aspirants require 300. Acceptance into the program also involves adhering to predetermined spending caps which were set at 33 times the number of registered Tucson voters in 2005, equating to $79,222 for council members and 64 times for mayoral contenders in 2003, amounting to $142,271. As compensation, they get matched monies from the city, maintaining a 1:1 ratio between public dollars and individual donations. A stipulation exists too - participants cannot surpass 75% of their spending cap before the primary elections. This approach has inspired numerous cities including San Francisco and New York City, who've implemented similar systems though featuring slightly different financial regulations.

The operation of the power grid is becoming more stressed, due to the addition of new large loads represented by Electric Vehicles (EVs) and a more intermittent supply due to the incorporation of renewable sources. As a consequence, the coordination and control of projected EV demand in a network of fast charging stations becomes a critical and challenging problem. In this paper, we introduce a game theoretic based decentralized control mechanism to alleviate negative impacts from the EV demand. The proposed mechanism takes into consideration the non-uniform spatial distribution of EVs that induces uneven power demand at each charging facility, and aims to: (i) avoid straining grid resources by offering price incentives so that customers accept being routed to less busy stations, (ii) maximize total revenue by serving more customers with the same amount of grid resources, and (iii) provide charging service to customers with a certain level of Quality-of-Service (QoS), the latter defined as the long term customer blocking probability. We examine three scenarios of increased complexity that gradually approximate real world settings. The obtained results show that the proposed framework leads to substantial performance improvements in terms of the aforementioned goals, when compared to current state of affairs.

Correlation never can imply causation in the most fundamental sense because correlation is always empirical whereas causality, in the strict metaphysical sense, is governed by ontological and epistemological principles. In terms of the scientific community, causality is most often expressed as a probability of sorts, in the form of either accepting or rejecting a null hypothesis rather than stating a causal case. Then you propose an alternate hypothesis to explain the scenario in which the former fails. The null hypothesis is always the more "neutral" or unchanging event. For example, the if you wanted to test whether or not a pen will drop if you let it go due to the effect of gravity, a simple test would be to state the null hypothesis as: "The pen will stay in its current state when I let go of it." When you perform the test and the pen in fact drops in every instance, then you are justified in rejecting the null hypothesis that gravity has no effect on the pen and you can then posit the alternative. How this is achieved is mostly through statistics. Keep in mind, empirical data is inherently coherentist in nature, meaning that there are no fundamental principles that are proven to be fundamental. In fact, this issue touches upon what is called the Aggripean Trilemma, something that is incredibly hard to address on the subject of causality. The Trilemma aside, scientists use statistical data in order to determine how likely a certain thing is to be a "significant factor" in a particular outcome. The significance is artificially defined by the researcher, with the common rule of thumb being a p-value of 0.05 in order to be considered statistically significant (i.e. a factor that is likely to cause a specific studied effect). The artificiality of this method of analysis can be best portrayed by the existence of Type I and III errors in which the alpha level (the threshold of significance) is adjusted to be either higher or lower depending on the sensitivity and size of the data set, because after all the threshold is a completely human construct. A p-value of 0.05 with a 95 confidence interval on a specific response by a specific factor simply means that there is a high probability that the null hypothesis ought to be rejected for the entire data population, even though you only tested a portion of the data set (i.e. it will apply to 95 of your experience with the overall population, since you cannot empirically test a full statistical population). We often see scientific articles that state: "A causes a X chance of increasing B" which can be an accurate albeit misleading statement with regards to statistical testing. However, it does not address the magnitude of the interaction, which might be negligible. In summary, causality is a completely different idea than correlation and its basis is in ontology and to a degree epistemology rather than in empirical science. We colloquially refer to "cause and effect" as a result of statistical testing, which provides solid a posteriori knowledge of the probabilities of causal relationships. I believe in a flat tax system, where everyone pays the same percentage of their earnings in income tax. I do not believe in a progressive tax system where richer people pay a higher percentage of their income in taxes than poorer people. The flat tax system is a simple, fair, and efficient way of taxing income. The progressive tax system is unfair, inefficient, and complex. The progressive tax system is unfair because it places an undue burden on the rich. In the United States, the top 5 of earners pay 50 of all taxes. The top 25 pay 80 of all taxes. The bottom 50 pay just 2. How fair is it that 50 of earners pay 2 of all taxes? The progressive tax system benefits the poor at the expense of the rich. The progressive tax system is inefficient because it encourages people to not work harder and earn more money. Why should someone work harder if they know they're going to be taxed more? This is known as the Laffer curve. If the goal is to maximize revenue, the tax rate should be high enough to collect the most revenue but low enough that people continue to work. It's not the purpose of government to punish the wealthy for being successful. The progressive tax system is complex because it is much more difficult to calculate and file taxes if you're paying at a progressive rate. If the goal is to simplify the tax code, a flat tax would accomplish this goal.

We propose a compressive sensing algorithm that exploits geometric properties of images to recover images of high quality from few measurements. The image reconstruction is done by iterating the two-stage process of phase-difference-minimization and a Landweber-type reconstruction method. The phase-difference-minimization step is a linear operation that solves for the angular-dependent gradient at each iteration step. The minimization of the angular-dependent gradient corresponds to a multi-stage image-processing method that is first used to compute the horizontal gradient of an image, then the vertical gradient of the image, and then the diagonal gradient of the image. This algorithm has been applied to images reconstructed using the method proposed by and the MRI images reconstructed using the method proposed by . In both cases, the proposed method reduces the number of measurements significantly while improving the quality of the reconstructed images.

Initially, we present the notion of weak adaptive submodularity—a broader form of adaptive submodularity—that effectively addresses complex adaptive state estimation tasks. Subsequently, regarding active diagnostics or discrete state estimation through active detection techniques, we demonstrate how an adaptive greedy strategy achieves nearly optimal results if the reward function exhibits this characteristic. Additionally, we reveal that the reward function utilized in collective active diagnostics, applicable in fields like healthcare and continuous state estimation amidst persistent sensor malfunctions, displays weak adaptive submodularity. The mixing time of a graph is an important metric, which is not only useful in analyzing connectivity and expansion properties of the network, but also serves as a key parameter in designing efficient algorithms. We introduce a new notion of mixing of a random walk on a (undirected) graph, called local mixing . Informally, the local mixing with respect to a given node s , is the mixing of a random walk probability distribution restricted to a large enough subset of nodes - say, a subset of size at least n for a given parameter - containing s . The time to mix over such a subset by a random walk starting from a source node s is called the local mixing time with respect to s . The local mixing time captures the local connectivity and expansion properties around a given source node and is a useful parameter that determines the running time of algorithms for partial information spreading, gossip etc. Our first contribution is formally defining the notion of local mixing time in an undirected graph. We then present an efficient distributed algorithm which computes a constant factor approximation to the local mixing time with respect to a source node s in O ( s) rounds 1 footnote 1 Footnote Footnote Footnotes Footnotes 1 footnote 1 The notation O hides a O (polylog n) factor. , where s is the local mixing time w.r.t s in an n -node regular graph. This bound holds when s is significantly smaller than the conductance of the local mixing set (i.e., the set where the walk mixes locally); this is typically the interesting case where the local mixing time is significantly smaller than the mixing time (with respect to s). We also present a distributed algorithm that computes the exact local mixing time in O ( s D) rounds, where D min { s , D } and D is the diameter of the graph (this bound holds unconditionally without any assumptions on s). Our algorithms work in the CONGEST model of distributed computing. Since the local mixing time can be significantly smaller than the mixing time (or even the diameter) in many graphs, it serves as a tighter measure of distributed complexity in certain algorithmic applications. In particular, we show that local mixing time tightly characterizes the complexity of partial information spreading which in turn is useful in solving other problems such as the maximum coverage problem, full information spreading, leader election etc.

Sounds are not pure tones, so even something like a loud whistle also contains frequencies lower than the primary sound your brain is identifying. When you cover your ears, you are putting mass between your ear and the sound. Lower frequencies have more energy and pass through mass more easily, so now you have less high-frequency sound waves hitting your ears and relatively more low frequency sound waves. It's the same reason that everything sounds muffled with those foam ear-plugs - low frequencies travel more easily through mass so they are less affected by the obstruction. If you were listening to a sine-wave generator (i.e. a single pure frequency), it would sound like a softer version of that sound, rather than a lower pitched version.

Energy-based models (EBMs) necessitate Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling within their learning algorithms' internal loops. Nonetheless, MCMC sampling within EBMs proves challenging when dealing with multimodal energy functions in the data space due to its non-mixing nature. These issues pose significant obstacles for EBM theory and application. Our research introduces a novel approach by incorporating a flow-based model into EBMs, enhancing them through correction or exponential tilting techniques. By conducting MCMC sampling in the latent variable space of the flow-based model—a simplified variant of neural transport MCMC—we demonstrate efficient mode traversal and improved mixing properties. Consequently, our method facilitates effective EBM sampling and learning processes.

While effective hunting can provide an increase in energy, there are always associated energetic expenditures involved with the process. Predators generally avoid pursuing prey when they aren't experiencing hunger because the efforts required often surpass the potential rewards. As an example, a satiated shark housed in an aquarium would ordinarily disregard the presence of smaller fish nearby; conversely, these small fish benefit from the absence of threat posed by the dominant predator. This situation diverges from typical predator behavior. Analyzing feeding habits through the lens of a balance between gains and losses is referred to as optimal foraging theory, which has proven valuable in understanding animal conduct. Usually, evaluations focus on the rate of energy acquisition over time, although additional considerations may include vital nutrients without calorie content that still play crucial roles in maintaining life and overall wellness.

A Hong Kong tycoon is suing the salesman that convinced him to use a supercomputer to handle his trading, a decision which cost him more than 20 million. It is a dispute that sounds almost comical - a salesman who sold a million dollar supercomputer to a billionaire; a billionaire who decided to use the machine for stock trading; and an end result of a 20 million loss. The lawsuit - which will be heard in Hong Kong court - has yet to be settled. How did this happen? The tycoon, billionaire Stephen Hung, was in the market for a supercomputer. He turned to salesman Dmitry Razumovsky to make the purchase. Hung wanted to use the computer to handle trading on his behalf. The two agreed to a 1 million dollar price tag. Razumovsky recommended a supercomputer that he believed would be ideal for the billionaire. Hung purchased the machine and installed it at home. He then gave it the task of buying and selling stocks for him. The plan was that the supercomputer would analyze the market and provide trading instructions. However, Hung's supercomputer took a few unexpected turns. At first, it bought and sold stocks and managed to earn a small profit. But, later, it began to make extremely risky trades that put Hung into the red. He lost 20 million. At that point, Hung turned to his lawyer, Gavin Haigh, who is now handling the lawsuit. Haigh says that the supercomputer's new trading strategies were flawed. "The stock market was not the problem," Haigh said. "The problem was the software." Hung and Razumovsky apparently disagree. "Mr. Hung entered into the agreement with Razumovsky with his eyes wide open," Razumovsky said. "He is attempting to blame his incompetence on the computer that he bought and the software that came with it." Hung, who is a very successful property developer, does not agree. His supercomputer may have helped him lose money, but he blames the salesman. "If you have no experience in this area then you need to find somebody with expertise, who can take you through a journey," Hung said. "It's my life's experience that if you find the right person to help you, then you can actually benefit from it." In spite of the lawsuit, Hung and Razumovsky have remained friends.

There are several drawbacks to using coaster brakes (those activated by pushing backward on the pedals) which prevent their inclusion in most adult bicycles: - Firstly, these brakes necessitate a taut chain while pedaling in reverse, making them incompatible with multi-gear bikes equipped with [derailleurs]. - Secondly, since braking converts kinetic energy into heat, it must be adequately dispersed; unfortunately, coaster brakes struggle with heat distribution, rendering them ineffective for decelerating heavier loads such as adult riders or swiftly moving cycles due to potential damage caused by excessive heat affecting the lubrication within the rear hub. - Additionally, the stopping power provided by the rear wheel alone is insufficient because shifting weight forward reduces traction, thereby compromising safety during rapid deceleration where utilizing primarily the front brake would be preferable. Consequently, coaster brakes are typically found on leisure 'beach cruiser' style bicycles designed for low-speed, level terrain travel without complex gear systems. Kids' bikes often feature coaster brakes owing to their user-friendly operation, minimal upkeep requirements, and lower production costs stemming from the absence of supplementary components associated with manual braking mechanisms.

In this paper, we study the problem of sampling from a graphical model when the model itself is changing dynamically with time. This problem derives its interest from a variety of inference, learning, and sampling settings in machine learning, computer vision, statistical physics, and theoretical computer science. While the problem of sampling from a static graphical model has received considerable attention, theoretical works for its dynamic variants have been largely lacking. The main contribution of this paper is an algorithm that can sample dynamically from a broad class of graphical models over discrete random variables. Our algorithm is parallel and Las Vegas: it knows when to stop and it outputs samples from the exact distribution. We also provide sufficient conditions under which this algorithm runs in time proportional to the size of the update, on general graphical models as well as well-studied specific spin systems. In particular we obtain, for the Ising model (ferromagnetic or anti-ferromagnetic) and for the hardcore model the first dynamic sampling algorithms that can handle both edge and vertex updates (addition, deletion, change of functions), both efficient within regimes that are close to the respective uniqueness regimes, beyond which, even for the static and approximate sampling, no local algorithms were known or the problem itself is intractable. Our dynamic sampling algorithm relies on a local resampling algorithm and a new "equilibrium" property that is shown to be satisfied by our algorithm at each step, and enables us to prove its correctness. This equilibrium property is robust enough to guarantee the correctness of our algorithm, helps us improve bounds on fast convergence on specific models, and should be of independent interest.

In bipartite matching problems, vertices on one side of a bipartite graph are paired with those on the other. In its online variant, one side of the graph is available in advance, and vertices on the other side arrive online, one at a time. A dynamic algorithm accepts each vertex online, if it has an available partner at that time. The offline version of the problem is to compute a maximum-cardinality matching in a given graph, without ever looking at the other side of the graph. We show that this problem can be solved in polylogarithmic time in the worst case, and in linear time in the average case. Our algorithm for the online problem works in time linear in the size of the input graph and the number of vertices that arrived so far. This algorithm has a constant competitive ratio for any input graph. The best previously known algorithm for the online problem has a competitive ratio of O (log n), where n is the number of vertices.

Quantum Clustering is a powerful method to detect clusters in data with mixed density. However, it is very sensitive to a length parameter that is inherent to the Schrodinger equation. In this paper we analyze the impact of this length parameter on the output of the algorithm. To do so, we use a likelihood function that mimics the likelihood of the Schrodinger equation. This function is used to reproduce a set of data with an underlying cluster. We find that the length parameter determines the most important aspect of the output of the algorithm. Our analysis is performed in a reproducible fashion and is applicable to other clustering methods.

Harmonic series. Essentially, sounds are waves. Sometimes, two different wavelength waves can overlap in such a way that they line up somehow. This sound comes off as naturally harmonious to us. Say you have two sounds. One has half the length of the other, and so fits inside the other twice nice and snugly. The two sounds are an octave apart, with the shorter wavelength being higher. If two wavelengths of one sound line up with three wavelengths of another, the sounds are a fifth apart. If it's 3:4, it's a fourth. These sounds are still harmonious to us even though not as much as the octave sound. This is why they are'perfect fifths' and'perfect fourths'. 4:5 gives us a major third, 5:6 gives us a minor third, 6:7 gives us something between a minor third and a major second (which we usually approximate to a minor third) and 7:8 does the same (which we usually approximate to a major second). Beyond that the intervals are no longer really harmonious enough for our ears to pick them up, and they just sound clashy. So because a minor third is more clashy than a major third, we perceive it as a little more off and this can translate into sad. The'harmonic series' is a set of notes that can be played on a wind instrument by overblowing each time. It's how flute players get really high notes even when flutes are actually quite big. Remember the ratios? The notes in the harmonic series go 1:2:3:4:5:6:7:8. Played together on, say, a piano, this really sounds kind of awesome. Basically, pick a low note (this is 1 wavelength), and play an octave up from that (2 wavelengths) a fifth up from that, a fourth up, a major third up, a minor third up, another minor third up, and a major second up. You will end up three octaves above your starting note (the ratio of start:end is 1:8, and 8 is 23). So say you pick a C. Play the C above that, then the G above that, then the C above that, then E, then G, then B flat, then C. Major chords consist of a major third and then a minor third. Minor chords consist of a minor third and then a major third. Minor chords are a lot more clashy than major chords because major chords are part of the harmonic series. Specifically, 4:5:6. Look up again at the notes. C, E and G are next to each other. This makes a C major chord. To make a minor chord you'd need a 5:6 ratio and then a 4:5 ratio. Essentially, this would work out at 5:6:7.5 (or 10:12:15) which is not as nice. (Actually, it's a lot better than say a diminished or augmented chord which is why the minor chord still sounds good to us and is used in a lot of stuff). I can't say why we interpret more clashy chords as sad or spooky; that may just be society. My theory is that they set you on edge just a little bit more. Bonus: This is also why certain configurations of a chord work together better than others. If you have a piano, go play F, the C above that, the A above that, and the F above that. Sounds nice, doesn't it? The ratios work out at 2:3:5:8 which is nice and whole numbery and low. Now play A to F above it then C above it then A. Doesn't sound as good, does it? The ratios here are 5:8:12:18 - much higher, meaning they clash more. This is even though the two chords are the same chord (F major). Analog Network Coding (ANC) is proposed in literature to improve the network throughput by exploiting channel diversity. In practical scenarios, due to the difference in channel characteristics an extra residual component, termed as ANC Noise, appears during the processing of the received signal. This ANC Noise component may suppress the ANC gain. None of the existing literature to our knowledge considers the effect of spatial correlation among channels on ANC noise. This paper develops a generic framework to investigate the effect of channel characteristics on ANC noise. We have modelled the channels as spatially correlated to take the (dis) similarity among them into account. Per node power constraint is also taken into consideration. In this work, we have characterized the behaviour of ANC noise and presented the results to analyze the network performance in terms of outage probability. Outcomes of our investigation show that spatial correlation among channels significantly affects the variance of ANC noise as well as the outage performance of the system. The proposed framework can provide better insights while selecting the system parameters in a correlated environment.

Microbes: yes; atoms: no. With a straight, magical scaling down of a human you'd hit the resolution limits of visible light which has a wavelength of about 0.5mm. This would mean that you could see everything that can be seen with an optical microscope but atoms are a challenge even for electron microscopes. If you delve into the kind of magic that would be required to scale a human then many more problems arise. The retinal cells in our eyes just don't scale down like that. Insect cells are roughly the same size as human cells; they just have way fewer of them. That's partly why insects have compound eyes which work in a very different way from human eyes. The most fundamental problem is that the square-cube law means that you can't just scale cells or organisms and expect them to work in the same way. There's a reason that the smallest mammals are bigger than insects.," "No, the world would look drastically different, but you wouldn't be able to see microbes or atoms or anything like that. Microbes are incredibly small, in many cases much smaller the cells in mammals or other complex life.," "Biology answer: as you shrink everything shrinks including your retina iris etc. so the amount of light let in would be tiny. This means the world would become very dark, if not black. Your ears wouldn't be able to accept sound waves, making you deaf. Your lungs would be too small to absorb oxygen, and the capellaries would be too small to transport oxygen which means you would suffocate in a dark silent world. So no you wouldnt be able to see microbes,The smallest ants - pharaoh ants at around 2mm - are about 11000th the size of the tallest humans - a little over 2m - so you can estimate that with the same visual acuity he would see things at effectively 1000x "magnification." We can perceive objects down to about 0.1mm, so our shrunken human would in principle be able to perceive down to 0.1mm (microns). Most bacteria are 2-100x that size so he could see them easily. You start hitting the limits of visible light at these scales though, which is why we move to things like electron microscopes at higher magnifications. There may be other optical effects I'm missing that would mess things up at such a small scale.

Safety risk assessment is an essential process to ensure a dependable Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) design. Traditional risk assessment considers only physical failures. For modern CPS, failures caused by cyberattacks are on the rise. The focus of latest research effort is on safety-security lifecycle integration and the expansion of modeling formalism for risk assessment to incorporate security failures. The interaction between safety and security and its impact on the overall system design, as well as the reliability loss resulting from ignoring security failures are some of the overlooked research questions. This paper addresses these research questions by presenting a new safety design method named Cyber Layer Of Protection Analysis (CLOPA) that extends existing LOPA framework to include failures caused by cyberattacks. The proposed method provides a rigorous mathematical formulation that expresses quantitatively the tradeoff between designing a highly-reliable versus a highly-secure CPS. We further propose a co-design lifecycle process that integrates the safety and security risk assessment processes. We evaluate the proposed CLOPA approach and the integrated lifecycle on a practical case study of a process reactor controlled by an industrial control testbed, and provide a comparison between the proposed CLOPA and current LOPA risk assessment practice.

Scientists in China have developed an extremely fast charging technology that can charge a lithium-ion battery to up to 60 percent capacity in under six minutes. The technology involves a special carbon composite material as the electrode, which has an exceptionally high specific surface area and conductivity compared with graphite electrodes used today for commercial batteries Researchers from Xiamen University were able to carry out this incredible feat by combining their existing electrochemical method of achieving supercapacitor levels of performance from solid polymer electrolytes (SPE) - they've now successfully applied it to Li-Ion cells too on top of being able to attain very rapid charge rates thanks to its unique nanostructure design. In addition, the team was also successful at extending this ultrafast recharge into larger sized batteries - making them not just suitable but ideally suited towards demanding applications such as electric vehicles or portable electronic devices where time is everything when you are running low on juice. The researchers published details about how exactly the process worked earlier this year detailing: Our] novel nanoplasmonic cathode exhibits enhanced capacitance and cycling stability with low impedance even after repeated 100 cycles... Moreover, we demonstrated a new type of SC system based on solid polymer electrolyte embedded fiber architecture using our newly designed nanoporous carbongraphite composite electrode. Our results demonstrate the possibility of ultrahigh rate capability (1Cmin) and long cycle life (500 h)." Now the scientists believe that these findings could be scaled up quickly resulting in commercially viable products sooner rather than later due to the fact there aren't any limitations involved here relating to safety concerns like those which would need to apply before commercialization took place if other technologies had been tested first. Instead, all improvements made will only improve each successive generation further allowing us to expect faster recharging times every single time while simultaneously increasing energy storage capacities over what already exists without compromising anything else e.g., cost, power density etc.. This research comes hot off the heels of report released late last month concerning scientists creating what may prove to become one of the most significant advancements ever seen within the field of chemistry; having discovered a way to combine two materials together through atomic bonding called van der Waals force. This allows both crystals usually found miles beneath the earths crust outer atmosphere, sodium chloride (also known as table salt), combined with copper sulfate (that makes your bath water stink slightly more than usual) to form a completely stable complex structure capable of absorbing light much better than either component alone! According to researchers from Northwestern University who carried out the original study titles: 'Sodium Chloride Energy Densifier via Intraface Bonding Between Sodium and Copper Sulfates': "Intramolecular cluster formation between NaCl 2O 3 6H2SO 4, CuSO43H2O colloids enables the direct absorption of visible solar radiation [...] We visualize optical properties of SrCl 5 doped Nd:YAG laser pumped suspensions showing unprecedented photoluminescence intensity enhancement upon excitation." They continue adding: "In comparison to pure solutions of NaCl CuSO43 H2O composed of individual compounds, [we find] exceptional thermal robustness due to nonstructural interdiffusion across interfaces during the heat treatment operation - no phase separation occurs between different components observed in previous studies."

The success of the human-robot co-worker team in a flexible manufacturing environment where robots learn from demonstration heavily relies on the correct and safe operation of the robot. How this can be achieved is a challenge that requires addressing both technical as well as human-centric research questions. In this paper we discuss the state of the art in safety assurance, existing as well as emerging standards in this area, and the need for new approaches to safety assurance in the context of learning machines. We then focus on robotic learning from demonstration, the challenges these techniques pose to safety assurance and outline opportunities to integrate safety considerations into algorithms "by design." Finally, from a human-centric perspective, we stipulate that, to achieve high levels of safety and ultimately trust, the robotic co-worker must meet the innate expectations of the humans it works with. It is our aim to stimulate a discussion focused on the safety aspects of human-in-the-loop robotics, and to foster multidisciplinary collaboration to address the research challenges identified.

Despite a decade of active research, there is a marked lack in clone detectors that scale to very large repositories of source code, in particular for detecting near-miss clones where a new and potentially large contribution (e.g., the rewriting of a large part of the code) is inserted into a larger and possibly very old code base. Existing clone detectors for large code bases tend to be ad hoc and unscalable, making it hard to know what constitutes a valid and useful code base. Furthermore, it is not always clear how to detect near-miss clones. We propose a novel framework for detection of near-miss clones in large code bases. Our approach uses a novel framework based on a learning machine that is capable of learning to detect near-miss clones. We first develop a baseline approach based on an unsupervised learning algorithm that has a reasonable performance on a large code base (10,000 lines of Java code) with an average size of 2,000 lines of code per repository. Next, we propose a framework that leverages two major improvements to our baseline: (1) we introduce a new approach to incorporate the available source code structure and the repository size in the training phase, and (2) we improve the performance of our unsupervised learning algorithm by introducing an unsupervised clustering step that groups the code lines into near-miss clones. Our framework outperforms the baseline on a large code base with an average size of 2,000 lines of code per repository, and can detect near-miss clones in repositories with a size as large as 500,000 lines of code. A computer-driven car that can tell when to brake and swerve has been unveiled by the UK's Advanced Technology Centre (ATC) in Oxfordshire. The new development is being tested with the aim of reducing driver distraction during reaction times tests. It also may reduce the need for drivers to look at their phones while driving - although this is not yet known whether it will help or hinder them. 'Game changer' Called "the first truly autonomous vehicle," the ATC said the system would make motorists safer than current systems because they were harder to control. "This technology is game changing," explained Paul Kyle, director of the centre, who helped launch the project in 2015. The team behind the project have already successfully tested computer control in a Nissan Navara SUV and on British roads as part of its 1m (1.4m; 1.7bn euro) Automated Vehicle Project. During the project, its three sensors - cameras, radar and lasers - tracked what was happening around it in real-time through a complex software system. Once this data had been analysed, a computer either turned on or off its lights accordingly, which allowed it to react quickly enough to avoid collisions and speed up. Mr Kyle added: "If you put the brakes on one second before impact, there is no difference between human intervention and computer interference." He believes that within five years automated vehicles could be on the market, but warned against taking too much liberty with autonomous features just yet. Short-term memory tends to go before long-term so pay attention to failure to keep track of where things are, times, dates, and appointments. [substeps] Try telling the person several pieces or parts of information at a time. For example, tell him that you will be picking up your friend in five minutes. After he has waited for about three minutes say "I'm ready now!" Then wait another minute or two until it is clear whether his brain remembers what was said. If not, repeat the request - maybe saying something else like "Honey? Honey?" as an inquiry rather than a command might help. Also try asking questions instead of giving instructions: "Where's my wallet?" with no further explanation. Instead ask if they have found their wallet yet, how do they feel when looking inside it. By asking simple yesno type questions, you can detect immediate interest (eagerness), confusion Is this thing on? annoyance This thing always does this..., fatigue Enough already!. [substep 5] Another test involves walking around while carrying five different items such as keys, purse, etc., without dropping any. The rules apply here too - make sure each item is visible from all angles. Notice what happens when you put down one item then pick up another. Does anyone notice? Repeat the process every few steps. When someone stops paying attention, take off running and see who follows. It shouldn't take them more than 30 seconds to catch up; and watch out for spontaneous explosions.[endnote]

There are two primary reasons for rising sea levels. Firstly, ice that floats on water occupies less space due to its lower density; hence, only a portion of the ice contributes to increasing water levels. The second reason involves vast quantities of ice stored within glaciers situated on landmasses like Greenland. As these glaciers melt, their previously trapped water flows into the oceans.

Furthermore, since most of this ice resides atop terrestrial regions rather than within the ocean itself, once it melts, it subsequently seeps into the marine environment. Consequently, even though the initial presence of ice may suggest otherwise, upon complete thawing, we witness an elevation in overall water levels. To illustrate this phenomenon, consider filling a cup partially with water and adding several ice cubes. Although the ice appears to increase the liquid's height initially, once it melts, the resulting water barely reaches near-full capacity. Similarly, as the land-based ice transforms back into liquid form, it ultimately contributes to escalating sea levels worldwide.

The study focused specifically on the high-level domain of memory access vulnerabilities detected by auditing the codebase used for copy protection against malicious attacks using primitives like C and Java and otherwise known vulnerabilities. The authors noted that attackers would need to learn how to exploit weaknesses exposed before attacking, which will require deep learning techniques including deep learning. In 1933, Herbert Chapman, wanting his players to be more distinctly dressed, updated the kit, adding white sleeves and changing the shade to a brighter pillar box red. Two possibilities have been suggested for the origin of the white sleeves. One story reports that Chapman noticed a supporter in the stands wearing a red sleeveless sweater over a white shirt; another was that he was inspired by a similar outfit worn by the cartoonist Tom Webster, with whom Chapman played golf. Regardless of which story is true, the red and white shirts have come to define Arsenal and the team have worn the combination ever since, aside from two seasons. The first was 1966-67, when Arsenal wore all-red shirts; this proved unpopular and the white sleeves returned the following season. The second was 2005-06, the last season that Arsenal played at Highbury, when the team wore commemorative redcurrant shirts similar to those worn in 1913, their first season in the stadium; the club reverted to their normal colours at the start of the next season. In the 2008-09 season, Arsenal replaced the traditional all-white sleeves with red sleeves with a broad white stripe.

A new survey suggests there may only be around a dozen left in English waters - down from 70 last year. But the endangered species still lives across Europe where sightings continue to occur despite its perilous status. Seahorses belong to the lily family growing up to 25cm long and are considered one of nature's "miracle" animals for being able to reproduce using sperm rather than eggs or ovaries as other fish do. At first sight it looks like any other sea animal, with shell-like plates that give them an appearance similar to those seen among molluscs. However, unlike barnacles which cling onto ships' hulls living inside bodies of water is not common among seamarspiders due to limited oxygen levels. They live almost entirely underwater feeding largely on microscopic plankton. Seahorses inhabiting inshore UK waters More than 300 different species of sea hares inhabit British coastal areas with some found in tidal rivers such as Avonmouth and Exmoor, while others are found in brackish inland waterways including Runnymede Creek near London. The IUCN estimates between 500 million and 1 billion sea hares worldwide, covering much of the northern hemisphere but also tropical waters. Sea harvesters scrape away unwanted detritus known as seaweed, taking advantage of its ability to absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. Find out more here. Their overall numbers in Britain dropped from 3,000 in 1990 to 2,700 in 2006 before rising again to 5,400 in 2015. Biologist here. Here's an attempt: Your muscles consume energy. A lot of it. They use this energy in the form of a molecule called ATP (Adenosine Triphosphate), commonly called the "energy currency" of cells. Cells use this molecule by essentially harvesting the energy that is released when a single phosphate is broken off. The ATP that once was "triphosphate" becomes "diphosphate" (ADP) and your cells take up the energy to use for whatever they need. ADP is not very useful as most of the energy comes from that third bond, and just two phosphates don't really have as much energy, so your body needs some way to replenish that ADP back into ATP to use again. This is done through a fairly complex mechanism called "cellular respiration" where your cells use other sources of energy (food) to convert ADP back into ATP. So how does creatine fit into this? Well I mentioned how your muscles consume energy and there's only so many places you can get that energy. You have stores of ATP ready to be used in a moment's notice in your muscles, but depending on how quickly you use it up your body will need to replenish that ATP to keep going. You could get it from breaking down food and fat and using cellular respiration, right? Sure, but that takes SO long and we don't have time for that when we need to get that next set of reps in. So what creatine does is whenever your body is resting and you have excess ATP just sitting around, creatine will actually take up a phosphate and just hold onto it. When you start doing an intense workout all of a sudden like lifting something heavy, your skeletal muscles quickly deplete ATP into ADP and "creatine phosphate," being the cool dude he is, will come and donate his phopshate to that ADP, becoming ATP and able to do work again. The thing is, the creatine is only useful for about the first 2-10 seconds of intense workout. Effectively that means that it may help you get that 11th or 12th rep in, but once it's depleted and you're still exercising, it won't really serve a purpose until you take a break and allow your body to replenish both ATP and creatine phosphate. The other thing is your body can only have so much creatine because of this thing called "homeostasis." Having excess creatine from supplements causes your body to in turn produce less creatine. The swelling of muscles from creatine supplements comesf rom water wanting to flow into your muscle cells to counterbalance the change in concentration. This isn't very long lasting nor does it really affect much aside from making you look "swoll.

It is prohibitively expensive to annotate a large-scale video-based person re-identification (re-ID) dataset, which makes fully supervised methods inapplicable to real-world deployment. How to maximally reduce the annotation cost while maintaining good recognition performance is an important yet challenging issue. In this paper, we propose to solve this problem using two complementary training schemes, namely, the class-level alignment (CLA) and instance-level alignment (ILA) schemes. The CLA scheme learns a set of class-level descriptors, while the ILA scheme learns a set of instance-level descriptors. We introduce a novel descriptor learning method called kernelised Fisher vector descriptor learning, which is based on an approximate Fisher discriminant analysis (FDA) and a novel loss function to further enhance the discriminative power of the kernelised Fisher vectors. An effective similarity matching method is also proposed, which makes use of the fact that the re-ID dataset is largely labelled with a noisy label (e.g., an incorrect person ID) problem. Finally, we introduce a novel two-level integration framework to integrate the CLA and ILA schemes into a unified framework to maximally make use of the collected labelled data. Extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed methods significantly outperform the state-of-the-art methods.

My stance is that jail terms are excessively commonplace and lengthy. Many people carelessly mention "five years behind bars" without comprehending the impact of such a decision on the remainder of someone's life. Moreover, I firmly maintain that legal history alone cannot sway my perspective regarding whether or not the privileged adolescent involved in the "Affluenza" case deserves incarceration. His acute observation skills and deductive reasoning had helped him solve some of the toughest criminal cases in history. However, this also meant that he couldn't help but find crime everywhere he looked - even while on a field trip with schoolchildren. One fine day, Detective Lewis received a strange request from the local school principal. She asked him to take a group of schoolchildren on a field trip to the local zoo. He called the zoo security and alerted them about his suspicions. They quickly took care of the situations he brought up, but nothing seemed to come of it. A man was following them around the herbivore's section, a woman seemed to be keeping an eye on the reptiles, and he even thought he could see someone trying to loosen the barriers around the lion's enclosure. Bode's sensitivity integral constraints define a fundamental rule about the limitations of feedback and is referred to as the waterbed effect. In a companion paper [35], we took a fresh look at the waterbed problem using this approach, assuming that an object would be sensitive only to its own position but not its orientation or shape (this, in fact, has been a standard formulation of the waterbed problem). While still being a useful tool for investigating mass wave propagation through nonuniform media, our improved formulation does not offer any insight into how changes in shape can affect the response to external perturbations. To address these two problems, we used a more general formulation based on the integration over time of geometric information contained within the diffusion equation and second-order perturbation theory. We developed an explicit algorithm for comparing the results from obtained with different versions of the NURBS model to those obtained by traditional methods without explicitly modeling the geometry of the objects diffusing along the surface. The resulting model was validated against numerical simulations and experimental data [36]. This work provides a novel procedure for deriving explicit formulae for evaluating the waterbed effect. It also establishes strong connections between feedback and the waterbed problem, providing insight into mechanisms controlling mass transport.

When a tree grows in an open area with stable soil and environmental conditions throughout its lifetime, it experiences swift growth during its early stages, which then tapers off over time. Initially, the tree's annual growth rings are broad, but these rings progressively narrow as the tree ages. Each new layer of growth forms around the existing structure, leading to increasingly slender rings if the rate of wood production doesn't significantly rise annually. Furthermore, as the tree matures, its canopy expands and reduces wood output, causing even finer growth rings. Forest-dwelling trees exhibit varying growth rates due to intense competition for resources like sunlight and nutrients, resulting in alternating periods of fast and slow development. Certain species, including some southern oaks, consistently produce rings of similar width for centuries. Generally speaking, though, the thickness of a tree's annual rings diminishes as its diameter enlarges.
