Stress is known to trigger various mental health conditions. Similarly, residing in densely populated societies can also induce these issues, despite having all basic necessities fulfilled. There was once an intriguing study conducted by John B Calhoun involving rodents. Named "Universe 25," this investigation involved providing mice with ample resources such as food, water, and medical attention. With no restrictions on breeding, the mouse population surged rapidly. Surprisingly, the increased density led to behavioral anomalies among the mice, including aggression, neglectful parenting, and random acts of violence. Eventually, this escalated into a 'behavioral sink,' where the mice ceased reproducing entirely, remaining abnormal even when the population decreased. Conducting the identical trial with rats yielded similar results; however, unlike mice, rats gradually returned to typical behavior patterns as their numbers declined. Reflecting upon our current global population of approximately 7.7 billion individuals - up from just a billion throughout much of human history - it becomes evident that feelings of insignificance may contribute significantly to prevailing mental health challenges within society. Moreover, empathy towards others tends to diminish amidst such overwhelming numbers.

Text-to-image synthesis seeks to create images based on user-provided textual descriptions, presenting significant complexity. This process encounters two primary obstacles: the heterogeneous gap that bridges abstract text concepts with concrete pixel data, and the homogeneous gap connecting artificially generated images with authentic ones. To overcome these challenges, we utilize powerful discriminative models like VGG19 to steer the development of a novel generative model capable of closing both gaps through multi-tiered guidance. By leveraging high-level insights, the generative model learns essential visual cues from texts, thus overcoming the heterogeneous divide. Additionally, using mid-level and detailed lower-level interpretations, the model acquires structural and intricate features of imagery, narrowing down the homogeneous gap. Consequently, our proposal introduces Symmetrical Distillation Networks (SDN), featuring an instructive discriminative model ("teacher") and a receptive generative model ("student"). Their mirrored architecture facilitates seamless hierarchical knowledge exchange. Furthermore, we segment the learning procedure into dual phases employing distinct distillation methodologies, enhancing the capabilities of the generative model. Testing across two popular datasets confirms the efficacy of our SDN approach.

Recent progress in deep learning enables us to assess city characteristics with high precision and across vast areas through analysis of street-level photographs. In this study, we concentrate on calculating the proportion of trees in urban settings via Google Street View (GSV) photos. Initially, we introduce a limited yet labeled verification dataset along with conventional measures for evaluating the accuracy of machine-generated estimates of arboreal coverage using GSV imagery. Utilizing cutting-edge deep learning algorithms, we contrast them against an earlier unsupervised approach's benchmark. Our unique training regimen for these deep learning algorithms involves leveraging plentiful publicly accessible, similarly annotated sets of street-level pictures for initial model development, followed by further refinement on a smaller collection of GSV images. Results indicate that deep learning approaches surpass the previous unsupervised technique substantially. A network of radio telescopes in the Netherlands made detailed recordings of a lightning bolt during a summer storm in 2018. The recordings, which were processed only recently, show lightning pulses with a duration of 50 microseconds. The new measurements are more precise than previous measurements, which lasted only 1 to 2 microseconds. The researchers behind the study published the results in the journal Physical Review Letters. Lightning pulses are very short electrical signals that can be generated by electrical discharges from a thundercloud. They have a length of a few microseconds, a duration that is too short to be measured directly with the technology available today. The radio astronomers recorded the lightning in such detail by connecting their telescopes to an electrical wire. The wires became antennas, which received the lightning signals. The signals were then combined and converted into sound waves. The new measurements are important because they are the first direct measurement of lightning pulses and will help scientists gain a better understanding of the physics behind lightning.

Courts have distinguished between two types of civil disobedience: "Indirect civil disobedience involves violating a law which is not, itself, the object of protest, whereas direct civil disobedience involves protesting against a law by violating it. A famous example of the former is the campaign of the African National Congress to defy the pass laws which required non-whites to carry their government-issued identification papers at all times." "The distinction between direct and indirect civil disobedience is not always clear; for example, an office worker who refuses to give his social security number to his employer is not violating any law, yet if he did so as a protest against a law he believed unjust he would be engaged in direct civil disobedience. Many types of direct action could be seen as civil disobedience. A more useful distinction might be between civil disobedience in the sense of a concerted campaign of breaking certain laws (the sit-in, the boycott, the refusal to pay certain taxes) and civil disobedience in the sense of a single, isolated act intended to demonstrate the illegitimacy of a law, such as the refusal of an individual to show his or her papers to a police officer. The latter type, a single act, is sometimes referred to as conscientious disobedience, and is usually described as the higher type of civil disobedience, though both have in common the deliberate and peaceful breaking of the law. The distinction between them is also drawn in law; in most countries, disobedience of a law (the lower type) is a crime, while conscientious disobedience is not, since it is usually seen as a justified protest against an unjust law. In any case, the two terms are often used interchangeably." American civil disobedience "The modern idea of civil disobedience begins with Henry David Thoreau's essay, "On the Duty of Civil Disobedience" (1849). Thoreau argues for disobedience to the government when a citizen believes that a government's laws are in opposition to the conscience of the citizen. He says that if a person can't follow the law without violating his or her conscience, then they must break the law. He suggests that laws which are unjust should be resisted rather than obeyed. Thoreau was a strict vegetarian, and he felt that the American government was not only allowing for slavery, but it was profiting from it. He felt it was his duty to break the law by not paying his poll taxes, because he did not believe it was right for him to support a government that allowed slavery. Thoreau was not the only American writer to advocate civil disobedience. For example, in 1893, writer and lecturer Helen Hunt Jackson wrote the essay "Civil Disobedience: A Chapter in American History," which was published in 1895 as part of the book "The Century" and included other American authors such as Ralph Waldo Emerson, Frederick Douglass, and Henry George. She describes the experiences of Native Americans and the many ways that they were denied their civil rights. For example, in 1888, the U.S. government had issued a "proclamation for the relief of the so-called 'starving Indians' of North Carolina." She believed that Native Americans were being denied their rights and were being treated very poorly, so she supported them through her writing. At the time, the American government was not receptive to the idea of civil disobedience. The idea that an individual could break the law if it violated their own conscience was not widely accepted. Thoreau's essay did not influence American culture until the 1950s and 1960s, when civil rights activists adopted his ideas to combat racial segregation. Martin Luther King Jr. and Mahatma Gandhi, for example, were both advocates for civil disobedience and nonviolence. In the United States, the term "civil disobedience" is attributed to Henry David Thoreau's essay "Resistance to Civil Government" (1849). Thoreau is known as one of the fathers of the American civil disobedience movement. In "Resistance to Civil Government," Thoreau argues that a citizen should not follow the law if it violates the citizen's conscience. He says that when an individual cannot follow the law without violating his or her conscience, then that individual should break the law.

Recommender systems have become integral across various fields, impacting daily life significantly. However, their influence has sparked debates over potential prejudices and unfair treatment they may perpetuate. Two main types of biases exist within these systems: observational bias and bias resulting from uneven datasets. The former arises from a self-reinforcing cycle where the algorithm learns to suggest items based solely on prior recommendations. Conversely, dataset imbalances occur when existing social, historical, or contextual disparities skew the data. To mitigate these issues, we introduce an innovative fairness-focused hybrid recommender system in our research. By integrating diverse factors like user and item relationships, content details, and demographic data into our methodology, we aim to offer precise and unbiased suggestions. Furthermore, our approach utilizes the robust capabilities of probabilistic soft logic—a sophisticated probabilistic programming tool—to execute the model. Upon testing with a well-known film recommendation database, our technique demonstrates superior performance in delivering equitable and improved recommendations relative to leading models focused on fairness.

The core issue in machine learning concerns how effectively trained algorithms can apply learned principles to new, unknown datasets. Despite the prevalence of oversized neural network-based models in contemporary machine learning practices, there remains an insufficient comprehension of their ability to generalize. Compounding this challenge is the complex nature of the associated non-convex optimization tasks. In response, we have developed a broad theoretical structure that evaluates the long-term generalization accuracy of single-layer neural networks—also known as generalized linear models—which incorporate any form of non-linear functions and are suitable for both predictive and categorical outcomes. This system allows us to examine the influence of various factors such as excessive parameters, the degree of non-linearity included, selection of the cost function, starting conditions, and regulatory techniques employed throughout the process. Additionally, our approach accounts for discrepancies between the sets of data used for training and testing purposes. To illustrate our findright, we delve into specific scenarios like linear and logistic regression. Furthermore, using our model, we're able to precisely and theoretically account for the occurrence of the double descent pattern observed within generalized linear models.

Educational psychology can in part be understood through its relationship with other disciplines. It is informed primarily by psychology, bearing a relationship to that discipline analogous to the relationship between medicine and biology. Educational psychology in turn informs a wide range of specialties within educational studies, including instructional design, educational technology, curriculum development, organizational learning, special education and classroom management. Educational psychology both draws from and contributes to cognitive science and the learning sciences. In universities, departments of educational psychology are usually housed within faculties of education, possibly accounting for the lack of representation of educational psychology content in introductory psychology textbooks (Lucas, Blazek, Raley, 2006).

The Very high-speed Backbone Network Service (vBNS) came on line in April 1995 as part of a National Science Foundation (NSF) sponsored project to provide high-speed interconnection between NSF-sponsored supercomputing centers. The vBNS project was completed in 1997, with 141 sites connected by high-speed 45 Mbps fiber optic cable. The vBNS now consists of two separate subnetworks. The first, the Fiber-Optic Network Subnetwork (FONS), is a fiber optic network operating at 45 Mbps that connects the vBNS sites. The second, the Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) Network Subnetwork (ANS), is a high-speed ATM network that provides connections between the vBNS sites and the Internet. The vBNS is currently being transitioned into a National Science Foundation (NSF) sponsored project to provide high-speed interconnection between NSF-sponsored supercomputing centers, and between these centers and major Department of Energy (DOE) and National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) supercomputing centers. D. Shields, "The Very High Speed Backbone Network Service (vBNS)," Proc. of the 31st Int. Conf. on Parallel Processing, (1998), pp. 433-438.

This paper discusses an efficient implementation of the generation of order conditions for the construction of exponential integrators like exponential splitting and Magnus-type methods in the computer algebra system Maple. At the core of this implementation is a new algorithm for the computation of coefficients of words in the formal expansion of the local error of the integrator. The underlying theoretical background including an analysis of the structure of the local error is briefly reviewed. As an application the coefficients of all 8th order self-adjoint commutator-free Magnus-type integrators involving the minimum number of 8 exponentials are computed.

This is called Proximity Pressure. As your brain recognizes you are getting closer to a bathroom, it signals your kidneys to release more urine to your bladder, so that the urine already there will be able to be released as quickly as possible.', "I don't buy the Proximity Pressure explanation offered previously. Does he think the brain releases less ADH instantly when your subconscious knows it's close to the bathroom? You normally produce 30 mL of urine per hour. I doubt in a few seconds your kidneys produce enough urine due subconscious cues to have a noticeable impact on the pressure you feel in your bladder. That doesn't explain how the defecation impulse is stronger the closer you get to a toilet. I think it has more to do with the autonomic control of both sphincters in the bladder and rectum. We have two sets of muscles that control opening of the urethra and rectum: one mainly controlled by our ANS and the other consciously controlled. We can't consciously control the ANS controlled sphincters through will or relaxing. This is why some people have trouble passing urine after a foley catheter has been removed, despite straining to void. They are relaxing one sphincter, but the other is still closed by some mechanism. So as you get closer to the bathroom, subconscious cues (thoughts of relief, thinking of a toilet or getting closer to a bathroom) may cause the autonomic sphincters to relax, which means you consciously controlled sphincters are now the only thing holding back the urinefeces. This extra pressure on those muscles then give you a greater sense of urgency to voiddefecate.," "My this has no gray transition area. Black and white. I leave work, I'm good. Driving home, fine. Dengue is a mosquito-borne disease which is prevalent in sub-tropical and tropical regions. It is a major cause of illness worldwide, causing about 100 million episodes of feverish illness a year. Its outbreak in Burkina Faso is causing alarm and officials are trying to avoid any widespread panic. One man told BBC Afrique's Yacouba Ouedraogo in the capital, Ouagadougou, that the disease had killed his brother quickly: "My younger brother did not even have a chance to say what was wrong. We just found him dead," he said. Dengue fever particularly affects young children and adults, but is not normally fatal, specialists say. Most people who get it will suffer from headaches and fever. Some get rashes, aches and pains and their symptoms usually last for two or three days. An infected person can feel tired for up to three months, but will not usually need treatment. Cases of the disease have been reported from all 12 districts of Ouagadougou, the World Health Organization says. Two other regions - the Sahel Region in the north and the Hauts-Bassins region in the west - have also reported cases.

The data revolution continues to transform every sector of science, industry and government. Due to the incredible impact of data-driven technology on society, we are becoming increasingly aware of the importance of privacy. This has led to the rise of data privacy laws around the world, such as the GDPR in Europe, which have the power to revolutionise the use of personal data. As more countries start to enforce data privacy laws, the regulation of personal data is becoming increasingly complex. For example, the EU's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) protects citizens of the EU, and data subject to the GDPR must remain in the EU or in a country that has been approved by the European Commission for the purposes of data protection. But what if your data is collected in Europe but stored in the USA? Which law applies? These are the types of questions that the Privacy Level Agreement (PLA) is designed to answer. PLA is a set of rules and policies for the use of data that is owned by individuals. The PLA helps organisations to determine which data privacy laws should apply to their data. The PLA is built on top of the concept of the Privacy Level. The Privacy Level of data is the set of rules that apply to the use of that data. These rules are defined by law, by contract, or by international treaties. For example, the USA has a Privacy Level with a single rule that says that US law applies to all data stored in the USA. Whereas the EU has a Privacy Level with three rules: the first two being that EU law applies to all data that is collected within the EU, and that EU law applies to all data that is collected outside the EU if it is about an EU citizen. The third rule is that international treaties must be respected. The PLA helps to identify the Privacy Level of a data item. It does this using a process called the Privacy Level Calculation (PLC). The PLC takes a data item and looks at the set of rules that apply to that data. For example, if the data is collected from an EU citizen within the EU, the EU Privacy Level applies and the PLC returns the three rules associated with the EU Privacy Level. If the data is collected from a US citizen outside the EU, then the USA Privacy Level applies, which has a single rule: that US law applies to all data stored in the USA. The PLC helps to answer questions such as: If a data item is collected from an EU citizen and stored in the USA, which data privacy laws should be applied to it? In this case, the answer is US law. If a data item is collected from an EU citizen and stored in the EU, which data privacy laws should be applied to it? In this case, the answer is EU law. If a data item is collected from a US citizen and stored in the EU, which data privacy laws should be applied to it? In this case, the answer is EU law. The PLC is designed to answer the question: "Which data privacy laws apply to this data item?" The PLC can be used to determine which data privacy laws apply to a data item in order to decide how the data can be used. For example, the PLC can be used to determine whether data collected in Europe about an EU citizen can be transferred to the USA. If the PLC says that US law applies to this data, then the data can be transferred to the USA. But if the PLC says that EU law applies to this data, then the data must remain in Europe. In the following sections, we will go through the PLC in more detail, and show you how it can be used to determine the Privacy Level of a data item. Research on generative models is a central project in the emerging field of network science, and it studies how statistical patterns found in real networks could be generated by formal rules. Output from these generative models is then the basis for designing and evaluating computational methods on networks, and for verification and simulation studies. During the last two decades, a variety of models has been proposed with an ultimate goal of achieving comprehensive realism for the generated networks. In this study, we (a) introduce a new generator, termed ReCoN; (b) explore how ReCoN and some existing models can be fitted to an original network to produce a structurally similar replica, (c) use ReCoN to produce networks much larger than the original exemplar, and finally (d) discuss open problems and promising research directions. In a comparative experimental study, we find that ReCoN is often superior to many other state-of-the-art network generation methods. We argue that ReCoN is a scalable and effective tool for modeling a given network while preserving important properties at both micro- and macroscopic scales, and for scaling the exemplar data by orders of magnitude in size. There are two elements to the "fiscal cliff" The first is government spending cuts. These were pre-negotiated and agreed upon two years ago by the Republicans and Democrats. Part of the cuts go to the military, which the Republicans don't want to be cut, and the rest go to various non-military programs, which the Democrats don't want to be cut. But, honestly, these "cuts" are inconsequential and not even really cuts at all. This is because of a practice known as "baseline budgeting," which takes a rising amount of spending as the zero point. The proposed "cuts" are not a decrease in actual spending but in the rate of growth of future spending. At any rate, it's hardly the drastic amount of cuts that is actually necessary to balance the budget. The other half of the "fiscal cliff" is the expiry of the Bush tax cuts. This would mean a significant rise in taxes for the middle and upper class. The Republicans want to keep these taxes where they are for everyone. But the Democrats are insisting on raising them for the "rich," those making more than around 200,000 per year. Now, the effect of going over this "fiscal cliff" depends on which economists you talk to. Pro-capitalist economists are most concerned about the effect on the economy of raising taxes, particularly on the rich. That is because they believe that economic growth is created by increases in savings. More savings means more money to go into expanding business and being able to make things in more capital-intensive but more efficient ways. This is sometimes called "supply-side" economics because the idea is that we get richer by allowing people to create more goods. Wealthier people put a much greater proportion of their money into savings, so the idea is that increasing the tax burden on them means less savings and thus less production. Those economists who support the mixed economy have essentially the opposite viewpoint and are more afraid of the reductions in government spending. These economists believe that the real trouble is that we do not have enough demand (spending) in the economy. That is why they support "stimulus" programs to encourage people to spend for consumption instead of saving. It is often called "demand-side" economists because the idea is that we will encourage more production by convincing people to want to buy more. All government spending is consumption, so it is supposed to be ideal for this purpose. These economists are afraid that if we decrease government spending, businesses will go under because there will not be enough demand for their goods. So, essentially, no matter one's beliefs, there is something damaging to the economy in this "fiscal cliff." At the same time, though, every sensible person knows that we have to contain the budget deficits somehow. So the rightists want to keep taxes the same (or lower them), while decreasing government spending, the leftists want to raise taxes and keep spending the same or increase it, and the politicians want to kick the can down the road because no one wants their taxes raised or their favorite programs cut.

Counsel General Mick Antoniw said he was "delighted" by the Supreme Court ruling against the UK government on Brexit. The Supreme Court said UK ministers were "not legally compelled" to consult the assembly and that AMs have no veto. Mr Antoniw said it is likely AMs would get a vote on the triggering process. But he said it will not be a veto on leaving the EU. AMs could decide to hold a vote in the assembly on article 50 if they feel that the legislation on article 50 affects devolution. There is a convention - called the Sewel Convention - whereby the assembly has a say on legislation in Westminster that affects devolution in the form of a vote in the chamber. But Tuesday's ruling that AMs do not have a veto on Brexit means that whether or not the vote has meaning will depend on the UK government's reaction. Mr Antoniw told AMs on Tuesday: "As the Article 50 Bill proceeds through Parliament, we would expect the UK government to respect the Sewel Convention, so that Parliament has the opportunity to listen to the assembly and to the other devolved legislatures." Mr Antoniw said there was "every likelihood of a vote (in the assembly) because a trigger bill will impact on Welsh legislation." The court ruled Theresa May cannot trigger Article 50 - the formal exit process from the EU - without the backing of MPs and peers. The court also said UK ministers were "not legally compelled" to consult the devolved legislatures in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. Analysis by BBC Wales political correspondent Daniel Davies It sounds like the eleven Supreme Court judges sent the Welsh Government packing. They all agree: there's no legal reason for Theresa May to consult the assembly. But there is a political reason for Parliament to listen. And if Parliament must vote on Brexit, it leaves the door ajar for the assembly to influence things. That means there might be a vote in the assembly on triggering Article 50, as well as in Westminster. I am also sorry to disappoint anyone who hopes that a vote in Cardiff Bay could stop Brexit. It will not. All sides agree the assembly does not have a power of veto.

Say and Yakarylmaz showed that the class of languages that could be verified by these machines within an error bound strictly less than sfrac 12 is precisely NL , but their construction yields verifiers with error bounds that are very close to sfrac 12 for most languages in that class. We characterize a subset of NL for which verification with arbitrarily low error is possible by these extremely weak machines. It turns out that, for any 0 , one can construct a constant-coin, constant-space verifier operating within error for every language that is recognizable by a linear-time multi-head finite automaton (2nfa (k. We discuss why it is difficult to generalize this method to all of NL , and give a reasonably tight way to relate the power of linear-time 2nfa (k) 's to simultaneous time-space complexity classes defined in terms of Turing machines.

Norman Daniel points out that the Arab equivalent of the Latin disputation, the taliqa, was reserved for the ruler's court, not the madrasa, and that the actual differences between Islamic fiqh and medieval European civil law were profound. Sociotechnical systems are intricate networks characterized by complex interactions between various entities, often making it difficult to identify cause-and-effect relationships. Due to the lack of effective tools to comprehend and instigate changes within these systems, managing them becomes challenging. Social forces known as influence and shaping act upon these systems to initiate transformations; however, they are typically addressed haphazardly without clear frameworks or measurement methods to ensure successful implementation. Additionally, both influence and shaping depend heavily on a thorough grasp of trust's underlying principles. A deficient understanding of trust hampers the ability to steer changes in a desired direction effectively. This research presents a succinct definition of these ideas, facilitating easier modeling and analysis of their behavior. Subsequently, we propose a model for influence and shaping that incorporates Computational Red Teaming techniques to illustrate its functionality. Our findings are validated using computational simulations set in a simulated societal context, thereby demonstrating the impact of social influence and shaping.

People with a DNA variation in a gene called PDSS2 tend to drink fewer cups of coffee, a study carried out at the University of Edinburgh has found. It suggests the gene reduces cell ability to break down caffeine. This causes it to stay in the body for longer and means those with the gene get the same caffeine hit through less coffee. One scientist working on the project said it suggests the "drive to drink coffee may be embedded in our genes." The researchers studied the DNA of 370 people living in a small village in southern Italy and 843 people from six villages in north-east Italy. The subjects were asked to complete a survey including a question about how many cups of coffee they drank each day. The team found people with the PDSS2 DNA variation tended to consume fewer cups of coffee than people without the variation - equivalent to one fewer cup daily on average. Researchers replicated the study in a group of 1,731 people from the Netherlands. The result was similar but the effect of the gene on the number of cups of coffee consumed was slightly lower. The scientists said the change could be down to the different styles of coffee drunk in the two countries. In Italy, people tend to drink smaller cups such as espresso whereas in the Netherlands the preference is towards larger cups which contain more caffeine overall. Dr Nicola Pirastu, a Chancellor's Fellow at the University of Edinburgh, said: "The results of our study add to existing research suggesting that our drive to drink coffee may be embedded in our genes. "We need to do larger studies to confirm the discovery and also to clarify the biological link between PDSS2 and coffee consumption." The study is published in the journal Scientific Reports and was conducted at the universities of Edinburgh and Trieste, the Burlo Garofolo Pediatric Institute in Italy, the Erasmus Medical Centre and PolyOmica, a data analysis company based in Groningen, the Netherlands.

Euclid's fifth postulate is also known as the parallel postulate, and afaik there wasn't really confusion so much as it's just weird. These five postulates were intended as an axiomatic foundation, the assumptions and rules from which everything else is proven, for what we now call Euclidean geometry. The other four seem reasonable and intuitive as postulates, but the fifth one, even with less awkward phrasing than Euclid used, seems like something you should be able to prove from the other four (spoiler warning, you can't). And there's no rigorous phrasing for that postulate that isn't awkward - the terms point and line aren't actually defined in geometry and adding more undefined terms is not a good thing (and that's why Euclid's postulates are all phrased the way they are, with most other terms in geometry defined in terms of points and lines on some level). Generally, mathematicians want to limit the number of assumptions they're working from, and given both the awkward and seemingly provable nature of E5P, there were a lot of attempts to prove it in order to get rid of it as a postulate. Then they tried ignoring it all together and seeing what they could prove without it, and non-Euclidean geometry was eventually the result. Spherical (ie what happens if you draw a triangle on a globe) and projective (ie drawing classes where you draw rail road tracks or a city street with a vanishing point) geometries are examples of non-Euclidean geometries where the parallel postulate does not hold. TLDR: 1. It was awkward and looked provable from postulates 1-4, and proving it would be good. 2. Lots of people tried, since if they succeeded they'd be famous. 3. They all failed, because 4. Non-Euclidean geometry is an interesting thing that you can get from postulates 1-4 and ignoringreplacing 5. Mostly. I'm going to mention the word metric and then recommend you not worry about it.

Ctenophores, similar to sponges and cnidarians, possess two primary cell layers enveloping an intermediary gelatinous substance known as the mesoglea—this term also applies to cnidarians but differs from the tripartite structure seen in more advanced organisms. This has led certain modern academic resources to categorize ctenophores as triploblastic, whereas other sources maintain the classification of them being diploblastic.

As I slowly turn to see, every moment explodes into a brand new universe, where space erodes my mind; where non-existence implores me to run. As I rotate my spectral head, every fiber of every muscle seems to hold a new way to remember, and a new way to suffer. I remember waking up feeling totally lost. I was only sixteen, how is it possible that neither of my parents wanted me? It had to be me. I had to be the reason they left. I was too much for them. Too much work; too much pain; too much to love. The cold, hard cement was all I had left. Turning more to take in a larger fraction of the scene, my body now screams in agony, begging me to leave; to once again swim inside the stars. Memories flood my being once again, as my skin feels like it's peeling off. I finally found people who loved me. Sure, it was the tough kind of love, but at least I found some family. Most people were terrified of us, and somehow that brought me comfort. While we didn't operate inside the law, we operated with each other in mind; the good of the group. We'd steal, rob, and even kill if it helped the group. Now my physical body is in full view. I can see it laying naked in the cold, damp alley; sprawled like piece of bird shit. My left arm, now visible in the light of the moon, lay noticeably separate from my body, clung only by the sharply barbed rose vines. As the vines bind my abdomen in a deliberate-looking pattern, blood oozes from every oversize thorn. Cherry petals swirl around me in the cool Chicago night, their sweet scent patronizing my agony. I have to get a closer look. As I move toward the scene, another figure becomes visible. It's her! It's Kendra! But. But that's not her real identity, is it? It was one I had created to escape the cruel reality of the situation. Just as I begin to realize the overwhelmingly painful truth, more memories flood my brain. I was doing a job. Just a routine break-in. Nobody was supposed to be home, and the loot was supposed to be out of this world. As I made my way to the closet with the safe, I started to feel kind of strange about the whole thing. The house didn't have any furniture, and it looked like nobody had lived here for months, maybe years. I figured it was just some rich dude hiding his cash in an inconspicuous location. So I continued on into the closet, and that's when things really got weird. It was some sort of shrine, and it was... it was a shrine to me! My picture was plastered on the ceiling, and what looked like hair, nails, and even bones adorned a cloth-covered table. I didn't waste any time even looking for a safe - I needed to run! Turning as quickly as I could, I quickly realized my path was blocked by some hooded figure. I immediately started swinging, but had no chance against this obviously beyond-human entity. I managed to knock its hood off, and I am still not sure if I should regret doing so. It was... It was my Mom! " What are you doing here?! " I spit at here in a rage that had been building for thirteen years. Without saying a word, she swung a lead pipe toward my face. The next thing I remember is, well, now. Looking at her, I have so many questions. Why would she do this? Why did she leave me? Why did I construct such a crazy story to avoid the truth? I know, though, that time is not enough to afford me an answer to any, let alone all, of my questions. Landing gently on the ground next to my body, I feel a deeper peace coming over me than anytime during my trips through the cosmos. My path is clear. I crawl back into my body, and feel every fiber of my being entrenched in pain. Moments become eternity, but moments are all it takes. Even as I feel myself laying naked in the alley, I can see that the cold, hard cement sings perfection as my hot, liquid blood steams across its surface. The contrast is stunning. I am going to die. The root and shoot systems rely on each other; typically non-photosynthetic roots need sustenance from the photosynthesizing shoots, while shoots require nutrients like water and minerals supplied by the root system. Each system's cells have the ability to generate counterpart cells and form extra shoots or roots. Examples include stolons and tubers, where shoots develop into roots. Surface-level roots, such as those found in willow trees, may give rise to new shoots and eventually full-grown plants. If one system gets damaged, the other has the capacity to regenerate it. A whole plant can potentially be cultivated from just a leaf, as seen in Saintpaulia species, or even from a lone cell, which transforms back into a versatile callus and then grows into a fresh plant. Vascular plants possess specialized conduits called xylem and phloem, facilitating resource movement among roots and shoots. Additionally, some roots serve as storage units for food reserves, including sugars or starches, as observed in sugar beets and carrots.

Stress can certainly bring out some mental health issues. So can living in a more crowded society even if all your needs are met. A while ago a man named John B Calhoun did an experiment on mice. The experiment was called Universe 25. In the experiment he had mice living in an environment in which all there needs were met. They had food, water, and health care! They were allowed to breed uncontrolled so their numbers climbed. Even though they always had enough food to eat, the mice started showing signs of mental health issues as they became more and more populated. The mouse equivalent of rapes became more common, mother mice started becoming shitty mothers, fights broke out even though there was no reason for them (random acts of violence). Soon things got even worse and the mice stopped behaving like mice (behavioral sink) and stopped breeding altogether. Even as they started dying off and numbers shrank, they never acted normal again. He did the same experiment in rats and saw the same thing, except that as the rats started dying off and their numbers got lower they did start behaving somewhat normal again. So... in our society of 7.7 billion people (noting that our population has more than doubled in the past 40 years alone and that for thousands of years our population was less than only a billion people) it's clear to see that some of the mental problems are likely the result of us feeling like nothing, like nobody, like one in 7 billion people... we lose compassion for others as well in such a society.

In October 1529, Philip I, Landgrave of Hesse, convoked an assembly of German and Swiss theologians at the Marburg Colloquy, to establish doctrinal unity in the emerging Protestant states. Agreement was achieved on fourteen points of doctrine, but when the subject of the Eucharist was raised, the Colloquy broke up without the hoped-for accord. Zwingli, unable to accept Luther's doctrine of Christ's "real presence" in the elements, confided to his friend, "They have more knowledge of the kitchen than of theology." Toward the end of the twentieth century, one hundred and fifty years after the Colloquy, I find myself in the theological position of Zwingli. If Luther and Calvin were correct, then the Protestant theology of the Lord's Supper, with its Christology as a whole, would have to be radically altered.1 Yet it is still Protestant theology, rather than that of the Orthodox or Roman Catholics, that presents a Eucharistic doctrine coherent with the doctrine of the Trinity, the hypostatic union of Christ's divine and human natures, and the communion of the saints. The central problem is this: Where does the theology of the Eucharist go from here? I One of the most perplexing problems of Christian theology concerns the relation between the infinite and the finite. Since God is infinite and we are finite, how can we relate to Him? The Bible, while affirming that we are created in His image, emphasizes the chasm between Creator and creature, and that God is "holy." How can the unholy relate to the Holy One? How can a finite creature relate to the Infinite One? The Incarnation, the becoming of God in human flesh, is the answer to this problem, for Christ is the mediator between God and man, the one who unites the infinite and the finite. The Bible teaches us that God Himself became finite, and that in the Person of Jesus Christ we can relate to God. And because Christ is both God and man, we can relate to God in the humanity of Christ. What does this mean? It means that Christ, while remaining God, also became man. It means that as God, He is the Creator, and as man, He is the creature. As God, He is the infinite, and as man, He is the finite. As God, He is eternal, and as man, He is mortal. As God, He is omniscient, and as man, He is ignorant. As God, He is omnipotent, and as man, He is weak. As God, He is omnipresent, and as man, He is limited in space and time. In other words, Christ is a divine Person with two natures. In His divine nature, He is infinite; in His human nature, He is finite. The two natures are united in the one Person of Christ, who is both God and man. The doctrine of the incarnation is the key to all of Christian theology. If we believe that Christ is both God and man, then we can relate to God in His humanity. And this is the doctrine of the Trinity. II The Christian doctrine of the Trinity, according to Scripture, is that within the one Being of God there are three eternally existing and equal persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Orthodox, Roman Catholic, and Protestant Christians agree on this. However, what do we mean when we say that God is a Trinity? What does it mean to say that God is one Being with three Persons? The answer is that we do not fully understand it. The doctrine of the Trinity is a mystery. The doctrine of the Trinity is an attempt to give coherent expression to the biblical data regarding the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. We know from the Bible that each of the three is fully God. Yet we know that there is only one God. The doctrine of the Trinity, therefore, affirms that there is only one God, and that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are eternally distinct Persons within the Being of this one God. In trying to understand the Trinity, it is important to avoid the error of tri-theism. The doctrine of the Trinity does not teach that there are three Gods. It teaches that there is only one God, and that this one God has three Persons. The Athanasian Creed is helpful in understanding the doctrine of the Trinity, for it states: We worship one God

Current Integrated Development Environments' (IDEs') source code recommendations primarily rely on static typing knowledge, frequently resulting in unrelated advice within specific scenarios. Lately, deep learning methods have demonstrated remarkable promise in crafting source code for diverse software engineering activities. Nevertheless, these strategies suffer from insufficient adaptability and resilience, hindering their application in genuine software creation settings. In our study, we introduce DeepVS, a comprehensive deep learning-powered code autocompletion solution that derives knowledge from existing code repositories through Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Units (BiGRUs). This innovative tool can deliver instant source code suggestions within an IDE utilizing a trained BiGRU network. Our assessment comprises both numerical and subjective evaluations. By conducting thorough tests across ten authentic open-source software frameworks, our approach exhibits notable improvements in efficiency and applicability. Additionally, our findings indicate that the DeepVS tool possesses the ability to propose novel (previously unencountered) code elements by recognizing coding conventions observed in real-life software applications.

While there may be debates about correlation versus causation, it seems evident that certain medications can lead to thoughts of self-harm or even suicide. This differs from innate impulses such as hunger or the need for rest, as deciding to take one's own life involves a deliberate choice, albeit potentially an irrational one. Individuals experiencing ongoing suffering may view suicide as a solution to their pain, and thus proceed with it. Although it appears unlikely for a medication to directly generate suicidal ideation, unlike other drugs that stimulate specific bodily functions like appetite or sleep, it's conceivable that changes in neurochemistry caused by medication could result in distress that prompts consideration of drastic measures like suicide. One example worth exploring further is antidepressants, which despite being intended to alleviate depression, have been linked to increased suicidal tendencies among patients. This connection raises questions regarding whether antidepressants provide depressed individuals with enough energy to act upon existing suicidal thoughts, something they may have previously lacked. In terms of clinical trials, if participants report having suicidal thoughts during testing, pharmaceutical companies must include this as a potential side effect since there's no means to predict such reactions accurately. Furthermore, considering how many of our emotions are regulated by hormones and substances within the body, medications that affect these levels can also impact mood and behavior, sometimes leading to unexpected outcomes such as uncontrollable crying episodes experienced personally when using a particular medication.

Neural networks for structured data like graphs have been studied extensively in recent years. To date, the bulk of research activity has focused mainly on static graphs. However, most real-world networks are dynamic since their topology tends to change over time. Predicting the evolution of dynamic graphs is a task of high significance in the area of graph mining. Despite its practical importance, the task has not been explored in depth so far, mainly due to its challenging nature. In this paper, we propose a model that predicts the evolution of dynamic graphs. Specifically, we use a graph neural network along with a recurrent architecture to capture the temporal evolution patterns of dynamic graphs. Then, we employ a generative model which predicts the topology of the graph at the next time step and constructs a graph instance that corresponds to that topology. We evaluate the proposed model on several artificial datasets following common network evolving dynamics, as well as on real-world datasets. Results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed model.

The reason for the majority rule is the high risk of a conflict of interest andor the avoidance of absolute powers. Otherwise, the physician has a financial self-interest in "diagnosing" a patient with a malady, which may result in ordering unnecessary tests andor procedures. When it comes to the field of medicine, there are different levels of informed consent. With basic or general consent, the physician informs the patient about the diagnosis, treatment and prognosis of the condition. In addition, the patient is provided information about the risks, benefits and side effects associated with the proposed treatment. With expanded consent, the physician provides the same information as well as information about alternative treatments. This type of consent is often used when there is a controversy among experts as to what's best for the patient. For example, there may be two different ways to remove an appendage. An expanded consent would include information about both options, as well as their risks, benefits and side effects. With full consent, the physician gives the patient all information about the proposed treatment, as well as about other similar procedures. The physician also provides the patient with information about the risks, benefits and side effects of each procedure. The patient is then asked to make a decision about which procedure to undergo. Full consent is usually required for elective procedures, such as cosmetic surgery. When it comes to emergency procedures, the patient may not be able to make a decision. In these cases, the physician must get the consent of the patient's next of kin or another authorized individual. If a patient is unconscious, the physician must get the consent of the patient's next of kin or another authorized individual.

Background When monitoring long periods of natural phenomena such as ocean temperature over thousands of years, it may be desirable to detect abrupt shifts in these fluctuations that are due either to an external physical trigger or to internal process dynamics leading toward new regimes. One method used widely to identify such transitions is based on statistical inference with respect to the likelihood function associated with observed values [1]. Another option is model selection through Bayesian statistics known as Baysian Model Selection (BMS), which has been introduced recently by others [2, 3 ]. Both approaches have strengths and weaknesses: while maximum likelihood allows arbitrary positivity constraints on the parameters involved, BMS can handle them easily but requires additional priors. Furthermore, when dealing with finite samples, both assume convergence towards the true parameter value distribution; however, BMS provides robustness against misspecification typically without imposing strong parametric assumptions (see Section 2). As such, BMS offers a valuable alternative to MLE under various conditions where weak regularity hypotheses must hold at each point along the horizon (e.g., stationary increments), which often cannot be verified empirically. This article proposes a solution to identifying local discontinuities, i.e., large jumps between two consecutive observations in a time series, which complements existing procedures. Our methodology consists of first estimating a latent variable representing the instantaneous mean logarithmic rate of return using weighted least squares regression and then combining this estimate with an outlier test that identifies a jump as significant if there is some evidence indicating that the real mode lies outside previous estimates. We call this procedure MODEST because "Mode Detection Estimation Switching Testing." Although similar ideas have appeared previously [4] 6], they did so with focus on stochastic models involving independent variables such as ARCH processes instead of queue lengths in queues. Moreover, our contribution includes several improvements including automatic sensitivity analyses on unknown lower bounds for weights appearing in the objective function (Section 6-7); calibration procedures aimed at improving precision and avoiding false positives; and clear distinction between conditional versus unconditional estimators for rare events. To showcase its performance, we analyze data from bank exchange rates collected during 40 months across four different currencies, namely USDJPY, EURUSD, GBPEUR and JPXGBP. By performing Monte Carlo experiments, we show that MODEST outperforms comparable competing procedures in terms of efficiency.Less

Deep learning models continuously break new records across different NLP tasks. At the same time, their success exposes weaknesses of model evaluation. Here, we compile several key pitfalls of evaluation and propose novel ways to deal with them. There are two main types of error in neural networks: (i) errors made by model training and (ii) errors due to testing data or noisy labels [119]. We focus on the former type as it is more relevant for our problem setting: when evaluating a language understanding system trained using large-scale publicly available datasets like BERT-Large 10, the ultimate objective is to use these models for better human-computer interaction systems and machine translation applications [120]. Error propagation The fact that one word might not have its correct meaning is a well-known issue with shallow embedding-based language representations [121]. In deep networks this can be handled via so-called 'error propagation' mechanisms such as dropout [122]: each layer's activation value depends only on other layers but does not depend itself directly on input words. However, some studies show that error propagation does not work properly for all languages because there exist many other factors which affect how humans understand words at any given moment [25], especially if they do not seem to fit into our current linguistic knowledge (e.g., foreign words). To illustrate this drawback further, consider an example where multiple synonyms are present within the same sentence; e.g., "see" in "He saw her standing next him." The output vector representation of "swim" will likely point towards the most frequent word in the English lexicon, while seeing may still imply swimming, flying, etc. This could cause problems during both semantic parsing like event extraction [71] and named entity recognition [123]. Dropout: Another way of reducing unwanted effects caused by various sources of noise is known as dropout [124]; i.e., randomly removing units from certain parts of a deep network to prevent overfitting. Dropout works well if the number of hidden nodes per layer is large enough so that activations tend to cancel out between neurons connected to those particular hidden nodes. Unfortunately, this means that even though unit removal prevents the wrongly activated node from influencing subsequent outputs, noise induced through dropouts would propagate throughout additional processing stages resulting in undesirable results [135]. In addition, dropout usually comes along with another kind of randomization -data shuffling, also called Galton-Watson noise 1 [148]. It has been shown that despite being often applied together with dropout, data shuffling actually leads to worse performance than either technique alone [149]. Perhaps surprisingly, although seemingly innocuous, dropping samples during data collection provides greater protection against bias compared with using the actual data drawn. As suggested by Ben-David et al., [210] whole corpus-level sampling plays a vital role here as it helps reduce cases where words strongly associated with individual speakers influence final scores, similar to the case described above. These studies provided us with important information about text properties that mattered for specific downstream tasks 2 and revealed the importance of distributional semantics, notionally tied to real-world contexts of events and entities [61]. For instance, one popular approach uses crowdsourcing platforms [169] 3 to collect ground truth ratings of sentences collected by researchers-whereas participants rate texts based on a set of predefined questions related to the topic under investigation. Based on this dataset, researchers create metrics fully tailored to individual downstream tasks. Although useful tools for benchmarking research progress, automatic approaches to measuring text quality suffer from limited generalizability since they rely heavily on the existing taxonomy used to annotate corpora 6. Furthermore, automatic proposal generation techniques add significant overheads to the annotation process without providing guarantees of high interannotator agreement [33]. Instead, manual scoring methods exploit expertise to assign numeric grades by combining qualitative judgments captured via open ended questions. Under Chapter IV, Article 25 of this convention, individuals within the armed forces who receive specialized training for tasks such as working as hospital attendants, nurses, or assistant stretch bearers during emergencies are entitled to equal rights and protections when engaging in activities related to locating, transferring, treating, or caring for the wounded and sick, even if they encounter hostile forces or are captured by them. Furthermore, according to Article 29, these personnel become prisoners of war once apprehended; however, they may still perform medical duties based on necessity. As per the Geneva Convention, intentionally attacking a medic displaying visible identification marks constitutes a serious violation. Presently, most combat medics are equipped with individual firearms for self-defense purposes and ensuring the safety of those they assist. However, using their weapons offensively would result in losing their protected status under the Geneva Conventions. In this paper, we propose a characterization of chordal bipartite graphs and an efficient enumeration algorithm for chordal bipartite induced subgraphs. A chordal bipartite graph is a bipartite graph without cycles of length 4 or greater where each vertex in one partite set is adjacent to all vertices in the other partite set that are reachable via a path of even length. Our enumeration algorithm iteratively selects a vertex from one of the partite sets and adds it to the current induced subgraph if it is adjacent to all previously selected vertices. The algorithm then either terminates if the induced subgraph is chordal bipartite or recursively calls itself to continue growing the subgraph. Our algorithm runs in polynomial time and can be used for applications such as maximum weighted independent set on chordal bipartite graphs.

The placenta-like structure found in male seahorses showcases an intriguing instance of convergent evolution. These creatures have developed brood pouches that perform similar functions to those of human placentas during gestation. Throughout their pregnancies, male seahorses nourish their developing offspring within these specialized pouches. As the fetuses increase in size, the walls of the pouch thin out and additional blood vessels emerge, mirroring the characteristics of a mammalian placenta, which facilitates respiration for the unborn seahorses. Remarkably, just 24 hours postpartum, the brood pouch returns to its original state before conception.

I remember the window being open during my last therapy session. A late September breeze tousled the curtains, as if the wind were self-aware and knew the power it held, the way it could blow the stale air out of the room and bring in the fragrance of fall. I remember thinking that that small moment of fresh air would be enough to chase away the lingering sense of doom that had clung to me, as if it were an unwanted guest, ever since I left the hospital. I was wrong. The sadness stayed. It was simply easier to deal with it outside the confines of the office, so I tried to embrace it. The darkness grew inside me, the way it always does during this time of year. I needed to stop it. I needed to cut it off, to figure out what was wrong with me, to face the dark and bring it to light. The weight of the sadness was heavy and immovable, like the sand I was always being buried in as a child, a sinister stand-in for the security of a warm blanket. I didn't want to fight it anymore. I was exhausted. It was easier to become the sadness, to embrace the darkness, to let it take me. But then I remembered the window, and the breeze. I remembered my therapist telling me to take a walk, that fresh air could do me good. I needed the fresh air. I needed a break from the darkness. I needed to stop embracing the sadness. I needed to face it, and I needed to bring it to light. The darkness was a well-worn pair of shoes, and it was time to get rid of them. It was time to let go of my past and move on, or at least try. I was getting older. I was in college now. I needed to grow up, to get past my childhood. But I needed to be careful. I needed to be careful because there was always the chance that I would be stuck forever in my childhood, in the sadness. I would be trapped in the darkness, and it would never go away. I remembered the window during my last therapy session and I remembered how the darkness had followed me out of the office. I remembered how I had brought it with me, like a secret that I carried with me. I remembered how I had tried to fight it, and how I had failed, and I remembered the window. It was time to stop trying to be strong and brave and fight the darkness. It was time to let it go, to let it take me. But then I remembered the window. It was time to move on, to let go. It was time to bring the darkness to light, so I could face it and be free. I made it outside. The darkness was following me, like a shadow, but it was not dark anymore. It was bright and it was beautiful, like a painting, like a photograph. The darkness was a picture of my childhood, and it was time to face it and let it go. It was time to bring it to light. I remembered the window, and I remembered the breeze. The darkness followed me, but I was not afraid. I had made it outside. I had made it. I had finally found the light. Data transmission within CPUs and RAM operates based on frequency levels. Higher frequencies result in circuits behaving similarly to transmission lines, leading to interference and other problems that cause data corruption due to excessive noise. Advancements in shielding techniques and architectural designs enable enhanced processing capabilities while mitigating these adverse effects. Conversely, storage presents additional complexities beyond mere transmission challenges; altering the physical state of materials holding data is necessary. While solid-state drives eliminate hard drive limitations, such as moving read/write heads through the device, they still require substantially more time spent modifying the storage medium's state compared to merely transferring electrical signals within the circuitry. Moreover, there exists an issue regarding the disparity in available data volume between different components - storage devices possess greater capacities than RAM, which itself exceeds CPU capacities. This results in data flowing sequentially from storage to RAM to CPU. To illustrate this concept, consider a large tub representing storage slowly pouring into a bucket symbolizing RAM before finally being transferred into a small cup depicting the CPU via a narrow passageway. Given the comparable conduit sizes, it invariably takes more time to fill the bucket than the cup.

Data densities have significantly expanded over time, resulting in accelerated read/write speeds for individual files. Furthermore, advancements in technology have led to reduced power consumption, allowing for smaller yet efficient 2.5" SAS drives running at 15,000 RPM. Five years prior, these types of drives required a larger 3.5" model along with a heatsink adapter. Presently, nearly all contemporary servers and SAN systems utilize 2.EE drives. Previously, 2.5" models weren't favored due to their lower storage capacity, slower performance, and elevated costs.

Conventional spinning disks faced constraints dictated by their inherent physical properties – a given disk size and composition possesses specific weight limits. Operating them at 7200 RPM demands a particular energy input. Although increasing rotational speed may seem viable, it would raise energy consumption, necessitate superior motor and bearing quality, generate more heat, among other factors. Fortunately, improvements in density allowed maintaining identical storage capacities while reducing disk size.

The task of cross-lingual document searching involves finding relevant documents when the query language does not match the document language. In this research, we examine the variability inherent in neural network-based document search methods and introduce a new comprehensive system designed to enhance results in multi-language document searches. Our innovative system features a unique metric called 'smooth cosine similarity' for assessing the relevance between queries and documents, along with a distinctive loss function termed 'Smooth Ordinal Search Loss'. Additionally, we offer assurances regarding the limit of the model's generalization error. Through comparisons with existing document search frameworks using standard ranking benchmarks, our method demonstrates notable improvements across various linguistic contexts within the realm of cross-lingual document retrieval.

There he was, in the flesh. The most notorious evildoer of antiquity. Adolf Hitler. Well, he was no Yfrshi, who had eclipsed Hitler's misdeeds by orders of magnitude only 500 years after him. But this was the most exciting trial scheduled for this decade; all the other trials were of less well known pirate warlords from the early days of space colonization. I could hardly believe I had actually secured tickets to Adolf Hitler's EGDC trial, especially for such a price. I still had a little bit left in savings after the purchase. " The Eptergalactic Defensive Court will now hear the case of the apologant, Adolf Hitler, " said the Butler, the overseer of the panel of judges. My clone sat up in her seat next to me. Everyone knew what the justification would be: investment in the future. He had already been convicted in another court, so there was no defense (his defense of insanity by medication had gone south after an analysis of his brain). Hitler had been in this time for over two years at this point, making his way through the top rungs of the galactic legal system. This was the end of the line, a sentencing court for his crimes against life in the Epterdisk of the galaxy. Fortunately for Hitler, the EGDC's prestige afforded him an excellent suite of lawyers: a powerful legal supercomputer and a team of six human psychopaths, all completely devoid of shame for finding the best justification possible for their client. And boy, was it a clever one. The judges, two humans, a computer, and one hothen, gave their first prompt. The apologant could only speak in response to the prompts of the judges, who themselves represented life in this half of the galaxy. " What justification does your client have for his actions against life over 8000 years ago? " Their client, by genetically pruning the human race at the end of its childhood, had prepared the future of the human species to venture forth wiser, stronger, and more capable of defending itself, they asserted. Such an event was a critical experience to have for a species which was to survive in the galactic ecosystem later on. They argued that their client's war had changed the species, not only in genetic composition, but also in a way only the magnitude and precision of such a war could have had. It had changed the outcome of the next several centuries, and taught the species several valuable lessons, both about its own nature and self defense. For the small price of a few million lives in the past, he had prepared the human species to save trillions of lives in the present day. The hothen, suspended by his somewhat loud bags of methane, eyed Hitler suspiciously. The human judges listened intently. The computer had no physical form in the room, but we all knew it was listening. Hitler sat completely motionless, with a bitter frown frozen into his face. A lower court had temporarily paralyzed him using a chemical concoction after his second suicide attempt while on the stand, and this decision had been preserved all the way up the court ladder. His lawyers kept his mouth tightly shut anyway, so they had no objections. I looked around at the audience, which was sectioned off by the time era they came from. All the way at the end I could see a few humans who held pamphlets for those from negative years. Their guides, I imagined, explained to them that the year system had been changed to center around their year 3500 or so, which was when humans first encountered another sentient species. It had taken us nearly 1500 years of space travel to find someone. My own guide had 9B0 - 11E1 shaped on it, which introduced me to the current year from my own, 2097 years ago. Paralyzed Hitler wasn't a very theatrical guy, which was kind of disappointing. The first trials, where he had ranted and attempted suicide must have been a lot more fun to watch. The story of his arrest was that the moment he saw them beam in, he had indeed tried to shoot himself. By the end of the day, a judgement was ready. It was a fast case. " The judges have determined that the apologant's actions are only marginally excusable, " they concluded. Though he remained motionless, his entire body was sweating. His upper lip had beaded sweat where his mustache once was. (His lawyers had insisted he shave it.) " And as retribution in the defense of all living beings in the Epterdisc of the galaxy, all living beings will have root access to the mind of Adolf Hitler. The apologant will endure this until the last day of his life, at which time he will be disassembled by nanobots. " The humans at the end, the ones from the negative years, stood up and cheered. I guess they still had memories of this guy in that time? Or maybe they were just happy with the retribution. Disassembly by nanobots was the most painful thing a human could experience, since the nervous system was always the very last thing to be torn apart. Trillions of nanobots shredding cells, eventually setting fire to every nerve simultaneously. But I think the pain was incidental to the retribution. Really, it was the twitch plays Hitler thing that was the main course. It wasn't just a physical control. No, they had said ' root access to the mind '. Trillions of people would wrestle for control of his very thoughts with him, in addition to having no agency over his person. He'd certainly never have a private thought again. Sure, there would be blocks in place to prevent death, but the public could be very creative....

Indeed, the majority of planets within a solar system align along the same plane since they originated from the same protoplanetary disk. Venturing away from Earth won't necessarily involve an 'upward' direction, as there is no universal orientation for 'up' and 'down' in outer space. Traveling perpendicularly to the ecliptic plane might lead one to encounter other star systems within our galaxy before leaving it altogether. After countless millennages, one could potentially come across another galaxy. However, considering the vastness of space, it is possible to traverse all solar systems and galaxies without interference or collision with celestial bodies. 

The structure of our solar system exhibits a relatively flat formation, with the planets orbiting approximately parallel to one another. Smaller celestial objects are dispersed throughout the system in a more spherical manner. While the solar system exists within the Milky Way galaxy, it does not encompass the entirety of the cosmos. Like our solar system, the galaxy possesses its own disc-like shape, resembling a grand spiral pattern. Although not every galaxy shares this feature, numerous others do possess similar structures. Galaxies tend to form their unique planes, such as the inclined plane observed in the neighboring Andromeda galaxy when compared to our Milky Way.

On a broader scale, various astronomical phenomena display a flattened nature. This characteristic arises from the phenomenon of rotation-induced flattening; as objects rotate, centrifugal forces cause them to adopt a disc-like configuration. Consequently, numerous cosmic entities, spanning multiple scales, appear flat while maintaining distinct orientations.

If you’ve decided to seek professional help, here are some things to think about before making an appointment. Firstly, ask yourself whether you would prefer to work one-on-one with a practitioner, or within a group setting. You could start by asking friends or family members for recommendations, or contact local community organisations for advice.

Once you have narrowed down your list of potential providers, try to meet them briefly before committing. Even if they don’t specialise in your particular issue, most will offer a free initial consultation session so you can decide whether you click with each other. During these trial appointments, ask questions such as “What experience do you have in treating my problem?” and “How does your approach differ from others?” Be honest with any concerns you have; it’s important to establish trust early on! Remember though that although price shouldn’t be a major factor in choosing someone, many services charge according to their expertise and/or qualifications – so bear this in mind too. Finally, check whether your chosen provider offers payment plans or accepts Medicare rebates where available. Many therapists now accept electronic payments via PayPal or credit card transactions online – both convenient options if cash isn’t handy!

This paper introduces the Packing While Traveling problem as a new non-linear knapsack problem. Given are a set of cities that have a set of items of distinct profits and weights and a vehicle that may collect the items when visiting all the cities in a fixed order. Each selected item contributes its profit, but produces a transportation cost relative to its weight. The problem asks to find a subset of the items such that the total gain is maximized. We investigate constrained and unconstrained versions of the problem and show that both are N P -hard. We propose a pre-processing scheme that decreases the size of instances making them easier for computation. We provide lower and upper bounds based on mixed-integer programming (MIP) adopting the ideas of piecewise linear approximation. Furthermore, we introduce two exact approaches: one is based on MIP employing linearization technique, and another is a branch-infer-and-bound (BIB) hybrid approach that compounds the upper bound procedure with a constraint programming model strengthened with customized constraints. Our experimental results show the effectiveness of our exact and approximate solutions in terms of solution quality and computational time.

Layout camouflaging (LC) is a promising technique to protect chip design intellectual property (IP) from reverse engineers. Most prior art, however, cannot leverage the full potential of LC due to excessive overheads andor their limited scope on an FEOL-centric and accordingly customized manufacturing process. If at all, most existing techniques can be reasonably applied only to selected parts of a chip - we argue that such "small-scale or custom camouflaging" will eventually be circumvented, irrespective of the underlying technique. In this work, we propose a novel LC scheme which is low-cost and generic - full-chip LC can finally be realized without any reservation. Our scheme is based on obfuscating the interconnects (BEOL); it can be readily applied to any design without modifications in the device layer (FEOL). Applied with split manufacturing in conjunction, our approach is the first in the literature to cope with both the FEOL fab and the end-user being untrustworthy. We implement and evaluate our primitives at the (DRC-clean) layout level; our scheme incurs significantly lower cost than most of the previous works. When comparing fully camouflaged to original layouts (i.e., for 100 LC), we observe on average power, performance, and area overheads of 12, 30, and 48, respectively. Here we also show empirically that most existing LC techniques (as well as ours) can only provide proper resilience against powerful SAT attacks once at least 50 of the layout is camouflaged - only large-scale LC is practically secure. As indicated, our approach can deliver even 100 LC at acceptable cost. Finally, we also make our flow publicly available, enabling the community to protect their sensitive designs.

While the concept of a Sparse Neural Network has been researched for some time, researchers have only recently made notable progress in the matter. Techniques like Sparse Evolutionary Training allow for significantly lower computational complexity when compared to fully connected models by reducing redundant connections. That typically takes place in an iterative process of weight creation and removal during network training. Although there have been numerous approaches to optimize the redistribution of the removed weights, there seems to be little or no study on the effect of activation functions on the performance of the Sparse Networks. This research provides insights into the relationship between the activation function used and the network performance at various sparsity levels.

The warning has been made by the Royal College of Emergency Medicine in its weekly update of AE performance. It showed nine in 10 hospitals are increasing bed numbers - but despite this they have problems seeing patients quickly enough and discharging them. The RCEM weekly report provides a snapshot of performance. It covers more than 40 hospital trusts - one in five of the total. Special report page: For the latest news, analysis and video Nick Triggle: The lost beds problem Hugh Pym: The Northern Ireland challenge Winter across the UK: A guide to how the NHS is coping Video: Why hospitals are under so much pressure Video: How a hospital can grind to a halt The update suggested that just over 86 of patients were seen and dealt with in four hours - below the 95 target. It also highlighted problems with delayed discharges - this is when hospitals cannot release patients because services or care are not available in the community. It said in some places a fifth of beds were being taken up by these patients. And it concluded that despite the best efforts of hospitals, winter was proving difficult and there was "insufficient capacity and capability" to respond to rising demand. Meanwhile, official data from NHS England, which also covers last week but does not include how hospitals are performing against the four-hour target, revealed visits to AE were increasing. There were nearly 340,000 attendances last week, up from just under 328,000 the week before. But Dr Barbara Hakin, of NHS England, said despite the increasing pressures staff continued to "deliver a first-class service." "We are working hard to make sure all parts of the NHS are well prepared for the busy winter period," she added. Scotland is also providing weekly figures for its major AE departments.
