Saints - the last visiting team to win at Ibrox 13 months ago - took the lead early on when Blair Alston curled in a fantastic strike. Joe Garner headed Rangers level from a corner before the break. The visitors had several chances in the second half with Alston firing against the post while Garner had a header saved for the hosts. With Aberdeen defeated at Hamilton Academical on Tuesday and Hearts beaten at Kilmarnock, Saints could have gone second with victory but instead they go level on points with the second-placed Dons, albeit having played a game more. Rangers, having taken 16 points from a possible 30 since being promoted, stay fifth edging to within a point of Hearts. The Ibrox side have won only two of their home league games this season, having also dropped points to Hamilton and Ross County. Mark Warburton's side had improved defensively in recent weeks with clean sheets in league wins over Partick Thistle and Inverness. However, with Wes Foderingham resuming goalkeeping duties from Matt Gilks - Rangers' best player in the 1-0 Scottish League Cup semi-final defeat by Celtic - the Ibrox side found themselves a goal down early on to Saints as Alston picked his spot after robbing Lee Hodson for his first Saints goal. Tommy Wright engineered an away win over Rangers in last season's League Cup when the hosts - then in the Championship - bringing an end to a 11-game winning sequence. And the Northern Irishman's team had several opportunities to go back in front early in the second half with Brian Easton, Liam Craig, Danny Swanson and Chris Kane all going close before Alston fired against a post. Garner had netted just once since his summer move from Preston North End but the striker broke his Ibrox duck with a headed finish off Harry Forrester's corner, having gone close from a similar situation moments before. And Garner threatened to nod Rangers ahead on 74 minutes but could not beat Zander Clark, who made good first-half saves to deny Jason Holt and Josh Windass. Warburton sought fresh impetus in attack with the introduction of Martyn Waghorn, Kenny Miller and Barrie McKay off the bench but St Johnstone held firm with David Wotherspoon clearing a Miller effort off the line. Rangers' Mark Warburton: "It was a decent first half but we didn't continue that and we gave the ball away cheaply. "We weren't brave getting out, despite the possession stats we didn't play the way we wanted to. "It's a demanding crowd because they're used to success. The players have to recognise it's an expectant crowd - and quite rightly. We have to respect that and learn from that." St Johnstone's Tommy Wright: "It's never easy coming here. We're happy to take a point but we could have taken all three as we had a few good chances in the second half. "We knew we'd stay above Rangers with a positive result. We're content with the return but there are no prizes given out so we're not going to get carried away with it." Match ends, Rangers 1, St. Johnstone 1. Second Half ends, Rangers 1, St. Johnstone 1. I've thought this for a long time, and the recent surge in media awareness has brought this idea to the forefront of my mind. "Resisting arrest" is currently a felony offense in multiple states (USA..) but anecdotally the charge is used to basically trump up the 'offenses' committed by the perp. For those of you who are unaware, it is still a felonyagainst the law to resist an unlawful arrest - meaning that as a citizen obeying the law, in a circumstance which gives the police officer no legal grounds to arrest you...they can still arrest you, and you aren't even allowed to flinch. I think this practice is toxic to our society. Psychologically and physiologically our first reaction to aggressive actions is defense, so resisting arrest statutes are legally punishing citizens for their natural instincts. Now I'm not saying civilians should be allowed to resist with deadly force or even excessive force - but there needs to be some protection for civilians 'resisting in a reasonable fashion'. That may not be the perfect wording or solution, but its coming from a layman. Edit The reason resisting arrest is illegal is to protect the civilian being arrested. If a cop grabs my arm and I pull away he may think in about to get aggressive and he'll tase me or tackle me or accidentally choke me to death for fear of his own safety so the problem is deeper than policy, it's the psychology involved with the entire arrest procedure. My mind is still set that USA arrests and policing are ripe with abuse but the root is not these laws, its the people and traditions. I'd still like to see more protection for civilians but "allowing" resisting arrest probably isnt the right avenue, a new generation of judges may be more lenient towards it but thats a different story. I don't think that's something we want either, otherwise we've just given the same dangerous latitude to civilians that we currently give to the police when we allow them to exercise deadly force if they "feel threatened." Especially when you circled back to: "it's a problem with individual officers, not the system" while I agree that the officer is obviously the main factor I think there is a systemically induced fear on both sides which is not addressed (and maybe even escalated) by allowing civilians to resist.

There are always two lawyers in a courtroom: The prosecution is trying to find the defendant guilty. The defense is trying to find the defendant not guilty. The prosecution does all the legal hard work by presenting evidence to convince the judge andor jury that the defendant broke the law and deserves to be punished. The defense tries to show that either the defendant did not break the law or should not be punished. If the defendant is guilty (which the defendant may tell the defense attorney under secrecy) then the defense will still try to show that the prosecution cannot prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant was the one responsible, etc. In the process of doing that, the defense will also try to show that the defendant should not be punished. For example, if the defense can prove that the police broke protocol when collecting evidence, that evidence may be thrown out and the defendant may go free even if the judge andor jury think the defendant was guilty.', "Their job is to get their client the most favorable outcome possible. It is a little different if they know their client is guilty, but not much. Lawyers are typically not allowed to provide evidence for things they know are not true, so they could not accuse someone else of committing the crime instead of their client. Two things to bear in mind. First, we have an adversarial legal system. The prosecutor's duty is to try to find the person as guilty as possible, and the defense is to show they are as not guilty as possible. Hopefully the true is found in the middle. Second, even when someone has clearly done something, it is often not entirely clear what, if anything, they are guilty of. You might have shot your spouse, but was in first degree murder, second degree, manslaughter, self defense, or just an accident? You lawyer will try to minimize the charges against you.

Cellular communications are evolving to facilitate the current and expected increasing needs of Quality of Service (QoS), high data rates and diversity of offered services. Towards this direction, Radio Access Network (RAN) virtualization aims at providing solutions of mapping virtual network elements onto radio resources of the existing physical network. This paper proposes the Resources nEgotiation for NEtwork Virtualization (RENEV) algorithm, suitable for application in Heterogeneous Networks (HetNets) in Long Term Evolution-Advanced (LTE-A) environments, consisting of a macro evolved NodeB (eNB) overlaid with small cells. By exploiting Radio Resource Management (RRM) principles, RENEV achieves slicing and on demand delivery of resources. Leveraging the multi-tenancy approach, radio resources are transferred in terms of physical radio Resource Blocks (RBs) among multiple heterogeneous base stations, interconnected via the X 2 interface. The main target is to deal with traffic variations in geographical dimension. All signaling design considerations under the current Third Generation Partnership Project (3 GPP) LTE-A architecture are also investigated. Analytical studies and simulation experiments are conducted to evaluate RENEV in terms of network's throughput as well as its additional signaling overhead. Moreover we show that RENEV can be applied independently on top of already proposed schemes for RAN virtualization to improve their performance. The results indicate that significant merits are achieved both from network's and users' perspective as well as that it is a scalable solution for different number of small cells.

This paper presents a novel framework for traffic prediction of IoT devices activated by binary Markovian events. First, we consider a massive set of IoT devices whose activation events are modeled by an On-Off Markov process with known transition probabilities. Next, we exploit the temporal correlation of the traffic events and apply the forward algorithm in the context of hidden Markov models (HMM) in order to predict the activation likelihood of each IoT device. Finally, we apply the fast uplink grant scheme in order to allocate resources to the IoT devices that have the maximal likelihood for transmission. In order to evaluate the performance of the proposed scheme, we define the regret metric as the number of missed resource allocation opportunities. The proposed fast uplink scheme based on traffic prediction outperforms both conventional random access and time division duplex in terms of regret and efficiency of system usage, while it maintains its superiority over random access in terms of average age of information for massive deployments.

Because the spring equinox was tied to the date of Easter, the Roman Catholic Church considered the seasonal drift in the date of Easter undesirable. The Church of Alexandria celebrated Easter on the Sunday after the 14th day of the moon (computed using the Metonic cycle) that falls on or after the vernal equinox, which they placed on 21 March. However, the Church of Rome still regarded 25 March as the equinox (until 342) and used a different cycle to compute the day of the moon. In the Alexandrian system, since the 14th day of the Easter moon could fall at earliest on 21 March its first day could fall no earlier than 8 March and no later than 5 April. This meant that Easter varied between 22 March and 25 April. In Rome, Easter was not allowed to fall later than 21 April, that being the day of the Parilia or birthday of Rome and a pagan festival.The first day of the Easter moon could fall no earlier than 5 March and no later than 2 April.

While humans may not excel in short bursts of speed compared to certain animals, we have developed an alternative mode of transportation that proves to be more beneficial over extended distances. Our unique ability to sustain moderate speeds for prolonged periods makes us exceptional endurance runners relative to our body size. Ancient hunters utilized superior cognitive skills and effective communication to monitor prey during chases, causing the target to tire out gradually. In contrast, humans possess the capacity to maintain consistent paces for hours, a feat rarely matched by other species.

Consider this analogy: If you find yourself being pursued by a predator, initially, you might dash off at full speed seeking refuge. However, due to their persistent nature, the predator eventually catches up once again. At each reiteration, you attempt to flee further yet notice diminishing returns due to fatigue and obstacles like water sources blocked by other predators. Over several days, despite human resilience, this situation typically results in defeat. Nevertheless, our survival doesn't rely solely on speed; we have adept thermal regulation systems and proficient energy consumption capabilities, ensuring longeership.

Additionally, bipedalism sets us apart from many other mammals who walk on four limbs, allowing them greater force generation through increased leg count. Nonetheless, our true prowess lies within collaborative efforts and inventiveness, which has led to constructing homes, harnessing electrical resources, and communicating across vast distances globally.

Predatory creatures renowned for swift movements generally belong to categories where rapid escape isn't essential for survival – these include both prey species and lone, stealthy hunters. Conversely, human beings thrive as group-oriented, resourceful predators. Due to our intellectual capacities and tool usage, we require significantly less velocity than comparable predators such as wolves. When facing a wolf pack, a potential victim merely needs to avoid engagement until the threat subsides. On the contrary, encounters with humans demand a higher level of strategy and teamwork.

Huguenot numbers peaked near an estimated two million by 1562, concentrated mainly in the southern and central parts of France, about one-eighth the number of French Catholics. As Huguenots gained influence and more openly displayed their faith, Catholic hostility grew, in spite of political concessions and edicts of toleration from the French crown. A series of religious conflicts followed, known as the French Wars of Religion, fought intermittently from 1562 to 1598. The wars finally ended with the Edict of Nantes, which granted the Huguenots substantial religious, political, and military autonomy. Huguenot rebellions in the 1620s resulted in the abolition of their political and military privileges. They retained the religious provisions of the Edict of Nantes until the rule of Louis XIV, who gradually increased persecution of Protestantism until he issued the Edict of Fontainebleau. This ended legal recognition of Protestantism in France and the Huguenots were forced either to convert to Catholicism (possibly as Nicodemites) or flee as refugees; they were subject to violent persecution by the dragonnades. Louis XIV claimed that the French Huguenot population was reduced from about 800,000-900,000 adherents to just 1,000-1,500. He exaggerated the decline, but the dragonnades were devastating for the French Protestant community. The remaining Huguenots faced continued persecution under Louis XV. By the time of his death in 1774, Calvinism had been nearly eliminated from France. Persecution of Protestants officially ended with the Edict of Versailles, signed by Louis XVI in 1787. Two years later, with the Revolutionary Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen of 1789, Protestants gained equal rights as citizens. The bulk of Huguenot emigres relocated to Protestant states such as the Dutch Republic, the Kingdom of England and Wales, the Channel Islands, Scotland, Denmark, Sweden, Switzerland, the Electorate of Brandenburg and Electorate of the Palatinate in the Holy Roman Empire, the Duchy of Prussia, the German Palatinate, the American Colonies, and even as far as South Africa and the Dutch East Indies. The exodus of Huguenots from France created a brain drain, as many Huguenots had occupied important places in society. The kingdom did not fully recover for years. By the 1790s, most French Huguenots had been assimilated, sometimes forcibly, into French society. By the 18th century, most Huguenots had been assimilated, sometimes forcibly, into French society. Today, most French people have forgotten about the Huguenots. Protestantism in France remains, but is largely concentrated among the Alsatian and Cevenole populations. The Huguenot cross is the distinctive emblem of the Huguenots (croix huguenote). It is now an official symbol of the Eglise des Protestants Reformes (French Protestant Church). Huguenot descendants sometimes display this symbol as a sign of reconnaissance (recognition) between them.

The concept known as Proximity Pressure suggests that as your brain realizes you're nearing a restroom, it prompts your kidneys to increase urine production for faster elimination from your bladder. However, I find this rationale unconvincing. Is it plausible that the brain reduces antidiuretic hormone (ADH) secretion instantaneously upon subconsciously perceiving proximity to a restroom? Considering we typically generate around 30 mL of urine per hour, it seems unlikely that the sudden surge of urine resulting from these subtle cues would significantly affect bladder pressure. Furthermore, this theory does not adequately address the intensified need to defecate as one approaches a lavatory. My belief is that this phenomenon relates more closely to the involuntary regulation of both the bladder and rectal sphincters via the autonomic nervous system (ANS). These dual sets of muscles manage the openings of the urethra and anus, with one set primarily governed by the ANS and the other under conscious control. Unfortunately, we cannot voluntarily manipulate the ANS-controlled sphincters using sheer willpower or relaxation techniques. Consequently, individuals who struggle to pass urine post removal of a Foley catheter, even though they attempt forceful expulsion, experience difficulty because while one sphincter relaxes, the other remains constricted by an unknown mechanism. Hence, as someone draws nearer to a restroom, subliminal signals such as thoughts of relief or visualizing a lavatory might trigger the looseness of the autonomic sphincters. In turn, this places additional tension on the voluntarily controlled sphincters, creating a heightened sensation of urgency to eliminate waste. Your description lacks any intermediate stage; it's either completely problem-free before reaching the bathroom, or once inside its vicinity, you encounter an overwhelming compulsion to use it, reminiscent of the anxiety experienced at the mere thought of Lake Erie bursting forth."

The term middle east as a noun and adjective was common in the 19th century in nearly every context except diplomacy and archaeology. An uncountable number of places appear to have had their middle easts from gardens to regions, including the United States. The innovation of the term "Near East" to mean the holdings of the Ottoman Empire as early as the Crimean War had left a geographical gap. The East Indies, or "Far East," derived ultimately from Ptolemy's "India Beyond the Ganges." The Ottoman Empire ended at the eastern border of Iraq. "India This Side of the Ganges" and Iran had been omitted. The archaeologists counted Iran as "the Near East" because Old Persian cuneiform had been found there. This usage did not sit well with the diplomats; India was left in an equivocal state. They needed a regional term.

Plotting the relationship between level of income and inequality, Kuznets saw middle-income developing economies level of inequality bulging out to form what is now known as the Kuznets curve. Kuznets demonstrated this relationship using cross-sectional data. However, more recent testing of this theory with superior panel data has shown it to be very weak. Kuznets' curve predicts that income inequality will eventually decrease given time. As an example, income inequality did fall in the United States during its High school movement from 1910 to 1940 and thereafter.[citation needed] However, recent data shows that the level of income inequality began to rise after the 1970s. This does not necessarily disprove Kuznets' theory.[citation needed] It may be possible that another Kuznets' cycle is occurring, specifically the move from the manufacturing sector to the service sector.[citation needed] This implies that it may be possible for multiple Kuznets' cycles to be in effect at any given time.

Never, ever walk into a dealership "just to see what they've got." Salesmen see that aimless stare on your face and they're like starving cartoon wolves they don't even see you as human anymore. They have one mission: to get you into a car, whether it's the right car for you or not. If you don't know what kind of car you want, they'll quickly find you one that costs more than you ever wanted to spend. What's the point? The point is that if you're just going to go in and look around, it might be best if you didn't go in at all. You could just look online at all the latest models and find one that you like. Then you can email a dealer to get some pricing info and ask questions about it. 3. Don't Get Tricked Into Buying a Used Car If you're looking to buy an affordable used car, make sure you really do get an affordable used car. Salesmen will often try to trick customers into buying a new car when what they actually wanted was a used car. For example, you ask about how much a used Ford Focus would cost. They say it's about 13,000. But then they say, "You know, we've got this brand-new Ford Fiesta that's almost exactly the same. It's only 500 more. Plus, there's a rebate on it that brings the price down even lower." It sounds like a good deal, but you didn't come in asking about a new Ford Fiesta. You came in asking about a used Ford Focus. You're getting artfully manipulated into buying a car you didn't even want. 4. Don't Let Them Talk You Into Getting a Loan If you're going to finance a car, that's fine. But don't let them talk you into financing the car when you don't even want to. A lot of people are afraid of car dealerships. They think that if they walk in with cash, the salesman is going to take advantage of them. In fact, the opposite is true. Dealers make a lot of money off of interest on car loans. If you don't want a loan, they're going to try to convince you to get one anyway. 5. Don't Buy the First Car You See This is another rule that people are afraid to follow. They see a car they like on the lot and they immediately start thinking about it as their own. They worry that if they wait too long, someone else will buy it. We get it. That car is cute. But here's the thing: There are so many cars out there. Most of them are pretty nice. Most of them come with lots of features. Most of them won't break down within two months of you buying them. All of them have four wheels. And some of them even have cup holders. The point is, there are tons of cars to choose from. So take your time. Go home and do your research. Try to find the best car for your needs and budget. Then come back to the dealership when you're ready to buy. 6. Don't Buy the Car at the End of the Month If you're planning on trading in your old car, you might want to wait until after the end of the month. This is because dealerships usually have sales objectives that they need to meet by the end of every month, and they'll offer extra incentives to encourage people to trade in their cars that month. You might be able to get a higher trade-in value if you wait until after the end of the month. Just don't tell the dealer that you know about this. He'll probably deny it and try to tell you that he gave you a great deal. 7. Don't Sign Up for Extra Warranty Coverage When you buy a new car, the manufacturer's warranty should cover you for at least three years or 36,000 miles (whichever comes first). However, a lot of dealers will try to sell you on extended warranty coverage. Here's the thing: These warranties aren't always worth it. In fact, most of the time, they're not worth it at all. 8. It seemed impossible, entirely impossible. This was something that happened to other people, how could it be happening to him. Philip still felt convinced he would not die, despite the overwhelming amount of evidence surrounding him that this was not the case. The sheer volume of death he had seen did not seem to cause him to feel anymore likely to die than he had done before this apocalyptic series of events. The remains of the last few months surrounded him, he could literally smell the decay in the air. He could feel it, pulling him into an endless sleep. His eyelids heavy, his body almost limp. Still his mind told him he would live, this was but a fleeting moment of suffering, he would awaken after a sleep and scold himself for being so ridiculous as to think he could die. The figure of death approached him, "Philip, you are dying. Yet I shall provide you with some comfort. Since you are the last of this species, you are burdened with a choice. Do you accept death and join your fellows in endless slumber or do you continue, alone, for the next 300 years and seek to make the world better than it was when the human race thought it had control?" Philip was stunned, was this simply one last cruel taunt, something that this figure could just gain twisted pleasure from, or was this a genuine offer, could he live on and escape the clutches of death for 300 years? But, what was the point of living without another for comfort, and how could he alter the world and improve it, how could he change it with no one left to aid him? Philip considered the offer, "No it ends here" he finally stated with as much conviction as he could muster. The figure of death smiled wryly, "as you wish" and with that the figure placed his hand just above Philip's eyes and let the smoky whisper of his soul pass through them, death then watched as Philip's soul slowly dissipated into the air. They do say the eyes are the window to the soul after all.

Jeremy Kauffmann had, by and large, lived a good life. He had been a good father, or at least, he had stayed out of the way. He was always punctual, valuing others' time as much as his own, which is really a divine quality in a small businessman. He also made it to church most Sundays, certainly enough times to build up a nest egg in the collection bin that most folks wouldn't shake a stick at, assuming those folks were cautious with sticks. So, when he collapsed into his oatmeal one day, the veins bursting through his head, Jeremy Kauffmann figured he was a shoe-in for Heaven. When he arrived at the pearly gates, he was greeted by St. Peter, who seemed very busy scribbling notes but still took the time to offer a wink and a smile. "Ah, Jeremy Kauffman! We've been expecting you!" Jeremy smiled and gave a small wave, which made him feel humble, even though he was wholly unsurprised that St. Peter knew him by name. After all, Jeremy supervised several accountants at Kauffmann and Kauffman, LLP. "Good morning, St. Peter." "Oh good heavens, it's not morning here. Time works very oddly in Heaven, you see. Although rather unfortunately, your timing isn't really the best." "What do you mean?" Peter frantically rearranged some parchment. "Well, I'm afraid Heaven is at capacity." "Capacity?" Jeremy was confused, but he didn't want to offend Peter outright." "Well, you see, we only have so much space up here. It wouldn't be a paradise if you had to wait too long at the cafeteria, you know." Jeremy's eyes moved past Peter, and he squinted to see the glow between the big golden bars on the gates of heaven's beautiful wall. "Of course, it may look like there's room," Peter interjected, as though hearing Jeremy's thoughts. "But there isn't. You see, we have to hold spots for the people who are coming in soon." "Whose coming in?" Peter glanced down at the parchment and flicked the edge with his thumb. "Well, the Pope is certainly getting up there. Two Popes, actually, the one fellow isn't dead yet. So, we have to hold plenty of space for them. Denzel Washington, he'll die pretty soon, between you and me, he's a revolutionary performer, but he has a weakness for cheeseburgers. So, he needs lots of space, because the Father really wants to discuss'The Manchurian Candidate' with him." Jeremy was trying not to look bitter, but he felt "The Manchurian Candidate" was a mediocre film. Certainly no better than "The Taking of Pelham 123." "Then there's going to be a few more mass shootings, we have to send those folks in, just to make amends since most of shooters believe in, well, I don't think I have to tell you that part. It's a little silly, but of course, you know how politics work. And of course, Betty White, got to save a place for her. So, I'm afraid you'll have to go on the waiting list." "How long will I have to be on the list?" Peter smiled. "The current estimated wait is 372,151 years." "What!?" "I know, what a deal! What's 372,151 years compared to eternal paradise?" Jeremy sighed. "So is the waiting list my only option?" "Well, if you're really itching to start the afterlife, you can try Hell. It's just down the street, although by the time you get there and get your name on the list, you may wish you had just stayed on this one. Time works very oddly in Heaven." Jeremy Kauffmann knew he deserved to be in Heaven, but he also deserved to be valued. "If Heaven doesn't care about me more than Betty White, maybe Hell will!" he declared. "Oh, I'm sure they will! They usually give a damn." So Jeremy Kauffmann marched off to Hell, and was disappointed to find that he still needed to clear a waitlist (as Lucifer calmly explained, there were an awful lot of mass shootings coming up, and the shooters usually didn't survive those). However, since the waitlist was only 527 years, he decided to stick it out. As he sat in the waiting room, he couldn't help but feel like a lot of people were headed down the street into Heaven with beaming smiles. He wondered if the wait would have been worth it. Still, the 527 years in Hell's waiting room seemed to take forever, so he was happy to stick it out, even though he heard whispers from the other pending souls that the cafeteria was far too crowded, and that time in Heaven went oddly quick.

Uplinkdownlink (ULDL) decoupling promises more flexible cell association and higher throughput in heterogeneous networks (HetNets), however, it hampers the acquisition of DL channel state information (CSI) in time-division-duplex (TDD) systems due to different base stations (BSs) connected in ULDL. In this paper, we propose a novel data-aided (DA) channel estimation scheme to address this problem by utilizing decoded UL data to exploit CSI from received UL data signal in decoupled HetNets where a massive multiple-input multiple-output BS and dense small cell BSs are deployed. We analytically estimate BER performance of UL decoded data, which are used to derive an approximated normalized mean square error (NMSE) expression of the DA minimum mean square error (MMSE) estimator. Compared with the conventional least square (LS) and MMSE, it is shown that NMSE performances of all estimators are determined by their signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) -like terms and there is an increment consisting of UL data power, UL data length and BER values in the SNR-like term of DA method, which suggests DA method outperforms the conventional ones in any scenarios. Higher UL data power, longer UL data length and better BER performance lead to more accurate estimated channels with DA method. Numerical results verify that the analytical BER and NMSE results are close to the simulated ones and a remarkable gain in both NMSE and DL rate can be achieved by DA method in multiple scenarios with different modulations.

Emily didn't have enough time to eat breakfast. She went to school on an empty stomach. By third period, she was so hungry. She was sitting in a quiet class eating her lunch when two black boys came into the room with bowls of lunch and sandwiches. She tried not to look at them as they sat down with their lunches. They were all between six feet tall and taller than her. One had brown hair that fell out past his shoulders. He smiled and waved goodbye before going back to his seat across the hall from hers. The other boy's hair was shorter but was just long enough to be brushed against his chin by his teacher. Emily wore baggy jeans and a white tee-shirt that said "Free to Be Me" underneath it. Her dark skin shone in the sunlight like golden milk in a glass, and pale blue eyes looked right through her. She wanted to laugh, or cry, because these little guys kept staring at her. And listening to every word she spoke. Their mouths moved silently, as if they weren't even breathing. They seemed to be giving Emily a side eye. Just saying hi and starting conversation. But then she realized something else: Their eyes scared her. This wasn't normal for kids! It wasn't normal for someone who lived here to feel uncomfortable around strangers. Didn't they know how scary people could be? Did he think she would hurt him? She got up and walked over to where one of them stood with another friend. When she reached them, she hugged each of them tightly but couldn't stop feeling nervous. The boys laughed and asked what year she was in. Emily told them and pressed her hand onto their cheeks just to make sure they really liked her. Then she gave them both hugs again and held them tightly until the bell rang. When she saw that they hadn't left yet, she turned back toward the two older boys. One of them grinned while whispering something in the other boy's ear. Emily knew exactly which one it was. "Are you going to the prom?" CHAPTER FIVE Emily woke up from her nap feeling tired. As soon as she hit the ground, she felt dizzy. She jumped off of the bed and started looking about the house. There was no one there except for her dog, who was curled up behind her. She wandered into the kitchen and found a plate of oatmeal waiting for her. After taking a bite, she noticed a bowl of fruit lying next to it. She took a piece and ate it within seconds without thinking. It tasted sweet and tart and the watermelon made her mouth water. She walked back outside into the cool September air. A breeze blew through her hair, blowing away any stray curls that had escaped under her pillowcase. At first, she thought that she smelled good; after all, she must've eaten a lot today. But once again, nothing. After walking a few steps farther, she heard voices coming from upstairs. She turned down a spiral staircase and saw the three children standing in front of the window wearing tattered brown shirts and pants. All three of them stared back at her through their hooded glasses. Even though it was late in the afternoon, the light that filtered through the small south windows cast a warm glow over them. Somehow, they still looked so innocent. They probably wouldn't understand why she was afraid of them. So maybe they shouldn't expect anything from her either. Maybe they should be surprised too. But then, isn't that part of most bullies' plans? To pick on bullied kids since they don't know better? If this is the case, then maybe the only thing they can do now is ignore her altogether. People are already talking about this girl's possible future being ruined by bullying, but nobody has actually done anything about it yet. Maybe they're waiting to see whether Emily will stand up to them or keep her head low and let things go. Or maybe they'll realize that maybe she deserved it. Prof Colin Riordan, the chair of Universities Wales and vice-chancellor of Cardiff University, said the policy of paying the majority of Welsh students' tuition fees has to change. He wants it replaced with a means tested grant to help poorer students. The Welsh government said its tuition fee policy has been a "huge success." Prof Riordan told BBC Wales' The Wales Report TV programme: "If you took the same approach to the tuition fee grant, as you do with maintenance grants, you could free up considerable funding to allow Welsh universities to compete in the same way as other universities in the UK and that's really critical to the future of our country. "There is no limit to the number of students that can go to university which means there is no limit to the money that is needed to fund the tuition fee policy and that means there is not enough money to fund Welsh universities." Yesterday, First Minister Carwyn Jones defended the Welsh government's university tuition fees subsidy and rejected the idea that tuition fee support should be limited to Welsh students who study at universities in Wales rather than anywhere they study in the UK. He was responding to Plaid Cymru leader Leanne Wood who said the current policy meant too much Welsh public money ended up going to English universities. On Sunday, outgoing Education Minister Huw Lewis told BBC Wales tuition fee grants would remain in place after May's assembly election if Labour retained power. Universities in Wales get the majority of their funding through the tuition fees paid by students. They also get an amount from the Higher Education Funding Council for Wales (HEFCW), around PS90m a year, which has been cut this year by the Welsh government. Prof Riordan said it had seen a 40 cut to funding which would result in job losses and would affect students. "The critical part is that the government needs to make sure than enough money is still available to fund all the areas that the tuition fee grant can't fund and that means making sure that funding is available to ensure that Welsh universities can continue to be the great success they've been over recent years," he said. "The future prosperity of the people of Wales is in the knowledge economy and the universities are the building blocks of that economy." A Welsh government spokesperson said: "There is no doubt that we have had to make some tough decisions within this budget and we recognise that the cut to HEFCW will present challenges. "We stand by our tuition fee grant policy which has been a huge success, has supported our learners to study a course and at an institution that is right for them, and has meant that Welsh graduates have left university with debts that are on average PS22,000 lower than graduates from England." In the United States, Lindlof and Taylor write, "Cultural studies [were] grounded in a pragmatic, liberal-pluralist tradition." The American version of cultural studies initially concerned itself more with understanding the subjective and appropriative side of audience reactions to, and uses of, mass culture; for example, American cultural-studies advocates wrote about the liberatory aspects of fandom.[citation needed] The distinction between American and British strands, however, has faded.[citation needed] Some researchers, especially in early British cultural studies, apply a Marxist model to the field. This strain of thinking has some influence from the Frankfurt School, but especially from the structuralist Marxism of Louis Althusser and others. The main focus of an orthodox Marxist approach concentrates on the production of meaning. This model assumes a mass production of culture and identifies power as residing with those producing cultural artifacts. In a Marxist view, those who control the means of production (the economic base) essentially control a culture.[citation needed] Other approaches to cultural studies, such as feminist cultural studies and later American developments of the field, distance themselves from this view. They criticize the Marxist assumption of a single, dominant meaning, shared by all, for any cultural product. The non-Marxist approaches suggest that different ways of consuming cultural artifacts affect the meaning of the product. This view comes through in the book Doing Cultural Studies: The Story of the Sony Walkman (by Paul du Gay et al.), which seeks to challenge the notion that those who produce commodities control the meanings that people attribute to them. Feminist cultural analyst, theorist and art historian Griselda Pollock contributed to cultural studies from viewpoints of art history and psychoanalysis. The writer Julia Kristeva is among influential voices at the turn of the century, contributing to cultural studies from the field of art and psychoanalytical French feminism.[citation needed]

Lately, intermediate attributes have demonstrated significant potential in the realm of image analysis. Attributes derived through the integration of category-specific knowledge can be more distinctive compared to conventional primitive elements. This study introduces a proficient approach for deriving these intermediate characteristics using Kinect skeletal data for recognizing three-dimensional human movements. Initially, we calculate the angles formed between pairs of skeletal joints and represent each angle with one of 27 possible states that depict their relative positions. Subsequently, these joints are grouped into sections and transformed into corresponding section states based on their individual states. We then utilize the technique of regular pattern extraction to identify the most common and pertinent states within consecutive sequences of images. Termed Frequent Local Patterns or FLPs, these components facilitate the construction of a robust 'bag-of-FLP'-inspired action model. Utilizing this innovative framework achieves unparalleled outcomes on both the MSR DailyActivity3D and MSER ActionPairs3D datasets.

In our study, we analyze a system where information and power are simultaneously transferred wirelessly from one point to another across a block fading channel. This process includes two main stages within each transmission block: a training stage followed by a data transmission stage. During the initial stage, pilot symbols are sent out which aid in estimating the channel conditions at the receiving end. The concept of Simultaneous Wireless Information and Power Transfer (SWIPT) is implemented through a power-splitting technique at the receiver's side. Here, part of the incoming signal is dedicated to determining the channel characteristics or decoding the message, while the rest is allocated for collecting energy. We have formulated an optimized strategy for dividing this power between the training and data transmission stages, ensuring superior overall capacity performance without compromising on the necessary energy collection rates. Our findings demonstrate the effectiveness of using a power-splitting approach in maximizing the benefits derived from both the pilot and data signals for achperformance in SWIPT systems.

One check on a magistrate's power was his collegiality. Each magisterial office would be held concurrently by at least two people. Another such check was provocatio. Provocatio was a primordial form of due process. It was a precursor to habeas corpus. If any magistrate tried to use the powers of the state against a citizen, that citizen could appeal the decision of the magistrate to a tribune. In addition, once a magistrate's one-year term of office expired, he would have to wait ten years before serving in that office again. This created problems for some consuls and praetors, and these magistrates would occasionally have their imperium extended. In effect, they would retain the powers of the office (as a promagistrate), without officially holding that office.

Some of the earliest recorded observations ever made through a telescope, Galileo's drawings on 28 December 1612 and 27 January 1613, contain plotted points that match up with what is now known to be the position of Neptune. On both occasions, Galileo seems to have mistaken Neptune for a fixed star when it appeared close - in conjunction - to Jupiter in the night sky; hence, he is not credited with Neptune's discovery. At his first observation in December 1612, Neptune was almost stationary in the sky because it had just turned retrograde that day. This apparent backward motion is created when Earth's orbit takes it past an outer planet. Because Neptune was only beginning its yearly retrograde cycle, the motion of the planet was far too slight to be detected with Galileo's small telescope. In July 2009, University of Melbourne physicist David Jamieson announced new evidence suggesting that Galileo was at least aware that the 'star' he had observed had moved relative to the fixed stars.

The duration required for a random walk on a (undirected) graph to reach equilibrium, known as the mixing time, plays a crucial role in assessing the network's connectivity and expansion attributes. Additionally, it acts as a vital element in crafting effective algorithms. In our study, we propose a novel concept termed "local mixing," pertaining to a specific node within a graph. Essentially, the local mixing refers to the mixing process of a random walk probability distribution limited to a substantial subset of nodes surrounding a designated node, denoted as 's.' Consequently, the period needed for the random walk originating from node 's' to achieve uniformity across this subset represents the local mixing time relative to 's.' This metric effectively gauges the immediate neighborhood's connectivity and expansion characteristics concerning node 's,' thereby influencing the performance of various algorithms involving information dissemination or gossip protocols.

Our primary advancement entails providing a formal definition of local mixing time for undirected graphs. Furthermore, we develop a highly efficient decentralized algorithm capable of calculating an approximate value for the local mixing time with respect to node 's' in just O(s) rounds, assuming an n-node regular graph. This result holds true particularly when the local mixing time is considerably lower than the overall mixing time related to node 's.' Moreover, we offer another decentralized algorithm that accurptaely computes the precise local mixing time in O(sD) rounds, where D denotes either the minimum between the local mixing time and the graph's diameter, or simply the graph's diameter itself; this outcome applies universally regardless of certain conditions. Both algorithms are designed to function optimally under the constraints of the CONGEST model employed in distributed computing environments. It should be noted that the local mixing time may occasionally exhibit values significantly below those observed for global mixing times.

Bayesian optimization (BO) is a powerful approach for seeking the global optimum of expensive black-box functions and has proven successful for fine tuning hyper-parameters of machine learning models. The Bayesian optimization routine involves learning a response surface and maximizing a score to select the most valuable inputs to be queried at the next iteration. These key steps are subject to the curse of dimensionality so that Bayesian optimization does not scale beyond 10-20 parameters. In this work, we address this issue and propose a high-dimensional BO method that learns a nonlinear low-dimensional manifold of the input space. We achieve this with a multi-layer neural network embedded in the covariance function of a Gaussian process. This approach applies unsupervised dimensionality reduction as a byproduct of a supervised regression solution. This also allows exploiting data efficiency of Gaussian process models in a Bayesian framework. We also introduce a nonlinear mapping from the manifold to the high-dimensional space based on multi-output Gaussian processes and jointly train it end-to-end via marginal likelihood maximization. We show this intrinsically low-dimensional optimization outperforms recent baselines in high-dimensional BO literature on a set of benchmark functions in 60 dimensions.

In most jurisdictions (such as the United States), pharmacists are regulated separately from physicians. These jurisdictions also usually specify that only pharmacists may supply scheduled pharmaceuticals to the public, and they may also limit pharmacy technicians' ability to function. History Since the mid-20th century, governments have implemented laws and regulations that restrict direct-to-consumer advertising of prescription drugs. These laws typically attempt to prevent drug companies from deceptively promoting drugs, and to ensure that consumers have the information necessary to make informed choices about their own healthcare. FDA regulations In the United States, the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FDC Act) regulates the advertising of prescription drugs. The United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) requires that all drug advertisements contain information required by the FDA. United States Supreme Court rulings In the 1976 case of Schaumberg v. Citrus Memorial Hospital, the Supreme Court held that the FDC Act prohibited prescription drug advertising directed to the general public. In 1997, the Supreme Court overturned this decision in United States v. Drug Emporium, Inc. and ruled that prescription drug advertising could be directed at the general public, provided that the advertisement included the complete prescribing information. In the 2001 case of Thompson v. Western States Medical Center, the Supreme Court held that the FDC Act prohibits prescription drug advertisements from including unapproved uses for a drug. Drug-specific regulations In the United States, drug-specific regulations dictate that a drug may only be advertised for its FDA-approved indications. In the United Kingdom, a drug must be registered with the Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) before it can be advertised. In the United States, a drug must be registered with the FDA before it can be advertised. Other regulations Other jurisdictions (such as the United States, the United Kingdom, the European Union, and Canada) also have regulations that restrict prescription drug advertising. In the United States, these regulations are primarily enforced by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), while in Canada they are enforced by Health Canada. Other jurisdictions There are other restrictions on the advertising of drugs. In many jurisdictions, prescription drugs must not be advertised directly to the general public. In some jurisdictions, they are allowed only in publications such as medical journals. See also Direct-to-consumer advertising

"This new funding represents an important investment in America's transportation infrastructure," said Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg. "These grants help ensure that motorists have access to affordable, reliable, clean charging options." Buttigieg also announced 1-billion federal investments this month aimed at supporting EV production across 11 states, with targeted incentives for manufacturers who commit to building zero emissions vehicles (ZEVs). While those funds are earmarked specifically for ZEV development, they could indirectly support EV sales as well: The White House estimates that each dollar invested in EV manufacturing generates up to 7 in economic activity elsewhere, such as parts purchases or expanded workforce training programmes.

The identification of a particle resembling the Higgs boson by CERN is considered a significant achievement in science from the 21st century. Our research examines how information dissemination occurred on Twitter prior to, during, and subsequent to the revelation of this new particle's existence, which mirrored the characteristics of the Higgs boson, on July 4th, 2012. We have discovered intricate spatial and temporal patterns in user engagement, including posting, sharing, and responding to tweets. Additionally, we offer an interpretation of the fluctuating activity levels among users throughout this event. By constructing a network based on those who shared a tweet regarding the Higgs boson finding, we modeled the propagation of information. Lastly, our results demonstrate an impressive approximation of the collective behavior of around half a million participants.

Caleb let his body go limp, and heard the sound of wings. It was feather-soft, near inaudible, the barest brush of air against his ear drums, along his jaw, across his face. There was someone giggling in the corner, a whole bunch of someones, and Caleb could open his mouth and feel the giggles drifting across his tongue, his lips, and wondered if maybe that meant it was him doing it. His jaw hung open, drifting, tenuously attached to the rest of his body. "I love you," he said, and looked to the air, and there were the wings batting at each other dizzyingly, building into a squall, his heart revving up feather-fast like a hummingbird, and then there were strong fingers pressing into his jaw and his head being tilted up and Brad's eyes looking into his. "Focus on my voice," Brad said, speaking at a distance, and the wings were flying away and the feathers unclouding the sky and there were the five points of contact anchoring his jaw and Caleb was slowly coming back. "Look at me. Focus on my voice. Look at me." "Yuh-yes," Caleb got out, his body slowly pulsing back into existence around him. Blood flowing. Muscles straining. He hurt. His wrists were hanging limply in the cuffs. The lines across his back burned, marking out the anchor points where wings would have connected. He wondered where the wings were now, if they were flying free without him. "You were floating," Brad said with a grin. His hand moved up the side of Caleb's face and tenderly closed on his hair. Caleb tilted his head skyward, listening like a prophet. "Flying," he corrected automatically, and then remembered himself and blushed. Brad squatted down in front of him, leather squeaking. "I - I heard the angels," he confessed. "Angels?" Brad said, and quirked an eyebrow. "That's a first for me. Don't worry," he said quickly, noticing Caleb's attempts to stay in position. "We're taking a break. How's the pain? You hungry? Thirsty? What about those angels, then?" Caleb let himself slump, the burning working its way across his back until the entire thing was a glowing mass of lines. "It's good," he said. "Good, good, good." He was warm. He was alive. "I was very religious growing up," he said. "Still am, really." "A fine tradition for that," Brad said, amused. There was the rich dark undercurrent in his voice, and Caleb licked his lips. "Jesus on the cross. Bet that got to you, huh?" The tip of the crop tapped a nerve in his thigh and Caleb flinched. "Naughty boy." "God became man," Caleb said. "Flesh and blood. All animating spirit." He touched his head to Brad's boot and his hair hung down wet around his face, brushing against the leather. "I'd pray for the Holy Spirit to come down into me." He lightly kissed the boot and tasted salt. "Angels. Cupids. Christ on the cross. All these - it wasn't sound theology. Just, when I'm thinking back on it now. That's what I prayed for. Some spirit to guide me, save me, make me fall in love, swoop down like fire and carry me away." With an effort he pulled himself back up, leaned backward, exposing his chest and throat. Caleb's eyes rolled up into his head. "I had to believe," he said, dreamily, "that God wanted me to be happy." Brad was grounded, feet tapping against the ground, quick violent strides. Swift and wingless. The crop tapped at Caleb's shoulders, temple, throat, guiding him back into position. "You believe that God wanted this for you?" Brad said, and there was the sneer, the distinct twist of cruelty in it. "Yes?" Caleb said, and giggled. "Or no." He set his shoulders, forced his spine into a straight line. "My guardian angel's got to hate you." "He ought to," Brad said softly, and then his hand was on Caleb's face, fingers digging into his jaw. "Jesus came down from Heaven to see what he was missing. No goddamn angel could give us that." He pressed his lips, his teeth, against Caleb's scalp, brushing up against the skull. "You're so fucking beautiful. All flesh and blood. The most beautiful goddamn thing in the world." And Caleb felt the feather touch dragging feverishly across his skin, all slick and weighted down with blood and spit and sweat, clinging to him as if they could no longer imagine flight, and in all the corners of the room, yes, yes, there was definitely someone laughing.

We do both. But "we" isn't just one person. Hardware engineers are constantly trying to improve computer systems. And software engineers are constantly trying to improve software. The thing is, with hardware, we can see how to make it better, it's just that the technology doesn't always exist to mass-produce that better hardware. Whereas with software, people have been studying the most effective ways of doing things for decades, and there's really very little extra that can be done with the current hardware. But every now and then, when there's a big improvement in hardware, there's might be a new generation of software that takes advantage of this hardware.... and then it might take a few years for software engineers to learn the best way to optimise this new generation of software.','We do both, but if you can expend the same amount of effort to double the power of a system as you would use to increase efficiency by 10 it makes more sense to expend that effort increasing your systems power. Yo can only make something SO efficient, but there is theoretically no limit in sight on how powerful we can make something.', "As others have mentioned, is that both are done. However, there is such a thing as'efficient enough'. There is a reason why we use software on computers as much as we do. We have a need for many millions of different kinds of machine to assist with many millions of different kinds of task but it would be impossible to make a'one-off' machine for all of these tasks. Instead, we make a'general' machine that we can manufacture easily and cheaply, and then the expensive customisation to make it do some specific thing can be programmed into it using software. Hence - the programmable computer is really a device which we can'instruct' it in such a way as to make it act as if it were one of these other single-task machines. There's not really any tool you can touch which is remotely similar. It's as if I could give you a toolbox that had just a single tool in it, but each time you reached into the toolbox, it could change from being a hammer, to a screwdriver, to a drill, to a spoon, to a crane. This.... is.... incredible. A lot of software is customisation to make a computer into a tool for some very specific task. It may be a task that only has to be done once, ever. It might be a task that is only of interest to one person, at one point of time, or one group of people in an office, or one department of one company. This is the bulk of all software. Instead of spending time making that kind of software efficient, it's almost universally better to just make it work, make it usable, and just run it on a more powerful computer. At the other end of the scale, there are software tools that are used by almost everyone (operating systems, compilers and other fundamental system software), and a lot of time is spent making these efficient.... but these tools only make up a tiny proportion of the software we actually use to make custom'tools' to help us. This is why we spend so much more effort - in general - making faster computers and not more efficient software. Faster computers runs all software faster. More efficient software - for almost all software - would barely be noticed.

The incredibly realistic effects you see in a movie are created over a period of many months, working to create something that will work particularly beautifully for one specific camera angle and one specific moment in a film. Once they've made the effect, they can still take hours to render a single frame of it - even using incredibly expensive, high-end computers. In a video game, that same effect has to run from every possible camera angle, with every possible combination of other things going on at the same time. And the game has to render 24 frames of that action every single second - using only the processing power of your 800 home PC.,A shortage of processing power is the problem.', "We're a long ways off from having the computing power in a consumer-level machine to do photo-realistic graphics. This has to do with the math used and the tradeoff between looking good enough and accuracy. The more accurate you get, the more math it takes (thus more computing power required). The jump in terms of computing power between good enough and accurate is huge. I'm going to get a bit technical here. Phong shading is the technique we use in games. It is essentially a collection of very simple mathematical formulas that give a very rough estimate of the color of something on your screen. In most cases it looks good enough, but the model goes a bit nuts when you go to extremes. For example reflections tend to be far too bright. The flaws get corrected with other mechanisms like shaders and so on. But again these are only approximations on the behavior of light. Over the years we've built better approximations and the expansion of computing power has allowed us to put a lot more stuff in there to make it look really good. We've gotten damn good at faking it, but at the end of the day all of this is built on an approximation of reality. Light isn't actually being simulated using this technique, therefore there will always be something that doesn't look quite right. It takes human intervention and an artist's touch to make it look better. But you don't have an artist sitting over your shoulder making adjustments to every frame in your game. So why are CG effects in movies so damn photo-realistic? Well that's because they actually do simulate light. They don't use the same technique and mathematical models that are used in computer games. They use a technique called ray tracing which is a physics simulation of the interaction of light and the environment. This technique is computationally expensive because it actually simulates light as it bounces off objects and how it interacts. This is so computationally expensive that they use server farms to render individual frames of a scene in a movie. Games run at 20-60 fps on your home pc. Ray tracing graphics a few years ago ran at days-per-frame (more like hoursminutes now) on server farms. There's one thing that is extremely hard to do well in normal game graphics but is fairly accurate using ray tracing. Human skin. Games have gotten really good at approximating the effect, but they're not perfect and there are small flaws that people will pick up on. It turns out that human skin is a bit translucent. Some light gets reflected at the surface, but some light will penetrate into your skin, bounce around, and re-emerge somewhere else. This effect is called sub-surface scattering. Game graphics using the current model will likely never get this completely right. Artists will get it pretty damn close or cover it up (Bloom oblivion for example), but it will always look a bit wrong. This leads to the uncanny valley a lot of people mention.

Quantization is essential to simplify DNN inference in edge applications. Existing uniform and non-uniform quantization methods, however, exhibit an inherent conflict between the representing range and representing resolution , and thereby result in either underutilized bit-width or significant accuracy drop. Moreover, these methods encounter three drawbacks: i) the absence of a quantitative metric for in-depth analysis of the source of the quantization errors; ii) the limited focus on the image classification tasks based on CNNs; iii) the unawareness of the real hardware and energy consumption reduced by lowering the bit-width. In this paper, we first define two quantitative metrics, i.e., the Clipping Error and rounding error , to analyze the quantization error distribution. We observe that the boundary- and rounding- errors vary significantly across layers, models and tasks. Consequently, we propose a novel quantization method to quantize the weight and activation. The key idea is to Approximate the Uniform quantization by Adaptively Superposing multiple Non-uniform quantized values, namely AUSN. AUSN is consist of a decoder-free coding scheme that efficiently exploits the bit-width to its extreme, a superposition quantization algorithm that can adapt the coding scheme to different DNN layers, models and tasks without extra hardware design effort, and a rounding scheme that can eliminate the well-known bit-width overflow and re-quantization issues. Theoretical analysis (see Appendix A) and accuracy evaluation on various DNN models of different tasks show the effectiveness and generalization of AUSN. The synthesis (see Appendix B) results on FPGA show 2 reduction of the energy consumption, and 2 to 4 reduction of the hardware resource.

Assessing conjunctive queries and addressing constraint satisfaction issues are essential challenges within database theory and artificial intelligence. Due to their NP-hard nature, numerous studies have aimed to identify manageable subsets or "islands of tractability" alongside developing smart strategies to tackle practical examples effectively. A common strategy involves imposing a characteristic referred to as local consistency, ensuring that in database terminology, each tuple corresponds to at least one tuple across all query atoms. Surprisingly, achieving local consistency alone often suffices for accurately resolving these types of queries, particularly those without cycles. Nonetheless, the exact capabilities of this technique remained uncertain until now, albeit for limited scenarios. This study presents definitive solutions to the enduring uncertaintres regarding the effectiveness of algorithms relying on local consistency adherence. It encompasses both the comprehensive model of tree projections – which demands local consistency maintenance among arbitrary views derived from the initial data set – and specialized situations involving structural decomposition techniques like extended hypertree width and component hypertree decompositions. While enforcing local consistency may yield accurate results for certain data sets, determining whether they belong to said category isn't feasible in an efficient manner. Consequently, the research concentrates on distinct categories characterized by the innovative concept of greedy tree projections. Demonstrated to be recognizable promptly and surpassing existing tractable regions significantly, these groups prove superior in both generic tree projection circumstances and when using various structural decomposition methodologies.

A database built with one DBMS is not portable to another DBMS (i.e., the other DBMS cannot run it). However, in some situations it is desirable to move, migrate a database from one DBMS to another. The reasons are primarily economical (different DBMSs may have different total costs of ownership or TCOs), functional, and operational (different DBMSs may have different capabilities). The migration involves the database's transformation from one DBMS type to another. The transformation should maintain (if possible) the database related application (i.e., all related application programs) intact. Thus, the database's conceptual and external architectural levels should be maintained in the transformation. It may be desired that also some aspects of the architecture internal level are maintained. A complex or large database migration may be a complicated and costly (one-time) project by itself, which should be factored into the decision to migrate. This in spite of the fact that tools may exist to help migration between specific DBMSs. Typically a DBMS vendor provides tools to help importing databases from other popular DBMSs.

Such attitudes could be seen as racially biased since judgments are made based solely on someone’s race or ethnicity rather than taking into account nonverbal cues such as body language and vocal inflection. In conclusion, would it not serve everyone better if we simply eradicated the word by ceasing to use it?

Once upon a time, there was a boy named Billy who loved spending time in the kitchen. He always admired his mother's cooking skills and wanted to be just like her. One day, his mother had to leave for an emergency meeting, leaving Billy in charge of preparing dinner for his family. Billy was excited about the responsibility, and he immediately got to work. He started chopping vegetables, seasoning meat, and boiling rice. The aroma of the food cooking filled the house, making his mouth water. As he was carrying a hot pot of soup to the dining table, he lost his balance, and the soup spilled all over the floor, making a mess. He felt embarrassed and frustrated, and he didn't know what to do. But then he remembered his mother's advice, "Mistakes happen, but it's how you handle them that counts." So, Billy took a deep breath and focused on cleaning up the mess. He wiped the floor with a cloth, picked up the broken pieces of the pot, and deftly cleaned the spilled soup off the table. Despite the accident, Billy didn't lose his motivation. He quickly got back up and started preparing the food from scratch. He dedicated all his attention to each step, and the whole process went smoothly. Finally, dinner was ready. His family was surprised by the delicious meal and appreciated Billy's effort. They enjoyed the food with a smile on their faces, proud of their little chef. After dinner, Billy's mother returned home and saw the clean kitchen, the happy faces, and the satisfied bellies. She was impressed by her son's progress and commended him for his effort. From that day on, Billy's passion for cooking grew even stronger, and he made sure to be more careful while handling hot pots. But most importantly, he learned that making mistakes was okay as long as you were willing to learn from them and take responsibility for your actions.

Desmond Ricks' lawyers say homicide detectives switched bullets in his mother's gun to pin a shooting on him. He was convicted of gunning down a friend outside a restaurant in Detroit, Michigan, in March 1992, and sentenced to at least 32 years in prison. Mr Ricks, 51, was released from prison last Friday. On Thursday, Wayne County prosecutor's office said Mr Ricks would not face a second trial. "I hope you enjoy your newfound freedom," Judge Richard Skutt told the exonerated man, who heaved a sigh of relief. Mr Ricks' case was championed by lawyers and students from the Innocence Clinic at the University of Michigan's law school. They managed to get the investigation reopened in 2016 after pointing out that two bullets taken from the victim, Gerry Bennett, looked different from the rounds presented at trial. Police investigators had maintained the bullets held up as key evidence were fired from Mr Ricks' mother's pistol. 'How I survived 22 years on death row' US man freed after 28 years in prison But a state police report last month established the bullets from the victim did not match the 38-calibre gun that belonged to Mr Ricks' mother. "I've got no time to be bitter at anybody," Mr Ricks said outside Wayne Circuit Court after Thursday's hearing, reports the Detroit News. "There's no excuse for what they did, but I have to move on. I just didn't want to die in prison. "Now, I'm just trying to get some semblance of my life back. I just want to pay my taxes and be a good citizen." David Moran, director of the Innocence Clinic, said the police conduct was criminal, but no retired officers can be brought to justice because too much time has passed. As Mr. Xi embarks on his first visit since assuming leadership in 2012, the occasion is imbued with significant symbolism, occurring against a backdrop of escalating political tensions. Plans include both official commemorative events and extensive demonstrations led by supporters of democracy and those aligned with Beijing. Prior to Mr. Xi's arrival, numerous prominent activists were detained, including student leader Joshua Wong, who had previously organized a protest centered around an iconic sculpture representing the transfer of power. This golden depiction of a bauhinia flower – the emblematic symbol of Hong Kong located near the harbor – was a present from China. Accompanied by his spouse Peng Liyuan, Mr. Xi landed at the primary airport in the city and received a warm reception from a brass ensemble and youngsters brandishing national flags. Delivering a concise address upon disembarkation, Mr. Xi expressed his enduring affection for Hong Kong and reiterated Beijing's unwavering commitment to supporting the region'sintegral aspects such as economic growth and improved quality of life. Furthermore, he voiced readiness to collaborate across various societal factions within Hong Kong to preserve the successful trajectory experienced over the previous two decades, ensuring the continued implementation of the 'one country, two systems' principle with sustained stability. Since being returned to Chinese sovereignty from British administration in 1997, Hong Kong has operated under this framework, providing unique liberties such as an autonomous judicial structure, partial democratic representation, and protected civil freedoms like peaceful gatherings and expression. Nevertheless, apprehension persists regarding potential encroachments by mainland forces upon the region's traditionally more progressive values. For years, advocates have called for increased self-governance in Hong Kong, leading up to forthcoming ceremonial festivities, including the swearing-in ceremony of the new chief executive Carrie Lam. Concurrently, heightened precautionary measures involving road closures and restricted access to certain areas of the urban center have been implemented due to anticipated dissent.

In conventional natural language understanding (NLU), slot filling employes a one-hot vector prediction per word. However, this approach does not account for semantic correlations, resulting in substantial issues related to data scarcity, particularly when transitioning an NLU system into a fresh domain. Our research introduces a groundbreaking slot filling technique rooted in label embeddings to remedy this shortcoming. We devise these embeddings by leveraging preexisting knowledge associated with every slot. By examining various encoding strategies such as atomical concepts, detailed slot definitions, and examples of slot usage, we aim to encapsulate diverse forms of antecedent information regarding slots. These embeddings facilitate pattern recognition across texts and enable efficient use of varying slot tags, thus enhancing the flexibility of adaptive NLU systems even with constrained datasets. Moreover, because our method operates independently from the underlying NLU architecture, it can be seamlessly integrated with most contemporary deep learning-based slot filling frameworks. Evaluation conducted on multiple datasets demonstrates that our label embedding strategy significantly outperforms both the classic one-hot label format and cutting-edge zero-shot techniques in terms of efficacy during standard domain applications and cross-domain transferability tasks.

According to Greek law, every Sunday of the year is a public holiday. In addition, there are four mandatory official public holidays: 25 March (Greek Independence Day), Easter Monday, 15 August (Assumption or Dormition of the Holy Virgin), and 25 December (Christmas). 1 May (Labour Day) and 28 October (Ohi Day) are regulated by law as being optional but it is customary for employees to be given the day off. There are, however, more public holidays celebrated in Greece than are announced by the Ministry of Labour each year as either obligatory or optional. The list of these non-fixed national holidays rarely changes and has not changed in recent decades, giving a total of eleven national holidays each year.

We introduce a novel class of adjustment rules for a collection of beliefs. This is an extension of Lewis' imaging to absorb probabilistic evidence in generalized settings. Unlike standard tools such as image recognition and machine learning, this approach is more scalable than other imaging methods. In contrast to many prior art approaches, we show that the effect of loss-of-awareness (LOD) is due not only to a general transform problem but also to the change approach of error correction using specialised processing techniques. The robustness of our new model offers important advantages over conventional LOD techniques because it allows us to handle a variety of proposed behavior choices in real time without adjusting to individual personalities. The aim of this study was to provide realistic estimates for the programmatic effects of loss-of-consciousness on the sensitivity of selected models. Results showed that the threshold value for the reversion coefficients Z and V were significantly higher when using an adaptive approximation with selected variables than when applying a traditional notion of loss of consciousness for different datasets (i.e., across all datasets). A similar result could be obtained by modeling how individuals respond to loss-of-consciousness.

Instant messaging is one of the major channels of computer mediated communication. However, humans are known to be very limited in understanding others' emotions via text-based communication. Aiming on introducing emotional content into chatbot dialogue, we study the utility of affective concepts in dialogue modeling. We evaluate a series of affective models with varying features, including latent variables of emotions, global affective states, and a new approach of exploiting sentimental lexicons. Our experiments show that the use of sentimental lexicons can significantly improve the performance of chatbots. To our knowledge, this is the first attempt to study sentimental lexicons in dialogue systems.

Until automation takes over these menial, low-paying jobs entirely, we will be dependent on these people to keep the streets clear.
