Come to the UK and try to find a bus driver, toilet cleaner, or postman that isn't Polish or Romanian or from some low income country like Bangladesh. You'll have a tough time finding a Briton in those jobs. Also, if college students are allowed to choose their degree, what would happen when there are too many students getting degrees in fields where there aren't enough jobs? That's been an issue for decades. We've always had more medical graduates than doctors, more law graduates than lawyers, and more science graduates than scientists. These people start careers in different fields; my uni lecturer is a qualified biology teacher, but he teaches computer security. How would it affect private universities? They'd have to offer a better standard. In the UK, public (private) schools offer education that goes above and beyond what the national curriculum demands. Latin, ancient history, modern foreign languages, calculus, and philosophy are common additions to the curriculum, and public school pupils tend to have a lot more experiences. My state school cricket trip was to Lords; the public school my friend went to took him to Barbados. We went to a dry ski slope, he went to Val-D'isere in the French Alps. Would the quality of education decrease? No. The universitycollege (whatever you want to call it) will still be receiving the same amount of money (at least it should be. If it isn't then the legislation was a scam), only this money is coming from the government instead of consumers. In the UK we use the term "statutory." Anything that is statutory is a service that is free at the point of delivery. If you break a leg, you don't get a bill, it's paid for through your National Insurance tax. When you go to a state school, you don't pay term fees, because it comes out of the tax you pay. We actually pay a very similar amount of tax to Americans (less actually, because overall we don't earn as much for doing the same jobs). The chief difference is that our tax money is spent on different things. If college education in the US becomes statutory, then you would see a lot more people going to college, and a lot more people getting degrees, but that would happen faster than the fields intended for those degrees could grow. But most people don't end up with the career they thought they wanted when they started university anyway, so it's a moot point.

The basic principle of arithmetic remains valid within unique factorization domains. One instance of this type of domain is represented by the Gaussian integers, denoted as Z[i]. These include all complex numbers expressed in the form of a bi, with 'a' and 'b' being any integer values, while 'i' represents the square root of -1. Within this system, prime elements are referred to as Gaussian primes. However, it's important to note that not all primes from the set of integers (Z) qualify as Gaussian primes when considered in the larger realm of Z[i]. For example, the number 2 can be broken down into the multiplication of two Gaussian primes: (1 + i) and (1 - i). Additionally, rational primes which take on the format of 4k + 3 remain Gaussian primes, but those conforming to the structure of 4k + 1 do not retain their primality status.

How far and how fast does information spread in social media? Researchers have recently examined a number of factors that affect information diffusion in online social networks, including: the novelty of content newness bias, its reputation, the degree to which it is shared by friends or unliked by enemies, and (in a recent paper) differences between non-technical and technical users. The authors found that different audience groups responded differently to each factor; this suggests that 'niche' communities of interest may be more vulnerable to rapidly spreading misinformation than broader audiences. In another paper, researchers looked at what type of message was most effective for countering misinformation about vaccination, and they analysed 1 million Facebook posts from parents in four countries who were concerned about children contracting measles after getting vaccinated with MMR. Their findings indicate that messages appealing to fear were less likely to persuade people to vaccinate their own kids, but among those who did so, pro-vaccine messages tended to perform better than anti-vaxxer ones, suggesting the existence of "pro-science" echo chambers on Facebook where only negative stories are propagated.

Software requirement analysis can certainly benefit from prevention and early detection of failures, in particular by some kind of automatic analysis. Formal methods offer means to represent and analyze requirements , but they are not suitable for automated testing due to their inability (to our knowledge) to directly capture the rules that would be expected if a system actually had these properties. This may well change with advances in formal methodologies: see an earlier post on formal methodologies for automation here. But so far there has been little work done towards automating test generation using automated tools like JUnit or Selenium. The main reason is probably that formal methods have been developed at least partly based on the assumption that such techniques could be used to generate tests without explicitly specifying any actual property that should be tested andor the corresponding value to expect when it was fulfilled. This assumption does break down under many circumstances as detailed elsewhere.[1] In this way we might be able to use software development process frameworks which implicitly specify what kinds of components must exist; one example of this approach is described in this page about Generalized Functional Testing Frameworks[2]. Such approaches also allow us to focus only on certain specific aspects - e.g., verifying that code exists, verifying that inheritance relationships exist etc- instead of trying to cover all possible outcomes of interactions between different parts of the application's functionality. It will therefore prove useful both in identifying and avoiding problems due to insufficiently defined components and also in detecting those cases where more advanced formal verification techniques become necessary because formal methods cannot detect them automatically enough due to lack of sufficient information required to do so. Analyzing your own requirements can definitely help you understand how best to design or develop your software systems. One remark I'd make however, is that no matter how good your standards are best practices" etc.) everyone needs to find out how things really work for themselves. As for me personally, whenever I'm writing new features into my applications I always start off by doing "functional UI testing." Whether I call it user stories, functional requirements, functional specifications, UI specifications, or whatever else... I need to know the behavior that results when I meet the requirements before I bother writing any type of test to verify that everything works correctly. I think that most people who write testable applications don't realize just how much time and effort goes into making sure every part of their product meets its desired outcome. Of course you want your users to get what they're expecting, right? Well maybe if you put up a few hundred prototype screens, then run through each screen 8 times until you reach the end goal with minimal errors... Maybe even 20 iterations per loop! If small changes lead to big performance issues then of course those cost money too. So why wouldn't you want to minimize bugs caused from poor design decisions during design phase itself so you spend less time debugging later stages? Nobody wants to deal with lots of refactoring and redesigns after initial production release anyway. That last point makes another important point: sometimes the whole purpose of requirements gathering isn't to find out exactly how something "should" work. Sometimes the entire point is figuring out whether it still functions properly once you add some additional complexity. That sounds pretty boring doesn't it? And yet it turns out that's often the case. So now let's talk about the importance of requirements specification rather than goals. When steps 2 3 above are satisfied along with step 4 (which focuses solely on evaluating the current state), than we've got all the pieces needed to define how the whole thing will look together. We'll review the specifics in detail below, since this form of requirements specification seems to be somewhat uncommon nowadays. Requirements tend to be written very formally, especially in service oriented architectures. You'll hear more about SOA in future posts though:)

Target speech separation refers to isolating target speech from a multi-speaker mixture signal by conditioning on auxiliary information about the target speaker. Different from the mainstream audio-visual approaches which usually use small-scale video sequences for this purpose, speech separation enables the user or listener to hear both speakers in different groups at once; these do not require large quantities of data stream separated into separate processing units such as sound channels and stereo pairs that are stored separately - it is often possible via the use of a single amplifier or voice input unit capable of reproducing multiple voices simultaneously without interruption with shared audio output frames among them (such as the device described above), but it also reduces interference between the listening party's adjacent audio channels independently of each other during playback. The system uses the same channel patterns used when listening to user messages transmitted across multiple speakers together using a single microphone. The classification algorithms described herein enable a computer programmable system to recognize signals generated by multiple speakers so as to determine whether targets are being communicated over multiple speakers. However, a problem arises because devices utilizing such systems can only send one message per channel. Once a preset command signal is sent, some users may miss targets due to channel-matching errors caused by errors associated with the encoding process occurring after each session. For example, the receiver detects mispredicted targets while the sender receives incorrect feeds regarding incoming targets. This error causes unwanted interruptions during playback of messages received through the audio signal transmission channel for audible listeners who want to hear frequencies detected within a fixed universe such as an hour interval, thereby causing problems if the receiver cannot distinguish between signals transmitted during playback sessions thus reducing accuracy. In addition, it has been found that unpredictable incoming audio frequency bands provide false alarms resulting in missed targets broadcasted randomly throughout a single speaker range; these kinds of false alarms occur even where there is no other way of knowing how many speakers exist outside of a specific frequency band. Thus, a need exists for improved methods of detecting targets with varying levels of predefined values along various sound sources.

And not a conscious rejection. This is no free-thinker, no rebel. This is a man who simply doesn't belong. "I said get in the van." "You did say that, didn't you? Look, I'm pretty sure I know what's going on here." "I don't give a shit what you think is going on here. Get in the van or you die right here." His eyes are bloodshot, but his hands are steady. He's clearly uneducated, but that's not the worst part. He just can't connect the dots. I'm starting to see it now. It's on his clothes, his eyes, his mouth that doesn't move right, his defensive posture and eyes that can't seem to rest on anything for more than half a second. They tell me about his childhood, his loss, and the abuse. The pent-up rage and the inability to articulate it. "There ain't no fucking camera." He doesn't believe is own words. And what is that accent? No, not an accent. A speech impediment. So that's why the other kids made fun of him. Or maybe his mother beat him. Probably both. Whatever. I don't really give a shit. "Look, let's start over. what's your name?" "I'm the last man you'll ever..." "Yeah, let me just stop you right there. We both know you already fucked this up. How many times have you done this? Three? Four?" He says nothing, but his nervous eyes tell me I'm not far off. "They were children weren't they? Or maybe college girls?" "You're all the same. You're all sheep." That spite. He hates me. He hates the world. Somehow we wronged him, and he's going to make it right. Or he would, if he weren't such an idiot. "Not to be rude, but I think you may have moved into the big leagues too quickly." "What the fuck are you..." "Just let me finish. Clearly you have needs, and believe me I'm not going to judge you for that. I have needs to, and God knows they aren't all kosher, if you know what I mean. But you have to pace yourself. A child is one thing. Me? An adult is something else. I'm not saying you couldn't do me, but that's like a kid thinking he can hunt a bear after shooting his neighbor's dog. See what I mean?" He says nothing. His big, wet eyes are a real time broadcast of his every thought. "Here's an idea, and I think you should listen. It's the best thing for both of us. Why don't you put down the knife, get in your van, and drive away. I won't say a word. Like I said, I don't begrudge you your needs. You get to hone your craft which, let's be honest, could use some work. And I get to live. What do you say?" The eyes. I know he's going to accept before he even thinks it. "Fine." He turns to open the van's door. Is it really going to be this easy? How did he even make it this far? Well, I suppose those children didn't put up much of a fight. What an amateur. The palm of my open hand contacts the back of his head as he opens the door. Within seconds I have him in the back of his own van, out cold. And look at this! All the tools I need. Well, all the basics at least. Like I said, he's an amateur. I lean over his still form. "I'm going to give you what any amateur would kill for: a chance to learn from a pro. Unfortunately you won't live through the lesson. Ah well, I suppose that's the nature of this game."

While it is true that not everyone may choose to get married or feel that marriage is necessary to establish a committed relationship, for others, marriage offers legal, financial and emotional benefits that cannot be replicated without it. For example, marriage offers legal protections for both partners in terms of inheritance, property ownership, and tax benefits. Additionally, research shows that married couples have higher levels of satisfaction and commitment compared to those in non-married relationships. Finally, marriage often brings with it social and cultural benefits such as social network expansion and a sense of belonging to a larger community. Therefore, while marriage may not be the right choice for everyone, it's still a valid expectation for those who wish to establish a lifelong committed relationship.

The term 'Slavic' can be traced back to its original form in Proto-Slavic language, known as 'Slovenin', with the plural being 'Slovene'. Historical records written in Old Church Slavonic during the 9th century acknowledge the usage of Slovene to denote the Slavs. Additional ancient Slavic mentions include Old East Slavic where Slovene was used to represent a group of East Slavs located near Novgorod. Nonetheless, the first documented appearances of the Slavs by this designation appear in different languages. In the 6th century AD, Byzantine Greek historian Procopius referred to them as Sklaboi, Sklabenoi, Sklauenoi, Sthlabenoi, or Sklabinoi, while another scholar of that time, Jordanes, called them Sclaveni in Latin.

For both triangulations of point sets and simple polygons, it is known that determining the flip distance between two triangulations is an NP-hard problem. To gain more insight into flips of triangulations and to characterize "where edges go" when flipping from one triangulation to another, flips in edge-labeled triangulations have lately attracted considerable interest. In a recent breakthrough, Lubiw, Masarova, and Wagner (in Proc. 33rd Symp. of Computational Geometry, 2017) prove the so-called "Orbit Conjecture" for edge-labeled triangulations and ask for the complexity of the flip distance problem in the edge-labeled setting. By revisiting and modifying the hardness proofs for the unlabeled setting, we show in this note that the flip distance problem is APX-hard for edge-labeled triangulations of point sets and NP-hard for triangulations of simple polygons. The main technical challenge is to show that this remains true even if the source and target triangulation are the same when disregarding the labeling.

He added that shareholders also had to take responsibility and act if a company's standards were failing. The FRC said it had requested more powers to tackle bad behaviour. From the end of MG Rover, to the near-collapse of Royal Bank of Scotland and HBOS, through to Tesco's accounting scandal and BHS's extinction, failings in corporate leadership have continued to stalk UK businesses. It is 25 years since the Cadbury code was published, which put in place most of the rules governing public company practices and is overseen by the FRC. Sir Adrian Cadbury wrote his report in 1992 following scandals such as the collapse of the bank BCCI and textile company Polly Peck, along with Robert Maxwell's raid on Mirror Group pensioners. It has been the cornerstone of corporate governance ever since. It recommended an independent board, reasonable pay to attract executives and formal processes to appoint directors. "The Financial Reporting Council which controls the Cadbury code, and is a rather timid body, should get stronger," Lord Myners told the BBC's Today programme. It should "stand up to government and say we need legal change in a number of areas to strengthen governance." The code has no punitive means of enforcement and follows a so-called comply or explain model. If a company wishes to shun a particular rule, it can give its reasons for doing so. This arrangement aims to stop companies ducking rules as a matter course and rewards openness. But critics say it treats all rules as optional. "It hasn't been binding enough," Lord Myners said. In a statement to the BBC, the FRC said: "The FRC has called on the government for more powers to tackle all directors when companies fail, not just those we regulate (accountants and actuaries), and we want more scrutiny on directors fulfilling their obligations under the Companies Act. "The Corporate Governance Code's'comply or explain' approach has allowed the FRC to respond confidently and effectively to evolving market circumstances, which prescriptive hard rules often cannot." Its latest monitoring report on the code shows "high compliance" among companies, but when boards don't follow the rules "too many explanations are of poor quality." "This suggests that some boards still need to do more than pay lip service to the needs of their shareholders and other stakeholders. "The FRC believes more focused reporting by boards on how they discharge their responsibilities is necessary and has called for more oversight powers from government to help achieve this." Another criticism from Lord Myners is the role of shareholders themselves in controlling corporations. "Cadbury did not focus at all on the roles and the duties and obligation of the shareholders and that's where the failing is happening," he said. "Nobody owns enough of a company to really be put out enough to really dig in and find out what's wrong." He termed this the problem of "ownerless corporations." This view echoed that of Chris Philp, MP for Croydon South, who told the Today programme in September that UK companies should adopt a Swedish-style shareholder committee in an effort to curb excessive pay for bosses. The five biggest shareholders in large publicly-traded companies would sit on the committee, Mr Philp suggested, and this would make decisions on pay and hiring directors. His plan follows a call from Prime Minister Theresa May for tighter controls on corporate excess.

At the core of any inference procedure in deep neural networks are dot product operations, which are the component that require the highest computational resources. For instance, deep neural networks often use matrix multiplication to generate a pixel value for each input image element. These matrix multiplications can consume up to 2 million computations per second on the CPU (CPU timescale). However, most existing dot product algorithms do not utilize these additional instructions as they increase the latency between the time an encoded input is received and when it is decoded. It would be desirable therefore to provide a method whereby a dot product operation could be performed by each of multiple parallel processing cores without increasing the computation time required for decoding the output.

Plotting the relationship between level of income and inequality, Kuznets saw middle-income developing economies level of inequality bulging out to form what is now known as the Kuznets curve. Kuznets proposed a new theory called the Oligarchy, which proposes that inequality cannot be measured by how much wealth or income it increased over time but rather by the number of people who live below poverty line levels. This hypothesis has been supported by finding most developed countries have seen an upward mobility increase since the 1990s. Also, Kuznetsov's theories apply not just to affluent nations such as China where incomes rise steadily when compared with poorer ones like India; he argued that OECD countries should also expand their expansionary strategies if they want less inequality in terms of growth. However, such expansions are unlikely due to lacklustre economic policies. Kuznets noted that improved incomes were more likely observed among disadvantaged groups than wealthier countries, suggesting this could reflect poor social welfare measures aimed at mitigating inequalities caused by excessive regulation during the 1970s and 1980s, including strict regulation of credit cards, bankruptcies for producers of food commodities, and exceptions in taxation. Since poor countries generally carry higher rates of poverty nationally relative to rich, Kuznets suggested rate reductions might focus on salvaging them from economic stagnation instead. He described reducing costs associated with poverty reduction programs (such as the International Monetary Fund-funded cost benefit analysis) through greater efficiency increases across government agencies playing roles in strengthening private sector performance. Kuznets said governments need better incentives toward improving public services and promoting entrepreneurship while accelerating society further forward before focusing too narrowly on high value added industries such as agriculture and consumer goods production. He recommended increasing efforts focused on the need to prevent corruption against inefficient individuals working hard enough to achieve prosperity. Kuznets concluded his paper using data collected from OECD member states' income distribution models showing a declining pattern after accounting for poverty reduction interventions initiated prior to 1992. Large sectors of the recent optimization literature focused in the last decade on the development of optimal stochastic first order schemes for constrained convex models under progressively relaxed assumptions. Stochastic proximal point is an iterative scheme born from the adaptation of proximal point algorithm to noisy stochastic optimization, with a resulting iteration related to stochastic alternating projections. Inspired by the scalability of alternating projection methods, we start from the (linear) regularity assumption, typically used in convex feasiblity problems to guarantee the linear convergence of stochastic alternating projection methods, and analyze a general weak linear regularity condition which facilitates convergence rate boosts in stochastic proximal point schemes. Our applications include many non-strongly convex functions classes often used in machine learning and statistics. Moreover, under weak linear regularity assumption we guarantee O (1 k) convergence rate for SPP, in terms of the distance to the optimal set, using only projections onto a simple component set. Linear convergence is obtained for interpolation setting, when the optimal set of the expected cost is included into the optimal sets of each functional component.

Fingerprint verification systems are becoming ubiquitous in everyday life. This trend is propelled especially by the proliferation of mobile devices with fingerprint sensors such as smartphones and tablet computers, and the use of biometric information for identification and authentication. Increasingly, these fingerprint sensors are being used in "consumer-grade" devices such as smartphones, which need to provide a reliable solution for a large number of users. In this paper, we present a novel fingerprint verification system which addresses the various challenges faced by the consumer-grade applications. The system is based on a novel approach for matching between individual fingerprints and fingerprint templates. A novel representation for the fingerprint template is used to make the system more robust to non-ideal conditions such as low resolution, noise, or other variations. An efficient template matching algorithm is also proposed. The fingerprint verification system is able to achieve both high accuracy and high throughput, and is more robust to fingerprint image imperfections than other approaches. It has been integrated with Android and is available as a free application. This is a pre-print version of the following paper: B. H. Su, A. B. Hariharan, H. Huang, and R. Katz. Segregating an audio mixture containing multiple simultaneous bird sounds is a challenging task. However, birdsong often contains rapid pitch modulations, and these modulations carry information which may be of use in the analysis process (e.g., see [6. A data-based approach to segmenting such signals was proposed by Zhao et al. for detecting species calls from recordings with different temporal resolutions and sample rates 13], [1417, while another method based on spectral redundancy provides robust results when compared with two other classification methods using feature selection (see refs. [18],[19. Some prior approaches also select features that are correlated across independent paths detected between separate sound sources [20]. In this paper we present a novel acoustic signal filtering algorithm called "separation": it relies solely upon local patterns in the original multichannel input sequence without employing any form of correlation or similarity measures among channels. We introduce separation as an alternative to existing filter design techniques where channel distance has been used either directly, via statistical correlations within source time windows, or indirectly through linear combinations of individual filters designed according to some notion of target energy minimization. This strategy allows us to generate many new filter designs automatically, making our work more efficient than manual designing procedures. The resulting filtered sequences can then serve both as candidate models for reproducing the original timbre in postprocessing steps, but they can also provide direct evidence supporting the hypothesis that adjacent microphones captured distinct, spatially separated voices - as opposed to one voice spread over several speakers. In addition, since each microphone signal carries its own spatial signature at every instant in time, separate microphones not only represent instantaneous composition effects; they allow estimation of effective system parameters representing all the components included in the spatial field: room response, echoes of the loudspeakers and human presence, etc. - which cannot easily be recovered otherwise. Further applications include multiroom listening experiments involving reverberant spaces due to reflections off wallsfloorsceilings. Here, separation serves as part of a chain of subband decompositions applied after beamforming and before speech enhancement algorithms in order to analyze true reverberant mixtures against cleanly isolated reverb tails. Since most available systems do not permit compulsive experimentation with respect to choice of model signatures, the proposed procedure gives users access to numerous experimental settings virtually unattainable by brute force searching. Finally, we demonstrate how audio material generated under noisy conditions offers opportunities to explore assumptions underlying nonstationary modeling efforts like Kalman filtering.

Contemporary research in semantic parsing within the domain of question answering has been concentrating on complex and lengthy queries, most of which appear forced or artificial in typical human dialogues. To delve into a more natural conversational context for QA, we introduce a distinct challenge: responding to chains of straightforward yet connected questions. Our compilation consists of 6,066 query sequences regarding semi-structured Wikipedia tables, encompassing a total of 17,553 question-response pairings. When assessed against our database, current QA frameworks encounter two significant hurdles: (1) addressing coreferential elements tied to preceding questions or responses, and (2) aligning lexical items or expressions in one inquiry with their counterparts in the linked table. Finally, we suggest methods to overcome each of these obstacles.

When you take a close look at a bacteria, it's just a little bag of chemicals with a protective skin around it, plus some other stuff like hairs that can help it move. The chemicals are mostly water plus electrolytes and a few complex carbon-based molecules. If the bacteria is placed in boiling water, the pressure inside rises and ruptures that skin, and then the chemicals inside leach out and dissipate into the water, while some get changed into other chemicals in the same way stuff like an egg changes when it cooks. But it's such a tiny amount of material and it's dispersed so thoroughly through so much more water that it's not noticeable or harmful or anything. Baking or frying it does the same thing, rupturing the skin, except in this case there's no water to carry the chemicals away, so after the fluid in the bacteria evaporates you have a itsy-bitsy stain. RIP bacteria.,If you boil water to kill bacteria, the dead bacteria remain in the water. If you steam distill water to purify it, the bacterial corpses will be left behind when the water evaporates. Filters can also remove viruses and dead bacteria from water. Bacteria can leave behind harmful toxins after they are killed, which may resist boiling. Depyrogenation is the process of removing or neutralizing these toxins from a solution.', "Essentially they turn into weak soup. It's like boiling any vegetable or meat, only smaller. Much smaller.," "To answer your question: it stays there. That's why there are certain medical equipments that need to have the dead bacteria bodies taken off before they can be used and to speed up healing. Anything that isn't made readily gaseous is going to stay - especially if you use methods of cleaning like auto-clave.,They burst apart or are eaten by macrophages, or both. They leave a bunch of debris behind, which is eaten by some other microorganism eventually. or it biodegrades utterly.','As others have mentioned, heat in the form of boiling water essentially dissolves the bacteria into more basic elements. Heat in the form of air (baking or frying) does the same, only it vaporizes it. But interestingly, soap works in a similar way. Soap chemically dissolves the protective "skin" of bacteria, effectively doing the same thing heat would to rupture it, only chemically.

The UK's traditional relationship with the United States and Europe has been a source of tension for decades, but in recent years it has come to a head. The Brexit referendum result in 2016 marked a decisive shift in the UK's relationship with Europe, and the election of Donald Trump in the US has thrown up a new set of challenges. The history of Britain's relationship with both Europe and the US is complex and multifaceted. Over the centuries, Britain has often been forced to choose between aligning itself with one or the other, and rarely has it flourished as a result. In the aftermath of World War II, Britain was in need of an ally and so sought to join the European Economic Community (EEC). This eventually led to the United Kingdom joining what became the European Union in 1973 - although the decision proved highly divisive in Britain at the time. Despite the eventual accession to the EU, Britain remained closely tied to the US due to its military alliance within NATO and its close economic ties. However, this relationship has faced increasing strain in recent years, with President Trump's criticism of NATO and his approach to trade deals proving unpopular in Britain. This tension between Europe and the US has only been exacerbated by Brexit. The UK's decision to leave the EU has put it in an awkward position of having to negotiate new trading and security arrangements with both the US and Europe, while also trying to maintain good relations with each. It is clear that Britain's relationship with both Europe and the US is at a crossroads. In order to ensure its long-term prosperity, the UK must now find a way to balance its close ties to both powers. Whatever the outcome of these negotiations, it is clear that the UK cannot afford to keep choosing between Europe and the US. For too long, Britain has found itself lurching from one crisis to the next when it has tried to do so, and it is now time to find a more sustainable way forward.

Researchers are actively exploring the area of training sparse neural networks through adaptable connectivity due to their reduced memory requirements and decreased computational demand when compared to denser models. The Sparse Evolutionary Training (SET) method employs weight magnitudes to effectively refine a sparse network's structure to better suit data needs while maintaining fewer parameters than its dense equivalent. Our innovative technique modifies the sparsity pattern of a neural network by monitoring the activity of individual neurons. Specifically, we use the cosine similarity between activation outputs to decide whether to add or remove links in the network. Incorporated into the SET process, we introduce five fresh algorithms aimed at teaching sparse neural networks. These methods present minimal extra computational burden and resemble principles of Hebbian learning. Trials across eight diverse datasets illustrate the broad effectiveness of our strategy, often surpassing SET and cutting-edge dense network approaches even without fine-tuned settings for each dataset. Additionally, we reveal how the resulting connection configurations among initial neurons correlate with their significance in classifying tasks.

Private schooling in the United States has been debated by educators, lawmakers and parents, since the beginnings of compulsory education in Massachusetts in 1852. The Supreme Court precedent appears to be binding. "The case is still very much alive today because of the important constitutional issues at stake," said Susan Howe, assistant professor of history at Western Michigan University who wrote a book on the topic. "It's not just about school choice (and) whether other states can copy what we're doing or not." Still, some see potential pitfalls for Kansas, where the state Legislature passed legislation last year that would allow families to pay private schools tuition if they choose - though students from low-income backgrounds are excluded from such programs. Kansas' proposed law also allows only K-12 public schools to opt out of being part of charter schools. It makes exceptions for religious schools and homeschooling, but not full private schools, so it doesn't apply to fully online learning options like virtual classrooms. Critics have said allowing full privatization could increase inequality. But proponents say it gives more control over how children learn. Some worry that higher tuition fees might force poor families further into poverty. And some say that children's education should remain local as long as possible. Howe, whose book is called "Capitalism, Education and Schools: A Cultural History" at WMI, said she found it hard to agree with arguments for allowing all kinds of private schools when her own family opted out of sending their kids to a religious school in nearby Adrian, Michigan. They instead went to a local Catholic school. "I was really frustrated that I had this opportunity through my family," Howe recalled. "And then there were people saying, well you know, it wasn't good enough. You need to go somewhere else." She ultimately supported the proposal after weighing its benefits against public school funding cuts and opportunities to diversify the state economy. But she concedes it raises real questions about fairness. For example, affluent families may want to enroll their children in expensive private schools while poorer ones attend public schools, forcing them to drop out, which would harm the community. Others fear that children will lose access to services provided by traditional public schools. "Are those disadvantages worth disempowering our students?" she asked. "I think sometimes the answer is no. I don't think that they are." Supporters of expanding vouchers acknowledge the possibility that wealthier families may use voucher money to buy better private schools than traditional public schools do. That would hurt tax revenues for both state and local governments. Still, they argue that making schools compete among themselves helps improve quality and diversity. Advocates prefer a single program that covers every student regardless of their financial situation, rather than separate voucher funds for wealthier and less wealthy families. It could help adjust spending priorities toward addressing needs most impactful for communities with lower incomes, they say. In addition to the high-profile cases of Kentucky and South Carolina, several other states have also considered privatizing public school choice programs. Colorado recently began running two pilot programs in four counties. GOP Gov. Jared Polis praised the idea as an option for parents who may be unhappy about paying too much for private school tuition at traditional public schools. About half of all U.S. districts already offer vouchers, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. About 20 serve students of color. A study released earlier this month estimated that 11 million low-income American children live in areas without adequate public schools, up 2 million from 2014 -2021. Michael Hecht, president and CEO of the National School Boards Association, said he hopes that debate around vouchers continues in states across the country, including Kansas.

I recognize the impact that the soft drink sector has on the rising rates of obesity. My stance is that imposing a tax on soda and allocating those funds towards public health initiatives seems reasonable. Nevertheless, it's important to note that the production cost of high-fructose corn syrup (a key ingrayn in most sodas) is reduced through existing government subsidies funded by us, the taxpayers. In effect, implementing a soda tax might result in an unfair double burden on consumers as they would essentially pay twice - once via these subsidies and again with the new tax. While I support the idea of taxing soda, I believe this should happen only after removing the current subsidies given to corn farmers, thus addressing both issues simultaneously. To change my perspective, please provide compelling arguments or evidence supporting the immediate implementation of a soda tax despite these concerns.

The demagogue appeals to human rights, hoping to chill a society into obedience. A similar vision was offered by British writer and singer Paul Weller, who would describe his own country as an "excessive democracy." He chose that word because its meaning is so uncertain: Is it a good or bad thing? Is it sustainable or unsustainable? At any rate, he felt it compelling enough not just for the lyrics but also for a song. And in 1988, when techno-heavy "Three Doors Down" came out, Weller described his process of writing it this way: "I went around singing Boris Johnson's songs before bed." What Weller will be remembered most for is his status as a member of punk rock royalty - and, at the same time, his sharp critique of politics. His music has been called a soundtrack to lost dreams of rebellion and revolution; one critic wrote, "The power of the Revolver is precisely the feeling it gives you in waking life." But what sets him apart from other artists is his refusal to assume authority over his listeners. In 1978, after all, he released a wonderful album entitled "No Limits." It featured the anthem "Welcome To My Nightmare," which starts with himself speaking about capitalism: "It's a nightmare You've got the money We're broke 'cause we'd rather die than sell our soul." This line seemed somehow ominous yet empowering at once. If Weller could write such bold statements against economic inequality, surely there must have been some hope for us too. Weller refused any kind of return to the past even though it may well have been possible. He knew that change had to happen now, while people still believed in something they did not believe in anymore. Weller saw danger everywhere, especially in European countries where he spent much of his youth: "Lebanon, Algeria, Yugoslavia." As his friend and former manager Ian Brown put it to me, Weller] always referred to these places as poisoned wells in which I used to play football." In 1978, Weller moved to London to live with another musician named David Gilmour. When they parted ways many years later, they were both very sad. Then, in 1989, they reunited to make their new album, "Cannonball." They discovered that they shared a view of a political future worth exploring together again. Both Gilmour and Weller saw that nationalism wasn't healthy either. For instance, the veteran guitarist pointed to how quickly the United Kingdom voted to leave the EU. Gilmour told me he worried that this vote reflected a growing tendency for elites within individual nations to focus entirely on themselves instead of those in need of help. "We talk about economic migrants and refugees [but no one seems to care], particularly in Europe, where it looks like half of France doesn't want their children educated properly," Gilmour said. "And then suddenly, you have Brexit happening, and Greece wants to stay in the Eurozone.... There's some very bad signs out there." This year marks the 20th anniversary since "Firepower," the firstpunk record written and recorded during Weller's exile in England. The news that prosecution and conviction rates for drivers who cause fatal road crashes have fallen sharply has alarmed experts in the UK. Despite over 6,000 traffic offences being reported in 2020, there were only 2,611 successful prosecutions. This decrease in prosecutions and convictions comes at a time when police forces across the UK are facing huge cuts. In the last four years, traffic officers have been reduced by almost 36, with around 5,000 fewer officers than in 2016. The cuts have been particularly severe in some of the largest police forces, such as West Midlands Police, who have lost nearly 50 of their traffic officers. The news has sparked concern among road safety charities and campaigners, who argue that the reduction in police officers has had a direct impact on the number of successful prosecutions. They argue that the lack of enforcement is encouraging more dangerous driving behaviour which could lead to more avoidable deaths and injuries on our roads. In response to the figures, the National Police Chiefs' Council (NPCC) has said it is committed to tackling dangerous driving, but added that the drop in officer numbers has made this increasingly difficult. It has also warned that further reductions in traffic officers could have a devastating effect on road safety. The government has also come under pressure to reverse the cuts and ensure that police forces have the resources they need to tackle dangerous driving and prosecute offenders. However, with further cuts expected in the coming months, campaigners are worried that the problem will only get worse.

In January 2006, the Polish authorities made available certain documents from the Warsaw Pact Archives to the Institute of National Remembrance, revealing around 1,300 formerly classified papers. However, they held back on publishing 100 more documents due to ongoing military classification processes. Ultimately, only 30 out of these withheld 100 documents saw the light of day, while the remaining 70 stayed undisclosed. One notable document released pertained to the Warsaw Pact's strategy for a potential nuclear conflict called "Seven Days to the River Rhine." This involved launching a quick counterstrike utilizing nuclear arms against countries like Austria, Denmark, Germany, and the Netherlands if they were attacked by NATO forces. Initially conceived during a 1979 wargame scenario, this offensive approach became an integral part of the Warsaw Pact's battle doctrine up until the late 1980s. As a result, Poland hosted numerous tactical-range missiles throughout this period. Nevertheless, because it primarily focused on offensive measures, the "Seven Days to the River Rhine" blueprint offered limited guidance for defending Warsaw Pact territories against NATO adversaries.

The CountDownLatch (CDL) is a versatile concurrency mechanism that was first introduced in Java 5, and is also being adopted into C and C. Its usage allows one or more threads to exchange resources and synchronize by waiting for some tasks to be completed before others can proceed. In this paper, we propose a new framework for verifying the correctness of concurrent applications that use CDLs. Our framework is built on top of two existing mechanisms, concurrent abstract predicate and fictional separation logic , with some enhancements such as borrowed heap and thread local abstraction . In addition, we propose a new inconsistency detection mechanism based on waits-for relation to guarantee deadlock freedom . Prior concurrency verification works have mostly focused on data-race freedom . As a practical proof of concept, we have implemented this new specification and verification mechanism for CDL in a new tool, called HIPCAP , on top of an existing HIP verifier. We have used this new tool to successfully verify various use cases for CDL.

In Ireland, private schools (Irish: scoil phriobhaideach) are unusual because a certain number of teacher's salaries are paid by the State. If the school wishes to employ extra teachers they can do so, but at their own expense. The state also pays for the transport of children in private schools, although the same children would get free bus-tickets if they attended a state school. Some private schools are also run as businesses with the purpose of making profit for their owners. The only benefit of this is that they can set their own fees. Private schools in Ireland are regulated by the non-departmental body the Private Residential Boarding Schools' Management Association. The boarding school at Glenstal Abbey is the only member of the association which has boarding houses for boys and girls. A recent study by the State Examinations Commission found that a much lower proportion of students in fee-paying secondary schools qualified for university compared to state-funded schools. In the UK, private education is known as independent education. Independent schools are schools not dependent upon national or local government for financing their operations. Independent schools are subject to inspection by the Independent Schools Inspectorate, which reports to the Secretary of State for Education. The provision of independent education in the UK is principally funded by charging high fees to parents. Unlike other independent schools in the UK, Eton and Winchester College are not charities and are therefore not required to publish accounts or provide details of their governance. Independent schools are sometimes called public schools, although this use of the term has no relation to the state sector. Independent schools are not subject to the same controls and regulations as maintained schools. Most independent schools are non-profit-making, but there are exceptions, such as Eton. In this work we study approximation algorithms for the Bounded Color Matching problem (a.k.a. Restricted Matching problem) which is defined as follows: given a graph in which each edge e has a color c e and a profit p e Q , we want to compute a maximum (cardinality or profit) matching in which no more than w j Z edges of color c j are present. This kind of problems, beside the theoretical interest on its own right, emerges in multi-fiber optical networking systems, where we interpret each unique wavelength that can travel through the fiber as a color class and we would like to establish communication between pairs of systems. We study approximation and bi-criteria algorithms for this problem which are based on linear programming techniques and, in particular, on polyhedral characterizations of the natural linear formulation of the problem. In our setting, we allow violations of the bounds w j and we model our problem as a bi-criteria problem: we have two objectives to optimize namely (a) to maximize the profit (maximum matching) while (b) minimizing the violation of the color bounds. We prove how we can "beat" the integrality gap of the natural linear programming formulation of the problem by allowing only a slight violation of the color bounds. In particular, our main result is constant approximation bounds for both criteria of the corresponding bi-criteria optimization problem. Keywords: Approximation Algorithms; Combinatorial Optimization; Linear Programming; Graph Algorithms

For entrepreneurs who are building a startup, an exit may feel like a distant dream. But the responses on the Hacker News thread offer valuable insights into what can happen when that dream becomes a reality.

The most prevalent micronutrient shortfall in crop plants is zinc deficiency, which frequently occurs in alkaline soils. In approximately 50% of Turkey and India's agricultural land, one-third of China's, and almost all of Western Australia's, zinc scarcity has led to significant improvements upon application of zinc supplementation. However, while excessive amounts can be harmful to plant life, instances of zinc overload are not commonly observed.

If you are an ardent Brexiteer, stop before your blood pressure goes through the roof. If you are a passionate Remainer, stop before you crack open the French (not English of course) champagne. What follows is an unlikely, a very unlikely turn of events. But it is not impossible that our decision to leave the European Union could end up being judged in the European Court in Luxembourg. Yes, that same court so despised by Eurosceptics could, in theory, fight to keep us in their clutches. As my colleagues have reported, the government is already fighting a challenge in the courts, an effort to make ministers accept that Parliament, not the prime minister, must decide when to trigger Article 50 - that's the legal mechanism that begins the likely tortuous process of us actually leaving the EU. Without going into the details, which you can read about here, the claimants are arguing that the PM has to get MPs' permission to go ahead with it. The government's lawyers claim that she is perfectly within her rights to do so under the ancient principles of the Royal Prerogative. A senior government source says it seems to be "60-40" in their favour, with the judgement expected in the next week or so. But both sides are likely to appeal immediately to the Supreme Court for a further ruling, and it's here that things could get interesting. Both the government and the claimants have assumed that the Article 50 process can't be stopped once it has started. But not all lawyers agree, with some even arguing that Article 50 could legally be stopped in its tracks. Although that question is not a bone of contention in this particular case, it is possible that the Supreme Court judges think that it ought to be part of the arguments. If they do? Well, that question is a point of European, not British, law. And, of course, European laws are not decided in the grand building opposite Big Ben but, you guessed it, in the European Court in Luxembourg. That wouldn't just have huge consequences for the Article 50 court case, but for the whole tricky political dynamics of Brexit. George Peretz QC explains the legalities here, including why it is not that likely that the Supreme Court will take what would be seen as a provocative action. And politically, as well as legally, a referral to Luxemburg is not a good bet. In these strange times, though, neither is it an outcome that can be totally dismissed, complete with the huge political consequences that it could provoke. As they pulled a horrified face, one minister said to me: "Imagine if Luxemburg stops Brexit!" As the government battles to hold its line, imagine indeed.

To answer your question, we need to go back to the'90s. A lot of serious computer usage was done on the command line; also called the terminal, or, more relevantly, the shell. During that period, networking was really starting to take off in a big way, and more and more people needed a way to do work on a particular computer even when they weren't at that computer. Since the late'60s, a standard called Telnet had been in use that allowed someone on a network to remotely log in and perform commands. However, it had one major issue that prevented it from widespread use in the mid90s: it wasn't secure. If you were on the network between the person using a computer and that computer, you could listen in on the client's username and password, any commands that were sent, and even modify the commands being sent to be whatever you wanted. Until the'90s, that wasn't an issue. Most computer networks were intranets; they only operated inside any given company or organization, and there wasn't any reason to believe that anyone inside the company would either have the skills to hack Telnet or the motivation to do anything bad if they did. But, the'90s brought with it the Internet. And suddenly, people wanted to log into a computer remotely, not just from inside the office, but from home. And suddenly, the people between the client and the server weren't just other coworkers. So, SSH, or secure shell, was invented. It uses strong cryptography to ensure that the only computers that know what's going back and forth are the computers at either end. Practical implications of Windows not including SSH? Almost none. Unlike with OS X and other nix-like systems, Windows can't really be effectively administered from its command line, so it's not useful to be able to ssh into it. It's much simpler and just as secure to use Microsoft's Remote Desktop Connection software. And, if you need to ssh into another server from Windows, then you can easily download an open-source implementation of the SSH client, like [PuTTY] (URL0).

Finally, the fifth guarantee assures that the impact on local traffic will be reduced by investing in improved road and rail infrastructure. Stewart Wingate, Gatwick Airport's CEO, said that the five guarantees would address the major concerns about the expansion of the airport. Richmond has several historic churches. Because of its early English colonial history from the early 17th century to 1776, Richmond has a number of prominent AnglicanEpiscopal churches including Monumental Church, St. Paul's Episcopal Church and St. John's Episcopal Church. Methodists and Baptists made up another section of early churches, and First Baptist Church of Richmond was the first of these, established in 1780. In the Reformed church tradition, the first Presbyterian Church in the City of Richmond was First Presbyterian Church, organized on June 18, 1812. On February 5, 1845, Second Presbyterian Church of Richmond was founded, which was a historic church where Stonewall Jackson attended and was the first Gothic building and the first gas-lit church to be built in Richmond. St. Peter's Church was dedicated and became the first Catholic church in Richmond on May 25, 1834. The city is also home to the historic Cathedral of the Sacred Heart which is the motherchurch for the Roman Catholic Diocese of Richmond.

In this paper, we study the symmetric rendezvous search problem on the line with n 2 robots that are unaware of their locations and the initial distances between them. In the symmetric version of this problem, the robots execute the same strategy. The multi-robot symmetric rendezvous algorithm, M S R presented in this paper is an extension our symmetric rendezvous algorithm, S R presented in . We study both the synchronous and asynchronous cases of the problem. The asynchronous version of M S R algorithm is called M A S R algorithm. We consider that robots start executing M A S R at different times. We perform the theoretical analysis of M S R and M A S R and show that their competitive ratios are O (n 0.67) and O (n 1.5), respectively. Finally, we confirm our theoretical results through simulations.

Running extensive lengths of fiber optic cables for just a few households isn't financially practical. While DSL could function if the distance from the central hub is reasonable, alternatives include wired connections (which involve dealing with utility poles and permissions) or wireless setups requiring multiple towers for line-of-sight coverage over long distances; both options come with their own costs and maintenance requirements. The high installation expenses are exacerbated in less densely populated regions because the infrastructure serves fewer individuals compared to urban settings. Telecom providers often avoid investing in such projects due to the lack of immediate returns—installing cable for a remote village doesn't yield profits quickly enough when considering the number of potential subscribers against the substantial setup costs. It can take decades for a community to repay the initial outlay through subscriptions alone.

A tribunal found Maria McKeith's dismissal from the Ardoyne Association was linked to her role as primary carer for her disabled daughter. This was contrary to the Disability Discrimination Act 1995, it said. Ms McKeith worked part-time for the association from 2010 until she was dismissed in March 2015. The tribunal said she had been unfairly dismissed and that the Ardoyne Association "did not put forward any convincing or coherent explanation for its decision." In her managers' minds, "because the claimant had a disabled child, her position was not properly in the workplace. Her daughter was'her priority'," it ruled. "That is not the legal position," it said. "People who are disabled themselves, or who are the primary carer of a disabled person, have a right to work within the protection afforded by the 1995 Act." The finding was appealed by the Ardoyne Association but the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. Maria McKeith said she was left in shock when she was made redundant. "I did not ask for any special treatment and I did not welcome it," she said. "I enjoyed coming to work, meeting people and being able to advise and help them and I knew my daughter was being cared for while I was at work. The tribunal awarded her PS10,000 for injury to feelings, PS6,760 for loss of earnings, and a total of PS2,126 in interest. Dr Michael Wardlow, Chief Commissioner of the Equality Commission said employers needed to be aware of their responsibilities. "The Disability Discrimination Act protects people against discrimination because of their disability," he said. It also protects people in Ms McKeith's position, who have a role as primary carer for a disabled person. "In this case, Ms McKeith was denied the opportunity to work as a result of her daughter's disability," he said. "The law makes such discrimination unlawful. "It is important also, as was referenced in these proceedings, to highlight that the purpose of the law is to assist disabled people and their primary carers to obtain work and to integrate them in to the workplace. "That is not a matter simply of money, but the dignity of, and the respect due to, the people concerned."

The use of microteaching and standardized students has the potential to aid in the professional growth and development of clinical teachers. Microteaching is a technique of teaching whereby a teacher delivers a brief lesson to a small gathering of learners, typically peers or other educators, and then receives feedback and possible suggestions for improvement. In this method, educators can enhance their teaching approaches in an amicable and helpful atmosphere. Microteaching in clinical teaching provides a useful way for faculty to enhance their teaching abilities, gain constructive criticism, and integrate innovative instructional techniques. On the contrary, standardized individuals are people who receive instruction on portraying and acting as patients while undergoing clinical training. The faculty gets an opportunity to hone their teaching skills by working with a steady and regulated group of "patients." This method assists in promoting a learning atmosphere that is more varied and participatory, as well as providing prompt feedback to teachers concerning their pedagogical approaches and communication proficiencies. Clinical educators can improve their teaching skills by using microteaching and standardized students simultaneously, which can result in better educational experiences for their students. Educators can help their students by cultivating valuable skills in communication, problem-solving, and clinical assessment through the provision of a secure and encouraging practice environment.

Since the fluid utilized in the system absorbs heat from its surroundings due to its lower temperature compared to the external environment while simultaneously emitting heat during the release phase because it has a higher temperature relative to the interior setting, the necessary arrangement would be as follows: Hot Operating Temperature - Indoor Room Temperature - Ambient Temperature - Cold Operating Temperature. This setup involves using a substance with a low boiling point as the working fluid. Initially, it gains thermal energy from outdoor air, then through compression, elevates in temperature surpassing the internal climate. Consequently, the acquired warmth dissipates within the building upon condensation, even though the fluid remains under significant pressure. To revert to its initial state, the fluid experiences a reduction in pressure via a throttle mechanism before restarting the sequence. Interestingly, refrigerators operate based on a similar principle.

As long as the exterior temperature isn't absolute zero, some amount of thermal energy exists in the atmosphere. Heat pumps and air conditioners rely on an identical concept involving two sets of coils—one located indoors and another positioned externally. A circulating refrrightant transitions between these coils depending on the system's operation. Normally a gas at ambient temperatures and standard pressure levels, the refrigerant becomes a liquid after compression by the device intended for indoor use. Liquid molecules exhibit reduced motion compared to their gaseous counterparts, resulting in decreased kinetic energy and consequent heat emission as the liquid warms considerably. This heat is then transferred to the indoor coil, subsequently dispersed throughout the living space by a fan. Upon reaching the outdoor coil, the refrigerant decompresses, reverting to a gaseous form and becoming substantially colder than the surrounding air. Subsequently, the chilled air interacts with the refrigerant, causing it to absorb thermal energy, which eventually returns to the interior as part of the refrigerant transforms back into a liquid during subsequent compression cycles. Reverse operations occur within air conditioners to achieve cooling effects instead.

Unlike the traditional dock-based systems, dockless bike-sharing systems are more convenient for users in terms of flexibility. However, the flexibility of these dockless systems comes at the cost of management and operation complexity. Indeed, the imbalanced and dynamic use of bikes leads to mandatory rebalancing operations, which impose a critical need for effective bike traffic flow prediction. While efforts have been made in developing traffic flow prediction models, existing approaches lack interpretability, and thus have limited value in practical deployment. To this end, we propose an Interpretable Bike Flow Prediction (IBFP) framework, which can provide effective bike flow prediction with interpretable traffic patterns. Specifically, by dividing the urban area into regions according to flow density, we first model the spatio-temporal bike flows between regions with graph regularized sparse representation, where graph Laplacian is used as a smooth operator to preserve the commonalities of the periodic data structure. Then, we extract traffic patterns from bike flows using subspace clustering with sparse representation to construct interpretable base matrices. Moreover, the bike flows can be predicted with the interpretable base matrices and learned parameters. Finally, experimental results on real-world data show the advantages of the IBFP method for flow prediction in dockless bike sharing systems. In addition, the interpretability of our flow pattern exploitation is further illustrated through a case study where IBFP provides valuable insights into bike flow analysis.

I saw the bright of morning before I even opened my eyes. I lay in my bed, in the fetal position, the dog curled at my knees. As I opened my eyes, I felt a tinge of fear, as was common most mornings. The surprise of looking at your own face unexpectedly never really wears off. My sister Angelina had an accident driving home from work when she was studying in undergrad. My parents mourned her death during continual trips to reproductive specialists, determined to replace one dead daughter with another. They poured hundreds of thousands into recreating their golden child, the one with social grace and a dazzling smile. I wasn't a black sheep by any means, but in comparison to Angelina, I was always a little substandard. Instead of pursuing college after high school, I worked at selling photos I'd taken around the city I lived in. Angelina stayed home while going to a prestigious local university; I bartended evenings while working on my portfolio in a shitty studio in LA. My conservative parents, both professors, did not approve. When Little Angie was born with light brown hair, not black like Angelina's was at birth, my mother nearly cried. As Little A progressed, my mother left Angelina's baby book on the coffee table, meticulously comparing her milestones. Little A's first smile and sneeze nearly mirrored the age of firsts outlined in my baby book. At first my mother didn't want to accept that Little A showed traits I had at her age. Mother insisted that she had mistakenly taken her accomplishments down in my book. When raising twin girls, you sometimes get things a little backwards. My mother eventually accepted that Little Angie was in fact a Little Ophelia, around her second birthday. She tried and failed to sue the specialists who performed Little A's gene therapy, draining the little remaining money she and my father had saved for retirement. By Little A's third birthday, mother withdrew from the world. She had to stop teaching, my often heard her talking aloud to Angelina around the house. Mother left Little A's care to my father, who begrudgingly cared for her while I worked. Weekdays she slept at my house, weekends in the guest room at my parent's house. My father had no desire to care for a child whose appearance took my mother's sanity. When my mother was committed, my father took Little A to my house. He handed me a check to cover rent for a year, the baby, and the key to his honda. The trunk was filled with all her clothes, bottles, and food. I pulled my blanket off my legs, looked at A, and sighed. She's an early riser like me. Just before she opened her eyes, I noticed her laying on her side, legs tucked to her chest, our pup curled at her knees.

People process their environment using their I.Q. and their emotional intelligence. Language skills are particularly important. If someoneone doesn't have a word for something, they can neither process nor remember it. (This is why you cannot recall your infancy. You did not yet have an active vocabulary to categorize and process the things you were seeing and experiencing.) Typically, a person with Down Syndrome has an I.Q. aproximating that of a child 8 years of age or younger. This means that they also have the vocabulary and reasoning ability of a very young child. Also, much like young children, Down Syndrome people may not have a clear division between the two hemispheres of the brain (as a normal adult does). This inhibits their ability to distinguish between fantasy an reality, between the truth and a lie. The creative side of their brain and the logic center do not correctly categorize information. Also, the transference of learned information from the short term memory to long term memory is compromised in Down Syndrome people. This is why they have difficulty learning new information and skills, and may not recall things like family vacations or certain birthdays unless something unusual happened that would act as a "place marker" to assist in categorizing the memory.', "Aside from the obvious physical problems, people with Down's are usually not exposed to the same kinds of harsh realities as people who function normally. For instance, it's rare to see someone with Down's worried about how they're going to pay their bills, whether or not their job is fulfilling, whether or not they have any real friends, etc. People generally are friendly when interacting with people who have Down's, so they're usually surrounded by a more cheerful atmosphere. Understanding the formation of subjective human traits, such as preference and opinions, is an important, but poorly explored problem. An essential aspect is that traits collectively evolve under the repeated influence of experience (i.e., they are "evolvable. Here we propose a simple model for evolvability by considering only the interactions between genetic variants encoding personality dimensions and their heritability (as a function of environment), rather than also including the interplay with environmental factors (such as parenting style or educational attainment) known to play a role in shaping individual differences. We argue that our approach improves upon other currently used approaches which attempt to incorporate broader environmental influences on trait variation into models of evolution. Abstract: Evolutionary psychology has been dominated recently by studies attempting to explain how genes can vary across individuals even though their environments are similar enough not to be expected to account for this pattern. The traditional view was that these patterns were due to inherited variance covarient with non-shared environmental effects (ESEEs), which have since become increasingly discredited; however, there remains a need to understand why some people share more similarities in personality over time despite sharing similar backgrounds. We suggest that these commonalities might instead arise from shared heritable components associated with certain aspects of personality that continue to interact with one another and change over generations. By modeling the interaction between genetics - represented through the dimension heritability - and the number of individuals exposed to specific experiences in each generation - modeled using exposure fraction - we show that evolving various aspects of personality requires heritability plus relative total exposure to relevant experiences. In contrast, ESEEs require neither heritability nor exposure fractionation. Our results clarify the important difference in requirements for explaining patterns of similarity among siblings who grow up together and find support for the idea that heritability alone cannot provide complete explanation of complex features of personality.

Well a server farm would have some serious AC going on so unless the power goes out a heatwave shouldn't be a problem even then if there's a power outage the servers wont be on anyways. Computers also aren't affected performance wise but stability wise by heat so you really only need to worry about keeping them from overheating not necessarily keeping them colder. Unless you pushing a computer to extremes (overclocking) just keeping it from overheating is enough and that's what most consumer computers are built to do. Now by stability we mean that when a computer get's to hot it will essentially start providing wrong answers to questions and thus eventually crash. earlier computers could actually get hot enough to cause physical damage but for a long time now modern processors have been designed to throttle themselves or even fully shutdown before they can even get anywhere close to being that hot so you really only have to worry about stability these days well that and not frying your processor with too much voltage again though this is generally only an issue for overclockers. Loss of stability happens because computers depend on electric signals traveling through the processors in a certain amount of time to function. This timing is based off the clock cycle of the processor and it's why processors have to be small to function so that the signal traveling distances stay manageable. As heat increases though these signals start to take longer to travel (resistance increases as heat does) and eventually they stop reaching their destination before the clock cycle rolls over. This causes errors in the processor at the binary level. Something that should have been a 1 might end up reading as a 0 and vice versa. These errors will cause issues in the software and eventually lead to a crash because proper continued functioning of a computer depends on the processor producing accurate results.

Crowd flow prediction has been increasingly investigated in intelligent urban computing field as a fundamental component of urban management system. The most challenging part of predicting crowd flow is to estimate the speed and direction of crowds using various techniques, such as optical flow visualization. Optical flow visualization requires the person viewing the visualization to be facing, or at least looking directly into the camera lens, while they are moving (e.g., walking). In order to obtain data on time-varying changes in velocity over time, it may also be necessary to perform rapid measurement. A few works have explored how to compute estimates from one or more images captured by telephoto lenses with cross-sectional imaging systems. For example, U.S. Pat. No. 6,716,488 B1 provides an image processing method for estimating population density in real time by acquiring images from different points along a street with two cameras and calculating average differences between them based upon changes in light intensity due to passing traffic. A time series of such images is then analyzed to determine when cross-sectional variations in intensity occur, so that real time calculations can be performed. U.S. Pat. Nos. 3,539,903; 4,163,372; 4,384,240; and 5,297,735 describe methods for obtaining estimates based on optical measurements taken for determining vehicle speeds across a road network but do not provide a means to calculate the estimated rates of change over time. Similarly, U.S. Pat. Nos. 2,843,683 and 4,183,482 disclose equipment used for estimating pedestrian speeds around an intersection but neither teaches nor suggests a scheme to use the measured velocities to infer the rate of change of various elements within the city environment.

The interior design of the International Space Station (ISS) is mainly based on functionality and safety considerations. The lack of gravity in space means that everything has to be carefully secured to prevent it from floating away and potentially damaging equipment or injuring crew members. Additionally, the ISS has limited space, so every object and piece of equipment needs to be carefully selected to ensure that it serves a functional purpose. That being said, efforts have been made to make the ISS feel more like a home. Crew members are allowed to bring personal items, such as photographs and mementos, with them to space. NASA has also experimented with adding greenery to the ISS, such as the Veggie experiment, which grew lettuce aboard the station. Finally, NASA has also experimented with colored LED lighting to help create a more soothing and comfortable environment, especially when crew members are working long hours. Overall, while the ISS may not look like a traditional "homely" environment, NASA has made efforts to ensure that it still feels welcoming and comfortable for the astronauts who live and work there.
