Urine isn't all that good for you. It's made up of water and some dissolved substances the body got rid of. These waste products make up a small part of what we ingest during our daily lives, but they are far from the only things we need to worry about in terms of sanitation. A University of Washington study published last year found that while most people don't think twice when it comes to their bodily fluids, experts say there is more than meets the eye-and this includes our toilet bowls. Although toilets may seem like an absolute must in modern society, researchers have found that many individuals still take surprisingly little care with them. The study was conducted by scientists at UW Medicine in Seattle and the UW School of Public Health, who relied on "a comprehensive survey of U.S. adults collected through online surveys." The findings were published recently in PLOS Biology: "Retention rates of faecal matter (FMC) from toilet bowls in nearly two-thirds of American households," according to PhysOrg.com. Researchers found that women were almost three times as likely to leave behind fecal matter in their homes compared to men. Women also said it took longer to flush their toilets after taking a dump versus using a public bathroom. That could be due to biological differences between the sexes or personal hygiene habits, however. "We might expect that flushing before making food preparations would increase FMC, because feces contain volatile components such as methane that cause gas emissions from landfills. But these gases tend not to produce odors or fogs indoors, so we did not find any associations between indoor FMC retention and odurant emission levels among households tested," explained lead author Sarah Bowman, PhD. Bowman added that the results could reflect other factors beyond human behavior. "There are environmental risks associated with indoor air pollution that affect septic systems and indoor humans. Perhaps these effects play a role in FMC retention." Many Americans still use single-use disposable diapers as a primary method of disposing of urine. In fact, approximately 19 million babies, toddlers, preschoolers, preteens, teens, postgraduate students, nursing home residents, and older persons use disposable diapers every day, according to the National Institute of Child Health and Human Development. The material can pose health concerns if flushed down the toilet instead of disposed of properly. Some people toss their used wipes in the trash or place them inside another item that may release toxic fumes into the environment. Older folks are just as guilty of leaving used medical instruments in sinks and under counters throughout their homes. Studies suggest that old pipes can contaminate groundwater if left unmonitored or ignored. This contamination can even result in disease outbreaks across several states. Other studies show that discarded medical supplies and pharmaceuticals on top of household garbage can cause problems within communities. Even so, less than half of U.S. citizens dispose of used medical equipment correctly, which means more than 5 billion pounds of these items enter the environment each year. It doesn't take much research time to connect dots regarding how often people leave their excrement around the house, but it does require extra effort to ensure you're following safe practices, regardless, says Wilson. He adds that one way to help keep your environment clean is simply to wash your hands frequently.

The growing popularity of Machine-to-Machine (M2M) communications in cellular networks is driving the need to optimize networks based on the characteristics of M2M, which are significantly different from the requirements that current networks are designed to meet. First, M2M requires large number of short sessions as opposed to small number of long lived sessions required by the human generated traffic. Second, M2M constitutes a number of battery operated devices that are static in locations such as basements and tunnels, and need to transmit at elevated powers compared to the traditional devices. Third, replacing or recharging batteries of such devices may not be feasible. All these differences highlight the importance of a systematic framework to study the power and energy optimal system design in the regime of interest for M2M, which is the main focus of this paper. For a variety of coordinated and uncoordinated transmission strategies, we derive results for the optimal transmit power, energy per bit, and the maximum load supported by the base station, leading to the following design guidelines: (i) frequency division multiple access (FDMA), including equal bandwidth allocation, is sum-power optimal in the asymptotically low spectral efficiency regime, (ii) while FDMA is the best practical strategy overall, uncoordinated code division multiple access (CDMA) is almost as good when the base station is lightly loaded, (iii) the value of optimization within FDMA is in general not significant in the regime of interest for M2M.

Everyone hates Comcast now, and Comcast either loses business (through its dislike with its customer base), or stops nickel-and-diming Netflix. We all hate when big business monopolizes. Net neutrality encourages monopolization through legal limits, and while it may seem that government regulation will preserve our internet, its important to remember that the internet has never been neutral, but nor has it been monopolized.

I had to applaud her; the tears on her wrinkled cheeks looked real. But I knew she was lying. The front of her car was wrapped around a lamp post, only two steps away from where I had been walking. She must have seen the shine in my hair, or the strut in my walk, and taken the dive. "Please she whimpered, gently nudging her car door open. I kicked the door shut, knocking her back into her seat. There was blood trickling down from her gray curls. "Please, I didn't mean to. It was an accident." I have to be honest; the tightness in her voice did something for me. A bug of empathy fluttered to life in my stomach. I flexed my abdominal muscles, newly-acquired from a twenty-year-old I found hiding out in a grocery store, and I crushed that fluttering bug until it was paste. "Please, you have to believe me. I have grandchildren," purple veins stood out as she struggled to pull a picture from inside her purse. She showed it to me, it's glossy finish tarnished with age. At the sight of the photograph, the bug fluttered back to life. Maybe she wasn't lying. There were three laughing kids, sitting one above the other on a slide. I don't know how old they were; it's been a long time since I've seen anyone that young. One of the kids was missing her front teeth. "How do I know they're yours?" "What?" she cupped her hand to her ear. Her eyes were huge in the lenses of her glasses. "I said," I leaned closer, "How do I know they're yours?" She gave me a warm smile, "Well, this one is Sara, and this is her younger brother Dav- HYYEEAAAAGH!" I leapt back as the blade of a knife darted out from the car. Instead of embedding in my stomach, it barely grazed my sweater. The old bitch swung her arm around a few more times, trying to snag me with her weapon, but I kicked her frail hand and the knife fell to the ground. She shoved open the door, and spilled out onto the ground. Her legs, broken, dragged behind her, and she crawled toward the knife. I stomped on her hand. She shrieked, and clawed at me with her other hand. With the butt of my firearm, I whipped her in the head. "Unph." That was all she said, like I'd somehow taken the wind from her lungs. The old woman laid still, and for a minute I thought it was another ruse. The front of the car was smoking, and it smelled like gasoline. "Hey," I nudged her with my boot, "Wake up." My boots felt heavier, and suddenly too large for my feet. I kicked her again, and she rolled over. Her old dress and the lower half of her face was covered in blood. She was grimacing, like she had just stuck her hand into something cold. "Fuck." I said to no one in particular. I could feel the arthritis settling into my bones. Now I have to go kill someone else.

Military chiefs in America have confirmed that a new, unmanned stealth bomber has successfully carried out its first test flight. The XQ-58A Valkyrie, developed by the US Air Force and Kratos Unmanned Aerial Systems, flew for just under an hour over Yuma Proving Ground in Arizona. The XQ-58A is designed as a low-cost, long-range, high subsonic cruise missile that could be used in long-range strikes and reconnaissance missions. It has been described by US Air Force officials as "the future of airpower." The aircraft was built using advanced composite materials, and is equipped with a range of sensors and avionics systems. It has a wingspan of 11 metres and a length of 8.2 metres, and weighs around 4,500kg. The pilotless craft is powered by a single turbofan engine and has a range of approximately 1,500km. This means it can fly further than many existing manned bombers. The successful test flight is seen as a major step forward for the US military's ambitions to develop unmanned systems. It follows the development of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) such as the MQ-9 Reaper and the RQ-4 Global Hawk, which are already being used in operations overseas. The XQ-58A is still in the early stages of development, and further flight tests will be needed to fully evaluate its performance. However, military experts say the successful first test is a significant milestone for the development of autonomous systems. If all goes to plan, the XQ-58A could soon join America's arsenal of unmanned strike and reconnaissance assets, providing the US military with a cost-effective solution for long-range missions.

That was why no one ever protested the Crucifixion - they were enraptured (often literally) by the most famous death in the Western world. It was fun to watch the tourists gather at more recent events - Obama, George VIII (then third in line), the Spratly Incident - and the media had simultaneously calmed down as it realized that certain events would be forgotten by history and turned up the sensation meter whenever there were lots of strange people crowding around a motorcade or a nuclear plant or whatever, especially if they were the sort that were mostly nude and kept talking about "the Event" and staring hungrily at supermarkets. Whenever some guy was walking along in the park followed by dozens of weirdos with cameras, the major networks and CNN would rush to the scene (unless that guy was Joseph Gordon-Levitt, in which case such following was normal, and people started guessing what was going to happen: "Oh, my God, that man there's going to shoot the President!" or "I don't think the waves will subside this time," and suchlike. I always wondered what I would do if such a thing happened to me, and then the clock struck 4:23 PM on August 28, 2023. I lived in a typical American household - myself (Arthur Weeks), husband (Jeremiah Weeks), 2.5 kids (Patricia, Sybil, and hn) - on a typical American street in a typical American town (New Bedford, Illinois), which I thought was the least likely setting for a major historical event. But then I spied with my little eye a gentleman wearing some sort of dress-thing trying to not be noticed behind a tree, and then a woman with long red hair setting up a folding chair, and then more and more people, and that was when I took my hand off the doorknob. "What are you here for?" I asked. They said nothing, but they were all keeping a bit of a distance from me. "I asked you a question!" I remembered that video I saw on the bystander effect, and I directed my next question towards the red-haired woman. "Why are you here? What is happening?" She merely put a finger to her lips and shook her head, indicating that she wasn't going to tell me, and the same was probably true for everyone else (at least, the ones who didn't want to face life in prison). I took out my gun - a handgun, nothing more, nothing you could shoot up a school with - and pointed it at one of the thin hungry people. "Why are you here? Why am I important?" There was still not a word from anyone, though some modern suburbanites were gathering around to witness a historical event live in action. I started turning around in the circle, and turned the safety off to show them I meant business. "If no one tells me what's about to happen, I will fire this gun and I will not take responsibility for the ensuing events. I have ten bullets." Still there was nothing, though the circle was shrinking backwards and a few had left. "All right, I'll give you to the count of five.." "One." "Two." "Three." "Four." "Five." One, two, three, four, five, six bullets were squeezed out in quick succession, and four tourists dropped to the ground. I couldn't tell whether they were dying or already dead, and frankly I didn't care. The others were starting to leave more rapidly now, with one of them remarking "Well, now we've seen everything." I fired two more shots, dropping two more people, and by then the others had already left. I walked towards the last person to be shot, a man who looked to be in his twenties. "Why did you come here?" I asked, though I'm not sure why I expected an answer when my previous iterations of the question had met with nothing. Coughing up blood, he was able to gasp out only the words "Look around you." A stunned realization came over me as my legs gave out from the shock of still only partially comprehending what I had just done. "Oh, my God. I fucked up. I fucked up so much." The key challenge in multiagent learning is learning a best response to the behaviour of other agents, which may be non-stationary: if the other agents adapt their strategy as well, the learning target moves. Disparate streams of research have approached non-stationarity from several angles, which make a variety of implicit assumptions that make it hard to keep an overview of the state of the art and to validate the innovation and significance of new works. This survey presents a coherent overview of work that addresses opponent-induced non-stationarity with tools from game theory, reinforcement learning and multi-armed bandits. Further, we reflect on the principle approaches how algorithms model and cope with this non-stationarity, arriving at a new framework and five categories (in increasing order of sophistication): ignore, forget, respond to target models, learn models, and theory of mind. A wide range of state-of-the-art algorithms is classified into a taxonomy, using these categories and key characteristics of the environment (e.g., observability) and adaptation behaviour of the opponents (e.g., smooth, abrupt). To clarify even further we present illustrative variations of one domain, contrasting the strengths and limitations of each category. Finally, we discuss in which environments the different approaches yield most merit, and point to promising avenues of future research.

The initial release by 3GPP regarding network slicing standards was introduced with Release 15. It outlined essential guidelines forming the basis of the standardized network slicing architecture; however, it did not include methods for maintaining continuous sessions across different slices, an integral aspect needed for seamless inter-slice movement. This study presents three strategies designed to facilitate session persistence within the existing 3GPP network slicing structure, leveraging prevalent and established standard techniques. Our first strategy employs the Return Routability Binding Update mechanism from the widely used Mobile IPv6 (MIPv6). The second strategy involves using the GPRS Tunneling Protocol User Plane (GTPv1-U), as defined by 3GPP, to create a tunneling link between preceding and succeeding slices for uninterrupted sessions. Lastly, our third approach combines aspects of both MIPv6-RRBU and GTPv1-U protocols into a single methodology. By conducting comparative analyses via mathematical modeling, we find that while the approaches incorporating GTPv1-U or the combined MIPv6/GTPv1-U exhibit reduced service interruption times, they also result in greater resource consumption and packet transmission expenses when contrasted against the MIPv6-RRBU technique and the conventional 3GPP Packet Data Unit Session Setup process.

In a recent interview with entrepreneur and former Apple executive, Tony Fadell, he unpacks the idea of how big companies kill innovation and what employees can do to combat it. According to Fadell, regardless of the size of the company or industry, the problem of stifling innovation is a common one. He claims that the primary reason big companies struggle to generate new ideas is that they are often focused on maintaining the status quo. Additionally, they can be reluctant to allocate resources to innovative projects or ideas when the return on investment is uncertain. Another major issue is the bureaucracy and red tape that come with large organizations. "The larger the company, the more process and politics can kick in, making it more challenging to drive new ideas and initiatives," says Fadell. However, Fadell believes that it's possible to fight back against these challenges and allow for innovation to happen. Here are a few tips he shared during the interview: 1. Embrace risk-taking: Failure is often seen as a negative in corporate culture, but Fadell says it's essential to take risks and learn from failures. Encourage employees to experiment and try new things, even if it's not always successful. 2. Empower employees: Fadell urges managers to trust their team members and give them the autonomy to innovate. The best ideas often come from the ground up, and empowering employees can create a culture where innovation can flourish. 3. Create a culture of openness: Fadell explains that it's essential to create a culture where employees feel comfortable sharing their ideas, even if they're not fully fleshed out. Encourage dialogue, collaboration, and constructive criticism and build a culture where all voices are heard. In conclusion, big companies should realize that innovation is not just an outcome, but it's a process. It requires patience, willingness to take risks and a culture where ideas are valued, and experimentation is encouraged. By adopting Fadell's tips, companies can foster an environment that promotes innovation and find ways to take advantage of new and emerging technologies that can help them stay ahead of the competition.

Radiation has the potential to unpredictably disrupt anything it encounters. In some cases, when exposed to radiation, genetic damage may cause cells to become malignant, leading to cancer. However, radiation therapy proves effective due to the rapid reproduction rate of cancer cells, making them highly vulnerable to radiation-induced harm. By directing multiple low-intensity radiation beams towards the tumor, causing significant damage at their convergence point, we aim to destroy the majority of cancerous cells. Although this approach may inadvertently affect healthy cells, the goal is to eliminate most of the tumor mass, allowing other treatments and medications to target any remaining cancer cells successfully. Essentially, radiation interferes with the normal growth signals within cells, prompting uncontrolled proliferation until the affected cells are destroyed through radiation therapy. This process concentrates on specifically damaging cancer cells while minimizing collateral damage to surrounding tissues.

In this paper, we study the waveform design problem for a single-input single-output (SISO) radio-frequency (RF) wireless power transfer (WPT) system in frequency-selective channels. First, based on the actual non-linear ity of SISO systems and the RF propagation channel model, we show that most energy is lost during transmission through impedance mismatch between the transmitter and antenna since their electric fields are strongly coupled to each other. Then using an approximate approximation scheme called MHDI, which uses parallel equations derived from Maxwell's equation, we derive new formulas for optimal WPT designs with minimal loss at high transmitter ratios. We also demonstrate that these idealized formulas can be used as starting points for designing practical solutions by providing simple numerical results. To assess whether our proposed models are valid, we apply them to solve a range of test problems generated from experiments conducted over a variety of frequencies in space and time domains. Our results suggest that our approach works well when applied to low-rate applications where long propagation times or constant radiated power levels exist.

The humpback has been seen at Pettycur Bay, Kinghorn in Fife. Humpback sightings are not uncommon in Scotland, but a large whale so far up the Forth estuary is a rare sight. Humpbacks travel up and down the east coast of Scotland throughout the summer, but this one is thought to be the first recorded so far up the Forth. Eileen Torrance, from St Andrews Aquarium, said: "It's been here for a few days now. It's quite a long way from the sea. "It's not unheard of for them to be here. But it's unusual." The humpback was first spotted by wildlife photographer Michael Pedgrift. He said: "I was just driving along the coast road by Pettycur Bay when I saw the humpback breaching so I pulled over right away. "I got my camera out and started taking pictures. I'm really glad I did because it's an amazing sight to see such a scruffy-looking creature doing what it does best."

In any courtroom setting, there are typically two types of lawyers - the prosecution aiming to establish guilt, and the defense striving to demonstrate innocence. The prosecution shoulders the responsibility of proving through evidence that the accused violated the law and warrants punishment. Converserally, the defense endeavors to refute the accusation, demonstrating the absence of wrongdoing or arguing against severe repercussions. Even if the defendant admits guilt privately to their counsel, the defense seeks to cast doubt on the prosecution’s ability to conclusively link the defendant to the offense. Additionally, they endeavor to lessen potential penalties by questioning the validity of evidence collection methods employed by the authorities. Ultimately, both parties seek to achieve the best possible outcome for their clients within our adversarial legal framework where each side vigorously contests opposing viewpoints, with the objective being to uncover the truth amidst varying degrees of culpability and appropriate sentencing.

The uncertainty surrounding the long-term health implications of sugar substitutes remains due to their relatively recent introduction, compared to the length of a human life span. Except for saccharin, which dates back approximately 130 years and was once deemed carcinogenic leading to its ban in various nations, these alternatives are newcomers. Several have already been phased out like cyclamate and aspartame, both linked to cancer concerns, causing skepticism among the public. Additionally, the complete understanding of how Splenda is processed by our bodies is lacking; although we comprehend where certain molecules go, others remain unknown. Emerging research suggests that these substitutes might trigger insulin spikes and consequent negative health impacts. From a natural perspective, traditional ingredients appear to be less detrimental to our wellbeing when consumed reasonably. Furthermore, there are three primary reasons why sugar continues to dominate over artificial sweeteners such as sugar and sucralose/aspartame: Firstly, their flavors differ significantly despite sharing sweetness. Secondly, producing sugar, particularly high fructose corn syrup in the US, incurs lower costs. Lastly, artificial sweeteners typically contain added fillers like maltodextrin, making them bulkier and reducing efficiency while increasing manufacturing expenses.

While the idea of using tranquilizer guns instead of firearms may seem like a humane solution, there are several reasons why it is not a viable option. First of all, tranquilizers take time to take effect, and during that time, the suspect could still pose a threat to themselves or others. In a dangerous situation where a suspect is threatening to harm others, immediate action is necessary, and tranquilizers may not be able to provide that. Additionally, the use of tranquilizers requires precise dosing, and incorrect dosage could lead to serious health complications, or death. This means that officers would need extensive training in using tranquilizer guns, which would be costly and time-consuming. It is also worth noting that tranquilizer guns would not be effective in situations where suspects are wearing thick clothing or armor, as the dart may not penetrate their clothing. In essence, while using tranquilizer guns may seem like an alternative to firearms, it is not a practical or safe solution for law enforcement.

New analysis for BBC News shows that many people relying on their savings income are worse off than ever before. Savings rates plummeted after the Bank of England slashed its base rate in the financial crisis. Since last autumn, as the economic outlook has worsened, they have fallen again. Tax-free Isas, fixed rate bonds and easy access accounts are all at or near their lowest points. In research carried out for the BBC, the rate-checking firm Savings Champion recorded 1,440 savings rate cuts last year and more than 230 so far this year. While low interest rates are welcomed by mortgage borrowers, they strike fear into those at or near retirement who had hoped that income from their nest eggs would help pay the bills. "There's no light at the end of the tunnel," says 76-year-old Mick Bridge, one of a group of ramblers from Chesterfield who all depend on savings. "Like most retired people, there was a plan and suddenly it's not like it was anymore. The pot's disappearing." Fellow walker Sharon Beresford is worried that low interest rates will leave more older people needing help to pay for care. "It's helping young people buy houses, but it's not helping me," she says, "There are a lot of us to be looked after." The fall in rates has come across the board, with significant reductions from National Savings Investments, Bank of Scotland, NatWest and Nationwide Building Society. The average return from the five best easy access accounts has dropped from more than 3 in 2012 to under 1.3. Tax-free Isa rates are at their lowest ever. The average variable rate Isa is down to 1, while a typical fixed-rate Isa pays 1.4. Another Chesterfield rambler, 63-year-old Judith Knowles, started dipping into her savings when she discovered she would have to wait for her state pension because women's pension ages were being raised. Low savings rates have forced her to dip in again. "It's worrying," she says. "I've had letters saying the rates are going down even more." Some rates of return are so tiny that savers can improve their situation by switching to a better offer. First Direct pays just 0.05 to customers in its Savings Account, while Santander has an Easy Isa with an interest rate of a mere 0.1. Anna Bowes, director of Savings Champion, traces the problem back to a decision by the previous Coalition government to supply banks with cheap money to boost their lending. "The competition between providers has been sucked out of the market," she explains, "They just don't need to raise money from savers any more, which has had a devastating impact." A spokesman for the British Bankers' Association said: "These have been frustrating times for savers. The Bank of England's base rate has remained at a record low for several years. "While this has been good news for borrowers, it has fostered a low-interest-rate environment which has not been easy for many savers to bear." The looming EU referendum has confused the outlook for savers, with George Osborne warning borrowers that a vote to leave could lead to higher interest rates and others speculating that uncertainty could prompt the Bank of England to cut its base rate again. Behind the scenes, senior bankers warn that very low savings rates are likely to be the "new normal," given the precarious economic situation across the world.

According to Tabatabaei, there are acceptable and unacceptable esoteric interpretations. Acceptable ta'wil refers to the meaning of a verse beyond its literal meaning; rather the implicit meaning, which ultimately is known only to God and can't be comprehended directly through human thought alone. The verses in question here refer to the human qualities of coming, going, sitting, satisfaction, anger and sorrow, which are apparently attributed to God. Unacceptable ta'wil is where one "transfers" the apparent meaning of a verse to a different meaning by means of a proof; this method is not without obvious inconsistencies. Although this unacceptable ta'wil has gained considerable acceptance, it is incorrect and cannot be applied to the Quranic verses. The correct interpretation is that reality a verse refers to. It is found in all verses, the decisive and the ambiguous alike; it is not a sort of a meaning of the word; it is a fact that is too sublime for words. God has dressed them with words to bring them a bit nearer to our minds; in this respect they are like proverbs that are used to create a picture in the mind, and thus help the hearer to clearly grasp the intended idea.

Sharding has emerged as one of the common techniques to address the scalability problems of blockchain systems. To this end, various sharding techniques for blockchain systems have been proposed in the literature. When sharded blockchains process personal data, the data controllers and the data processors associated with the sharded blockchains need to be compliant with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). To this end, this article makes the first attempt to address the following key question: to what extent the existing techniques developed by different communities such as the distributed computing community, the distributed systems community, the database community, identity and access control community and the dependability community can be used by the data controllers and data processors for complying with the GDPR requirements of data subject rights in sharded blockchains? As part of answering this question, this article argues that there is a need for cross-disciplinary research towards finding optimal solutions for implementing the data subject rights in sharded blockchains.

The towers were self-contained enclaves, shining monuments of man's brutalist urban designs, and vertical remindersenforcers of man's self-destructive need to socially stratify. James had grown up on the 22nd floor. But he was a big boy now. He could probably handle the stairs and the novelty of being able to walk through the tower after work without worrying about falling down and cracking his skull open like a walnut. He caught glimpses of the long staircases that led upward from the lower levels. It would take him an hour or two to get all the way back, but it still seemed like such a short trip. The once bustling streets became somewhat empty, but they weren't so deserted as to be dangerous either. There wasn't any signposts guiding people along the path to their destination. It must have been around midnight when someone finally decided to follow them up, watching for robberies and other criminal activity. The hotel was just across the street, right in front of the empty lot where the old Sears Roebuck store used to stand. James didn't know what was going on at that particular moment. All he knew was that the place had boarded over into an abandoned building which looked quite ominous. In fact, everything about the place looked ominous except for the large steel bars covering the huge windows. The night was clear and cold with no wind, making it feel almost like Christmas morning. A few years ago, before the economy went south, there had been a lot more people wandering this area looking for jobs. Now that's gone and everyone seems desperate to stay afloat instead of trying to make some money off of a collapsing economy. This lack of traffic even made it hard to hear each other. It was a little eerie not knowing who you might run into down here. Maybe if there was a sign saying "We're Closed" or something like that? The elevator doors opened and he lowered himself onto the concrete floor. He took one look around and then grabbed onto a railing near the bottom of the escalator. When pushed upwards, it slowly began to move. Although it felt kind of slow at first, it soon picked up speed again until it reached the top and stopped. For just a second, he thought maybe he should hang on for dear life because he wouldn't be moving anymore very soon. But he managed to hold on for himself. His legs got tired fairly quick and he couldn't keep going forever. At least not without getting too close to the edge. It only takes a couple seconds to hop down a flight of stairs on this thing. Still though, he thought, I can go faster... And he did! He started picking up speed and as fast as he could go. He traveled 45 feet per minute and eventually came to a stop in front of the reception desk. After entering his name and receiving his room key, he turned around to see a nice, young blonde woman sitting next to her computer looking at the clock on her wall. She smiled warmly and waved her hand in greeting. James hadn't spoken much since he arrived at the hotel. As far as anyone knew, he slept most of the time. So when she spoke to him, it kind of startled him a bit. "Miss?" James asked politely. "Yes," she said flippantly, "what are you doing here?" She gestured toward the door and motioned him inside. "I'm sure your night got... interesting." A small smile appeared on James' face. Well, actually it looked more like a grimace than anything else. "Yeah..." he admitted quietly. She stared at him intently and waited patiently for another answer. Eventually James released a sigh and shrugged. "Well...it depends on how you slice it. You don't really want me talking to you anyways." She nodded briefly. "Okay," she agreed oblivious to James' expression, "you seem upset." She glanced away quickly at the clock on the wall. "Is it too late to come out for dinner?" James shook his head. "No. I'll just wait outside." He extended his hand in invitation. "Say hi to Elsie for me. She always has a great meal waiting inside." She walked ahead of him down the hall towards the main entrance. James gave her a wave goodbye as he headed down the halls. Just a few minutes later, he heard her say hello to Elsie. Then he saw her leave through the door. Smiling slightly, he stepped out onto the sidewalk and watched her disappear behind it.

The agents are assumed to be fed by self and neighboring output measurements, while the states are not available from any independent measurement. We find that the network of agents shared in the network can be described as a modified form of 'collective forked' indexing (CCI). To translate the CCI into an abstract framework we will evaluate the CCI model from the acquired data extracted by RTP-ranked (RF) networks. A comparison of the CCI model between the acquired data of four identified target subgroups (JU, UCI, JUI and JUSY), as well as two other types of indices (SVSRM) shows that CCI models differ significantly from each other. Neural networks have been a topic of significant interest among scholars seeking to enhance the efficacy of their training techniques. While stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and analogous gradient-based approaches remain prevalent, they encounter persistent issues like diminished gradients and minute learning rates, resulting in sluggish progress and volatility within SEE algorithms. Inspired by error backpropagation (BP) and proximal strategies, our team introduces an innovative semi-implicit backpropagation technique designed to refine neural network training processes. This approach mirrors traditional BP by advancing errors backwards through neurons while updating parameters via proximal mapping. By incorporating implicit updates across hidden neurons and parameters, it enables larger step sizes during training. Additionally, evidence shows that every stable solution derived from this method corresponds to a stationary point of the target loss function. Empirical tests on MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets reveal that our novel semi-implicit BP surpasses both SGD and a comparable ProxBP algorithm in enhancing loss reduction and validation accuracy throughout training.

A man from an unspecified U.S. state received a prison sentence for raping and killing a child under one year old. Some people criticized the leniency of the punishment, arguing that a life sentence would be more appropriate. Conversely, there are instances where individuals in countries such as India receive harsher penalties for extreme acts of violence, yet others suggest they deserve to spend their lives in prison instead. While some may perceive my stance as supporting capital punishment, I want to clarify my perspective. When an irreplaceable loss occurs, retribution rather than justice becomes the prevailing option. For example, if someone steals a valuable item from your home, you cannot fully recover what was taken even if caught and prosecuted. Similarly, victims of severe physical assault cannot regain their previous state through punishment alone. Therefore, although I believe in holding criminals accountable, I question the notion of justice being served in cases involving grievous harm. Our research introduces a machine learning (ML)-based strategy to differentiate between eruption and pre-eruption indicators of Chimayo geyser (located in New Mexico, USA), even amidst noisy surroundings. Given its similarity to CO2 injection into shallow water aquifers, examining this geyser provides insperience about the emergence of CO2-laden fluids from below, which holds significance for leak surveillance within a CO2 storage initiative. Although methods like Random Forests (RF) have proven effective as resilient multiclass classifiers operating optimally in suboptimal noisy settings, their effectiveness remains uncertain when applied to CO2-induced geysers. In pursuit of assessing the efficacy of RF-based classifiers in identifying geyser states, our investigation commences by detailing the seismic information procured via a nearby sensor installed at the geyser site. These recordings include various disturbances stemming from factors such as diurnal temperature shifts, seasonal patterns, wildlife movements, and human activities. To eliminate extraneous noise while preserving pertinent precursor and eruption signals, we implement a sequential combination of the Butterworth-Highpass filter alongside an AutoRegressive technique. Subsequently, we apply RF analysis on the processed data to categorize the geyser condition into one of three categories: residual noise, precursor stage, or eruption phase. Results demonstrate over 90% precision achieved through RF on the cleansed dataset. Thus, our ML model presents promising applications for distinguishing events and enhancing signals under challenging acoustic environments, particularly beneficial for tracking breaches during CO2 confinement projects.

Algorithmic statistics has two different (and almost orthogonal) motivations. From the philosophical point of view, it tries to formalize how the statistics works and why some statistical models are better than others. After this notion of a "good model" is introduced, a natural question arises: it is possible that for some piece of data there is no good model? If yes, how often these bad (non-stochastic) data appear "in real life"? Another, more technical motivation comes from algorithmic information theory. In this theory a notion of complexity of a finite object (amount of information in this object) is introduced; it assigns to every object some number, called its algorithmic complexity (or Kolmogorov complexity). Algorithmic statistic provides a more fine-grained classification: for each finite object some curve is defined that characterizes its behavior. It turns out that several different definitions give (approximately) the same curve. 1 1 footnote 1 Road-map: Section considers the notion of (a, b) -stochasticity; Section considers two-part descriptions and the so-called "minimal description length principle"; Section gives one more approach: we consider the list of objects of bounded complexity and measure how far some object is from the end of the list, getting some natural class of "standard descriptions" as a by-product; finally, Section establishes a connection between these notions and resource-bounded complexity. The rest of the paper deals with an attempts to make theory close to practice by considering restricted classes of description (Section) and strong models (Section). In this survey we try to provide an exposition of the main results in the field (including full proofs for the most important ones), as well as some historical comments. We assume that the reader is familiar with the main notions of algorithmic information (Kolmogorov complexity) theory. An exposition can be found in [, chapters 1, 3, 4] or [, chapters 2, 3], see also the survey. In this extended abstract we present the gubs Upper Bound Solver. gubs is a dedicated constraint solver over the naturals for inequalities formed over uninterpreted function symbols and standard arithmetic operators, where the operator symbols are defined by an orthogonal matrix of rational coefficients. We prove that gubs can solve all problems in differential geometry and estimation based on finite difference methods (with respect to a given set of constraints). In particular, there exists some arbitrary function symbol which satisfies several sets of non-trivial equations, while maintaining a natural form. The resulting solutions satisfy all practical constraints, at the same time preserving their natural form. We discuss the application of this solver to two important applications: routine problem formulation using mononormality assumptions; and the representation of strictly bounded systems in geometrical space

We present a dictionary learning approach to compensate for the transformation of faces due to changes in view point, illumination, resolution, etc. The key idea of our approach is to force domain-invariant sparse coding, i.e., design a consistent sparse representation of the same face in different domains. In this way, classifiers trained on the sparse codes in the source domain consisting of frontal faces for example can be applied to the target domain (consisting of faces in different poses, illumination conditions, etc) without much loss in recognition accuracy. The approach is to first learn a domain base dictionary, and then describe each domain shift (identity, pose, illumination) using a sparse representation over the base dictionary. The dictionary adapted to each domain is expressed as sparse linear combinations of the base dictionary. In the context of face recognition, with the proposed compositional dictionary approach, a face image can be decomposed into sparse representations for a given subject, pose and illumination respectively. This approach has three advantages: first, the extracted sparse representation for a subject is consistent across domains and enables pose and illumination insensitive face recognition. Second, sparse representations for pose and illumination can subsequently be used to estimate the pose and illumination condition of a face image. Finally, by composing sparse representations for subject and the different domains, we can also perform pose alignment and illumination normalization. Extensive experiments using two public face datasets are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach for face recognition.

Individuals in various stages of transition, such as trans women unable to assimilate into cisgender groups, transgender youth, and those whose trans status is widely recognized in settings like work, face significant challenges. Those who seamlessly integrate within cisgender communities likely avoid harassment. However, trans individuals whose ability to blend remains uncertain could encounter confrontations in facilities like restrooms if others suspect their gender identity. Particularly vulnerable are trans women who cannot pass as cisgender, trans youth in well-informed school environments, and trans colleagues facing hostility in the workplace. Achieving complete concealment is arduous both emotionally—constantly fearing exposure through interactions—and practically—altering aspects of one’s life to evade recognition by altering location, career paths, or cutting ties on social platforms. Furthermore, should any undisclosed aspect of their past emerge, it poses additional risks. 

Additionally, legislation mandates that educational institutions prevent individuals assigned a certain biological sex from utilizing facilities designated for another. Schools must ensure transgender students adhere to restrooms corresponding with their assigned sex. Although these laws don't specify repercussions for violators, potential consequences include financial sanctions. Given that schools possess access to birth records, compliance is enforceable.

This research focuses on creating an easily implemented distributed graph visualization algorithm suitable for processing extensive graphs without necessitating significant hardware or software expenditure. Our approach involves developing, executing, and testing a force-directed algorithm within the Giraph environment - a widely-used open-source distributed computing framework utilizing a vertex-centric methodology. Tests were conducted on both genuine and synthetic graphs comprising up to a million edges through a cost-effective Amazon PaaS infrastructure. Results demonstrate the efficiency and scalability of our solution relative to a conventional centralized version of the same force-directed algorithm. Our findings reveal that it takes under eight minutes to render graphs containing approximately one million edges while incurring around $1 in cloud computing costs.

In most contemporary learning-based tracking methods, costly annotations are required for optimal results. Conversely, the Lucas-Kanade (LK) technique functions effectively even without annotations. Nevertheless, it relies heavily on the brightness constancy principle within the imagery and can easily deviate due to significant movement, occlusions, or the aperture dilemma. To diminish these constraints and reduce the likelihood of deviation, we introduce CyLKs, an innovative method for teaching the Lucas-Kanade approach in an autonomous fashion. By employing CyLKs, we utilize CNNs to learn a feature transformation that renders the input visuals into a more conducive feature environment for LK tracking. Throughout the training phase, we execute differential Lucas-Kanade operations both forward and backward across the convolutional feature maps before aiming to lower the reprojection discrepancy. When evaluating, the LK tracking operates on the acquired features. Our application involves landmark tracking tasks, with tests conducted using THUMOS and pta=300VW datasets.

Angiogenesis leads to the formation of new blood vessels that link the arterial and venous systems within an amputated stump. Contrary to common belief, blood flow doesn't extend to every part of our limbs. For instance, the blood supply to your biceps diverges from the primary artery, proceeds through its course, and ultimately joins with the principal returning vein, bypassing the forearm entirely. This particular route remains intact even if you were to undergo a forearm amputation. 

Capillaries serve as the sites where nutrient and gas exchanges occur; they essentially facilitate communication between larger arteries and veins. Think of it like this - just because there's congestion on a highway doesn't imply that smaller streets will become unusable. In fact, capillaries branch out extensively throughout the body, and additional blood vessels can develop when necessary.

The World Economic Forum's'Future of Jobs Report' surveys corporate executives in 35 countries around the world about how they think the workforce will change in the next five years. Its findings show that while automation may bring job loss in some areas, new jobs will also be created for human workers. Businesses across the world expect to reduce their number of permanent employees and increase the use of freelance workers and automation. The World Economic Forum's (WEF) 'Future of Jobs Report' surveyed 350 executives across 15 of the world's largest economies, as well as 20 developed and emerging economies, to find out how they thought the workforce would change in the next five years. Overall, 53 of executives said their company will have fewer full-time employees in five years' time, while 44 expect to have more freelancers, contractors, and temporary staff. The survey also found that 62 of firms expected to have more automation in their workplace within the next five years, and 74 expect to have expanded their use of gig workers. In terms of the skills required by businesses in the future, there were some unexpected findings. While technical skills and capabilities remain a priority for most executives, some other skills, such as creativity and social intelligence, are expected to rise in importance, too. "The workforce of the future will need to align its skillset to keep up with these changes," the report said. "This means that technical skills, such as programming, app development, and data analysis, will be highly valued, alongside other skills such as creativity, originality, and initiative. In an age of automation and outsourcing, distinctively 'human' skills such as social and emotional intelligence, leadership, and creativity are increasingly valuable." However, the report also found that businesses believe the workforce is unprepared for the changes ahead. "Businesses in every industry expect to create new roles in the next five years, but the growth will be unevenly distributed across industries," the report said. "Furthermore, while executives expect the pace of innovation to increase, the majority (85) do not believe that their organizations are ready to harness the benefits of these advances." We've highlighted the most important findings from the report below. Businesses across the world expect to cut their permanent staff and expand their use of freelancers. Source: World Economic ForumFuture of Jobs Report In terms of skills, executives said that technical skills will be a priority in the future. "Technical skills and capabilities will remain a priority for all industries, particularly for those that already employ large numbers of highly skilled workers," the report said. These skills include app development, programming, and data analysis. "Technical skills such as programming and data analysis are also identified as critical for many roles, as are skills that will enable people to effectively harness the benefits of technology, such as user experience design," the report said. "The ability to analyze, organize, and evaluate information are also highlighted as key skills that will be required across roles." However, some other skills are also expected to become more important as more automation enters the workforce. From video streaming to security and surveillance applications, video data play an important role in our daily living today. However, managing a large amount of video data and retrieving the right information from it is still more difficult than expected due to the complexity of human vision. This thesis addresses this challenge by introducing multiple video feature extraction methods that are capable of extracting features for different purposes such as motion detection or semantic segmentation from videos. The proposed algorithms have been tested on synthetic datasets with varying degrees of realism to determine which approaches work best under certain conditions. Additionally, these new algorithms are compared against several existing state-of-the-art solutions such as YOLO cite1, VISION cite19, STRIDE cite21. The baseline method used in this research aims at improving upon the widely known YOLO algorithm. In order to accomplish this goal a novel dimensionality reduction technique called SRMs (Scale Reducing Mapping) was introduced. In addition to being faster than YOLO, SRM allows us to focus better when designing features through its unsupervised nature. Furthermore, another notable improvement over YOLO comes in the form of an interactive mode where users can easily change their selection of keyframes via mouse movements. Other improvements include introducing a variable frame rate user interface so that we can preserve high quality images while reducing file size. Another approach examined in this work focuses on spatial-temporal difference learning, also known as STDL cite3. Instead of using hand crafted features like many other approaches do, MRF cite4 provides a framework that learns the discriminative properties between videos automatically based solely on the temporal content. To recognize certain regions of interest within videos, VLDA cite20 uses attentional mechanisms similar to what has already been described in various works including SLIC cite17. These two methods were specifically applied to detecting pedestrians both indoors and outdoors in real life settings during daytime and nighttime respectively. For indoor pedestrian detection, the results provided here indicate that outdoor performance may not be affected much if any since there are fewer shadows available for use. Another interesting finding from this analysis indicates that attentional systems perform slightly worse than visual similarity measures even though they seem intuitively simpler and more robust for use in low lighting environments.

Lots of ways. Here are some examples: Poetry - poetry, puns, and other sorts of "language play" often directly involve the sounds of spoken language. Look at English rhyming poetry from the 16th-18th centuries, for instance, and you'll often find a bunch of rhymes that don't seem to work, such as rhyming something like "love" and "move." This sort of thing implies that the words rhymed at the time. Similarly, we can learn about things like stress from poetic meter. Misspellings - even people 2000 years ago misspelled. Someone a thousand years from now could see that "should have" is often misspelled "should of," and could reasonably conclude that both phrases are (at least in some contexts) pronounced identically. SpeechWriting Guides - on a related note, even people 2000 years ago were annoyed when other people misspelled or used "improper" grammar or pronunciation. There are several well-known pronunciation guides for Classical Latin that simply list the ways people pronounce words "incorrectly" and how they should properly be pronounced. The Comparative Method - one of the most important techniques used by historical linguistics, this essentially entails combining our knowledge of how sounds tend to change in languages with our knowledge of existing descendants of the language in question. As a simple example, we know that in Vulgar Latin (the language of the common people, as opposed to literary Classical Latin), the consonant H was frequently dropped entirely, as is evidenced by the fact that all of the Romance languages have lost Latin H (and it is far more likely that this consonant was lost back when everyone was still speaking the same language, rather than positing that the exact same change happened individually in each of the Romance languages). Borrowings - when a word in Language A is borrowed into Language B, it is now (usually) exempt from any future pronunciation changes in Language A. Both "castle" and "chateau" come from the French word, but were borrowed into English several centuries apart. The much older "castle" makes it clear that the French word originally started with a k sound, even though the modern French word begins with S sh. I'm no expert in Ancient Egyptian, but my understanding is our knowledge of its pronunciation largely comes from a combination of foreign borrowings, examination of its descendants (Coptic, which was written with an alphabet and is still in use in a liturgical context by Coptic Christians in Egypt), and some degree of internal reconstruction based on our knowledge of the somewhat-distantly-related Semitic languages. However, Egyptological tradition predates modern historical linguistics, so most Egyptologists actually use a special scheme that is not intended to accurately portray the original pronunciation, consisting mostly of pronouncing the glyph for "Y" as i ee, "W" as u oo, and inserting e eh wherever needed to render the word pronounceable. In this particular case, most of the ways you usually hear Egyptian names pronounced are probably not very accurate historically, at least as far as vowels are concerned. We have a fairly good idea of how Ancient Egyptian consonants were pronounced given how various well-known non-Egyptian names were rendered in hieroglyphs.', "In some cases, we don't. A PID controller takes input, processes it, determines the current "error" (or the deviation from what the input is, to where it should be), and then issues a command to try to correct the error. For example, imagine a controller that tries to maintain a level flight for a quadcopter. Its input might be the angle of flight. If the angle of flight is not horizontal, then there is an error, and the PID controller will issue a command to try to correct it. The main reason PID controllers work so well is that they don't just look at the current error. They look at the accumulation of past errors, as well as a prediction of future errors. This allows the command the controller issues to be much more precise.

It seemed to last an eternity, the sharp, pinching bite, the hot, steamy blood, and then the cold, unforgiving nothingness. It was as if I had been like that for years, decades, centuries. And then I was back, but not..... there. Who is that? I think, looking at a familiar cadaver. Oh my god! That's..... I cover my mouth with my hand in disbelief. It's me. I whisper. The corpse began to stir, rising back up..... but..... it wasn't me. It stood there for half a second, then immediately ran out of the building I was in, straight to the nearest living thing. My eyes widened as I came to the realization of exactly who that was. I run ahead of myself to my family "Get the hell out of here!" I shout, "What in god's name are you waiting for, goddammit!?" Then I saw their faces. Tears streaming down their face, their lips pouted, and their brows furrowed. They knew. They knew what happened. They knew what was about to happen. They all knew. They didn't even jump when I broke down the door. All they did was look in horror, because not only were they going to die a horrible, painful death, followed by an eternity of unrest, but it was going to be by their father's, their brother's, and their husband's hands. In their eyes I saw the thing that will never leave me. It was not only dread, not just horror..... but also betrayal. It was me! Out of millions of undead, I was the one to end their lives. I was the one who tore out my brother's eyes. I was the one to take a chunk out of my wife's thigh. I was the one that ripped out my little girl's heart and eat it in front of her dying mother. I was the last thing that they saw.

Six other people, including Bobby Storey, Sinn Fein's northern chairman, will also not face charges linked to the 1972 killing. Jean McConville, 37, a widow, was abducted from her west Belfast home, shot and secretly buried. Mr Adams said the decision was "long overdue." "There was never any real basis for questioning me in respect of this case. I played no act or part in Jean McConville's death," he said. Mrs McConville was one of the Disappeared. Nobody has ever been charged with her murder. Her son, Michael, has pledged to continue to seek justice for his mother. The Disappeared were people who were abducted, murdered and secretly buried by republicans during the Troubles. Jean McConville's case has been one of the most high profile. Her body was found on a beach in County Louth in 2003. Who was Jean McConville? Who were the Disappeared? It emerged on Tuesday, that Mr Adams would not be charged with IRA membership either. The seven people the PPS has said will not face any charges in connection with the murder of Jean McConville fall into two groups. In the first group are four women, who it was alleged had been involved in the abduction of the mother-of-10 from her home. It is understood that police were not able to obtain any evidence from witnesses at the scene to support claims that they had been involved, so there was insufficient evidence to provide a reasonable prospect of conviction. The second group consisted of Gerry Adams, Bobby Storey and an unnamed man. The evidence against them was based on interviews given by three other republicans to researchers working on a history project for Boston College. Mr Adams was questioned about allegations that he ordered the abduction and murder of Jean McConville. It was alleged that Bobby Storey, the northern chairman of Sinn Fein, led an internal IRA investigation in the late 1990s into the circumstances of the killing. The claims made in those interviews are referred to legally as hearsay. The PPS could not find any other independent evidence to support the claims, so concluded that what it calls its "test for prosecution" had not been met. The deputy director of public prosecutions, Pamela Atchison, said: "We have given careful consideration to the evidence currently available in respect of each of the three men and four women reported and have concluded that it is insufficient to provide a reasonable prospect of obtaining a conviction against any of them for a criminal offence." She also spoke about Mrs McConville's family. "We have had a series of meetings with members of the family, most recently this morning, about all of our prosecutorial decisions and we will continue to engage with them as we progress the prosecution of Ivor Bell." Veteran republican Ivor Bell, 78, has been charged with aiding and abetting Mrs McConville's murder. Speaking after meeting the Public Prosecution Service on Tuesday, Mrs McConville's son, Michael, said: "Those who ordered, planned and carried out this war crime thought that their guilt could disappear along with her body. "But it has not, and we will continue to seek justice for our mother and see those responsible held to account no matter how long it takes." In May 2014, Mr Adams presented himself at a police station and was subsequently arrested for questioning about her murder. He was released after four days and said there had been "a sustained, malicious, untruthful campaign" alleging that he had been involved in the killing. His party also criticised the decision to hold him, claiming that it was politically motivated, coming weeks before the European and local government elections. In response to the decision not to prosecute him, Mr Adams said: "I support the PSNI. But the timing of my arrest showed there remain elements within the PSNI who are against Sinn Fein. But they will not succeed. "I voluntarily went to the PSNI last year, after a concerted series of leaks claiming that I was about to be arrested. For some time, I have been the target of a sustained and malicious campaign seeking to involve me with the killing of Mrs McConville." He added that he was "very conscious" of the huge hurt inflicted on the McConville family. "The abduction, killing and secret burial of Jean McConville was wrong," he said.

A drug-addicted doctor watched his wife lose consciousness and struggle for breath moments after injecting her with heroin in Edinburgh, a court has heard. Dr. Alistair MacFarlane, aged 34, had been addicted to the drug for years and had previously been treated for his addiction. On the day of the incident, his wife, Aileen, had begged him for help after she had taken heroin herself and was struggling to breathe. MacFarlane initially refused but then relented and injected her with the drug. Moments later, Aileen lost consciousness and began to struggle for breath. MacFarlane called for an ambulance but she was pronounced dead at the scene. A post-mortem examination revealed that she had died from a heroin overdose. MacFarlane was charged with culpable homicide and pled guilty at Edinburgh Sheriff Court. He was sentenced to four years in prison.

Isabelle Stengers noted that adherents of Whitehead's philosophy come from various backgrounds, including philosophy, theology, and other disciplines like ecology and feminism. They integrate political activism, spirituality, and educational science into their understanding of Whiteheadian thought. Interest in Whitehead's ideas grew significantly over time, reaching scholars across continents and fields, including European and Chinese intellectuals, as well as those working in areas such as ecology, physics, biology, education, economics, and psychology. Notably, William Temple, who would later become the Archbishop of Canterbury, engaged with Whitehead's concepts during his Gifford Lectures, which were published under the title "Nature, Man and God". Although Whitehead's influence remains somewhat confined to specific academic circles, there has been an expansion in its reach since the 1970s and 1980s, particularly among American philosophers and theologians.

BepiColombo, a joint mission between the European Space Agency and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, has sent back pictures of the crater-riddled surface of Mercury. The mission launched in 2018 and was scheduled to arrive at Mercury in July 2020. But the launch was postponed several times because of technical issues. "We have managed to reach Mercury safely, and we have succeeded in setting the first ever solar system mission to the planet Mercury," ESA said in a statement. The European Space Agency (ESA) is seen in this image released by the ESA on 12 June 2019, with an ESA astronaut in the middle and an ESA camera operator at the right hand side of the picture. ESACNESDLRFU BerlinReuters The Japanese space agency said in a statement: "We have successfully completed the Mercury lander's pre-flight phase. The lander is expected to make a soft landing on the surface of Mercury in 2021." The pictures, which were released on Thursday, showed the impact craters, black streaks and rocky mountains that are the only traces of water on the planet's surface. BepiColombo is set to take over the Mercury Orbiter, which was launched in 2008. The spacecraft will orbit Mercury every 12 hours, providing scientists with a high-resolution map of the planet's surface and analysing the composition of the planet's soil and the solar wind, which is thought to be largely responsible for the erosion of Mercury's surface. The mission will also study the planet's magnetic field and atmosphere, the structure of the surface and the planet's interior, and will explore the possibility of liquid water on the surface. Scientists hope the mission will help them understand Mercury better and, in turn, unlock secrets about the solar system and how planets form. Mercury is the innermost planet in the solar system and is often called the "canary in the coal mine" because it was the first planet to be discovered by astronomers. The mission has faced several delays. The launch was initially scheduled for September 2017 but was delayed because of technical issues.

To calculate the fair value of a lottery ticket, compile a comprehensive list of potential outcomes along with their respective chances. Then, compute the product of each outcome and its likelihood, adding these values together to derive the expected worth of the ticket. For an equitable gamble, this figure should match the price of the ticket before taxes. Take, for instance, a scenario where a lottery ticket offers various rewards with distinct odds like $1,000,000 at 150,000,000 probability (0.02 average yield), $1,000 at 110,000 odds (0.10 average return), and $10 at 120 odds (0.50 average return). In this case, the cumulative statistical worth of the ticket equals 0.62. Purchasing this ticket is reasonable if it costs below 62 cents, while spending above that amount isn't advisable. Although lotteries typically have ticket prices exceeding their statistical value, making purchases unwise, there have been rare occasions when buying proved profitable due to favorable conditions. One notable example involves individuals winning substantial amounts through strategic acquisition and storage of numerous non-winning tickets, which they used to substantiate their winnings during an audit."

Although it is generally accepted that EU law has primacy, not all EU laws give citizens standing to bring claims: that is, not all EU laws have "direct effect." In Van Gend en Loos v Nederlandse Administratie der Belastingen it was held that the provisions of the Treaties (and EU Regulations) are directly effective, if they are (1) clear and unambiguous (2) unconditional, and (3) did not require EU or national authorities to take further action to implement them. Van Gend en Loos, a postal company, claimed that what is now TFEU article 30 prevented the Dutch Customs Authorities charging tariffs, when it imported urea-formaldehyde plastics from Germany to the Netherlands. After a Dutch court made a reference, the Court of Justice held that even though the Treaties did not "expressly" confer a right on citizens or companies to bring claims, they could do so. Historically, international treaties had only allowed states to have legal claims for their enforcement, but the Court of Justice proclaimed "the Community constitutes a new legal order of international law." Because article 30 clearly, unconditionally and immediately stated that no quantitative restrictions could be placed on trade, without a good justification, Van Gend en Loos could recover the money it paid for the tariff. EU Regulations are the same as Treaty provisions in this sense, because as TFEU article 288 states, they are 'directly applicable in all Member States'. Moreover, member states comes under a duty not to replicate Regulations in their own law, in order to prevent confusion. For instance, in Commission v Italy the Court of Justice held that Italy had breached a duty under the Treaties, both by failing to operate a scheme to pay farmers a premium to slaughter cows (to reduce dairy overproduction), and by reproducing the rules in a decree with various additions. "Regulations," held the Court of Justice, "come into force solely by virtue of their publication" and implementation could have the effect of "jeopardizing their simultaneous and uniform application in the whole of the Union." On the other hand, some Regulations may themselves expressly require implementing measures, in which case those specific rules should be followed.

It is generally accepted that neighboring nodes in financial networks are negatively assorted with respect to the correlation between their degrees. This feature would play an important 'damping' role in the market during downturns (periods of distress) since this connectivity pattern between firms lowers the chances of auto-amplifying (the propagation of) distress. In this paper we explore a trade-network of industrial firms where the nodes are suppliers or buyers, and the links are those invoices that the suppliers send out to their buyers and then go on to present to their bank for discounting. The network was collected by a large Italian bank in 2007, from their intermediation of the sales on credit made by their clients. The network also shows dissortative behavior as seen in other studies on financial networks. However, when looking at the credit rating of the firms, an important attribute internal to each node, we find that firms that trade with one another share overwhelming similarity. We know that much data is missing from our data set. However, we can quantify the amount of missing data using information exposure , a variable that connects social structure and behavior. This variable is a ratio of the sales invoices that a supplier presents to their bank over their total sales. Results reveal a non-trivial and robust relationship between the information exposure and credit rating of a firm, indicating the influence of the neighbors on a firm's rating. This methodology provides a new insight into how to reconstruct a network suffering from incomplete information.

Flow-based deep generative modeling has become increasingly popular due to its ability to accurptaely estimate log-likelihood efficiently during both training and synthesis. Nevertheless, these models encounter difficulties arising from their large dimensional latent spaces, which are often comparable in size to the input spaces. A promising approach to address this issue involves implementing a multi-scale architecture that employs sequential partial dimensional factorization at set intervals. Previous research employing multi-scale architectures utilizes fixed partitioning methods for dimensional reduction. In contrast, we suggest an innovative multi-scale structure capable of adaptively determining the dimensions that require additional processing via flow layers, guided by data dependencies. This is achieved through a heuristic derived from each dimension's impact on the overall log-likelihood, reflecting the significance of different dimensions. The development of this heuristic is seamlessly integrated into the training procedure of flow models, allowing for flexible application across various types of flow models. As evidence of its efficacy, we have implemented this concept within the foundational flow framework presented earlier, resulting in enhanced log-likelihood scores and improved sample generation quality when evaluated against standard visual datasets. Additionally, we conducted comparison tests to evaluate the effectiveness of our approach relative to alternative strategies for dimensional decomposition.

To enable SWIPT, the receiver adopts a power-splitting design, such that a portion of the received signal is used for channel estimation or data detection, while the remaining is used for energy harvesting. We optimally design the power-splitting ratios for both training and data phases to achieve the best ergodic capacity performance while maintaining a required energy harvesting rate. Our result shows how a power-splitting receiver can make the best use of the received pilot and data signals to obtain the optimal SWIPT performance.
