Age UK's latest research has found that around 20,000 people who are eligible for free personal care are still waiting for an assessment or for their care arrangements to be put in place. Free personal care is a government-funded programme that offers elderly individuals support with daily tasks such as washing, dressing and eating. Despite the fact that free personal care has been available in Scotland for over a decade, it was only introduced in England in April 2020. However, the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on the health and social care sector have led to significant delays in assessments and care arrangements being carried out. According to Age UK, the consequences of these delays are severe. Many elderly individuals are left to manage on their own without any support, which can lead to isolation, poor health and a loss of independence. Others are forced to pay for their own care, which can use up all of their savings and assets. Charity officials believe that more needs to be done to ensure that elderly individuals receive the care they are entitled to. Some of the recommendations being made by Age UK include greater investment in social care services, better communication between health and social care providers, and the streamlining of the care assessment process. Age UK's director, Caroline Abrahams, said: "Free personal care is a lifeline for many elderly individuals who struggle to carry out the most basic tasks. We need to ensure that everyone who is entitled to this support receives it in a timely and efficient manner. It is time for the government to take action and address the issues that are preventing elderly individuals from accessing the care they need."

Regulator NHS Improvement had wanted to publish data on the scale of hospital deficits but was advised against it by the government. NHS Improvement said it was "disappointing" the results could not be published until after the election. The Department of Health and the Conservative Party did not comment. In a statement, NHS Improvement said a date for the publication of the figures had to be agreed with the Department of Health, but this had not been done when the election for 8 June was called. "We sought advice and clarification in the hope that a date for publication could be agreed but it was clear, after discussions with the department, that this would not be permitted without breaching Cabinet Office guidance. "It is disappointing, but the financial results for the provider sector will have to be published after the general election." The financial state of the NHS in England has been debated intensely. In the 2015-16 financial year, hospitals and other trusts ran up deficits totalling PS2.4bn. The latest figures covering the three months until the end of March will confirm the deficits for the most recent financial year, 2016-17. They are usually published ahead of NHS Improvement board meetings with the next one due before the end of May. It is understood that NHS Improvement wants to publish the figures in line with normal practice, which should be within the next week. But Whitehall officials have advised that because of so-called purdah rules there should be a delay until after polling day. The purdah convention limits civil service announcements during election campaigns. Some have argued that the rules are too restrictive. Dr Mark Porter, BMA council chairman, said: "The government is clearly running scared, refusing to face up to the funding crisis that has put the NHS at breaking point. "Delaying the release of the figures won't magically solve the very real problems our health service is facing." Dr Mark Holland, president of the Society for Acute Medicine, said: "The general election and purdah appear to be putting a number of important NHS decisions on hold. "I would argue that it is only right and just that important data pertaining to the NHS in England is published. " Shadow health secretary Jon Ashworth said: "It's a cover-up to deny the public the true picture of the NHS. "We demand full transparency so everyone knows the real state of the NHS when casting their vote." NHS England caused some raised eyebrows at the start of the campaign by announcing that the monthly performance figures, including AE waiting times, due on 8 June would not go out then because it was polling day. A spokesman said the figures would be published on 9 June on the advice of the national statistician. Meanwhile, leading scientists, in a letter co-ordinated by the Science Media Centre, have written to the head of the civil service, Sir Jeremy Heywood, calling for clarification of the purdah rules. The signatories said that the public "are being denied access to the best experts" because university researchers felt unable to provide comment to journalists. Liberal Democrat health spokesman Norman Lamb said: "It would be wrong to try and hide this vital information until after the election. "The public deserves to know the scale of the financial crisis facing the NHS before they vote."

In this paper, we propose a novel algorithm for matching faces with temporal variations caused due to age progression. The proposed generative adversarial network algorithm is a unified framework that is more powerful than existing methods. The proposed algorithm consists of two components: a generative network and a discriminative network. The generative network takes in the original face image as input and generates age-progressed faces with temporal variations. The discriminative network then compares the generated faces to the original ones and decides whether or not they are similar. The two networks are trained together and the results show that our method can significantly improve the accuracy of matching faces with temporal variations. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on real-world datasets such as the FG-NET aging database. The proposed algorithm has several advantages over existing methods. First, it is a unified framework that can be applied to any temporal face matching problem. Second, it is more robust to noise and other factors that affect the accuracy of matching faces with temporal variations. Third, it is able to generate realistic age-progressed faces with temporal variations accurately. Fourth, it requires less data and computational resources than existing methods. Finally, it is easy to implement and can be used for various applications. In conclusion, we have presented a novel generative adversarial network algorithm for matching faces with temporal variations caused due to age progression. Our proposed algorithm is a unified framework that is more robust to noise and other factors, requires less data and computational resources, and can generate realistic age-progressed faces with temporal variations. We demonstrated the effectiveness of our method on the FG-NET aging database and showed that it can significantly improve the accuracy of matching faces with temporal variations.

I re-arranged the other pieces of artwork on the refrigerator and grabbed one of the few remaining magnets to keep the new drawing in place. " It's my monster! " Micah said. I smiled at him. It was one of his better drawings. The arms were too large on the body, but they appeared symmetrical. The orange fur that covered the " beast " stayed neatly within the black outlines. The eyes were dark pin points of mashed crayon, and two red fangs peeked out from a nearly straight line that turned up at the last second - a vague hint of a smile. Unlike Micah's other drawings this one seemed composed and practical, almost like a portrait. Micah's other drawings were confused compositions of a child trying to keep a single image fixed in his mind, and failing. " It's a very good monster. " I said. " Not a monster, mommy! My monster. The one that's been scaring me. He wanted me to draw a picture of him. " " That's nice sweetie, I'm sure you did a great job. " There had been a few nights he had come to my bed with tears in his eyes. The nightmare must've looked something like this monster. I took a step back and regarded my son's gallery of art. A colorful collage of children, dogs, dragons, and monsters with wide open mouths screaming to escape the pages. I smiled at the collage and vaguely wondered if he had found his talent. Perhaps I should keep these as artifacts for his future biographer to paint a picture of a genius's artistic development. I dreamed what every parent wanted for their children: a better life. " Go clean up for dinner, Micah, " I said. He was already walking away leaving behind a mess of half colored pages and worn down crayons. " Come back and clean this up! " I called, but he ignored me and walked down the short hallway to his room. He shut the door, and a moment later I could hear his muffled voice. I sighed to myself, and dropped the fire to low before chasing after him. Things were getting harder. All year, ever since his father left, I felt control slipping further and further away. As I got to his door I could hear him talking a little more clearly, enough to pick out a few words. I got closer and pressed my ear against the door. " She didn't listen, " Micah said. " I think you were right. She doesn't believe me. " You I repeat to myself. My heart sinks and a thousand scenarios start running through my head: personality disorder, intruder, imaginary friend, real friend with drugs (Micah was only four, but the thought emerged with frightening clarity). All of these things came down to one clear problem. My son could be in danger. In one quick move I turned the knob and pushed open the door. Micah stood up suddenly and twisted around to see his mom. His short curly hair bounced on his forehead, and he took several steps away from his mother without looking where he was going. His foot found a misplaced Hot Wheel. The toy car slipped out from under him and he fell hard, breaking his fall with his wrist. It was the shock, however, not the pain that made him start crying. I didn't see this happen to Micah, from the moment I opened the door I stood transfixed at the impossible figure dominating the room. Standing just outside the open closet door was an seven foot tall orange-furred beast. Its huge arms hung off its small body, making it look like a gorilla standing on two legs. Pin point black eyes watched me and its mouth opened revealing several red fangs. It was the monster from Micah's drawing. The room began to narrow and spin around me. My legs grew weak, and the tunnel vision brought the last remains of my focus to the monster standing dumbfounded in my son's bedroom. It was starting to raise a giant paw. Razor sharp claws extended out of those paws. Micah's drawing hadn't shown that. I would've fainted then had Micah not fallen and started crying. The high pitched wail broke the shock filling my mind and brought me back to reality. The reality of an impossible monster was no longer the top priority on my list. My son was in pain. " I'll get to you in a minute. " I said to the monster trying my best to sound confident. I even waggled my finger at him, though no part of my conscious being directed me to do that. Perhaps it was my subconscious pulling up memories from how my mother talked when she disciplined me. Micah was sitting on the ground his legs sprawled out under him. He was holding his left hand in his right, and tears were rolling down his face. He wasn't screaming anymore, just sobbing occasionally. " Oh, sweetie, what happened? Did you fall and hurt your hand? " Micah nodded. " Here, " I said, " let Mommy kiss it and make it all better. " I grabbed his hand and checked for any serious damage. There wasn't any. I covered it quickly with kisses until Micah started giggling and pulled his hand free. " Stop it! " He said, " You're embarrassing me! " That single comment rang our with all the weight of the future when Micah would start to pull away from me. When he would ask for my car keys and not come back until the next morning. When he would say goodbye and leave me to fill the emptiness in my home. The weight of that future settled on my heart, but I brushed that away and focused on something a bit less scary: the seven-foot orange monster in my son's bedroom. The attention-based end-to-end (E2E) automatic speech recognition (ASR) architecture allows for joint optimization of acoustic and language models within a single network. However, in a vanilla E2E ASR architecture, the decoder sub-network (subnet), which incorporates the role of the language model (LM), is conditioned on the encoder output. This means that the acoustic encoder and the language model are entangled that doesn't allow language model to be trained separately from external text data. To address this problem, in this work, we propose a new architecture that separates the decoder subnet from the encoder output. In this way, the decoupled subnet becomes an independently trainable LM subnet, which can easily be updated using the external text data. We study two strategies for updating the new architecture. Experimental results show that, 1) the independent LM architecture benefits from external text data, achieving 9.3 and 22.8 relative character and word error rate reduction on Mandarin HKUST and English NSC datasets respectively; 2) the proposed architecture works well with external LM and can be generalized to different amount of labelled data.

Scientists from the University of Portsmouth have made a groundbreaking discovery in the field of plastic recycling. They have created a mutant enzyme that is capable of breaking down plastic bottles in just a matter of hours. The enzyme works by speeding up the natural process of plastic degradation, which can take hundreds of years. The research team used a combination of biochemistry and computer modeling to redesign an existing enzyme, called PETase, which is capable of breaking down PET plastic. The new enzyme, described as a "supercharged" version of PETase, is able to break down plastic bottles into their raw building blocks at an unprecedented rate. According to the study, published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the mutant enzyme is able to break down 90 of the plastic in a 24-hour period. This groundbreaking discovery has the potential to revolutionize the plastic recycling industry, which has long struggled to find efficient and cost-effective methods of breaking down plastic waste. Dr. John McGeehan, the lead author of the study, said: "This is a major step forward in the fight against plastic pollution. Our mutant enzyme is the first example of an enzyme that can break down PET plastic on a large scale, and offers a real solution to the plastic waste crisis." The discovery has already attracted the attention of major companies in the plastics industry, who are now exploring ways to commercialize the mutant enzyme. This development could significantly reduce the amount of plastic waste that ends up in landfills or the ocean, and lead to a more sustainable future for our planet. Environmentalists have welcomed the development as a major breakthrough in the fight against plastic pollution. However, they urge caution, as the mutant enzyme is not capable of breaking down all types of plastic. This means that we still need to reduce our dependence on plastic and find alternative solutions to packaging and other single-use plastics. Overall, the discovery of the mutant enzyme is a significant step towards a more sustainable future, and serves as a reminder of the power of science in addressing some of the world's most pressing issues.

We don't know how gravity works. A lot of very educated guesses are in lines with the idea that every particle deforms space itself a little bit. Larger collections of particles deform things so much that the effect is measurable by us very easily. Outside of that, all we truly know is how strong gravity is. Many very advanced experiments, such as work being done at the Large Hadron Collider seek to understand gravity a bit more clearly, via a particle known as the Higgs Boson. Recently, researchers found direct evidence for the Higgs particle. It had existed only as a mathematical model prior to that. What this means for us, is that since we now know the particle is there, it is thought that the particle itself may play a role in "carrying" gravity. That is, it somehow makes gravity happen. This is EXTREMELY simplified, mind you. The idea is that particles interact with a universal mechanism (called the Higgs Field) which exists everywhere. The Higgs Boson is the key component that makes a particle have mass, and thereby interacts with the Higgs Field. Right now, it can't be said that we truly even understand WHY things have mass, while some other things don't. As for the moon, no thing has an effect on the gravity of another thing. Think of it like throwing stones into a pond. A big stone makes big waves, small stones make small waves. Each thing (planet, moon, person, etc) is its own stone that you throw into this pond. No stone directly changes the other, but their gravity interacts in the form of the waves on the pond. When you consider the moon and the earth together, they are both pulling one another towards themselves. The earth, being far larger, is only affected a little bit. The moon is pulled so much that it falls into orbit. The moons gravity still shifts things around on earth though, which is part of why we have tides, and a few other things.

From atop Ayers Rock Australia seems red, endless and lifeless, like some displaced piece of Mars. "There's life everywhere," Alice tells me, gesturing at the desert. Her hat's made of serpent skin. Her own skin could just as well be, too. "Nasty, vicious life. Most of it is venomous or poisonous - I don't recall fhe difference, but most are both. Trouser snakes, anklebiter spiders, drop bears, stinger dingos, scorpion rats, vampire'roos - and get to the ocean, and the sea kittens will eat you alive." I shudder, and she leers at me. "The people ain't entirely harmless either." "W - what does this have to do with I wave a hesitant hand downwards. "Right. Keep up, I'll show you, London boy." And so I follow Ms. Springs of the Bushmaster Service to the depths of Ayers Rock, down a narrow tunnel, its walls full of aboriginal graffiti - skulls, screaming faces, dismembered corpses, people and animals running - warnings, or some forgotten prehistory of shock rock. The tunnel's end is dark, chill, and red. There are no wall-pictures in this hall, only irregular angles of rock, as if set down by a Mother Nature who didn't want to linger here. Then there's the door. "So you found this..." She - Alice - I'm unsure how formal I should be - shrugs. "Found, maybe thirty years ago. Told anybody..... there are strange types in the Service. Me, I heard about this last week, when Bruce vanished." "He's the, um, the one who went through this door?" She scowls, as if about to give me a dissertation on the local dearth of Bruces, and then nods. "Yep. And came back raving. Hair all white. Babbling, shaking, drooling, trembling - like a limey on vegemite, begging your pardon, sir." "Shush. And you..." "I looked in." She puts a hand on the doorknob. The door's metal, rust-red, and looks older than the Rock itself. "And it was like he said. So I thought, we need a special kind of a guy..." "And that's me." "Right. So, you ready, London boy?" "Show me." She swings the door open, and I see the truth about Australia, the reason why it is a desert of deadly things, dynamite fishers and trouser snakes and drop bears, all kinds of crazed, off monsters, full of malicious vitality. Ayers Rock isn't a rock at all. It's a vast, rust-encrusted, muck-covered, aeons-disfigured conning tower, and Australia is a UFO. "It makes sense," Alice Springs says behind me. "All the wildlife's as if designed to tell you to fuck off..... because it is."

One of the most important landmarks in Nis is Cele Kula (Skull Tower). It is a monument to the bravery and courage of the Serbian people in their struggle for freedom and independence. It was built after the First Serbian Uprising , when the Serbs rebelled against the Ottoman rule. During the uprising Serbia was liberated and recognized as an autonomous principality. When the Ottomans regained control over the region in 1813, they built the tower using the skulls of Serbian soldiers and rebels, killed in the Battle of Cegar in 1809. The tower was originally built in 1809 and was 14 meters tall. It was later demolished by the Turks in 1892 and rebuilt in 1895. This tower is one of the most important memorials of that period. The building was damaged again during the NATO bombing in 1999, and it was restored and reopened to the public in 2001. The theatre is still active today. Across the National Theatre you will find the monument to Stevan Sremac , one of the most famous Serbian novelists and short story writers. The monument was designed by the sculptor Zivojin Lukic and built in 1932. Today the National Theatre is one of the most important and most visited buildings in the city. A flat tax refers to either charging an equal fixed sum from each individual or applying a uniform percentage rate across all earners. The drawback of this approach is its disproportionate impact on lower-income individuals compared to wealthier ones, given the absence of any exceptions or reductions. The entirety of a low-income person's earnings could be significantly affected by such a tax, whereas higher-earning individuals may hardly notice the difference. To compensate for potential revenue shortfalls, governments often have to set relatively high percentages. On the other hand, a progressive tax model considers the varying financial capabilities of citizens. It involves increasing tax obligations incrementally based on income levels, creating a gentler burden for those least able to afford it. While opinions vary on what constitutes equitable taxation, these two systems represent contrasting methods of achieving fiscal balance within society.

So imagine you have a lemonade stand and you want to sell lots of lemonade. You might ask your friends to come and help you sell lemonade too! And then they could ask their friends to help sell lemonade too, and so on. Network marketing is kind of like that. You join a company that sells things, like beauty products or essential oils. And then you tell your friends and family about these products and if they want to buy them, you get some money. But then, if your friends want to join the company too, they can tell their own friends and family about the products and sell them too. And then they can make some money, but you also get some money because you helped them start selling. So you keep telling more and more people about the products and helping them start selling too, and eventually you have a big network of people selling these products together. Now, a pyramid scheme is different. In a pyramid scheme, you only make money by recruiting other people to join the scheme. There's no actual product that you're selling, it's just all about getting more and more people to join and give you their money. That's not fair or right! But in network marketing, you're actually selling products that people want to buy. And just like your lemonade stand, you're getting help from your friends to sell even more. So it's not a pyramid scheme, it's just friends helping each other out to make some money!

Creating human activity suggestions within long, raw video footage presents a significant challenge with numerous practical uses. Existing techniques typically struggle with unclear borders and subpar reliability ratings for identifying relevant clips. This study introduces BSN, an innovative approach employing dual boundary regression and interrelated sequence analysis for producing time-based recommendations. Initially, we put forward a unique boundary predictor using a U-shaped network structure equipped with cross-linked shortcuts to harness comprehensive contextual information and a bidirectional border alignment method to enhance accuracy. Additionally, our design incorporates a module focused on understanding relationships between various segments by implementing dual self-focusing mechanisms considering location and feature space. We also address potential discrepancies arising from uneven distribution of positive and negative instances as well as varying lengths through a balancing resampling technique. Our extensive testing on recognized datasets like ActivityNet-1.3 and THUMOS14 confirms that BSN outperforms existing models in generating high-quality activity suggestions.

Tucson is known for being a trailblazer in voluntary partial publicly financed campaigns. Since 1985, both mayoral and council candidates have been eligible to receive matching public funds from the city. To become eligible, council candidates must receive 200 donations of 10 or more (300 for a mayoral candidate). Candidates must then agree to spending limits equal to 33 for every registered Tucson voter, or 79,222 in 2005 (the corresponding figures for mayor are 64 per registered voter, or 142,271 in 2003). In return, candidates receive matching funds from the city at a 1:1 ratio of public money to private donations. The only other limitation is that candidates may not exceed 75 of the limit by the date of the primary. Many cities, such as San Francisco and New York City, have copied this system, albeit with more complex spending and matching formulas.

In this paper, we consider molecular communications in one-dimensional flow-induced diffusion channels with a perfectly absorbing receiver. In such channels, the random propagation delay until the molecules are absorbed follows an inverse Gaussian (IG) distribution and is referred to as first hitting time. Knowing the distribution for the difference of the first hitting times of two molecules is very important if the information is encoded by a limited set of molecules and the receiver exploits their arrival time andor order. Hence, we propose a moment matching approximation by a normal inverse Gaussian (NIG) distribution and we derive an expression for the asymptotic tail probability. Numerical evaluations showed that the NIG approximation matches very well with the exact solution obtained by numerical convolution of the IG density functions. Moreover, the asymptotic tail probability outperforms state-of-the-art tail approximations.

On average, a European employee generates more output per hour compared to a worker from an Asian nation. For instance, a garment maker in Bangladesh would yield fewer results than someone working on an assembly line at a Volkswagen factory. This higher productivity stems from Europeans possessing greater access to resources, including tangible assets like factories and intangible ones like education.

Within a contemporary service-oriented economy, most occupations do not contribute significantly to overall wealth creation. Jobs directly involved in producing wealth, such as those in manufacturing, research, agriculture, and mining, represent just a fraction of the workforce. Instead, the majority of employees engage in tasks related to distributing existing wealth, such as sales, marketing, financial services, administrative duties, taxation, and compliance. These roles essentially involve transferring wealth between parties without creating new value; envision this as multiple pairs of individuals paddling against each other in small boats, causing minimal movement despite exertion. Whether they represent rivals or different entities within the same organization, the outcome remains the same – increased effort without significant progress.

European governments tend to adopt a more proactive approach towards regulation when compared to their Asian counterparts, enforcing stricter labor laws. As a consequence, these governments often advocate for reduced working hours among employees, which may lead to negligible changes in individual earnings or national prosperity.

Furthermore, European culture generally views excessive work commitments as detrimentoal to personal happiness and equates it with servitude. Thus, embracing a balanced lifestyle by avoiding overworking becomes crucial.

Our understanding of gravity remains limited. Various theories suggest that each particle slightly distorts space, resulting in noticeable effects when large numbers of particles come together. Current knowledge primarily revolves around the strength of gravity rather than its underlying mechanics. Advanced experiments, including those conducted at the Large Hadron Collider, aim to shed light on gravitational mysteries through the study of the Higgs Boson—a particle recently confirmed experimentally after existing solely as a theoretical concept. Some speculate that the Higgs Boson could influence gravity, possibly acting as a mediator due to its interaction with the ubiquitous Higgs Field. However, these explanations greatly oversimplify the complexity surrounding our grasp of mass generation and the reasons behind certain objects lacking it. In terms of celestial bodies like the Earth and Moon, their mutual gravitational attraction resembles dropping stones of varying sizes into a body of water; although individual actions do not affect others, collective interactions create ripples or 'waves.' Consequently, while the Earth experiences minimal impact from the Moon's gravitational pull, the Moon succumbs significantly to Earth's force, resulting in its orbital path. Nevertheless, lunar gravity does exert subtle influences on Earth, contributing to phenomena such as oceanic tides.

The third evaluation report showcased a chart titled "Reconstruction of Temperature in the Northern Hemisphere since the Millennium," derived from a study conducted by Michael E. Mann, Raymond S. Bradley, and Malcolm K. Hughes in 1999 (referred to as the 'hockey stick graph'). It expanded upon a comparable figure presented in the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change's (IPCC) Second Assessment Report released in 1995. Contrastingly, the initial assessment report contained only a conceptual illustration without specific temperature measures. While this earlier representation suggested more significant temperature fluctuations throughout history, particularly during the Medieval Warm Period, compared to the mid-20th century, it wasn't backed up by empirical data. Rather, it relied on historical records such as medieval wine production in England. Despite adjustments made to accommodate these findings, even the highest values indicated during the Medieval Warm Period fell short of those experienced in Central England in 2007. The results achieved by MBH99 received further backing from research carried out by Jones et al., Pollack, Huang Shen, Crowley Lowery, and Briffa between 1998 and 2000, who used diverse datasets and techniques. The cones are responsible for color vision and fine details. There are three different types of cones, each with slightly different functions. L-cones respond to long wavelength light, which is blue in color. These cones give your cat the ability to see blue colors. M-cones are sensitive to medium wavelength light, or green light. M-cones allow your cat to see greens and yellows. S-cones respond to short wavelength light, which is purple, red, and orange. These cones enable your cat to see shades of orange and red. The S-cones also help your cat see better in dim lighting. Do cats need all 3 types of cones to see? No, cats apparently don't require all three types of cones to see. In fact, we don't even know if cats can see in color. Some studies have shown that cats can distinguish some colors, but many experts believe that your cat probably only sees in black and white. How many rods and cones does my cat have? In comparison to humans, cats have very few rods and cones. A human eye has around 100 million rods and 6 million cones. A cat eye has about 6 million rods and 250,000 cones. Because cats have far fewer cones than humans, it makes sense that they probably only see in black and white. Can a cat get glass in their eye? Yes, your cat can get glass in their eye. If you think your cat has gotten glass in its eye, take them to the vet right away. Glass can cause severe injuries to your cat's eye. Your cat may start rubbing at their eye with their paw if they have something in their eye. You should be able to see the glass if there is any on the surface of your cat's eye. However, you won't usually be able to see glass beneath the surface of the eye, so it's always best to take your cat to the vet whenever you think there may be something wrong with their eye. Clear cornea The cornea is the clear part of your cat's eye that covers the iris. It should be clear and free from any cloudiness or spots. 2. Bright iris The iris is the colored part of your cat's eye. It should be bright and free from any redness, swelling, or discharge. 3. Clear pupil The pupil is the black part of your cat's eye that gets bigger and smaller to control how much light enters the eye. It should be black and free from any spots or damage. 4. Clear lens The lens is the clear part of your cat's eye that helps focus light onto the back of the eye. It should be clear and free from any cloudiness or spots. 5. The increasing prevalence of Machine-to-Machine (M2M) communication in mobile networks necessitates the optimization of these networks according to the unique features of M2M, which differ considerably from the parameters used in current network designs. Primarily, M2M involves numerous brief sessions rather than the few prolonged ones typical of human-generated traffic. Additionally, many M2M devices operate on batteries and are situated in fixed locations like basements and tunnels, requiring higher transmission power levels than conventional devices. Moreover, it may not always be possible to replace or recharge the batteries of these devices. These disparities underscore the necessity for an organized approach to examine the optimum power and energy system design tailored for M2M, which serves as the central theme of this paper. We analyze various coordinated and non-coordinated transmission methods, establishing the optimal transmit power, energy per bit, and the maximum load that can be handled by the base station. This leads us to recommend the following design principles: (i) Frequency Division Multiple Access (FDMA), with equal bandwidth distribution, proves most efficient in terms of total power consumption under low spectral efficiency conditions; (ii) although FDEMA remains the preferred strategy generally, Uncoordinated Code Division Multiple Access (CDMA) performs nearly equally well when the base station experiences minimal usage; (iii) optimizing within FDMA typically does not yield substantial benefits in the context relevant to M2M.

Yves Jego has launched a drive on the Change.org website calling for vegetarian alternatives to be compulsory in all schools. More than 73,000 people have so far backed the petition. The move comes after a town in eastern France banned all pork substitutes in school meals last week. The conservative mayor of Chalon sur Saone had earlier launched his own campaign on Change.org, reiterating France's secular values. His campaign has gained 2,750 supporters. "Messages of support and of encouragement have come from every corner of France and from French people of all backgrounds, faiths and professions," the mayor, Gilles Platret, wrote. A court in the city of Dijon last week rejected an appeal against Mr Platret's intention to ban pork substitutes. "Can we force a Catholic child to eat meat on Good Friday because nothing else is proposed, or a Jew or a Muslim to eat pork?," Mr Jego asked in his petition, set up in response to Mr Platret's. He said he would propose a law if the petition received 75,000 signatories. France insists on the separation of religion and the state, and in 2004 introduced a ban on headscarves in schools. France has five million residents of Muslim descent, half of whom are under the age of 24. It also has the largest Jewish population in Europe. A secular solution to the problem of school meals was possible, said Mr Jego, of the left-wing Radical Party. The petitions have led to a debate in some quarters on the nature of secularism and what is ethically correct. "Secularism is not the denial of religions and beliefs, but the respect of all religions," wrote Houari Zeidouni, who signed Mr Jego's petition. But France's Agriculture Minister, Stephane le Foll, wrote in a tweet: "Supporting French livestock with vegetarian menus: that's Yves Jego's programme! Let's be consistent."

These campaigns expanded Han sovereignty into the Tarim Basin of Central Asia, divided the Xiongnu into two separate confederations, and helped establish the vast trade network known as the Silk Road, which reached as far as the Mediterranean world. The territories north of Han's borders were quickly overrun by the nomadic Xianbei confederation. Emperor Wu also launched successful military expeditions in the south, annexing Nanyue in 111 BC and Dian in 109 BC, and in the Korean Peninsula where the Xuantu and Lelang Commanderies were established in 108 BC.

Traditional mobile data packages tie data usage to a predetermined duration, typically one month, after which any remaining data expires. Recognizing the diverse needs of users over various timespans and aiming to offer greater temporal adaptability, certain cellular service providers now present customers with data plans featuring varying durations. This study delves into devising an effective data package structure for a singular provider catering to clients with distinct data consumption patterns through differing package terms. Adopting a framework based on contract theory, we suggest offering data plan contracts characterized by a selection of term-and-fee pairings, specifying charges corresponding to varied package lengths. The investigation focuses on optimally structuring these contracts within two distinct frameworks: one assumes discrete consumer categories, while the other considers them as part of broader segments. Each framework addresses ensuring fairness and mutual benefit between the provider and the customer by incorporating conditions related to choice encouragement and participant satisfaction. Additionally, our research identifies the most profitable contract configuration possible without breaching these established guidelines. Through simulation outcomes, it has been determined that the optimized contract yields a notable 35% profit enhancement when contrasted with standard monthly-term data packages.

The Endangered Species Act (ESA), established in 1973 under Public Law 16 U.S.C. 1531 et seq., represents one among several environmental statutes adopted during the 1970s within the US. Its purpose is to implement measures required by The Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES). Enacted by then-President Richard Nixon on December 28th, 1973, its objective was to prevent endangered species from becoming extinct due to unregulated economic expansion and industrialization. In interpreting this Act, the U.S. Supreme Court concluded that Congressional intention was to stop and counteract the decline towards species extinction, regardless of expense. Temporal visual field defects can indeed be associated with monocular inattention in chiasmal pathology. Chiasmal pathology refers to disorders or damage affecting the optic chiasm, where the optic nerves from each eye cross and partially exchange nerve fibers. This area is responsible for relaying visual information from the eyes to the brain. In chiasmal pathology, the damage on the optic chiasm can lead to various visual field defects, including temporal visual field defects. Temporal visual field defects are characterized by loss of vision or impaired vision in the outer (temporal) part of the visual field in one or both eyes. Monocular inattention, on the other hand, refers to a patient's inability to pay attention to or process visual information coming from one eye, typically the eye contralateral to the lesion. This can result in worsened visual performance and can be associated with temporal visual field defects due to the impaired processing of visual information from the affected eye. So, while temporal visual field defects in chiasmal pathology can be associated with monocular inattention, it is crucial to have a thorough assessment by an ophthalmologist or neurologist to determine the exact cause of visual impairments and formulate appropriate treatment plans.

You could build a paper mountain out of all the plans to give vocational education the same status as university degrees, There are several reasons why vocational education has struggled to achieve the same status as university education. First, there is a long-standing cultural bias that values academic education over vocational education. This bias is particularly strong in many Western countries, where university degrees are seen as the key to social mobility and success, while vocational education is often seen as a second-best option. Second, vocational education has often been associated with low-status jobs and low pay. This has led to a perception that vocational education is less valuable than university education, despite the fact that many vocational careers can be highly rewarding in terms of job satisfaction and financial remuneration. Third, there has historically been a lack of investment in vocational education and training, particularly in terms of resources and infrastructure. This has made it difficult for vocational education to keep pace with changing industry needs and maintain high standards of quality. Despite these challenges, there has been a growing recognition in recent years of the importance of vocational education, particularly in the context of addressing skills shortages and improving economic competitiveness. Initiatives aimed at promoting vocational education, such as apprenticeship programs and public-private partnerships, have gained traction in many countries, which is a positive step towards giving vocational education the same status as university education.

The cosmic calendar serves as an illustrative tool to comprehend the vast expanse of time elapsed since the Big Bang. This concept does not attribute specific importance to individual moments; rather, it breaks down the entire timeline of the universe into segments of approximately 26,000 years each. Essentially, this approach employs mathematical calculations—for example, aligning 14 billion years across a conventional calendar reveals that the final minute corresponds to roughly EEK years. Human existence pales in comparison to this colossal duration, constituting only a minuscule portion of our known history. In terms of mathematics, one can determine the length of a cosmic 'minute' by dividing the age of the universe (approximately 14 billion years) by 525,000, resulting in nearly 26,000 years per unit. Drawing parallels between these units and the actual passage of time helps us appreciate the sheer scale of events preceding our arrival on Earth's stage. Although each moment seems constant, the ever-advancing nature of time means that future measurements may show slight increments due to the continuous expansion of the universe. To illustrate further, should humankind persist for another 13.7 billion years, they might consider their origins as occurring in mid-June within this cosmic framework, yet they would remain within the concluding seconds of its overall timespan.

My friend and I decided to get a job at Little Caesars. We were hired on the spot, and worked there for a month. After a month, we found out that the boss was paying us a lot less than the minimum wage. We quit working there, but the owner still owes us money. I want to know if he still has to pay us for the work we did before we quit. A: Yes, he does. Your employer is still obligated to pay you for the time that you worked for him. In Ontario, employees are entitled to be paid for the work they do, regardless of whether they are fired or they quit. You are entitled to be paid for the time you worked before you quit, as well as any money you are owed for vacation pay and overtime. In Ontario, the minimum wage is 10.25 per hour, and employees who work more than 44 hours per week are entitled to overtime pay. In this case, your employer has violated the Employment Standards Act (ESA), which is a law that sets the minimum standards of work in Ontario. If you do not receive the money that is owed to you, you have the right to file a claim with the Ministry of Labour. This may be done in person at one of the Ministry's offices, or you may complete an Employment Standards Claim online and send it to the Ministry by mail. You must file your claim within two years of the date when you should have been paid. When your employer receives your claim, he will have 15 days to respond. If he agrees to your claim, you will be paid within a week. If your employer refuses to pay you, an Employment Standards Officer will be assigned to your case and will decide whether you are entitled to the money you are owed. You may want to get advice from an employment lawyer or a community legal clinic before you file your claim. You can find the contact information for a clinic in your area on the Legal Aid Ontario website, or by calling their free, confidential hotline: . If you have more questions about filing a claim, you can contact the Ministry of Labour's Employment Standards Information Centre by phone at or toll free at . Got a question? A suitable state representation is a fundamental part of the learning process in Reinforcement Learning. In various tasks, the state can either be described by natural language or be natural numbers. For example, a suitable state representation for a game of chess could be represented as a set of 64 natural numbers that correspond to the pieces on the board. Each number would represent the type of piece in each location on the board, such as 1 for a pawn, 2 for a rook, 3 for a knight, etc. This state representation would allow the agent to understand the current state of the game and make decisions accordingly. In other tasks, the state may need to be described by natural language or symbols. For example, in a navigation task, a suitable state representation could be a set of coordinates that represent the current position of the agent. This would allow the agent to understand its current location and plan its next move accordingly.

Interestingly, while the British originated it, they do not utilize the term 'soccer.' This term emerged during the 1880s as an informal contraction of 'association,' associated with Oxford University students who enjoyed condensing words like 'breakfast' into 'brekkers' or 'rugby football' into 'rugger.' Author Clive Toye remarks that the Brits have a penchant for making names more approachable through truncation; hence, they formed 'soccer' from taking the third to fifth letters of 'Association Football.' In contrast, Americans avoid using this term to prevent confusion with their version of American football, distinguished by its protective gear and physicality, where typically just one player per team uses their feet on the ball.

A total dominating set of a graph G (V , E) is a subset D V such that every vertex in V is adjacent to some vertex in D . Finding a total dominating set of minimum size is NP-hard on planar graphs and W [ 2 ] -complete on general graphs when parameterized by the solution size. By the meta-theorem of Bodlaender et al . [FOCS 2009], it follows that there exists a linear kernel for Total Dominating Set on graphs of bounded genus. Nevertheless, it is not clear how such a kernel can be effectively constructed , and how to obtain explicit reduction rules with reasonably small constants. Following the approach of Alber et al . [J. ACM 2004], we provide an explicit linear kernel for Total Dominating Set on planar graphs. This result complements several known constructive linear kernels on planar graphs for other domination problems such as Dominating Set , Edge Dominating Set , Efficient Dominating Set , or Connected Dominating Set . Keywords: parameterized complexity, planar graphs, linear kernels, total domination.

Highly concentrated sources of oxygen promote rapid combustion. Fire and explosion hazards exist when concentrated oxidants and fuels are brought into close proximity; an ignition event, such as heat or an oxidizing agent, can ignite a fuel and produce a large volume of combustion products. 3. Safety concerns are also present when working with concentrated oxidants and fuels. A worker may come into contact with an oxidant or fuel while attempting to separate or purify a fuel from an oxidant. For example, when working with oxygen or hydrogen, a worker may come into contact with these materials as they are introduced into a system. Likewise, when working with nitrogen or argon, a worker may come into contact with these materials as they are removed from a system. Contamination of these materials may occur when the materials are stored in an unsealed container. Exposure to concentrated oxidants and fuels may also occur when a worker inhales or ingests these materials. Exposure to concentrated oxidants and fuels may also occur when a worker is subjected to intense heat, such as when an oxidant is burned to produce a high temperature. As noted above, the health and safety concerns presented by concentrated oxidants and fuels can be exacerbated by the presence of other materials, such as fuel. For example, a fuel may cause oxidants to become concentrated. Similarly, a fuel may cause a oxidant to become concentrated. A fuel may also interact with an oxidant to create a concentrated mixture of oxidant and fuel. A concentrated oxidant may also be created when a fuel is burned to produce heat. It is therefore desirable to develop an apparatus for separating and purifying a fuel from an oxidant that minimizes the health and safety risks presented by concentrated oxidants and fuels.

Four people were badly injured when a carriage on the Smiler ride hit an empty one on 2 June. Leah Washington, 18, from Barnsley and Vicky Balch, 20, from Lancashire, later each had a leg amputated. Ms Washington's boyfriend Joe Pugh, 18, also from Barnsley and Daniel Thorpe, 27, from Buxton, Derbyshire, suffered leg injuries. Twelve other people were trapped 25ft (7.6m) off the ground for several hours as emergency services attempted to rescue them. "My first words to the [fire] crews were this is probably going to be the most technical rescue they will ever carry out in their careers," Incident Commander Dale Harrison said. The Staffordshire Fire and Rescue officer, with 21 years' experience, was in charge on the day of the crash. "The first thing was the difficulty in getting access to the ride itself," he said. "We had to go down steep steps to get to the accident itself.... there were a lot of people already there and we could see that this was not going to be an ordinary rescue." He said a helicopter filming the incident as it unfolded and streaming pictures to news channels around the world, coupled with running commentary on social media, made the rescue all-the-more challenging. "There was scrutiny of every move we made," he said. "I don't think I've been under that level of scrutiny before." More than 30 firefighters worked alongside ambulance crews and engineers from Alton Towers. It took four hours to free the last passengers. Watch Manager Paul Hewson was on a special platform built to help remove the most seriously injured. "The courage of those individuals on that ride in a horrible situation was phenomenal," he said. Three hospital trauma team consultants were brought in to help treat passengers at the scene. Accident and Emergency consultant Richard Hall said they also helped surgeons and nursing teams at the Royal Stoke to prepare and get the most critically injured into operating theatres as quickly as possible. Some of the firefighters involved in the rescue, including Mr Hewson, have since visited the crash victims in hospital. Describing them as "inspirational," he said he was able "fill in some of the gaps" for them. "They were obviously in a lot of pain [at the time], in an awful situation and were unaware and couldn't see quite a lot of what was happening," he said. Mr Hewson said his last images from the scene were "quite distressing" and meeting the victims helped him come to terms with the incident. One of the most badly injured Leah Washington tweeted pictures from her 18th birthday celebrations on Tuesday evening. Well-wishers on Twitter praised her as "courageous" and inspiring." Calcified plaque in the aorta and pelvic arteries is associated with coronary artery calcification and is a strong predictor of heart attack. Current calcified plaque detection models show poor generalizability to different domains (ie. pre-contrast vs. post-contrast CT scans). Many recent works have shown how cross domain object detection can be improved using an image translation model which translates between domains using a single shared latent space. However, while current image translation models do a good job preserving globalintermediate level structures they often have trouble preserving tiny structures. In medical imaging applications, preserving small structures is important since these structures can carry information which is highly relevant for disease diagnosis. Recent works on image reconstruction show that complex real-world images are better reconstructed using a union of subspaces approach. Since small image patches are used to train the image translation model, it makes sense to enforce that each patch be represented by a linear combination of subspaces which may correspond to the different parts of the body present in that patch. Motivated by this, we propose an image translation network using a shared union of subspaces constraint and show our approach preserves subtle structures (plaques) better than the conventional method. We further applied our method to a cross domain plaque detection task and show significant improvement compared to the state-of-the art method.

It was a dark stormy night in October 1955. I, a Western Union employee, received a peculiar assignment that would take me back in time. I was to deliver a letter from 1885 to a random kid in 1955. The letter had been perfectly preserved for seventy years and was written by a notorious outlaw, Jesse James. I embarked on my mission, intrigued and fascinated by the prospect of delivering such an important letter. The address on the letter indicated a small town just outside of Kansas City. I quickly packed my bags and headed toward my destination. The storm was raging, with heavy rain and strong winds. The old car rattled as it struggled to carry me through the treacherous weather. I wondered if I would make it to my destination before nightfall. Finally, I arrived in the small town, which looked like it had not changed since the 19th century. I made my way to the local post office, where I asked the postmaster for the address of the random kid. He looked at me indifferently and told me that there was no such person in the town. Frustrated and exhausted, I decided to take a stroll around town. As I walked around, I noticed a group of kids playing in the park. I approached them and asked if any of them was the random kid I was looking for. An older boy stepped forward and introduced himself as Tommy. I showed him the letter and explained its significance. His eyes widened with amazement as he took the letter from me. He eagerly read the contents and asked me how I managed to secure such a valuable item. I shared my story with him, and he listened intently. It was like he knew the significance behind the letter, which was strange for a kid his age. Before I left, Tommy told me that he would never forget the significance of the letter and that he would treasure it forever. As I made my way back to the post office, I was glad that I had fulfilled my mission. I was exhausted but happy that I had played a small role in connecting the past with the present. I knew that Tommy would cherish the letter forever and would share the story with future generations. It was a night that I would never forget.

If any of you frequent rbadhistory, there is a rather infamous [chart] that captures a popular perception of the Middle Ages as a "dark age" that retarded scientific progress by a thousand years. The chart in question is known as the "Frazer-Gow Chart," created by two historians, Arthur Frazer and James Gow. The chart shows the development of scientific knowledge from 500 BC to 1900 AD, with each period divided into five distinct categories: Pre-Christian, Early Christian, Medieval, Renaissance, and Modern. According to the chart, science stagnated or even regressed during the Middle Ages, with the lowest point being in the medieval period. However, this chart has been widely criticized for its lack of evidence and historical accuracy. Many historians have argued that there was significant scientific progress during the Middle Ages, especially in the fields of mathematics, astronomy, and medicine, and that the Renaissance was more of a continuation than a revival of ancient knowledge.

The "fiscal cliff" comprises two components. Firstly, there are predetermined government spending reductions that were mutually accepted by both Republican and Democratic parties two years prior. While some funds from these cuts affect the military sector (which Republicans oppose trimming) and others impact different non-military initiatives (which Democrats resist cutting), these adjustments are relatively minor due to the concept of "baseline budgeting." In essence, this approach sets an escalating level of spending as its benchmark rather than reducing actual expenditure. Moreover, such modest decreases fall short of what would truly achieve fiscal equilibrium. Secondly, the conclusion of the Bush-era tax breaks represents the remaining part of the "fiscal cliff," potentially resulting in substantial tax hikes for the middle and affluent classes. Republicans advocate maintaining current tax rates across the board, while Democrats propose increased taxation for high earners above approximately $200,000 annually. Opinions vary among economists regarding the potential repercussions of surpassing this "fiscal cliff." Advocates of pro-capitalist ideology express concerns related to the negative effects on the economy when imposing higher taxes on wealthy individuals since they argue that economic expansion stems from enhanced savings, leading to further investment and improved efficiency through capital-intensive methods—referred to as "supply-side" economics. Conversemenly, supporters of mixed economies tend to emphasize the risks associated with diminished government spending, considering alternative perspectives on fiscal matters.

Exploring automated design of neural network structures customized for distinct tasks holds immense potential yet poses significant challenges. Although substantial advancements have been observed primarily in image classification and natural language processing domains, this study focusages on pixel-level tasks like semantic image segmentation employing fully convolutional networks (FCN). Fully convolutional networks necessitate different design decisions compared to other fields, involving modifications such as utilizing dilated convolutions or addressing complex optimization issues. Our aim is to identify efficient, resource-friendly FCN designs capable of executing in real-time without compromising performance. We accomplish this by deliberately expanding the model's parameters during training through supplementary cells offering additional guidance which are later discarded during testing. These support cells are generated by a separate neural network called a 'controller,' fine-tuned via reinforcement learning techniques. Furthermore, we illustrate effective methods for discovering optimal architectures within restricted timeframes and computational constraints, including a process that halts underperforming models early on, along with Polyak averaging combined with knowledge distillation to enhance convergence rates. In just eight days of GPU computing, our method yields competitive architectures comparable to current leading compact models across various applications, including semantic segmentation, pose estimation, and depth prediction. Around 1890, a political movement developed in the United States to mandate private executions. Several states enacted laws which required executions to be conducted within a "wall" or "enclosure" to "exclude public view." For example, in 1919, the Missouri legislature adopted a statute (L.1919, p. 781) which required, "the sentence of death should be executed within the county jail, if convenient, and otherwise within an enclosure near the jail." The Missouri law permitted the local sheriff to distribute passes to individuals (usually local citizens) whom he believed should witness the hanging, but the sheriffs - for various reasons - sometimes denied passes to individuals who wanted to watch. Missouri executions conducted after 1919 were not "public" because they were conducted behind closed walls, and the general public was not permitted to attend.

NASA scientists discovered cyclopropenylidene in the atmosphere of Saturn's moon Titan. The simple, carbon-based molecule has never been seen in an atmosphere before. Titan has long been considered one of the most Earthlike places in our solar system, and has been theorized to be similar to our planet during its early days. The Cassini spacecraft, which orbits Saturn and has been sending back data since 2004, found that the simple hydrocarbon is a chemical precursor to life. "This molecule existed on the primordial Earth," said Martin Cordiner, an astrochemist at NASA Goddard Space Flight Center. "This tells us that complex organic chemistry can happen in alien environments, and that the building blocks of life are everywhere in the universe." Cyclopropenylidene is a simple molecule containing carbon and hydrogen atoms, and it's surprisingly common in the universe. It's produced in chemical reactions in laboratories on Earth, and exists in carbon-rich environments like meteorites and the atmosphere of Titan. The Cassini spacecraft, which was launched in 1997, has been studying Saturn's moons since 2004. Scientists first discovered methane in Titan's atmosphere during a flyby in 2004, and suspected that complex organic chemistry existed on the moon. But until now, the instruments on the spacecraft weren't sensitive enough to pick up the signal from cyclopropenylidene. The data showed that the molecule's abundance is comparable to methane's. The scientists believe that the molecule is formed when sunlight interacts with methane and other molecules in Titan's atmosphere. This causes the carbon-hydrogen bonds to break, allowing the molecule to form. "We are very confident in our findings because we were able to detect the molecule multiple times at various altitudes," said Conor Nixon, a planetary scientist at NASA Goddard and lead author of a paper on the discovery published in Science Advances. "We are now bringing together all of the data we collected in order to create a detailed picture of the chemistry of Titan's atmosphere." This discovery, along with others, suggests that Titan's atmosphere is a chemical factory, and has a complex network of reactions similar to Earth's. "We can't say for certain what forms of life may exist in Titan's methane-rich lakes and seas, but this new information will provide valuable insight into chemical processes occurring in the environment of this intriguing moon," said Scott Edgington, Cassini deputy project scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Our research focuses on developing approximation methods for the Bounded Color Matching issue, also known as the Restricted Matching challenge. The problem involves finding a maximum cardinality or profit matching within a graph, with constraints on the number of edges sharing a specific color. Such issues not only hold academic value but also find practical applications in multi-fiber optical network systems, where different wavelengths represent distinct colors used to facilitate communication between system pairs. By utilizing linear programming techniques and polyhedral descriptions, we explore approximation and bicriteria algorithms that permit minor deviations from the prescribed color limits. Our primary achievement is demonstrating constant approximation solutions for both the profit and color boundary violation aspects of the bicriteria optimization task. Key terms include Approximation Algorithms, Combinatorial Optimization, Linear Programming, and Graph Algorithms.

In Oklahoma, there are thirty-nine tribal governments representing Native American tribes. These governments possess restricted authority within their respective territories. Unlike other regions in the US where Indian reservations exist, Oklahoma lacks this structure. Instead, these tribal authorities manage lands that were allocated during the period known as the Indian Territory era. Their power is confined and they lack influence over local government structures like cities and counties. Despite being acknowledged by the federal government as having self-governing capabilities including administrative, legal, and legislative aspects concerning their members and activities, their sovereigpta can be revoked or curtailed by the U.S. Congress. Moreover, all tribal constitutions and changes made to them must receive Congressional endorsement.

The shortcomings of Aristotelian physics would not be fully corrected until the 17th century work of Galileo Galilei, who was influenced by the late Medieval idea that objects in forced motion had an inherent inertia. This led him to develop a theory involving many bodies contained within one gravitational field expanding outward at different rates - or rather, as he said: "One body falling to earth will not fall equally into all parts of the Earth... but some shall fall very fast." Galileo's use of words and concepts borrowed from Greek philosophy were intended to describe his new scientific discovery (one whose ultimate consequences are still hotly debated today). But this is where things dramatically diverge with Newton's world view. While he has been much admired for how easily it allowed mankind to understand gravity, there have also been charges against him of playing fast-and-loose with the truth. To assign fault solely to Newton seems unfair given his extraordinary contribution to modern science. He laid out the law that explains these various motions through the relationship between mass, velocity, acceleration and time. It remains active even now two centuries after its publication. And while the fact remains that he then used those laws to construct the universe we live in can hardly be unkindly described as breathtaking - we owe him a debt no other scientist could ever hope to repay.

Emergent narratives provide a unique and compelling approach to interactive storytelling through simulation, and have applications in games, narrative generation, and virtual agents. However the inherent complexity of simulation makes the design of emergent narratives a challenging problem. In this paper we present the application of computational intelligence to the design and generation of emergent narratives in simulation. We provide a general overview of emerging narratives, including key concepts and common approaches to their generation. We describe how computational intelligence can be used to solve problems in the design and generation of emergent narratives. We survey the application of computational intelligence to emerging narratives, and we discuss future directions for research. Emergent narratives are defined as stories that emerge from complex simulations. They are often seen as a type of interactive fiction, in which the player's actions affect the course of the story. Emergent narratives have been used in games, narrative generation, and virtual agents. The concept of emergent narratives was first introduced by A.I. researcher Michael Mateas in 2001 [1]. Mateas defines emergent narratives as "complex fictional worlds in which stories emerge through the interactions of autonomous characters." He notes that emergent narratives are different from traditional narratives in several ways: Emergent narratives are generated by simulations, rather than being written by authors. Emergent narratives are open-ended, meaning that they do not have a predefined ending. Emergent narratives are nonlinear, meaning that they do not have a fixed sequence of events. Emergent narratives are dynamic, meaning that they can change over time. Mateas also notes that emergent narratives are similar to traditional narratives in some ways: Emergent narratives have characters that interact with each other. Emergent narratives have plots that unfold over time. Emergent narratives have themes that give them meaning. Since Mateas introduced the concept of emergent narratives, there has been a growing body of research on the topic. In 2005, Mateas and Stern published a book on the topic [2]. In 2007, the journal AI Society published a special issue on emergent narratives [3]. And in 2008, the International Conference on Interactive Digital Storytelling (ICIDS) held a workshop on computational approaches to emergent narratives [4]. There are several common approaches to the design and generation of emergent narratives. One approach is to use artificial intelligence techniques to generate stories from simulation data [56]. Another approach is to use evolutionary computation to evolve stories that are consistent with simulation data [78]. A third approach is to use simulation models to generate stories from scratch [9]. This approach has been used in the field of game design, where it is known as procedural content generation (PCG) [10]. PCG is a type of generative art, in which computer programs are used to generate artifacts that are aesthetically pleasing. PCG has been used to generate game levels [11], characters [12], and items [13]. It has also been used to generate stories [14], dialogue [15], and cutscenes [16]. Simulation-based PCG has been used to generate emergent narratives in games. For example, the game Spore uses PCG to generate stories about the player's creature [17]. The game Facade uses PCG to generate stories about the player's interactions with two virtual characters [18]. And the game The Sims uses PCG to generate stories about the player's Sims [19]. Simulation-based PCG can also be used to generate emergent narratives outside of games. For example, Mateas and Stern used PCG to generate stories about the interactions between virtual agents [20]. And Preteux and colleagues used PCG to generate stories about the spread of a virus in a virtual city [21]. Computational intelligence (CI) is a type of artificial intelligence that is inspired by natural intelligence. CI includes a wide range of subfields, such as evolutionary computation, neural networks, and fuzzy logic. CI has been used to solve a wide variety of problems, including optimization, control, and prediction. It has also been used to generate artifacts, such as images, music, and text. CI has been used to generate emergent narratives. For example, Riedl and Young used evolutionary computation to generate stories about virtual agents [22]. And Liapis, Yannakakis, and Togelius used evolutionary computation to generate stories about the interactions between virtual agents [23]. In this paper, we survey the application of computational intelligence to emergent narratives. We begin with a brief overview of emergent narratives. We then describe how computational intelligence can be used to solve problems in the design and generation of emergent narratives. Finally, we survey the application of computational intelligence to emergent narratives, and we discuss future directions for research.

Until 1932 the generally accepted length of the Rhine was 1,230 kilometres (764 miles). In 1932 the German encyclopedia Knaurs Lexikon stated the length as 1,320 kilometres (820 miles), presumably a typographical error. After this number was placed into the authoritative Brockhaus Enzyklopadie, it became generally accepted and found its way into numerous textbooks and official publications. The error was discovered in 2010, and the Dutch Rijkswaterstaat has published the complete overview of measurements.[citation needed] The river has an average discharge of about 2,900 m3s (100,000 cu fts) and an average basin area of 275,000 km2 (106,000 sq mi). The Rhine begins in the canton of Graubunden in the Swiss Alps, forms part of the Swiss-Austrian, Swiss- Liechtenstein border, Swiss-German border (See Upper Rhine) and then forms the Franco-German border (Middle Rhine), then flows through the Rhineland and eventually empties into the North Sea in the Netherlands. The largest city on the Rhine is Cologne, Germany, with a population of more than 1,050,000 people. It is the second-longest river in Central and Western Europe (after the Danube), and the 12th-longest river in Europe, at about 1,230 km (760 mi), with an average discharge of about 2,900 m3s (100,000 cu fts). The Rhine and the Danube formed most of the northern inland frontier of the Roman Empire and, since those days, the Rhine has been a vital and navigable waterway carrying trade and goods deep inland. Its importance as a waterway in the Holy Roman Empire is supported by the many castles and fortifications built along it. In the modern era, it has become a symbol of German nationalism.

In a tense exchange between the US and Russia, a Russian fighter jet reportedly flew dangerously close to a US Air Force plane while they were flying over international waters near Japan. US officials have confirmed that in April, the Russian Su-35 fighter jet flew within 100ft (30m) of the US reconnaissance aircraft, which is considered an unsafe distance for two planes travelling at such speeds. The incident happened during a routine flight by the US plane, which was conducting "a routine intelligence collection mission" in international airspace over the Sea of Japan, according to Lt Col Dave Westover, a spokesman for the US Pacific Air Forces. Lt Col Westover said in a statement: "Although the Russian aircraft was operating in international airspace, this interaction was irresponsible. We expect them to operate within international standards set to ensure safety and to prevent incidents, including the 1972 Agreement for the Prevention of Incidents On and Over the High Seas." The US has since lodged a complaint with the Russian government about the incident and called for "better airmanship" from the Russian pilots in the future. The US has also raised concerns about a series of similar incidents involving Russian jets and other US and NATO planes in the past year. In December, a US Air Force F-22 fighter jet intercepted two Russian Su-25 fighter planes over Syria, and in February of this year, a Russian fighter jet came within five feet of a US surveillance plane in the Black Sea. It is not yet known how the Russian government will respond to the latest incident, but it is likely to be met with strong condemnation given the heightened tensions between the two countries.

The man, who was in his 20s, was rescued by a volunteer crew from Bangor RNLI.
