The War of the Austrian Succession (whose North American theater is known as King George's War) formally ended in 1748 with the signing of the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle. The treaty was primarily focused on resolving issues in Europe. The issues of conflicting territorial claims between British and French colonies in North America were turned over to a commission to resolve, but it reached no decision. Frontiers from between Nova Scotia and Acadia in the north, to the Ohio Country in the south, were claimed by both sides. The disputes also extended into the Atlantic Ocean, where both powers wanted access to the rich fisheries of the Grand Banks off Newfoundland.

The primary factors influencing penis size are genetics and certain environmental influences. Genetic makeup sets the potential range for penis size. Androgen levels present in utero play a role in determining a male infant's degree of masculine characteristics. A high number of androgen receptors leads to more significant responses when androgens attach, ultimately increasing penile growth. Consequently, an individual's ultimate penis size is largely established at birth but may continue to grow during puberty until reaching the predetermined limit set by their genetical blueprint. Partial androgen insensitivity syndrome serves as evidence that this trait is generally fixed from conception since those affected often exhibit underdeveloped penises or ambiguous genitalia. Neither diet nor lifestyle choices appear to influence penis size, suggesting that products claiming to increase penile dimensions are likely fraudulent. The development of flattop vessels produced the first large fleet ships. In 1918, HMS Argus became the world's first carrier capable of launching and recovering naval aircraft. These conversions gave rise to the Lexington-class aircraft carriers (1927), Akagi and Courageous class. Specialist carrier evolution was well underway, with several navies ordering and building warships that were purposefully designed to function as aircraft carriers by the mid-1920s, resulting in the commissioning of ships such as Hosho (1922), HMS Hermes (1924), and Bearn (1927). Federated learning (FL) allows decentralized entities to jointly develop a shared model while keeping their data separate; however, it doesn't safeguard user privacy from attacks aimed at extracting sensitive information from the collective model. Consequently, integrating differential privacy into FL, creating DPFL, appears promising. Current techniques using encrypted gradient summation necessitate numerous communications, often fail to reach convergence, and struggle with scalability for extensive models due to dependency on dimensions within the injected noise. This study introduces an adaptation of the private learning framework through knowledge transmission established by previous researchers, incorporating elements of their PATE algorithm and the subsequent PrivateKNN technique into a federated context. Instead of merging gradients like prior methods, our approach combines label votes, circumventing dimension reliance and reducing communication overhead. Our analysis indicates that substantial gains in accuracy and robust, variable-based differential privacy can be achieved if voting score margins remain high. Empirical results demonstrate a marked enhancement in balancing privacy concerns with utility compared to existing top-performing DPFL approaches.

This paper considers a nonlinear multi-hop multi-user multiple-input multiple-output (MU-MIMO) relay channel, in which multiple users send information symbols to a multi-antenna base station (BS) with one-bit analog-to-digital converters via intermediate relays, each with one-bit transceiver. To understand the fundamental limit of the detection performance, the optimal maximum-likelihood (ML) detector is proposed with the assumption of perfect and global channel state information (CSI) at the BS. This multi-user detector, however, is not practical due to the unrealistic CSI assumption and the overwhelming detection complexity. These limitations are addressed by presenting a novel detection framework inspired by supervised-learning. The key idea is to model the complicated multi-hop MU-MIMO channel as a simplified channel with much fewer and learnable parameters. One major finding is that, even using the simplified channel model, a near ML detection performance is achievable with a reasonable amount of pilot overheads in a certain condition. In addition, an online supervised-learning detector is proposed, which adaptively tracks channel variations. The idea is to update the model parameters with a reliably detected data symbol by treating it as a new training (labelled) data. Lastly, a multi-user detector using a deep neural network is proposed. Unlike the model-based approaches, this model-free approach enables to remove the errors in the simplified channel model, while increasing the computational complexity for parameter learning. Via simulations, the detection performances of classical, model-based, and model-free detectors are thoroughly compared to demonstrate the effectiveness of the supervised-learning approaches in this channel.

Across a majority of modern learning-based tracking systems, expensive annotations are needed to achieve state-of-the-art performance. In contrast, the Lucas-Kanade (LK) algorithm works well without any annotation. However, LK has a strong assumption of photometric (brightness) consistency on image intensity and is easy to drift because of large motion, occlusion, and aperture problem. To relax the assumption and alleviate the drift problem, we propose CyLKs, a data-driven way of training Lucas-Kanade in an unsupervised manner. CyLKs learns a feature transformation through CNNs, transforming the input images to a feature space which is especially favorable to LK tracking. During training, we perform differentiable Lucas-Kanade forward and backward on the convolutional feature maps, and then minimize the re-projection error. During testing, we perform the LK tracking on the learned features. We apply our model to the task of landmark tracking and perform experiments on datasets of THUMOS and 300VW.

Metric-based few-shot learning methods concentrate on learning transferable feature embedding that generalizes well from seen categories to unseen categories under the supervision of limited number of labelled instances. However, most of them treat each individual instance in the working context separately without considering its relationships with the others. In this work, we investigate a new metric-learning method, Memory-Augmented Relation Network (MRN), to explicitly exploit these relationships. In particular, for an instance, we choose the samples that are visually similar from the working context, and perform weighted information propagation to attentively aggregate helpful information from the chosen ones to enhance its representation. In MRN, we also formulate the distance metric as a learnable relation module which learns to compare for similarity measurement, and augment the working context with memory slots, both contributing to its generality. We empirically demonstrate that MRN yields significant improvement over its ancestor and achieves competitive or even better performance when compared with other few-shot learning approaches on the two major benchmark datasets, i.e . mini Imagenet and tiered Imagenet.

Recently, amidst the NSA controversy, I observed numerous individuals—especially here—employing the "infringement upon my liberties" defense along with an oft-quoted statement by Benjamin Franklin to justify their apprehension and indignation regarding PRISM and the NSA's latest activities. Interestingly, most of these people align with a progressive political stance, which may explain their lack of support for existing firearm regulations in the US. Although I intend to discuss the NSA and PRISM separately at a later time, the contradiction within this mindset cannot go unnoticed. Arguing vehemently against the government breaching your Fourth and Fifth Amendment rights, yet endorsing their encroachment on Second Amendment rights appears absurd to me, undermining the essence of our Constitution, suggesting that some freedoms hold greater significance or deserve stronger protection than others. Rights ought to be treated equally; otherwise, we risk establishing a precedent whereby the judiciary might declare something unconstitutional due to prioritizing one freedom above another. Legislation could then potentially emerge, compromising one liberty solely to safeguard another perceived as more vital. Both the Constitution and its authors envisioned the same country, so this issue serves as a prime illustration. For example, I find it equally illogical when proponents of the Second Amendment oppose exercising First Amendment rights, like participating in LGBTQ+ rallies in specific regions. Consequently, I maintain that every American advocating for any particular Constitutional right must champion all of them. Otherwise, they're selectively adhering to portions of the Constitution that suit their personal lives and conform to their political views.

A software for managing simulation jobs and results, named "OACIS," is presented. It controls a large number of simulation jobs executed in various remote servers, keeps these results in an organized way, and supports the analysis of these results. It is designed to be a flexible tool, which can be easily expanded to manage other kinds of simulation. The software is written in Java, and it can be used in various platforms. Optical properties of dusty plasmas can be studied by scattering light off an electron plasma in a dusty gas. In order to better understand the influence of dust on the propagation of light in the plasma, we performed a Monte Carlo simulation. The software "OACIS" is employed to help manage the large number of simulation jobs executed in various remote servers. A few selected figures of the simulation results are presented here. Dusty plasmas are produced in a gas of rf-generated electrons and charged micron-sized grains. In these plasmas, the interaction between dust particles and electrons can be significantly different from those in a normal plasma, and the electron temperature can be much higher than the ion temperature. These unusual properties provide dusty plasmas with some unique optical properties, such as the existence of negative index of refraction. Another example of using "OACIS" to control remote simulation jobs is the study of electrostatic waves in dusty plasmas. The results of the simulation are presented in this paper. Motivation: In the absence of horizontal gene transfer it is possible to reconstruct the history of gene families from empirically determined orthology relations, which are equivalent to event-labeled gene trees. However, horizontal gene transfer (HGT) can alter the gene tree and it is hard to determine how much it has done so, and thus how much the orthology data can be trusted. Methods: Here we propose a new method for reconstructing gene trees from orthology data, which is based on a lineage-specific model of HGT. It infers the gene tree by maximizing a likelihood function for the gene tree under a suitable prior on the gene family history. We show that this likelihood can be computed in polynomial time, so it is tractable even for large gene families. We also derive two approximate methods for gene tree reconstruction, which avoid the computation of the likelihood entirely. Results: We apply our methods to 1298 orthologous gene families, which were previously studied using phylogenetic inference methods, and we find that our reconstruction methods yield gene trees which are similar to the ones obtained using phylogenetic inference methods. For 1222 of the gene families, we also find a history of horizontal gene transfer which agrees with previously found histories of gene duplication and HGT. In addition to the results for the 1298 gene families, we also find that our methods identify 102 gene families in which there is a likely history of HGT that was not previously identified. Had it not been for the hangover, I wouldn't have noticed her. It was at some local dive, in Cartagena, in July. I sat outside, sipping water in the enveloping heat, a heat which seemed to pierce straight through the awning and roast my insides. I had three glasses of water and alternated looking through each, trying to distill the world into something less headache-inducing. I saw someone with a mustache, and a straw hat, and a loose-fitting button-down shirt (Hawaiian-print, no less), with skin was so goddamned bright in the light - like made of mirrors - I pulled my head up from the table just to shout at that someone to get a tan. At least, I was about to, but when I looked up I noticed that someone's mustache was crooked - comically so - and then my head really started to swirl. " Liz? ," I muttered. I felt as confused as a kangaroo set out on a frozen lake. She - clearly she I could recognize those eyes from anywhere - pulled a German-language newspaper in front of her face. I kept staring for several minutes, ignoring the many-legged mass of ceviche that had summoned itself to my table. " Liz? ," I said, even quieter, which - strangely enough - was what got her attention. She replied in German, but then waved me over. I grabbed my ceviche and two of the three glasses of water. " What the hell is going on? You were. " She lowered the newspaper, her already askew moustache becoming even more askew as she spoke. " Dead? " " Yeah? What? I have no - Liz what - I can't. You're alive? I am asleep? I am way too hungover for this. " " Aren't we all, Al, aren't we all? And keep your voice down! Do you know any German? Can you speak to me in German? Ah, it doesn't matter. I don't think this place is planted; I haven't been here before. It would just be a shot in the dark for them. " " You died. Twelve years ago. I was devastated, Liz. " " Were you, though? ," she said, raising an eyebrow. " Yes! " " Well, actually, Al, I know you were. I saw you at the funeral. You looked pretty beat up. " " You attended your own funeral? " " Wouldn't you, given the chance? " I felt like throwing up, but more of a throwing up of my whole body, which I imaged would look like a sea cucumber stepped on by a boot. I couldn't eat, I couldn't think, I just watch those long-lost eyes flit back and forth between my face and the surroundings. " Al, walk with me. " I stood, automatically. " Am I dreaming? " We followed the side-street to its terminus at a major road, one where she talked a little more openly in the din of early afternoon. " Alice, you're really down the rabbit hole now, you know. Ha! You really think I died in a jet-ski accident? And that my body was so badly-damaged that they couldn't go open-casket, like my parents would have wanted. " " They told me you looked like a crash-test dummy that had been filled with ground beef. " " I told them to tell you that, Al. I thought you'd think it was funny. I mean, it is, right? " " Why would you do that? That's not funny? " " Al, humor is the only thing that keeps me going. Also, you need to call me Eugene Steinereiner when we're in public. And why didn't you tell me my moustache was crooked?! Christ, Al, you need to pay more attention. But that's all beside the point. Are you aware of the textbook definition of an amphibian vis-a-vis a reptile? Really, Al - this is important. " " Is this a joke? " I grabbed her hand and she whipped her head back at me. " There are no jokes! Not anymore! I mean, there certainly are jokes, Al, I didn't mean to say it so absolutely. There are jokes - but not this! Amphibians, Al! " " What, why? " I followed Liz to a run-down hotel, Paraiso Perdido. She beckoned me up the rundown stairway, passing a concierge wearing a coconut-white three-piece suit, who she addressed in German and broken Spanish. Before she opened the door to her room, she turned back to me, wild-eyed. " Al, I'm going to need you to promise me something before I tell you. At this point, you already know I'm alive and not a broken-up bag of hamburger meat, so I can't have you going back state side without a little debriefing. And then - you know - your life definitely will get weird afterwards. But hell, everyone's lives are a little weird, and you were always want for adventure, right? " " Liz, what are you talking about? " " Al, it's not lizard-people. It's frog-people. They had it wrong the whole time. Global warming, rising sea levels? Bad for frogs; great for frog-people. " " Liz..... " " Al, as soon as you step through this door, there's no stepping back. " She adjusted her mustache again, as if by a nervous tick. The key clicked in the door, unlocking a path so unimaginable that I even as it unfolded I could scarcely believe it was happening.

Additionally, he created the technique of pasteurization as a measure to hinder the transmission of diseases via dairy products and various edibles.

In the grand scheme of things, Germany losing WWI ultimately had negative consequences for the global community. Following the conflict, the Treaty of Versailles imposed severe limitations on the nation while compelling them to pay exorbitant reparations for the damages caused during the war. Consequently, the economic downfall of Germany adversely affected other countries as well since the funds paid by the Germans were funneled back to the U.S., contributing significantly to the prosperity of the Roaring Twenties and eventually playing a role in precipitating the Great Depression. Furthermore, the devastation faced by both Germany's economy and national morale provided an opportunity for Adolf Hitler and the Nazis to seize control, thus paving the way for WWII. Had Germany triumphed over Russia more swiftly, the rise of the oppressive Bolshevik regime may have been prevented, potentially sparing millions of lives from Stalinist atrocities. Alternatively, even if history unfolded differently, it seems plausible that the West would have preferred alliance with Imperial Germany rather than the USSR; particularly considering scenarios wherein Germany achieves victory early in battles such as the First Marne or captures Paris prior to engaging the United States militarily via events like the Battle of the Atlantic or the infamous Zimmermann Telegram. It's unlikely that under these circumstances, a second World War would occur due to the formidable combined forces of the USA, Germany, the UK, and France being able to thwart the Soviet Union. Additionally, the urgency for developing nuclear weaponry might have been diminished in this alternate timeline. Lastly, despite the probable collapse of the Ottoman Empire in the Middle East, reduced Western interference might have allowed for smoother resolution between the empire and its territories, thereby averting some of the current regional conflicts observed today, including groups like ISIS.

Article content Theories include: 1) each person's brain produces and processes thoughts in a unique way (such as by using different pathways), 2) everyone experiences their own emotions differently (and thus have distinct emotional reactions based on how others feel about you), 3) some emotions require more cognitive processing than others, 4) specific combinations of certain neurons may be involved in any given emotion neuronal magnets and 5) there could be a general mechanism at play which allows all human beings to experience the same basic thoughts - even if we don't know exactly what it is. There isn't much evidence to support these theories, however, since no studies really look into the question. Photo by Dan KitwoodGetty Images In fact, only a few people with severe mental illness actually report feeling like they're having multiple separate thought processes going on simultaneously. Are feelings just part of our brains' weird workings? Well ... kind of. Feelings are made up of chemicals released from the body when the right set of receptors are activated; they can also activate brain cells naturally during physical activity such as moving through space or breathing deeply. But so far, researchers have found little scientific proof to back the hypothesis that feelings evolve over time. As a result, this idea hasn't been widely accepted among scientists. If you've ever noticed an intense night-time feeling while lying in bed thinking hard enough, then after several minutes your mind begins to wander off, without causing pain or anxiety, and eventually fades away. It sounds like something out of science fiction, but physiologists call those kinds of deep, long-lasting sensations "drowsiness." Scientists believe drowsy feelings arise because our bodies shut down deep neural networks (the complex systems embedded within the brain) that control limb movement and alertness, allowing us to sleep. The theory goes that we get sleepy once we reach the point where executive function shuts down, leaving us free to go do whatever we want instead of being focused on staying awake. People often attribute anxious behaviour to depression; interestingly, though, both conditions involve decreased levels of neurotransmitters dopamine and serotonin, which would seem to suggest similar mechanisms driving the two disorders. And although panic disorder suggests strong connections between the brain and heart, research indicates stress hormones have relatively little influence on either condition. So why does every single person experience fear and sadness, whether everything seems normal or the world looks scary? One popular explanation holds that humans aren't wired to handle negative emotions very well. Einstein's solution to the problem of gravitational time dilation is called "spacetime" theory, which posits four dimensions instead of three dimensions for spacetime. The Maui Shell is a new convergent Linux shell that aims to work on both mobile and desktop. It is still a work in progress, but there are some usable features already. It works with Ubuntu, Debian, Elementary, and Fedora, and I was able to test it on Ubuntu 16.04. The software is still under heavy development, but I've been using it for several weeks and it is stable enough to be useful. The Maui Shell can be installed from the PPA repositories. I've also created a live USB image that you can use to test it. The Maui Shell's goal is to make it easy to use your phone as a desktop computer. The main goal is to make the phone and desktop apps work seamlessly, and this is mostly accomplished. The Maui Shell is currently based on GTK3, and this means that it is not possible to run GNOME Shell or KDE Plasma 5 apps. These will probably change in the future. The new shell is designed to work with the Android 9.0 Pie and upcoming Android 10 Pie. The phone apps are not very good yet, but they are usable. For example, you can run the phone's built-in web browser, which is much better than any web browser you'll find on desktop. The keyboard is also pretty good. It is better than the stock Android keyboard, and it also has predictive text. It's not perfect, but it's usable. The shell's desktop is based on GTK3 and includes a very basic shell and apps. It is not yet possible to run KDE Plasma 5 or GNOME Shell apps, but the desktop is usable and has some useful apps. For example, you can run the web browser, the file manager, the system monitor, and the battery monitor. The battery monitor is a bit strange because it uses a time-lapsed screen, but it's at least usable. The battery monitor also shows a live percentage of the battery, so you can see how much charge you have left. I've also been using the Maui Shell's messaging app. It is based on a custom GTK app that runs on top of the stock Android messaging app. It works reasonably well, but it's not very polished. The messaging app has the Android's unified inbox, so you can view all your messages in one place. You can also do some actions on your messages. For example, you can delete or reply to messages. You can also set a message as read, which will mark the message as read on your phone. You can also set a message as read on your desktop, which is useful for marking messages as read when you're on the go. The Maui Shell has some interesting features, and it's very stable. I would recommend it to anyone who wants to use their phone as a desktop.

The city lies on approximately 200 deep canyons and hills separating its mesas, creating small pockets of natural open space scattered throughout the city and giving it a hilly geography. Traditionally, San Diegans have built their homes and businesses on the mesas, while leaving the urban canyons relatively wild. Thus, the canyons give parts of the city a segmented feel, creating gaps between otherwise proximate neighborhoods and contributing to a low-density, car-centered environment. The San Diego River runs through the middle of San Diego from east to west, creating a river valley which serves to divide the city into northern and southern segments. The river used to flow into San Diego Bay and its fresh water was the focus of the earliest Spanish explorers.[citation needed] Several reservoirs and Mission Trails Regional Park also lie between and separate developed areas of the city.

The United Nations has welcomed the coming into force of a global arms trade treaty regulating the multibillion-dollar business. The landmark agreement, which was adopted by the UN General Assembly in April 2013, will impose restrictions on international transfers of conventional weapons. UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon hailed the treaty's entry into force today as "a new chapter" for international peace and security. He noted that it sets out the highest possible standards for preventing the diversion of arms to rogue regimes, terrorists and organized crime networks. "This is an exceptional achievement," Mr. Ban said. "For the first time, the international community has established common standards to regulate the global arms trade." The treaty requires governments to assess whether there is a risk that arms will be used to commit serious violations of international humanitarian and human rights law before authorizing any export. It also prohibits states from transferring arms if they know the weapons would be used to violate international law. Under the agreement, countries must also establish national systems to regulate their arms exports, including regular reports on transfers. The treaty has been signed by 130 states and ratified by 60 countries so far. Supporters say its entry into force marks a historic step towards greater control over the global arms trade, estimated to be worth around 85 billion a year. Speaking at a ceremony at UN headquarters in New York, Mr. Ban called on all states to sign and ratify the treaty "without delay." He said it offered an opportunity to reduce the suffering caused by armed conflict and to strengthen international security. "The Arms Trade Treaty is an important tool in the pursuit of peace and stability," he said. "I urge all countries to join this endeavor."

Offline reinforcement learning seeks to utilize offline (observational) data to guide the learning of (causal) sequential decision making strategies. The hope is that offline reinforcement learning coupled with function approximation methods (to deal with the curse of dimensionality) can provide a means to help alleviate the excessive sample complexity burden in modern sequential decision making problems. However, the extent to which this broader approach can be effective is not well understood, where the literature largely consists of sufficient conditions. This work focuses on the basic question of what are necessary representational and distributional conditions that permit provable sample-efficient offline reinforcement learning. Perhaps surprisingly, our main result shows that even if: i) we have realizability in that the true value function of every policy is linear in a given set of features and 2) our off-policy data has good coverage over all features (under a strong spectral condition), then any algorithm still (information-theoretically) requires a number of offline samples that is exponential in the problem horizon in order to non-trivially estimate the value of any given policy. Our results highlight that sample-efficient offline policy evaluation is simply not possible unless significantly stronger conditions hold; such conditions include either having low distribution shift (where the offline data distribution is close to the distribution of the policy to be evaluated) or significantly stronger representational conditions (beyond realizability).

The sheriff said she was resisting arrest and tried to handcuff her. She kicked the officer and struggled to get free. The sheriff was unable to subdue her. He then went to a nearby home for help. Two officers arrived and Paisley continued to resist arrest. One of the officers was injured in the struggle. She was eventually subdued and placed under arrest. 3 A preliminary hearing was held and the judge found probable cause to believe that Paisley had committed the offense of resisting arrest. At the time of the incident, she was also charged with assault on a peace officer. 4 Paisley moved to suppress the evidence obtained as a result of her arrest, alleging that the arresting officers had no probable cause to arrest her. The motion was denied and she was convicted of both charges. 5 On appeal, Paisley claims that the arresting officers did not have probable cause to arrest her for resisting arrest. In reviewing the denial of a motion to suppress evidence, we apply a two-step process. First, we determine de novo whether the police had probable cause to make the arrest. See United States v. Brignoni-Ponce, 422 U.S. 873, 880 (1975); United States v. Taylor, 10 F.3d 1441, 1445 (9th Cir. 1993). If the officers had probable cause, then we must determine whether the arrest was supported by an exception to the warrant requirement. See United States v. Delgadillo-Velasquez, 927 F.2d 619, 621 (9th Cir. 1991). 6 Probable cause exists if the facts and circumstances within the officers' knowledge and of which they had reasonably trustworthy information are sufficient to warrant a person of reasonable caution in believing that an offense has been or is being committed. See United States v. Kincade, 975 F.2d 845, 847 (9th Cir. 1992). The determination of probable cause is made on the basis of the "totality of the circumstances" and not on a consideration of each fact in isolation. See Illinois v. Gates, 462 U.S. 213, 238 (1983). 7 In this case, the arresting officers were investigating a possible domestic violence incident involving Paisley. Paisley had earlier refused to allow the officers to enter her home and had also told them that she was not going to make any statement. She had been charged with obstructing an officer and with assault on a peace officer. 8 It was at this point that the arresting officers decided to investigate whether Paisley was intoxicated. They found that she had an empty bottle of alcohol on the table and that she was wearing only a bra and panties. She also had a beer can in her hand and was very drunk. It was reasonable for the officers to believe that Paisley was intoxicated and to conclude that she was likely to become violent. The arresting officers also had reasonable grounds to believe that she was resisting arrest. She was kicking the officer, trying to get away, and resisting arrest. 9 Under these circumstances, the officers had probable cause to arrest Paisley for resisting arrest. Stars are fueled by nuclear fusion - hydrogen forced together into helium, then helium forced into lithium, beryllium, and so on. As you may know from humanity's continued attempts to create fusion power plants, fusion gives off a ton of energy, but it takes a ton of energy to make it go. In a star, fusion is caused by the intense gravity of the star crushing down on the elements in the core, squeezing them together until they fuse (and also quantum tunneling, but that's another ELI5). If a star is more massive, the fusion at its core goes faster. More mass means more pressure forcing the atoms together, and more atoms to force together. Big stars burn much hotter than small stars, but they can't burn forever. Fusing light elements together gives you more energy out than it took going in to fuse them. But fusing heavier elements gives you less energy and takes more energy, [shown in this graph] (URL0). The opposite is true of fission - bigger elements release more energy when they're split than smaller elements, and that makes a kind of intuitive sense. When you fuse elements, you're investing the energy into the atom that it took to fuse the two smaller elements. With bigger elements, it takes way more energy to fuse them, so you're investing more in than you get out with fusion. When you split them, you release that invested energy so you get more out of fission than fusion (with heavier elements; you get less energy from splitting lighter elements). The point where the two meet is iron. Up until iron, the star gets more energy out of fusion than went into fusing the atoms. That extra energy is what balances the star against the gravity crushing the elements down. The star is kind of self-limiting - if gravity overpowers the fusion energy, more atoms are crushed into the core and fuse, which creates more energy pushing out against gravity. If the fusion energy overpowers gravity, the atoms move away from each other and fewer fuse, so there's less energy to fight gravity. When the star reaches iron, that balance stops. Fusing iron absorbs energy instead of releasing more of it, so for every iron atom fused there's less energy pushing against gravity. More atoms are pulled downward into the core, crushing the core harder, so more iron fuses, so there's less energy, so gravity pulls more atoms into the core.... There are still lighter elements fusing outside of the core, so it's not immediate, but once a star starts fusing iron, its life is almost over almost" being a relative term - the star will still live for thousands or millions of years). The iron fuses into heavier elements that absorb even more energy, so there's even less pushing against gravity, and that reaction accelerates faster and faster as heavier elements are created. Each stage of fusing heavier elements takes less time, from thousands of years for iron to hundreds, to a decade, a day, then a few hours, until the last stage of fusion, in which every single atom in the core of the star gets fused within fractions of a second and the mass outside of the core collapses at significant fractions of the speed of light, crashing into the super dense core of the star, creating one last massive explosion of fusion, fission, and the reflection of the mass bouncing off the core. That explosion is a supernova. As XKCD pointed out, if you replaced our Sun with a supernova, and also detonated a hydrogen bomb that was literally touching your eyeball, the supernova in place of the Sun would deliver more energy to your retina than the hydrogen bomb. Even though big stars have much more fuel to go through, they burn through it much faster than small stars and reach the stage when they fuse iron much sooner. Smaller stars may not have enough mass to fuse iron at all, and will never go supernova, they'll just stop fusing their mass and slowly cool off over trillions of years. Our Sun is one of those - it doesn't have enough to mass to go supernova, it'll just slow down until it stops. Some of the largest stars will only last for a few millions or hundreds of millions of years, but will burn incredibly brightly until they explode. The smallest stars will burn through their fuel slowly, and stay super dim, but last for billions, if not trillions of years. And some stars are just older. They formed from the very first dust clouds after the big bang and were big and exploded. Remember, matter doesn't go anywhere, so after those stars explode their matter is flung out into space where it can collect and form new stars. Some stars are big and old and had enough time to reach the end of their fusion and explode, and some are still forming from the remnants of the old stars that already exploded. EDIT: Some typos and clarifications. Also worth mentioning: some stars can go nova (not super) and explode a "little bit" (again, "little bit" being a relative term - it's still a big boom). If the mass of the star is high enough, when it goes supernova the remnants of the star are so dense, and there's so much energy in one place, that it collapses into a black hole. But not all stars go supernova, and not all supernovas end in black holes! Some end in neutron stars, which are very weird.','Additionally, some are much older. We present a channel spectral estimator for OFDM signals containing pilot carriers, assuming a known delay spread or a bound on this parameter. The estimator is based on modeling the pilots in the frequency domain and performing an FFT over them which yields all spatial information about the channels (i.e., time-frequency masks). We consider different data representations, on which different kinds of multi-class classifiers are trained. Both raw data and high-level features are utilized. In the considered examples, a filter based on the classifier's score can be trained to retain 99 of the interesting events and reduce the false-positive rate by more than one order of magnitude. By operating such a filter as part of the online event selection infrastructure of the LHC experiments, one could benefit from a more flexible and inclusive selection strategy while reducing the amount of downstream resources wasted in processing false positives. According to Lindlof and Taylor, cultural studies in the United States originated within a practical, pluralistic framework. Initially, it primarily focused on exploring how audiences interpret and utilize popular culture, emphasizing its empowering qualities. Over time, the differences between American and British perspectives have diminished. Early British scholars often employed a Marxist lens when examining cultural phenomena, drawing inspiration from the Frankfurt School and figures like Louis Althusser. Such thinkers believed that the creators of cultural content held significant power over society's collective interpretation of their work. However, alternative methodologies, including feminist cultural analysis and other contemporary American approaches, reject these notions. These methods argue that various consumption practices can alter the significance of cultural products. As COVID-19 grabs the attention of the world, the war against antibiotic-resistant bacteria wages on. The number of people dying from bacterial infections could grow from 700,000 annually last year to 10 million by 2050, according to a new report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. As the world races to find effective new treatments, antibiotic-resistant bacteria are quickly learning new tricks for how to beat the medications we have today. So how do we fight back? First and foremost, doctors have to stop prescribing antibiotics so indiscriminately. Antibiotics are often recommended for viral infections, like the flu, where they are useless. And overuse in hospitals and clinics leads to the development of antibiotic-resistant bacteria, which then infect patients. Secondly, pharmaceutical companies must develop new antibiotics, especially those that fight the latest resistant bacteria. In the past, the pharmaceutical industry has not been rewarded for developing antibiotics. This is because they can be used only for a short period of time, and then the bacteria will inevitably develop resistance and patients will need new drugs. It doesn't pay to make a better toaster when it will just get thrown away. But there is a new drug in the pipeline that just might change all that. With a grant from the US National Institutes of Health, a team of scientists led by researchers at the University of Michigan Medical School is trying to create a new type of antibiotic that will work against the most common antibiotic-resistant bacteria. The approach is radical, but it might be the solution to the antibiotic resistance crisis. The team's novel approach is to screen a library of antibiotics for those that can kill bacteria by disrupting the process by which they synthesize DNA. They identify the bacteria that are resistant to the new drugs. Then they screen a library of chemicals for those that can kill the resistant bacteria, and screen again for new chemicals that can kill the resistant bacteria again. This screening-and-rescreening process continues until only one kind of resistant bacteria remains. Then they develop that drug into a commercial product, which they hope will be effective against a broad range of resistant bacteria. It's not the first time scientists have taken this approach to drug discovery. But it's never been tried before on an antibiotic. And it's never been done with the type of urgency needed to combat the current crisis. The strategy could work. And it might even work faster than the traditional approaches to finding antibiotics. The researchers hope to have a drug that works against resistant bacteria in three years. The researchers hope their approach will get the attention of pharmaceutical companies, who might find it less risky to invest in a new drug that has a higher chance of success. The researchers are making the results of their work open source. They are publishing details of their experimental protocols, their screening data, and their analyses of the data on the preprint server bioRxiv. That way, other researchers can evaluate their results and improve on their methods. Their preprint can be found here. Learn more about antibiotic resistance here.

The shortest path (SP) and shortest paths tree (SPT) problems arise both as direct applications and as subroutines of overlay algorithms solving more complex problems such as the constrained shortest path (CSP) or the constrained minimum Steiner tree (CMST) problems. Often, such algorithms do not use the result of an SP subroutine if its total cost is greater than a given bound. For example, for delay-constrained problems, paths resulting from a least-delay SP run and whose delay is greater than the delay constraint of the original problem are not used by the overlay algorithm to construct its solution. As a result of the existence of these bounds, and because the Dijkstra SP algorithm discovers paths in increasing order of cost, we can terminate the SP search earlier, i.e., once it is known that paths with a greater total cost will not be considered by the overlay algorithm. This early termination allows to reduce the runtime of the SP subroutine, thereby reducing the runtime of the overlay algorithm without impacting its final result. We refer to this adaptation of Dijkstra for centralized implementations as bounded Dijkstra (BD). On the example of CSP algorithms, we confirm the usefulness of BD by showing that it can reduce the runtime of some algorithms by 75 on average.

RAM can be read and written to anytime the CPU commands it, but ROM is preloaded with data and software that never changes, therefore the CPU can only read from it. ROM is typically used to store the computer's initial start-up instructions. In general, the contents of RAM are erased when the power to the computer is turned off, but ROM retains its data indefinitely. In a PC, the ROM contains a specialized program called the BIOS that orchestrates loading the computer's operating system from the hard disk drive into RAM whenever the computer is turned on or reset. In embedded computers, which frequently do not have disk drives, all of the required software may be stored in ROM. Software stored in ROM is often called firmware, because it is notionally more like hardware than software. Flash memory blurs the distinction between ROM and RAM, as it retains its data when turned off but is also rewritable. It is typically much slower than conventional ROM and RAM however, so its use is restricted to applications where high speed is unnecessary.

On the other hand, Professor Minford reiterated his concerns over the proposed plan being excessively costly, discouraging higher-earning citizens burdened with funding the initiative through increased taxes. Nonethptaetly, he acknowledged the challenge of persuading the general public concerning the advantages of such a program. Another of the Egyptian groups which employed violence in their struggle for Islamic order was al-Gama'a al-Islamiyya (Islamic Group). Victims of their campaign against the Egyptian state in the 1990s were both secularists and Islamists. The group was founded by al-Sayyid Imam al-Sharif, better known as Dr. Fadlallah (d. 2010), a Lebanese Shiite cleric and a teacher at the Lebanese University. Sharif, who was also the spiritual guide of Hezbollah, was accused of having encouraged the 1983 attack on the U.S. Embassy in Beirut. He himself denied involvement and blamed the attack on the CIA. Sharif's more radical views and militant rhetoric led to his expulsion from the Lebanese city of Tripoli in 1982. He then moved to Cairo, where he established the al-Gama'a al-Islamiyya. The group was founded to oppose the perceived corruption of the Egyptian regime and to introduce sharia law. The group, which was also active in Jordan, had some 3,000 members at its peak, but its membership declined after the 1990s. The group's first attack took place on October 8, 1981, when it bombed the Cairo building of the Egyptian Tourism Authority. That same year, it carried out its first assassination when it killed the Minister of Religious Endowments. In 1984, the group murdered President Sadat. From 1987 to 1988, the group carried out many attacks. In May 1988, it seized the al-Azhar University and held the students there for a week. In 1991, the group kidnapped and killed a number of Western tourists, and the Egyptian government consequently began hunting the organization's members. The group claimed responsibility for the 1995 assassination of Egyptian Prime Minister Atef Sidqi. The group's most deadly attack was carried out on October 17, 1995, when the group detonated a bomb in the resort town of Luxor. The attack killed fifty-eight people, most of whom were tourists. After al-Jihad and other terror organizations in Egypt were neutralized in the 1990s, al-Gama'a al-Islamiyya began to distance itself from the terror organizations that had sprung up in the wake of the 2011 revolution in Egypt. Hamas was founded in 1987, one year after the first Intifada broke out in the Palestinian territories. The organization is an offshoot of the Muslim Brotherhood and was founded by Sheikh Ahmed Yassin, Abdel Aziz al-Rantissi, and Muhammad Taha. The name "Hamas" is an acronym for Harakat al-Muqawama al-Islamiyya (Islamic Resistance Movement). The organization began as a branch of the Muslim Brotherhood, but split from it and became a separate organization. Hamas was established in order to replace the Muslim Brotherhood as the Palestinian branch of the Muslim Brotherhood, because the latter had been banned in Egypt. The organization was formed after the outbreak of the Intifada, and it was designated as a terror organization by Israel and the U.S. in 1997. Amid the 2011 revolution in Egypt, the Muslim Brotherhood's political branch, the Freedom and Justice Party, was established in 2011 and won a majority in the Egyptian parliamentary elections, which were held in 2012. The Freedom and Justice Party and Hamas became close after the 2011 revolution. The Egyptian army, which had ousted the Muslim Brotherhood from power in 2013, accused Hamas of collaborating with the Muslim Brotherhood in Egypt and supporting the organization's objectives. This led to a security deterioration in the Sinai Peninsula, where Hamas is active, and to restrictions imposed on the movement of people from the Gaza Strip to Egypt and Jordan. Hamas has been involved in armed attacks against Israel since 2001. Another Palestinian organization, Fatah al-Islam

In 1226, immediately after returning from the west, Genghis Khan began a retaliatory attack on the Tanguts. His armies quickly took Heisui, Ganzhou, and Suzhou (not the Suzhou in Jiangsu province), and then divided to take Xiliangfu and Xining. The Tangut emperor hurriedly surrendered, and the Mongols soon controlled all of the Tangut lands except for Lintao. Genghis Khan had a long-standing fear and hatred of water, and he would never sail on any river or sea. When his armies approached the Yellow River, he refused to cross it, and instead ordered his generals to follow the river south until they could find a place to ford it. This eventually led to the Battle of Mount Yinshan. The Imperial Taoist temple of Quanzhen had been located at Mount Yinshan for many years, and had been the source of much turmoil in previous years. During the reign of Emperor Zhangzong, the Quanzhen monks there had rebelled, and in the ensuing battle the abbot and most of the other monks had been killed. In 1182, the temple was rebuilt, and in 1187 another rebellion occurred, and again the abbot and monks were killed. In 1222, the Quanzhen monks had joined the war against the Jin, and after the fall of Zhongdu, they returned to Mount Yinshan. Genghis Khan's armies had taken Lintao in 1226, and the next year they attacked the Hexi Corridor. Two armies followed the Yellow River south, while a third army moved south through the Ordos Desert. When they reached Mount Yinshan, they found the Quanzhen monks had fortified their temple. The Mongol generals sent a messenger to parley with the monks, asking them to submit to the Mongols. The monks refused, so the Mongols attacked, taking the northern half of the mountain, while the monks retreated to the southern half. The Mongol general Doqolqu led an attack on the southern half of the mountain. He and his men climbed the mountain, but found themselves trapped and were soon killed. The Mongols tried again, but again the monks were able to push them back. Seeing that they were unable to take the temple by force, the Mongol generals decided to lay siege to it, surrounding it with troops. The siege lasted for more than a year, but the monks were able to hold out, even in the face of a smallpox epidemic. They were aided in this by the weather, as heavy snows fell that winter, and the Mongols could not get their siege engines into position. In the spring of 1228, the monks were still holding out, so the Mongol generals decided to launch another direct assault. On April 11, the Mongols began their final assault. One group attacked the front gate, while a second group attacked the back gate. However, the defenders were able to hold both attacks, and then counterattacked. The Mongol general Ming'an was killed, and then the defenders flooded the area, washing many of the attackers down the mountain. The Mongols finally realized that they could not take the temple by force. Instead, they cut off the water supply, and after two months the defenders surrendered. The Mongols massacred all of the Quanzhen monks and burned the temple to the ground. The monks' leader, Qiu Chuji, was able to escape to Liangzhou, but he was captured in 1229 and imprisoned in Ganzhou. He was eventually released, and died in 1227 in Chang'an. After the fall of Mount Yinshan, the Mongol forces were able to advance into the Hexi Corridor. They were delayed by the Great Wall, but in 1227, they defeated a Jin army at the Battle of the Tang River, and then took Yinchuan, the Jin capital. The Jin emperor surrendered, and the Jin dynasty came to an end.

E-Mail SPAM: A lot of the email addresses are acquired though spammers buying lists from sites that you input you email into when signing up. Others are from people breaking into databases with a lot of users (forums, blogs, etc) and selling the emails listed in the database to spammers. Some are from bots crawling sites where emails are in plain text or from phishing sites (a site that looks exactly like a popular legitimate site but is not) The addresses are then put into a file that a program reads. The program sends out an email to each of the addresses in that file. BlogForum SPAM: A bot goes to the site and attempts to register as a user. It is programed to use a certain username, email address, and password. The tricky part is getting around the Captcha vitrifaction.... There are a few ways they circumvent it. One way is to have a room of people just sit there all day and enter them as the bots encounter them. The other is to send the capcha to a site owned by the spammers where a regular user will input the answer thinking he is registering for a legitimate site. Like anything on the internet though, the Captcha is vulnerable to insecurities that allowing bypassing the Captcha completely. There are also character recognition programs that attempt to simply read the Captcha no different than a human would. Once the bot is registered, it just goes and makes a post or thread.

Alex McKechnie, then 16, was in the crowd for that first show and went on to be a regular at the club: "I saw The Beatles a few times in the north end of Liverpool and was working in Liverpool city centre as a messenger boy in a printing works when I heard that they were on at the Cavern in a lunchtime session. "The Cavern was in the basement of a three or four storey warehouse. The public went down one flight of stone stairs and then there were three long arches. "At the end of one of the long arches was a little tiny stage. That's where the Beatles performed 292 times. "I remember it being very highly charged with excitement. The music sounded even more exciting [than the previous gigs] because The Cavern was this little squashed space so the music sounded a bit louder, a bit more exciting and a bit more vital. About 20 to 30 people were there. "The Beatles were the complete package - they didn't just have a great singer, they had two great singers. They always did harmonies right from the very first time I saw them. "They could probably only afford two microphones, and so when one was doing the lead singing the other two were facing each other on the mic, and it was quite charismatic, it was nice to look at. They had a camaraderie about them. "I never heard them singing one of their own songs because they were just a straight covers band at that time, as was everybody else in Liverpool. "The standard songs that they sang - them and the other bands in Liverpool - were [by] Chuck Berry, Little Richard, the Everly Brothers, Buddy Holly. The sound that I very clearly remember the Beatles playing in the Cavern was a Chuck Berry riff. "As well as doing the stock standards, the Beatles were a bit different because they were better at playing complicated chords. The Beatles were a bit more adventurous. "It wasn't just the music and the singing, it was their lack of respect for the audience. At the Cavern for those first few gigs, they were quite irreverent to the audience and other people. They were sort of the first punk band. The Beatles were a law unto themselves on the stage. "They were still doing that when they went to America - if someone asked them a question they didn't give a serious answer, and that's how they behaved on stage in the Cavern, and that's why I think they liked it in the Cavern. "They were the epitome of rebellion in Liverpool because they weren't trying to imitate Cliff Richard and the Shadows doing little in time steps. They would dance out of step on purpose. "That was their purpose in life - to upset the apple cart. They were so cheeky and so entertaining all around. They were a little bit of a voice for us against authority. I think they were rebels. We were mini rebels supporting them. "Of course when I went back to work I used to stand gazing out of the window thinking about the Beatles and the girls at the Cavern. I couldn't really concentrate on doing any work. "Just in a few weeks they'd gained a bigger following. When word went around, the crowd grew and people kept coming back. Once you'd seen them, not many people didn't go to see them again. "They had big long queues, right down the length of the street and even round the corner at the bottom. But at that stage I'd dumped them. "They started talking about going to London and making records and things like that. Betrayal. "I wasn't the only one. I think the ones who thought that they'd discovered them were a little clique and really did give up on them when the masses found them. It was only when I heard Love Me Do on the radio that I started getting interested in them again. My wife subsequently bought all the LPs but that first era of The Beatles was over for me." Alex McKechnie was speaking to BBC News entertainment reporter Ian Youngs. The Cavern is celebrating the anniversary with a series of tribute events on Wednesday. A documentary about the first gig will be broadcast on ITV1 at 2240 GMT on Wednesday.

Most of us who live in Las Vegas have quietly accepted the fact that restaurants on the Strip are notoriously over-priced. However there is one place where you can still find remarkably inexpensive choices for high quality food: the buffet. Buffets began popping up along the Strip late last decade when a number of casinos decided they wanted to boost traffic by offering some form of cheap dining experience without offending guests with lower cost options like pizza slices or pasta salads. While most buffets offer three main courses - and often several side dishes - prices remain low compared to other restaurants. Be sure to check what's being served first because it will give you an idea of which flavor profiles are popular. For example one area might feature specialties like Italian meats or chocolate mousse, another French favorites, and yet others Indian foods. Favorites change frequently depending upon customer demand. A great strategy when visiting the buffet is to keep an eye out for desserts near the entrance. Finally use all of your coupons, especially ones related to specific meals because you'll want to buy extras ahead of time. This is particularly important during peak hours, and crowds do tend to force merchants to raise prices to cover increased overhead costs. You can also enter your loyalty card information directly on the app rather than having someone fumble with paperwork. Be aware that the selections offered varies greatly across locations. "I suspected that this had something to do with the composition of the soil, but I never thought that there was a genetic component." Potatoes can store a large amount of carbohydrates, which the plants use as energy. Valois decided to study whether the genes responsible for this storage process were the same in potato and humans. The team spliced the human gene into potato plants and tested them for changes in size and metabolism. They found that the plants grew about 50 percent larger than normal and had higher levels of glucose in their tubers, which suggests that they were storing more energy. "We had no idea that the human gene would work in potatoes, but it did," Valois says. The potatoes also had higher levels of starch and sugar, which is a good thing for the plant because it makes them more productive. The results suggest that potato growers may be able to increase yields by inserting the human gene into their crops.

The standard half-wave dipole, likely the most prevalent antenna configuration, comprises two 14-wavelength components positioned in sequence and parallelly, each linked to a separate conductor on a dual-wire transmitter. These elements' orientation causes them to operate 180 degrees out of sync; consequently, one component feeds current into the cable while the other withdraws it simultaneously. A monopole antenna can be considered as half of a half-wave dipole - a singular 14-wavelength element connecting its opposite side to either a ground surface or an analogous ground plane (counterpoise). Due to their smaller size, being only half that of a dipole, monopoles are frequently employed in long-wavelength radio transmissions where using a full dipole would prove unwieldy. Additionally, another widespread model is the folded dipole, consisting of two adjacent dipoles joined at both extremities, resulting in a combined one-wavelength antenna.

Samples drilled from beneath the Indian Ocean are being used to reconstruct past rainfall and temperature records. Scientists are studying how the Indian monsoon behaved in the past, to shed light on the impact of climate change. The research will lead to a better understanding of how the monsoon over India might change, said Dr Kate Littler of the University of Exeter. As part of the larger-scale Asian monsoon, the monsoon over India is formed due to intense heat from the Sun in late spring, which warms the Northern Indian Ocean, along with the plains of northern India and the Tibetan Plateau. This results in 75 of the year's rain falling between June and September. Simulations of future climate generally suggest a 5-10 increase in monsoon rainfall over India, which could influence the economy and agriculture. Palaeoclimatology - the study of changes in climate taken on the scale of the entire history of Earth - can give valuable clues to how the Earth might respond to future climate change. Dr Littler was part of an expedition to the Indian Ocean, Bay of Bengal and the Andaman Sea on a scientific drill ship belonging to the UK International Ocean Discovery Program. The team of international scientists collected sediment samples from the deep-sea at several locations. These are being analysed to reconstruct what the regional and global climate was like during the period when the small fossilised marine creatures contained in the sediments lived. "We wanted to capture the whole evolution of the India monsoon from when it intensified about 8 million years ago," said Dr Littler. "By analysing these hard-to-reach deep-sea sediments we will make important discoveries about the behaviour of the Indian monsoon in the deep past, and how its behaviour and intensity may change in the near future. "The data will give us a holistic idea of the past behaviour of the monsoon." Some of the samples came from sites that had never been drilled before. Others contained volcanic ashes, which can be matched to ancient volcanic eruptions, helping in dating the sediments. Their chemistry, geology and biology will be analysed to build up a record of how the annual Indian monsoon cycle has historically been affected by climate change.

Most historians[who?] consider Caliph Muawiyah (661-80) to have been the second ruler of the Umayyad dynasty, even though he was the first to assert the Umayyads' right to rule on a dynastic principle. It was really the caliphate of Uthman Ibn Affan (644-656), a member of Umayyad clan himself, that witnessed the revival and then the ascendancy of the Umayyad clan to the corridors of power. Uthman placed some of the trusted members of his clan at prominent and strong positions throughout the state. Most notable was the appointment of Marwan ibn al-Hakam, Uthman's first cousin, as his top advisor, which created a stir among the Hashimite companions of Muhammad, as Marwan along with his father Al-Hakam ibn Abi alAs had been permanently exiled from Medina by Muhammad during his lifetime. Uthman also appointed as governor of Kufa his half-brother, Walid ibn Uqba, who was accused by Hashmites of leading prayer while under the influence of alcohol. Uthman also consolidated Muawiyah's governorship of Syria by granting him control over a larger area and appointed his foster brother Abdullah ibn Saad as the Governor of Egypt. However, since Uthman never named an heir, he cannot be considered the founder of a dynasty.

Time is the ultimate factor relied on by everything in this world. Although man can control its environment, it can never tame time. Time only moves forward. It can not be reversed, replicated, or in any means at all be manipulated. When time runs, we have no other choice but to move along with it, and when it runs out..... we can only accept the fact that it has finished. One thing, though: in this reality, time can be paused. It can be stopped for a short, brief moment. Through this, an individual can take a while to sit back and relax, and see everything for what they are..... or at least, what they seem to be. I have lived knowing this fact for as long as I can remember, and though it proved to be pointless most of my life, I have actually used it in two very crucial instances. The first time being three years ago. I attended..... or should I say was forced to attend a camp held on the other side of my town back then. It was boring really, and the only engaging parts were the buffet dinners and the after-party where I got to meet some new friends. One girl, to be specific, named Jessica Andy. It has been a habit of mine to'check out' some fine women here and there, but when I first saw her, I switched on pause mode almost instantly. She was unbelievably beautiful. Only afterwards did I realize that it was the first time I actually toggled my ability to intermit time. I tagged along with Jessica throughout the entire party that night, and boy, was it a blast. "It's really rare to meet genuinely nice guys like you here in the city. And you know what? I feel like I've seen or even met you before! I don't know why, but you seem like those kind o' guys that I feel I've been friends with for a very long time." she said giggling, while we were strolling down the sidewalk going home after the event. I gave her a little smirk, "This isn't really an act of kindness in the name of being nice though. This is just a guy walking a girl home. I mean, why would I let a lady walk all alone at this time in the night? There are a lot of trippy dudes here in the neighborhood, and I can't afford letting them get their hands on you." She smiled and turned away from me. "Well here we are! " , she exclaimed as we stopped across a house, "This is home sweet home for me, Andrew! Thank you so much bringing me home, this was so nice of you!" "Yeah, anytime. No problem." I replied. There was an awkward silence between us at that moment right there. "So, hey, if you didn't know..... there's a really great pizza place nearby this area that we could hangout at..... and you know I just want to know, if uh, are you free tomorrow night..?" I asked her as I had my hand on my hair. "Oh..... I'm so sorry Drew, but I need to catch a flight home tomorrow, mum and dad expect me to back immediately after this camp." "Flight? Home? But I thought I mumbled as I pointed at the house that we just stopped at. "Oh, this is my Aunt's house here in town! I actually reside in Sydney with my mum, dad and 3 brothers. I just made a visit here to attend the event." For some reason I don't know, I felt like my heart just got hit hard with a baseball bat when I heard the word'Sydney'. That's so far away from here. "Sydney? You mean you're from Australia!? No wonder you're so gorgeous!" I told her in a silly manner..... At this point I realized that this was most probably the last time I'll see her again, "So..... it was nice to meet you, Jessica Andy." "It was nice to meet you too, Andrew Alvarez." " ..... So should we hug?" Laughter bursted out, "No, no we shouldn't." she said, as she leaned in on me and kissed me on the cheek. "Thanks for being a good friend, Drew. See you again sometime." "Yeah, I'll see you again..... sometime......" hopefully. I watched as she paced towards the front door. She looked at me again and gave me a big smile before entering. I waved at her and returned an even bigger smile. Yes, it may seem a bit over-exaggerated, we've known each other for only what? 4 hours? And it developed so fast for sure..... but whatever. It felt great. And although that was already 3 years ago, I still can't forget about her. It was 3 years ago..... the first time I ever used the ability to pause time. So when was the second time I used it? Just today actually. As I was taking a walk around my university..... there she was, again. Jessica Andy in the flesh. Not a daydream anymore. Not just a Facebook photo of her..... It was her, the real her, right there. How could it be, that a girl from Sydney is back here again? Was there another camp? Or what? I called her out from afar and she looked my direction to see who was shouting her name. She was just as surprised as I was when she saw me. I was so excited, I ran for it. As I was so happy and giddy about this entire situation..... all of a sudden, time paused involuntarily. I didn't want it to stop, but it did. I looked around and saw everything in a frozen frame. The falling leaves from the trees, the birds and the clouds in the sky, the civilians walking by, Jessica in front of me looking as wonderful as I first saw her years ago..... they were all standing still. I looked to my rear left, and saw the raging police car about to run me over. It may seem that it's standing still right now, but as soon as time gets away from this pause screen that I am in, my whole existence will have been put to an end. Time can be paused..... but it can not be permanently stopped. It is a linear process..... it has a point of beginning, and a point of conclusion. Death is imminent. It can not be escaped. All of this is reality, and it can not be denied, but only accepted. I am not afraid of dying..... I am more afraid of missing the opportunity to live this life fully and appreciate it, not only for what it seems to be, but for what it really is. I can not pause time forever. This was the third time I have used the ability to intermit it, and was it an absolute strike.

During the latter part of the 1EE70s, numerous key thoroughfares underwent transformation into "ejes viales"; these high-capacity one-way streets traverse across Mexico City's heartland horizontally. The design of the eje vial system follows a nearly Cartesian layout, featuring north-south routes like Eje 1 Poniente, Eje Central, and Eje 1 Oriente, while east-west paths include Eje 2 Sur and Eje 3 Norte among others. Additionally, there are circular routes such as the inner-city Circuito Interior or Anillo Periférico, the outer-ring Circuito Exterior Mexiquense state highway encircling the northeast and east segments of the metropolis, the Chamapa-La Ventan toll road along the northwest perimeter, and the Arco Norte circumventing the entire urban sprawl in a curved trajectory extending westward towards Atlacomulco, then northwards towards Tula, Hidalgo, before veering eastwards toward Puebla. Moreover, the second tier of the Anillo Periférico where fees apply, known informally as the "segundo piso" or second floor, was inaugurated in 2012, albeit certain portions remain unfinished. To facilitate transit between Observatorio and the international airport, the city is bisected by the east-west running Viaducto Miguel Aleman. Finally, the year 2013 witnessed the inauguration of the Supervía Poniente, a paid passage connecting the burgeoning Santa Fe commercial hub with the southwestern regions of Mexico City.

The immune system serves as a defense mechanism for living beings against infections through multiple layers of protection that become more precise at each level. Essentially, it employs physical barriers to block harmful microorganisms like bacteria and viruses from penetrating into the body. When these defenses fail, the innate immune system kicks in promptly, though not specifically tailored to any particular invader. This type of immunity exists across both plant and animal species. However, if pathogens manage to dodge the innate response, creatures with backbones have another safeguard called the adaptive immune system. Triggered by the initial response, the adaptive immune system adjusts itself throughout the course of an infection to enhance the identification of the intruder. After defeating the pathogen, the system remembers the encounter via an immunological memory, enabling quicker and more potent reactions upon subsequent exposures to the same threat.

"Will I be safe?" Asked Christopher. There was a moment of silence. The words came slithering from the dark in a low and comforting tone. A whisper. "Of course..." A thin smile spread across his face as he nodded, smiling back at her. The door opened quietly behind him. He glanced out cautiously into the hallway. No one else seemed to have heard them or seen them come in. Darren stepped forward slowly with his hand on one shoulder. "I'll wait for you here." His voice held that same reassuring tone she had found in him, and it felt good to hear it again after all this time. Even though they'd only known each other casually since he left here two weeks ago, she could feel how strongly linked they were right now. That safety was as real as it ever would be. She smiled warmly as well, feeling her heart swell with happiness just thinking about it. Looking down at her hands, she began picking up small bits of debris where the pieces had landed during the fight against Tzadera and those who tried to kill her along the way. It was a few days before the full effects of what happened to her began to show themselves; fatigue, nausea, dizziness, weakness... But these things eventually subsided in their own time. At least she knew she wasn't alone anymore. She kept the necklace around her neck anyway...just to remind herself not to let go when she needed a little bit more strength than usual. Soon enough, she saw them step out in front of her and started to turn away to walk towards them. They made no attempt to stop her, but instead looked straight ahead and continued on together. They passed Christian without saying anything, and then Christopher turned and walked past her. Her gaze followed him until his back disappeared beneath their hoods, leaving her wondering if he really did know who she was or why he hadn't addressed her by name yet. Without another word, Darren took off running in between two buildings and nearly collided head-on with someone trying to cross the street. Traditionally, architects drew out the designs on semi-transparent paper. When it came time to copy these for the various people (City planers office, construction company, individual contractors) they used a tool called a drafting machine to make a blueprint. The process for making blueprints is so called because the chemicals used were a combination of ammonium ferric citrate and potassium ferricyanide. These chemicals reacted when exposed to ultra-violet light. The blueprint, or cyanotype, was then washed in water and hung up to dry. Blueprints are no longer used as much, but there is still a fascination with them. Many architects have a sentimental attachment to them as well. If you have a blueprint from an old building, or a special one from a family home, you may want to keep it in good condition. First, blueprints should be stored flat. You can store the blueprint in a polyester sleeve, and place the sleeve in a box. Keep the box in an archival box, with an acid free tissue. Finally, the box should be kept in a cool dry place, like a climate controlled storage unit.

When you hit send, your mail is delivered to the Mailserver of your mail provider. Your computer knows which one that is because it was part of your initial mail setup on your computer. Once the mail reaches'your' Mailserver it'll look at the domain (the part behind the sign in the mail address) and looks up the IP address of that domain using DNS (think of it as the phone book of the internet). Once the server knows the IP of the recipients mailserver it'll send your mail over there. The recipients Mailserver then looks at the account name (the part before the sign in the mail address) and puts the mail in the correct mailbox. Edit: the recipients computer is set up to know the recipients Mailserver and thus checks there for new mail. So in the end, the two computers themselves don't communicate directly at all but the servers do.,It works kind of like the post office. Think of it like this. The stuff after the symbol is the city. The stuff before the is the street address. When you hit send the email gets given to the post office of the "city" you specified which can be google, yahoo, comcast or hotmail. The city then looks at the "street address" and figures out where to put it. You then go and pull it out of your mail box.

The Rhine River holds the title for being Germany's most extended waterway. Within this region, significant tributaries like the Neckar, the Main, and eventually the Moselle join the Rhine, with the latter contributing over 300 cubic meters per second.
