Nearing the Netherlands' boundary, the Rhine boasts an average flow rate of 2,290 cubic meters per second and spans approximately 400 meters across on average.

The day it happened was a good day. People who had previously felt the pain of incurable illnesses and weakness from old injuries had now become stronger. They had become alive. These were people who were once told they would never be able to walk again. People who were told nothing could be done about a malignant tumor in their body. There were the people in third world countries who would have previously succumbed to illnesses that were now healthy. People who were going to experience death had a pass. Those who had no idea how to cope with the sense of impending expiration were free from the constraints previously placed on them. Everyone was finally happy. Everyone was at peace. Everyone would never have to suffer another loss ever again. That was everyone but Daniel Smith. The poor thirty-two year old was not one of the lucky ones. Everyone else was a lucky or chosen one except for Daniel. Daniel had been declared the loser of this immortality jackpot. He knew he would never have to experience the loss of his parents, the loss of his brothers and sister. He would never experience the defeated inability to help his loved ones manage pain, loss or suffering. This was a good thing for him. Instead, this burden was placed on his loved ones. His loved ones would watch Daniel progressively age as everyone else stayed the same. His brothers and sister would stay their same ageless young selfs doing whatever they pleased, without any care or remorse. His mother and father would watch their son turn gray and age with wrinkles deepening in his skin, his bones becoming brittle, his muscles becoming weaker, and his body slumping with the weight of his mortality on his shoulders. His parents who should never experience the pain of burying one of their children would have to endure that pain just once. His brothers and sister would have to figure out how to deal with their own pain, their own sadness while trying to support their own parents. Daniel could not accept his mortality. He was the only mere mortal in a world filled with immortality. This wasn't fair. This wasn't something he wanted. This wasn't something he had signed up for. Instead, he was just unlucky. He never wanted to experience the emotional pain, he was feeling now. The pain of knowing there was no way to dull what was to come. His family would not be able to escape their own feelings of loss, regret, anger, suffering, and mourning. They would have to live forever knowing that one of their own family members had to perish because of mortality. To Daniel, this was impending doom. How was he supposed to live with all of this in the back of his mind? How could he handle knowing that at one point he would stop breathing and stop living? Daniel sat with a gun in his right hand resting against his thigh. In his shaking left hand was a picture of his smiling family standing in their matching Christmas sweaters in front of their Christmas tree. He felt the heaviness in his stomach looking at the happiness emitting from that single moment in time. Was it worth living his life knowing one day his family would have to suffer because of his mortality? Or should he just get the inevitable over with? What was the right thing? He no longer knew.

Basic overview: Early animation of the simpsons was very similar to how comics used to be made (and in some ways, comics are still done this way). An animator used a light table to draw pictures onto transparent paper, then a camera photographed the drawings onto film. Before I got the story straight from the horse's mouth, I was under the impression that this guy (who looks kinda like a hand model) was the only one who did the animation for the first season of the simpsons. But as it turns out, there were in fact several people who did the drawings. (The original image was full of noise so I had to reduce the resolution. The image at the top of this page is a cleaner version of the original. It's what this guy actually drew on a light table.) The original creators of the simpsons, Matt Groening, James L Brooks, Sam Simon and David Mirkin were the ones who did most of the work on the show during it's first year. They would come up with a bunch of ideas and sketches of their characters, and then they'd send them to this guy. One of the animators, Ken Keeler, wrote an article about this process, which you can read here. After the first season, the production of the simpsons slowed down quite a bit. Instead of animating all the characters in every episode, only the main characters (Homer, Marge, Bart, Lisa and Maggie) would get animated. The other characters would just be redrawn onto the light table by the same guy using reference pictures that the animators gave to him. This guy is considered to be the "Official Simpsons Animator." If you look at the line of the characters in this picture, you'll see that it's very clean and straight. This is because the drawings were done with a grease pencil on a light table. That's what he uses to draw the characters. This guy is currently living in Australia. He's still doing the same thing for the simpsons, but he's not getting paid for it. The one thing that makes this job special is the fact that you can't be anonymous. People recognize you if you walk down the street, so you have to be careful. If you'd like to learn more about this guy, I would recommend reading this interview. How to draw the Simpsons To draw the Simpsons, you need a piece of paper, a pencil and a light table. Draw the outline of the character with the pencil on a piece of paper. After you're done with that, make sure you're using a light table. Draw the line again with the grease pencil (or a crayon) onto the light table. The character will be drawn from a front view, but you can also do the back and side views. And that's all there is to it. You can use reference pictures, but it's best not to. The original pictures are often hard to find so you have to draw them yourself. A simpsons episode usually has several scenes in it. Some of them are just full of static drawings, while others are full of movement. Each drawing is called a cel. You can see the front view (the direction the character is looking) of the drawing on top, and the back view of the drawing on the bottom. The character's head is the top half, and the rest is the bottom half. Some of the characters don't have a back view. Maggie is an example of that. Here's an example of a drawing that's full of movement. The character's head is at the top of the drawing, and the bottom of the drawing is the character's legs. The drawing is stuck to a glass plate. You can see the reflection of the drawing on the glass plate in this picture. The glass plate is placed in a plexiglass box. To play the movie, the plexiglass box is placed in front of a camera. The camera takes a picture of the drawing. The plexiglass box is placed on the light table, and the image is flipped over. You can see how the characters look at this point in time in the following pictures. Here's an example of a drawing with some static movement. The characters in this scene are moving left to right, but the camera is moving right to left, so the characters are still in the same spot. The plexiglass box is placed in front of a camera, the camera takes a picture, and the characters on the drawing move. The image

I woke from my dreams by the sound of my phone having a seizure on the desk. It was rolling across the desk, chirping out a familiar song. Jill insisted on making it her ringtone. "They tell me I'm too young to understand. They say I'm caught up in a dream. Well life will pass me by if I don't open up my eyes, well that's fine by me." I hesitated. "Am..... is it really...?" "Do you need me to prove to you?" Jill demanded, angry. "Just listen to me and then you can ask all the stupid living person questions you need..... if there is time." "Time?" "Listen!" Jill said, her voice unnaturally deep. "You need to go into my room, right now." When I didn't move, she snarled, "Diana Jane! You need to do this. Do it now. I please?" "Fine, turn on the light and go over to my dresser." I walked slowly into her room, shuffling across the hardwood floor. "In the underwear drawer," Jill said. The phone was making weird noises, static, and she sometimes broke up. "Did you call me from..... wherever to tell me to hide your toys?" "No. I need you to take out the box in the drawer, inside will be a golden necklace. Do not touch it. Open the box only when you have filled the sink with salt water..." She broke off for a moment. "Did you..... hear..... Drop the whole box in there, then get..... out..... of the apartment." It was there, under her lacy bras. I took it out, listening to Jill tell me what to do over and over again. I filled the sink with hot water then dumped a whole tub of salt in it. The box seemed red in the kitchen light and where it sat on the counter was a large, red stain, like blood. I used a paper towel to wipe it up. It smelled like blood. I dropped it into the water. Nothing happened. Jill told me to get out, but I just wanted to sleep. I walked to my room, the phone forgotten on the floor. I woke up the next morning completely refreshed. I went into the kitchen to find it spotless. No box. My phone was on the counter, plugged into the wall. There were two places set at the table. I finally recognized that the apartment looked a little weird. It was missing some things, the boxes I had of Jill's stuff, the floral picture she painted for me. The walls were hung with pictures of farm animals. There were daisies in the sink. It looked like it had when I first moved in with Jill and her grandmother. I was about to turn and go back to my room, when I saw my reflection in the window. Jill was staring back at me, her red hair short around her face. She winked and was gone. I headed to my phone, just in time for it to ring. I answered it with a tired tone, "Hello?" "Where the hell have you been?" my mother asked. "At home." "You haven't answered your phone for over two weeks. We sent the police to look for you," she said. "Jake has been worried sick." "Jake? I haven't spoken to Jake in two years," I said. "I broke up with him Freshman year." "I don't think it is funny. I think it might be best to move back home..." "I am not moving back home. I am 27 years old, I don't need I began. "I am coming over," my mom said, sounding very worried. "I think you need to see a doctor." I hung up the phone. Fifteen minutes later there was a knock on the door. Jake and my mother stood there. Jake rushed to grab me and I stepped away from him. My mother, looking years younger, stood wearing a very concerned look. "We need to take you to a doctor," my mother said. "I think there is something wrong with you..." "There is nothing..... Jill's dead and all you can think about is..." "Jill isn't dead..." Jake said. "She called us, to come talk to you. She sounded really worried." "What..... what day is it?" "March 15th, 2009."

An illustration of eugenics gone wrong would involve the affluent group being able to pay for gene editing, leading to desirable traits in their children, which exacerbates the gap between the rich and poor. When it comes to using gene modification for preventing diseases, there isn't as much debate if it's clearly defined and executed properly. For instance, pregnancies with conditions that don't allow survival after birth are usually terminated; thus, making changes inside the womb wouldn't raise concerns in such situations. However, when considering potential applications of gene modification, "preventing diseases" becomes less relevant compared to commercial purposes aimed at "enhancements" or "upgrades." Regarding medical reasons alone, our understanding of the consequences of altering a single gene is still limited since many genes perform various functions or interact with others. Consequently, our current level of knowledge does little to reassure us that we won't cause additional issues while attempting to solve existing ones.

The issue revolves around ownership of the historical narrative surrounding Alexander the Great and the associated cultural legacy and identity. This raises several questions regarding the true nature of the Macedonians - were they genuinely Greek or merely 'barbarians' assimilating aspects of Ancient Greek culture? Moreover, there are wider considerations about whether a particular culture can persist beyond its geographical origin, and if current inhabitants of a nation hold exclusive rights over an ancient civilization's cultural heritage after centuries of transformation. Additionally, we must ponder how interconnected culture and history truly are, and how past biases may shape modern perceptions of ancient societies. According to Greece, the Macedonian Empire established by Alexander was an integral part of Ancient Greece's cultural heritage, and thus only those of Greek descent can lay claim to it. However, this perspective is contested due to significant migration patterns and linguistic changes that occurred between the 5th and 6th centuries AD. Although many historical accounts portray Macedonians as Greeks, some argue that such descriptions stem from external sources like the Romans, who lacked interest in recognizing internal distinctions within regional groups. Presently, citizens of the Republic of Macedonia (FYROM) assert that Ancient Macedonians had distinctive cultural and ethnic traits compared to Ancient Greeks, challenging the notion that Modern Greeks exclusively possess Macedonian identity. For instance, one hypothesis suggests that the Macedonians might have been a northern Greek tribe that experienced Hellenization, incorporating select elements of Greek culture while retainsindeedpreserving certain unique characteristics.

This quote - attributed to a Professor Aaron Levenstein - perfectly captures the dangers of making miscalculations, or generalisations, based on data sets. When it comes to data, nothing is ever clear cut. And'The Thinning Blue Line' report released today by Reform Scotland, on how more Scottish police officers are solving fewer crimes, is a good case study. Here, I pose and attempt to answer some key questions......... On the face of things, the report's findings are correct. On a per officer basis, the clear-up rate has decreased from 12 to 8 between 20067 and 201314. The report argues this shouldn't be happening when crime rates are falling, and there are now more than 1,000 additional officers to work on fewer recorded offences. There are a couple of problems I found when I quickly dug a little deeper into how the report presented the data. One must also try and place these figures into context. Surely more officers won't necessarily equate to more crimes solved. Each crime should be taken on its own merit. What leads are there? What forensic evidence is left behind? What about crimes that maybe take more than one year to solve? What about the rise of internet crime and its online perpetrators who can be trickier to bring to justice? And, as one freedom of information request that I submitted earlier this year shows, what about the average 58 officers who were on stress-related leave between April 2013 and December 2014? On paper there are more officers, but in reality a number were on the bench unable to work on solving crimes. The report makes assumptions, which may well be true, that any increases in unsolved crimes are due to more officers being placed into positions previously held by civilian staff - essentially taking officers off the streets. However, the report doesn't seem to have the data or proof to categorically support this claim, but rather relies on "Underpants Gnomes" logic (go on - look it up). Indeed the report quotes Chief Constable Sir Stephen House in stating to Holyrood's Justice Committee that "under the terms on which staff go, jobs are in most instances closed down, so in the vast majority of cases there is no backfilling [by police officers] to be done." So if backfilling is happening, how many officers is it really impacting? To what extent is this a permanent occurrence, or to just fill in to cover an occasional civilian staff absence? If ever a freedom of information request could be used to strengthen an argument, this would be it. Although to be fair, backfilling civilian or administrative posts with police officers was a point the government failed to address in its official response.

Sir Charles Lyell first published his famous book, Principles of Geology, in 1830. This book, which influenced the thought of Charles Darwin, successfully promoted the doctrine of uniformitarianism. This theory states that the geological features of the earth can be explained by means of natural processes presently in operation, without the need to postulate catastrophic events. Lyell's book continued to be reprinted and revised over the years, with a twelfth edition being published in 1872. Although this statement in itself might seem innocuous enough, he was actually attempting to deny the Genesis Flood. He had been reading the first edition of Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species, and he was attempting to extend the theory of biological evolution to the earth's crust. He was seeking to explain the sedimentary rocks and the fossils contained therein without invoking Noah's Flood. The following quotation is from a letter written by Sir Charles Lyell to a friend of his in 1836. I am really amazed at the more than stupid audacity of theologians. I have scarcely read a sentence yet, but I have found a contradiction. I have just been reading the accounts of the deluge. If you read the account in Genesis, it is plain that the waters did not rise above the highest mountains. It is also plain that they did not rise above the highest mountains. But according to Moses' account, the waters rose fifteen cubits above the highest mountains. Now it is impossible to conceive how these facts can be reconciled. The one is a contradiction of the other, and either must be false. I cannot help thinking, from what I have read, that the account of the deluge is an Eastern story that was handed down to Moses. There are similar stories in the Hindu and Persian mythology. Thus the two theories (the uniformitarian and the catastrophist) of the origin of the earth's strata are both inconsistent with Moses. Now the question is, are we to abandon the facts and the certain conclusions drawn from them because they are inconsistent with Moses, or are we to give up Moses because he contradicts the facts? I will not have any more to do with the Old Testament if it contradicts my reason. "Let us accept the truth, whatever it may be, and take for our motto those words of Boyle: 'In necessary things, unity; in doubtful things, liberty; in all things, charity. Sir Charles Lyell died in 1875, and was buried in Westminster Abbey. It is said that his funeral was attended by many of the leading men of science. These are but imperfectly known in their present operation; how much less completely in their remote effects! What causes skeletal muscle to contract is when a little neurotransmitter (a chemical messenger from your brain) called Acetylcholine binds to its specific receptor on skeletal muscle. However, acetylcholine is used for more than muscle contraction, it is also used for the parasympathetic nervous system as stated below. When Acetylcholine binds to parasympathetic receptors, it causes effects that allows your body to "rest and digest," such as salivation, digestion, urination, etc. The muscle relaxers you are taking probably block acetylcholine release higher up in the chain of command, meaning they affect more than just skeletal muscle. Some muscle relaxers can act right at the skeletal muscle and prevent the Acetylcholine from binding to the receptor on that muscle. Others are less localized (like preventing the release of Ach from your neurons) which will affect other body systems as well.

Transistors come in two varieties with minor distinptaions in their application within circuits. The first type, known as a bipolar junction transistor, consists of three terminals named base, collector, and emitter. In this device, a modest electric current entering the base terminal influences a significantly greater current traversing from the collector to the emitter terminals. On the other hand, the second kind, called a field-effect transistor, features three differently designated terminals: gate, source, and drain. This variety operates by utilizing a voltage applied to the gate terminal to regulate the electrical current flowing between the source and drain terminals.

Regulator Ofgem said there were 3.8 million switches in the first six months of the year. This was the second six months in a row that the switching total broke three million, and was nearly one million higher than the first half of 2015. The data follow a major report into competition in the energy market. According to the Competition and Markets Authority's (CMA's) two-year investigation, two-thirds of UK households were paying "over the odds" for their energy compared with those who have switched to a different tariff. Ofgem said that customers could save more than PS300 by ditching expensive standard variable tariffs for the cheapest deal, often a fixed-term tariff. The average standard variable tariff of the larger energy suppliers as of 28 July was PS1,066. The cheapest tariff available on that date - a one year fixed tariff - was PS758, a saving of PS308. "Great deals are there for the taking. There are very competitive offers and many more suppliers to choose from, and that's why more consumers are switching," said Rachel Fletcher, of Ofgem. To encourage more switching, Ofgem is planning to trial "more effective prompts" on customers' bills to encourage them to compare different tariffs. However, Ofgem said it would not be capping standard variable energy tariffs. The regulator's response to the CMA report, and the investigation itself, was criticised by some as not being bold enough. Separately, the Energy Networks Association has launched a new service in England, Scotland and Wales allowing people to contact their network in the case of a power cut by calling 105 or visiting a dedicated website.

Our method provides a systematic way to construct multi-D non-separable wavelet filter banks from two 1-D lowpass filters, with one of whom being interpolatory. A number of pubs claim to be the oldest surviving establishment in the United Kingdom, although in several cases original buildings have been demolished and replaced on the same site. Ye Olde Trip to Jerusalem in Nottingham is claimed to be the "oldest inn in England." It has a claimed date of 1189, based on the fact it is constructed on the site of the Nottingham Castle brewhouse; the present building dates from around 1650. Likewise, The Nags Head in Burntwood, Staffordshire only dates back to the 16th century, but there has been a pub on the site since at least 1086, as it is mentioned in the Domesday Book.

In Brazil, the pinnacle of the judicial system is represented by the Supreme Federal Tribunal (Supremo Tribunal Federal), which serves as both the country's constitutional court and its ultimate legal authority. Its scope encompasses reviewing potential violations of the Constitution and issuing verdicts on conclusive habeas corpus petitions related to criminal offenses. Additionally, it exercisers original jurisdiction over disputes concerning officials such as congressional representatives, senators, cabinet members, top court justices, along with the nation's President and Vice-President. Complementarily, the Superior Court of Justice (Tribunal Superior de Justica) functions to evaluate appeals against decisions from State and Federal Circuit Courts in areas pertaining to civil and penal legislation tied to federal statutes or inconsistent adjudications. Moreover, the Superior Labour Tribunal (Tribunal Superior do Trabalho) specializes in labor law case assessments, while the Superior Electoral Tribunal (Tribunal Superior Eleitoral) acts as the supreme arbiter for electoral laws and supervises national election processes. Lastly, the Superior Military Tribunal (Tribunal Superior Militar) holds preeminence regarding issues within the realm of federal military regulations.

Learning energy-based model (EBM) requires MCMC sampling of the learned model as the inner loop of the learning algorithm. However, MCMC sampling of EBM in data space is generally not mixing, because the energy function, which is usually parametrized by deep network, is highly multi-modal in the data space. This is a serious handicap for both the theory and practice of EBM. In this paper, we propose to learn EBM with a flow-based model serving as a backbone, so that the EBM is a correction or an exponential tilting of the flow-based model. We show that the model has a particularly simple form in the space of the latent variables of the flow-based model, and MCMC sampling of the EBM in the latent space, which is a simple special case of neural transport MCMC, mixes well and traverses modes in the data space. This enables proper sampling and learning of EBM.

The semi-final between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest took place on Saturday 15 April, 1989. The match was sold out, meaning more than 53,000 fans from the two sides would head for Hillsborough for the 15.00 kick-off. Despite being a far larger club, Liverpool supporters were allocated the smaller end of the stadium, Leppings Lane, so that their route would not bring them into contact with Forest fans arriving from the south. Football crowds at the time had a reputation for hooliganism and strict segregation was enforced. Fans began arriving at Leppings Lane at about midday. The entrance had a limited number of turnstiles, of which just seven were allocated to the 10,100 fans with tickets for the standing terraces. Once through the turnstiles, supporters would have seen a wide tunnel leading down to the terrace and signposted "Standing." As was common practice in grounds at the time, the terrace was divided into "pens" by high fences that corralled fans into blocks and separated them from the pitch. The tunnel led directly into the two pens behind the goal, pens 3 and 4. Access to other pens was poorly-marked - a sign for refreshments was bigger than one showing the way to pens 1 and 2, the inquests heard. There was no system on the day to ensure fans were evenly distributed across the pens and no way of counting how many were in each pen. The match commander was Ch Supt David Duckenfield. He was new in his post and had limited experience of policing football matches. Police expected supporters to "find their own level" by spreading out across the pens in search of space, but this was difficult to do as movement between the pens was by narrow gates at the rear. By 14.15 a crowd had started to build outside the Leppings Lane turnstiles and it swelled rapidly over the next quarter of an hour. Progress through the seven turnstiles was slow and by 14.30 just 4,383 people had entered, meaning 5,700 ticketed fans were set to enter the ground in the half hour before kick-off. The inquests were told Mr Duckenfield and Supt Bernard Murray discussed delaying the kick off to allow fans to enter but decided against it. By 14.45 CCTV footage showed there were thousands of people pressing into the turnstiles and alongside a large exit gate, called Gate C. The funnel-shaped nature of the area meant that the congestion was hard to escape for those at the front. The turnstiles became difficult to operate and people were starting to be crushed. The police officer in charge of the area, Supt Roger Marshall, told the inquests he thought somebody was "going to get killed here" unless the exit gates were opened to alleviate the pressure. He made several requests and at 14.52, Mr Duckenfield gave the order and the gates were opened. About 2,000 fans then made their way into the ground. Most of those entering through Gate C headed straight for the tunnel leading directly to pens 3 and 4. This influx caused severe crushing in the pens. Fans began climbing over side fences into the relatively less packed adjoining pens to escape. The pens' official combined capacity was 2,200. It was later discovered this had not been updated since 1979, despite modifications made to the ground in the intervening decade. At 14.59, the game kicked off. Fans in the two central pens were pressed up against the fences and crush barriers. One barrier in pen 3 gave way, causing people to fall on top of each other. Those who survived told of seeing people lose consciousness in front of their eyes. Supporters continued to climb perimeter fences to escape, while others were dragged to safety by fans in the upper tiers. At 15.06 Supt Roger Greenwood ran on to the pitch and told the referee to stop the game. In the chaotic aftermath, supporters tore up advertising hoardings to use as makeshift stretchers and tried to administer first aid to the injured. The authorities' response to the disaster was slow and badly co-ordinated. Police delayed declaring a major incident and staff from South Yorkshire Metropolitan Ambulance Service at the ground also failed to recognise and call a major incident. The jury decided this led to delays in the responses to the emergency. Firefighters with cutting gear had difficulty getting into the ground, and although dozens of ambulances were dispatched, access to the pitch was delayed because police were reporting "crowd trouble." Only two ambulances reached the Leppings Lane end of the pitch and of the 96 people who died, only 14 were ever admitted to hospital. For the jury in the inquests, police errors in planning, defects at the stadium and delays in the emergency response all contributed to the disaster. The behaviour of fans was not to blame. Match commander Ch Supt David Duckenfield had a duty of care to fans in the stadium that day, the jurors decided. They found he was in breach of that duty of care, that this amounted to gross negligence and that the 96 victims were unlawfully killed. The jury also concluded:

Deep learning techniques have achieved top-notch outcomes in various medical imaging applications, including the segmentation of distinct anatomical components. As deep learning research proliferates and related source codes become readily accessible, selecting an appropriate model for novel tasks can be challenging given finite time and computational resources. Meta-learning emerges as a viable strategy for efficient model selection; it leverages previous model performances to forecast their effectiveness on fresh tasks. In our study, we explore meta-learning's application to segmentation using data from ten diverse organ and modality datasets. Our proposal includes four methods for representing each dataset through meta-characteristics: one employs image statistics, while the other three utilize deep learning characteristics. Support vector regression and deep neural networks serve as tools to establish correlations between meta-attributes and past model efficiency. When tested with three independent validation datasets, our methods yielded Dice scores that closely align with actual performance, evidenuming the promise held by meta-learning in medical imaging domains.

John, the child of Henry II of England and Eleanor of Aquitaine, entered this world on December 24th, 1166. His father, Henry, possessed vast territories along the western coastline, including Anjou, Normandy, and England, further expanding his realm by subjugating Brittany. In matrimony, Henry joined forces with the formidable Eleanor of Aquitaine, sovereign of the Duchy of Aquitaine, holding questionable rights to Toulouse and Auvergne within southern France; she was also previously wedded to Louis VII of France. This union led to the creation of the Angevin Empire, bearing the name derived from Henry's hereditary title as Count of Anjou or more accurately, its capital city in Angers. Nonetheless, the integrity of this empire remained delicate due to the distinct historical backgrounds, cultures, and governing systems among its constituent regions. Progressively moving towards the south through Anjou and Aquitaine, Henry's influence gradually dwindled, hardly echoing contemporary notions of an empire. Meanwhile, longstanding connections like those between Normandy and England started fading away. Upon Henry's demise, the future of the empire appeared uncertain. While European practices favored primogeniture, wherein an elder male offspring would inherit all parental estates, the English norm differed. Many anticipated that Henry might distribute the empire equally amongst his sons, trusting they would maintain amicable relations posthumously. Further complexities arose since numerous portions of the Angevin empire were technically owned by Henry as a vassal of the French king, hailing from the opposing House of Capet dynasty. Additionally, Henry frequently formed coalitions with the Holy Roman Emperor against France, exacerbating the already intricate feudal dynamics.

The distinction between morality of abortion and its legality is often missed when discussing the pro-life and pro-choice positions. Granted, there's usually someone that brings it up somewhere down the line, but it doesn't appear to be on a national level at all. As far as I recall, Bill Nye the Science Guy has been given an award by the IHSA for his work as a "national consultant" on abortion issues in the U.S., and he also provides access to one of IHSA's web sites which specifically addresses the question of whether or not Roe v. Wade violated human rights. The website addresses each question with some commentary: But what if abortions are designed more literally than merely leaving patients sick? And how can we take advantage of this ambiguity when many clinics provide just a few abortions every day without any hassle? Because unlike Roe V. Wade, we do have access to care from our physician services. Abortion is only legal in certain cases where, after a successful procedure performed on an indigenous alien or woman who was conceived with rape on her mind, an autopsy results show she had no conception again. We would be legally able to terminate a pregnancy if it was medically necessary, or they were found to cause serious bodily harm to the woman. I use the phrase "abortion is illegal under 18 U.S.C. 1152" because I consider abortion "legal" in some clinical contexts (for example, in the United States), but not in others - even though our laws are so strict that doctors do not need to carry out an abortion or abort in order to perform it. In essence, the distinction between morality of abortion and its legality is often missed when discussing the pro-life and pro-choice positions. So why does it matter? One thing about abortion is that if you're being charged with murder, no amount of time will mean anything. You'll most likely end up in jail, no matter what your case may involve. There simply isn't much evidence to back these claims up; however, there is something intrinsically wrong with demanding that physicians and other health professionals be allowed to remove abortion from their practice, including requiring them to operate in state hospitals for whom abortion is not legal in most states. The right to choose should be protected in all circumstances, including those involving minors and people with diseases that might otherwise define themselves before a doctor could provide treatment or care to them. If abortion is somehow illegal under 17 U.S.C. 1152, then the federal government has no place to regulate its activities, unless Congress allows the removal of such an act. So if you want private entities to enforce rules that violate human rights while doing business, remove abortion from your practice. In my view, it's the institution of the U.S. Constitution that fundamentally protects us against the tyranny of law at all levels. It serves two purposes: first, it protects individual liberty and Second, it makes clear that the country as whole is a democracy running through a system of checks and balances. What difference does it make that the judiciary, which controls the executive branch, cannot impose justice on citizens?

Pesticides are used to control organisms that are considered to be harmful. For example, they are used to kill mosquitoes that can transmit potentially deadly diseases like West Nile virus, yellow fever, and malaria. They can also kill bees, wasps or ants that can cause allergic reactions. Insecticides can protect animals from illnesses that can be caused by parasites such as fleas. Pesticides can prevent sickness in humans that could be caused by moldy food or diseased produce. Herbicides can be used to clear roadside weeds, trees and brush. They can also kill invasive weeds that may cause environmental damage. Herbicides are commonly applied in ponds and lakes to control algae and plants such as water grasses that can interfere with activities like swimming and fishing and cause the water to look or smell unpleasant. Uncontrolled pests such as termites and mold can damage structures such as houses. Pesticides are used in grocery stores and food storage facilities to manage rodents and insects that infest food such as grain. Each use of a pesticide carries some associated risk. Proper pesticide use decreases these associated risks to a level deemed acceptable by pesticide regulatory agencies such as the United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and the Pest Management Regulatory Agency (PMRA) of Canada.

Integrating basic geometric forms into 3D point cloud data serves as a link connecting raw digital 3DN data and complex structure details inherent in 3D objects. This integration facilitates numerous subsequent tasks within 3D data manipulation. Traditionally, RANSAC-oriented techniques were considered the pinnacle of solution for these fundamental shape fitting issues; however, their dependency on meticulous customization for each specific dataset limits their scalability across extensive collections containing various form factors. Our study presents the Supervised Primitive Fitting Network (SPFN), which operates as a comprehensive neural network capable of identifying multiple primitives of differing dimensions autonomously. SPFN relies on predefined surface coordinates and classification labels associated with the individual data points during training. Rather than outputting the primitives straight away, our system initially determines distinct attributes for each data point followed by employing a module designed for estimating the type and characteristics of the primitives. Upon testing against a new benchmark comprising 3D mechanical components conformant with ANSI standards, our method shows considerable advancements compared to prevailing RANSAC approaches and those based on neural networks alone.

Orthogonal signal-division multiplexing (OSDM) is an attractive alternative to conventional orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) due to its enhanced ability in peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR) reduction. Combining OSDM with multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) signaling has the potential to achieve high spectral and power efficiency. However, a direct channel equalization in this case incurs a cubic complexity, which may be expensive for practical use. To solve the problem, low-complexity per-vector and block equalization algorithms of MIMO-OSDM are proposed in this paper for time-invariant and time-varying channels, respectively. By exploiting the channel matrix structures, these algorithms have only a linear complexity in the transformed domain. Simulation results demonstrate their validity and the related performance comparisons.

Quantizing weights and activations of deep neural networks results in significant improvement in inference efficiency at the cost of lower accuracy. A source of the accuracy gap between full precision and quantized models is the quantization error. In this work, we focus on the binary quantization, in which values are mapped to -1 and 1. We provide a unified framework to analyze different scaling strategies. Inspired by the pareto-optimality of 2-bits versus 1-bit quantization, we introduce a novel 2-bits quantization with provably least squares error. Our quantization algorithms can be implemented efficiently on the hardware using bitwise operations. We present proofs to show that our proposed methods are optimal, and also provide empirical error analysis. We conduct experiments on the ImageNet dataset and show a reduced accuracy gap when using the proposed least squares quantization algorithms. 1 footnote 1 1 footnote 1

Indeed, the term "reasonable person" can vary significantly depending on the context. Generally, it refers to someone acting reasonably under specific conditions, such as encountering a car crash while driving their vehicle. Over time, societal norms influence how we define this concept, shifting away from historical interpretations. Informally, it could be likened to an ordinary individual commuting on public transportation. Rather than having a static meaning, it serves as a guideline for jury members when evaluating actions and responses during trials.

Furthermore, each new cohort of legal professionals possesses unique perspectives based on contemporary standards. Nevertheless, established legal principles shape our understanding of the 'reasonable person.' These include concepts such as stare decisis, which emphasizes consistency through previous court decisions. Although evolving societal values may alter perceptions of what constitutes reasonable behavior, existing case law provides some boundaries within which these judgments operate.

In instances lacking explicit precedents, attorrights rely on drawing parallels between relevant past rulings, resorting to personal judgment when necessary. Thus, although the notion of a "reasonable person" adapts over time, its evolution remains influenced by foundational legal doctrines and previously settled cases.

Walt Disney and his brother Roy contacted Goldenson at the end of 1953 for ABC to agree to finance part of the Disneyland project in exchange for producing a television show. The Walt Disney Company was incorporated on January 9, 1955 with an initial stock offering that raised 2 million (equivalent to today). Goldenson designed much of Mickey Mouse's early appearance - a black-and-white silhouette against bright colors representing lightness and happiness; later color drawings were also influenced by Cubist art.[citation needed] He developed the character using assistants named Ben Hardaway and Ub Iwerks who animated him through the use of paper cutout animation techniques. This pioneering technique became known as cel animation because it used "cels" or small individual plastic figures instead of traditional painted cels (painted celluloid) which had been done since the dawn of film animation but proved expensive to produce quickly enough for TV programs. As well as developing new cartoon characters such as Oswald the Lucky Rabbit and Donald Duck Goldenson produced many classic cartoons including Plane Crazy, Make Mine Music, Whacko Bird, Barnyard Buddies, Epic Yarn, Pets 'n' Animals, Popeye series, Felix the Cat, Thimble Theatre, Goofy's Circus Train, Mickey Mouse Clubhouse, Tale Spinners Academy stories based off Grimm fairy tales, Winnie the Pooh, the Chipmunks and more recent movies like Frozen and Ratatouille among countless others. During this period he created one of the most iconic images associated with animation: Milt Kahl portraying Mr. Incredible from the movie Incredibles wearing only red pants. In addition Max Fleischer directed several shorts starring Mickey Mouse during these years too, although none have survived except for two very rare outtakes. In 1959 Wheatley Associates hired Goldenson away from Disney Productions where he remained until retiring in 1970 after being diagnosed with Parkinson's disease. According to Pixar cofounder John Lasseter, "What impressed me about Bob when we first met is how incredibly happy he always seemed while working - never complaining about anything, no matter what crazy hours he might be pulling." Following retirement, Goldenson published the book Designing Animation Comics in 1976 detailing his career and work processes. Over the next few decades he continued fighting for disability benefits so other artist could get treatment without going bankrupt.[123] He died due to complications related to Parkinson in 1984 leaving behind over 150 credits under both name[4]. He has received nine honorary degrees, three Emmys, eleven Annie Awards,[5], five Annie Award nominations [6] and seven Oscar nominations.

For instance, one area may receive 250 inches of snow in a single season, while another receives only four or five feet the following year—a substantial difference. Moreover, utilizing stationary cable support structures proves more cost-effective and secure compared to adjustable ones. However, certain resorts employ the latter. Secondly, longevity and capacity play crucial roles. Ski lift installation incurs substantial expenses, often amounting to millions of dollars. Similarly, replacing the cables to which the chairs are attached entails considerable financial investment. Over time, the main cable elongates slightly, causing the chairs to descend below their usual position amidst support towers. Setting the towers too low might pose safety concerns; therefore, elevated placement allows extended usage of the same cable despite its gradual lengthening. Observing various ski lifts reveals a common feature: a loading platform situated at the base, equipped with a movable pulley system powered by a counterweight, typically made of heavy concrete. Depending on passenger volume, the counterweight's position alters accordingly. Fully occupied lifts result in the counterweight being raised, whereas less crowded rides see it remain closer to the ground. This mechanism influences the height of the chairs relative to the ground. Given that chairs can experience dips of approximately ten to fifteen feet between support towers based on passenger load and cable extension, understanding these dynamics becomes essential.

A new privacy-focused cryptocurrency has become popular recently, and not only because of its Harry Potter theme. Grin promises to create a cryptocurrency that is both 'light' and completely anonymous. The system will be created with the help of an existing proof-of-work protocol called CryptoNight V7, but it's quite different from other cryptocurrencies using this same algorithm like Monero or Zcash. CryptoNight operates on one specific function which means that mining calculations need to be stored in RAM, making for slower transaction times compared to more advanced protocols such as Segwit2x or even Bitcoin Core. The group working behind Grin want to use CryptoNight while changing its hashing algorithm so transactions are faster than what they already offer. This can cause miners to switch over easily if they're made aware that another coin offers better speeds when it comes to transferring funds. Other advantages include cheaper fees thanks to reduced blockchain bloat and no ASICs since it won't have any nodes running at all (only regular computers). Grin isn't alone though: there are two others projects out right now trying to do something similar including Electric Coin Company who hope to bring back "the anonymity that bitcoin was designed around." The team says their currency is inspired by the original whitepaper written regarding Bitcoin itself. It also uses the CryptoNight algorithm along with Ring Confidential Transactions (RingCT) which keeps users' private data hidden.

On 9 December 2010, The Sun published a front-page story claiming that terrorist group Al-Qaeda had threatened a terrorist attack on Granada Television in Manchester to disrupt the episode of the soap opera Coronation Street to be transmitted live that evening. The paper cited unnamed sources, claiming "cops are throwing a ring of steel around tonight's live episode of Coronation Street over fears it has been targeted by Al-Qaeda." Later that morning, however, Greater Manchester Police categorically denied having "been made aware of any threat from Al-Qaeda or any other proscribed organisation." The Sun published a small correction on 28 December, admitting "that while cast and crew were subject to full body searches, there was no specific threat from Al-Qaeda as we reported." The apology had been negotiated by the Press Complaints Commission. For the day following the 2011 Norway attacks The Sun produced an early edition blaming the massacre on al-Qaeda. Later the perpetrator was revealed to be Anders Behring Breivik, a Norwegian nationalist.

Scotland is facing an obesity epidemic, and a new study suggests that supermarkets and other food retailers may be contributing to the problem. According to the research, these retailers are offering an abundance of unhealthy food options, and little support or encouragement for healthier choices. The study, conducted by the University of Glasgow, found that supermarkets and other food retailers in Scotland overwhelmingly stock an excessive amount of high-fat and sugary products, such as chocolates, crisps, cakes and sugary drinks. These products can be seen in prominent display areas, making it too easy for consumers to be enticed by them. Despite over a third of Scots being overweight or obese, the researchers noted minimal sales promotions for healthier food options. They also discovered that products marketed as "low fat" or "low calorie" often contain high levels of sugar, which can have an adverse effect on weight as well as overall health. Although the study was focused on Scotland, the issue of unhealthy food choices in supermarkets and food retailers is not unique to the country, but a problem across the UK as well as many other parts of the world. Health experts have been calling for more government intervention and industry responsibility to help promote healthier food options, especially in areas where obesity is prevalent. In response, various initiatives have been launched such as the Scottish Government's Healthy Living programme, which aims to improve dietary habits and promote physical activity. Supermarkets and food retailers have also begun to develop new products and services to help support healthier choices. However, the onus is on these companies to ensure that they are not compounding the problem. Do you want to know about the theory behind them, or about which ones are better in which situations and how to use them? Video is a series of still images (called frames) played rapidly in a row. Most commonly, people will use 24 frames per second (24fps) for video; that's 24 still images played quickly enough that it seems like smooth motion. Each of these images is made up from many tiny coloured squares, called pixels. Think of a [mosaic art piece] (URL0); the more pieces of mosaic pixels you use, the more detailed the image can be. The number of pixels used in an image is called its resolution. To illustrate the differences in resolution: a DVD has 345,600 pixels per frame, HDTV has around 921,000, and Blu-ray has over 2 million. For every second of video you see on a Bluray, the player is putting 49.76 million tiny coloured squares on the screen in a specific order. That's a lot of information. The player would have to say "Put a red square first. Then a blue square. Then a yellow square. Then a green square" to the TV almost 50 million times a second. When it's speaking in plain English like that, just saying what squares go where, we call it uncompressed video. Uncompressed Blu-ray video takes up 149.3 megabytes per second (without even counting audio). Codecs are our solution to that problem. They encode the video that is, they turn that list of "Put red square here" plain-English instructions into a special kind of code that's a lot faster and takes less space to store. They will also change parts of the video to make it easier to describe in this code. One trick they might use is to keep non-moving portions of the screen static. Imagine your video is a Simpsons episode where Homer is mowing the lawn. Your uncompressed video, which doesn't use a codec, will describe every single part of the scene 24 times per second, using a LOT of space. You use a clever codec that says "Oh, look Homer and the lawnmower are moving, but the house stays perfectly still in the background. We'll describe the house once, and just say keep that on the screen for 10 seconds, so we don't have to keep describing it over and over." You've saved a lot of space that way. Likewise, while your uncompressed video describes Homer's face as "yellow pixel, then yellow pixel, then yellow pixel, then yellow pixel" over and over again a million times, your clever new codec would say "Repeat yellow pixel 500 times," saving space. It might even say, depending on what codec you've chosen and what settings it has, "That tree in the background is made up of 500 shades of green, but let's trim that down to 300 shades, it won't look that much different but it'll save some more space." After enough of these tricks, your 900GB video is down to 8GB, small enough to put on a DVD. Why are there so many different codecs? Well, it takes a lot of computer brainpower to process a video using an advanced codec. Back in 1990, when computers were slow and computers were just starting out, they would've made quite simple codecs that didn't take a million years for the computer to understand. Now in 2011, because our computers are hundreds of times faster, we can write new codecs that employ very in-depth and complicated tricks. Our priorities have also changed now that we can stream videos online without worry, and now that we have 2TB hard drives instead of 2GB ones, we prefer to have big-but-pretty videos, while 1990s folks wanted to keep them as small as they possibly could. The codec used on DVDs is called MPEG-2. MPEG-2 dates from 1996, and was written with the goal of being decoded by cheap, low-power DVD players, so it's not very thorough or clever. The codec used on Blu-ray, iTunes video and many online sites is called H.264 or AVC. It is much newer, and was written knowing that it would be used on the strong computers of the late 2000s, rather than low-power devices from the mid-90s. As such, it is much smarter and more powerful because it knows it'll be played by powerful processors and provides a much higher quality of video. If you yourself are looking to encode video, the three most popular codec formats are MPEG-2 (used only for DVDs nowadays), Xvid (used in the AVI files you find online, good for making sure everyone can see it, or that it can be played on phones and other low-power devices) and H.264 (used for most online, Blu-ray, and HD videos; the best choice in 95 of cases). Now, as a footnote, let's note what a container format is. Many people are confused by this. Containers are things like AVI, MKV, or MP4. These file extensions do not tell you what codec was used to make the video. Think of them more like ZIP files. Most video files contain the video, one or two audio tracks, maybe some subtitles, and some chapters. Each of those things is a separate piece, in a different format, messily separated. So you put them together into a container, one file that contains them all, just like ZIP. The exact same video can be represented inside an AVI, an MKV, or an MP4, but they have different features. For example, AVI is 20 years old, made specially for Windows, and only really supports one video with one piece of audio on the top but everyone can view it. MKV is more modern, and supports multiple viewing angles, chapters like a DVD, built-in subtitles, multiple audio tracks (so you can embed director's commentary or different languages), but because it's relatively modern, older software doesn't know how to deal with it. When you make a video, you choose what container you want based on your needs, but it has absolutely zero effect on the image quality, and it is very easy to change later. For example, today I made a file where the video format was H.264, the audio format was MP3, the subtitle format was SRT, and the container format was MKV. That's an MKV file, but the video isn't MKV, it's H.264. MKV's just the container I put all the stuff in.','So you have the data corresponding to some movie, and you want your computer to play it. How does the computer make this happen? It would be simplest if the data that your computer uses to store the movie were the instructions to your screen and speakers to make it work. Problem is, this would be incredibly inefficient; it would be like having a book say READ THE FOLLOWING before every single word in the book. So instead, we just store the data, and have some program whose job it is to convert the data into display instructions. That program is called a codec.', "Codec stands for compressor-decompressor. When you encode the video, it's compressed so you can fit more movie into the same space. Audio and video are handled separately because you can compress them in different ways. You need the same codec to decompress the movie back into usable audio and video. Files like AVI are actually containers that hold the audio and video streams often as separate files. This is why audio and video can become desynchronized.

I hated going to the meetings. But there was only so much time I could spend alone in the attic before going a little stir crazy. Harvey sat next to me. He wasn't a bad sort. Tended to go off on philosophical ramblings about time and space. He had these funny soft ears and hard buck teeth. They clacked when he spoke. Nose was across from us. Wasn't sure what his real name was. He had giant nose in the middle of his face. No eyes. No mouth. When asked his name he'd written something intelligible. So he was Nose. He'd sometimes get up and pace but never tried to speak. Nobody sat near him after the last meeting. He'd had this awful cold. It was like a pipe burst. Me, I was normal. At least I thought so. No bunny ears or gigantic features. I had all my arms and legs. Most of my fingers. I'd lost the pinky on my right finger somewhere and had never managed to find it again. "You have anything to share?" Greg asked. Or lisped, actually. His mouth was too wide for his face, giving him this unnatural slash of red from cheek to cheek. He wore a bow tie and shoes that laced up to his calves. I'd attempted to avoid his eyes but he caught me anyway. I sighed, standing up. "Hi, my name is Paul and I am imaginary." "What's your real name?" one of the new kids shouted. I blinked. "Popple was my original name. I'm not that anymore. None of us have to be that anymore." Greg nodded. "Your creator gave you that identity. Here, you choose your own." "What if he comes back?" someone whimpered. "Won't he be mad?" I leaned against the podium. "Let me tell you about that. They never come back. I was born the same day as my girl. Went to school with her. Slept in the same room. Played games all day. It was me and her. Then she starts to hear that it's weird to be friends with me. At first it's a few people. Her other friends. Then it's her parents. One day she tells me, "You're not real." Just like that, I'm gone. Living in the attic with the rats." Greg patted me on the back. I shifted away. He had those wet hands. No idea who dreamed that up. "We're here to support each other. Maybe your creator will come back. If you're patient enough and good enough." I hissed through my teeth. Liar. Greg was such an asshole. Inventing some mythos that our suffering would be worth it. That the hours of loneliness would earn us a place somewhere better. We existed. Until we didn't. Some said we were reborn as other playmates in other places. Me, I was staying in my attic. People often underestimate the need for the touch of another human being- a gentle caress, perhaps. A kiss on a good day. On April 20, Kennedy sent a memo to Vice President Lyndon B. Johnson, asking Johnson to look into the status of America's space program, and into programs that could offer manned spaceflight opportunities. On May 25, 1961, Kennedy presented the idea to Congress as a part of his budget speech, and asked for a boost in funding for the space program, specifically the NASA. The budget speech was a result of Kennedy's concern about the Soviets' success in the Space Race, and his desire to beat the Soviets to the Moon. A few days later, Kennedy met with Vice President Lyndon B. Johnson to discuss the possibility of a manned spaceflight. Johnson was particularly interested in the idea of a circumlunar flight. The president then commissioned a three-person committee to study the plan and make recommendations. The committee's findings were presented to Kennedy on July 2. The committee recommended that a manned circumlunar flight was possible, and that it would require an expendable rocket. Kennedy and Johnson decided to launch a manned flight by the end of 1968. The president ordered the NASA to develop a three-stage Saturn V rocket that would be used to send astronauts around the Moon. On July 29, 1961, Kennedy publicly announced his goal to send an American to the Moon. Goals Kennedy wanted to catch up to the Soviets in the Space Race. The president believed that an American in space would help the country's prestige. He also thought that the space program was an effective stimulus to the economy. First goal The first goal of Kennedy's Space Program was to put a man in orbit by 1965. Second goal The second goal of Kennedy's Space Program was to land on the Moon by the end of the 1960s. Massively multiplayer online games serve as widespread platforms for socializing among countless users worldwide. Yet, there's scant information available regarding the intricate social connections formed within these digital environments and their progression over time. By examining the intricacies of interpersonal relationships in expansive virtual gaming landscapes like Halo: Reach, we can gain valuable insights into broader social behaviors and enhance the design of captivating interactive experiences. Our research delves into an extensive dataset comprising nearly 18 billion social exchanges across 44 weeks involving some 17 million participants in Halo: Reach, resulting in what may be considered one of the most comprehensive and temporally resolved networks analyzed thus far. The data uncovers fascinating trends such as the initial rapid decline followed by eventual stability in the network's size and connectivity, contradicting previous assumptions of continuous growth (non-densification). Additionally, it reveals that sustained player involvement correlates with increased local cohesion at a community level. Consequently, our investigation not only underscocreates the significance of video games as effective tools for scrutinizing social structures but also offers fresh perspectives on recurring patterns observed in real-world relational graphs while challenging prevailing theories concerning the expansion of network density.

EDIT1: I feel I need to rephrase the view I currently hold: Under almost no circumstances is it morally permissible to shoot and kill an unarmed individual. The caveat being situations in which someone has threatened harm andor is in the act of trying to harm you, the use of force is permissible. That said, killing someone when you have the capacity to disarmrender them a non-threat is still wrong. Over the past year a number of cases made the news wherein someone armed with a gun has shot and killed an unarmed person due to negligence, misunderstanding, or the escalation of a trite conflict. While I don't want to want to delve too deep into identity politics, I think it's noteworthy that a large percentage of these victims are young minority men; a population that is not often protectedgiven empathy by the general public. I'm hesitant to say that this type of crime is increasing in frequency, but our awareness of it has skyrocketed due to the way in which media has become interconnected. What prompted this CMV was [this case in particular.] Long story short: a father found a 17 year old boy in his 16 year old daughter's bed at 2:30am, the daughter said she didn't know him and the dad ends up shooting him in the head, killing him. Turns out the guy was her boyfriend and completely unarmed. Talking to some acquaintances that grew up in Detroit during the 70s80s, the attitude that it's okay to use deadly force on unarmed individuals is acceptable is relatively new, even in the case of home intruders. To some extent I get the desire to protect oneselfone's familyone's community, but it seems like too often this results in "shoot first, ask questions later" situations in which an innocent person is killed. In the context of this article, the father had a 17 year old, and I would guess at least partially undressed boy at gunpoint and kills him because he moved his hands in a way that the father interpreted as reaching for a weapon. The argument that the father did this in self-defense completely ignores the inherent power dynamic of that situation by casting the person with the gun as the "victim," and thereby justifying harsh actions they choose to take. I'm all for Second Amendment rights, but with the caveat that gun owners use their guns responsibly. Over and over we hear people talk about how they own a gun for protection, but rarely do we hear about that resulting in the saving of a life. Particularly in the case that the person is visibly unarmed and authorities are on their way, I believe it's irresponsible and unacceptable to shoot an individual. The Apple Store went down for just over an hour on Tuesday and came back with a brand-new look. The new design is filled with cards, similar to Apple's Store app for iOS, and is more about helping you buy a product, rather than just shopping for one. The site now features a card-based design similar to Apple's iOS and tvOS apps, including Apple Pay support for purchasing items directly from the site, along with the addition of a new account preference allowing for site-wide dark mode to match the dark mode option in macOS Mojave. The redesign includes a "Shop Now" button on the top right, which takes you to the site's full catalog. In the left-hand navigation bar, the old "iPhone" option has been replaced with "Apple," which will take you to all of the company's devices, including the iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, Apple TV, HomePod, and more. The left-hand navigation bar also includes categories for Services, Apple Store, Support, and Apple Newsroom, while the right-hand side has options to log in to your account, check your order status, chat with a Specialist, set up an appointment at an Apple Store, or find your local Apple Store. On the homepage, Apple highlights its latest and greatest products with larger images and fewer words, a major change from the previous design that featured many products with smaller images and a lot of text. The website is also full of touches from Apple's "beyond the page" design language, including curved page corners, drop shadows, and more. In the navigation bar for individual product pages, there's now a "More Details" option that can be toggled to show more specs about the product, and Apple has added a new "Compare" feature to make it easier to see the differences between products. The new Compare feature is also available on iOS in the Apple Store app. The site's checkout process now supports Apple Pay, allowing you to complete a purchase with Touch ID on the iPhone or Mac, or Face ID on the iPhone X. Apple Pay can be used in the browser to complete purchases on the new Apple Store, even when using an iPad or Mac without Touch ID. The redesigned Apple Store website was first noticed by users in early October. Apple is in the process of revamping its online store experience to better highlight products. These new store pages are built on a completely new platform that Apple is calling "WebKit2," which will be replacing the company's old e-commerce platform, "Yosemite." For Apple, this means that the online store will be updated more frequently with new content, and new products will be easier to launch. Apple's website is designed in a way that allows the company to launch new products, pages, and even site designs, without having to go through the App Store review process like third-party developers. Update 1023: Apple has also introduced a new "Dark Mode" option in the footer of its website. When enabled, the Apple Store's website design and content will have a dark tint to it, matching the new "Dark Mode" option in macOS Mojave. The most reliable indications of oligochaetes date back to the Tertiary era, starting approximately 65 million years ago. It is proposed that their evolution coincided with that of angiosperms during the initial phase of the Cretaceous, between 130 to 90 million years prior. Potential proof of their existence could be found in an early Triassic period trace fossil (251 to 245 million years ago), featuring a twisted burrow partially lined with diminutive excrement spheres. Although there are body fossils dating as far back as the mid-Ordovician (472 to 461 million years ago) that might belong to oligochaetes, such attributions remain speculative and contentious.

In the coming decades, pharmacists are expected to become more integral within the health care system. Rather than simply dispensing medication, pharmacists are increasingly expected to be compensated for their patient care skills. In particular, Medication Therapy Management (MTM) includes the clinical services that pharmacists can provide for their patients. It was a cold, dark night when I nervously approached my partner's house. I had been struggling with this decision for weeks and now it was time to tell them that our relationship was over. I knocked on the door and my partner welcomed me in with a warm hug and smile. In the short moments that followed, I felt my heart breaking into a million pieces as I tried to find the right words. Finally, I told them that we had come to the end of our relationship and that it was time to say goodbye. But then I said something that I never thought I would ever have to say: "I need you to run and never contact me or come back ever again." The look of shock on their face was all too familiar and I knew that they had expected something else from me. I could see the tears in their eyes, but I knew that I had to be strong and stay firm in my decision. I explained that it was for the best and that I wanted them to move on with their life without me. I hugged them one last time and asked them to take care of themselves before I left. The next morning, I woke up to an empty house and a broken heart. I had known that this day would come eventually, but I had never expected it to be so hard. I stayed in bed for days, grieving the loss of my partner and trying to come to terms with what I had done. No matter how much pain I was in, I knew that I had made the right decision. I had to let them go so that they could find the happiness they deserved. I will always miss them, but I know that this was the only way.

It was a last resort. That's what needed to be done..... The extinction of my race was at stake! No one could've known what they planned to do.... For those of you reading this log, My name is Kul'Thrat, Lead Biomancer of the Technocratic Hegemony. We were a peaceful race. We were masters of the sciences. Physics, Biology, Engineering, Medicine.... Everything. It was the one thing our race had above our galactic neighbors. For what seemed like an eternity, there was peace. It was all a ruse, of course. Those of us in the High Council knew what lurked inside the false promises of the peace. The Empire of the Von. A despotic, tyrannical empire set on destroying anything that didn't bend to their will. The Von controlled such huge swathes of territory, that a small nuisance like the Technocracy could be completely eradicated and no one would bat an eye. This was the High Councils greatest fear. We tried to surround ourselves with allies, promising to advance all of their tech in return for protection. Everyone accepted at first. Then the Empire made their advance. Like flies, the other Empires dropped out of the Alliance. We did not curse them, it was the smart thing to do. Of course, we tried to defend ourselves. We constructed massive weapons platforms to the best of our abilities. These worked, for a time. But the Von had endless legions to push against our small defense. One by one, our worlds fell. Our cities were glassed. Entire stations sucked into wormholes. They were at the gates, when we sent out a distress to all Empires. We promised to share our FTL tech with whoever accepted our plea. At the time, the only means of travel were through the Artificial Wormholes. One Empire accepted. Humanity. They were a new race to the galactic scene, but one already feared for their tenacity. Within a short timespan of them being uplifted, they had already amassed one of the largest fleets in the local sector. Within hours, what seemed like their entire fleet warped into our system. Thousands of ships, of all sizes. It was a beautiful sight to behold. The planet erupted in celebration. Our Human Protectors had come to rescue us. Anxiously, we waited for the Von to enter the system, and for the bloodbath to begin. It never came. For weeks we waited, nervously. The Humans seemed.... almost too calm. We should've known something was wrong. A week, and four days after the Humans arrived in our system, we recieved the unconditional surrender of the Von Empire to the Humans. In excited confusion, we asked why they surrendered while they were winning. Silently, they handed us a vidscreen, and exited the chamber. It was the last transmission of a battleship in order around their Capital. A massive fortress of battlestations, and capital ships. All seemed normal, before a blinding flash of light covered the screen. Once it cleared.... We stared in horror. A black hole now resided where their capital once was. It began to destroy everything in the system, before the vid cut to static. Over the course of the next few months, The Humans began to annex the territory of the former Von Empire. They had set themselves up to be the dominant power in the galaxy. We are grateful to them, no doubt. But.... Scared. Very, very scared.

It is a logical extension of the compound engine (described above) to split the expansion into yet more stages to increase efficiency. The result is the multiple expansion engine. Such engines use either three or four expansion stages and are known as triple and quadruple expansion engines respectively. These engines use a series of cylinders of progressively increasing diameter. These cylinders are designed to divide the work into equal shares for each expansion stage. As with the double expansion engine, if space is at a premium, then two smaller cylinders may be used for the low-pressure stage. Multiple expansion engines typically had the cylinders arranged inline, but various other formations were used. In the late 19th century, the Yarrow-Schlick-Tweedy balancing'system' was used on some marine triple expansion engines. Y-S-T engines divided the low-pressure expansion stages between two cylinders, one at each end of the engine. This allowed the crankshaft to be better balanced, resulting in a smoother, faster-responding engine which ran with less vibration. This made the 4-cylinder triple-expansion engine popular with large passenger liners (such as the Olympic class), but this was ultimately replaced by the virtually vibration-free turbine engine.[citation needed]

The claim: Membership of the European Union guarantees rights on equal pay, sexual harassment and maternity leave, and rights for part-time workers. Those rights would be in jeopardy if Britain voted to leave. Reality Check Verdict: The EU has been influential in the development of equality legislation but leaving would not necessarily mean those rights would be lost. The Treaty of Rome included the commitment for member states to ensure "that men and women should receive equal pay for equal work." And the rules were strengthened following the 1975 Equal Pay Directive, and subsequent rulings by the European Court of Justice (ECJ), which have set out further what counts as equal work. Similarly, the right of part-time workers to join occupational pension schemes was determined by rulings of the ECJ, which found that excluding them constituted indirect sex discrimination. If Britain leaves the EU those rules could, in principle, be revoked. However, in some cases the UK government has gone further than the rules set by the EU. For example, the 52 weeks of statutory maternity leave in the UK is considerably longer than the 14 weeks guaranteed by EU law. Leave campaigners say there's no reason to suppose that a future British government would undermine women's rights. But Ms Harman believes that many of the people leading the campaign for Brexit - including Boris Johnson, Nigel Farage and Iain Duncan Smith - cannot be trusted to protect women's rights. She admits that this part of her argument is speculative, but she warns that women's rights could be eroded under the guise of pushing for deregulation and cutting red tape. Uses of underwater videos to assess diversity and abundance of fish are being rapidly adopted by marine biologists. Manual processing of videos for quantification by human analysts is time and labor intensive, so we developed a computer program that automatically recognizes individuals in video sequences based on key characteristics such as fin shape (bipodal or caudal), scales, coloration, and arrangement of the dorsal-ventral fins. The program first categorizes each individual into one of three classes: abundant ( 5 cover with at least 10 individuals per square meter), commonplace (0-5, 10 indm2), and rare (1 cover). Then it filters out common species using threshold values of 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 19, 20, 21, 22, 25, 26, 27, 28, 30, 31, 32, 33, 34 based on the maximum frequency of occurrence across locations during field trips. This provides an alternative approach for fish identification beyond visual examination of video frames because it can be used more widely than conventional methods such as morphology. In addition, our approach allows users to identify fish from multiple angles simultaneously within a single sequence, which cannot be done manually without extensive analysis. We tested this method using two monitored sites located between 1200 m depth and 400 km off western Australia. Our results show that we were able to accurately classify 81 of all fish encountered in these areas. These data suggest that computer programs such as ours have great potential in improving current approaches for automated fish recognition.
