Jim Watson was eating an apple when the Devil appeared before him, but he didn't stop. It was juicy with just the right balance of sweet and tangy, a honeycrisp he'd picked up from the Farmer's Market just that morning. The acrid smell marking the presence of the Dark One threatened to sour Jim's enjoyment of his succulent treat, so he put a dishtowel to his face and walked into the dining room. " Please, just stay in there. I can hear you just fine, " he said, talking around chewed up apple. A deep purple light beamed from underneath the door, and tendrils of smoke crept out, but the door itself didn't move. The sharp sound of clacking could be heard from the kitchen. Claws. When the Devil spoke, the sound of it should have made Jim's skin crawl; it sounded like the voice of an average, congenial man, the sort of man who would shake your hand with a smile, imitated poorly. " Jim, buddy. It's done. She's not gon na bother you no more. " " Now that don't sound like Sheila, Mr. Satan, " Jim said. " You sure we're talking about the same woman? She's got a tendency to just turn up on you. That's the whole reason I had to come to you in the first place. " " Oh, don't you worry now, Jim, " said the Devil. " You won't be seeing your wife no more. " " And you can't bring her back? She's gone? " " I said you won't be seeing her again, Jim, and you won't. " The voice was stern now. Jim gaped his jaw like a snake to gob an extra big bite of apple. He chewed loud and long, sucking out the juice from the tender pulp as he gnashed it between his molars. He nibbled errant bits of peel as it all went down his throat, and then he went for another bite. Jim smacked his lips and dashed to lick the dripping juice from his fingers before it fell to the carpet. He made a scene of eating a damn apple, and the Prince of Lies waited patiently for his reply. Not a claw clacked on the tile as Jim ate; the only sound was the man's gluttonous glee. Jim set the half-eaten apple on the table, and wiped his hands with a napkin. " Mr. Satan? " he said. " Yes, Jim. " " How'd you do it? " " Oh, Jim. Now, I wouldn't want to tell you that. " " And why not? " " Well, there are a lot of reasons, really, but think about it. When the police come knocking, and you realize they will, right? " " I guess I hadn't thought about it. " " You should think about it. Tell me, Jim, when they tell you what they found, do want to fake surprise, or do you want to really be surprised? " " That's a good point, Mr. Satan. " " Well I'd hate to see someone get what they want and then not be able to enjoy it. " Jim fingered the apple, rotating it slowly on the surface of the table. " Mr Satan, I thank you for what you've done, sir, but I think it's time we parted ways. I've got a dinner to cook, and I'm sure, well, I'm sure you're pretty busy yourself. " " You could say that. " " Well, then. " " Jim, " said the Devil. His voice was a poorer imitation than before. " Aren't you forgetting something? Jim grinned. " I don't think so. " " Jim, " said the Devil. The purple light began to pulsate slowly, swirling with midnight blues and bloody reds. " Your soul belongs to me. " Jim picked up the apple and took another bite. His mouth full, he shook a finger at the door slowly, saying, " Now that's where you're wrong, Mr. Satan. Now now, I know I promised you my soul in exchange for your little favor. That's true. But I didn't tell you that I'd already traded my soul away before I ever called you up. " " You gave it away, " said the Devil. Jim hacked off another chunk of apple with his incisors, smacking as loudly as before. " That's right. My friend Sam and I traded each others' souls about a week ago. I've got his, and he's got mine. I signed that weird paper you showed me, and I know I said I'd give you my soul, but I don't have it. It ain't mine to give any more. But hey, make me an offer and I might be willing to part with Sam's soul. I doubt he'd even miss it. " " No thank you. I don't really want it. " " Well good bye, Mr. Satan. You're not getting mine. " " I'm not? Then what's this? " There was a crinkle of paper, and then a single sheet slid out from under the kitchen door. It was a note, rumpled slightly, a yellow page from a legal pad handwritten in pen. Jim's heart fell into his stomach. " That's my- " " Contract. " " My contract. " " Amended. Slightly. " Jim lost his grip on the apple, and it fell to the floor. " Sam sold it to you, " he whispered. " What did he want? " " Your wife. " " But you said, you said she was..... " " I said you won't be seeing her again, Jim, and you won't. " The purple light went out. The kitchen door swung open.

One of the roadmap plans for quantum computers is an integration within HPC ecosystems assigning them a role of accelerators for a variety of computationally hard tasks. However, in the presence of multiple computational resources, the information about which of them is quantum and which is classical is crucial. If we know the resources' nature, we can perform data transfer to and from quantum devices, transfer quantum state, apply quantum algorithms and algorithms for quantum state transfer, and perform fault tolerant quantum computing. The knowledge of resources' nature is also important for classical machine learning, as quantum information can be used to improve training procedures. In this paper, we propose a novel quantum information transfer method for HPC architectures. We assume that the user knows the resource nature and performs classical data transfer. In order to perform the quantum data transfer, we implement quantum state transfer algorithm in software and hardware and exploit classical data transfer for the classical resources. The proposed approach is applicable to HPC environments with limited resources (CPUs and FPGAs). In our approach, the user can control the quantum state transfer by means of a classical computer. Moreover, it is possible to implement the quantum algorithm with the help of classical resources only. We evaluate the proposed method by using a sample data transfer algorithm and a modified version of a famous quantum state transfer algorithm. The results show that the proposed method outperforms classical data transfer and quantum state transfer algorithms in terms of speed and precision.

There are many styles of mandolin, but four are common, the Neapolitan or round-backed mandolin, the carved-top mandolin and the flat-backed mandolin. The round-back has a deep bottom, constructed of strips of wood, glued together into a bowl. The carved-top or arch-top mandolin has a much shallower, arched back, and an arched top - both carved out of wood. The flat-backed mandolin uses thin sheets of wood for the body, braced on the inside for strength in a similar manner to a guitar. Each style of instrument has its own sound quality and is associated with particular forms of music. Neapolitan mandolins feature prominently in European classical music and traditional music. Carved-top instruments are common in American folk music and bluegrass music. Flat-backed instruments are commonly used in Irish, British and Brazilian folk music. Some modern Brazilian instruments feature an extra fifth course tuned a fifth lower than the standard fourth course.

Subsequent sections explore concepts like (a,b)-stochasticity, minimal description lengths, standardized descriptions derived from lists of objects constrained by their complexity, and connections to resource-limited complexity. Later portions investigate aligning theoretical frameworks with practical applications through examining limited-description classes and robust models. Recognizing objects from simultaneously sensed photometric (RGB) and depth channels is a fundamental yet practical problem in many machine vision applications such as robot grasping and autonomous driving. In this paper, we address this problem by developing a Cross-Modal Attentional Context (CMAC) learning framework, which enables the full exploitation of the context information from both RGB and depth data. Compared to existing RGB-D object detection frameworks, our approach has several appealing properties. First, it consists of an attention-based global context model for exploiting adaptive contextual information and incorporating this information into a region-based CNN (e.g., Fast RCNN) framework to achieve improved object detection performance. Second, our CMAC framework further contains a fine-grained object part attention module to harness multiple discriminative object parts inside each possible object region for superior local feature representation. While greatly improving the accuracy of RGB-D object detection, the effective cross-modal information fusion as well as attentional context modeling in our proposed model provide an interpretable visualization scheme. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly improves upon the state of the art on all public benchmarks.

A new method for estimating the relative positions of location-unaware nodes from the location-aware nodes and the received signal strength (RSS) between the nodes, in a wireless sensor network (WSN), is proposed in this paper. This method is based on the Manhattan distance, which is a widely used metric for measuring the distance between objects, and the RSS values. The method estimates the relative positions of nodes using a WSN with only four location-aware nodes. The estimation error is evaluated for various scenarios using both real and simulated data. The results show that the proposed method can estimate the relative positions of location-unaware nodes with a relatively low estimation error.

In July 1968, ABC Radio launched a special programming project for its FM stations, which was spearheaded by Allen Shaw, a former program manager at WCFL in Chicago who was by then running ABC's FM division. The ABC Network would pay for the programming. In exchange, the stations were expected to make it available to ABC affiliates (there were 85 of them at the time) for use on their AM stations. The project was called The First Eleven, and it featured a mix of original programming and music, live and pre-recorded. There were two original weekly shows, each 30 minutes long. One was called "The Happening," and featured music from the first 11 songs on the "Billboard Hot 100" chart. The other was called "The ABC Countdown," which ran down the top 11 songs in the country, as determined by Billboard. The shows were hosted by Peter O'Brien and James Eastman. ABC also aired a countdown of the top 11 hits of the week on its 35-station AM network, which was anchored by Detroit's WXYZ-AM (760). In November 1968, the ABC AM countdown was renamed "The Top 11." The weekly show, which ran for five years, continued on the AM side until it was discontinued in 1973. Courtesy of Jonathan Butler Here's a photo of Butler with a copy of the July 20, 1968 edition of Billboard, which reported on the new ABC radio programming project. Here's an excerpt from an article in Billboard that year, titled "ABC-FM Set to Launch Radio Project." In July, ABC will launch The First Eleven, a series of 30-minute programs for each of ABC's 21 FM stations. The program will be produced by ABC's FM division, headed by Allen Shaw. The ABC network will fund the programs, and the stations will air them on their AM outlets. The First Eleven will feature a mix of original programming and music, live and pre-recorded. Music will be drawn from "Billboard's Hot 100," with two original weekly shows, The Happening (30 minutes) and The ABC Countdown (15 minutes). Both will feature the first 11 songs on the Hot 100. One show will focus on contemporary rock and roll, while the other will be a pop music survey. ABC has yet to announce who will host The First Eleven. The First Eleven was ABC's attempt to beat rival FM station WCFL-FM (100.3) at its own game. A lot of other radio broadcasters took notice of the WCFL-FM program, called "The Real Gone Experience," which was produced by Al Michaels and hosted by Terry Clark. In October 1968, a month after ABC launched its special programming project, Detroit's WXYZ-FM (97.1) started running a similar program, called "The New Hour." It was hosted by morning man Chuck Sullivan and was produced by a Detroit radio veteran named Bob Francis. "The New Hour" featured live interviews, pre-recorded features, recorded music and a mix of original music programming, which included a program called "The Countdown," which was co-hosted by Sullivan and Francis. But WXYZ's program was terminated after three months, and its host, Chuck Sullivan, moved to WCFL-FM, where he stayed until 1973. He later became an NBC TV news anchor in Chicago. Today, there are hundreds of specialized radio shows on the FM dial, including shows devoted to current music, nostalgia, talk, sports, comedy, news, religion and more. Partial label learning (PLL) is a class of weakly supervised learning where each training instance consists of a data and a set of candidate labels containing a unique ground truth label (or none at all). The goal of PLL is to learn a classifier that can accurately predict the ground truth label for each instance, given only the candidate labels as input. PLL is often used in cases where obtaining the ground truth label for every instance is prohibitively expensive or time-consuming, and only a small subset of the instances have known labels.

Monitor is looking into the financial sustainability of Southend University Hospital Foundation Trust "on behalf of patients," the NHS regulator said. Finances became a concern when a planned PS7.8m deficit grew, for which Monitor could see no recovery plan. The hospital blamed the larger-than-anticipated deficit on growth in demand and increased staff recruitment. Hospital chairman Alan Tobias OBE, said: "The overspend is a result of vital investment in services and more staff to ensure high standards of patient care as well as the rise in attendances. "We welcome this review to clearly demonstrate to Monitor - as well as patients and stakeholders - our future financial plans are both robust and sustainable." The hospital has pledged to cut the deficit while maintaining "high quality care for local people" and said it was committed to returning to a surplus within three years. Monitor said its investigation will look into the state of the hospital trust's finances, assess the strength of its financial management and explore ways of improving its sustainability, on behalf of patients across the region. The investigation will also examine how the trust works with other local health and care organisations to respond to the financial challenges it faces. Katherine Cawley, regional director at Monitor, said: "People are relying on Southend to provide them with quality healthcare now and in the future, and we are concerned that this may be at risk because of the trust's poor financial performance. "We have launched this investigation to find out more about the financial situation at the trust and to establish what can be done to improve things."

Consider entropy as randomness or disorganization. For instance, imagine an organized deck of cards – there’s just one arrangement with them perfectly sorted out, meaning the level of entropy is minimal. However, when we shuffle them even slightly, the entropy rises because numerous arrangements become possible. This explains why rooms often appear cluttered and belongings get tangled up easily; disarray is naturally preferred over organization due to higher entropy levels. According to the Second Law of Thermodynamics, the entropy within any system tends to escalate without external intervention. To reduce the disorder in your surroundings or untie knotted items requires investment of energy. Solid objects possess lesser entropy compared to liquids, given their fixed atomic positions versus the fluid movement of atoms in liquids. In essence, entropy symbolizes disorderliness. Think of constructing a card tower – considerable effort yields a structured creation, which is swiftly ruined upon being disturbed. Hence, creating order necessitates energy expenditure whereas maintaining chaos demands less effort. Lastly, while the First Law of Thermodynamics postulelles that energy can neither be produced nor eliminated, the Second Law addresses entropy."

Various elements merge to form unique compounds with distinct characteristics compared to their constituent elements. For instance, water possesses different attributes from its individual components, hydrogen and oxygen. Similarly, heme, an iron-containing substance found in our blood, exhibits varying traits from pure elemental iron. Since heme lacks attraction to magnets, MRI scans pose no threat; moreover, there are no solid iron pieces present in our bloodstream. It's worth mentioning that iron ions within our circulatory system lack magnetic properties due to the absence of unpaired electrons. However, if someone were to possess iron filings instead of ions in their blood, this could potentially cause significant health concerns. In addition, these iron filings wouldn't react as ionic forms typically do.

Unlike eukaryotic cells, bacteria lack a nuclear envelope surrounding their DNA; instead, their singular, circular chromosome resides within the cytoplasm's nucleoid region. This area comprises the chromosome along with its associated proteins and RNA. However, some bacteria like those from the Planctomycetes phylum or the potential Poribacteria group might possess internal membranes encasing their nucleoids, as well as additional intracellular membrane systems. All bacteria feature ribosomes, which are commonly found in clusters known as polyribosomes, facilitating protein synthesis. Nonetheless, these ribosomes differ structurally from those present in eukaryotes and Archaea. With a sedimentation coefficient of 70S, the bacterial ribosomal subunits measure at 30S and 50S. Certain antibiotics can selectively target these 70S ribosomes, disrupting protein formation in bacteria while leaving the larger 80S ribosomes in eukaryotic hosts unharmed.

In this study, we introduce methods utilizing Gibbs sampling for determining the best locations for storing content within a cellular network infrastructure. We examine scenarios involving several base stations distributed across an area, each servicing an individual cell that might intersect with others. Users moving about the network seek to access a limited variety of digital materials, whose demand patterns could be predetermined or undiscovered by the base stations. Given that each base station possesses restricted storage capacity and cannot maintain every available content simultaneously, there arises a need to fetch requested data from a centralized source if unavailable locally. Our objective is thus to optimize the positioning of these contents to reduce reliance on external sources, effectively enhancing local retrieval success rates. Notably, in densely populated base station environments, simply stocking the most sought-after items isn't always ideal. Despite the complexity and computational intensity inherent in solving this challenge, we employ Gibbs sampling strategies to devise straightforward iterative procedures for deciding content retention and replacement based on neighboring station inventories. These tactics have proven effective towards achieving optimal arrangements regardless of initial conditions. Additionally, we adapt the approach to accommodate evolving estimations of both consumer preferences and network structure, ensuring eventual alignment with the ideal setup even amidst uncertainty. To illustrate our methodology's efficacy, we provide numerical examples.

Islamic art frequently adopts the use of geometrical floral or vegetal designs in a repetition known as arabesque. Despite this, there is a presence of depictional art in some Muslim societies, notably the miniature style made famous in Persia and under the Ottoman Empire which featured paintings of people and animals, and also depictions of Quranic stories and Islamic traditional narratives. Another reason why Islamic art is usually abstract is to symbolize the transcendence, indivisible and infinite nature of God, an objective achieved by arabesque. Islamic calligraphy is an omnipresent decoration in Islamic art, and is usually expressed in the form of Quranic verses. Two of the main scripts involved are the symbolic kufic and naskh scripts, which can be found adorning the walls and domes of mosques, the sides of minbars, and so on.

The authorities say they want to check whether the organisations are operating legally - particularly whether they comply with a controversial law requiring all NGOs receiving overseas funding to register as "foreign agents." But human rights watchdog Agora says at least 90 NGOs have used its hotline since last week to complain about visits by officials from the prosecutor-general's office, the justice ministry and the tax authorities. Foreign NGOs - such as Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and Transparency International - have been among those targeted. Marina Gridneva, from the prosecutor-general's office, said the checks were being conducted "in strict compliance with the current legislation." Russian officials typically arrive unannounced, or at short notice, and request groups to hand over legal and financial documents, eyewitnesses say. Yelena Panfilova, who heads Transparency International's office in Moscow, said she was surprised that it was being checked again - just a month after a similar inspection. Law enforcement agents visited her office on Wednesday and gave her 24 hours to hand over paperwork. Ms Panfilova's links the checks with the new NGO legislation. "We are on the list of NGOs that are visible and presumably receive foreign funding. As far as I understand, there is a big search for'foreign agents' among the NGOs," she told the BBC. When the controversial law on NGOs was approved in November, a number of prominent Russian groups said they would not comply - even if that risked closure. They regard the term "foreign agents" as insulting, saying it harks back to Stalin-era purges. Memorial, an NGO gathering information about victims of Communism, reiterated this position earlier this week when law enforcement agents turned up at its office. "Memorial... has carried out a research of people who 70 years ago were called agents by the authorities and then shot. For us, taking on the label of a foreign agent is unacceptable," Memorial's Alexander Cherkasov told Reuters news agency. The "foreign agent" bill was one of several controversial laws adopted in the aftermath of last year's pro-democracy protests in Moscow. Other measures introduced tougher internet restrictions, outlawed "gay propaganda" and banned adoptions of Russian orphans by US parents. "The scale of these inspections serves to reinforce the menacing atmosphere for civil society created by the adoption of last year's laws," Human Rights Watch's Rachel Denber told Reuters. The group's Moscow bureau was inspected last Thursday. Several NGOs, including Transparency International, reported that the visiting officials were also looking into the organisations' compliance with anti-extremist legislation. Russia's law gives an extremely vague definition of extremism, allowing officials much leeway in choosing their targets.

Swansea City's Supporters' Trust has expressed its disappointment over what it calls a "lack of engagement" over the club's takeover. The Trust, which owns almost 21 of the club, has said that it has not been consulted or kept in the loop about the ongoing negotiations and that it was forced to find out about the deal through the media. Many Swansea City fans have expressed their concerns about the takeover, which involves an American consortium led by Jake Silverstein. The consortium reportedly plans to buy a controlling stake of the club from the current owners, who include chairman Trevor Birch and majority shareholders Jason Levien and Steve Kaplan. The Supporters' Trust, which was established in 2001 to give fans a voice in the running of the club, has been at the forefront of efforts to ensure that the interests of supporters are taken into account. However, according to the Trust, its concerns have been ignored and its efforts to engage with the current owners have been rebuffed. In a statement, the Trust said: "We are disappointed that we have had no direct communication from the current owners or the proposed purchasers since the news broke on Friday. This seems to contrast with other trusts and clubs where the communication with the supporters' organisations has been much more positive." The Trust also expressed concerns that the potential new owners may not have the best interests of the club at heart. "We are not opposed to change or the involvement of new investment - but that change must be done in the right way and in the interests of the long-term future of the club," the statement said. The takeover is expected to be completed within the next few weeks, subject to approval from the Football Association and the Premier League. It remains to be seen whether the Supporters' Trust will be able to exert any influence over the new owners, but the group has vowed to continue to fight for the interests of Swansea City fans. As one of the few fan-owned football clubs in the UK, Swansea City has long been seen as a model for how supporters can play a meaningful role in the running of a club. The Supporters' Trust will be hoping that its concerns are taken seriously and that it still has a role to play in shaping the future of the club.

The right to create private schools in Germany is in Article 7, Paragraph 4 of the Grundgesetz and cannot be suspended even in a state of emergency. It is also possible that the Bundesrat will have to take over some of the functions reserved for the Chancellery at Section 5 (2) Cf., s1.3b). The Federal Constitutional Court may decide whether this would fall within their jurisdiction or not: "In theory, the concept of the principle of subsidiarity does not apply to the state of emergency as it now stands" (Judgement of 12 November 2003). If they do not consider that such an interpretation of the law applies then I think there are other possibilities which could justify reconsidering this provision on behalf of Germany. This is because although under the German constitution the only way to ensure the existence of self-governing communities with equal rights is through democratic means the German constitutional court should still be setting up communities based on fair elections.

The word "metal" can mean a variety of things. Let's start with the Chemistry definition, please bear with me as I give a little background here so nobody ends up in an argument: Metal is any chemical element that forms solid solutions or compounds (solids and liquids are either solids or liquids), has no free electrons, atomic number above 58, most easily liquefied at 1 atm [1] or 532 K 183 C) [2], and does not react readily with other elements.[3] The metal ion is the more common form of the element. All metals have at least one stable isotope,[45] which means they do not undergo radioactive decay.[67] Most notably among radioisotopes is uranium-238, whose half-life is 4.47 billion years,[8] which has made it difficult to date rocks older than about 3.9 billion years by radiometric methods[9]. However, we don't use this classic definition often anymore for several reasons. First off, direct dating techniques supersede it but let that pass. Second, some people would argue even from the original definition that gold isn't really all that chemically unique compared to certain others like silicon, oxygen, chlorine, etc., and probably wouldn't want to claim that iron is truly similar only because it is a metallic element too. Thirdly, modern technology makes disparate items look similar on many different levels. And lastly, although there are still plenty of scientists who love arguing over what constitutes a true metal today, you'll find very few geologists doing so. In a magnet, all of the atoms are aligned with their poles in a single direction with the positive ends all facing one direction and the negative facing the opposite. For example, if an atom is shown as being oriented along its polarity which makes up north or south, that means it has to be seen from this perspective only; however since these magnets do not lie directly next to each other they cannot always have exactly the same orientation. Atoms can even move (relatively) sideways within their magnetic field so some may appear to be bent at right angles when viewed through both polarities. This effect was first described by Arthur Samuel Thomson in 1842 and led to his concept known as magnetometry which tells you about how many different ways there are for any given pair of particles to interact with another due to exchange forces between them in a magnetic field. The idea of repulsion could refer to any type of interaction including attraction, but up until now has been used exclusively to describe attractions such as those arising from strong interactions like electrons and protons. Datasets from the fields of bioinformatics, chemometrics, and face recognition are typically characterized by small samples of high-dimensional data. Among the many variants of linear discriminant analysis that have been proposed in order to rectify the issues associated with classification in such a setting, the classifier in , composed of an ensemble of randomly projected linear discriminants, seems especially promising; it is computationally efficient and, with the optimal projection dimension parameter setting, is competitive with the state-of-the-art. In this work, we seek to further understand the behavior of this classifier through asymptotic analysis. Under the assumption of a growth regime in which the dataset and projection dimensions grow at constant rates to each other, we use random matrix theory to derive asymptotic misclassification probabilities showing the effect of the ensemble as a regularization of the data sample covariance matrix. The asymptotic errors further help to identify situations in which the ensemble offers a performance advantage. We also develop a consistent estimator of the misclassification probability as an alternative to the computationally-costly cross-validation estimator, which is conventionally used for parameter tuning. Finally, we demonstrate the use of our estimator for tuning the projection dimension on both real and synthetic data.

Galicia's interior features rolling hills and elevations reaching up to 2,00right meters high in the eastern and southern regions. Industrial development remained limited until post-mid-century, excluding sectors such as shipbuilding and food production. As of 2012, Galicia had a GDP valued at $56 billion when adjusted for purchasing power parity, alongside a nominal GDP per capita amounting to roughly $20,700. Population density primarily exists along two sections of the coast: stretching from Ferrol to A Coruña in the northwestern part and extending from Pontevedra to Vigo in the southwestern area. Smaller communities also exist near the central towns of Lugo, Ourense, and Santiago de Compostela. Although Santiago de Compostela serves as the administrative hub, Vigo boasts the highest number of inhabitants among municipalities, totaling over 294,000 people in 2014, whereas A Coruña holds the distinction of being the most densely populated urban center, housing more than 215,000 residents during the same year.

A hollow point refers to a type of bullet whose tip has been partially removed or shaped differently than usual. This modification causes the bullet to create extensive internal damage within soft tissue rather than penetrating deeply into the target. On the other hand, armor-piercing rounds are specifically engineered to breach protective barriers such as body armor. These projectiles consist of dense materials like tungsten and maintain their shape upon impact with conventional defensive gear. Furthermore, they feature sharp tips to facilitate piercing through armor effectively. Essentially, bullets can be classified based on their intended purpose - either to pass through targets while minimizing damage or to remain in place and inflict significant harm, albeit with increased susceptibility to being halted by armored protection.

Unable to cancel Leno's program outright due to his contractual obligations, NBC reduced its duration and shifted its slot to where The Tonight Show used to air. In this study, we propose a randomized misfit technique for efficiently solving sizable PDE-constrained inverse issues involving extensive datasets. Our objective is to establish a foundation based on random projections within these inverse problems. We examine the stochastic approximation of the misfit through random projection theory. Enhanced analysis of randomized misfit convergence beyond mere mean estimator convergence is offered. Theoretical outcomes derived herein apply to all recognized random projections found in existing research. Compared to prior stochastic misfit approaches, our class of possible distribution options is both wide-ranging and straightforwardly identifiable. These include highly sparse random projections that yield significant computational advantages. Additionally, we supply an alternate demonstration supporting a version of the Johnson-Lindenstrauss theorem, leading to novel insights into the (-2) component in the bounds established by the Johnson-Lindenstrauss findings. Central to this work is a theoretical finding illustrating how the technique ensures accurate solutions even when dealing with diminished misfit dimensions. Moreover, it underscores the critical role played by combining Johnson-Lindenstrauss principles with Morozov's discrepancy concept. Finally, we address potential reductions in computational costs associated with large-scale PDE-restricted issues featuring extensive datasets. To validate the theories put forth, numerical tests were conducted on model problems aimed at deducing a distributed parameter from an elliptical partial differential equation. Comparative analyses utilizing various random projections have been performed to substantiate the effectiveness and precision of the suggested methodology.

The uneven and fluctuating utilization of bicycles necessitates essential rebalancing procedures, highlighting the importance of accurate predictions regarding bike traffic flow. Although various predictive models for traffic flow exist, they often lack transparency, hindering their usefulness in real-world applications. We present the Interpretable Bike Flow Prediction (IBFP) framework designed to accurately forecast bike traffic while providing clear explanations for the observed trends. Our approach involves segmenting urban areas based on bike usage intensity and employing graph regularized sparse representation to depict the interregional bike flows over time, incorporating the graph Laplacian to capture recurring patterns within the dataset. Furthermore, we identify comprehensible traffic patterns via subspace clustering and sparse representation techniques that help formulate understandable foundational matrices. Using these matrices alongside learned variables, bike flow projections become possible. Empirical evaluations performed on genuine datasets demonstrate the superiority of the IBFP technique in anticipating bike flows in dockless systems. Additionally, a case study emphasizes the interpretative aspect of our model, offering insightful perspectives on analyzing bike movements.

When you request a page from reddit with your browser it first connects to a "edge server" - this server is a distributed network of servers from a content distribution acceleration provider (like akamai, cdnetworks, amazon cloudfront, etc.). These servers are located near users, much moreso than Reddit's "native" servers. This edge server then requests on your behalf (it is a "proxy to the "origin server" (e.g. reddit's real servers). Once at Reddit reddit's own web servers sit in front of their application servers and data-stores, etc. So...if something further downstream fails, the upstream components can return to your browser "something is wrong." The only time you'd get no response at all would be if the very front of the communication chain is unresponsive. TL:DR: A series of proxy servers (at least on the edge, likely 2 with the second being the web tier within reddit's infrastructure) exist between you and the "real reddit servers." If the real reddit servers are down, the proxy servers can still respond to you, just not with the ideal content.','You can think of a website as having multiple tiers. That top tier is a receptionist. It takes your information and forwards it to the lower tiers that actually to the work, which involve querying a database and and building the web page. If the lower tier takes to long or sends and error message, the reception can send you a simply, low effort static web page telling you the site is down.

Recent research has shown significant interest in attributed network embedding, which seeks to create versatile, compact, and smooth vector representations for nodes that encapsulate both structural and characteristic data. Many current techniques, including those based on random walks and graph convolutional networks (GCNs), primarily concentrate on neighboring attributes, making them effective for homogeneous networks but less so for heterogeneous ones like multipartite, hub, or mixed-structured networks. Addressing this gap, we introduce a probabilistic, block-oriented generative approach to attributed network embedding that caters to both types of networks. This involves grouping nodes into distinct blocks with analogous connection patterns that may represent either cohesive community structures in assortative networks or diverse configurations in disassortative networks. Furthermore, we incorporate hidden embeddings associated with these blocks to retain attribute details using a neural network to capture complex relationships between node features and their respective embeddings. Our comprehensive evaluations across various real-life and artificially constructed attributed networks demonstrate that our novel technique surpasses contemporary embedding strategies in terms of performance for clustering and categorization challenges, particularly within disassortative network contexts.

Very roughly, your cells are sort of floating in water. They're connected to each other by proteins and things, but they're surrounded by water. Inside that water, there are all sorts of things dissolved or suspended. All the stuff your cell needs is in that solution, which has a name that I forget. I think it's "intercellular solution." To get from the intercellular solution into the cell, nutrients can take a lot of different paths. Some of them enter "passively," meaning that it just sort of happens automatically (the process is called "diffusion. The cell membrane, which is the "border" of the cell, is semi-permeable, which means that some stuff can just pass right through it. There are also proteins embedded in the cell membrane which essentially are "tubes" that certain nutrients can get through. So, something that can't penetrate the membrane itself might be able to sneak in through a protein. Stuff will only diffuse into the cell if there's more on the outside than on the inside, though. So, there are also proteins that act like "pumps," which force nutrients inside (or, sometimes outside) of the cell. The pumps take energy to run, though. The way that nutrients get from your blood to the intercellular solution is similar to how stuff gets into the cell. There are little tiny blood vessels called "capillaries" in all of your tissues. The capillaries are surrounded by the same solution as the other cells. So, stuff can get pumped or diffuse out of the blood, through the capillary walls (which are only one cell thick), and into the intercellular solution. Once it's in the solution, it can get to the other cells. Each cell doesn't have its own capillary, though. I forget the exact numbers, but I believe that each capillary serves maybe a few dozen to a few hundred cells, depending on what part of the body it's in. You have a ton of capillaries in your face, for example, but not many on, say, your feet. edit: it's "interstitial fluid," not "intercellular solution." I was close!

Your stomach produces hydrochloric acid (HCl) which plays a crucial role in breaking down food particles along with enzymes, eliminating harmful bacteria present in your meals. Since most individuals consume their meals at regular intervals throughout the day, the quantity of HCl produced is regulated; an excess amount might destroy essential digestive enzymes within the stomach. In instances where you abstain from eating, the unused hydrochloric acid accumulates, potentially causing damage to the lining of your stomach. Although the stomach lining is designed to endure acidic environments, an overabundance of acid can still lead to its degradation, resulting in discomfort. Moreover, when fasting, your body resorts to consuming stored fats first, followed by carbohrighties, and finally proteins comprised of muscle tissue. Consequently, undernourished individuals often exhibit reduced muscle mass since their bodies utilize muscle fibers for energy. Ultimately, without sufficient sustenance and nutrients, one risks collapsing, possibly entering a comatose state before succumbing to starvation-related death. While survival duration varies depending on individual factors, complete deprivation of food and water typically leads to demise after several weeks to four days respectively.

We analyze two types of summation-by-parts finite difference operators for approximating the second derivative with variable coefficient. The first type uses ghost points, while the second type does not use any ghost points. A previously unexplored relation between the two types of summation-by-parts operators is investigated. By combining them we develop a new fourth order accurate finite difference discretization with hanging nodes on the mesh refinement interface. We take the model problem as the two-dimensional acoustic wave equation in second order form in terms of acoustic pressure, and prove energy stability for the proposed method. Compared to previous approaches using ghost points, the proposed method leads to a smaller system of linear equations that needs to be solved for the ghost point values. Another attractive feature of the proposed method is that the explicit time step does not need to be reduced relative to the corresponding periodic problem. Numerical experiments, both for smoothly varying and discontinuous material properties, demonstrate that the proposed method converges to fourth order accuracy. A detailed comparison of the accuracy and the time-step restriction with the simultaneous-approximation-term penalty method is also presented.

VR headsets require rapid rendering of dual images at high frame rates. Developers must compromise on graphical resolution and effects due to limitations in costly equipment to achieve this performance. 

Virtual reality games necessitate displaying two perspectives simultaneously which demands increased computational capacity over standard single-screen games. Maintaining a smooth frame rate in VR is crucial to prevent motion sickness; thus, while conventional games may operate well at 30fps, VR games typically need a baseline of 60fps, ideally reaching 90fps for optimal user experience. This means generating twice or thrice the number of images within the same timeframe, requiring significant GPU capabilities. As such, to function on average computers rather than top-of-the-line machines, VR games often sacrifice detailed graphics to maintain consistent display across both screens. The situation is even more pronounced with devices like the PlayStation VR, given its comparatively weaker hardware against modern PC setups.

One of the primary reasons for reducing graphic details is to avoid discomfort caused by fluctuating frame rates. Without advanced computing resources capable of handling high-resolution textures at 60fps or higher, adjustments must be made to ensure compatibility. Beyond these technical aspects, it's worth mentioning that high-profile VR titles similar to those found in mainstream gaming are relatively scarce. Indie games frequently exhibit similar quality levels but rely on distinctive artistic styles to compensate. Major studios allocate fewer resources towards VR development compared to their traditional counterparts, resulting in less sophisticated VR experiences due to underdeveloped technologies relative to non-VR gaming platforms.

A quantum effect called superabsorption allows a collection of molecules to absorb light more efficiently than if each molecule were acting individually. Researchers have used this phenomenon to create a multicolored light-emitting crystal. Artist's concept of a superabsorbing crystal Understanding how a crystal absorbs and emits light is critical to the development of quantum technologies, such as quantum computers, according to the researchers. The scientists at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and the University of Maryland, College Park have published their findings in the journal Nature Communications. Scientists have long known that if you add more molecules to a thin film of a material, such as a semiconductor, the film will become more absorbent, but it has been unclear how this happens. In this study, the researchers studied a very thin film of pentacene, a semiconductor. They found that when the film had 5000 molecules per square centimeter (1.2 square millimeters), it became superabsorptive and emitted light in three different colors simultaneously. The scientists used a microscope to study how the light changed when they added and removed molecules. They measured the temperature of the material and also its optical density, which determines how much light can pass through it. Superabsorption occurs when light interacts with a thin layer of material. The light excites electrons in the material to a higher energy level, and this process continues until the electrons reach the top of the material. This creates a wave of light that spreads out. The electrons fall back to the lower energy level, and the wave collapses, producing light in the form of a shorter wavelength. This causes the color to shift, and the light is emitted at a lower frequency. The scientists found that the light waves in the film have "hot spots," or places where the waves are particularly intense. By changing the temperature of the film, the researchers could control the number of hot spots in the film. They observed that the hot spots also interact with each other, and these interactions can change the color of the light. They found that if one hot spot is removed from the film, the light intensity in the remaining spots will increase. This means that the film produces three different colors of light simultaneously because it has three different hot spots. The team plans to use this research to create quantum sensors that can be used to detect the presence of single molecules in a thin film. Deep learning has led to state-of-the-art results for many medical imaging tasks, such as segmentation of different anatomical structures. With the increased numbers of deep learning publications and openly available code, the approach to choosing a model for a new task becomes more complicated, while time and (computational) resources are limited. A possible solution to choosing a model efficiently is meta-learning, a learning method in which prior performance of a model is used to predict the performance for new tasks. We investigate meta-learning for segmentation across ten datasets of different organs and modalities. We propose four ways to represent each dataset by meta-features: one based on statistical features of the images and three are based on deep learning features. We use support vector regression and deep neural networks to learn the relationship between the meta-features and prior model performance. On three external test datasets these methods give Dice scores within 0.10 of the true performance. These results demonstrate the potential of meta-learning in medical imaging.

The term "biased discrimination" was used as a placeholder since I wasn't sure how to accurately describe it. Here, I refer to negative perceptions associated with various forms of prejudice present within communities known for their strict opposition to racial bias. Similarly, platforms such as Reddit and Imgur may exhibit these sentiments. To illustrate my perspective using a Reddit scenario: A popular thread titled 'Racist store owner follows a black guy around his store,' insinuates that the owner is being racially biased by monitoring a Black customer. However, suppose the owner has managed the business for a year and observed that a significant percentage of Black patrons engage in theft compared to others. In that case, wouldn't it be reasonable for them to monitor those who pose a higher risk of causing financial loss? Differentiating between racism and caution informed by either personal experiences or extensive statistical evidence can be demonstrated through a Youtube comment related to the mentioned video. For instance, statement (1) suggests avoiding unnecessary surveillance if crime rates among different races were equal, whereas statement (2) unfairly blames individuals for behaviors attributed to their race, reflecting true racism. Thus, I believe: 1. Disliking someone solely due to their ethnicity constitutes racism deserving disapproval, and 2. Exercising heightened vigilance towards members of a particular race when informed by reliable sources does not equate to racism unless generalized assumptions lead to unjust treatment of individual persons belonging to that group. TL;DR - Discriminatory behavior arises from both unwarranted bias against someone's race and baselessly attributing criminal actions to entire racial groups. Distinguishing between cautious awareness based on factual evidence and outright racism helps us understand the issue better.

"Help!" Ser Galen's eyes narrowed at the shriek, though he struggled to remain outwardly calm. He had been a witch-hunter for years, and this would not be the first trap he'd been led into by his own compassion. Nor the last, he thought grimly, spurring his mount toward the sound. It was late. The witching hour, it was called - the time just before midnight when the barrier between the world and the next was thinnest. The ideal time to strike back at a pursuer, or lash out at a victim. It was possible that the cry for help was issued from someone with a perfectly innocent reason to be here on the moor in the dead of night - but unlikely. "Hail, the desperate!" Galen shouted after checking the wards on his shield. "Are you in need of aid?" "Yes!" Not the voice of a young woman - perhaps just old enough to be a grandmother. "Help me, please! My daughter, she's not breathing!" He saw her come running toward the light of his lantern, silhouette plain against the starlit brambles. "How far?" Galen asked, gently urging his steed forward. "Across the brook, milord, about a league. Please, she needs a priest!" "Direct me, then," he instructed, making the sign of the cross and throwing salt across his shoulder. "Ride with me. I would not separate a woman of God from her imperiled kin." The woman ran up to the horse and mounted it behind him with an ease that bespoke years of horsemanship. Unusual, but not impossible - and any witch who tried to mount his horse would be met with intense pain. "Forward here, ser, and turn to the left as you cross the brook!" she commanded confidently. That was more unusual, for a peasant addressing a knight. Curious. They came upon the girl laying unconscious against a tree. The woman leapt off immediately and cradled her, pulling one of the girl's hands up to brush her face. She conceals knowledge of medicine, Galen realized. "Does her blood yet flow?" he asked, watching the reaction. "Yes, her heart is beating, milord. Please, we need to bring her to a church! She may yet confess her sins and enter God's kingdom in a state of grace." A trap, but not for me, Galen mused. Fell creatures may not enter hallowed ground unbidden. "She doesn't need a church, mother." What am I doing? he wondered, but continued: "She needs her blood let, and tea made of willow. She's been bitten by a snake, don't you see? Her blood will curdle and rot if we are not quick to push it from her." "Ser knight, she's been here cavorting with the Devil himself. Small wonder if she's been bitten by a serpent. I would not want her to live in sin any more than to die in it, do you understand? Take us to a church at once!" She threw her arms about in a commanding gesture. Galen pushed the old woman away and threw a quick circle of salt about the girl. "Do you think you have authority over death, woman? Has all of your wickedness driven from you the memory of compassion?" She spat at this, but he continued. "Until the moment of death, all of God's creatures may find redemption. Even this girl. Even you. Please do not make me end your life, and hers, tonight." Two grotesque punctures about the left breast marked the poison's entry. Quickly, he set to the bloodletting. An initiation ritual. He had seen these marks before. The next step, the profane resurrection on an altar of our Lord. Grimly, wordlessly, he pushed the tainted blood from her wound. He was there for some time, intent enough that he did not see the witch return. She placed a small clay cup of willow tea at the boundary of the circle and said, "Do you truly think she can be saved?" "Her wounds are not fatal. She may yet live through the night." "Stubborn as ever, I see. That's not what I meant." She looked away, pensive. "How long have you been chasing after me now?" "Nine-hundred and sixty-two days," Galen replied, not looking up. "Though if you count the days I spent as page to Ser Thalus, God rest his soul, the total is increased by eight hundred and twelve." She smiled at that. "He was never as careful as you are, Galen. Nor so concerned with the lives of blasphemers." "All are rendered equal before the Lord," he quoted in a monotone. "We shall not turn away those in need until they have turned away from our Lord God." "And do you think, even now, that she has not turned? That I have not turned? Would you stoop over even me, to push poison from my veins?" "My lady," Galen exhaled, extending one hand from the circle and picking up the tea, "It saddens me that you do not understand that is what I am doing now. All children of God are given the opportunity to repent until they are dead. My mission is to ensure that you meet with one outcome or the other." As he poured the tea across her lips, the girl began to cough and breathe more deeply. "I will not forsake anyone, even a mistress of the Adversary." "I daresay you will not," she said, seemingly whispering into Galen's ear. He stood up, shield raised and sword drawn, but she was long gone.

Chloroplasts have their own DNA, often abbreviated as ctDNA, or cpDNA. It is also known as the plastome. Its existence was first proved in 1962, and first sequenced in 1986. It was, at one time, thought to be an organelle, but it is now known to be a genetic element found in the chloroplasts. The ctDNA encodes the proteins of the photosynthetic machinery, and other essential chloroplast functions. It is arranged in a single circular molecule, like the mitochondrial DNA. The ctDNA is a small genome, consisting of about 160,000 base pairs, and contains 114 genes, of which 78 encode proteins. There are also 8 ribosomal RNA genes, and 30 tRNA genes.

Hello everyone at CMV! I sincerely want to grasp this viewpoint since hearing discussions about it across various platforms such as media, Reddit, etc., makes me uncomfortable. We're all familiar with the phrase "America is the land of the free," which evokes strong emotions. In my opinion, this statement serves more as propaganda than anything else, just like any discourse promoting national superiority. Those who subscribe to such beliefs often lack critical thinking skills regarding this topic. To begin with, the term 'free' lacks clear definition within the social context referenced by these remarks. For instance, someone speaking loudly conflicts with another person choosing silence, illustrating how individual freedoms may clash. Moreover, every organized society imposes certain limitations on its citizens – countries form alliances and elect leaders to establish regulations, levy taxes, and perform essential functions for smooth operation. These guidelines differ minimally among developed nations; the U.S. and Canada share fundamental laws against actions like murder, assault, and robbery. While some might argue that these constraints hinder personal liberties, I find them necessary and reasonable. Consequently, America isn't entirely 'free.' If we were to dissect this assertion further, would it imply that Americans face fewer prohibitions compared to residents of other nations? It's hard to confirm whether that holds true, especially considering the United States maintains strict policies surrounding alcohol consumption, such as prohibiting underage drinking and public imbibing. This limitation alone significantly curbs individual autonomy, highlighting that complete freedom remains elusive even in seemingly progressive nations.

I grew to like the hospital at night, at least like it as much as I could. At night the halls were quiet, nurses and doctors talked in hushed voices or quietly walked by, but there was no sound of children crying in the background. It reminded me of my time with Chaz. He took great pains to make sure that I understood what he said because if I didn't know how to ask him for something, he wouldn't be able to understand either. We would talk about our day and sometimes even when we weren't talking about anything else he would ask questions such as "When are you going home?" or "Are you hungry?" But not only did they help us both cope during this difficult period, but also bring a sense of security throughout our entire relationship. The fact that she wasn't born at the hospital really helped her bond with the staff while at the same time giving her an opportunity to experience new things without being tied down by any bed restrictions. When asked what she liked most about the hospital, she responded simply with "the food." She then proceeded to describe all the different foods served there from hamburgers to desserts and added, "more desserts please!" The doctor's office immediately followed after the cafeteria with their own restaurant where she earned enough cash to have a pizza delivered daily. I loved hearing her say those words; I never thought of myself as having ever been fat until this moment. It made me realize just how far I had come and how much work still needed to be done. Once again, I couldn't wait to go back there to visit with her each week so that I could show her off. They transformed my days into gloom, but why? Their indifference seemed spiteful, causing distress. Nevertheless, amidst lingering soreness, determination grows stronger. Dawn inches closer, dispelling the remnants of night; clarity emerges as light reappears. At long last, tranquility replaces turmoil, fulfilling desires once fervently held. As you talk, your vocal cords produce vibrations, creating sound waves that leave your mouth during exhalation and spread outwardly. This expansion encompasses transmitting these sound waves along your face and reentering your ear. These sound waves enter your inner ear via the ear canal, impacting the eardrum and allowing you to perceive your spoken words. However, this explanation doesn't fully capture the phenomenon. In addition to entering the ear through the air pathway, these vibrations also propagate through solid structures like your jawbone and temples before reaching the inner ear within your head. Human voices comprise numerous sound frequencies ranging typically between 300 Hz and 3400 Hz. While higher frequencies possess greater energy, they dissipate rapidly over distance. When compared to air, flesh and bones offer significantly denser mediums for sound transmission; thus, the high-frequency components of your voice experience substantial energy loss by the time they reach your eardrums, whereas lower frequencies retain more energy and appear louder. Consequently, while listening to yourself speak, you hear not just the complete spectrum of your voice, including its bass tones, unlike others who only receive the frequency range carried by air. My insight comes from having worked alongside an audio engineer with a background in music. Additionally, your perception of your voice may differ due to how the sound waves navigate both the bodily channels and airways, leading to some degree of distortion.

In the Amazon lives a tribe of men with no concept of time. They have no history, oral, written, or drawn no stories of the past or hopes for the future. This tribe of men is known as the Yanomami people and they live in the Amazon rainforest in northern Brazil, southern Venezuela, and parts of Colombia and Peru. They are a hunter-gatherer culture, living off the land and relying on the resources of their environment for survival. As such, they have no concept of time, instead living in the present moment and appreciating each day as it comes. The Yanomami have no written language and so have no history or stories of the past. They do not plan for the future, instead focusing on the moment and taking each day as it comes. They also have a spiritual belief system which is based on the natural world around them, with spirits inhabiting plants, animals, and other elements of the jungle.

Lossy compression introduces imperfections known as artifacts into an image, negatively impacting its visual appearance. Over the past few years, several techniques employing convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for removing these artifacts have shown promising outcomes. Nevertheless, most existing models are tailored to work within a narrow range of quality factors, leading to subpar performance when applied outside their designated range. Hence, in light of this issue and considering real-world applications, this study proposes a resilient compression artifact removal framework. This singular model can be trained to handle diverse quality levels, yielding consistent or even enhanced results compared to previous methods. For illustrative purposes, we examine JPEG compression at various quality factors between 1 and 60. A key feature contributing to our method's efficiency is incorporating quantization tables directly into the training process. Additionally, our system consists of dual branches operating simultaneously – one focusing on rectifying localized artifacts like ringing effects and another concentrating on improving overall image quality by addressing widespread issues like blockiness and color distortion. Comprehensive experiments conducted on both color and grayscale imagery confirm the efficacy and reliability of our unified model in eliminating compression artifacts from processed images.

On everything from music to microwaves, and taxis to train tickets. Consumers save money by doing their transactions on a computer or mobile phone. But not when it comes to banking. Customers of UK banks who use the internet pay just as much for overdrafts and fees as everyone else. These low-maintenance customers rarely need to call their bank, let alone visit the local branch. From the bank's point of view, they are cheap to look after. Yet they get no price reductions. On the face of it, digital customers are getting a raw deal. Lloyds - the UK's biggest retail banking group - boasts that is has 10 million customers who access its services via the internet. In effect, those 10 million are paying for the other 12 million customers who still want a premium and personalised service; namely the ability to go in to a centrally-heated, business-rate paying, well-decorated and well-staffed High Street branch, to speak to a human being. "If I'm just using online, and never go into a branch, or never ring a call-centre, I would expect to get a better price, because otherwise I am subsidising those people who go into a branch," says Kevin Mountford, head of banking at MoneySupermarket. No bank will say how much its branch network really costs them. But Lloyds has no fewer than 1,300 such branches in England and Wales alone. And Royal Bank of Scotland (RBS) spent PS400m last year on refurbishments. Either way, transactions on the internet cost banks a tiny fraction of those in-branch, or compared to the cost of processing a cheque. "As a customer, if I am seeing that my behaviour brings down the operational cost, what's in it for me?" says Mr Mountford. "I would expect something back. But unfortunately it doesn't happen." None of the big High Street banks offer their customers separate internet banking directly. However HSBC and The Co-operative Bank do so under separate brands. One of them is Smile, the first full internet bank to be set up, in 1999, and owned by the Co-op. Smile customers borrowing PS500 for a month benefit significantly. The cost is just PS7.34, as opposed to PS17.40 with the Co-op. The other is First Direct, which - as a telephone and internet bank only - has much lower running costs than its parent brand, HSBC. Yet First Direct charges PS83.05 to fund a PS500 overdraft for a month, only marginally cheaper than HSBC's PS87.52. Mark Mullen, the former chief executive of First Direct - and now boss of Atom Bank - is not impressed. "I think it is astonishing that you can have banks with very different cost bases, very different sizes of banks, and very different histories of technology, yet somehow miraculously they price just about the same." Others might wonder why, if Smile charges PS7.34 for an overdraft, and HSBC charges PS87.52 for exactly the same thing, more customers aren't switching; or why the self-evident benefits of internet banking aren't available more widely. The banks concerned argue that customers are unlikely to be charged the amounts listed above, as they would be advised to take out a personal loan instead of the more expensive overdraft option. In any case, the mainstream banks believe consumers should not be getting lower prices for banking online. They are acutely aware that differential pricing would make life more expensive for older and vulnerable customers, who rely on a branch network, and often still use cheques. James Daley, the managing director of Fairer Finance, and a former campaigner with Which? believes that banks have a social responsibility to provide an equal service for everybody. "You start telling pensioners that they're going to have to pay twice as much for their banking services because they aren't comfortable with the internet - I don't think that would be the right solution. "I wouldn't want to advocate a world where people who bank predominantly online end up with significantly better deals than those customers who have to use branches." So are online customers going to have to continue tolerating paying over the odds for banking? The answer to that could depend on the launch of Atom, the UK's first truly internet-only bank, sometime before Easter. Built from scratch, with just 150 staff at its Durham headquarters, Atom will only offer access via the internet or an app. No branches, no call centres. As a result of its low cost base, it is promising cheaper prices. "We would expect to be more competitive when it comes to some - not all - of our charges, and some of our costs," says Mark Mullen. For example, customers will not be forced to pay both an interest charge and a fee for an overdraft. And there will be no distinction between an authorised and an unauthorised overdraft. "That's just nonsense," says Mr Mullen. But even if Atom does offer its users a significantly better deal, the rest of the industry may not feel obliged to follow suit. In this market, competition does not work as it should. So without a significant shift in banks' attitudes, digital customers may continue to argue they're not getting a good deal. But they may just have to lump it. Monday: Do other countries offer consumers better banking than the UK?

For any Borel probability measure on R n , we may define a family of eccentricity tensors. This new notion, together with a tensorization trick, allows us to prove an energy minimization property for rotationally invariant probability measures. We use this theory to give a new proof of the Welch bounds, and to improve upon them for collections of real vectors. In addition, we are able to give elementary proofs for two theorems characterizing probability measures optimizing one-parameter families of energy integrals on the sphere. We are also able to explain why a phase transition occurs for optimizers of these two families.

The Classification of medical images and illustrations in the literature aims to label a medical image according to the modality it was produced or label an illustration according to its production attributes. It is an essential and challenging research hotspot in the area of automated literature review, retrieval and mining. The significant intra-class variation and inter-class similarity caused by the diverse imaging modalities and various illustration types brings a great deal of difficulties to the problem. In this paper, we propose a synergic deep learning (SDL) model to address this issue. Specifically, a dual deep convolutional neural network with a synergic signal system is designed to mutually learn image representation. The synergic signal is used to verify whether the input image pair belongs to the same category and to give the corrective feedback if a synergic error exists. Our SDL model can be trained 'end to end'. In the test phase, the class label of an input can be predicted by averaging the likelihood probabilities obtained by two convolutional neural network components. Experimental results on the ImageCLEF2016 Subfigure Classification Challenge suggest that our proposed SDL model achieves the state-of-the-art performance in this medical image classification problem and its accuracy is higher than that of the first place solution on the Challenge leader board so far.

Deep learning models have gained great success in many real-world applications. However, most existing networks are typically designed in heuristic manners, thus lack of rigorous mathematical principles and derivations. Several recent studies build deep structures by unrolling a particular optimization model that involves task information. Unfortunately, due to the dynamic nature of network parameters, their resultant deep propagation networks do not possess the nice convergence property as the original optimization scheme does. This paper provides a novel proximal unrolling framework to establish deep models by integrating experimentally verified network architectures and rich cues of the tasks. More importantly, we prove in theory that 1) the propagation generated by our unrolled deep model globally converges to a critical-point of a given variational energy, and 2) the proposed framework is still able to learn priors from training data to generate a convergent propagation even when task information is only partially available. Indeed, these theoretical results are the best we can ask for, unless stronger assumptions are enforced. Extensive experiments on various real-world applications verify the theoretical convergence and demonstrate the effectiveness of designed deep models.

It gradually grew louder until it was unmistakable. Bees. Hundreds of them, buzzing around in circles. I opened my window and stuck my head out to get a better look, and sure enough, the sky was filled with a massive swarm of bees. I didn't know what to make of it. Was this some kind of prank? Or was it a sign of something more sinister? Whatever it was, I knew I wasn't safe. I scrambled to grab my things and make an escape, but it was too late. The bees were everywhere, blocking my path and swarming around me. I tried to swat them away, but it was hopeless. Finally, I gave up and just stood there, surrounded by the buzzing of the bees. After a few moments, the noise died down and the bees slowly began to disperse. Once again, everything was silent. I looked around, trying to make sense of what had just happened. I still had no answers, but one thing was certain: I wouldn't be sleeping through any more air raid sirens.

Modern embedded technology is a driving factor in satellite miniaturization, contributing to a massive boom in satellite launches and a rapidly evolving new space industry. Miniaturized satellites, however, suffer from low reliability, as traditional hardware-based fault-tolerance (FT) concepts are ineffective for on-board computers (OBCs) utilizing modern systems-on-a-chip (SoC). Therefore, larger satellites continue to rely on proven processors with large feature sizes. Software-based concepts have largely been ignored by the space industry as they were researched only in theory, and have not yet reached the level of maturity necessary for implementation. We present the first integral, real-world solution to enable fault-tolerant general-purpose computing with modern multiprocessor-SoCs (MPSoCs) for spaceflight, thereby enabling their use in future high-priority space missions. The presented multi-stage approach consists of three FT stages, combining coarse-grained thread-level distributed self-validation, FPGA reconfiguration, and mixed criticality to assure long-term FT and excellent scalability for both resource constrained and critical high-priority space missions. Early benchmark results indicate a drastic performance increase over state-of-the-art radiation-hard OBC designs and considerably lower software- and hardware development costs. This approach was developed for a 4-year European Space Agency (ESA) project, and we are implementing a tiled MPSoC prototype jointly with two industrial partners.

Let me simplify this by comparing it to a child named Tim who owns two different kinds of playsets. Playset X consists of a single toggle and a light, while Playset Y has two toggles and a light. With Playset X: The light illuminates when the toggle is switched off, and dims once the toggle is activated (analogous to a NOT gate in electronics). For Playset Y: The light shines only when both toggles are deactivated; otherwise, it remains dark (similar to a NOR gate in electronics).

Now picture connecting Playset Y to Playright X so that whenever the light from Playset Y goes off, its corresponding toggle does too. Consequently, if both toggles on Playset Y are turned off, Playset Y's light will illuminate, leading to activation of Playset X's toggle, thereby turning off Playset X's light. Furthermore, if both toggles on Playset Y are active, or just one of them, Playset Y's light stays off, resulting in Playset X's toggle being deactivated, thus lighting up Playset X's light. This demonstrates how an OR gate can be built using a combination of NOR and NOT gates in electronic systems.

Using a specialized software called Verilog (a tool for describing electronic systems), one can outline the actions of these playsets as part of a larger circuit. An example rule might state: if either Playset A or Playset B is lit, then the main output should also be lit. However, if both Playset A and Playset B remain unlit, the main output should also stay unlit. Imagine now that these playsets are composed entirely of DNA. Instead of physical toggles and lights, there are proteins and enzymatic processes involved. By utilizing specific DNA sequences capable of mimicking NOR or NOT functions, Cello enables users to design genetic circuits, which it then assembles through the construction of relevant genetic modules containing these functionalities.

However, our research reveals difficulties in broadening this methodology to counter diverse attack models, particularly in scenarios involving high dimensions. Specifically, for numerous classes of independent and identically distributed smoothing distributions, we've established that the maximum achievable radius, denoted by 'p', diminishes proportionally to O(1/d^(1+1/p)) as the dimensionality 'd' increases, provided p^2 conditions are met. Significantly, under p^2 constraints, this relationship between 'd' and 'p' does not surpass the performance observed through standard isotropic Gaussian smoothing, implying a comparable lower limit for robustness radius. Furthermore, when confined to generalized Gaussian smoothing, these limits appear nearly identical at large scales, affirming that Gaussian smoothing delivers optimal outcomes, modulo constants, given p^satisfactory conditions. Our empirical findings based on the CIFAR dataset substantiate our theoretical analysis. Moreover, alternative smoothing methods like uniformly distributing points inside an L1 or Lp norm sphere yield less favorable bounds expressed as O(1/d) and O(1/d^(1+1/p)), respectively, exhibiting significantly inferior scalability with respect to 'd'.

North Carolina's party loyalties have undergone a series of important shifts in the last few years: While the 2010 midterms saw Tar Heel voters elect a bicameral Republican majority legislature for the first time in over a century, North Carolina has also become a Southern swing state in presidential races. Since Southern Democrat Jimmy Carter's comfortable victory in the state in 1976, the state had consistently leaned Republican in presidential elections until Democrat Barack Obama narrowly won the state in 2008. In the 1990s, Democrat Bill Clinton came within a point of winning the state in 1992 and also only narrowly lost the state in 1996. In the early 2000s, Republican George W. Bush easily won the state by over 12 points, but by 2008, demographic shifts, population growth, and increased liberalization in heavily populated areas such as the Research Triangle, Charlotte, Greensboro, Winston-Salem, Fayetteville, and Asheville, propelled Barack Obama to victory in North Carolina, the first Democrat to win the state since 1976. In 2012, North Carolina was again considered a competitive swing state, with the Democrats even holding their 2012 Democratic National Convention in Charlotte. However, Republican Mitt Romney ultimately eked out a 2-point win in North Carolina, the only 2012 swing state that Obama lost, and one of only two states (along with Indiana) to flip from Obama in 2008 to the GOP in 2012.
