We introduce an integrated optimization approach that merges neural networks with dictionary learning for representing intricate relationships between resting state fMRI scans and associated behavior patterns. The process involves breaking down correlation matrices specific to each patient into common foundation networks along with individualized weight distributions. Concurrently, these personalized attributes serve as inputs to a neural network designed to forecast various dimensions of clinical data. Our cutting-edge methodology integrates the gradient details derived from both the neural network and traditional matrix decomposition techniques. Through this joint estimation strategy, we determine the foundational networks, individualized coefficients, and neural network parameters that best reflect clinical condition intensity. We put our hybrid model to test on a comprehensive scoring task involving 52 individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), demonstrating superior performance compared to existing top-tier approaches during ten iterations of cross-validation across multiple criteria measuring clinical gravity.

The US tech giant sold 74.8 million iPhones in its fiscal first quarter, compared with 74.5 million a year ago. Apple said revenue for the next quarter would be between 50bn (PS34bn; a'!46bn) and 53bn, below the 58bn it reported for the same period a year ago. This would mark Apple's first fall in revenues since it launched the iPhone. Despite first-quarter iPhone sales being below the 75 million expected by analysts, it was still a record quarter for the company. Apple revenue in the three months to 26 December was 75.9bn and net profit was 18.4bn, both of which are the highest ever recorded by the company. Sales of iPhones accounted for 68 of the company's revenue in the period. Any other company announcing record profits and revenues might expect a warm welcome from investors. But now that Apple has scaled so many peaks the worry is that the only way is down - and there's evidence in these figures to back up those concerns. Sales of the iPhone, surely the single most profitable product any company has produced, were basically flat. What's more, the revenue outlook for the next three months indicates we can expect the first fall in sales since the iPhone's 2007 launch. Then there's China - still growing but far more slowly. The iPhone is still an object of desire there, but at a time when Apple says it's seeing softness in the economy, the attractions of cheaper rivals from local firms like Xiaomi may grow. Of course, the worries about "peak iPhone" have surfaced before and evaporated with the hugely successful iPhone 6. Last year's upgrade to the 6S was a minor one, and we can expect something more radical in September. But the pressure is now mounting on Apple to deliver another blockbuster product to keep the profit engine running. The Apple watch will not fill that role - we've still not even heard any sales figures for the product. Perhaps the 1,000 engineers rumoured to be working on an Apple Car will come up with the exciting innovation which Apple's fans and investors await with growing impatience. Is the mighty iPhone in decline? Apple boss Tim Cook credited "all-time record sales of iPhone, Apple Watch and Apple TV" for the performance. But the firm's chief financial officer, Luca Maestri, said the company was operating in "a very difficult macroeconomic environment." He added that "iPhone units will decline in the quarter" and that the company was not projecting beyond those three months. Mr Maestri partly blamed the strong US dollar for Apple's flat sales, estimating it had knocked 5bn off the company's revenues. Apple's sales in Greater China - defined by the company as China, Hong Kong and Taiwan - rose 14, but that was much slower than the 70 increase a year ago. Mr Maestri said the softness in China was "something that we have not seen before," Reuters reported. China accounts for almost a quarter of Apple's sales, more than all of Europe combined. The profitability of Apple's business improved, with gross margin - or how much the company makes per product - increasing to 40.1. Geoff Blaber, an analyst at CCS Insight, said Apple was "generating industry defying margins" and had cash of almost 216bn. Speaking to analysts, Mr Cook said the company had "the mother of all balance sheets" and that its financial position had never been stronger. Apple's shares were down 2.7 in after hours trading at 97.28. Daniel Ives, an analyst at Capital Markets who owns shares in Apple, said given the "white knuckles fears" ahead of the results, he would "characterise the overall headline performance as better than feared."

Infection initiates when a foreign entity gains access into the body, proliferates, and establishes itself, known as colonization. Typically, most people do not fall prey to infections easily; however, those suffering from illnesses, poor nutrition, cancer, or diabetes may be more prone to recurring or long-lasting infections. Moreover, individuals with compromised immune systems are especially vulnerable to opportunistic infections. The point of contact between the host and the invader often lies at natural openings such as the mouth, nostrils, eyes, reproductive and digestive tracts, or skin lesions. Although certain microbes remain localized at their points of entry, others disseminate throughout the body affecting various organs. Pathogens either replicate inside host cells or thrive unimpeded in bodily fluids.

A debtor is someone who owes money, while a creditor is a person seeking repayment of funds. Bankruptcy is a legally recognized procedure designed to provide relief to individuals facing excessive financial obligations. Its primary objective is to prevent debtors from becoming homeless due to insurmountable debt. Bankruptcy laws vary across countries; however, the United States tends to be more accommodating towards debtors. Within U.S. jurisdiction, bankruptcy falls under the purview of federal legislation known as the [US Bankruptcy Code] (URL0), which spans approximately 500 pages, requiring careful study to comprehend its contents fully. Ordinary citizens typically encounter two types of bankruptcy: Chapter 7 and Chapter 13. Currently, Chapter 13 is mandated for high-income debtors, involving a structured payment plan managed by the court along with a regulated budget. Should a debtor fail to adhere to this schedule, the court might convert the case to Chapter 7 proceedings. Chapter 7 represents the conventional route to bankruptcy, entailing asset liquidation followed by debt settlement. There exists a roster of non-negotiable properties shielded from seizure, such as treasured personal belongings, essential modes of transportation, and potentially one's home depending on the respective state guidelines outlined within the Bankruptcy Code. Although filing for bankruptcy will negatively impact an individual's credit score, this stain diminishes gradually over time, often fading entirely within five years. Business entities experience less favorable treatment during bankruptcy proceedings. While corporate bankruptcies may occur via Chapter 7 - effectively dissolving the business entity - Chapter 11 reorganization is a more prevalent alternative aimed at restructuring management strategies when faced with unfavorable circumstances.

The basic primary colors of red, yellow, and blue are used to create the secondary colors. Tertiary colors are created by mixing primary and secondary colors together. Primary colors have a maximum brightness that is determined by their saturation as well as by their color temperature (the higher the Kelvin number, the more intense its light). Secondary colors do not reach those maximums but can be made brighter or darker to match other colors, so they tend to be much more saturated than the primary colors. The primary and secondary colors are relatively similar in hue, but each has differing intensity; even if all three primaries were combined into one color, it would still differ from the primary-secondary combination only slightly. In this example, we will consider the relationship between complementary colors: black, white, and green - [1] In order to make these colors complementary, we need two different sets of primary colors that complement each other, so let's start with a single set whose primary colors form the primary and secondary colors. Because you don't know which parts of the primary and secondary colors are complimentary, you'll want to mix them together until they're both mixed together. You might also handmix them to see what happens. If there is too little mixture, then adding another part may bring out the differences further. Mixing the first colored objects in this way gives us the same result we wanted when we started with the single object: a complex combination of colors without any apparent difference in brightness or saturation. But if there was some concentration on the second color, then we will notice a great difference in color, somewhere near our original object. We can use the laws of thermodynamics in this case to test how many degrees Celsius the new and old colors have been altered, since we expect that the temperature of the new material increases at a constant rate while the temperature of the old material stays the same. This will give an indication of whether or not the materials change in appearance. On average, the materials undergo no significant changes, though it's possible for small variations to occur. It's important to note that the schemes described above display only a gradual increase in brightness over time, which means that every system will look very different after just a few minutes. So like any experiment involving matter, it's best to continue doing it until you get some useful results.

In 1983, the Radio Communications Sector of the International Telecommunication Union (ITU-R) created a group called IWP116. Their goal was to establish one global high-definition television (HDTV) standard. A major challenge they faced involved choosing an appropriate framefield refresh rate, as different regions had adopted either 2550 Hz or 3060 Hz standards based on their local power supply frequencies. Over the course of the decade, the IWP116 group facilitated advancements in various aspects of video digital processing technology, including techniques for converting between the primary framefield rates by utilizing motion vectors. Although they did not succeed in developing a complete HDTV standard, they were able to reach a consensus regarding the aspect ratio.

When expressing distress through yelling, what message are you conveying? Using a sharp, sudden 'rrrruff,' similar to a dog's alarm bark, can prompt most dogs to bark along, mimicking how they interact with one another upon sensing unfamiliar presence. Additionally, growling may deter dogs from intrusive behavior like begging. However, dogs eventually disregard fake howls. Interestingly, I can elicit barking responses from strangers' dogs due to my authentic-sounding bark. Shifting gears, do dogs worldwide comprehend each other's vocalizations, potentially forming a universal 'dog language' enabling basic communication? For instance, specific sequences might indicate agreement ('bark yes'), invitations to investigate something ('two barks - let me sniff'), or excitement about prey ('three barks - squirrel'). Dogs respond well to such sounds; however, despite being adept at noticing variations, they primarily rely on nonverbal cues—body language accounts for the vast majority of their interactions. While human impersonation of these signals may succeed temporarily, effective two-way dialogue remains challenging without understanding their primary mode of expression.

(My first time writing anything. Here goes!) I was awakened by the sensation by a searing pain on my wrist. I bolted upwards, jerking my head around to see what asshole was responsible. Unfortunately, my sudden movements caused a trombone case to fall over into the aisle, waking up a number of groggy band kids on the bus, all of them muttering their disapproval of being woken so suddenly. Sidney jumped awake next to me, startled. "What's up with you?" she grumbled. She looked at me with her tired eyes. She didn't like to be disturbed from her sleep, especially not after a performance. Sleeping on the bus ride back home wasn't comfortable, but it was usually inevitable. I rubbed my wrist, feeling nothing but my bare skin. Must've dreamt it. "Nothing," I said. I picked up the trombone case and propped it back up to where it was before. Sidney rolled her eyes, and leaned on my shoulder. She quickly fell back asleep. I chuckled. Careful not to disturb Sidney, I cautiously took my phone to check the time. 9:39 pm. Huh. It felt like it was much later. Just as I was about to put my phone away, something caught my eye. On the same wrist where I felt that pain, there was a mark. My heart felt like it dropped down to my stomach. I looked away from my wrist before I could see what the tattoo looked like, my chest feeling constricted. No way. I couldn't have done it, I couldn't have killed someone. I didn't want to look at it; what if it was someone I knew? I wouldn't have been able to bear it. I'll have to look at it eventually. But not now. Not in front of everyone. My god, how would I tell my family? Sidney? I tried not to think about it. 30 more minutes and we'll be back in town. I kept trying to sleep, but all I did was rub that spot on my wrist until it was even more raw. The next few weeks at school, I showed up wearing an oversized sweatshirt. I knew I looked ridiculous, but I'd take the public ridicule. It's driving me insane. It would be so much easier to just look at it and see who it was, but no matter how I tried, I just couldn't do it. Everyday, I'd check and see who was at school and who wasn't. I've been anxious and I haven't been eating. I'm a generally quiet kid at school; I don't have many friends who would've noticed my strange behavior. But Sidney, she noticed. One day, as we were walking home from school, she confronted me. "Jay, I miss the old you," she said. "I wish you would tell me what's wrong." I shook my head. "I-I can't," I stammered. I clenched the left sleeve of my sweater out of habit. I saw her eyes flick down to my trembling hands, then back up to meet mine. Her gaze softened. She took a step forward, reaching her hand out to grab mine. "You know, you can tell me anythin "NO!" I shouted, panicking. I didn't want her to know. I pushed her away, a little too hard, and she fell back. She looked up at me, her eyes wide with shock. My eyes filled with tears. I hurt her. I hurt her. I could see the blood welling from the scratches in her hands. "I'm sorry," I said, my voice quivering. But before she could say anything, I turned and walked away as fast as I could, making the biggest mistake of my life. In the following week after our incident, I avoided Sidney. I wanted to talk to her, I really did. But I don't think she wanted to see me. I never realized how lonely she was during school. It's not like I was the only person she ever talked to; but when she would talk to other people, she didn't have that same spark, that passion that I adored so much when she was with me. It was all just meaningless small talk. I finally decided this weekend that it was time to set things straight. I missed her. I wanted to have my friend back. I'm so sick of being miserable all the time. However, it's my own fault. Sometimes I wonder how much grief would I have saved if I had just looked at my tattoo from the beginning. My heart started to pound. I knew what I had to do. I pulled up my left sleeve and examined the tattoo closely. It was a peculiar little tattoo. So simple, yet there was beauty in its simplicity. A white lily flower, with its stem in the shape of a treble clef. I've never seen this tattoo before. I was still trembling, but this brought me a little relief. I pulled out my cellphone and, with shaking fingers, dialed Sidney's number. It rang and rang, but there was no answer. Of course; she never picked up her phone. But a feeling of doubt got into me. I pushed that feeling aside and opened the messenger app. "Hey Sid..... it's Jay" I waited a few minutes. No answer, and she hadn't read it. I typed another message. "I want to talk to you about what happened, can we meet up later?" No reply. No read. Suddenly a chilling thought crept it's way into my head. Sidney's never shown me her tattoo before. What if..... No. That's silly. As the hours passed, I grew increasingly more worried about her. She lived just down the street, it wouldn't hurt to visit and check on her. I walked to her house with urgency in my step. Once I got to her doorstep, it took about a minute to muster up the courage to ring the doorbell. And it took another minute for someone to come and open the door. The door swung open, the smell of cigarettes and alcohol wafting from the house. "What do you want kid?" said Mr. Brown, a cigarette in his hand. "Is Sid home?" I asked. He stared me down. "Should be in her room. She's been in there all day," he puffed on his cigarette. I frowned. Not a good sign. He opened the door wider and let me in. It took a lot to not sprint to her room. I knocked on her door. "Sid?" No answer. I knocked louder. "Sid!" No answer. Consumed with worry, I enter without permission. And became immediately mortified at what I saw. There was blood all over the sheets, and Sidney was lying, motionless, in the middle of her bed. I stood, frozen, until my eyes came to a rest on her ankle. A white lily tattoo with a treble clef stem. Then the world went black.

According to Tabatabaei, esoteric interpretations can be categorized as either acceptable or unacceptable. Acceptable ta'wil involves deriving meanings from a verse that go beyond its literal sense, focusing on the hidden significance that only God knows fully and cannot be understood solely through human reasoning. These interpretations often attribute human characteristics such as movement, contentment, and emotions to God. On the other hand, unacceptable ta'wil entails altering the straightforward meaning of a verse using evidence, leading to contradictory outcomes. Despite its prevalence, this approach is flawed when applied to the Quran. Instead, the true interpretation lies in understanding the actual situation being addressed in each verse, regardless of whether it is clear-cut or vague. This deeper meaning transcends mere linguistic expression, representing profound truths that God conveys through language to make them somewhat accessible to us. In essence, these verses function similarly to metaphors, painting mental images to aid listeners in grasping the intended message more effectively.

A Full Duplex Base Station (FD-EE) has the capability to support two Half-Duplex (HD) Mobile Units (MUs), each operating either on the uplink or downlink channels concurrently. This function can also be accomplished through the utilization of two linked yet distinctively positioned Half-Duplex Base Stations (HD-ESs), known as CoMPflex (CoMP for In-band Wireless Full Duplex). Here, an FD-EE can be considered as a specific instance of CoMPflex where the distance between them is negligible. Within this study, we analyze the effectiveness of CoMPflex within a two-dimensional mobile network environment employing stochastic geometry techniques, contrasting its outcomes with those obtained from FD-ESs. Through the derivation of Cumulative Distribution Functions, our findings indicate that CoMPflex enhances proximity between base stations and their respective mobile units, whilst expanding the gap between a mobile unit and any nearby interfering units. Additionally, the data suggests that CoMPflex offers improved communication dependability compared to FD-ESs. Given the growing trend towards denser wireless networks, CoMPflex presents itself as a promising approach for maximizing the efficiency of existing half-duplex installations.

This was a hugely significant fixture for the visitors too, Louis van Gaal and his players arriving with their fate in their own hands but little margin for error. They knew victory here, amid a heady mix of nostalgia and fierce hostility, would leave them needing only to beat Bournemouth at Old Trafford on Sunday to secure Champions League football. It was later suggested United had not missed out but that Van Gaal had actually vetoed the deal - and why would the club let him do that if he was not going to be in charge next season? Indeed, so buoyed was Van Gaal by the sudden upturn in his position that he was even able to point out to the media that they were finally posing tactical questions before a game rather than asking about his possible sacking. And for four tantalising second-half minutes it all seemed on for Van Gaal. Antony Martial's brilliance had turned the game, undeservedly on its balance, in United's favour with two goals. At 2-1 up, they were 14 minutes from a win that could have offered the opportunity to put a different spin on their season. It was not to be. Old vulnerabilities quickly returned and saw United beaten by two headed goals from Michail Antonio and Winston Reid - leaving Van Gaal back on the rack. The players dragged their manager out of a hole then threw him back in again. The intention may still be to keep him next season but that decision would have been made a lot easier and more palatable with victory. Now it all goes on the line again on Sunday - but with Manchester City at the controls. The equation is simple. Manchester United must beat Bournemouth and hope Manchester City lose at Swansea - and therein lies that sliver of hope for the 64-year-old Dutch coach. City have been so unreliable, unpredictable and uninspired at times this season that you would not risk too much on the certainty of Manuel Pellegrini's side getting the job done. Of course City will be favourites and only need a point - but they are not a team to be trusted, as seen in their heavy defeat at Southampton and disappointing draw at home to Arsenal in their last two Premier League games. And after beating Liverpool 3-1 and, more impressively, thrashing West Ham 4-1 at Upton Park on Saturday, Swansea are also running into the sort of relaxed good form that makes them dangerous opponents. Confidence has been renewed to such an extent that head coach Francesco Guidolin is expected to be confirmed on a new contract after a Swansea board meeting on Wednesday. City can be fragile and United will hope that vulnerability haunts them one last time. And then all it needs is for United to beat Bournemouth - but United cannot be trusted either. Manchester United's players may have been affected by an arduous coach journey that ended in such disgraceful scenes outside Upton Park - and West Ham co-owner David Sullivan's dismissive response that the visitors should simply have arrived earlier did no credit to him or his club on this landmark night. The kick-off was delayed by 45 minutes but there was still no excuse for a tepid Manchester United first half that lacked urgency, organisation and anything that would be reasonably expected with stakes so high. They were lucky to only trail to Diafra Sakho's early goal, their defence going missing in its entirety shortly afterwards when Andy Carroll raced clear only to shoot straight at David de Gea. It was as if Van Gaal had not impressed upon his players that a door to the Champions League that had looked shut for so long was suddenly ajar. Instead it looked like meaningless, end-of-season stuff. The superb Martial offered brief hope, the normally passive Van Gaal leaping from his seat to punch the air - but the joy did not last long as the visitors' vulnerability in defence was exposed. They simply could not cope with West Ham's pressure. For long spells this was a performance that made you question how such an ordinary side could even be in contention for a top-four place. They were that poor. True, they missed the aerial strength of suspended Marouane Fellaini, who operated with such success to not only combat the likes of Carroll but also score when Manchester United won 2-1 at Upton Park in the FA Cup quarter-final replay. In the final reckoning, however, this defeat was deserved after a display that produced much of the evidence that has left so many United fans questioning Van Gaal's future. Van Gaal will still believe his side can reach the Champions League but the odds are against them now so he may well end up looking to the FA Cup for success. If United win he will undoubtedly paint this as progress - and he will have a point as it would be the club's first major trophy since Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013. It may not be enough, however, to suggest Van Gaal is pointing United in the right direction, despite his willingness to play youth with the emergence of 18-year-old Marcus Rashford and the signing of 20-year-old Antony Martial - who increasingly looks like a bargain at PS36m from Monaco. Executive vice-chairman Ed Woodward clearly wants his man to succeed and his thoughts on the future remain a mystery but there is no doubt an FA Cup win is a much harder sell than an FA Cup win and Champions League football. With the Sun in an active part of its cycle, there are concerns that some storms could disrupt technology on Earth including satellite navigation signals and aircraft communications. The Sun may seem to change little from our viewing position on Earth. With the right equipment, it is possible to see dark regions called sunspots. But up close, our Sun is a dynamic, violent beast. Bright loops of matter arch and twist like fiery fountains above the surface of this gigantic natural nuclear reactor. And every so often an intense burst of radiation called a solar flare appears when magnetic energy - stored in our star's atmosphere - is suddenly released. Solar flares are sometimes associated with the release of high energy particles into space - eruptions that are known as coronal mass ejections (CMEs), though these can also occur on their own. A large CME can contain billions of tonnes of gas and other matter that pours into space at several million km per hour. The charged particles in this cloud stream towards any planet or spacecraft in its path. When these particles collide with the Earth, they can cause a geomagnetic storm - a disturbance in the magnetic sheath (or magnetosphere) that surrounds our planet, protecting its denizens from the worst effects of cosmic rays. Many of the effects of charged particles hitting the Earth's magnetosphere are benign, such as polar lights - the Aurora borealis and australis. Geomagnetic storms - often referred to as solar storms - cause these northern or southern lights to become visible at lower latitudes. However, they also disrupt technology on Earth, such as communications systems - including those used by aircraft, satellite navigation signals and electrical power grids. As such, they could wreak long-lasting havoc with communications and power infrastructure across the globe. A 2008 report by the US National Academy of Sciences concluded that an extreme storm could cause up to 2 trillion in initial damages by crippling communications on Earth and causing chaos around the world. As such, several agencies around the world are working to better understand the changing conditions near our planet - known collectively as space weather. Forecasters at the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Space Weather Prediction Center monitor activity using data from a network of sensors, including those on satellites, and US Geological Survey instruments that detect magnetic fields (magnetometers). The Sun goes through cycles of high and low activity that repeat approximately every 11 years. It is currently gaining in activity and is expected to peak in 2013 or 2014, although nobody can be sure. This means we can expect more solar flares and more coronal mass ejections over the next few years. The solar cycle we're currently in has been a relatively quiet one in compared with previous ones. But that does not mean that there could not be a large event in the build up to the next "solar maximum." Yes. In 1994, a solar storm caused major malfunctions to two communications satellites, disrupting television and radio services throughout Canada. In March 1989, another event caused the Hydro-Quebec power grid in Canada to go down for over nine hours. The resulting damages and loss in revenue were estimated to be in the region of hundreds of millions of dollars. But the most significant historic event remains the great solar storm of 1-2 September 1859. This disturbance shorted telegraph wires, starting fires in North America and Europe, and caused bright aurorae to be seen in Cuba and Hawaii. In 1859, our technological infrastructure was in its infancy, but a storm with the magnitude of the so-called Carrington Event would be much more damaging today.

Under the same objective, many NE methods calculate high-order proximity by the powers of adjacency matrices, which is not accurate and well-designed enough. Our research focuses on addressing the challenge of Robust Outlier Arm Identification (ROAI). The objective here is to pinpoint those 'arms' that possess anticipated rewards significantly divergent from the norm through dynamic sampling from respective reward distributions. To establish an outlier benchmark, we utilize the median along with the median absolute deviation of the prospective returns. Compared to traditional methods employing means and standard deviations, this method proves more resilient against anomalous data points, enabling us to detect outliers effectively. Unlike conventional exploration issues where thresholds are predetermined either numerically or ranked, our approach excels when seeking potentially advantageous entities without prior knowledge of quantity; for instance, discovering potential medicines for novel illnesses or discerning popular items among specific demographics. In our work, we introduce two -PAC algorithms tailored for ROAI, featuring the inaugural UCB-based technique for spotting outliers, while simultaneously presenting established upper limits regarding sample requirements. Additionally, we demonstrate corresponding, albeit logarithmically varied, worst-case lower boundaries, suggesting these superior constraints cannot be further refined. Empirical findages reveal our algorithms exhibit remarkable durability alongside approximately fivefold greater efficiency in terms of samples than current leading solutions.

We introduce neural networks for end-to-end differentiable proving of queries to knowledge bases by operating on dense vector representations of symbols. These neural networks are constructed recursively by taking inspiration from the backward chaining algorithm as used in Prolog. Specifically, we replace symbolic unification with a differentiable computation on vector representations of symbols using a radial basis function kernel, thereby combining symbolic reasoning with learning subsymbolic vector representations. By using gradient descent, the resulting neural network can be trained to infer facts from a given incomplete knowledge base. It learns to (i) place representations of similar symbols in close proximity in a vector space, (ii) make use of such similarities to prove queries, (iii) induce logical rules, and (iv) use provided and induced logical rules for multi-hop reasoning. We demonstrate that this architecture outperforms ComplEx, a state-of-the-art neural link prediction model, on three out of four benchmark knowledge bases while at the same time inducing interpretable function-free first-order logic rules.

Under the agreement, a national unity government will be installed and a presidential poll will be held by the end of the year. The deal, reached after mediation by EU foreign ministers, also sees electoral reform and constitutional changes. Ukraine's parliament has voted to reduce the president's powers. It also approved laws which could see the release of jailed opposition leader Yulia Tymoshenko. The deal follows hours of talks and months of demonstrations on the streets of Kiev and other cities. Dozens of protesters were killed by security forces on Thursday. The deal has been met with scepticism by some of the thousands of protesters who remain on Independence Square in Kiev, with some saying they still did not trust President Yanukovych. The opposition leaders who signed the deal were booed and called traitors by a crowd in Independence Square, the focal point of the protests, the BBC's Gavin Hewitt reports from Kiev. BBC News The primary aim of any new government - which could be in place with a week or two - will be to restore peace and political stability to a country that has been on the brink of civil war. Alongside the political changes is the challenging task of reforming the police and dismantling the whole apparatus of repression. Corrupt prosecutors and judges will have to be replaced. The agreement was later signed by Mr Yanukovych and opposition leaders Vitali Klitschko, Arseniy Yatsenyuk and Oleh Tyahnibok at the presidential administration headquarters in Kiev. This paper presents a survey of the currently available hardware designs for implementation of the human cortex inspired algorithm, Hierarchical Temporal Memory (HTM). In this review, we focus on the state of the art advances of memristive HTM implementation and related HTM applications. With the advent of edge computing, HTM can be a potential algorithm to implement on-chip near sensor data processing. The comparison of analog memristive circuit implementations with the digital and mixed-signal solutions are provided. The advantages of memristive HTM over digital implementations against performance metrics such as processing speed, reduced on-chip area and power dissipation are discussed. The limitations and open problems concerning the memristive HTM, such as the design scalability, sneak currents, leakage, parasitic effects, lack of the analog learning circuits implementations and unreliability of the memristive devices integrated with CMOS circuits are also discussed.

But for the average backbench MP, the chance to make laws can seem a distant possibility. Their best chance comes around once a year, in the form of a random ballot. The prize? A chance for MPs to promote their pet project in the House of Commons by introducing it as a Private Members' Bill. Private Members' Bills can be introduced in three different ways. The first are "Ten Minute Rule" bills, where MPs make a speech of no more than 10 minutes to outline their position. Second are presentations to the Commons, where an MP might formally introduce the title of their bill. The third and most likely to make it onto the statute book are the "Ballot Bills," so-called because MPs take part in a random draw to decide who gets to propose a bill in the Commons. The system has its critics, among them the SNP MP who sponsored the "Turing Bill" to pardon gay men for obsolete sexual offences. "It is absurd for legislation to be decided by the deputy speaker pulling balls out of a jar. It seems altogether too random," John Nicolson says. If this sounds confusing, it's probably because it is. In a report on Private Members' Bills, the Commons' Procedure Committee called the process "impenetrable" and "enormously damaging to the reputation of the House and to the legislative process." Chairman of the committee, Broxbourne MP Charles Walker, says: "One thing you have to do in this house is accept failure, but you need to have a fair crack at failure, and I don't think most backbenchers now have a fair crack at failure." Even if an MP is lucky enough to propose their Private Members' Bill to the Commons, it is far from guaranteed that it will become law. Opposing MPs can stop these sorts of bills progressing by "filibustering" or "talking them out" during debates held on 13 Fridays throughout the year - a process the Procedure Committee report describes as "speaking at inordinate length on the bill to ensure that the debate cannot conclude" before the set time limit. Mr Nicolson's Private Members' Bill, the Sexual Offences (Pardons) Bill, fell after a government minister used up the time allotted for debating it by speaking for 25 minutes. There were cries of "shame" and "shameful" from some MPs as Justice Minister Sam Gyimah's speech brought the debate to a close. Speaking to the BBC Mr Nicolson said: "I think voters consider filibustering to be wrong. And I agree with them. "Filibustering is archaic, and often used to frustrate the Private Members' Bill process. If a minister doesn't talk out a bill, a hard core of obstructionist MPs often do it, talking nonsensically for lengthy periods until the time allocated for the bill is over." Mr Gyimah defended his opposition to Mr Nicolson's bill, saying "I understand and support the intentions behind Mr Nicolson's bill, however I worry that he has not fully thought through the consequences." Conservative MP Philip Davies, a regular attendee of Friday debates on Private Members' Bills, mounted a passionate defence of talking out. Speaking to a Procedure Committee evidence session Mr Davies said: "I support a bill by not speaking at all, and stop a bad bill from going forward by running out of time. "If the purpose of me contributing to the debate is to try to stop bills that I think are bad, this is the mechanism that I have to use, under the rules," he continued. "If there was another mechanism of blocking them that didn't involve me speaking in the debate, the chances are that I would use that mechanism and therefore nobody would hear another point of view. You would only hear one side." Mr Davies concluded: "When we have a debate, whether people like the outcome or not, at least people get to hear that there is a different opinion on a particular bill." Green Party co-leader Caroline Lucas had a similar experience of a bill being talked out in 2015. Her "NHS Reinstatement" bill ran out of time after MPs spent four-and-a-half hours debating the two-clause Foreign National Offenders (Exclusion from the UK) bill. Ms Lucas told the Procedure Committee the bill was one that "certain MPs have'on the shelf' for the purpose of clogging up Private Members' Bill time on Fridays." The Brighton Pavilion MP told the BBC: "What really turns the public off politics is witnessing the childish way some MPs speak for a huge amount of time in order to'talk out' bills and prevent them from being concluded and voted on." While talking out has many opponents, there are ways of clamping down on the practice that already exist. In its recommendations for changes to the Private Members' Bill process, the Procedure Committee suggested that the Speaker and his deputies overseeing debates on them should make greater use of their existing ability to impose time limits on speeches. Equally, an MP sponsoring a Private Members' Bill can attempt to close a debate before it runs out of time. The problem is that to do so 100 MPs have to be present in the chamber - a requirement the committee's report called a "a formidable hurdle" to overcome on Fridays, when many MPs have already returned to their constituencies. In the end, opponents of talking out may be disappointed, because the Procedure Committee stopped short of calling for a ban. Warning against applying more rules to Commons debates, the committee instead suggested limiting opportunities to indulge in the practice. "The more rules there are, the greater the opportunities to game them," it said.

Observations with Japan's Subaru telescope reveal the likely icy body to be some 15.5 billion km from the Sun - about three times further away than even far-flung Pluto. Scientists had previously thought it was closer, putting its age at around 8 to 10 billion years old and implying that a recent impact might have pushed it into interstellar space Subaru Telescope image of K2-18b (8) created by scientists using data from NASA Hubble Space Telescope, which reveals the red dwarf star, located in Virgo near the constellation Lyra, is visible as an elongated blue spot just below, leftmost part of the object's face. The star is spinning rapidly but appears still because light passes through the Earth very quickly when traveling between our planet and the background stars. The size of this dot represents how fast the spin rate varies over time relative to the sky. Credit: HSTNASA ESA "We are thrilled to announce the discovery of K2-18b," said Alan FitzSimmons, principal investigator for the Subaru Telescope at Waikato University. "This is one of the most exciting discoveries we've made so far." K2-18b probably formed after a giant collision on another galaxy a few hundred million years ago. It then moved onto our own, where its orbit has brought it close enough to our sun to heat up hydrogen gas clouds before they collapse under their own weight. This process makes them shine brightly, like supernovae explosions. Another possibility is that K2-18b formed inside the Milky Way itself; however, astronomers suggest these collisions aren't common among young galaxies, making such a scenario unlikely. The red dwarfs found orbiting nearby objects can easily outshine planets by thousands or even tens of thousandths of magnitudes based upon what we know today. Astronomers don't yet understand why this type of star would gravitationally attract planetary systems toward themselves instead of away from each other. However, if there were any massive metallic ice giants - i.e., rocky exoplanets similar to our moon - inhabiting these cold open clusters, they could get swept outward by the gravitational field of the galactic core and eventually escape altogether. Or perhaps they simply burst apart once they hit the hot gas cloud layers higher up in the cluster. From two separate telescopes deep within the remote Kuiper Belt region, astronomers observed that K2-18b may indeed possess the inherent qualities needed for life. Observations also confirm that the planet's atmosphere seems rich in methane, suggesting water vapor is present along its surface. Astronomer Takashi Kubota of the National Institute of Astrophysics in Tokyo led observations of K2-18b while working alongside astronomer Masaaki Ishiwatari of Kyoto University. They used the Subaru Telescope and Keck Observatory in Hawaii for their research, including potential measurements of atmospheric composition via spectroscopy - the study of chemical elements' colors and atomic masses-on K2-18b. They say that both observations show no signs of carbon monoxide, methane or oxygen, all substances necessary to sustain life. In fact, they speculate that absorption from stellar winds alone could make such conditions too hostile for the existence of living beings.

We develop the theory and practical implementation of p-adic sparse coding of data. Rather than the standard, sparsifying criterion that uses the L 0 pseudo-norm, we use the p-adic norm. We require that the hierarchy or tree be node-ranked, as is standard practice in agglomerative and other hierarchical clustering, but not necessarily with decision trees. In order to structure the data, all computational processing operations are direct reading of the data, or are bounded by a constant number of direct readings of the data, implying linear computational time. Through p-adic sparse data coding, efficient storage results, and for bounded p-adic norm stored data, search and retrieval are constant time operations. Examples show the effectiveness of this new approach to content-driven encoding and displaying of data.

Researchers have used CRISPR gene editing to eliminate a genetic liver disease in mice. This breakthrough means that CRISPR might be usable in human fetuses even before traditional gene editing (which requires replacing the full gene). CRISPR is very targeted, it's like using find and replace to fix a typo rather than retyping the entire document (like in traditional gene editing). In the late 1970s many arterial roads were redesigned as ejes viales; high-volume one-way roads that cross, in theory, Mexico City proper from side to side. The eje vial network is based on a quasi-Cartesian grid, with the ejes themselves being called Eje 1 Poniente, Eje Central, and Eje 1 Oriente, for example, for the north-south roads, and Eje 2 Sur and Eje 3 Norte, for example, for east-west roads. Ring roads are the Circuito Interior (inner ring), Anillo Periferico; the Circuito Exterior Mexiquense State of Mexico outer loop toll road skirting the northeastern and eastern edges of the metropolitan area, the Chamapa-La Venta toll road skirting the northwestern edge, and the Arco Norte completely bypassing the metropolitan area in an arc from northwest (Atlacomulco) to north (Tula, Hidalgo) to east (Puebla). A second level (where tolls are charged) of the Periferico, colloquially called the segundo piso second floor, was officially opened in 2012, with sections still being completed. The Viaducto Miguel Aleman crosses the city east-west from Observatorio to the airport. In 2013 the Supervia Poniente opened, a toll road linking the new Santa Fe business district with southwestern Mexico City.

Placing mitochondrial Eve isn't an exact science- it's really only accurate to a large region, like "Southeast Africa." To trace our lineage back to Eve, geneticists examined placental mtDNA from a few hundred people from various regions. First, they found that each region shared mtDNA- Asians were most similar to Asians, and so on. Then they found that Africans were the most different from all other groups, meaning mtDNA analysis put humanity in to two major "branches," African and Non-African. All the other groups (Asian, European, Pacific Islander, etc.) had their own differences to identify them by, but were similar enough to be contained within the Non-African mtDNA group. Further, this Non-African group had large sections of African mtDNA in their mitochondrial genome. This suggested that the original "trunk" of our mtDNA family tree was in Africa, and lent credibility to the Out of Africa Hypothesis. As a final piece of evidence for an African origin of Eve, we can look at the variability within each population. The oldest mtDNA group should have accumulated the most mutations, meaning their mtDNA would have the highest in-population diversity. As expected, it's Southeast Africa. The tracing stops at mitochondrial Eve because she was the earliest female to produce an unbroken line of daughters into the modern age. She is estimated to have lived around 150,000 years ago. Eve also isn't a fixed individual- there may have been others (of whom the current Eve may have been a descendant of, on her father's side). Once the line of daughters is completely broken, the title shifts to the most recent woman with an unbroken line of daughters. However, since half of the current human population makes up her line of daughters, Eve will retain her title. There are no longer any contenders. On a related note, there may be a "Y-chromosome Adam" who is estimated to have lived 150,000 or 500,000 years ago, depending on who you ask.

Abrupt cessation of alcohol intake among individuals heavily reliant on it could cause severe health consequences, including death. Hence, seeking professional medical assistance during detoxification is highly recommended.

The ordinary half-wave dipole is probably the most widely used antenna design. This consists of two 14-wavelength elements arranged end-to-end, and lying along essentially the same axis (or collinear), each feeding one side of a two-conductor transmission wire. The physical arrangement of the two elements places them 180 degrees out of phase, which means that at any given instant one of the elements is driving current into the transmission line while the other is pulling it out. The monopole antenna is essentially one half of the half-wave dipole, a single 14-wavelength element with the other side connected to ground or an equivalent ground plane (or counterpoise). Monopoles, which are one-half the size of a dipole, are common for long-wavelength radio signals where a dipole would be impractically large. Another common design is the folded dipole, which is essentially two dipoles placed side-by-side and connected at their ends to make a single one-wavelength antenna.

A total dominating set T(G) within a graph G = (V, E) comprises a selection of vertices from V where each vertex in V has at least one neighboring vertex in T. The challenge of locating a minimal total dominating set is recognized as NP-hard for planar graphs and W[2]-complete for arbitrary graphs when considering the parameter related to the solution's size. According to the theorem proposed by Bodlaender et al. [FOCS 2009], graphs with limited genus possess a linear kernel for the Total Dominating Set problem. However, the methodology for efficiently assembling this kernel remains ambiguous, along with devising concrete reduction guidelines featuring reasonable constant values. Building upon the strategy introduced by Alber et al. [J. ACM 2004], we present an explicit linear kernel tailored specifically for planar graphs concerning the Total Dominating Set issue. Our discovery augments existing linear kernels applied to various domination challenges—such as Dominating Set, Edge Dominating Set, Efficient Dominating Set, or Connected Dominating Set—on planar graphs. Key terms include parameterized complexity, planar graphs, linear kernels, and total domination.

The result is that there are hundredsof library functions available for most graph algorithm problems. It can be difficult to findand understand which graph algorithms do well on the various platforms forwhich they were designed."Until now," says Andrew Patterson from Oregon State University, "there have been notools or techniques developed to help TIP implement high performancegraph algorithms efficiently across multiple instances of TIP. In thiswork we introduce two high level primitives we call 'clips' and 'cores'. Clippedsense graphs are short trees built using only simple primitives likeBuckets, Rings, Connections and Sequences, while cores represent largeintersections of sequential components. These features make them ideal forembedding standard graph algorithms inside TIP's semantic model andinstantiating graphics processing engines capable of simulating fastcomputations over complex graph graphs.By introducing clips what really matters is how you define the graphproblem. That meansyou don't always want to build your complete representation initially; justadd nodes until you hit the right match." said School of ComputerScience Assistant Professors Christopher Peabody and Jonathan Wyatt. "Essentially all of the results suggest that any efforts made inthe future toward faster graphics processors based upon the latestGPU silicon may not necessarily translate directly to faster TARGETprocessors" says Zachary Kallio, who worked closely with Pattersonon creating the benchmarks and testing predictions performed here.The researchers believe these findings open the door to optimizingmany commonly used graph algorithms including SVD, Mcbain,SVD adjacency construction, reordering along paths, edge insertion,filtering, clustering, and polynomial regression. We analyse the way in which the principle that 'the whole is greater than the sum of its parts' manifests itself with phenomena of visual perception. For this investigation we use a modified version of the famous Gestalt test of 'Wertheimer's 'Phenomenon'. We analyse the way in which perception and cognition are influenced by the specific visual environment. We compare the results obtained in an ordinary situation of normal vision with those obtained in different visual environments characterised by spatially homogeneous but coloured visual backgrounds. We find that the results are very different and depend on the type of visual background. We also observe the fact that the 'Phenomenon' is dependent on the position of the stimulus (test patch) in the visual field. The results have implications for perception in environments such as driving a car, or flying an aeroplane.

A (k, d)-hopset refers to an edge subset in a graph, which enables traveling between two nodes within k hops while keeping the distance within d. There could be a few reasons why your phone battery continues to drain even when it's turned off: 1. Background processes: Some processes on your phone may still be running in the background even when your phone is switched off. This can cause battery drain. 2. Connected devices: If your phone is connected to other devices such as Bluetooth earphones, smartwatches, or other accessories, it can drain the battery even when the phone is turned off. 3. Battery health: If your phone battery has degraded, it may drain faster than usual even when the phone is turned off. To troubleshoot the issue, try turning off any connected devices and check your battery health. If the problem persists, you may need to reset your phone or take it to a repair center for further evaluation.

Literature reviews enable scholars to build upon previous work by highlighting potential areas of study, consolidating advancements, and pinpointing current issues within their field. However, performing an exhaustive literature review can be both time-consuming and costly. Recent investigations into utilizing crowd-based approaches for literature reviews are scarce. The purpose of this article is to investigate whether crowdsourcing could aid the literature review process efficiently regarding outcomes, time allocation, and resource expenditure while also determining optimal crowdsourcing techniques given specific budgets. Our primary emphasis lies in evaluating the initial stage of the literature review procedure; hence, we analyze various methodologies aimed at defining test sizes, label requirements per document, classifier functionality, and phased implementation of crowdsourcing activities to enhance effectiveness. We conclude with insights drawn from empirical trials conducted using Crowdflower's platform.

Currently, self-driving cars rely greatly on the Global Positioning System (GPS) infrastructure, albeit there is an increasing demand for alternative methods for GPS-denied environments. One of them is known as Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM). Through the SLAM method, which is a combination of mapping and tracking, the car can determine where it is, where it is going and how it can get there without the need for GPS. A team of researchers from the University of Michigan are now developing a new SLAM method called Relative Pose Graph SLAM (RPG-SLAM) that can help self-driving cars and robots in real-time without requiring GPS. The system uses a monocular camera to identify and track 3D objects in the environment. In a paper published in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters, the researchers from the University of Michigan, led by Matthew Johnson-Roberson, Associate Professor in the University of Michigan's Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science and the team's leader, detailed the new SLAM method. During the team's tests, they noted that the new SLAM method was able to map, explore, and navigate in 3D environments in real-time. Aside from that, the researchers also noted that the method performed better than previous approaches. The researchers noted that most of the existing SLAM methods in the past do not work well in large-scale environments. In addition, the existing methods also failed to address the problems that arise in 3D environments with textures and surfaces that do not vary much. The team's new RPG-SLAM method works by processing the data from the camera in real time and then estimates the location of the vehicle relative to the objects in the environment, such as parked cars, trees, and buildings. The team noted that the RPG-SLAM method can function in GPS-denied environments such as in underground parking lots, tunnels, and urban canyons. The new SLAM method is also capable of performing in environments with many 3D objects that do not vary much, such as buildings that are next to each other, rows of houses, and trees. According to the researchers, the key to the system's success is the way they treated the mapping and tracking problems as one, instead of solving them separately. In addition, the team's new method also continuously estimates the vehicle's location, its orientation, and the position of the landmarks that the camera sees. The researchers noted that their new SLAM method is better than existing methods because it is more efficient and it is better at tracking the car's location in relation to its environment. They also noted that their new method is capable of handling large-scale environments and it is also better at handling large parking lots, which is something that most of the existing methods struggle with. In addition, the researchers noted that their new method is also more accurate at mapping and tracking than the existing methods. The team is now planning to make their new SLAM method even more accurate and more efficient. The researchers are also planning to test their new method in different environments.

Attacks involving the exposure of source code can endanger embedded systems by enabling adversaries to pilfer proprietary information or exploit it in control-flow manipulation assaults. The implementation of execute-only memory (XOM) offers defense against such threats; however, conventional XOM strategies necessitate a memory management unit unavailable on ARM-based embedded systems or introduce considerable efficiency penalties. Our introduction of PicoXOM addresses this issue, providing an efficient and innovative approach to XOM tailored for ARMv7-M and ARMvEE8-M architectures, utilizing the ARM Data Watchpoint and Tracing module alongside basic memory security features inherent in the processor. In testing across two benchmark suites and five practical software instances, PicoXOM demonstrated an average processing delay increase of just 0.33% and a code expansion of 5.89%.

A common thing I see on many news stories, etc. is how expensive people on social assistance are to society and how we need to start taking more actions to support them. At the same time that you're hearing those things, there's also a lot of other information out there about how difficult it can be for clients to get benefits in some provinces (here's one example). I think this happens because too often, people - especially politicians - don't understand what goes into getting someone access to these supports, as well as just how complex our system already is. Our systems were built up over decades with no thought given to their complexity or potential impact on vulnerable populations like seniors and children. It puts us at odds when programs are being cut because they aren't working but not enough attention is paid to why they might not work. In short: Our agencies have done really great work building our programs from scratch! And now we want to try something new? We've got a whole bunch of new kids coming through the door each day who need a little help finding their place in life. How do we make sure that all these little individual pieces come together? (As an aside, if anyone knows any good books articles about learning about computer programming, please let me know!) Anyway, here are my thoughts ... 1. There's nothing easy about figuring out what kind of program works best for someone. No two situations are exactly alike so trying to fit everyone into a cookie cutter model is bound to fail anyway. 2. For every person whose situation is unique, there could potentially be 10 others in similar circumstances who may benefit from another type of program. People automatically assume there only needs to be one solution "right" way to approach the problem. 3. Each person will require different levels of support depending upon how long they'll need it and where they live within the province. This means that funding should follow individuals rather than agencies. 4. Funding should go toward meeting actual need rather than paying for things like administration overhead which would ultimately be the responsibility of whoever receives the money anyway. 5. Right now, government pays out less per capita on social assistance than most Western European countries. 6. The majority of social assistance recipients work part time jobs during the week and school full time at night while raising families. They still struggle to afford groceries, clothes, gas and shelter. 7. Poverty shouldn't be used as a political tool. If Minister Grellet wants to see poverty decrease, then she needs to look honestly at her own department. She seems hell bent on making cuts instead of saying "this isn't working." 8. Even if the provincial government said that the current level of social assistance was satisfactory, there'd always be room for improvement. Any measurement against the standard set by other developed nations must include a comparison to the minimum wage rate. 9. Social Assistance payments should increase along with inflation. 10. Our tax dollars belong to us, not to Billionaires who figure out ways to pay themselves millions without lifting a finger. 11. Your choice is between doing everything yourself or relying on someone else to take care of your basic human necessities. 12. Forgetting about politics, I'm pretty tired right now and it looks like I won't get much sleep tonight. When do I say "enough"? That's all I wanted to share today. Ok, seriously, maybe 13 is actually the point.

Our method compares favorably to SpecAugment on English-French and English-Romanian automatic speech translation (AST) tasks as well as on a low-resource English automatic speech recognition (ASR) task. Further, in ablations, we show the benefits of both quantity and diversity in augmented data. Finally, we show that we can combine our approach with augmentation by machine-translated transcripts to obtain a competitive end-to-end AST model that outperforms a very strong cascade model on an English-French AST task. The Decentralised Web (DW) has recently seen a renewed momentum, with a number of DW platforms like Mastodon, PeerTube, and Hubzilla gaining increasing traction. These offer alternatives to traditional social networks like Twitter, YouTube, and Facebook, by enabling the operation of web infrastructure and services without centralised ownership or control. Although their services differ greatly, modern DW platforms mostly rely on two key innovations: first, their open source software allows anybody to setup independent servers instances that people can sign-up to and use within a local community; and second, they build on top of federation protocols so that instances can mesh together, in a peer-to-peer fashion, to offer a globally integrated platform. In this paper, we present a measurement-driven exploration of these two innovations, using a popular DW microblogging platform (Mastodon) as a case study. We focus on identifying key challenges that might disrupt continuing efforts to decentralise the web, and empirically highlight a number of properties that are creating natural pressures towards re-centralisation. Finally, our measurements shed light on the behaviour of both administrators (i.e., people setting up instances) and regular users who sign-up to the platforms, also discussing a few techniques that may address some of the issues observed.

The outlying villages have been evacuated and the populace is being directed into the massive shelters dug into the mountain. The titanium ore that lured immigrants here left massive tunnels and caverns empty. Though it was a heavy tax, the installation of fresh air ducts and lighting along with water pipes is a godsend to the people, as are the massive blast doors installed. He arrives at the hanger and past the salutes of the MP's. Going into the ready room, he removes his uniform and dons his equipment. Ragged cargo shorts and an ancient t-shirt make up his combat clothes. A cooling vest and a neuro-helmet he also pulls out of his locker. Shrugging on the heavy vest, he makes his way into the main hanger. Sparks fly as mechanics and technicians make last minute repairs. The whine of power tools and smell of spilt oil and coolant fill the air. Forgoing a lift, he climbs up the flank of his mech manually and drops down into his seat. Plugging in his cooling vest and his helmet, diagnostics and other readings scroll forth from his screens. He checks the displays and adjusts the mech until the statuses are green. He rotates the torso to the right and left, nodding satisfied at the smooth motion. He aims his left arm, the mounted Rotary Autocannon follows his gaze. He rolls his right arm. The mounted mace does as well. He gives a thumbs up signal to the waiting mechanic, who then raises twin glow rods. Guiding the mech, he leads it out of the hanger and into the rising dawn. The battle has begun. Six hours later. The tide has turned against them. The initial landings of the foe were one of disorganization and Friedrich's brother took advantage of the chaos, tearing into the dismounting forces. A running battle took place over the rich fields of corn and sugar beets. Numerous mechs and tanks fell or were otherwise forced to retire. The charred and burnt out remains dotted the plains for miles. Lieutenant Von Amling threw his lance into the fray, accounting for several mechs and many more vehicles. One of his own mechs was destroyed and another one crippled. There is a lull in the fighting, as both sides seek to catch their breaths and to rearm and regroup. His brother was taken to a hospital. Spalling from missile strikes struck him. It was a miracle he didn't bleed out in his cockpit. Now the enemy forces are gathering, preparing to mount the final attack to seize the city. The leader of the enemy can be seen in his mech, instilling the attackers with words of encouragement. His father is considering terms of surrender. The young noble will hear none of that. Ignoring protests he climbs back into his mech and walks it out of the underground hanger and into the later afternoon sun. "This is Baron Friedrich Von Amling, Lieutenant of the Duke's Own Camden Hussars. Who leads this force?" A moment passes before the open channel crackles. "This is Knight-Colonel Alan Samuel of Count de Bernham's host. I lead this action." "Sir Alan. It is my intention to challenge you to single combat if you so choose to accept it." There is another pause. "Very well Lord Friedrich. I accept. Do you wish to begin now or at later time of your choosing." "Now if it would not inconvenience you sir." "Very well let us begin." They start a kilometer away from each other. Their two mechs walking slowly towards the other. Lieutenant Von Amling's mech has the greater range. Placing his target reticule over his opponent's mech, his thumb presses the firing switch, his rotary autocannon spits rounds downrange. Though plenty miss, enough find the foe and slam into armor, chipping away at plates. Another burst rips forth, more depleted uranium rounds contact with the enemy. Then the foe fires. Lasers scores across the young noble's armor, drawing angry red lines across the left torso. More firepower crosses the closing distance. Great swaths of armor of torn off from both opponents. The rotary cannon spins empty. His ranged weapon useless, he raises the massive four ton mace and charges in. The knight also has a melee weapon on his machine, a long and wicked two ton lance. He pours on speed. The pair hurl themselves down the field, neither wavering, both intent on destroying the other. The lance of the foe finds purchase first, tearing into the Lieutenant's left arm, shearing it clean off. The amputated limb drops to the ground. Von Amling replies with a smashing blow that crumples the enemy's missile launcher. Secondary explosions from the ammo rip into the hull of the mech. Another mace swing collapses the foe's left knee. In return, the lance stabs deep into the torso of Amling's mech. Another mace swing connects with the foe's head, stunning the pilot. Lieutenant Von Amling takes this opportunity to unleash a torrent of blows. Hammering down on the helpless mech with a half dozen strikes. Armor is almost non existent on the enemy's mech. Eventual the foe breaks away from the melee and lowers his battered machine to the ground, powering it down in surrender. "Baron Friedrich. I yield. The field is yours. Cease your attack." The young noble wipes the perspiration from his brow. He is drenched in sweat. "Very well, I accept your surrender. With respect to your bravery and skill at arms. I permit you and your men to depart this world peacefully. Any machines that can not move under their own power are to be left here, as spoils. Do you agree?" "I agree to these terms. Thank you. We will leave by nightfall. I congratulate you on your victory. It was well won." "Thank you. Depart in peace. I hope we will not see each other again soon. Lieutenant Von Amling out." The noble steers his battered machine back towards the city, to the waiting arms of its cheering people. Their young warrior has protected them for another day. Such is the price for his position in life. With his rank and status, he must shield the people from harm, with his own body is required. There is a reason for the statement, noblesse oblige. Nobility obliges. It is his duty.

Israel's legal system combines three legal traditions: English common law, civil law, and Jewish law. It is based on the principle of stare decisis (precedent) and is an adversarial system, where the parties in the suit bring evidence before the court. Court cases are decided by professional judges rather than juries. Marriage and divorce are under the jurisdiction of the religious courts: Jewish, Muslim, Druze, and Christian. A committee of Knesset members, Supreme Court justices, and Israeli Bar members carries out the election of judges. Administration of Israel's courts (both the "General" courts and the Labor Courts) is carried by the Administration of Courts, situated in Jerusalem. Both General and Labor courts are paperless courts: the storage of court files, as well as court decisions, are conducted electronically. Israel's Basic Law: Human Dignity and Liberty seeks to defend human rights and liberties in Israel.

While anecdotal evidence can be convincing and relatable, it's important to acknowledge its limitations. Anecdotes are personal stories, based on a single individual's experience. They aren't necessarily representative of the larger population or provide enough statistical data to make a factual conclusion. But the move has led some residents to question why the pallets have been stored in an area used by children who play nearby. A concerned father from Belvoir on the Upper Newtownards Road said he feared his child could be injured if they tripped on a pallet. He told Belfast Live: "It's a public place, where people bring their kids to play. "It's right next to the football pitches and there are hundreds of pallets all over the place. "There's no barrier around them, so if a kid fell onto one they could hurt themselves. "I've asked why they were brought here and what they are doing here. "They said it's because they need to store them somewhere. But I don't see why they would store them in a public place like this. "Why can't they just store them in the yard at the back of the town hall? "They told me that the council's depot is full, but I don't understand why they have to bring them here. "You don't see this kind of thing happening anywhere else." Another resident, who did not wish to be named, said that having the pallets being stored in such a high-profile spot could encourage illegal dumping in the area. "We're trying to tidy up the area, but this doesn't look very good," she said. "The pallets are stacked up high and they are just lying there. They will probably stay there until next summer. "People use this place all the time, especially at weekends and during holidays. "I've been asking why they are here, but I haven't had any response." A spokeswoman for Ards and North Down Borough Council said the pallets needed to be stored in an accessible location in case they were needed late at night or early in the morning. "The Council has been storing salt pallets at this site to maximise their availability should they be required out of normal working hours," she said. "It is a conveniently located site with good access and a gate for security purposes. "The pallets are stacked in line with health and safety regulations and the site is regularly inspected for any signs of deterioration. "The Council appreciates the concerns raised and will monitor the situation to ensure the site remains secure." The council said the pallets would be removed once the risk of ice and snow had passed. "The pallets will be removed once the Winter Maintenance Programme has ended and the Local Resilience Forum has advised that the risk of ice and snow has passed," the spokesperson added. There are 56 cases involving 97 deaths. They include killings by police officers and soldiers, and others where there are allegations of state collusion. As the review got under way in Belfast, the time taken by police to security-vet and disclose classified case files was repeatedly highlighted as an obstacle in the way of progress. Twenty-two of the cases are more than 40 years old. Lord Justice Weir, the presiding judge of the Coroners' Service, is spending the next two weeks conducting preliminary hearings to assess the state of readiness of each case. Families of those who were killed and their legal teams have been asked to inform the court of the issues which are outstanding in each of the cases. The stalled inquests into the Army shootings of 10 people in Ballymurphy, west Belfast, in 1971, and of five more civilians in nearby Springhill a year later, were examined on the opening day in Laganside Courts. The cases focusing on nine deaths linked to the Royal Ulster Constabulary's (RUC) alleged "shoot to kill" policy in the 1980s were also assessed. A barrister for families of two INLA members shot dead by the RUC in 1982 - Seamus Grew and Roddy Carroll - criticised police after they said disclosure could not be completed ahead of a proposed September 2017 inquest date. A Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) representative told the court at least another year would be required. The barrister for the Grew and Carroll families accused the police of failing to honour a series of similar disclosure commitments since the cases were re-opened in 2007. "Obviously there is the suspicion within the families that the PSNI have been dragging their heels over disclosure in order to protect the RUC," he said. "They are fighting a rearguard action on behalf of the RUC, which they have done successfully to date." Ahead of the review, a senior police officer said the disclosure delays were due to the huge pressures being placed upon the PSNI's Legacy Support Unit (LSU). Dep Ch Const Drew Harris said attempting to run the 56 inquests at the same time, rather than sequencing them in order, resulted in the LSU continually jumping from one case to the other. When the review is completed, a coroner will be appointed to hear inquests identified as ready to proceed. In the others, relevant parties will be instructed to provide any outstanding material needed for an inquest to take place. Some of the hearings are expected to take place later this year. The most complex and controversial ones are likely to be heard by a High Court judge, while others will be heard by a County Court judge. Justice Minister David Ford last year authorised the Northern Ireland Courts and Tribunals Service to recruit "investigative support" for coroners dealing with the legacy inquests. The review was announced by Lord Chief Justice Sir Declan Morgan in October, a month before he was appointed president of the Coroners' Courts. Sir Declan said he wanted to assure the families of those who were killed that he was "fully committed to doing all that I can, within my sphere of influence and with the resources at my disposal, to ensure that justice is delivered." But he also warned that it could be "many years" before most of the cases could be dealt with. Only nine legacy cases have been disposed of during the past five years, and 13 cases in total in the past 10 years. In November 2014, Sir Declan warned that inquests into deaths involving alleged state collusion and cover-up could go on until 2040 unless the coronial inquests system was changed.
