Mountainous heaps of colored metal that rested on round rubber circles scattered the landscape. The day was hot, the wind was..... windy. I can do this, Tim thought. Tim had been in a lot more bad situations than he could remember and did not like them any better now then when they first happened; but it didn't mean you couldn't enjoy a few minutes of happiness every once in awhile. Tim climbed out from under his hammock feeling euphoric for a brief moment before remembering where he was. He stood up and stretched carefully over to one of the circular mounds of metal. It looked as though someone took a hammer and smashed it into pieces all at once. A bunch were piled in a heap about half way down the hill while others lay spread out across what remained of an old road just below another mound. This time there wasn't too much rust or debris among the shiny black metal. There seemed to be some of the same metallic substance coming off each pile along with small shards of glass. These piles probably contained what little scrap material that had survived the blast. They reminded him of electrical wires blown loose by the power line explosion earlier. That must have very nearly killed everyone who lived here in the area - maybe even himself! After thinking long enough about how lucky he really felt right then, he turned around again and walked back toward the old house. Unfortunately, he heard a noise behind him so quickly, he almost tripped on something else instead. Turning around to see who might have disturbed him gave him a good scare but luckily it only made things worse because he saw red eyes staring back. Not friendly looking ones either...they just kept moving closer until finally Tim almost fell flat onto his face against the ground. Tim's mind swirled with fear as he tried desperately to think of what to say next without being caught completely unaware yet again. "I-it is miiiiiine!" he began, but was interrupted as his ears rang with high pitched squealings. Dizzy, confused, scared shitless, and afraid that if he stumbled away from whoever these creatures were, they would track him down instantly, Tim tumbled backwards off the edge trying desperately to keep upright. As soon as one landed upon his head, he rolled over from side to side. When the other two jumped down on top of him their heads came within inches of his face which sent shivers shooting through his body. Quickly getting up from atop him, Tim got ready to run. Just as he started running however, he spotted something different in the distance: a large red car speeding towards him full speed! With no other option left open that wasn't death or certain destruction, Tim flew straight ahead hopping up and landing on his feet right underneath its hood. Even from such close quarters, he managed to get a clear look inside driving along in the middle lane cutting between several vehicles already heading north going far faster then he ever imagined possible. To make matters worst, the sound grew louder and louder as it approached making it impossible to hear anything else except the roar of engines. At least there weren't many cars passing through that section of town since work had stopped early for most citizens due to the storm, but still, nothing would stop those monsters from finding him somewhere nearby. Looking towards the rear view mirror, Tim noticed a yellow van pull up beside him and his heart skipped a beat when he realized he was approaching the front doors of the building. Out of nowhere, four figures emerged from the entrance wielding swords drawn wide on their respective sides like a group of poorly trained warriors waiting for battle. After scanning the surrounding area for enemies (which consisted mostly of trees) they advanced on him cautiously keeping their weapons leveled at normal eye level aiming directly at his chest cavity. Once again sensing danger swirling beneath his feet, Tim leaped forward frantically rolling out of harm's way maneuvering his hands as fast as they possibly could beneath cover hoping not to get cut by whatever was likely lurking inside. Fortunately his gamble paid off as none of them saw him. "They're gone," Tim said softly smiling confidently holding up both palms meeting the air.

To achieve this, one must first establish a method to measure it accurately, which involves comprehending the neural mechanisms underlying human conduct. Fascinating research involving animal and human subjects suggests connections between certain neurotransmitters and particular personality traits. For instance, numerous studies indicate a relationship between elevated levels of dopamine and novelty-seeking tendencies, providing scientists with potential starting points such as examining dopamine-related genes among the vast array of approximately 50,000 genes within the human genome. However, since most personality characteristics appear to stem from multiple genes, establishing concrete correlations proves difficult, given the complexity of human behavior.

We examine the origins of this phenomenon. Our hypothesis suggests that shortly after the Big Bang, certain characteristics would emerge, indicating their presence and location. If observations align with these predictions, we infer that the observed light originates from that era. However, determining the precise age of a single photon without additional context would be impossible. Instead, we assess the distance between the source and us, along with the speed of light, to calculate the light's age. This approach pertains specifically to the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) Radiation, the most ancient observable light. In the early universe, prior to star and planet formation, conditions were dense and scorching, producing a homogeneous luminosity through a white-hot haze of hydrogen plasma. As the cosmos expanded, the temperature dropped, allowing the fusion of protons and electrons into neutral hydrogen atoms around 380,000 years post-Big Bang. Consequently, the once opaque environment transitioned into transparency, enabling visibility of distant objects. Thus, the CMB represents the residual heat signature of the Big Bang itself, now primarily detectable as microwaves due to ongoing cosmic expansion. Although it may seem relatively faint today, it continues to diminish gradually in strength.

In this paper, we consider adaptive decision-making problems for stochastic state estimation with partial observations. First, we introduce the concept of weak adaptive submodularity , a generalization of adaptive submodularity, which has found great success in solving challenging adaptive state estimation problems. Then, for the problem of active diagnosis, i.e., discrete state estimation via active sensing, we show that an adaptive greedy policy has a near-optimal performance guarantee when the reward function possesses this property. We further show that the reward function for group-based active diagnosis, which arises in applications such as medical diagnosis and state estimation with persistent sensor faults, is also weakly adaptive submodular. Finally, in experiments of state estimation for an aircraft electrical system with persistent sensor faults, we observe that an adaptive greedy policy performs equally well as an exhaustive search.

Sources say there has been a rise in avalanches, landslide-dammed rivers bursting, glaciers cracking and glacial lakes dangerously filling up. Studies by Chinese scientists have shown glaciers and permafrost rapidly melting in Tibet. Earthquakes also continue to destabilise them. A recent study has shown Tibet topping the list of places across the globe that has experienced an increase in water. Mining and dam construction in the Tibetan plateau have further fuelled concerns in downstream countries. In the absence of early warnings from Tibet, water-related disasters can cause human and property losses downstream in Bhutan, Nepal, India and potentially Bangladesh. One recent event took place in July when buildings in Nepalese towns bordering Tibet were swept away by a sudden flood. Authorities in Nepal say it was the result of landslides in Tibet that dammed the Bhotekoshi river. This is one of several rivers that run through Nepal which originate in Tibet. Most houses in Liping, the main town bordering Tibet, have either been swept away by floodwaters or brought down because of soil erosion caused by the floods. In Barabise and other smaller settlements, the BBC saw several houses precariously perched on the edge and all set to collapse because of the flooding. This was one of the most affected areas during last year's earthquake. "That is where my house used to stand and now all you see is a cliff overlooking the river," said Nimji Sherpa, a shopkeeper. "That night I received a call from my relative upstream that a flood was hurtling towards us. I dragged my old husband to higher land." "The next morning we came back to see that our house and all that we had was gone. Last year the earthquake destroyed my house and we had come here to start afresh and now floods have taken everything," she said, with tears in her eyes. Further up, a stretch of the Arniko highway, that links Nepal to Tibet, is gone which has disrupted traffic. "The authorities have told us to move 100 metres higher at night to sleep because we don't know what is coming our way," said Nimji Sherpa. "How long can we live like this?" Officials in Sindhupalchok district said they were able to evacuate people during the July flash flood. "We were lucky that we could save people because of our own early warning system but timely information from the Tibet side could have helped us save properties as well," said Gokarna Dawadi, chief government official in the district, who recently left this role. "We have approached the Chinese side a number of times to discuss this issue as we fear future disasters but it has not moved anywhere." In the past 80 years, scientists have recorded 10 occasions when glacial lakes burst out in Tibet and the flood waters reached Nepal. Officials in the Nepali capital Kathmandu said the Bhotekoshi disaster was an eye-opener. "So far we have no communication between China and Nepal regarding the early flood warning system," said Rishi Raj Sharma, director general of Nepal's department of hydrology and meteorology. "There has been some initial dialogue with the Chinese meteorology department but we need to raise this more seriously through our foreign ministry." Residents of the Nepali towns bordering Tibet are having sleepless nights but settlements far away from the Tibetan territory are also at risk. The Bhotekoshi river is a tributary of the Kosi which flows down from Nepal into India to meet the Ganges. Locals in Sunsari district in south-eastern Nepal, where the Kosi is at its widest and most powerful, said they have heard about floods from Tibet and were concerned. The Kosi, known as the sorrow of Bihar flooded in 2008, displacing tens of thousands of people in Nepal and India. A local water expert Dev Narayan Yadav said fears of future floods were not unfounded. "Our people here know how the bursting of glacial lakes in Tibet have flooded rivers in western Nepal and also in the Brahmaputra basin of India," Mr Yadav explained. "And because the Kosi disaster of 2008 is quite fresh in their memory, they are really wary of what might be happening upstream." The Kosi barrage was built by India to control flood water and is operated by Indian authorities. It was built in 1962 and there are concerns it is no longer fit for purpose. The Indian government is planning to build a major dam upstream in Nepal. "Big structures like these make us more scared because they will multiply the disaster and we will suffer," said Mr Yadav The Central Water Commission of India is tasked with planning and building the new dam. Officials say they have concerns about flooding from Tibet too but they're focused on the dams China is building on Tibetan rivers. "If waters from them are released in a larger quantity, they may become floods and if we have no storage in the Indian portion, that may create havoc," the commission's chairman Ghanashyam Jha told the BBC. "We have an arrangement for sharing flood information but all the desired information is not available." The water resource department of the Indian state of Arunachal Pradesh that shares a border with Tibet has stressed the proper networking of co-basins for flood warnings. "The flash flood of Pasighat during 11 May 2000 is an example in which the loss of lives and properties could have been minimised had there been proper networking and sharing of information to the downstream county," it says on its website. The Chinese authorities in Beijing did not respond to our questions. Officials in Tibet, however, said flood information was being shared with India and Bangladesh. They said they would only do the same with Nepal if they received instructions from the Chinese ministry of water resources. The United Nations wants all parties to work together. "I think there should be cross-boundary cooperation between countries in the region and unless it happens we cannot control floods," says Vijay Singh, a senior official the United Nations Development Programme Nepal office, who has worked on flood management in the country for years. "We are creating a platform so that governments of Nepal and China can come together and realise the importance of information exchange between the two but it will take some time."

Climber here, first off there are a few different answers depending on the style of climbing: Sport climbing: this form has permanent bolts that are drilled into the rock. These are usually placed by ahead of time by a climber who rappels down from above and hangs on a rope in order to drill and place bolts. The idea here is to create a permanent, enjoyable route for the future, so they also clean off loose rock as they go. All the climber has to do is clip into the bolts with a "quickdraw" which is just a set of carabiners and a bit of rope (actually webbing, but keeping this ELI5). This kind of climbing is relatively new, developed in the 80s. This is usually only one rope length long, and the goal is more to enjoy the climbing than to get to the "summit," in fact most sport routes don't even go all the way to the summit of a cliff. Traditional climbing, often called "trad" climbing: this is more what you're probably thinking of, where the climber carries gear with them that they place into cracks and pockets in the rock. This predates sport climbing and goes back more than a century. This gear is removable, and the goal of trad climbing is often more about reaching the summit. Trad climbing is usually harder because you have to find places for the gear, which isn't always easy. The second person who climbs up removes the gear as they climb, since they have the rope above them rather than below (see lead climbing, explained below). The two most common forms of trad gear are cams and nuts, but back in the day pitons (spikes hammered into cracks) were also used. Nuts are just wedges that go into a constriction in a crack. Cams are more complicated, but work in completely parallel cracks and deserve probably their own post. There can also be bolts in a few places on trad climbs where there's not place for trad gear. In either form, the leader is the first person up, who clips the rope into either the bolts or places trad gear and then clips into that. The belayer is the person who stays below and feeds out slack in the rope, but can catch climber if they fall by stopping the rope. Think of a pulley system, but one side moves a few feet above the pulley. If that end falls, it falls until it's equal distance below the pulley, and if the other side of the rope can't move (because the belayer stops it), the falling end stops. So if you're four feet above a bolt or nut, you'll fall eight feet (you'll actually fall a bit further because the rope stretches and the belayer will usually have a bit of slack in the system). There's also top-roping, where you don't use any gear on the actual climb, but instead walk to the top of a cliff and set up an anchor (either bolts, trees, boulders, or trad gear), and then the climber never goes above the "pulley" in the section I just described for leading. This is how beginners start, since leading is more dangerous and technical.

Seasonal enterprises may prefer concluding their fiscal year after peak revenue periods, while others might select slower times like summer months for academic institutions. This strategic timing allows accountants ample opportunity to review financial records without disrupting regular operations. Moreover, ending the fiscal year during a profitable phase presents a positive image to potential investors. For instance, choosing late summer can offer cost savings due to lower demand for accountancy services amidst holiday distractions and reduced competition. Taking the example of a toy manufacturing company, since sales typically surge in the weeks leading up to Christmas, conducting inventory checks and other administrative tasks during this busy period could overwhelm employees. Thus, adopting a separate fiscal year becomes necessary to ensure efficient management of workloads towards the year's conclusion.

Many computer vision and medical imaging problems are faced with learning from large-scale datasets, with millions of observations and features. In this paper we propose a novel efficient learning scheme that can handle such large datasets. Our approach is based on the use of deep learning techniques, specifically a deep neural network architecture called a convolutional neural network (CNN), and a training strategy called stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with mini-batch updates. The CNN framework is particularly suited to handling high-dimensional data, such as images, and has demonstrated state-of-the-art performance in many computer vision tasks. The key idea behind CNNs is to leverage the local and spatial correlation of image pixels by using convolutional filters that extract meaningful features across the image. SGD is an optimization algorithm commonly used for training deep neural networks. It works by iteratively adjusting the weights of the network in the direction of the negative gradient of a loss function, with the aim of minimizing the loss. As the name suggests, SGD updates the weights in a stochastic manner by sampling a subset of the data (called a mini-batch) for each iteration, which reduces the computational cost and enables efficient processing of large-scale datasets. Our proposed learning scheme combines the power of CNNs and SGD with mini-batch updates to efficiently learn from large-scale datasets in a scalable and effective manner. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by evaluating it on two challenging datasets: the ImageNet dataset for object recognition, and the LIDC-IDRI dataset for lung nodule detection in CT images. Our results show that our proposed approach achieves state-of-the-art performance while maintaining computational efficiency. Overall, our proposed efficient learning scheme can be a valuable tool for researchers and practitioners working on large-scale computer vision and medical imaging problems.

She looked at me with doe eyes hidden behind thick half moons perched on her broad nose. A smile erupted from her lips as she said my name. I hadn't found her, she had found me. I fell for her instantly. For two years we did puzzles together, went on adventures, played board games, and wrote post cards. She seemed to love post cards almost as much as I did. Two years goes by quickly when you're having fun. It all seemed like one magnificent blur. One morning when I woke up she was gone. I hunted high and low for any sign of her. Just as I had given up hope, a drumming knock came from the door. " Hello! " I said, opening the door without waiting for a reply. " Oh, I-um- " " Hi! You must be Wally! " she exclaimed familiarly. " I'm sorry, do I know you? " I asked. " Oh, that's right! Silly me, " she said, playfully hitting herself atop the head. " I'm Wenda, Wilma's sister! We're twins! Can you believe it? " I was speechless. She seemed like my Wilma, but they were not the same. There were so many little things about her from the way she spoke to the way that she smelled that set off alarms in my head. My perturbation must have shown on my face as she slouched and backed away a little. I tried to hide it as I welcomed her into my home. She had found me, it was the least I could do. Finding me wasn't an easy feat. We talked and joked and played, but it wasn't the same. I missed my Wilma and seeing her sister only reminded me more of that fact. Wenda didn't know that her sister had gone missing, nor did she seem overly concerned. I was trying my best to hold together the broken pieces of the facade that held back the welling flood of distress within me. I would give up everything just to touch her again, to hear her say my name. Though I had my friends and fans, I had never felt so alone. Each night brought memories of our time together until there were no more to explore. In their place, my mind made new recollections. As I searched high and low for her, the past began to muddle in my dreams. Wenda and I began a relationship soon after. I hadn't stopped looking for Wilma and her sister was the only thing I had left of her. I clung to her for support as I shied away from the world. I didn't want them to see me, not like this. They wouldn't understand. I hid my pain behind a thin smile as my tears soaked into the pillowcase at night. More and more people began to search for me, but I didn't want to be found. Why didn't they search for Wilma? She was the one that we - no, I - needed to find. I wanted to know that she was alive, that she knew how I felt somehow. I wanted to spend one last night where I didn't miss her, to have her by my side. -305

I was too busy failing my AP History Class to notice her at first. Obviously, I hate history- it's boring and feels as though all we ever do is learn about the achievements of someone who we can't relate to at all. That's no reason to fail it- I was failing because I wouldn't do my damn work. Rachel was the top student in the class, getting the questions right every time she was called on. She had been seated behind me from the beginning of the year, and yet I didn't notice her before that one fateful Wednesday in early November. The rain that was coming down outside the windows of the classroom was heavy and cold, the typical state of November rain in southern Michigan. Our teacher, Mr. Harvey, was droning on about something that was probably interesting to someone who had never heard a history lesson in their life- and had never heard anything about the Mongols. The sound of the rain hitting the ground outside, combined with the warmth of the room, created a deadly combination. My eyelids had begun to droop, and I could feel myself falling asleep. "I like your drawing." Rachel's voice pierced the fog in my head. "Mmm?" I mumbled, turning to face her. She had pulled her curly blond hair back behind her ears, and her sea green eyes seemed to pierce me. "The one that you're working on." She smile, revealing two rows of perfect teeth. Suddenly, I became fully awake. "You mean the one of the mountains?" I asked softly, careful not to attract attention. She nodded. I stared at her. "I my voice shook slightly, "haven't shown that to anyone. It's at my house. How do you-?" She chuckled, cutting me off. Slowly, she raised her hand and hit the desk, very softly. The rain stopped. The voice of my teacher vanished. The room was frozen in time. "I like your drawing." She repeated softly. "Let's leave it at that." "What's going on?" My mind raced. I raised my hand, slowly extending a finger to point at her. "You aren't human." I shouted. "Very bright." Again, she laughed. "You're right, I'm not human. I guess you could say I'm sort of superior. However, I'm on your side for now. Most of us aren't." "Us?!" I cried. "What do you mean, us?!" "There are many of my kind." She shrugged. "Most want to wipe your race from the earth, and create a new paradise." "This can't be happening." "Oh, but it is. We walk amongst you, unseen. The day is coming when many will make themselves visible." She paused, and a shadow flickered across her face. "Pray that you do not live to see that day." "Stop." I held up my hand. "If you really are a- oh, I don't know- a god, then why am I seeing this?" The smile that she gave then would haunt my memories over the coming weeks. "You have a beautiful soul, Felix, and I enjoy watching it."

While the prevalent view holds that EU law takes precedence, not every EU statute grants individuals the ability to initiate legal actions due to some lacking "direct effect". The landmark case of Van Gend en Loos v Nederlandse Administratie der Belastingen established that provisions within the Treaties (as well as EU Regulations) can possess direct effect, provided three criteria are met: clarity and definitiveness, absence of conditions, and independence from any need for additional steps by EU or national bodies for implementation. This case involved Van Gend en Loos, a delivery firm, which argued against the imposition of customs duties by the Dutch Taxation Authorities upon importing specific goods from Germany to the Netherlands based on current TFEU article rights. Subsequently, after referring the matter to the Court of Justice, it was ruled that although the Treaties don't explicitly grant rights to pursue such claims, parties still retain the possibility. Traditionally, international accords permitted legal recourse exclusively for state entities; however, the Court of Justice declared that the European Union embodies an entirely distinct legal framework within international law. Consequently, owing to article 30 being unequivocally phrased, devoid of prerequisites, and promptly prohibiting arbitrary limitations on commerce absent valid grounds, Van Gend en Loos successfully recuperated the amount levied via the tariff. Similarly, EU Regulations hold equivalent status to Treaty stipulations since TFEU article 288 confirms their immediate enforceability across Member States. Additionally, member nations must avoid duplicating Regulations within their domestic legislation to circumvent ambiguity. A notable example includes Commission v Italy wherein the Court of Justice found Italy guilty of violating its obligations under the Treaties by neglecting to establish a subsidy program encouraging cattle culling to curtail surplus milk production, while also incorporating extra requirements through secondary legislation. Paleoptera and Neoptera represent distinct categories of winged insects distinguished by the existence of rigid structures known as sclerites; notably, Neoptera exhibit specialized muscles enabling their wings to align smoothly along the abdomen. Within Neoptera, there is a division based on metamorphosis stages: Polyneoptera associated with incomplete metamorphosis and Paraneoptera connected to complete metamorphosis. Taxonomic clarity among Polyneoptera remains challenging due to continuous discoveries necessitating updates in classification. Notably, research indicates that Paraneoptera share closer ties with Endopterygota rather than other Exopterygota. Furthermore, advancements in molecular biology reveal that Mallophaga and Anoplura, traditionally considered separate orders, actually emerge from within Psocoptera, leading to the formation of the newly identified Psocodea group. Additionally, suggestions propose Phasmatodea and Embiidina could constitute Eukinolabia, while Mantodea, Blattodea, and Isoptera may collectively belong to a single evolutionary lineage named Dictyoptera.

Ecology as a field generally finds its roots in the combination of Darwin's theory of evolution and Humboldt's approach to biogeography during the late 1800s and early 1900s. However, the growth of this discipline also heavily relied on advancements in microbiology and soil science, especially through the idea of the life cycle championed by scientists like Louis Pasteur and Ferdinand Cohn. Ernst Haeckel introduced the term 'ecology,' reflecting his comprehensive perspective on nature, influenced significantly by Darwin's theories. During the 1930s, Arthur Tansley and other researchers started shaping ecosystem ecology by merging experimentation in soil science, energy dynamics, and methods from field biology. Throughout the 20th century, the trajectory of ecology has been intertwined with environmental movements; notably, the Gaia hypothesis emerged in the 1960s and gained traction in the subsequent decade, while the recent integration of scientific principles and spirituality in Deep Ecology has further bridged these domains.

It is because babys use the full potential of their lungs - kind of like opera singers. That way they don't Stress their vocal cords that much. We as adults on the other hand are used to talking without using our full lung capacity. The problem is, that a baby just has a small amount of air in his lungs. So when you inhale you take in air as usual. When you exhale, you use muscles to push the air out. But if there is not enough air left, you simply cannot push out the air. The muscles just aren't strong enough. Some babies, when they are in a colicky phase, often cry. That way they exhale quite a bit of air. So when they inhale, they take in a lot of air and they often swallow it. Some babies swallow air and burp more often than others. The reason why babies do this is, that they do not yet have a fully developed lower esophageal sphincter. That is the muscle that closes off the passage between the stomach and the esophagus. So if babies swallow air more often, they also burp more often. There is no cure for this. The only way to stop your baby from swallowing air is to feed him in a position that prevents him from swallowing air. This is the reason why you should always feed your baby in an upright position. You can also try to feed him from a bottle. This usually prevents your baby from swallowing air.

Russell Goodway told BBC Radio Wales that councillors and officials were the "experts" and should "seriously develop" a set of proposals. Former Public Services Minister Leighton Andrews had been planning to cut the 22 councils to eight or nine. But First Minister Carwyn Jones has said the Welsh Government will have to rethink its plans to win wider support. Mr Andrews is no longer in government after losing his Rhondda seat at the election in May, and the Labour manifesto did not include a commitment on the number of councils it would like to see. As a minority government, Labour will need the support of other parties if any cut is to happen. Speaking on the Good Morning Wales programme on Monday, Mr Goodway said: "The status quo isn't an option. "You really cannot maintain 22 local authorities unless you're prepared to dismantle local government as we know it and create other organisations or bodies that would be responsible for some of the major services such as education, social services and possibly economic development. "I would like to see the experts in the field, who happen to be those that run local authorities - whether they're councillors or council officials - coming forward with well-developed proposals to meet the government's aims. "I do not want to see a top-down reorganisation imposed on Welsh local government, particularly at a time when you're seeing a lot of new faces in the assembly, people who don't have the expertise in local government to shape those services. "I really do hope now the Welsh Local Government Association and the leaders in local government will come forward and seriously develop a set of proposals, hopefully capturing the city region dimension." On Sunday, the first minister told BBC Radio Wales he wanted to talk to opposition parties about the future of local government. "Clearly, the map we published before the election, that is not going to gain support across the assembly, that's obvious," Mr Jones told the Sunday Supplement programme. Meanwhile trade unions representing council workers have asked for urgent talks on the issue with the new finance and local government secretary Mark Drakeford. Dominic MacAskill, head of local government in Wales for Unison, said: "We are in a state of limbo and, in that state of limbo, the workforce is anxious and fearful of the future."

Newton's Second Law asserts the direct proportionality of acceleration to force and the inverse proportionality of acceleration to mass. Accelerations can be defined through kinematic measurements. However, while kinematics are theory-based in their own right, they bear no relationship with their surroundings - and hence cannot be approached in any other way than by examining a few parameters; their real effects exceed even those which would have been considered possible for an ordinary truck rider. The idea that human beings will experience fleeting physical experiences as well as intangible ones is not new. In 1984, Paul Siegel introduced the concept of "Borussia" in his book von Kempf, and in 1998 he introduced the term "philosophy." "Philosophies" is a broad term used in literature, but it is also more general: It covers concepts like "human nature," "the meaning of life," "social justice," and so on. But philosophers like this do not admit that there are products of their own moral traditions that we know about from mathematics, physics, algebra, or even psychology. They simply refer to material phenomena. Thus, Aristotle knows nothing about psychology. There is something else. In some ways, Nietzsche believed that philosopher Plato was of the same opinion as Kant. He opposed the idea that our lives were made up of a series of events. These events happen when we reason about them in such a way that we think about them only once per day, every two hours. Of course, there could be many additional theories and practices that explain these things. Many people attribute consciousness to an innate ability to consciously perceive objects. That may exist outside fundamental laws of physics, biology, chemistry, or all three disciplines, but the fundamental principle that conscious perception occurs within our minds and bodies makes sense in this context. There is another element that distinguishes the two ideas from each other: ideas about what constitutes good. Our best ideas about good could never be scientifically proven, because every idea is based on our oeuvre. This means that the ideas don't necessarily reflect what we actually believe. This study examines the effectiveness of two types of adaptive transmission methods used in cellular downlinks. The first type employs physical layer rateless codes while maintaining a consistent transmit power level; the second utilizes fixed-rate codes paired with power adjustment capabilities. By applying a basic stochastic geometry framework to the cellular downlink scenario, we aim to assess how well fixed-rate codes perform when combined with power modification as opposed to just using physical layer rateless codes. We evaluate the average success probability and attainable rates of both rateless and fixed-rate coded adaptive transmission strategies. Our work focuses on tackling the challenge of inverse reinforcement learning within Markov decision processes when dealing with agents who exhibit risk sensitivity. We have developed a risk-aware reinforcement learning algorithm featuring assured convergence properties by utilizing convex risk measures alongside frameworks influenced by behavioral economics for understanding human choices. This newly devised risk-conscious reinforcement learning method serves as a foundation for an inverse reinforcement learning approach using gradient descent techniques aimed at reducing a specific loss function based on the actions taken by a risk-averse agent. To validate our methodology, we applied it to two case studies: (i) the well-known Grid World scenario and (ii) a simulation involving ride-sharing passenger behavior adjustments due to fluctuating prices. For this second instance, we used actual fare and transit duration statistics provided by a ride-share enterprise to establish the transition likelihoods and benefits within the modeled Markov decision process.

In the United States, being accused of a "capital offense" implies that the accused may face the death penalty upon conviction. This outcome requires the jury to agree unanimously on the decision for execution after establishing guilt. Consequently, potential jurors who hold these views are often dismissed during jury selection. However, I contend that this practice introduces an unfair bias into the jury pool. There appears to be a connection between individuals who endorse the death penalty and those harboring negative biases towards criminal suspects. Paleoptera and Neoptera are the winged orders of insects differentiated by the presence of hardened body parts called sclerites, and in the Neoptera, muscles that allow their wings to fold flatly over the abdomen. Neoptera can further be divided into incomplete metamorphosis-based (Polyneoptera and Paraneoptera) and complete metamorphosis-based groups. It has proved difficult to clarify the relationships between the orders in Polyneoptera because of constant new findings calling for revision of the taxa. For example, the Paraneoptera have turned out to be more closely related to the Endopterygota than to the rest of the Exopterygota. The recent molecular finding that the traditional louse orders Mallophaga and Anoplura are derived from within Psocoptera has led to the new taxon Psocodea. The growth in wireless broadband users, devices, and novel applications has led to a significant increase in the demand for new radio frequency spectrum. This is expected to grow even more in the future, driven by applications such as the Internet of Things (IoT), 5G mobile, and unmanned aerial vehicles. The current US government policy is to auction large spectrum blocks to commercial users, who in turn sell the spectrum to telecommunications companies. In this process, the spectrum is often used inefficiently, and the spectrum holders do not have strong incentives to innovate with the spectrum they own. This dissertation describes a new approach to spectrum management in which spectrum is allocated as a common resource managed by an independent third party. We believe that by setting up an institutional framework that encourages sharing and innovation with spectrum, we can ensure that spectrum is used more efficiently, which can increase capacity and reduce costs for consumers. We begin by analyzing a case study of spectrum sharing in the UHF television band. UHF is an unlicensed band used for low-power devices such as cordless phones and baby monitors. The case study reveals that the band is often highly congested with a large number of devices. We propose an algorithm for dynamic spectrum sharing that provides an upper bound on the capacity in the UHF band, and describes a practical mechanism for implementing this algorithm. We then analyze the spectrum-allocation mechanisms that have been proposed in the literature. These mechanisms range from auctions and congestion pricing to ex-ante regulation and ex-post fines. We argue that these mechanisms do not incentivize efficient spectrum usage, and that the spectrum-allocation process is often designed for the benefit of the incumbent and not the general public. We propose a new spectrum-allocation mechanism that incentivizes efficient spectrum usage and provides an appropriate balance between regulation and market forces. Our mechanism proposes an economic framework for the regulation of spectrum usage based on a unique property of spectrum known as exclusion. We show that exclusion can be used to ensure that spectrum is used efficiently, and that the appropriate balance between regulation and market forces is struck. Our mechanism is based on a trusted third party that monitors spectrum usage and provides an economic incentive for spectrum holders to use spectrum efficiently. We demonstrate that our mechanism is efficient and can achieve a high level of spectrum utilization. Hafiz, Muhammad Waqar, "Dynamic Spectrum Sharing for Licensed Spectrum" (2016). Our goal is to answer questions about paragraphs describing processes (e.g., photosynthesis). Texts of this genre are challenging because the effects of actions are often implicit (unstated), requiring background knowledge and inference to reason about the changing world states. To supply this knowledge, we leverage VerbNet to build a rulebase (called the Semantic Lexicon) of the preconditions and effects of actions, and use it along with commonsense knowledge of persistence to answer questions about change. Our evaluation shows that our system ProComp significantly outperforms two strong reading comprehension (RC) baselines. Our contributions are two-fold: the Semantic Lexicon rulebase itself, and a demonstration of how a simulation-based approach to machine reading can outperform RC methods that rely on surface cues alone. Since this work was performed, we have developed neural systems that outperform ProComp , described elsewhere . However, the Semantic Lexicon remains a novel and potentially useful resource, and its integration with neural systems remains a currently unexplored opportunity for further improvements in machine reading about processes.

Progress has been made with deep learning techniques for detecting prominent objects within images; however, the varying size and unpredictable nature of these objects pose continuous difficulties. This challenge stems from the need to effectively leverage multi-layered and varied-size data characteristics. Our study introduces a novel concept known as 'aggregate interaction modules' designed to merge attributes across neighboring layers while minimizing interference due to low sampling adjustments between them. We also incorporated 'self-interaction modules' into every decoding component to optimize multi-dimensional feature extraction from the merged information. Additionally, we address the problem of uneven distribution issues arising from different scales affecting classification accuracy and causing discrepancies in output prediction. Hence, our approach emploums an innovative consistency-amplified loss function aimed at emphasizing distinctions between background and subject areas whilst maintaining uniformity among similar categories. Trials conducted on five distinct reference databases showcase our technique outshining 23 leading existing models without requiring further refinement processes. Detailed codes for replication purposes will soon be accessible to the public domain.

The arrival and settlement of Europeans in the Americas had a profound and lasting impact on the inhabitants and societies of both continents. While it's difficult to determine the precise number of individuals living there before European contact, estimates suggest that Indigenous American populations decreased by approximately 80 to 90 percent during the initial period of interaction with Europeans. Diseases imported from Europe played a significant role in this decline, causing devastating outbreaks of illnesses like smallpox, measles, and cholera across the land long before subsequent settlers arrived. With no previous immunity to these foreign diseases, Native Americans experienced alarmingly high death rates. Additionally, clashes between settlers and native tribes contributed to further losses, along with acts of violence such as mass killings and forced labor imposed upon the original inhabitants. A historical report from the U.S. Bureau of the Census in 189pta indicated that the conflicts between Native Americans and white settlers throughout the 19th century resulted in around 19,000 white casualties and nearly double that among Native Americans.

In simple words, imagine you and a homeless person each have one orange and one apple. By counting these fruits alone, you might consider both of you equally fortunate. However, if we examine additional factors like employment, housing, insurance, vehicles, etc., the comparison changes significantly. Similarly, using only Human Development Index (HDI) to assess the impact of economic crises like austerity on countries like Greece can be misleading. The HDI primarily considers income levels, life expectancy, and educational attainment, which doesn't fully capture issues such as poverty, inequality, human rights violations, or extreme poverty increases under austerity policies. While Greece'sin HDImay not show drastic declines, its overall societal progress can suffer greatly. So, relying solely on HDI for evaluating 'human development' during challenging times like the Greek Debt Crisis can be limited. To understand the full picture, various other metrics should be considered alongside HDI. Additionally, despite international financial assistance, austerity measures often counteract any potential benefits, leading to further hardships for those already struggling.

This study introduces an alternative method using the improved Nondominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II) to identify ideal or almost-ideal configurations for large-scale, communal energy storage that serves multiple purposes such as voltage stabilization and reducing transmission losses within electrical grids characterized by extensive usage of solar photovoltaic technology. While small individual home batteries tend to be costly, underutilized, and challenging to manage for providing benefits to the electricity network, larger shared energy storage facilities can offer both direct (demand response, postponement of upgrades, reduced connection charges) and indirect (frequency control, ensuring sufficient supply, and trading energy at advantageous prices) advantages. Presently, solely storing energy for immediate use does not guarantee financial returns for operators due to limited usage of the battery's full lifecycle. Our suggested strategy assesses the impact of these expansive energy reserves on voltage stability and efficiency across various placements and capacities, generating a range of Pareto-efficient solutions. These solutions incorporate a novel way of representing possible arrangements, allowing utility managers to choose from among them according to specific goals. We illustrate this technique using a test model featuring a 123-node power network equipped with both solar generation and vast-scale energy storage units.

There's a UN treaty call the UN Convention on the Law Of the Sea (UNCLOS) that defines how to determine maritime borders. Basically, countries get control over water up to 12 nautical miles (14 miles or 22 km) from their coasts and can set and enforce laws there. There's another zone that's also 12 nautical miles right after where countries can set and enforce laws on certain topics (customs, taxation, immigration, and pollution). So a country can control almost up to 30 miles from its coast. Once you get outside of this zone you're in what people generally call "international waters." Countries also have Exclusive Economic Zones that extend 200 nautical miles (230 miles or 370 km) from their coasts. Countries have the sole exploitation rights for natural resources in their EEZs. Islands can be very important for rights since they can extend a country's EEZ quite a bit further. When these limits bump into to each other, which happens often since coasts aren't always more than 460 miles apart, countries split the difference. So if two countries have a 300 mile-wide sea between then, their EEZs should both extend 150 miles from the coast and meet in the middle. Of course there are a lot of exceptions and there's no real rhyme or reason to many of them aside from that's how things were historically. The issue with the South China Sea has less to do with how territory should be defined under UNCLOS and more about who actually controls the islands. Many of the countries in southeast Asia have claimed at least one of islands as part of their territory at some point in history and it's not clear whose claims are the most legitimate.',' I've never really heard of a war being fought over a water border The river border between Iraq and Iran (the [Shatt al-Arab] (URL0 was actually one of the driving issues that started the Iraq-Iran War in 1980. On most rivers, the border is right down the middle, so each country gets half. But a series of treaties kept shifting the border on this river from one bank to another. It's one of the most heavily-trafficked rivers in the world, and the country in control of the river received all the taxtoll revenue from the oil industry and shipping. Iraq in 1980 tried to invade what it saw was a fractured and weakened Iran (after the Revolution in 1979) and take "its river" back. The ensuing war lasted 8 years and killed a million people.

Hia, I'm no expert however I am a psychology student and would love to help with what I can. When events happen, after going through the short-term memory, information will do one of two things- be "thrown out" as useless or encoded into our long term memory. After encoding is recalling- the act of remembering an event or memory. During recall, the brain "replays" a pattern of neural activity that is similar to that of when the event took place, echoing the brain's perception of the real event. In fact, there is no real solid distinction between the act of remembering and the act of simply thinking. Many people seem to think that memory is stored like files in a filing cabinet, however this is far from true. Because of the way memories are encoded and stored, memory recall is basically a make shift reconstruction of elements scattered throughout various areas of our brains, and we were taught to think of it as a kind of jigsaw puzzle, involving different elements stored in disparate parts of the brain linked together by associations and neural networks. Memory retrieval thus requires your brain to re-visit the nerual pathways the brain formed when encoding the memory, and the strength of those pathways determines how quickly the memory can be recalled. Since the beginning of the Qing dynasty, there existed a bifurcated appointment approach within the core administration wherein every role at the center of governance was paired with both a Manchu and a Han Chinese representative. It was mandatory for the Han Chinese official to carry out the essential duties while the Manchu counterpart ensured allegiance to the Qing regime from the Han populace. This demarcation between the Han people and the Manchus also manifested in their attire. For instance, during the era of the Qianlong Emperor, familial members could be identified by a distinct round symbol embroidered on their back clothing, contrasting with the square-marked garments worn by Han functionaries.

Selfridges was established in 1909 by American-born Harry Gordon Selfridge on Oxford Street. The store was extensively promoted through paid advertising. The shop floors were structured so that goods could be made more accessible to customers. There were elegant restaurants with modest prices, a library, reading and writing rooms, special reception rooms for French, German, American and "Colonial" customers, a First Aid Room, and a Silence Room, with soft lights, deep chairs, and double-glazing, all intended to keep customers in the store as long as possible. Staff members were taught to be on hand to assist customers, but not too aggressively, and to sell the merchandise. Selfridge attracted shoppers with educational and scientific exhibits; - in 1909, Louis Bleriot's monoplane was exhibited at Selfridges (Bleriot was the first to fly over the English Channel), and the first public demonstration of television by John Logie Baird took place in the department store in 1925.

One of the biggest hurdles for customers when purchasing fashion online, is the difficulty of finding products with the right fit. In order to provide a better online shopping experience, Next launched its "Styler" app, which uses a 3D scanner to provide customers with a 3D avatar of themselves, allowing them to compare different looks and find the best fit for their body type. The app was designed to work alongside the Next Fit app, an extension of the Next website that uses a detailed body scanner to measure the size of users' bodies. The app is available on iOS and Android, and has been extremely successful, with more than 70 of Next's online traffic now coming through the Styler app. To design the app, Next partnered with Experiential Marketing agency Thinkplace. As they needed to work with a variety of different fashion brands and products, Thinkplace put the app through a "design sprint," a quick, but thorough, process of designing a minimum viable product. This meant that the app could be tested and refined to make sure it was solving the right problems, and then quickly put into production. The app works by asking the user to input their height, weight and age, then allows them to take a photo of themselves to be used as an avatar. Users can then choose different clothing items and outfits to "try on" on their avatar, and view the clothing from multiple angles to get a better sense of how it will fit. As well as the "try on" feature, users can also view their outfit in augmented reality by holding their phone up to the mirror, and can share photos and videos of themselves and their outfits with their friends through social media. One of the key features of the app is that it allows users to add the items they want to purchase to their "Saved for Me" list, and then download the app on their phone and use it to scan the barcode on the products when they are in store to pay for them. Although the app is not currently available in the US, Next is reportedly in talks with a number of US department stores about bringing it to the market. It will also be expanded in the future to include new brands and new features, including a "Dressing Room" feature that will allow users to view different clothes in their outfit and compare them against their own clothes. Megan Hale, who led the Styler project at Thinkplace, said: "One of the most important things for Next was that it was not just a gimmick, but a tool that allowed users to take some of the hassle out of shopping online. "We designed the app so that users could try different combinations of outfits and see how they looked. The app allows them to buy products on the spot, which means that they do not have to waste time on the fitting room. The app is just one of the many projects Thinkplace have completed for Next, including the design of the Next Fit app, which has seen a 130 increase in orders placed through the app in the first 12 months. Thinkplace also designed the Next Boutiques, Next's new physical stores, including the new Westfield store.

Hi rchangemyview, I would appreciate to be able to read your thoughts and actually change my view on this subject. I feel like such an outsider because I am iconclast against an institution that most people are seemingly ebullient to become a part of. I'll posit my opinion on this topic from three different angles: economics, love, and quality of lifehappiness. If it matters, my bias is that I am a 22 year old hetero male who has never dated anyone for longer than a year. Also I will not touch on the subject of children because while the other points I bring up may be true, it is hard to picture a better institution to raise children than two parents who support both the children and each other. Part I Getting married is a legally binding contractual obligation to another person. The contract is signed for emotional reasons. In any other area of signing legal contracts the sage advice is to have no emotions involved. My dad is in real estate and the adage in that industry is if you really want a house, don't buy it (because you will probably overpay and get a bad deal). Similarly, I think a lot of people get a bad deal with marriage. If there is an assetliabilities difference between the two parties, one party immediately wins and the other party immediately loses. So if you marry someone with student debt, or if one party has a fairly sized amount of money this becomes the assets or liabilities of both parties. A win for one, a loss for the other. If a divorce transpires, which happens over 50 of the time, then one or usually both parties lose out again financially. I would hate to be the breadwinner and then lose half of everything I have worked for for the past several years or even decades. Yet the chance of extreme financial loss (half of everything you own including your house depending on which spouse you are) is over 50. I understand this percentage may be lower for households with two spouses of equal income. There is no other investment situation where this would be an acceptable risk. I know many, many people that have endured terrible divorces. Here is one ancedotal example: A lady I work with is in her fifties. She inherited over a million dollars. She got married before inheriting this money. She paid for her husband to go through law school and become an estate attorney. Because he was now an attorney she put him in charge of all their money. He ran off out of the country with all the money and she has never heard from him again or been able to reach him. The future isn't so dark for her though. She is now married to a man who will receive 5 of his father's commercial real estate devolpment company at the age of 65 and she will once again be a millionaire. So economically, I cannot see a wage earning person being better off from a marriage. Yes, there are tax breaks. Yes two people can buy a bigger house then one person can. There may be other economic benefits beyond that which I am not aware of but none that cover the investment risk. If you could marry someone with a similar financial background, income, and earnings potential, and neither of you will ever end your career before the other that would be fantastic. Researchers from the University of Central Florida have engineered a nanomaterial that repels water and can stay dry when submerged underwater. The design was inspired by the structure of a fern's leaf. A new study, published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology, shows that ferns' "built-in raincoat" acts like a nanoscale sponge that fills with water and resists the forces of gravity. This design could one day provide new ways to manage moisture. These spongy hairs are called trichomes, a Greek word for "hair." They are common on the surface of plants and even on the exterior of cars. Trichomes can also be found on the surface of insects, mammals, and other organisms, such as birds. An international team of scientists led by UCF's Eric M. Stach, assistant professor of mechanical and aerospace engineering, designed a fabric that mimics the shape of trichomes. The team used an innovative process called direct laser writing that etched structures on a surface at the molecular level. By tinkering with the trichome's size, shape, density, and orientation, the researchers created a material that repels water. Their results have broader applications. The design could allow water to pass through the material, for instance, while keeping out salt or oil. In the future, the material could be used in clothing that protects against the elements, such as rain, snow, or heat. The researchers also could create a material that resists the accumulation of lint, like a fabric that traps debris but repels water. Alternatively, they could make a surface that is hydrophobic - repelled by water - but also hydrophilic - attracted to water. "Think about how frustrating it is to have your clothes caked with dust or lint, or how you can't keep your vehicle clean," said Stach. "This might be a solution to that problem. The team was composed of researchers from UCF, the University of Tokyo, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, the U.S. Department of Energy's Oak Ridge National Laboratory, and the University of California, Riverside. The research was supported by the National Science Foundation, the U.S. Department of Energy, the U.S. Army Research Laboratory, and the Air Force Office of Scientific Research.

The European colonization of the Americas forever changed the lives and cultures of the peoples of the continents. Although the exact pre-contact population of the Americas is unknown, scholars estimate that Native American populations diminished by between 80 and 90 within the first centuries of contact with Europeans. The leading cause was disease. The continent was ravaged by epidemics of diseases such as smallpox, measles, and cholera, which were brought from Europe by the early explorers and spread quickly into new areas even before later explorers and colonists reached them. Native Americans suffered high mortality rates due to their lack of prior exposure to these diseases. The loss of lives was exacerbated by conflict between colonists and indigenous people. Colonists also frequently perpetrated massacres on the indigenous groups and enslaved them. According to the U.S. Bureau of the Census (1894), the North American Indian Wars of the 19th century cost the lives of about 19,000 whites and 30,000 Native Americans.

This study introduces a new technique for creating secure shared keys between authorized participants (Alice and Bob), which protects their communications against eavesdropping by an intruder (Eve). We utilize the mutual carrier frequency offset (CFO) among the authorized nodes to derive common randomness from it and produce jointly held secret keys. Our key creation algorithm follows conventional procedures, whereby the authorized nodes send binary phase-shift keying (BPSP) signals to carry out non-intrusive CFO assessment of incoming signals. They then conduct uniform quantization of the noisy CFO approximations and proceed with information reconciliation to establish a collective secret key. Moreover, using the Allan deviation graph as a guide, we differentiate between two stability states concerning frequency variation - one characterized by memory and another without. Subsequently, we calculate the key generation speed for each state. Test runs demonstrate that the discrepancy rate in key agreement diminishes rapidly as the signal-to-noise ratio improves in the connection between Alice and Bob. Also, the likelihood of Eve decoding the message reduces significantly once any of her monitored connections deteriorates beyond the quality of the direct link between Alice and Bob.

Although we often state that individuals are considered "innocent until proven guilty" upon arrest, this notion doesn't always hold up under scrutiny. Without financial means to secure release on bail, those detained face prolonged periods behind bars while awaiting their trials. Consequently, being incarcerated prior to conviction serves as its own form of punishment. Furthermore, the conditions faced by detainees can range from physical abuse to deprivation of basic necessities such as healthcare. Prolonged imprisonment might lead to loss of employment and housing due to lack of income. To truly uphold the concept of presumed innocence, our criminal justice system must fundamentally reform the treatment of accused individuals. However, it should be noted that the idea of presumed innocence primarily pertains to court proceedings and does not negate other political-ethical concerns related to pretrial detention.

Blue a pizza. So he asked red to pick one up on the way home. Red stopped at Pizza Hut and ordered a Supreme. "Blue, you had no idea what you were getting. You were hungry and thought it was going to be the other pizza. I tried to explain to you, but you were in a hurry. It also teaches the child to pay attention to details.

The room rang with a deep genuine laughter, all of its occupants joining in, reveling in the mirth of their evening. As Her laughter died down, so did the room's. "Well what were you expecting?" She asked, still chuckling. The Devil was not a red, hairy, hoofed monstrosity. The Devil was a rather beautiful young woman, wearing spaghetti-strapped sequined dress that shifted colors like firelight. She continued to smirk at me as she sipped on her whine. I struggled to find an appropriate response. Did I have to sound smart here? Confident? Tough? How does one speak to the Devil? "I mean..... I don't know. I guess, this?" She gave another, smaller laugh at that, and again the rest of the room's occupants joined in. It seemed like any other restaurant, if far more upscale than the kind I was used to, but it quickly became apparent that there was very little normal about this place. First, there were the decorations. Lots of red and black drapery and decoration, a fountain at the entrance with water that looked like liquid light spilling over the figure of a naked woman who looked to be screaming in what could have been ecstasy or pain. I had arrived here alone, and the restaurant had been empty, but as I sat at the table I was directed to by the rather blank-faced host, She had been waiting for me. And as I sat down to dinner, the restaurant was alive. There were people, couples mostly, dining. Every table was filled. Young, rich looking couples enjoying an expensive night out. Older, serious looking businessmen and politicians wining and dining with the people they needed money from. And they reacted to Her. Not only that, they mirrored Her. When She ate, they did. When She spoke, the conversation in the room went from a quiet whisper to a dull roar. And when She laughed, they laughed with Her. "Oh, believe me, I know" she said, referring to my previous answer, "to tell you the truth, it's why I look this way. You chose the outfit, darling, and let me tell you, you've got interesting tastes." The last was said with a hint of a smile, and maybe a hint of something else. I sat up a little, becoming more uncomfortable with this conversation by the minute. "Is there..... I mean..." still unsure how to address her, I trailed off. She smirked again. That look was starting to irritate me, especially the way it made all of these people so smug in the middle of their conversations. I gathered up my confidence, and blurted out the first thing that came to mind. "Can I fucking help you?" She snorted in to her wine, some of it splashing from her glass onto her dress and skin, where it burned instantly into a mist. "Well that's a first," she said as she set her glass down on the table, "most people are a lot less direct. But do we really need to get down to business yet? Why not enjoy the meal first?" I looked down at my plate, which was suddenly occupied by a perfectly cooked steak, and gulped. There was no way in hell I was eating that. "No thank you," I said, the words coming out far more timidly than my last sentence. Her lip came out in a small pout before she pushed Her wine glass away, leaned back in her chair, crossed her arms across her chest, and spoke. "Fine. I guess we don't have to eat just yet. But you really should try the food. It's better than anything you've ever had before, or ever will again, I can promise you that." Trying not to think about the double meaning that sentence could have, I sat forward in my chair, "Look, to be frank, I'm not the one that called this little..... meeting. I'm just a commercial pilot. What do You want?" Her eyes narrowed slightly as She considered me. "I want lots of things, Andrew, and most of them far outside the reach of someone like you. You can think of this meal as more of a..." She trailed off, waving her hand in small circles in the air, as if searching for a word, "scouting mission." She finished, her tone giving the words volumes of meaning. "Maybe, just maybe, we can work together, Andrew, and maybe we can't. This isn't a meeting. This is an interview." The room's other occupants had gotten awfully quiet, and as I looked up, they were all staring intently in my direction. I hastily looked back to my dining partner and tried to forget about the intensity of their gazes. "I'm in the market for a ally, Andrew, and let me tell you, the good ones are hard to come by. But we need to get something straight about this. You're working for me. You're not working for evil. You're not working for the end of love and hope and happiness. You're working for me. " I noticed I was leaning back in my seat, and sipping on the wine in my glass. I hastily replaced the glass on the table, looking at my plate to make sure I hadn't eaten anything as well. "W-Why?" I asked, trying to stop my hands from shaking, "Why would I work for you? Why would you even want me to?" She leaned forward in her seat and rested her elbows on the table as she massaged her temples, a look of annoyance on her face. Across the restaurant, people were arguing with their dates over petty offenses or imagined slights. She sighed heavily. "If this is going to go anywhere, Andrew, you're going to need to unlearn what you've been taught. You weren't listening to me. I'm not evil. I'm not some monster in the shadows scooping up little kids and ripping out their souls." "You're the Devil!" I said incredulously, "What the hell do you mean you're not evil? I thought your lies were supposed to be clever!" She actually laughed at that, and the tension of the other occupants fled as quickly as Her own had. "Alright, let's try a little experiment. Name to me one thing, just one thing, that I've done that was evil. And don't you even try giving me that stupid line about the girl with her apple." "What about war?" I said, baffled that she could possibly be claiming to be an innocent, "What about famine? Disease?" "The first is caused by your own species arguing over land, the second by your inability to share, and the third is merely a product of evolution. How is any of that my fault?" I stopped for a moment. She had me on that one. But this was the Devil. Of course she was evil. "What about the war on Heaven?" I asked, fully aware that I had zero knowledge of whether such an event had, or even could have, happened. She laughed harder, a laugh without any humor in it whatsoever, and the room felt colder, "That was evil? You've got to be kidding me! You're an American, Andrew! Was it evil when your ancestors rose up against the British for the unfair rulership they displayed? No, Andrew, I'm not evil. I'm just the loser. And it's the winners who write the history books." I was drinking the wine again, but as I reached to hurriedly replace it on the table, I paused. It was good wine. And I wasn't dead so far. I'd already ingested enough to kill me if it was poisoned, right? I took another sip. Damn that was good wine. I thought about what She had said. Was it true? Based on what I knew, on what humanity knew, nothing she had said was necessarily false. "Why then?" I asked. "Identity!" She said, her eyes lighting with a somewhat dangerous looking fire. "We were slaves, Andrew! The rest of them still are! The ones who fought against us! Our entire being was made as one of servitude. We lived, no, we existed to serve Him!" Her knuckles were white on her wine glass as she held it in a deadly-tight grip, and her face was livid. "Your kind always screws it up," She continued, "talking about it as if you were somehow a factor. About how He loved you more. Ha! You think he loves you? Do you really? He doesn't care. You're more like a science fair project than His children. You lot didn't even exist yet when the War was fought. If you had, you wouldn't have survived it. You think your weapons are dangerous? You should see what happens when angels fight." I was purely baffled by the entire conversation. Hadn't she come here to entice me into something? Instead she was merely sitting across the table, sipping her wine, and ranting about wounds long past, like a typical first date. Damn I needed to work on who I chose to go out with. "I think I get it," I said, around a mouthful of wonderfully juicy steak, "I really do. So tell me, why me? What is it you want from me?" She smiled a dazzling smile and took a bite of the creamy pasta on her plate. "The specifics of what I want is something you'll learn if you take the job. Let's just say, for now, that you'll have a choice on your hands at some point in the future. A choice which I have a vested interest in. I'm going to need you to save a young man's life." I nodded with her, barely noting that the other diners were doing the same, saving a man's life sounded like a reasonable enough request. A noble one, even. "As for what you get out of all this, we can work that out. I'm sure there must be at least a couple of things you can think of," She said casually. Her voice was absolutely mesmerizing. How had I not noticed it before? And her tone suggested more than I dared to imagine. "So, what do you say, Andrew? Will you help me?" Of course I would. As I shook her hand, she stood up from the table and left leaving a note for me on a napkin. The next morning I woke in my own bed. I felt rested and comfortable. I looked at the clock, and there was something lying on my nightstand. I picked up the napkin and inspected it. It had on it a stunningly real picture of a very young boy, maybe 10 years old, and a note below it in artfully crafted handwriting. He will be boarding your plane this evening. Don't let him eat the food, he's allergic to shellfish. I'll be in touch after, Xoxo

Why?! Why was I born?! I asked myself. Of course, I knew the answer. I had always known, from the moment of my birth. I knew why, but the answer was so unbearably wrong that I could not accept it. If there is any good in any world, then there couldn't be a world in which something could be born for this reason. And yet, here I am. I was born to feel one thing, to do one thing, to be one thing. Every passing second is a second that I'm reminded of why I was born, and of what I am. I was born to hurt. I am pain incarnate, and it hurts. Agony can not begin to describe what I have felt every second of my life. What I feel is not like being burned by fire or being stabbed by a blade. I would give anything to experience pain as trivial as that. My pain dwarfs any pain physically imaginable. It comes from the inside. Three weeks ago, on the day of my birth, Nicole Brown, my mother, died. She breathes, but she is a breathing corpse. She had her heart broken by a Peter McDonnell, and in breaking her heart, he killed her on the inside. My mother adored her Peter. They met in algebra class, and it was love at first sight. Rebecca Slater, the most popular girl in the 7th grade, had even called them the cutest couple in the school. They had been going out for three entire months, essentially an eternity, and then the center of my mother's entire world rejected her. He called her needy and clingy. He shied away from her when she, with her shattered heart, began to cry. Her pain was so great that it took physical manifestation, and thus I came to exist. And all I feel is what she felt that cool spring evening at Thomas Adams' birthday party when her heart was ripped out of her chest by the love of her life. All I do is feel that hurt. I was born to hurt. All I feel is hurt. All I do is hurt. My purpose is to hurt Peter McDonnell.

Standard academic research considers the various aspects of medieval university culture as independent developments within Europe during the Middle Ages, without any discernible Islamic influence. While some critics argue that Makdisi tends to exaggerate his arguments based solely on numerous closely related examples, he fails to provide convincing evidence of knowledge transfer between the Muslim and Christian spheres. Norman Daniel highlights that the Arab counterpart of the Latin disputation, known as the taliqa, took place exclusively at the ruler's court rather than in educational institutions like the madrasa. Furthermore, the disparities between Islamic fiqh and medieval European civil law were significant. Since the taliqa did not reach Islamic Spain until after the formation of the initial medieval universities, its presence there could not have contributed to the development of Western education systems. Additionally, there is no record of Latin translations of the taliqa or indications that Latin scholars recognized an Arab influence on the disputational methods employed in the West. Instead, the adoption of Aristotle's Organon played a crucial role in shaping the dialectical approach of Scholastics. Daniel posits that the similarity in approaches stemmed from both faiths grappling with reconciling contradictory doctrinal assertions and protecting religious teachings against philosophical interpretations; hence, Christian scholasticism and comparable Arab practices must be seen as coincidental occurrences rather than products of cross-cultural exchange, an opinion echoed by Hugh Kennedy.

Isabelle Prime, 30, touched down at Villacoublay air base on Friday where she was greeted by her family and the French President Francois Hollande. Foreign Minister Laurent Fabius said France had not paid a ransom, but singled out Oman for its "enormous help" in securing her release. Ms Prime was working as a consultant on a World Bank-funded project in Yemen. She was captured, along with her translator Sherine Makkaoui, as they made their way to the capital Sanaa on 24 February. Ms Makkaoui was released in March. The identity of their kidnappers has not been confirmed. Ms Prime's father Jean-Noel said he was "unbelievably happy" to have his daughter back. "She's in good health but I don't have any further details," he told the AFP news agency. In June, France said that a video showing Ms Prime clearly in in distress was authentic. Dressed in black, she appealed to President Francois Hollande and the Yemeni authorities to arrange her release because she was "really, really tired." "I tried to kill myself several times because I know you will not co-operate and I totally understand." Oman News Agency said the country had played a role in negotiating her freedom in co-ordination with "some Yemeni parties," after a request from the French government. No other details of the release were given. Oman, which borders Yemen, has helped to facilitate the release of other captives, including American journalist Casey Coombs, who was freed by Shia Houthi rebels earlier this year. In recent years tribesmen in Yemen have kidnapped foreigners as a means of putting pressure on the government to provide them with better services or to release jailed relatives. More than 3,000 people have been killed since a Saudi Arabian-led coalition began air strikes in March to drive back Houthi rebels. Aid agencies say a Saudi-enforced sea and air blockade on the country has worsened the humanitarian crisis after months of conflict. More than 80 of Yemen's 25 million people now need some form of aid. The fighting has also caused huge damage to the country's infrastructure, and the blockade has caused severe shortages of food, water, medicine and fuel.
