Chloroplasts are one of many types of organelles in the plant cell. They are considered to have originated from cyanobacteria through endosymbiosis - when a eukaryotic cell engulfed a photosynthesizing microorganism, which then took over chloroplast function and became its own. Green plants use complex biochemistry for converting sunlight into energy that they can use in forming carbohydrates (fossils) and proteins (living things). Photosynthesis is at the heart of this process because proteins called chlorophylls absorb light with an absorption wavelength between 420 and 570 nanometers while other molecules such as nucleotides, large organic molecules, or lipids absorb visible light wavelengths below 400 nm. During green-colored photosynthesis, chlorophyll converts solar radiation into chemical bonds that combine with oxygen and hydrogen atoms to form water and carbon dioxide ions. The oxygen released by the reaction combines with free radicals produced inside cells to create several compounds including nitrates, carboxylates, sulfate ions and hydroxyl acids that help make up the coloration.

The net benefit is about PS257m each year and takes into account the impact on public services such as the NHS. In 2014, 34,670 students travelled from outside the European Union to study in the UK. Universities UK, which represents higher education institutions, said the figures showed how important international students were to the country. It said the government must do more to reassure international students that they are welcome here. Universities UK said the government's latest net migration figures would "undoubtedly raise concerns among our staff and students." "This is a global market and we are competing with other nations who recognise the benefits of international students and want to attract them," said Dame Julia Goodfellow, president of Universities UK and vice-chancellor of the University of Kent. "We must do more to communicate that the UK is open to students who want to study here, and that we are keen to support them in their studies. "We welcome the government's decision to extend the post-study work visa to all students and look forward to seeing the detail of the consultation." Many students who come to the UK from outside the EU do so under the Tier 4 student visa scheme. The scheme was introduced in 2008 to replace a previous system of issuing a series of separate visas. It covers students from overseas who want to study a bachelor's or master's degree, or a post-graduate certificate in education, a doctorate or a professional qualification such as accountancy. Tier 4 students must show that they have enough money to pay for their course and living costs, and are given a "conditional" visa. They must then apply for a "confirmatory" visa at the end of their course to allow them to stay on and look for work, or apply for a student entrepreneur visa if they want to set up a business. The government has previously said that international students in the UK are worth about PS10.8bn to the economy. However, many people have questioned whether the government is doing enough to attract students to the UK. Britain is struggling to fill its net migration target of below 100,000 people a year, and in the year to June 2016, net migration was 327,000. A report by the Migration Advisory Committee (MAC) last year said the government's immigration policy should prioritise attracting skilled workers and making it easier for "bright international graduates" to stay in the UK after finishing their studies.

Thrombomodulin-dependent protein C activation has been shown to play a role in various processes in the central nervous system, including maintaining the blood-brain barrier, reducing inflammation, and promoting neuroprotection. Some research has suggested that activated protein C (APC) may help promote oligodendrocyte differentiation and myelination. Additionally, APC has been shown to have anti-apoptotic effects in various cell types, which might indirectly support mitochondrial function and overall cell health. However, more research is needed to determine the specific roles and mechanistic pathways through which thrombomodulin-dependent protein C activation may affect mitochondrial function and myelination in the central nervous system.

Indeed, animals can develop dental cavities, as evidenced by this image of an otter skull with visible decay. However, the occurrence might be somewhat reduced due to the natural abrasive action of certain food items that help maintain dental hygiene. For example, gnawing on bones and connective tissues assists in keeping teeth clean. Some species, like sharks, have evolved unique mechanisms such as continuously replacing lost teeth. Humans began practicing dental care after discovering the causes of cavities and developing effective tools for prevention over millennia. Our increased consumption of processed sugars has made regular brushing essential today. Modern diets may negatively impact dental health; losing several teeth before age 50 could lead to significant challenges, including financial burdens associated with restorative treatments. Just as with humans, poor dental condition in animals can impede feeding capabilities, potentially leading to starvation in predators or difficulties finding alternative sustenance sources. Teeth consist primarily of bone material vulnerable to acid damage and bacterial erosion when exposed to high-sugar environments. If these factors are avoided, teeth can remain functional for extended periods. Fortunately, having multiple sets of teeth allows for continued function even if some become compromised.

An average European worker tends to produce more value in a given hour of work than the average worker in an Asian country. A seamstress in Bangladesh will produce less value than a line operator at a Volkswagen plant. Europeans have far more capital (embodied both in physical stuff like the plant in my example as well as non-physical things like education) that allow them to be more productive, on average.','In a modern service economy most jobs don't generate a lot of wealth. Wealth generating activities, such as manufacturing, research, agriculture and mining, only employ a minority of workers. The bulk of workers is employed in wealth redistributing activities, such as sales, marketing, finance, administration, tax, regulatory affairs, etc. Those activities are zero-sum. Think of the economy as a collection of row boats. Pairs of "workers" sitting in each row boat are rowing in opposite directions and the boats stay more or less stationary. Each worker is fighting for his employer's share of wealth. Those opposing sides might be two competitors but could also be a government bureaucrat vs. a corporate bureaucrat. Now, if one side rows harder the other side also has to row harder in order to win back their slice of the pie. But the end result is that both sides are rowing harder but the boat still hasn't shifted position. In Europe, the government is more interventionist than in Asia (there are stricter labor laws) and mandates that both sides should row a little less hard. Since both sides are forced to oblige, it doesn't make much of a difference to their individual incomes, neither to the aggregate wealth of the economy.', "Culture - Europeans believe that life is worth living and that having to work every waking hour is basically slavery. We're not going to put up with it and neither should you.

Reactive oxygen species, such as superoxide ion (O- 2) and hydrogen peroxide (H 2O 2), are dangerous by-products of oxygen use in organisms. Parts of the immune system of higher animals that respond to reactive oxygen species have been identified as being important for protecting against them [3]. Immune responses include a number of components involving cytokines produced from specialized effector cells within the lymphatic system; these intercellular signals can be either proinflammatory or antiinflammatory [4]. Cytokine production is controlled via cell surface receptors on T helper (Th) cells. The Th12 balance between regulatory and inflammatory cytokines has evolved after decades of studies which revealed how different signaling pathways control their activity during development and disease progression. In general, an increase in the quantity and expression of proinflammatory mediators occurs when there is a shift toward a more activated state. On the other hand, it appears that overproduction of inflammatory markers leads to tissue injury and eventually death. Thus, regulators of inflammation play key roles throughout cellular physiology including regulation of homeostasis and metabolism.

I am an agnostic atheist and would even call myself antitheist, but my folks were religious. Not very, and they never forced stuff on me. Is a description of my experience with it growing up. I was brought up by nonreligious parents who identified as Hindu. My grandparents are Hindu and strongly so. Now it's a pretty lax religion with no central doctrine - which is why I'm not so much against it, but I am glad for that upbringing. It gave me things that a purely atheistic upbringing would not have. Primary the food and tradition. Festivals were a time for families to get together, brush misunderstanding under the table and have fun for a day. Sure there were some prayers, but we kids always sneaked off and were never any worse for it. It was like Christmas and Santa - except it happened multiple times in a year. And we had a little house garden on the roof, and I used to wake up early in the morning and pluck flowers for the prayer. It was a ritual - but it was hardly religious for me. That's not to say that Hinduism is harmless - far from it. But a lot of the ills came from the state of society at the time, and there are some aspects of the festivals I would have changed. And a number of ills in Indian society are as a result of Hinduism. But the religion is so lax that with a changing society the only things that have more or less stayed the same are the celebrations. There aren't social rituals or traditions which are atheistic in nature which I have been part of which had the fun-ness of the religious festivals of my childhood. Religion creates stories, an oral tradition, encourages fun for its sake, creates a vibrant culture that is communal in nature. Atheism is deeply personal and is not defined by anything. So in essence - having treated, and being allowed to treat religion as nothing more than some rituals with little of the actual devotion I think a lot of it is something I would consider worth preserving. Now I like the fact that these festivals existed and people take time to celebrate them. It's kind of like a fan convention - with great food and celebration. Diwali, Holi, Christmas, Eid and many more. Perhaps you can say Halloween, but it is a very exclusionary holiday (kids trick or treat, teens are in some weird limbo, college kids go crazy and it is less accepting of older people). Men's events are floor exercise, pommel horse, still rings, vault, parallel bars, and the high bar. Gymnastics evolved from exercises used by the ancient Greeks that included skills for mounting and dismounting a horse, and from circus performance skills.

The initiation of coagulation and fibrinolysis processes within the joint as well as in the bloodstream can be seen in both inflammatory and degenerative joint disorders. Inside the joint, it's probable that inflammatory actions causing tissue factor-induced coagulation pathway activation followed by fibrin accumulation account for the observed results. However, in the blood, the connection between inflammation (evidenced by CRP elevation) and tissue factor activation appears less robust; thus, an alternative, tissue factor-independent process might elucidate these observations. Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) demonstrates notably greater levels of thrombin-antithrombin complexes (TAT) in both synovial fluid and blood when compared to other types of arthritis. While there is a correlation between fibrinolytic action and inflammation, the heightened presence of TAFI in the joint—particularly in cases of RA—could shed light on the predominance of fibrin generation in this disease relative to others affecting the joint.

Peng was convinced that the war would be protracted, and that neither side would be able to achieve victory in the near future. In contrast to conventional, univariate analysis, various types of multivariate analysis have been applied to functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data. In this paper, we compare two contemporary approaches for multivariate regression on task-based fMRI data: linear regression with ridge regularization and non-linear symbolic regression using genetic programming. The data for this project is representative of a contemporary fMRI experimental design for visual stimuli. Linear and non-linear models were generated for 10 subjects, with another 4 withheld for validation. Model quality is evaluated by comparing R scores (Pearson product-moment correlation) in various contexts, including single run self-fit, within-subject generalization, and between-subject generalization. Propensity for modelling strategies to overfit is estimated using a separate resting state scan. Results suggest that neither method is objectively or inherently better than the other.

You may consume liquids from either side; however, if it's a cube-shaped container, consumption should occur exclusively along the edges to avoid spills. Round containers prove more convenient since their design allows for easy stacking without misalignment. In terms of efficiency, the round shape holds the greatest volume relative to the amount of material utilized. Although our beverage intake doesn't typically involve consuming from spherical containers due to impracticality, we opt for cylinder shapes instead. Historically, the production methodology favored roundness, making it simpler to fashion using rotating equipment. This shape also eliminates vulnerability points within the structure.

Today's glassware has roots in ancient cups crafted through various methods including pottery wheels, wooden materials, and metals—all favoring the round shape. Square or polygonal designs emerged later. The primary benefit of round glassware is ease of maintenance. While there exist square options, their usage highlights their inferior functionality. Tradition plays a significant role in maintaining the prevalence of round glassware, stemming from the fact that naturally occurring objects used as early drinking vessels, such as animal horns and shells, had rounded forms. Additionally, potters discovered that creating round vessels via coil or wheel techniques resulted in superior quality compared to slab construction, as no visible seams appeared. Similarly, glassblowing results in orb-like creations rather than square ones. Observing professionals produce wine glasses reveals that shaping occurs primarily through blowing rather than casting in molds, further affirming that the round configuration remains dominant due to simplicity in fabrication processes.

Twelve nations comprising approximately 40% of global GDP agreed upon the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP) but have yet to formally approve it. Leaders from the Asia-Pacific region convened at a recent economic gathering in Peru and committed themselves to advancing free trade agreements, even against former President Trump’s disapproval. However, the future of the TPP remains uncertain now that the U.S. has opted out. Reactions vary regarding how much involvement the incoming American government might demonstrate towards either the original TPP framework or its potential revisions. Despite this uncertainty, there exists considerable enthusiasm amongst the remaining eleven TPP member states to move ahead with implementation. From an Australian perspective, increasing market access across various sectors within these major economies would clearly serve national interests. While the United States cannot isolate itself completely from international trade, the current administration must ultimately decide based on what they believe aligns best with American welfare. As the soon-to-be inaugurated President, Donald Trump holds the prerogative to set policies according to his judgment. Nevertheless, fostering trade development and collaborative initiatives within the Asia-Pacific region are essential for mutual prosperity. Although disheartening, the anticipation is to cooperate with President-elect Trump towards common objectives such as fortifying security measures while promoting equitable, sustained, and broad-based economic expansion. Withdrawing from the TPP could signify a shift away from U.S.-centric global commerce leadership and possibly lead to stagnating growth amidst already sluggish economic conditions. Contrary to Trump’s criticism during his presidential bid, experts argue that the TPP had notable benefits for the United States.

Uber is having a very public fight right now with NYC Mayor Bill de Blasio, basically arguing that they should be allowed to compete with yellow cabs in a free market. But it turns out that that's not actually the case, and NYC cabs have been paying up to 1 million for the right to operate. Annual medallion sales have fallen to just 242,000 this year, down from a peak of 1.3 million in 2013. Last year, the city reported that the value of a medallion had fallen to 600,000 from a peak of 1.3 million. NYC has some pretty strict requirements for cabbies, including a knowledge test and a lengthy apprenticeship, but with new ride-sharing services like Lyft and Uber eating into their business, cabbies have been protesting in the streets. The medallion sales have gone down for a couple of reasons: a new taxi law has limited the number of new medallions, and a new credit card surcharge that has been added to cabs. Children's childhood experiences were undergoing substantial changes due to diminished chances of spending time outside, noted experts. They cautioned against potential adverse effects of reduced interaction with nature over time. Proposing the creation of an "outdoor learning center", they aimed to assist educators while influencing policy formation. Studies pointed towards busy familial schedules coupled with growing societal anxiety leading to decreased accessibility to natural surroundings for kids. Such conditions adversely impacted their ability to develop socially, emotionally, physically, and affected overall mental health. Hence, educational institutions should acknowledge the significance of outdoor learning in addressing these challenges. According to Sue Waite, a co-author and expert in outdoor learning from Plymouth University, the current inclusion of outdoor activities within school syllabi primarily stemmed from teacher initiatives valuing its importance amidst increasing emphasis on academics. She emphasized that without recognition and support from decision-makers, outdoor learning may continue to linger on the fringes of mainstream education. The study advocates incorporating outdoor learning into national curricula and suggests establishing a "policy-research hub" to consolidate research findings, identify areas requiring further investigation, and align such insights with policymaking efforts. Additionally, the report recommends implementing a "Framework for 21st Century Student Outcomes" via routine classes held in outdoor settings.

A new book from a long-time Android engineer offers a behind-the-scenes look at early Android development. This article features two chapters from the book that covers the startup's search for an operating system, and how it became available on Intel PC in 2001 (and why they ended up with QNX instead). The first part of "Inside Google Mobile" is about what companies like Facebook and Yelp were doing to find Android competitors back when there was only one OS out by Microsoft: Windows CE. Back then, Google had just launched their own browser called Chrome, which was quite popular among developers but hardly used outside the company itself. By contrast, Windows Phone 7 looked set to become a serious competitor against iOS as soon as Apple released iPhone 3G - but Google never made any effort to actually develop apps for WP7. Google Eric Schmidt Asks Why There Aren't Great Apps For The New Smartphone Era 1of2 Back Then, Google's Eric Schmidt asked himself "Why aren't there great mobile apps?" In his book Inside Google Mobile, he goes into more detail about this question than you might expect Getty Images Drew Angerer Buy Photo Wait 2 minutes 15 seconds Play GIF BACK TO SLIDE Instead, Gmail cofounder Larry Page took over Android development to attract users away from iOS, which had become so dominant by 2007 that no other phone manufacturer cared enough about it anymore to make anything close to even a decent version of its UI. At around 1999 or 2000, Page realized they needed something better than what Palm had been putting together based on Qt for phones, since none of the existing platforms were very good either in terms of user experience, developer tools, or app selection - especially compared to Nokia's Symbian platform. At the time, Nokias were still the big smartphone leader; not too many people would have considered building a successful webapp store for them back then because even though they appeared pretty competent, most devices running those software stacks didn't seem to work very well anyway (they ran well on paper, but really didn't do much else), plus the actual hardware wasn't all that great either. And while there are some cool webapps that work surprisingly well and are usually awesome for getting your hands dirty with programming, I've found few third party programs that work reliably okayish on real world phones these days. Page decided BlackBerry was the best bet thanks to its excellent business model of selling cellular modems directly to carriers via licensing deals, unlike HTC and Motorola who chose to go with carrier subsidies and lower profit margins. So getting a strong relationship between Blackberry and Verizon was critical. It also seemed like the biggest barrier down the road would be convincing manufacturers themselfes to use BB10 rather thaniOS. "In hindsight," page writes, we] should probably have worked harder to get BB to open source Linux." But even if he'd done that, "it wouldn't have solved everything we wanted, as Linus Torvalds' kernel sources can attest." Existing browsers like Netscape Navigator hadn't yet matured into mature applications themselves, nor did Mozilla Firefox. Neither had Opera, although both built on top of the same underlying technology. Even after years of using IE, MS NTXP, MacOS 8, Win98SE, etc., Page knew there could never be a single standard for web design that everyone agreed upon. Instead, it was important to try different approaches until someone got it right... and after years of experimenting with various ideas, Page finally settled on a system that runs smoothly everywhere, has high quality fonts, lots of animations including backward scrolling, customizable backgrounds, rich media support including video, audio, and games, and comes bundled with tons of useful third party addons. He calls it the WebKit approach. As far as he knows, nobody has come anywhere near reaching WebKit's level of polish and responsiveness today - probably partly due to lack of competition during the past decade. Getting the balancing act right between performance, battery life, AND usability is tough stuff! It seems kind of obvious now that the perfect balance ultimately lies somewhere in the middle... and once you find it, things just start working beautifully. On top of that, designers started copying each others styles without realizing it and plugging them into their sites altogether. That led to huge forks where every feature went into separate browser engines and eventually cascading effects like alpha transparency in old web pages turned into infinite scroll loops across pages full of interactive content. Once everything gets out of sync, fixing it becomes impossible unless maybe you're willing to leave major parts of your site broken forever. Also, don't forget the inertia of millions of websites being built around certain older versions of the core HTML block structure. It takes several months to update such legacy code properly; meanwhile, hundreds of thousands of developers build new stuff using the latest standards, leaving poor compatibility and incompatibility issues behind. Those factors combine to ensure that almost nothing works perfectly on nearly any device ever. For mobile robots navigating on sidewalks, it is essential to be able to safely cross street intersections. Most existing approaches rely on the recognition of the traffic light signal to specify where the robot will go and when it should move. For example, a small robot can walk into a busy intersection without having to turn in front of the pedestrian if the vehicle approaches from behind. As is known from U.S. Pat. No. 5,935,872, an approach for man-to-woman walking has been developed. In such a concept, an operator is instructed to place a plurality of markers along one side of the road at predetermined intervals between pedestrians. When the marker sets off, she enters a sign area or other control section. A user then places each marker along the path that leads to the next entry point. The user makes a first stop on the path beside the marker before crossing the trail or initiating another advance. The user may use the skills acquired during this step to determine how long the walk follows the path indicated by the marker. If the marker appears to skip ahead, the user may proceed further down the path, until the marker stops itself at some point after stopping. The user's action motivates her to continue across the map even behind the marker as she knows the path ahead.

Typically, when using SR procedures as part of these algorithms, the outcome isn't utilized if its overall expense surpasses a certain threshold. For instance, in time-restricted predicaments, any routes discovered via the least-time SR method but exceeding the temporal limitation of the initial issue won't be incorporated into the construction of the solution by the overarching algorithm. Consequently, due to these limits and the fact that the Dijkstra SR approach unveils routes sequentially based on their costs, we have the option to halt the SR examination sooner—specifically, when it becomes apparent that routes with higher cumulative prices will be disregarded by the primary algorithm. By doing so, we can decrease the processing duration of the SR procedure, which consequently reduces the execution period of the main algorithm while still yielding the same end results. We call this modified version of Dijkstra tailored for centralized operations "bounded Dijkstra" (BD). Severe storms in December 2013 caused damage to an existing dune system to the east of Barkby Beach in Prestatyn. A report, to be considered by Denbighshire councillors, says there should now only be 'minimal' changes made as a result of this incident The stormy weather, on 2 and 3 December, was part of a sequence brought across from Scandinavia that also triggered huge waves at Porthmadog beach elsewhere along that stretch of coast. However it is at Barkby where the impact came home most dramatically with its extensive dunes being damaged or destroyed. Now a new report has been prepared for consideration by the county council which concludes that just small-scale adjustments need to be made. In his report, John Nixon said: "There are two issues - one around the original construction, which has since had further reinforcement put into place; and another about future management of both the wider area and any specific protection needed." He recommended work be carried out by officers together with North Wales Fire Service (NWFRS). The latter body will carry out risk assessments to guide possible alterations. Both bodies have already begun some preliminary investigations during January 2014. Work undertaken so far includes assessment of scenedismemberment photographs, topographical surveys, aerial photography planning permission procedure advice and initial tree identification works. Particular concern centres upon one area of high sand concentration west of Waunfawr Lighthouse and adjacent to the sea wall near the car park entrance towards the centre of Barkby. This section consists mainly of long narrow prefabricated sections held together by steel mesh and concrete anchor blocks placed within the sand deposit beneath them. In addition to this arrangement, two additional rows of steel mesh panels were added laterally up either side of this assembly. It is not known whether these panels were present when originally constructed but they are thought to have been installed recently after the storm event. At the time of writing, NWFRS personnel were involved in the process of removal from the site of the former dune formation and preparation for replacement. On Monday 28 October, the park authority received formal notification from the Welsh Government's Roads Agency confirming that the coastal defence scheme ongoing between Dulas Bay and Tywyn would not go ahead due to lack of funding. Responding to that news, Councillor Richard Williams, leader of the authority explained how important the project was, describing the loss as 'devastating'.

Scientists have found that planting large numbers of jatropha trees in desert areas could be an effective way to reduce the amount of carbon dioxide (CO2) in the atmosphere. A recent study has found that jatropha trees can absorb large amounts of carbon dioxide and grow in harsh desert conditions. This breakthrough could have significant implications for global efforts to tackle climate change. The study also found that jatropha trees can help to combat desertification - the process of land turning into desert - by reducing soil erosion and increasing soil fertility. This is because the deep root system of the trees helps to stabilize the soil and prevent it from being blown away by wind erosion. The researchers suggest that planting jatropha trees in desert regions could provide significant benefits, reducing CO2 emissions and improving the living conditions for people in these regions. However, the planting of jatropha trees should be carefully managed to prevent unintended consequences. For example, large-scale planting of these trees could have an impact on ecosystems and may require large amounts of freshwater for irrigation. The findings of this research are extremely promising, but they are not a panacea for tackling climate change. Instead, they should be seen as part of a suite of solutions, including reducing emissions from fossil fuels, investing in renewable energy, and increasing energy efficiency. Nevertheless, the discovery that jatropha trees can be grown in harsh desert conditions and absorb large amounts of CO2 provides a glimmer of hope in the fight against climate change. Planting trees may sound like a simple solution, but it could be a powerful tool in our battle against a changing climate.

Flexible or so-called "unbreakable" records made of unusual materials were introduced by a number of manufacturers at various times during the 78 rpm era. In the UK, Nicole records, made of celluloid or a similar substance coated onto a cardboard core disc, were produced for a few years beginning in 1904, but they suffered from an exceptionally high level of surface noise. In the United States, Columbia Records introduced flexible, fiber-cored "Marconi Velvet Tone Record" pressings in 1907, but the advantages and longevity of their relatively noiseless surfaces depended on the scrupulous use of special gold-plated Marconi Needles and the product was not a success. Thin, flexible plastic records such as the German Phonycord and the British Filmophone and Goodson records appeared around 1930 but also did not last long. The contemporary French Pathe Cellodiscs, made of a very thin black plastic, which uncannily resembles the vinyl "sound sheet" magazine inserts of the era, were similarly short-lived. In the US, Hit of the Week records, made of a patented translucent plastic called Durium coated on a heavy brown paper base, were introduced in early 1930. A new issue came out every week and they were sold at newsstands like a weekly magazine. Although inexpensive and commercially successful at first, they soon fell victim to the Great Depression and production in the US ended in 1932. Related Durium records continued to be made somewhat later in the UK and elsewhere, and as remarkably late as 1950 in Italy, where the name "Durium" survived far into the LP era as a trademark on ordinary vinyl records. Despite all these attempts at innovation, shellac compounds continued to be used for the overwhelming majority of commercial 78 rpm records during the lifetime of the format.

There is limited evidence showing a direct relationship between desmoglein 2 and kallikrein 7 in the context of pancreatic cancer. Desmoglein 2 is a cadherin-type cell-cell adhesion protein primarily involved in cell adhesion and maintaining tissue integrity, while kallikrein 7 is a serine protease associated with various biological processes such as skin desquamation, inflammation, and cancer progression. Individual roles of desmoglein 2 and kallikrein 7 in pancreatic cancer have been investigated. Desmoglein 2 has been reported to be overexpressed in various cancers, including pancreatic cancer, and may be involved in cancer progression and invasion. Kallikrein 7, on the other hand, has been implicated in the degradation of the extracellular matrix and the promotion of tumor invasion and metastasis in several cancers. However, current literature does not provide sufficient evidence that directly links desmoglein 2 as a substrate of kallikrein 7 in pancreatic cancer. Further research is needed to explore this potential relationship and its implications in cancer biology and targeted therapy.

During the 17th century, amidst the prevalent "continental rationalism", philosopher John Locke presented his significant perspective in "An Essay Concerning Human Understanding" (1PM), suggesting that all human knowledge stems solely from a posteriori reasoning—information obtained through lived experiences. He popularized the notion of the human brain being akin to a blank slate ("tabula rasa"), asserting that one's thoughts and beliefs evolve via experiential inputs throughout their lives. Our ideas originate from two main sources: sensations and reflections. Both categories encompass elementary and compound concepts. Simple ideas cannot be further deconstructed, comprising primary and secondary characteristics. Primary traits form the essence of an object; alter these, and you change the object itself. Conversely, secondary features refer to the tangible aspects that we can detect from primary properties. Though the physical appearance might vary, if the fundamental composition changes, so does the identity of the item. Compound ideas amalgamate single ones, categorizing them into substances, modes, and relationships. Unlike Descartes who sought absolute certainty, Locke believed understanding arises from comprehending how ideas relate to or contradict each other.

Historically, Microsoft would release significant upgrades for Internet Explorer concurrently with major Windows system updates. This approach impacted various aspects such as security, standardization, and others. Consequently, there arose an unusual scenario wherein Internet Explorer versions for Windows lagged behind their Mac counterparts in terms of both quality and safety; eventually leading to the cessation of Mac-based development. Additionally, during the era spanning IE5 through IE6, the integration of Internet Explorer into Windows Explorer resulted in its imposition upon countless individuals unaware of superior alternatives available. Furthermore, security vulnerabilities became increasingly critical and widespread due to the browser's extensive usage.

Internet Explorer 9 marked a drastic departure from earlier iterations, specifically IE6. Some reasons users may prefer avoiding it include slower page loading speeds, reduced overall efficiency when executing JavaScript tasks, heightened risk of virus exposure via the internet and drive-by downloads concealed within online advertisements, limited availability of additional functionalities provided by add-ons compared to competitors like Firefox and Google Chrome, and administrative permissions required for installing certain add-ons—which may not always be granted by company administrators.

On the flip side, web developers often faced challenges working with IE6 since it remained prevalent among certain organizations seeking customized software solutions exclusively tailored for it. As technological advancements surpassed IE6, these companies continued relying on it, forcing designers to spend excessive amounts of time modifying websites to display correctly in IE6 environments. Attempts to enhance cross-browser compatibility, known as 'standards support,' proved insufficient even with later versions such as IE7 and IE8.

Despite these drawbacks, IT professionals appreciate several benefits offered by Internet Explorer. For instance, group policies enable simultaneous configuration changes across vast computer networks. Although rival browsers are gradually improving in similar capacities, Internet Explorer remains dominant in this regard, simplifying large-scale network management for IT administrators.

First off, let me clearly define what I'm going to be talking about. I'm referring to parking spots in a car park, NOT parallel parking on streets. Backing in reversing into the spot. Pulling in driving head on into the spot. Backing out reversing out of the spot when you're leaving the premises. When parking in a car park, you have two options: 1. Back into the spot when you're entering the carpark. Drive straight out when you're leaving . 2. Pull straight into the spot when you're entering the carpark. Back out of the spot when you're leaving. In my personal driving experience (little under 4 years so not that much), I have found backing into parking spots to be infinitely easier than backing out. Unless someone is a dick and is tailgating you when you're trying to back into the spot, you generally have unobstructed vision as you reverse. If you are skilled, and know how to use your side mirrors (!), then backing into the spot can be generally done in 2 quick moves without needing any further adjustments to straighten the car. On the other hand, backing out of spots is problematic as you need to make sure that there are no oncoming cars, and your vision to check this is obstructed by the car parked adjacent to you. More often than not, you will need to inch your car slowly backwards as you make sure no cars are oncoming. And god forbid if you're unlucky enough to have a 4WD parked next to you. Furthermore, I've found pulling straight into a spot to be more difficult than one would seem. Maybe it's because I drive a SUV and my mirrors are inadequately placed, since I can barely see the lines on the ground when I'm driving straight on. But I can very visibly see the lines when I'm reversing. So, the issue here is that when parking in a carpark, either the entry or exit is easy peasy, while the other is "difficult." Maybe in an alternate universe, someone can invent a carpark layout such that both entry and exit of a spot are trivial. But right now, it seems that the "backing in" option is easier at both the "easy" and "difficult" maneuvers. It's easier to pull out than to pull in, and it's easier to back in than to back out. If everyone started to "back in" when they're at carparks, then it would be more efficient as a whole. Now I personally see 2 issues with my conclusion (trying to be as unbiased as I can here!): Firstly, in this example [here] and if you look at the red car, you can see that heshe has pulled into the spot. However, as there is no car in the spot "in front" of the red car, the red car can simply pull out of the spot when heshe chooses to leave. Hence in this case, there is no difficult driving maneuver required. But my counter to this would be that you cannot bank on this happening oftenly, unless the carpark you are visting is not a very busy one. Secondly, for the less skilled drivers, both backing in and out would be difficult and time consuming. However, depending on the customs of whatever country you're in, oncoming drivers may be accustomed to having right of way when someone is backing out of a spot. Hence the lack of skill of some drivers would not be a detriment to others. On the other hand, if a less skillful driver is trying to back into a spot, oncoming drivers will have to wait for the parking driver to finish before they can go on their way. Despite these two points I just discussed, I still think that the backing in option is much more efficient than pulling in. In Czech, grammatical cases are employed to express the role of words within sentences, offering flexibility in their arrangement, unlike English which depends heavily on word sequence. Being a pro-drop language, Czech allows an intransitive statement to comprise solely of a verb since the subject's details are incorporated within it. Clitics, mainly auxiliary verbs and pronouns, are obligated to occupy the second syntax position post the initial emphasized segment. The Great Suspender, a popular Chrome extension that automatically suspended open tabs that haven't been used for a while, has been removed from Google's Chrome Web Store. Apparently, some sketchy developers were using the extension to force pop-up ads on unsuspecting users and start charging them money to remove those intrusive ads. "As soon as we were able to identify this malicious activity in our user base, we took action by removing it immediately," said Google's official statement regarding the removal of The Great Suspender from its store. "We have alerted affected users about changes to their browsing experience." What is 'the Great Suspender'? Developers behind the extension noted that they had added a feature called "the Great Suspender" which kept browsers from closing inactive tabs without user interaction (although that function was intended to be an optional toggle). However, according to reports, the extension turned out to be being abused by shady webmasters who could use it to prevent users from exiting or accessing other pages, forcing them to watch unwanted advertisements instead. This kind of abuse resulted in serious security issues and even allowed fraudulent websites to hijack essential systems such as passwords and credit cards before any warning appears. Google officially announced the extension's suspension after receiving over 97 complaints from users - all regarding payment requests made with fraudulent e-mails supposedly sent by The Great Suspender itself. Some of these users reportedly paid up to 3.50 each for the privilege of getting rid of the annoying ads. And because of that fact alone, Google couldn't keep the extension available anymore.

I'm not an expert on firearms nor strongly opinionated about gun control. However, I'd like to posit the following: We can develop a biometric device that prevents a gun from firing unless it recognizes that the hand holding it belongs to its registered owner. Perhaps this tech could be integrated into the gun itself, so there's no bulky detachable lock or it could be a detachable lock. Whatever gun people prefer. Once the gun is unlocked, it won't lock again unless you put it down for some significant period of time. So if you're hunting in cold weather, pick up your gun, unlock it, then put on your gloves and venture out. The technology is reliable and does not jam, or refuse to unlock for the rightful owner, with any statistically significant degree of frequency. If it's unrealistic to imagine a device without a failure rate, we should assume the failure rate is the same as what we tolerate in other life-or-death situations (e.g. jet engines, airbags, or the technology comprising the gun as-is). I'm proposing that the U.S. government require this technology be installed for any newly manufactured guns sold to civilians. As to how this would apply to guns purchased by citizens abroad, or other technicalities let's imagine we use the same parameters used under current gun laws when it comes to other restrictions on gun design. While "legacy" guns already in circulation would not have the technology, they would inevitably exit the market one day. Over time, a larger and larger of American guns would be operable only by their owners. If multiple members of a household co-owned a gun, we could calibrate the gun to recognize everyone's handprint but anyone with a recognized handprint would need to satisfy whatever the current law requires before you can legally shoot a gun. I imagine this would exclude (for example) toddlers. The calibration could be performed by a licensed firearms dealer. This would prevent tragedies such as Newtown, incidents where kids stumble upon their parents' guns and accidentally shoot themselves in the face, and similar nastiness. It would not interfere with self defense or other legitimate uses. CMV.

The name Rijn, from here on, is used only for smaller streams farther to the north, which together formed the main river Rhine in Roman times. Though they retained the same general character as the other rivers of Holland and Zeeland, there was no doubt that this small stream bore at one time much more similarity than any with its larger counterpart; it flowed northward through a number of meadows and valleys, crossed a broad valley where the woodlands were broken by hills, entered the rich polder around Emmen, and took up its most northerly course along the banks of the high swampy plain between the walnut groves and vineyards that cover part of the district now known as Emmenland. The signs are evident enough: the narrow rivulet often becomes wide-spreading like a mighty ocean when swollen by heavy rains, while at low water it presents all the features familiar to those who have seen or heard of gales near the sea. Further east and out beyond Dordrecht we find very distinctly the trace of various former channels diminished in width by reclamation, so that even at low tide they are visible but dimly already lost beneath the rising waters. First off, UBI has much less bureaucracy. You don't have proof of income for benefits, no welfare offices, no proof that you're looking for work, nothing. The only criteria are "Are you legally allowed to be here?" and "Are you an adult?" (childcare is handled by different systems under most UBI proposals to prevent people from having tons of kids). This results in much less waste, and much more of the money going to people rather than salaries. Second, current welfare systems create incentives to not work. Right now, if you are poor enough to get welfare, but then start working, you might get pushed over the threshold and stop receiving benefits. As a result, getting a job could decrease your household income and will definitely cut off your access to healthcare. This is a problem which is fixed under UBI because everyone receives healthcare (through some form of single-payer system) and everyone gets the money regardless of need. In addition, UBI allows for some really interesting compromises such as abolishing the minimum wage. Since everyone can afford to live with or without a job and any additional money can be spent on leisure, if someone doesn't want to work for a stupidly low wage, they don't have to. Companies which fail to pay wages anybody wants will simply fail to get applicants, rather than people working for slave wages right now because it's all they have access to. UBI swings power out of the hands of the employers and puts it firmly with the employees, because nobody will, strictly speaking, need the work. If you hate your job, you can just quit and not have to worry about starvation or health. Eventually, as technology rises, all jobs will be automated. As that happens, UBI payouts can increase until nobody wants to work. Which will be convenient because there will be no work to be had.

In this paper we present the problem of saturation of a given morphism in the database category DB, which is the base category for the functiorial semantics of the database query language Datalog. We present a general method for saturation in DB which reduces the saturation problem of a morphism f to the saturation problem of a smaller morphism g, with the saturation of g in DB easier to compute than that of f. In addition, we show that our method provides a fixpoint-free semantics for Datalog. Finally, we present some experimental results that show that our method outperforms other methods for computing saturation of morphisms in DB.

Object detector training usually necessitpta large collection of labeled images using bounding boxes, but creating them manually can be laborious. This study introduces center-click annotations where annotators simply click at the center of a hypothetical bounding box around the target object. These points are integrated into current Multiple Instance Learning methods used for semi-supervised object location. Tests on datasets like PASCAL VOC 2007 and MS COCO indicate that our method produces superior detectors compared to other weakly supervised approaches with minimal additional labeling efforts. Moreover, the performance aligns closely with models trained on hand-labeled data. Additionally, because clicking centers is quick, our approach cuts down overall annotation times by 9 to 18 percent.

Dean Owens, from Leith, knew that his great great grandfather Ambrose Salvona was buried somewhere in Inverness. After telling this to his audience at Perth's Southern Fried Festival, Inverness resident Judi Menabney came forward and offered to find the grave. Salvona's resting place has since been found in Tomnahurich Cemetery. Owens' research of his family tree influenced the writing of Dora, a track on his Nashville-recorded album Into the Sea. The song is about his grandmother, Dora Salvona Owens, who grew up in a circus that Salvona started in Scotland. Salvona was thought to have arrived in Scotland from Italy in the company of a dancing bear, sometime in the late 19th Century. Owens' lyrics of the song include the lines: "Somewhere way back there's a lion tamerAmbrose and his dancing bearHe's buried in the Highlandsbut we're not sure where." Ms Menabney works for High Life Highland, an organisation that runs archives, registration and family history services on Highland Council's behalf. With help from her colleagues at the Highland Archive and Registration Centre in Inverness she was able to find the grave in one of the city's largest cemeteries. Family historian Anne Fraser said: "It was great fun investigating Ambrose's story. "He turns out to have been a very colourful character - which may not be a surprise - but we have also finished up raising as many questions as we've answered." The staff at the centre found out that Salvona was married twice and was the father of at least 10 children. He was 80 when he first arrived in Inverness and was, at the end of his life at the age of 88, a resident of a poor house that later became Hilton Hospital and is today a block of flats. Salvona appears to been a popular figure in the Highland town. A procession of people carried his body to a prominent position at Tomnahurich following his death on 13 October 1917. The inscription on the gravestone acknowledges his career as a lion tamer. Owens said: "I can't believe the final resting place of my great great grandfather has been found. "I'm very grateful to Judi, Anne and their colleagues for all the work they've put into discovering his story. "I'm delighted they want to use it and my song Dora - which started the search - in their own presentations." The singer added: "You really don't know what's up there, way up in the family tree. And maybe there's another song in that."

Software development includes diverse tasks such as implementing new features, analyzing requirements, and fixing bugs. Being an expert in those tasks requires a certain set of skills, knowledge, and experience. Several studies investigated individual aspects of software development expertise, but what is missing is a comprehensive theory. We present a first conceptual theory of software development expertise that is grounded in data from a mixed-methods survey with 335 software developers and in literature on expertise and expert performance. Our theory currently focuses on programming, but already provides valuable insights for researchers, developers, and employers. The theory describes important properties of software development expertise and which factors foster or hinder its formation, including how developers' performance may decline over time. Moreover, our quantitative results show that developers' expertise self-assessments are context-dependent and that experience is not necessarily related to expertise.

Smooth pursuit eye movements can reveal valuable insights about an individual's behavior and health status. However, they might interfere with the effectiveness of conventional fixation-saccade classification algorithms under certain conditions. Consequently, it is crucial to develop an automated and effective method to detect such eye movements during eye-tracking studies utilizing dynamic stimuli. This study introduces the Bayesian Decision Theory Identification (I-BDT) algorithm, a cutting-edge approach for categorizing eye movements into three categories - fixations, saccades, and smooth pursuits - while functioning efficiently in real time, even with low-quality eye trackers. We have tested the algorithm using four different datasets featuring various combinations of eye movements, captured at a frequency of sinusoidal motion, and involved six participants, resulting in 24 test sets. Our findings showcase the algorithm's robust and stable performance across all tests and movement types when contrasted against a manually annotated dataset by an expert (recall: 91.42, 9.52; precision: 95.60, 5.29; specificity 95.41, 7.02), demonstrating a noteworthy enhancement over the current leading technique, I-VDT (recall: 87.67, 14.73; precision: 89.57, 8.05; specificity 92.10, 11.21). Interested parties seeking access to our algorithm and its accompanying datasets should reach out to the principal investigator.

Steam engines can be said to have been the moving force behind the Industrial Revolution and saw widespread commercial use driving machinery in factories, mills and mines; powering pumping stations; and providing transportation on both land and sea. Steam engines are still used today to power ships, locomotives and in some cases, electricity production. Steam engines use the energy stored in pressurized steam to do work. This energy is produced by burning a fuel such as coal, petroleum or natural gas. The resulting hot gases are then used to heat water in a boiler, creating pressurized steam which can be directed through a piston, turbine or other device, thus providing mechanical energy. Steam engines are characterized by their ability to convert heat energy into mechanical energy efficiently, making them a reliable and cost-effective form of power generation. Additionally, their relatively simple design makes them easy to maintain and repair, meaning that they can remain in service for many years.

A method to lessen the magnitude of this heating and cooling was invented in 1804 by British engineer Arthur Woolf, who patented his Woolf high-pressure compound engine in 1805. In the compound engine, high-pressure steam from the boiler expands in a high-pressure (HP) cylinder and then enters one or more subsequent lower-pressure (LP) cylinders. The complete expansion of the steam now occurs across multiple cylinders and as less expansion now occurs in each cylinder less heat is lost by the steam in each. This reduces the magnitude of cylinder heating and cooling, increasing the efficiency of the engine. By staging the expansion in multiple cylinders, torque variability can be reduced. To derive equal work from lower-pressure steam requires a larger cylinder volume as this steam occupies a greater volume. Therefore, the bore, and often the stroke, are increased in low-pressure cylinders resulting in larger cylinders.

The concept of prime number is so important that it has been generalized in different ways in various branches of mathematics. Generally, "prime" indicates minimality or indecomposability, in an appropriate sense. In number theory, a prime number is a natural number greater than 1 that has no positive divisors other than 1 and itself. In abstract algebra, a prime element is an element of a ring or algebraic structure which cannot be decomposed into a product of smaller elements. In group theory, a prime group is a group whose order (number of elements) is a prime number. In geometry, a prime line is a line that does not intersect itself.

This research focuses on exploring the symmetric rendezvous challenge for two robots placed along a straight path without knowledge of each other's positions or the distance separating them initially. Both robots follow identical strategies in this scenario. Within this paper, we introduce the Multi-Robot Symmetric Rendezvous Algorithm, abbreviated as M S R, which builds upon our previously developed Symmetric Rendezvous Algorithm (S R). Our investigation encompasses both simultaneous (synchronous) and non-simultaneous (asynchronous) instances of the issue. For the asynchronous model, we have devised the Asynchronous Multi-Robot Symmetric Rendezvous Algorithm, known as M A S R, wherein the robots initiate execution at varying intervals. Through theoretical examination, we establish that the competitive ratios for M S R and M A S R algorithms stand at O(n^0.67) and O(n^1.exeptly) correspondingly. Ultimately, our findings are corroborated via simulation trials.

Operationalizing AI has become a major endeavor in both research and industry. Automated, operationalized pipelines that manage the AI application lifecycle will form a significant part of tomorrow's infrastructure workloads. To optimize operations of production-grade AI workflow platforms we can leverage existing scheduling approaches, yet it is challenging to fine-tune operational strategies that achieve application-specific cost-benefit tradeoffs while catering to the specific domain characteristics of machine learning (ML) models, such as accuracy, robustness, or fairness. We present a trace-driven simulation-based experimentation and analytics environment that allows researchers and engineers to devise and evaluate such operational strategies for large-scale AI workflow systems. Analytics data from a production-grade AI platform developed at IBM are used to build a comprehensive simulation model. Our simulation model describes the interaction between pipelines and system infrastructure, and how pipeline tasks affect different ML model metrics. We implement the model in a standalone, stochastic, discrete event simulator, and provide a toolkit for running experiments. Synthetic traces are made available for ad-hoc exploration as well as statistical analysis of experiments to test and examine pipeline scheduling, cluster resource allocation, and similar operational mechanisms.

Conventional neural networks show a powerful framework for background subtraction in video acquired by static cameras. Indeed, the well-known SOBS method and its variants based on neural networks were the leader methods on the large-scale CDnet 2012 dataset during a long time. Recently, convolutional neural networks which belong to deep learning methods were employed with success for background initialization, foreground detection and deep learned features. Currently, the top current background subtraction methods in CDnet 2014 are based on deep neural networks with a large gap of performance in comparison on the conventional unsupervised approaches based on multi-features or multi-cues strategies. Furthermore, a huge amount of papers was published since 2016 when Braham and Van Droogenbroeck published their first work on CNN applied to background subtraction providing a regular gain of performance. In this context, we provide the first review of deep neural network concepts in background subtraction for novices and experts in order to analyze this success and to provide further directions. For this, we first surveyed the methods used background initialization, background subtraction and deep learned features. Then, we discuss the adequacy of deep neural networks for background subtraction. Finally, experimental results are presented on the CDnet 2014 dataset.

Females are born possessing approximately 1 - 2 million undeveloped eggs which gradually deteriorate over their lifetime via a phenomenon known as atresia; beginning immediately after birth. Upon reaching adolescence, typically there remains around 400,000 eggs due to hormonal changes causing surrounding tissues to encapsulate these eggs into follicles. Monthly cycles trigger hormone production leading to maturation of certain follicles wherein one eventually outgrows the rest. Consequently, this dominant follicle is discharged from the ovaries along with its egg for potential fertilization. Unfortunately, roughly 1000 other follicles perish in each cycle. In essence, across a span of 38 years, females experience the loss of between 456,000 - 910,000 eggs.

She vanished on 19th November 2014 and her remains were located over two weeks later in Hope Street, West Bromwich. According to the West Midlands Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), Cherrington, an electrician, lured Ms. Pascale, who resided in Smethwick, West Midlands, and Coventry, into his residence before assaulting and killing her with no less than 11 blows to the head. Presiding judge Melbourne Inman described him as "a highly perilous individual prone to extreme unprovoked aggression," emphasizing that he hadn't displayed any form of remorse or penitence. Evidence provided by mobile phone records indicated that Cherrington had communicated with multiple escorts, including Ms. Pascale, on the day she was tragically murdered. Increasing technological sophistication and widespread use of smartphones and wearable devices provide opportunities for innovative and highly personalized health interventions. A Just-In-Time Adaptive Intervention (JITAI) uses real-time data collection and communication capabilities of modern mobile devices to deliver interventions in real-time that are adapted to the in-the-moment needs of the user. The lack of methodological guidance in constructing data-based JITAIs remains a hurdle in advancing JITAI research despite the increasing popularity of JITAIs among clinical scientists. In this article, we make a first attempt to bridge this methodological gap by formulating the task of tailoring interventions in real-time as a contextual bandit problem. Interpretability requirements in the domain of mobile health lead us to formulate the problem differently from existing formulations intended for web applications such as ad or news article placement. Under the assumption of linear reward function, we choose the reward function (the "critic parameterization separately from a lower dimensional parameterization of stochastic policies (the "actor. We provide an online actor-critic algorithm that guides the construction and refinement of a JITAI. Asymptotic properties of the actor-critic algorithm are developed and backed up by numerical experiments. Additional numerical experiments are conducted to test the robustness of the algorithm when idealized assumptions used in the analysis of contextual bandit algorithm are breached.

We investigate GPU-based parallelization of Iterative-Deepening A (IDA). We show that straightforward thread-based parallelization techniques which were previously proposed for massively parallel SIMD processors perform poorly due to warp divergence and instruction scheduling in the operating system. In contrast, an interactive message passing algorithm enables us to achieve a throughput on par with single-threaded performance using modern NVIDIA-K80 GPUs. For this work we use the Python toolkit for distributed computing (Pycon) along with its cgi module to implement three different IDA implementations: Smooth, Humboldt, and CP2.0 cite22. To enable our analysis we instrument each implementation by recording the execution time of several instances over two GPUs in an attempt to capture both convergence rates as well as deadlock scenarios. Afterwards, we compare our results against theoretical guarantees provided by modern supercomputers cite8, achieving a statistical error of less than 0.04 per iteration. Our experiments are conducted under Linux OpenGL graphics drivers version 3.6.15 at a resolution of 1600x900. For all installations, CUDA 8 is installed but not enabled. While toll roads may seem frustrating to some people who are used to free highways, there are some benefits to having toll roads. Firstly, tolls generate revenue that can be used to fund road maintenance and improvement projects. Without tolls, these projects might be postponed or even cancelled due to budget constraints. Secondly, toll roads can help alleviate traffic congestion by providing drivers with a faster and more direct route to their destination. This can save drivers time and reduce fuel consumption, which in turn can help to reduce air pollution. Overall, toll roads may have some inconveniences, but they do serve a purpose and can benefit both drivers and the community as a whole.

John decided that he would try to learn how to jump higher. He found a basketball trainer in his town that would help him. After 4 weeks of training he was able to increase the height by 3 inches. When John started school, as expected there were differences between himself and the students around him. Most of them did not understand what it meant to have ADHD or ADD because they didn't suffer from similar problems themselves. One thing that John noticed right away was that their teachers often treated them differently than other children with special needs such as speech disorders or learning disabilities. The kids with these types of issues often had to be left out on their own but John wanted to make sure that he wasn't like that at all. As he grew older John learned about social skills and made some friends so that later when he went off to college no one called him weird or said he couldn't do something just because he has ADHDADD. He also discovered that talking to adults helped better explain things so instead of trying to talk to someone who was nearby he talked directly to his teacher more than once if necessary - this proved very helpful for him throughout high school. After graduation John attended Stanford University. In addition to taking classes there is he took many time-consuming vocational courses including Business Management and Accounting which are typically taken after your undergraduate degree (think IBS courses). He soon realized that attending a top university does not guarantee you good grades; as much as he loved studying music and getting involved with campus activities he still struggled academically. It was hard work but eventually he got used to it. While John was earning degrees in both music performance and accounting he continued working toward an MBA. During his time in college John became involved with the student orchestra and played the French horn while attending. His first job once graduating was with a large financial firm where he worked as a portfolio manager. For two years he managed over 40 billion dollars worth of assets - although it turned out to be too stressful for him to handle. Being exposed to several different fields really broadened his knowledge base and he saw a lot of similarities across industries. Still he knew that someday he wanted to go back into teaching or possibly become a professor. At this point in his life he realized the importance of finding happiness within yourself before focusing too heavily on others. We spend most of our lives doing what we think people want us to do rather than following our true passions. In fact, he believes that it isn't until you stop caring what other people think that you can find meaning in your life. This realization gave him a new perspective of everything he had been through. He then transitioned into a career with a professional sports team. During his 11 year tenure here he earned the respect of his co-workers and superiors alike. However, having lived through several seasons where the team underperformed he felt the need to get away from sports altogether. Although he was happy with his accomplishments during his short stint at sports, he missed being able to play every day with his band mates especially since they had performed together for over ten years. Since leaving sports John tried playing drums again only to discover that his hands had gotten weaker due to arthritis. More recently he began writing songs and recording demos. Eventually he plans to release music alongside friends and family members. Long term goals include opening up his own studio and getting a doctorate in education.

However, the majority of these methods work only for text summarization. This is because there are two main reasons why automatic QE algorithms need to operate on sentences: firstly, many natural language processing tasks require sentences rather than tokens; secondly, most existing QA systems do not yield good performance at query term identification and answer selection but can still perform well when given high-quality summaries generated from input documents. The current state-of-the-art research on documentlevel quality assessment has mainly focused on correctness (CQA) [18], which measures how much an output summary deviates from its corresponding ground-truth description or reference, while ignoring other important aspects such as fluency [56] and coherence [61]. In this paper we propose an end-to-end representation learning framework that simultaneously encodes multiple forms of content information relevant for the generation of highly informative textual descriptions. Our approach builds upon recent insights into deep image captioning [4, 5] by proposing a novel multi-task network architecture called CoherenceNet that learns three different types of representations related to coherence: lexical consistencycohesion between words (LexCohe), semantic relation between topics (SemRel) and logical relationships among them (LRC). The contributions of our method are: We introduce a new task-specific objective function designed specifically for document-level CQA, focusing explicitly on three major sources of coherent lexis: synonymssynonyms redundancy detection, partial matching with neighboring topics and similarity within each topic area. To encode lexical relations more effectively than single word embeddings alone, we employ both graph convolutional networks [21] and hybrid attention mechanisms over Word2Vec vectors [22]. We propose an approach to estimate the 6DOF pose of a satellite, relative to a canonical pose, from a single image. Such a problem is crucial in many space proximity operations, such as docking, debris removal, and inter-spacecraft communications. Our approach combines machine learning and geometric optimisation, by predicting the coordinates of a set of landmarks in the input image, associating the landmarks to their corresponding 3D points on an a priori reconstructed 3D model, then solving for the object pose using non-linear optimisation. Our approach is not only novel for this specific pose estimation task, which helps to further open up a relatively new domain for machine learning and computer vision, but it also demonstrates superior accuracy and won the first place in the recent Kelvins Pose Estimation Challenge organised by the European Space Agency (ESA).

In 1854 at Ballarat there was an armed rebellion against the government of Victoria by miners protesting against mining taxes (the "Eureka Stockade. This was crushed by British troops, but some of the leaders of the protest subsequently were elected to the Victorian parliament. Between 1855 and 1890, the six colonies individually gained responsible government, managing most of their own affairs while remaining part of the British Empire. The Colonial Office in London retained control of some matters, notably foreign affairs, defence, and international shipping. On 1 January 1901, the colonies of New South Wales, Victoria, Queensland, South Australia, Western Australia, and Tasmania federated, forming the Commonwealth of Australia. The new constitutional monarchy of Australia came into being under the Commonwealth of Australia Constitution Act (Imp). This had been passed by the British parliament in 1900. The Australian Capital Territory (ACT) was formed in 1911 as the location for the future federal capital of Canberra. It was formally brought under the jurisdiction of the Commonwealth by the Seat of Government (Administration) Act 1910. The Northern Territory was transferred from the control of the South Australian government to the Commonwealth's in 1911. In 1927, the United Kingdom Parliament passed the Statute of Westminster, conferring a large degree of power on the Dominions, including the Australian Commonwealth. Under the statute, the United Kingdom could no longer make new laws for the Australian Commonwealth without its consent. However, the Australian Commonwealth did not ratify the statute until 1942. Australian history is characterised by a strong emphasis on political and economic liberalism. The most important event in the 20th century history of Australia is the increase of economic ties between the Australian economy and the economies of the east Asia region, which started in the 1960s and 1970s. This led to economic reform through the 1980s and 1990s. There was less emphasis on government regulation and protection of Australian businesses. In the late 1960s, Australian Prime Minister John Gorton, Labour Prime Minister Gough Whitlam and Democrat Senator Don Chipp, were involved in an intense debate about multiculturalism in Australia. Australia has always had a very multicultural society, but in the 1960s the population of Australia had its largest percentage of people from British background. In the 1960s Australia's population was very different to that of the 21st century. There was a policy of assisted passage, which meant that the Australian government paid part of the air fare for people to migrate to Australia from Europe. The immigration policy of the 1960s encouraged European people from Britain, Ireland, Italy, Greece and Yugoslavia to migrate to Australia. In the 1970s there was a second wave of immigration from Asian countries like Vietnam. Multiculturalism was a policy of the Whitlam Labour government. Whitlam abolished assisted passage and did not encourage new migrants to Australia. This meant that the Australian economy had a shortage of labour in the 1970s. In 1972, the Australian population was 13 million. In 2009, the population was 22 million, with over 45 of the population born outside Australia or having a parent born outside Australia. During the 1980s and 1990s, the Australian economy was hit by a severe economic recession, which led to a change of government. The government of the day made large cuts to education and public services. During this time, the Prime Minister, Paul Keating, said in a speech in 1992 that Australia should not be a monocultural society. In the 1990s, Australia continued to have a large immigration program. The immigrants came from many different countries. In 1996, Pauline Hanson was elected to the Australian House of Representatives for the party One Nation. She made a speech in parliament, in which she said Australia was being swamped by Asians.
