He opened his eyes as the sun started to peek through the curtains. The crack in the ceiling was getting wider. It had been for a while now, but nobody else really looked up in that direction for more than a second or two. He, on the other hand. Well, that's the only thing he was able to see until someone came in to position him. It was early yet. He could tell that by the way the light refracted gently through the panes of glass, not yet searing his face. The whoosh of the ventilator and the beep of the heart rate monitor soothed him, as he steeled himself for the onslaught of burning pain that came as the rest of his body awakened slowly. It was Sunday. He missed the time when he didn't dread Sunday mornings. When that meant that he and his beautiful wife could spend time together, without health aides, without doctors, with as minimal equipment as necessary. They'd had great chats back then, as she gently massaged his contracted muscles, stretching his legs to relieve the pain. He'd crack a joke, and she'd squint her eyes, her left one closed completely, right one mostly closed, tilt her head back and just gaffaw. It occurred to him that he couldn't remember the last time he'd seen her smile. He'd queued up a couple of zingers on his speech device, waiting for the right time to let them go, but they sat idle much of the time, like his device itself. She had recently put that in the closet, declaring the voice harsh and mechanical; too painful to listen to. He tried to please her, mouthing his words silently, but she wasn't adept at lip reading, so he spent a lot of energy trying to get his point across. More and more it seemed as though she was trying to mute him. Pretend like he wasn't there. They had gotten more hours from the agency; he had agreed to go into respite care for two weeks every summer. But it hadn't helped. Every day, he could feel her slipping further and further away from him. The door to his room opened slowly. She looked exhausted, deep purple bags under her eyes almost made it look like he'd punched her. The way she looked through him this morning chilled him to the bone. She mashed the button on the bed that sat him up, way too fast. The raw fear running through his veins caused his arms to contract inwards, towards his chest. His hands in fists so tight blood started dripping down his palms. His arms, she noticed. The way they were positioned made it hard for her to maneuver him onto the lift to get him to the bathroom. She huffed and roughly pried his arms away from his chest. He opened his mouth in a silent scream. His arms snapped back to their original position, contracting so tightly he was afraid his tendons would snap. She veritably threw him onto the lift, which carried him slowly and steadily into the bathroom. His body slumped to the left, almost falling out of the hoist. Damn, she had done an ugly job with the positioning. Her hands slipped as she was guiding him onto the bath chair and he could sense his legs slowly sliding out from underneath him. He tried getting her attention as she turned her back to grab the shampoo, but as he did, his mouth dipped below the waterline, and water started pouring into his lungs. His eyes stared up at her, pleadingly. Water gurgled out of his mouth as his lips turned blue. She stared back at him, as if willing him to fight back. " What a shame, " she sighed, as his vision dimmed, " Out of all the decisions you could have made today, you chose to die. "

Laura fumbled to unlatch the carabiner from her belt loop and separate her apartment key from the half dozen others that dangled from it. Her arms seemed to be shaking independent of her body. Finally, she found the small brass key among the others and held it out steadily with both hands. The world around the key twisted and distorted, corrupted by the entire bottle of wine that was meant to be shared with Abby and the tears that seemed endless. Makeup ran and smeared down her cheeks as if it was insoluble with such a wretched shell of a woman. Voices echoed in her head; " How stupid are you? You'll never be good enough for her. No wonder she wants nothing to do with you. " Inside the apartment that she wouldn't let anyone else see sat dirty dishes piled high in the sink, a hill of trash surrounding the bin she'd promised she would take out once a week, and empty liquor bottles that represented every spare penny she'd ever earned. Laura threw her keys onto the floor and dove for the first bottle within reach, sticking her tongue out and hoping for one final drop, but finding none. " Look at this place. You're pathetic. You're no better than the filth you live in. " With a tormented cry, she threw the glass bottle at the hardwood floor where it shattered into a million fragments and spread out across the apartment. Spotting a bottle across the room with two shots of bourbon still sitting in the bottom, Laura tried to bring herself to her feet, but her legs had lost all motivation, and she slumped back down against the nearby wall. Finding herself completely helpless to go anywhere or do anything, she broke down into a fit of weeping tears, snot, and spit. "Why is it always like this?" she cried out to her empty apartment. " Because you're a worthless pile of rubble. " The voices in her head echoed back. " You're broken. You're a mess. You let everyone down. You're barely even human. " Laura wrapped her arms around herself and rocked rhythmically back and forth on the floor as she muffled her cries and screams into the arm of her sleeve. And then, among the tears and the constricting pain in her stomach, came a moment of clarity. Laura took a deep breath and wiped her eyes and face clean. She propped her left arm up on her knee, held it out in front of her, and slowly began to fold the sleeve up past her elbow, revealing the faded hesitation marks from previous nights that webbed up and across her forearm like broken glass. She picked up a shard of the broken bottle in her other hand. " Remember, deeper this time. Don't be so weak. It only takes one good cut and all this will be over" Laura arched her head back against the wall, shut her eyes, and pictured Abby. She gently ran the shard up the length of her arm, getting a feel for the path it would take as she put an end to all the pain, guilt, and emptiness that she felt every minute of every day. Then she cut, long and deep, down her arm. The feeling was both unbearable and euphoric. She waited, eyes closed, for death to come. There was no such relief. After what felt like several minutes, Laura felt no different. She opened her eyes to survey her work out of morbid curiosity, thinking that perhaps she hadn't cut as deeply as she meant to. Strangely, the cut had in fact been deep, but it had stopped bleeding. Laura dropped the bloody shard to her side, stuck her fingers into the cut, and parted her skin. Rather than muscle and bone, she saw a stream of wires running down her arm in brilliant colors, underneath which were two pale plastic rods shaped like what should have been her radius and ulna bones. Laura gripped at the layer of warm outer flesh and pulled as hard as she could until it ripped off her hand like a glove. She no longer felt pain. She no longer felt anything. She held her robotic hand in front of her face, turning it this way and that, bending the digits and rotating the wrist. " You've got no soul. " Laura located what appeared to be the primary wire that ran at the center of the bundle, grabbed it in her human-like hand, and ripped it out. First, let me clarify by saying I don't support actual, intentional bashing of any kind, however: We see jokes about it (especially on Reddit) all the time: political correctness is reaching a ludicrous level in our everyday society. It is getting to the point where you can't even make jokes or off-hand remarks without being considered rude, distasteful, ignorant, what ever. I think this is not only not really helpful to a person or group of persons who are facing adversity, it is detrimental. It causes issues that could be making actual progress to falter and nit-pick all of the tiniest little problems they can find rather than strive for real change. It is inadvertently focussing on the negativity in society rather than trying to find a positive solution. It is my opinion that the only way to get past adversity in life is to toughen up and become immune to it and push your way through it. Real change comes about because of real actions. This post was inspired by the earlier discussion on the use of the word "cisgendered" and wether it is "normal" or wether we should then be differentiating the difference between diabetics and nondiabetics and so forth. I don't think this is a helpful debate overall. sure, if you are asking what gender someone is, it is okay, even good, to distinguish, but all I keep seeing around here, and in real life, and at an increasing rate, is how we all need to check our privilege and be more and more sympathetic; how white people can't relate to minority problems, men can't relate to women's suffrage, cisgendered people can't really understand what transgendered people go through... it just keeps getting more and more specific, and in my opinion, its just focussing everyone's attention on what is wrong with the world, and doesn't actually help us make it better. Adversity is everywhere, it hits everyone. I may be a man, but maybe my dad sexually abused me and locked me in the basement my whole childhood. That girl may be white, but maybe she was raised in a seedy part of town with a drug addicted prostitute mother. Maybe that guy is a straight white male from a nice neighborhood, but he was somehow infected with HIV and now he has AIDS. My point is, none of those people are going to get through their hardships by focussing on those things they can't change, doing so would only hinder their own growth. I can't help but think the same thing when I hear about someone getting upset about someone else using language they find to be offensive. Again, I'm not saying bullying is okay, but the line between what is considered okay to joke about, and what is borderline a hate crime seems to be getting thinner and thinner. In my eyes, trying to further political correctness is only babying everyone and hindering actual growth. TL;DR There is no relative degree of suffering, everyone has a hard life, and trying to force everyone to walk on eggshells all the time doesn't help anyone make their life better. Quebec seeks separation from Canada due to a persistent linguistic and cultural conflict between the English-speaking majority and the French-speaking minority. This tension dates back to colonial times when England conquered France's North American territories. Asserting its distinctiveness, Quebec strives for acknowledgment as a 'nation within a nation.' By becoming independent, they aim to safeguard their unique heritage and gain autonomy from the predominantly English authority they perceive as hindering their progress. However, contrary to their claims, there isn't a deliberate plot against them. If Quebec becomes a sovereign state, it may face financial challenges like debt accumulation and decreased revenues since the region presently depends on monetary transfers from other provinces. Their aspirations to retain unhindered travel to Canada, increased tourist influx, continued use of the Canadian currency, and participation in the Bank of Canada might not materialize. Probability suggests that Quebec could become insolvent within two decades and reluctantly reunite with Canada. Alternatively, forceful annexation could occur before then. Moreover, the likelihood of passing another referendum appears low based on present support rates similar to those seen in the 1980s. Another factor includes negotiating Indigenous peoples' rights and land agreements, who typically favor the central government over Quebec. Furthermore, considering the stark cultural disparities between Quebec and the remainder of Canada, particularly evident during recent elections where minimal votes went towards the Conservative party despite holding power, unity remains uncertain.

In between these two extremes lies a wide array of less extreme terrain such as the Cajon Pass area where the seismic activity has had an impact upon local flora and fauna. Zipporah Lisle-Mainwaring, 71, was accused of painting the candy stripes to "get her own back" on neighbours who objected to her property plans. She wanted to demolish her Kensington house and build a new one in its place A woman convicted of defacing white chocolate with red paint has been ordered by an appeals court judge to pay 1,000 compensation for inflicting "psychological distress" on her neighbours. The ruling followed an appeal against her conviction after she was found guilty at Leeds crown court last year for painting lines through pictures of sweets on to bars that ran along two properties close together in south London. Her actions were thought to be part revenge from being made homeless after attempts to stop developers building flats in her home next door had failed; but they left residents feeling angry about how much damage the unexpected marks did. One neighbour said: 'I feel outraged. How could you do this? It's like graffiti.' A second added: 'It seems quite petty. And what does it get them?' At first, Mrs Zipporah Lisle-Mainwaring - now aged just over 70 - admitted spraying some 30 cans containing the gaudy paint onto buildings near her Bloomsbury Road home where she lived alone before the renovations began. But when police searched her garden following complaints from other local people, she denied any involvement. When questioned again Ms Main-Waring denied saying anything to anyone else during the episode. In his judgment Lord Justice Gross told Lady Justice Arden QC there was nothing wrong with drinking or using intoxicating drinks as amusement, even if these resulted in drunkenness. But he ruled that Ms Main-Waring was not taken into account enough consideration when sentencing her for criminal damage because she hadn't appeared drunk when pleading guilty to the offence. He went on to say that although he accepted that looking forward to the future is "a natural human instinct," destroying others' built up hopes was unacceptable behaviour which breached public order laws. Appeal prosecutor Mark Easton said that he hoped the decision would make sure such deliberate acts never happened again. Mrs Main-Waring, prosecuted under the Criminal Damage Act 1971, tried unsuccessfully to overturn her sentence in January 2017, losing another bid after appealing against her conviction last May. According to evidence heard in front of three judges sitting in the Court of Appeal, the defendant became distressed while trying to clear out personal possessions stored above her former kitchen worktop so that renovation work could begin. Accompanied by her brother John James Main, 54, and friend Julie Roberts, 61, Mrs Main-Waring poured around 20 litres of water down their sink in a futile attempt to wash away traces of orange paint believed to have come from the same canisters used to cover the pink walls surrounding both houses. During cross examination by Mr Easton, Richard Robinson, defending, suggested there was no guarantee that nobody living across the road might actually find the marks offensive themselves. Under questioning by Jane Albin, Lord Justice Gross asked whether the women knew what the word vengeance meant, or took pleasure from making mischief. On Wednesday morning, Justice Gross ruled on his verdict, finding Mrs Main-Waring guilty of causing serious harm despite denying responsibility himself. In his written judgement he described the incident as an example of low level crime by deliberately injuring someone's sense of well-being and stability within their life structure, adding that 'breaks down social boundaries between individuals'. After conceding that she should have considered seeking help rather than carrying out the act herself, he concluded: 'Having regard to all the circumstances of (the case), I consider that you caused psychological distress without reasonable excuse or justification. You must therefore repay your victim... for the distress suffered by reason of your conduct."

One key figure in the plans for what would come to be known as American Empire, was a geographer named Isiah Bowman. Bowman was the director of the American Geographical Society and an early proponent of this new concept of "world government." "Bowman's vision did not focus on territorial expansion alone; he also advocated the use (of military) force to achieve hegemony," noted Michael Hudson, who is now professor emeritus at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and was a graduate student at Harvard when Bowmans' ideas were developed. "And, to further that goal, Bowman strongly promoted international relations as one means by which to secure control over the world." Toward that end, Bowman founded a think tank called the "American Pan-Atlantic Association" in the summer of 1877. The idea was to bring together people from all parts of Europe to promote cooperation among them. In doing so, it hoped they could pave the way for Americans to take over more of the globe especially Asia. While European governments continued fighting the worst civil war since the French Revolution in 1870, Bowman saw another opportunity: China had recently risen up against foreign influence and colonization. In response, Bowman organized conferences with European statesmen in advance of the symposia held in New York City in 1880 and Chicago in 1886. He took German leaders like Otto von Bismarck, Franz Koerner and Maximilian Schutz as well as Japanese Prime Minister Kanjo Kato to lecture participants about their own imperial ambitions. The most important outcome was the creation of the League of Nations. While it remained focused only on maintaining peace between nations, Europe grew closer toward this notion of global governance and empires began emerging across Eurasia. That led to the formation of the United States and its founding and subsequent wars of conquest, such as the Mexican War of Independence. For many years, this divided America along political lines: Republicans favored unifying the country while Democrats opposed it. But after years of political struggle, President Theodore Roosevelt recognized American imperialism as a reality. Its roots lay deep within the very fabric of the nation itself. As he put it, its aims were beyond the reach of reason or morality but it needed at least two things to succeed. First, it needed allies across Eurasia. Second, there needed to be some kind of global order around which to function. Roosevelt understood these two basic requirements and thus set out to form a "Great Game": his attempt to create an alliance of equals through diplomacy and propaganda. This became the basis of the U.S.-China relationship going forward. There are good reasons why the rise of French nationalism and British colonialism during the same time period coincided with the emergence of American empire. They both sought to establish spheres of influence across Eurasia and show off how powerful they were to those outside of them. And while France and Britain each won significant victories abroad in their respective empires, they failed ultimately because of internal strife that eventually forced them to abandon their goals. President Woodrow Wilson, however, managed to escape that fate. Although in opposition to Roosevelt, he maintained a close friendship with Germany and remained a staunch opponent of Anglo Colonialism. After his election to office in 1920, Wilson worked tirelessly to maintain that cordiality in both economic and diplomatic terms. By the end of World War II, the United States had become the largest economy on earth. It boasted the second-largest military budget in history behind only Great Britain. As a result, it was able to sustain its position as the dominant player in world affairs without major effort. Wilson also saw the benefits of pursuing an imperial strategy: by combining military power and financial might into a single entity, Washington could build alliances across the world to combat any potential threats posed to its self-interests. Not surprisingly, this served as a useful playbook for American presidents past and present.

In Afghanistan, the mujahideen's victory against the Soviet Union in the 1980s did not lead to justice and prosperity, due to a vicious and destructive civil war between political and ethnic rivals. But the mujahideen's successes created political space in which the Taliban were able to come to power. A Taliban victory would not lead to justice and prosperity either, because it would be a brutal, misogynist, theocratic state, enforcing strict Sharia law. It would be a regime that, among other things, would reimpose many of the restrictions on women's lives that were removed in the wake of the Soviet withdrawal. In Pakistan, the military's decision to join with the United States in a war against Al Qaeda and the Taliban has weakened the military's grip on civilian politics. The country has elected a civilian president, even if he is not as independent as we would like. But the military is not the only institution that has to be reformed in Pakistan. The country's weak civilian institutions and the grip of the tribal elites on the political process have kept Pakistan from achieving a more just and democratic society. Afghanistan and Pakistan are not the only countries that have seen the spread of Islamist violence. But they are the only ones that have a central role in our struggle against terrorism. So we must think carefully about the best way to help those countries achieve the justice and prosperity that most people there crave, and make sure that our own actions do not unintentionally prevent that goal from being achieved. To see the full story, check out "Pakistan and Afghanistan: Two Ticking Time Bombs" by Stephen P. Cohen and Sarah Holewinski in Foreign Policy.

Your body temperature, which typically hovers around 37 degrees Celsius, is maintained through a state of equilibrium. This involves generating heat from various bodily functions necessary for survival while simultaneously losing heat to the surrounding environment. To sustain a consistent body temperature, these two processes must be balanced. The disparity between your internal temperature and that of the ambient air plays a crucial role in dictating the speed at which heat is dissipated. When the external temperature approaches your internal temperature closely, you may not be able to shed heat quickly enough without perspiring. Recent advances in deep learning have made it possible to quantify urban metrics at fine resolution, and over large extents using street-level images. Here, we focus on measuring urban tree cover using Google Street View (GSV) images. First, we provide a small-scale labelled validation dataset and propose standard metrics to compare the performance of automated estimations of street tree cover using GSV. We apply state-of-the-art deep learning models, and compare their performance to a previously established benchmark of an unsupervised method. Our training procedure for deep learning models is novel; we utilize the abundance of openly available and similarly labelled street-level image datasets to pre-train our model. We then perform additional training on a small training dataset consisting of GSV images. We find that deep learning models significantly outperform the unsupervised benchmark method. Our semantic segmentation model increased mean intersection-over-union (IoU) from 44.10 to 60.42 relative to the unsupervised method and our end-to-end model decreased Mean Absolute Error from 10.04 to 4.67. We also employ a recently developed method called gradient-weighted class activation map (Grad-CAM) to interpret the features learned by the end-to-end model. This technique confirms that the end-to-end model has accurately learned to identify tree cover area as key features for predicting percentage tree cover. Our paper provides an example of applying advanced deep learning techniques on a large-scale, geo-tagged and image-based dataset to efficiently estimate important urban metrics. The results demonstrate that deep learning models are highly accurate, can be interpretable, and can also be efficient in terms of data-labelling effort and computational resources.

In this paper, we present a novel attack against authorship attribution ofsource code. We exploit that recent attribution methods rest on machinelearning and thus can be deceived by adversarial examples of source code. Ourattack performs a series of semantics-preserving code transformations thatmislead learning-based attribution but appear plausible to a developer. Theattack is guided by Monte-Carlo tree search that enables us to operate in thediscrete domain of source code. In an empirical evaluation with source codefrom 204 programmers, we demonstrate that our attack has a substantial effecton two recent attribution methods, whose accuracy drops from over 88 to 1under attack. Furthermore, we show that our attack can imitate the coding styleof developers with high accuracy and thereby induce false attributions. Weconclude that current approaches for authorship attribution are inappropriatefor practical application and there is a need for resilient analysistechniques.

Yes. If you use a one-time-pad you can encrypt something in such a way that it absolutely cannot be decrypted unless you have the key. It's actually an incredibly simple process, but nonetheless this is how AES works: Suppose we map all plaintext m to ciphertext c and v mapping all keys k to corresponding desymetric keys dk derived from them. Then simply pick some message M with length L (say 16 bytes) and "encrypt" it as follows: x DesEnc (M). We now apply our encoding function f which maps every byte of input into between 0..255 values. So for example if an ASCII character had value 96 then f will return 97 or 255 depending on whether m 128. Next take each bit of the encrypted text and write its position in binary using only bits 1 through 8 inclusive. For instance suppose first bit was 1 so decimal representation would be 00100101b, then set every other bit except the last two based on where there might previously been ones: 10100011110b - 11101111100b. The resulting number is called's' since we started by writing everything in base 2, e.g., means s31687. Note that while the original encryption scheme uses modulo arithmetic in practice most people just stick to multiples of 4 to simplify things - I'm sticking to in base 10 here because doing otherwise makes code diagrams look rather weird:P Repeating last stage... Now perform another DES Encryption operation, but this time map the output back to the actual plaintext using the same fixed transformation list used to convert ciphertext to plaintext above. In fact it will work even if we didn't know any of the keys; we just need to make sure we always do the translation correctly. Finally add up all these numbers together, strip off leading zeros and voila! You've created a cipher whose strength depends solely on the block size chosen when you prepared your secret key and thus can apparently not be cracked without knowing what the exact key word is. This type of construction has become known as "one-way encryption." The reason why nobody really ever bothered developing anything like this is that it requires two completely different modes of thinking about data processing: One where instead of transforming data randomly it transforms it deterministically according to a certain rule based on string manipulation, i.e, sorta quasi-linear algebraic stuff (which seems quite complicated and arcane), and a second mode where instead of applying transformations continuously fairly new blocks are always added yielding a fully random looking result. " A woman " said the old man, hand absently fondling the worn silver revolver as he looked across the table at the youth. " What? I'm right aren't I? " asked the old man, dragging his thumb downwards in a flick, spinning the barrel around with a whirring hypnotic sound. The old man grinned at his young companion, tobacco stained teeth gleaming from behind his ragged silver moustache. The youth nodded his assent, hair matted to his head with sweat, upper lip quivering slightly as he watched the old man spin the barrel of the pistol, over and over. " Yeah, I guess so, but you know not just that " he spoke now, voice firmer as he trod once more on familiar ground. Comforting respite from this chaotic, yammering jungle of humanity where he found himself. The old man grinned a feral grin suddenly and rapidly raised the pistol to his temple. The noise of the crowed stilled with a pop as the atmosphere fled at one hundred breaths all held at once. The old man gazed into his young mirrors clear blue eyes with his yellowing bloodshot green. Smiling wider as his finger tightened on the trigger. All movement in the room ceased, every heart skipped a beat, all eyes stared unblinking on his face. A click. The crowd erupted. Foreign voices shouting over one another, money passed this way and that, shouted lamentations and celebrations raised a cacophony of sound. The old man grinned again, in relief this time and slid the gun across the table to the youth. " She break your heart? " asked the old man, quaffing from a filthy bottle of local whisky at his elbow, hissing his satisfaction as it burned down his throat. The youth didn't answer, eyes pinning the pistol to the uneven boards of the roughhewn table. At the exhortations of the crowd he reached a shaking hand and gripped the tape wrapped handle of the gun drawing it to his chest where he cradled it in both of his quivering hands. " No, I, err, I broke hers " he spoke still staring at the weapon clasped now like a baby bird to the filthy stained yellow of his singlet. " Oh, ho ho " chortled the old man. " Doesn't seem hardly a reason to end up here in this little piece of hell. You must have done something bad, something really bad ." The young man nodded slightly head wobbling crookedly on a neck gone to loose taffy with the heat and his terror. The crowd chanted now, baying for blood, begging and screaming with foreign voice for him to raise the gleaming instrument to his head. England's Chester Zoo and a tissue bank called Nature's SAFE have partnered up to cryogenically freeze genetic material from animals that pass away at the zoo. The preserved material could one day be used to clone endangered species. The Chester Zoo has been freezing animal tissue for two years. The material is stored in a nitrogen-cooled tank and can be preserved for hundreds of years. So far, the zoo has stored material from more than 100 species. The genetic material is collected from animals that have died from natural causes, like old age, as well as those that have been euthanized, usually because of illness. Chester Zoo's Dr. Nick Davis, who is the zoo's director of conservation and science, said it's "a bit like saving money in the bank." "The idea is to try and preserve as many different species as possible," he said. "We're very keen to do our best to preserve the genetics of a species that we can't preserve the animal itself." Davis believes that cloning may one day be a conservation tool to help repopulate species that have become endangered. "I think it's a really exciting opportunity to help safeguard the future of endangered species," he said. But he added that the zoo doesn't advocate cloning for reasons other than conservation. "I don't think that cloning is a sensible way of producing a healthy, successful animal," he said. "It's not an exact science by any means, so you have to have very good reasons and you have to be very confident that you're doing it for the right reasons."

In response, we present a consistent methodology for encoding whole graphs into features that enhance the precision of both CNN models and conventional graph kernel techniques when paired with an SVM classaire. Our contribution marks a breakthrough in scalable, unsupervised acquisition of cutting-edge graph representations without reliance on specific tasks.

My arguments are: 1. There's no logical reason for CP possession to be treated differently from possession of any other crime video 2. Re-victimization of the victim is not reason enough to imprison the viewer 3. Decriminalization of CP doesn't effect demand for abuse and has off-setting benefits if it does The common opinion is that viewing images; even when they are disturbing, depict crimes, are taboo, etc., is protected by law and the viewers are not criminals. There's no reason why CP media is different from media of other crimes. Why is viewing media of other crimes not criminalized (and profited from through advertising dollars on websites) but viewing CP worthy of years and years behind bars? Many claim viewing CP re-victimizes the victim and because of that viewers must be imprisoned. Why can't victims of other recorded crimes call for the imprisonment of those who have viewed their victimization? It seems to be an arbitrary distinction. Victims in both cases suffer long-term damage and embarrassment but they are given entirely different rights. Secondly, if you're convinced that the victims of CP are a special case, appeasing the victim's mental suffering has limits. For example, if the victim of CP wanted the state to torture and murder the viewer, the state would refuse. Even if the victim claimed imprisonment wasn't enough and mental suffering was had as long as the viewer was alive andor free the state still would not acquiesce. The viewer still has rights that can't be removed at the request of the victimized. So, how much physical and mental suffering (via imprisonment) is owed by the viewer to the victim? Isn't it logical that it's the same amount owed by the viewer of every other crime to the victims they watched? Many claim that viewing CP will lead to more abuse by increasing demand but far fewer claim that for any other crime. Most would deny that viewing murder, theft, assault, etc would lead to more of those crimes - they would probably say that the correlation is ridiculous. Do videos of school shootings increase the demand for school shootings? And do they do it so much that viewers of school shooting videos must be imprisoned? I believe most would say no yet that same group claims that CP must be criminalized because those that view it will be encouraged to commit what they have seen. Also, isn't it strange to imprison the viewer for the "crime" of potentially altering the behavior of others slightly? It seems a strange principle that one could be responsible for the actions of others through such a small medium as viewing a video. Do magazines showing children in swimsuits increase the demand for CP? What about the bookstore that sells Lolita? I'd say those active producers of material have greater impact on demand than an anonymous consumer (and they get paid for it). Tangentially, I question whether or not increased demand for CP would lead to more supply. How much of a demand increase would be necessary for someone to abuse a child who wasn't already going to? My guess is an increased demand would just cause more viewing of images that already exist. The amount of people who would go from normal non-offenders to child rapists because of more non-monetary demand seems an incredibly low number. I believe, if there is a greater supply of CP produced, it would be by current abusers videotaping the abuse they were already committing. This could be argued as a positive. If someone is going to commit a crime it is better that they video it then not. Video provides evidence and identification of abusers and victims. If CP legalization leads to more CP circulation it may reduce the supply and reduce abuse. CP producers and victims would be viewed by more eyes that could potentially recognize them or other identifying details in the video. Law enforcement and concerned citizens could more easily find CP, identify the rapists and bring them to justice. Increased CP circulation could save a child from the crime they're scared to admit is happening.

This work presents and analyzes space-time finite element methods on fully unstructured simplicial space-time meshes for the numerical solution of parabolic optimal control problems. Using Babuska's theorem, we show well-posedness of the first-order optimality systems for a typical model problem with linear state equations, but without control constraints. This is done for both continuous and discrete levels. Based on these results, we derive discretization error estimates. Then we consider a semilinear parabolic optimal control problem arising from the Schlogl model. The associated nonlinear optimality system is solved by Newton's method, where a linear system, that is similar to the first-order optimality systems considered for the linear model problems, has to be solved at each Newton step. We present various numerical experiments including results for adaptive space-time finite element discretizations based on residual-type error indicators. In the last two examples, we also consider semilinear parabolic optimal control problems with box constraints imposed on the control.

Shana Grice, 19, was found with her throat cut in her bedroom at her Brighton home in August 2016. Her ex-boyfriend Michael Lane, 27, of Portslade, had placed a tracker device on her car, Lewes Crown Court heard. Miss Grice contacted police several times about Lane's unwanted attention before she died. The police watchdog has begun an investigation. A statement by her mother, Sharon Grice, read out in court by counsel, said: "We firmly believe her murder could have been avoided if her fears had been taken seriously by police. "Michael Lane had been harassing, stalking and pressurising her for over a year. Her life became a nightmare which we believe had affected her mental and physical health. "The brutal death of our daughter has ruined our lives forever. We have become mere shells of our former selves." Speaking after the verdict, Deputy Chief Constable of Sussex Police, Bernie O'Reilly, said the force had apologised to the Grice family. "When we looked at the circumstances leading to Shana's murder, we felt we may not have done the very best we could," he said. During the two-week trial, Lane admitted he had stalked Miss Grice and had lied to police in interviews, but denied murder. He had claimed he found her body and left her home without raising the alarm because he was in shock. But the jury returned its guilty verdict after just over two hours of deliberation. The court heard Lane refused to accept their break-up and was incensed when Miss Grice rekindled her relationship with ex-boyfriend Ashley Cooke, vowing to a friend: "She'll pay for what she's done." Prosecutor Philip Bennetts QC said: "During their relationship, he stalked her. He put a tracker on her car and followed her movements. "That obsession with her translated into killing her. He would not allow anyone else to be with her." Two days before Miss Grice was killed, she met Lane at a hotel in Hove to insist their relationship was over, but Lane claimed they had sex earlier that day. The evening before he killed her, he filled a red petrol can with fuel, but claimed he bought it to kill himself due to depression following his grandfather's death. The car mechanic waited until she was alone at the bungalow she shared with two housemates before cutting her throat and trying to set fire to her room. Prosecutors said one fire was started on the bed and another on the carpet, and Lane dismantled the smoke alarm in the hallway. After the killing, Lane withdrew PS60 from Miss Grice's bank account and went to check a lottery ticket before he went to work at SE Tyres in Burgess Hill, where he was arrested. He is due to be sentenced on Thursday. Mr Justice Green warned Lane he faces a life sentence with a "very substantial minimum term." During the trial, the the court heard Miss Grice complained about her ex-boyfriend to police several times. The Independent Police Complaints Commission (IPCC) is conducting an investigation into the contact between Miss Grice, Mr Lane and Sussex Police in the lead-up to her death. Mr O'Reilly said: "Within days of her murder I personally visited Shana's family to apologise on behalf of Sussex Police and we made a referral to the IPCC. "We have thoroughly reviewed all aspects of how we deal with cases of stalking and harassment and we have now taken on the learning and our approach is more robust." An IPCC spokesman said investigators had already interviewed a number of witnesses and further interviews would be carried out now the trial had finished.

The paper deals with the problem of deciding if two finite-dimensional linear subspaces over an arbitrary field are identical up to a permutation of the coordinates. This problem is referred to as the permutation code equivalence. We show that given access to a subroutine that decides if two weighted undirected graphs are isomorphic, one may deterministically decide the permutation code equivalence provided that the underlying vector spaces intersect trivially with their orthogonal complement with respect to an arbitrary inner product. Such a class of vector spaces is usually called linear codes with trivial hulls. The reduction is efficient because it essentially boils down to computing the inverse of a square matrix of order the length of the involved codes. Experimental results obtained with randomly drawn binary codes having trivial hulls show that permutation code equivalence can be decided in a few minutes for lengths up to 50, 000.

Other predecessors of the Reformed church included the pro-reform and Gallican Roman Catholics, such as Jacques Lefevre (c.). The Gallicans briefly achieved independence for the French church, on the principle that the Catholic Church had been established by Christ in Rome. The church owes its independence to the Great Synod. The atom core is protons and neutrons. The atom gets shot with more neutrons. It gets so heavy that it collapses and the strong force in the atoms core gets released. That means energy in form of heat is radiating. Also more netrons get shot at other atoms and a big variety of electromagnetic waves.', "You take an atom that's somewhat unstable, like Uranium 235. You then fire neutrons at it. Since the U-235 is already unstable, the neutrons push it over the edge and it splits into parts, releasing energy. But there's more! It also releases more neutrons. And those neutrons go split more U-235. And so on. Every split releasing energy. Sooner or later, you've split most of the U-235 from a huge block, and it's released LOTS and LOTS of energy.," "This is not really something that can be easily explained, but I'll give it a shot. Hopefully it satisfies your curiosity until someone more versed in nuclear physics comes along. Atoms consist of protons, neutrons and electrons. An atom is defined by the amount of protons and electrons it has, so for example Hydrogen, being the lightest element, has one of each. The amount of protons and electrons is equal. The amount of neutrons determines the isotope of the atom, so there is regular hydrogen, which has one proton, one electron and no neutrons. There are also the rarer isotopes, known as deuterium or (2) H with one proton, one electron and one neutron, and tritium, or (3) H, with two neutrons and one proton (and electron). Now, regular 1) H) and (2) H are what are called stable elements. They will happily keep their forms until the end of time, if nothing is done to them. But tritium is radioactive. What this means is that the atom is, in essence, unstable, and will decay into other atoms, in this case helium-3, which is an isotope of helium. As it decays, it releases radiation and a small particle called a neutrino. These decaying products vary, depending on the decaying atom, but all you need to know is that the atoms lose energy and emit radiation and particles as they decay. The time it takes to do this is called half-life. Most isotopes have fairly long half-times, and even tritium, which is considered quite active, has a half-life of 12.32 years. Now, there are other isotopes of hydrogen, with more neutrons, but they are highly unstable and can only be produced in laboratories as they will break down, or decay, very quickly. So, as you may be able to deduce, we can make a stable, or mostly stable, atom into a more unstable, or radioactive, atom, by adding neutrons. This is what splitting the atom is all about. Most atom bombs work by using nuclear fission, which works in the manner described above. A mass of atoms of a relatively stable substance (Uranium-235 with a half-life of approximately 704 millin years, or Plutonium-239 with a half-life of approximately 24 000 years) is bombarded with neutrons, thus transforming them into more unstable atoms, that will quickly break down, releasing more neutrons that will hit more atoms, that will again break down and release more neutrons, and so on. This produces massive amounts of energy as radiation and as kinetic energy as the resultant atoms generated by the splitting of a uranium or plutonium atom are forced away from one another. The forces between the particles in an atom are extremely strong, which is why splitting an atom can only be achieved by causing it to become unstable. The amount of energy generated by the decaying or splitting must therefore be greater than the forces holding the particles together, ie. very large. As the forces between particles in atoms are very strong, and it is possible for an atom to break down into two lighter atoms, we of course get curious if it is possible to combine two lighter atoms into one heavier atom and harness this force as well, and the answer is yes. That is called fusion, and as you would suspect, fusion bombs exist too, called thermonuclear weapons. They are often called hydrogen bombs, as currently they use deuterium and tritium (which are isotopes of hydrogen, as we learned earlier on) to produce the boom. Fusion bombs actually have a smaller fission bomb inside them to start the fusion, as it requires immense amounts of energy that could not otherwise be produced. But doesn't this break the first law of thermodynamics? Couldn't we just break up and then re-build atoms in an endless fission-fusion-fission-fusion-loop to produce infinite energy? The answer is no. Fusion normally only produces a net release of energy when the resulting atom is lighter than iron-56 or nickel-62. So only those fusion reactions that result in those isotopes or lighter ones will actually produce energy, and those producing heavier atoms will require more energy than they will release. Conversely, the fission reaction only produces energy when the atoms involved are heavy enough. TL;DR: In nuclear reactions, a subatomic particle collides with an atomic nucleus and causes changes to it. This releases a huge amount of energy, even if the mass that is converted is really small. The atom is initially split by shooting a high energy particle at it, ripping the atom apart, and giving it the energy to split and release even more energy. With three defeats in his previous six bouts, the Scottish boxer's career seemed to be on the wane. Italy's Michele Di Rocco, at 34 a year older than Burns, hadn't lost a fight since September 2007. He arrived with a record of 40 wins and a draw from 42 bouts. He left a lesser figure. The referee deemed the man from Assisi to be in no state to continue in the eighth round, the result of a welter of blows to his head and body and made all the more unbearable by the hostile acoustic energy generated by 8,000 Scottish fans. Surely, for Burns, this was time to shout about his record, the ideal moment to counter all those who had written him off and questioned the wisdom of him leaving trainer Billy Nelson two years ago to work with Tony Sim in Essex? No. Instead, the champion spoke of his disbelief at the ease of his victory, his gratitude that he was safe, of his thanks to promoter Eddie Hearn, manager Alex Morrison and coach Sim for believing in him, and of his desire to celebrate with a fast-food burger and 20 chicken nuggets. "When I got in the ring after the fight, I said,'You've done it! You've done it!'," reported a beaming Hearn at the post-fight media conference. "And you know what Ricky said?'Can you get a picture with me and Michael Buffer [the legendary American boxing ring announcer]? When he has time to reflect during a well-earned holiday, Burns will take immense satisfaction at being only the third British-born fighter, after Bob Fitzsimmons and Duke McKenzie, to be a three-weight world champion. In Scottish terms, his achievements must mean that he is in the very top tier of boxing greats, comfortably mentioned in the same breath as former world champions Benny Lynch, Walter McGowan, Jackie Paterson, Ken Buchanan and Jim Watt, for example. Burns' record stands at 40 wins from 46 bouts. Remarkably, 11 of those have been world title fights. Buchanan's exploits in the United States add lustre to his legacy, but while Burns may never have fought someone like Roberto Duran, should Hearn manage to set up a bout against Cincinnati's Adrien Broner, the four-time world champion stripped of the WBA title because he could not make the weight, then Burns could achieve little more in the sport. "There are some big fights out there for me," said Burns. "I want to fight the top names. I will fight anybody. I do super-lightweight comfortably and lightweight is still an option. I would fight Terence Crawford again if it came down to it. "That's nearly two years I have been with Tony and things have just started clicking. "I had a bit of a bad run in the last year with stuff. Who'd have thought I'd be sitting here world champion again?" Hearn said suitors could "make all the offers they want, we'll listen." "If they want to come with a sack-load of money for Ricky to defend his title against Broner in Vegas, I'm sure there are a few Scots who would like a trip there as well." At that point Burns quipped: "I'd be one of them." The lovely thing is, you suspect Burns was speaking in the guise of a fan rather than that of a three-weight world champion who could enjoy a profitable title defence.

We propose a compressive sensing algorithm that exploits geometric properties of images to recover images of high quality from few measurements. The image reconstruction is done by iterating the two step modulated sensing process which consists in first modulating the sensor with an auxiliary signal and then measuring the resulting sensor response at different phases (or pitches) of this modulation. The method has been implemented on three common sensors: charge coupled device (CCD), complementary metal oxide semiconductor (CMOS) active pixel sensor, as well as silicon photo diode array (SiPDA). Experimental results show that using only four measurements one can reconstruct the original image over a large number of pitch variations.

In the summer of 1521, Luther widened his target from individual pieties like indulgences and pilgrimages to doctrines at the heart of Church practices. In On the Abrogation of the Rights of Princes he contended that princes have no rights over their subjects save when they are willing; in The Babylonian Captivity of the Church he argued that Christ came not only for the Jews but also for gentiles too - a doctrine which had deep impact on European politics. He felt free to take up new matters because of this: "I thought it my duty fully to understand all articles and propositions concerning faith and theology." How far did his own theological progress accede with these broadening strokes? Luther's following reestablished him as the principal spokesman for Protestantism (for a while), then dispersed. His work was translated into more languages than any other source except Scripture itself, yet we know relatively little about what he read during those years before he took communion at Wittenberg on 5 October 1517. We do know something of his reading habits thanks to an autobiography by Jakob Spener. It is known that one day in 1518 Luther borrowed John Eckhart's Third Book against Humanistic Philosophy, perhaps needing reassurance that humanists were still regarded as heretics. Tablets in Reformation Studies suggest that there must have been some serious scholarly leanings (as well as ladies' handkerchiefs) among Luther's bookshelf, including works by Erasmus, Agricola, Peter Martyr Vermigli and Edward Lee. Four years later a friend wrote that Luther's library contained seven hundred volumes, supervised by Hermann von der Hardt, though the contents were entirely unknown. This implies that many of them belonged to the safe deposit box kept under the innkeeper's bed rather than being classed among the bookshelves. One of the few scholars who studied Luther thoroughly was Georg Neumark, whose book Notes on the Life and Works of Martin Luther gives us an insight to Luther's early intellectual formation. However, since most of Neumark's studies concern the later stages of Luther's life, he reinforces the impression that Luther spent much time travelling or studying alone, away from people. From the beginning of his career he seems to have adopted a solitary style. The first letter dated 14 September 1505 has become famous as Luther's soliloquy asking whether God could possibly love anyone else apart from himself. It makes clear that Luther preferred solitude and even rejected Jesus Christ as if he were in fact another person! There is little doubt that in his letters to friends such as Melanchthon, circulating privately after the Diet of Worms, Luther expressed similar sentiments. Thus around 1524, Melanchthon noted how Luther would write in isolation when things went wrong, particularly over doctrinal issues where he "pleads out loud." But we cannot be sure just what kind of religious education Luther received until we examine his earliest correspondence. When Luther arrived at Leipzig University in April 1512, he soon fell ill again. Writing home about nine months earlier from Greifswalder Oie, he said he would probably study medicine if he could learn Latin quickly enough. After this setback, he began attending lectures given by Gabriel Zwillinge, professor of logic, ethics, physics and metaphysics at Leipzig. As a leading exponent of Aristotelian philosophy, Zwillinge stressed the importance of natural law, arguing strongly that reason should direct our actions. A liberal arts master, lecturing occasionally in Greek and Hebrew, Zwillinge used Aristotle's Categories as his main textbook for teaching students. Normally, however, he taught mainly to students intending to enter the legal profession, partly reflecting the university curriculum targeted at apprentices. For example, the course included Logic I-IV (the whole syllabus for five days a week); Ethics II-III (also part of the weekly timetable); Physics I, II and Metaphysics I-II (all delivered two times daily). So although Zwillinge knew that Aristotle was considered suspect due to his attacks on Plato, he never questioned that the philosopher really existed nor did he venture further into questions regarding creation ex nihilo without proof. Unfortunately, for reasons of health, the majority of Zwillinge's students found themselves unable to continue with his lectures, so Luther attended less often than would usually occur through regular attendance (though he may well have heard someone give the same lecture at least once). Yet despite this irregularity, in February 1513 Luther asked why nothing bad ever happened to the best philosophers. We address the problem of using hand-drawn sketches to create exaggerated deformations to faces in videos, such as enlarging the shape or modifying the position of eyes or mouth. This task is formulated as a 3D face model reconstruction and deformation problem. We first recover the facial identity and expressions from the video by fitting a face morphable model for each frame. At the same time, user's editing intention is recognized from input sketches as a set of facial modifications. Then a novel identity deformation algorithm is proposed to transfer these facial deformations from 2D space to the 3D facial identity directly while preserving the facial expressions. Rapper Dizzee Rascal to Headline at Wickerman Festival 2021 The celebrated rapper, Dizzee Rascal, has been announced as one of the headline acts at Scotland's Wickerman Festival 2021. The festival, held annually, has a reputation for showcasing diverse and dynamic acts from across the music spectrum. This year, the event will take place at the picturesque site of Dundrennan in Kirkcudbrightshire, Scotland, from 23-24 July. Dizzee Rascal, real name Dylan Kwabena Mills, is one of the biggest names in UK rap and grime music. His debut album 'Boy in da Corner' released in 2003, won the prestigious Mercury Prize, setting the stage for a career that has since spanned almost two decades. His music has consistently challenged socio-political issues in addition to celebrating the culture and roots of UK urban music. Wickerman Festival has become a firm fixture in the Scottish summer calendar since it first launched in 2001. Known for introducing exciting new acts alongside big names, the festival has previously hosted artists such as Primal Scream, The Coral, and Texas. There are several stages for showcasing a broad range of musical genres, including electronic, indie, rock, and dance music. In recent years, Dizzee Rascal has become increasingly politicized and vocal about social injustices. Thus, his appearance at the festival is expected to bring a thought-provoking set of songs and lyrics to the event. The festival organizers are thrilled to have secured his performance. Stuart Clumpas, organiser of Wickerman Festival, said, "We're delighted to announce that Dizzee Rascal will be headlining the Wickerman Festival this year. He's an incredible artist, and we are looking forward to hearing his unique blend of grime, hip-hop, and electronica on stage again, showcasing his socially conscious lyrics to the world. We are looking forward to welcoming him back to Wickerman." The Wickerman Festival has always boasted an inclusive atmosphere, attracting music fans from all over the UK and beyond. With a focus on sustainability, the festival provides green energy, biodegradable plates and cutlery, and encourages patrons to recycle and leave no trace. This year the festival plans to reduce the environmental impact of the event even further. Advance tickets for the festival are available now, and music fans in Scotland and beyond are eagerly anticipating what is set to be a fantastic weekend of live music, featuring some of the most exciting artists of the moment, including the iconic Dizzee Rascal. In this paper, we propose a novel deep convolutional neural network (CNN) -based algorithm for solving ill-posed inverse problems. Regularized iterative algorithms have emerged as the standard approach to ill-posed inverse problems. However, these algorithms have their limitations, including slow convergence rates and sensitivity to initialization. Deep learning-based methods have shown promise in solving these issues, but most existing methods rely on fully connected layers or shallow networks. Our proposed algorithm utilizes a fully convolutional architecture, which can efficiently learn high-level information from low-level features. It also employs a residual learning framework, which speeds up convergence and enhances the stability of the algorithm. Additionally, by incorporating a skip connection into the network, our algorithm can leverage prior knowledge and improve accuracy in the reconstruction process. We tested our algorithm on several different inverse problems, including image deblurring and super-resolution, and achieved state-of-the-art performance compared to other deep learning methods and traditional iterative algorithms. Our proposed algorithm has potential applications in medical imaging, remote sensing, and computer vision.

Embedded in the thylakoid membranes are important protein complexes which carry out the light reactions of photosynthesis. Photosystem II and photosystem I contain light-harvesting complexes with chlorophyll and carotenoids that absorb light and transfer the energy to the reaction center. The photosystems are organized in the thylakoid membranes as a series of enzyme complexes in a linear arrangement. The reactions catalyzed by the complexes occur simultaneously, and each step leads to the next in the electron transport chain, allowing the transfer of electrons from water to NADP. The light reactions of photosynthesis occur in two steps: the light dependent reactions and the light independent reactions. The light dependent reactions use light energy to make the energy-storage molecule ATP and the reduced electron carrier NADPH. During the light dependent reactions, the absorption of light by chlorophyll in the antenna complexes of photosystem II and photosystem I is used to pump protons across the thylakoid membrane. The pumped protons are used to make ATP in the cytoplasm by chemiosmosis. The energy-storage molecule NADPH is made by the light-dependent reactions when electrons derived from water are transported through photosystem I and photosystem II. The light independent reactions, also called the Calvin cycle, use the energy-storage molecules to make organic molecules from carbon dioxide. Erkle never got violent, never snapped at him. He asked again for a few days, till Erkle finally gave in. " Fine kid, fine. I'll tell ya. No there's no sense spreading this around, as nobody'd believe you, and those that would, might kill ya. When I was about your age I ran away. Daddy was a drunk and mom didn'care. Same story you're gon na hear a lot of if ya stay down and out in these parts of town. I took a few hits from Da'on the way out, you see. Got cut up a bit. ," Erkle waved his hand generally around his face. He had scars on his cheeks and the left side of his head, though Trit couldn't tell which were from what, or when, they seemed so old. " Now, that was when I learned I's a mite sturdier than I thought. Grab that there bottle Trit. ," Erkle said. Trit picked up the glass beer bottle, not sure what Erkle had in mind. " Now take that, and smash ' er and get a sharp piece an bring it here. " Trit brought the glass over, Erkle held out his arm. " Now slash my wrist. Don't worry none now. ," Erkle said. But Trit was afraid. He didn't do it, just stood there staring at Erkle. " Fine boy, fine! I'll do it myself. " Erkle snatched the glass from Trit, faster than he'd ever seen anyone move. Before he knew it, Erkle had run the blade down his arm, sliced open a series of scars to reveal... green. And metal. Wires, tubes. Trit had seen his fair share of violence and injuries, that's not how a person's insides worked. " You... you a robot? I thought that was a myth, that them all got destroyed. ," Trit said. " Aye boy, I'm a robot. ," Erkle said as he looked down at his arm and flexed his hand. " I don'feel nothing. Just like back then. I knew it was wrong, knew I was different. After I ran, took me a few days to realize what I was. Not sure I ever got fully used to the idea. Went back and took care of my daddy, you know? Hit him so hard that he didn't get back up. " Trit said nothing. It was far too large a thing, the last thing he expected. That one of his only trustworthy friends was a robot. A light patter of rain began, sounding a discordant tune on the tin roofs above them. " Now Trit, you best not tell nobody bout this. They're watching you know. Looking. Not like I got money for a regular prosthetic, even if I was human. " Erkle sighed and scratched absently at the arm of his old wooden chair. He looked far older than he first appeared as his shoulders slumped. " Now you know. Maybe I'll tell you another story later. You should try and stay warm till this rain stops, eh kid? Judge Thokozile Masipa ruled in December that prosecutors could appeal against the acquittal. She had sentenced Pistorius to five years in prison for the lesser charge of culpable homicide, or manslaughter. Pistorius shot dead his girlfriend Reeva Steenkamp in February 2013. He said he mistook her for a burglar, while prosecutors argued that he shot her after a row at his upmarket home in the capital, Pretoria. The double amputee athlete was acquitted by Judge Masipa of both premeditated murder and the lesser murder charge of dolus eventualis, also known as common-law murder. In South African law, this charge applies if the accused knew they might kill someone but still went ahead with their course of action. Prosecutors argued that Judge Masipa misinterpreted the law when she cleared Pistorius of murder on the basis that he did not intentionally shoot Ms Steenkamp. Giving them permission to appeal in December, she said: "I cannot say.... that the prospect of success at the Supreme Court of Appeal is remote." The BBC's Milton Nkosi in Johannesburg says that defence lawyers are now challenging the judge's decision, and do not want the culpable homicide verdict to be overturned. On 13 March they will appear before Judge Masipa and intend to cite previous cases to back their argument that the appeal should not be allowed. Pistorius was one of South Africa's most celebrated sportsmen until his arrest. He made history by becoming the first amputee sprinter to compete at the Olympics in London in 2012.

Data is just a series of 1's and 0's. When something is "deleted," like others have mentioned, often it just sits there and the space is marked as available for new data. When new data goes there, the data is just overwritten. Think of it like this - if I arranged toothpicks to write my name on a table, and then you rearranged those toothpicks to write your name, where did my name go? That is essentially the same thing that happens once data is overwritten.','If you're talking about deleting data on a a hard drive, it works like this. There's an index at a specific place on the disc. This index lists the "addresses" of every file on the disk. A file is a series of binary ones and zeroes that starts at a particular location on the disk and it continues until the end of file. (This is simplified. Sometimes a file is "fragmented, meaning that part of it is is on one place, it continues in another, and so on.) When you "delete" a file, what a typical operating system does is just erase the entry on the index. When you "delete" MyExamplePicture.JPG, the corresponding entry is overwritten in the index and the address blocks that were assigned to it are marked as "empty" (meaning that it's okay to write data there when needed since it is not being used.) Now if you search for the deleted pic, the index is searched, and no result is found. It appears to be gone. But the file is still there. There are utilities that can ignore the index and instead look at the actual sectors themselves. Assuming they haven't been overwritten, it is possible to retrieve them. This is sometimes called "undelete." Some operating systems or utilities work differently because they can securely delete files. They go a step further and instead of simply deleting the index entry, they overwrite the corresponding file sector where the file existed with random ones and zeroes so that it impossible to retrieve the data - it has been overwritten. There are many theories on how to do this. Sometimes they overwrite the same address block a number of times (seven or more) so that even a very sophisticated agent attempting to retrieve the data will be thwarted. (It's theoretically possible to retrieve overwritten data due to minor fluctuations in the strength of those ones and zeroes on magnetic media like a hard drive. Multiple overwrites make this impossible.)

The word pharmacy is derived from its root word pharma which was a term used since the 15th-17th centuries. However, the original Greek roots from pharmakos imply sorcery or even witchcraft. However, the term pharmacy is a relatively modern one, the term pharmacopoeia being more appropriate for ancient medical practice. History Pharmacy has a long history dating back to the 3rd millennium BC. The origins of pharmacy can be traced back to the earliest civilizations, as evidenced by Egyptian hieroglyphics, where pharmacists were mentioned. Ancient Egyptian pharmacists were involved in the preparation of medicines, and they were called "prescribers of the gods." Ancient Egypt also possessed a pharmacopoeia. Many of the medicines used in ancient Egypt were imported from the Far East, such as the use of a Chinese herbal remedy for snake bites. In the 3rd millennium BC, Chinese physicians began to use herbal remedies, but these were still prepared and administered by other specialists. The Romans introduced a pharmaceutical school to the Greek cities of the Eastern Mediterranean. As well as studying the Greek and Egyptian classics, the physicians studied texts on the ancient Chinese and Indian medical systems. The study of pharmacy was a fundamental part of the medical curriculum, and in the 1st century AD, a library was built in the Roman forum in Rome to house all the texts on pharmacy. The first university in Europe, the University of Padua, was founded in 1223 by the Italians. Padua was an important center of the Renaissance, and this influenced the development of pharmacy, as it introduced new drugs and technologies. A notable contribution was the discovery of insulin by John Russell Young, in 1821. The beginnings of modern pharmacy can be traced back to the middle of the 19th century, with the development of analytical chemistry and the isolation of the active principles of many drugs. This led to the publication of many texts on pharmaceutical chemistry and therapeutics. In 1858, the first pharmacist in the United States, Samuel Bronson, opened a pharmacy in Boston. His son, Dr. George S. Bronson, was a pioneer in the study of drugs and the pharmacology of drugs. In 1880, he founded the Journal of the American Pharmaceutical Association, and in 1883, he founded the Pharmaceutical Society of America. In 1889, the American Pharmaceutical Association was founded. In 1893, the American Pharmaceutical Society was founded. In 1914, the International Pharmaceutical Association was founded. In 1928, the American Association of Pharmaceutical Scientists was founded.

Although deep learning has achieved appealing results on several machine learning tasks, most of the models are deterministic at inference, limiting their application to single-modal settings. We propose a novel approach based on temporal probability distributions (TDDs) that can be used for modeling many kinds of conditions in multi-modal settings with high levels of similarity between inputs and outputs. Our TDDs allow us to extend existing methods by combining them into a larger system. The aim of this thesis is to develop an efficient algorithm for efficiently computing a classifier from one or more feature vectors. The task is solved using convolution which does not require a memory leak or data processing overhead since it only requires a single branch per feature vector. This allows us to solve problems where big datasets contain lots of features directly without passing through any intermediate step. In particular, we address the problem of finding a signature-based model for image classification in geospatial data where both image features and related points such as roads or buildings have been included. To achieve our goal, we implement an important but difficult design choice: static feature selection when the dataset contains sparse features rather than dynamic selection during training. We then apply some algorithms to find the best matches among the selected feature vectors (e.g., sequential matching), and finally combine these result sets to form a simple classifier. Our method successfully performs well in all types of geospatially distributed datasets including text, images, and GIS datapoints. We present a framework for extracting proposed features from a large corpus of real time video streams of multiple frames simultaneously using sparsely sampled shape embeddings. The framework aims to exploit the robustness of many existing methods while improving efficiency by reducing the computational burden typical with these methods. To realize this objective, we first establish robustness criteria for each type of feature extraction and use these criterion to select optimal constraints for shape embedding. For example, for linear support vector machines, we consider the correct size of L2 secretaries and quadratic color gradients to extract key features from CNN filters. Artificial intelligence (AI) studies of visual perception rely heavily upon three main techniques: vision theory, object detection, and recognition. Vision theory deals primarily with light objects, whereas object detection concerns the identification of specific patterns within large scenes that may contain other objects. Recognition is about identifying distinct objects in complex scenes, either manually or automatically. However, all three approaches face significant limitations: they cannot reliably detect humans; they cannot classify objects correctly if there are similar objects; they do not deal reliably with motion; and they often fail to recognize human gestures because they typically involve a range of movements andor motions and gestures overlap significantly. This dissertation examines these issues from different angles - from the perspective of social cognition and artificial neural networks, from that of speech recognition systems, and from that of computer vision systems. We focus particularly on speech recognition, but we also show how these techniques suffer from questions of action semantics (i.e., when human actions occur). We argue here that these shortcomings go hand-in-hand with the need for improved AI ability to understand spoken language, which underlies the emphasis placed on understanding linguistic structures over comprehension. Finally, we document much work underway in this area and investigate the promising areas of natural language retrieval and active voice control in speech recognition.

He sat there, mesmerized, chasing his mind around in circles, as if to force an answer to the surface. He was sure of it now, the desk appeared out of tune to its surroundings. The more he stared at it, the more glaringly obvious it became. Until Paul could no longer think or look at anything else. The desk now seemed to demand his attention, almost communicating something. In regards to lunges, the extra weight requires your legs to work harder to control the weight and stabilize your body as you lower into the lunge. The reason why the hack squat is so effective is because the additional weight forces your legs to work harder to stabilize your body as you lower into the squat. The same concept applies to lunges. [substeps] The timing for the lunges is very important. If you have a hard time keeping your balance, do not add additional weight. The best time to lunge is when your quads are fresh. This means the best time to do your lunges are at the end of your workout after you have completed your squats. If you are doing your lunges after your squats, make sure you have a chair in front of you in case you lose your balance and fall backwards. Three weeks of late nights pouring through the data, triple checking the accounts, only to find that the sole problem their company had was having a tax accountant who was too stupid to realize that the laws had changed the previous year, and the entire approach to deductions for the offshore accounts was bogus. Generative models are pivotal in the nascent domain of network science, examining the creation of statistical patterns observed in actual networks through established rules. These models serve as the foundation for devising and assessing computational techniques applied to networks, alongside facilitating validation and simulation endeavors. Over recent years, numerous models have been developed aiming to achieve high levels of authenticity when generating networks. This paper presents our novel generator, ReCoN, investigates its ability to adapt to preexisting networks, generates significantly larger versions of those networks, and concludes with potential future research areas. Our experiments reveal that ReCoN frequently outperforms several advanced network generation methodologies. We contend that ReCoN serves as a versatile and proficient instrument for reproducing specific networks while maintaining critical features across various scales, and enabling extensive expansion of the initial dataset. Key terms include network generation, multiscale modeling, network modeling, and community structures.
