Your phone's speaker transforms your speech into electrical impulses, which travel along telephone lines to reach someone else's device, where these signals revert to audible sounds. Telephones operate based on this fundamental concept. While mobile devices communicate with nearby cell towers using radio frequencies, subsequent connections follow similar procedures. Directing calls accurately presents the primary technological hurdle. Previously, calls were routed via a central hub, requiring manual input from operators who physically connected the caller and recipient. Although current systems retain this core principle, computers now handle all operations, eliminating the necessity for live personnel and tangible wire manipulation. Automated communication necessitated methods allowing data transfer without human assistance. Dialing initiates electronic signals representing digits, while other indicators like busy signals or dial tones are merely intricate circuits. Terms such as 'pulse' and 'touch-tone' refer to two types of dialing techniques employed by traditional landlines to ensure compatibility with outdated infrastructures, whereas mobile phones exclusively utilize touch-tones. Modern technology favors assigning distinctive tones to each digit rather than relying solesinvolving specific voltage patterns, simplifying extensive data transmission. Hearing certain tones during dialing indicates the corresponding notes being relayed to the exchange center.

In conventional mobile data plans, the data is associated with a fixed period (e.g., one month) and the unused data will be cleared at the end of each period. To take advantage of consumers' heterogeneous demands across different periods and meanwhile to provide more time flexibility, some mobile data service providers (SP) have offered data plans with different lengths of period. In this paper, we consider the data plan design problem for a single SP, who provides data plans with different lengths of period for consumers with different characteristics of data demands. We propose a contract-theoretic approach, wherein the SP offers a period-price data plan contract which consists of a set of period and price combinations, indicating the prices for data with different periods. We study the optimal data plan contract designs under two different models: discrete and continuous consumer-type models, depending on whether the consumer type is discrete or continuous. In the former model, each type of consumers are assigned with a specific period-price combination. In the latter model, the consumers are first categorized into a finite number of groups, and each group of consumers (possibly with different types) are assigned with a specific period-price combination. We systematically analyze the incentive compatibility (IC) constraint and individual rationality (IR) constraint, which ensure each consumer to choose the data plan with the period-price combination intended for his type. We further derive the optimal contract that maximizes the SP's expected profit, meanwhile satisfying the IC and IR constraints of consumers. Our numerical results show that the proposed optimal contract can increase the SP's profit by 35 , comparing with the conventional fixed monthly-period data plan.

After pressing send, your email is transmitted to your email service provider's mail server, a detail known by your device due to its initial configuration during mail setup. Upon reaching 'your' mail server, it identifies the domain from the email address and retrieves the corresponding IP address through DNS - essentially the internet'sinternet directory'. With the IP information, the message is forwarded to the recipient's mail server, which determines the appropriate mailbox based on their username within the provided email address. To clarify further, the recipient'smail server and their device are configured to receive emails via the former; hence they don't exchange data directly. This process resembles how postal services operate, with the email provider acting as the local post office and the email addresses serving as physical addresses.

Human activity recognition based on wearable sensor data has been an attractive research topic due to its application in areas such as healthcare and smart environments. In this context, many research studies have proposed the use of machine learning techniques to classify human activities from wearable sensor data. The most commonly used approaches include supervised learning algorithms such as decision trees, support vector machines, and neural networks. These techniques are based on the assumption that labeled training data is available, where each instance in the dataset corresponds to a particular activity and its associated sensor readings. In order to use these techniques, the data must be pre-processed and transformed into feature vectors. Commonly used feature transformations include normalization, feature selection, and dimensionality reduction. Additionally, for optimal performance, parameters such as kernel type, regularization, and network topology must be tuned. Once the model has been trained, it can then be evaluated using metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. Finally, the trained model can be deployed in an application and tested in real-world conditions.

Southampton, Portsmouth and Isle of Wight councils applied to the government in October to create an authority to boost economic growth. They said they had been allocated PS900m over 30 years by the government. Portsmouth Council leader Donna Jones said the money now appeared to have been lost because of opposition by Hampshire County Council. Ms Jones said it was "highly unlikely" that the government would agree the deal, because "there isn't consensus." The situation was discussed at a meeting at Westminster on Wednesday involving Hampshire MPs and council leaders. The new Isle of Wight Council leader Dave Stewart said he confirmed to the meeting that his recently-elected Conservative administration would not support the existing bid. Isle of Wight Conservatives had previously said the island's needs "could easily be overridden" by Southampton and Portsmouth. Hampshire County Council leader Roy Perry said: "I'm not surprised that the deal is now dead. "It would not have helped the local economy and would have led to the dismantling of vital county-wide services - such as transport, health and social care." Keith House, the leader of Eastleigh Borough Council, which had been in talks to join the Solent Combined Authority (SCA), said the bid was "almost certainly dead," but Fareham Borough Council leader Sean Woodward urged the government to "press ahead" with the deal. The Department for Communities and Local Government said devolution applications should be accompanied by "local support," but did not say whether the Solent bid had been refused. The Conservative MP for Havant, Alan Mak, said: "The money is still very much there. "This is an opportunity for the council leaders to come forward with new proposals that are viable."

Warsaw was occupied by Germany from 4 August 1915 until November 1918. The Allied Armistice terms required in Article 12 that Germany withdraw from areas controlled by Russia in 1914, but because of the indecision of the Supreme War Council over the future of Poland they were not enforced until after the armistice. The city was occupied by the 1st and 3rd Guards Regiments of the 1st Guards Division, 1st Army on 5 August. The 1st Guards Division had been withdrawn from the Eastern Front for rest and refitting, and took part in the Gorlice-Tarnow Offensive in May 1915. It was then moved north to take part in the siege of Novogeorgievsk, and was withdrawn to the rear again when the fortress surrendered on 20 August 1915. Although Polish nationalists had been offered their independence by Germany in the Proclamation of 5 November 1916, the Germans remained in occupation of Warsaw, and did not withdraw until November 1918. Warsaw was the capital of Russian Poland and the residence of the Grand Duke Constantine, Viceroy of Poland. The city was defended by the Warsaw Fortress, commanded by Lieutenant-General M. A. Svechin. The fortress lay to the west of the city, on the other side of the Vistula, and was entered through the Warsaw Gate. The fortifications consisted of two inner defensive rings first' and 'second and an outer defensive ring (the 'third, the latter being the most important. The inner defensive rings had a perimeter of about 32 kilometres and a width of about 2 kilometres. The third defensive ring had a perimeter of 50 kilometres and a width of 3.2 kilometres. The first and second defensive rings were armed with over 600 guns, the third with about 1,500. The Russian forces in the Warsaw Fortress numbered 80,000 troops and 1,000 officers. The garrison was divided into the Western and Eastern Groups. The Western Group comprised the 29th Infantry Division, 4th Grenadier Division and the 5th Rifle Brigade, and was under the command of General A. E. Blagoveshchenski. The Eastern Group comprised the 2nd Grenadier Division, 48th Infantry Division, 1st Cavalry Division and the 1st Siberian Infantry Brigade, and was commanded by General A. I. Denikin. The fortress was defended by 16 forts. The fortifications were made of earth, with some concrete, and were armed with a total of 862 guns. The forts were of various sizes, with the largest being Fort Zegrze, which was 2.5 kilometres long and 1.2 kilometres wide. The Warsaw Fortress was protected by a system of interlocking defensive positions and a network of trenches and strong points. The Warsaw Fortress was defended by the 50th Infantry Division and the 16th Cavalry Division, under the command of General P. O. Lechitsky. The Russian forces were in disarray following the defeat in East Prussia. The men were exhausted and the command structure was in chaos. General M. V. Alekseyev, Chief of Staff of the Russian South-Western Front, ordered General Svechin to leave 40,000 men and 200 guns to defend the fortress, and to retreat to the Ivangorod fortress with the rest of the troops. Svechin and Lechitsky were opposed to this, but had little choice but to obey the order. On 13 August 1915 the garrison of the fortress consisted of 53,000 men and 460 guns. On 16 August the garrison was reduced to 40,000 men and 200 guns. The 9th Army began its advance on Warsaw on 12 August, and the first troops reached the Warsaw fortress on 14 August. Light Deteptaion and Ranging (Lidar) technology enables precise object identification within expansive regions by generating high-resolution data known as point clouds. These point clouds are produced constantly at rapid speeds, providing valuable insights for autonomous operations in cyberphysical systems. A primary challenge lies in effectively grouping these point clouds to retrieve relevant information. Implementing methods capable of addressing this issue continuously could enhance processing efficiency, particularly in fog computing environments where data is processed near its source. In response, we introduce LISCO, an innovative method designed for ongoing, streamlined, distance-based clustering of LiDAR point cloud data. This approach optimizes the detail level throughout our data processing workflow. Our comprehensive analysis includes rigorous experimentation, demonstrating performance enhancements up to threefold over standard techniques and emphasizing its adaptability across diverse datasets—both actual and simulated—to thoroughly test extreme scenarios.

I remember feeling a bit smug, listening to all my friends spilling out their grand ideas for living forever. Until I win the lottery..... two days in a row. Until I get married. Until I move to the USA, or Australia (or anywhere else for that matter). They all had plans and theories of how they could achieve immortality, but most of them were based on the premise that they would be dead in the first place. If they didn't die, then they couldn't achieve immortality. I had a plan too, but it was more like a hope than anything else. I hoped that I could find a way to stay alive forever, without ever dying. It seemed a bit far-fetched, but it was my only hope. And then I met her. I was working in a lab at the time, and she was one of the new interns. I don't remember her name, but she was beautiful. And she had a plan. She told me about a way to achieve immortality. It involved a lot of science, and a lot of math, but the basic idea was this: You take a healthy person, and you put them into a medically induced coma. You then hook them up to a machine that sustains their life, providing them with the nutrients they need to survive. The machine also monitors their vital signs, and if any of them start to decline, the machine automatically injects them with the appropriate medication or adjusts the IV drip accordingly. In short, the machine keeps them alive indefinitely. Of course, there are a few caveats. The first is that the person has to be healthy to begin with. If they have any underlying health conditions, they will likely not survive the coma. The second is that the machine has to be well-maintained. Current motion capture (MoCap) systems generally require markers and multiple calibrated cameras, which can be used only in constrained environments. In this work we introduce a drone-based system for 3D human MoCap. The system only needs an autonomously flying drone with an on-board RGB camera and is usable in various indoor and outdoor environments. A reconstruction algorithm is developed to recover full-body motion from the video recorded by the drone. We argue that, besides the capability of tracking a moving subject, a flying drone also provides fast varying viewpoints, which is beneficial for motion reconstruction. We evaluate the accuracy of the proposed system using our new DroCap dataset and also demonstrate its applicability for MoCap in the wild using a consumer drone.

He also coauthored two books in this area during the 1920s: The Long Wave Theory of Electricity and Magnetism (1923) and On the Shortwave Theory of Electricity and Magnetism (1926). Tesla retired in 1934 and died in 1959. Tesla is buried alongside Howard Hughes at Mt Hope Cemetery, Los Angeles.

Variational autoencoders (VAEs) are commonly utilized in natural language generation tasks; nevertheless, they face persistent challenges such as information underrepresentation and posterior collapse. Information underrepresentation occurs because only the final hidden state from the encoder is converted into the latent space, leading to inadequate data summary. Posterior collapse stems from an uneven balance between the reconstruction loss and the Kullback–Leibler divergence within the objective function. In response, this study introduces a novel discrete variational attention model employing categorical distributions over the attention mechanism due to the inherently discrete quality of languages. By integrating an autoregressive prior, our method captures sequential dependencies among observations, thereby improving the latent space's effectiveness in language production. Additionally, our approach benefits from the distinct advantage of using a discrete latent space instead of a conventional continuous one based on the standard Gaussian distribution. Through extensive testing in various language generation scenarios, our proposed technique has proven to outperform existing advanced methods.

Whilst the permanent building at Holyrood was being constructed, the Parliament's temporary home was the General Assembly Hall of the Church of Scotland on the Royal Mile in Edinburgh. Official business usually took place there between 1749 and 1817 but after this date it became a venue for debating sessions or for attending meetings of other organisations such as trade unions, professional bodies and committees. The first session of the new Scottish parliament met at the church hall on 27 October 1749 with its presiding officer (or deputy) being Andrew Melville who had been appointed by the Lords to act as their representative during the period when the lower house had not yet sat. The House then adjourned until 2 November for the election of members in each constituency. An Act of Union was passed that same day which merged England and Wales into one Kingdom of Great Britain; however, due to the rapid growth of population in Scotland, most constituencies were too small to elect more than 4 Members of Parliament and so only 56 representatives arrived from across the country. First Parliament (November-March): First Session On 3 December the newly elected chamber convened in the church hall and came under the presidency of Robert Dundas, 1st Lord Melville. His office is traditionally referred to as "first lord of the parliaments." On his appointment he declared: "I have come hither to be your servant." However, within three months he would lead the opposition against the government of the day over issues including land reform and the abolition of slavery. He died suddenly while out riding on 12 April 1751 before receiving any official notice of his election - leaving William Robertson, an independent Whig MP, in charge pending the arrival of his successor. Following the death of Dundas' widow Elspeth Anderson at Stirling Castle in July 1753, her son David was chosen to succeed him but was prevented from taking up his seat whilst his brother John ran against him unsuccessfully in Perthshire in August. When John announced his intention to stand again in January 1754, David moved to challenge him but on 25 June was forced to withdraw having failed to secure support from anyone else. Instead he supported William Graham, whose candidacy was backed by David's brother-in-law James Smith, and both men stood again unopposed at the next general election in September. Both returned to serve in the second parliament of the union. William Bruce, 4th Earl of Carrick, known as the "Lion of Battle," held the post of Speaker from 19 February 1755 to 15 March 1756 when Thomas Henderson succeeded. It later emerged the latter had been secretly involved in plotting against the reigning king Charles Edward Stuart which led to an investigation that resulted in him resigning from the chair. His replacement, George Gillespie, served until 16 May 1757 when he resigned following a vote of no confidence brought about by accusations of corruption in his administration. The government then formed a coalition consisting of Tory MPs and Independents headed by William Maitland and Robert Erskine, Bishop of Dunblane. This arrangement continued until March 1759 when the two sides reentered full-scale conflict. Whilst Erskine agreed to continue serving as Speaker on condition his followers could also hold office in the House, Maitland rejected all concessions and withdrew from the government, taking his supporters along with him. In June of that year, the Duke of York deposed King Charles II and established the British Empire. Although a general election took place on 21 July before the creation of the North American colonies in 1763, the Second Monarchy Party opted not to contest these elections, instead remaining politically inactive until after the Glorious Revolution of 1688. Second Parliament (October-December): Second Session In October 1761, Parliament gathered once again at the church hall where they remained until 7 November 1762 before moving to the New State Rooms in Whitehall. They officially opened on 22 December 1764 when Sir William Dalrymple launched proceedings by reading a message written by Queen Anne and received by the Duke of York from the Prince Regent. Despite some early difficulties - Parliament only met twice for less than six weeks - the House proved popular amongst ordinary Scots for improving medical care systems, introducing legislation to protect children from child labour and banning smoking indoors among other things although complaints of lack of time allocation resulted in the suspension of sittings on several occasions. With the restoration of monarchy in 1770, Parliament was dissolved ahead of a general election that saw the return of the Tories under Jacobite leader Charles Edward Stuart. This paper studies social cooperation backed peer-to-peer energy trading technique by which prosumers can decide how they can use their batteries opportunistically for participating in the peer-to-peer trading. The objective is to achieve a solution in which the ultimate beneficiaries are the prosumers, i.e., a prosumer-centric solution. To do so, a coalition formation game is designed, which enables a prosumer to compare its benefit of participating in the peer-to-peer trading with and without using its battery and thus, allows the prosumer to form suitable social coalition groups with other similar prosumers in the network for conducting peer-to-peer trading. The properties of the formed coalitions are studied, and it is shown that 1) the coalition structure that stems from the social cooperation between participating prosumers at each time slot is both stable and optimal, and 2) the outcomes of the proposed peer-to-peer trading scheme is prosumer-centric. Ambient RF (Radio Frequency) energy harvesting technique has recently been proposed as a potential solution to provide proactive energy replenishment for wireless devices. This paper aims to analyze the performance of a battery-free wireless sensor powered by ambient RF energy harvesting using a stochastic geometry approach. Specifically, we consider the point-to-point uplink transmission of a wireless sensor in a stochastic geometry network, where ambient RF sources, such as mobile transmit devices, access points and base stations, are distributed as a Ginibre -determinantal point process (DPP). The DPP is able to capture repulsion among points, and hence, it is more general than the Poisson point process (PPP). We analyze two common receiver architectures: separated receiver and time-switching architectures. For each architecture, we consider the scenarios with and without co-channel interference for information transmission. We derive the expectation of the RF energy harvesting rate in closed form and also compute its variance. Moreover, we perform a worst-case study which derives the upper bound of both power and transmission outage probabilities. Additionally, we provide guidelines on the setting of optimal time-switching coefficient in the case of the time-switching architecture. Numerical results verify the correctness of the analysis and show various tradeoffs between parameter setting. Lastly, we prove that the sensor is more efficient when the distribution of the ambient sources exhibits stronger repulsion.

When examining how income levels correlate with economic disparity, Kuznets identified a pattern where mid-level developing countries exhibit a peak in inequality, forming what we refer to today as the Kuznets curve. The hypothesis presented by the Kuznets curve suggests that over time, income inequality should diminish. For instance, the period encompassing America's High School Movement (1910-1940) witnessed a decline in income inequality within the country. Yet, post-1970s statistics indicate a resurgence in such disparities, which doesn't automatically invalidate Kuznets' proposition. There could be potential shifts in sectors influencing these patterns; transitioning from manufacturing to services might instigate new Kuznets' cycles simultaneously.

Alloys can be formed when melting and combining different elements through two main processes - atom exchange and the interstitial mechanism. The sizes of the individual atoms involved determine which process takes place. If the atoms have comparable sizes, they tend to substitute for one another within the metallic structure, resulting in what's known as a substitutional alloy (e.g., bronze and brass). However, if there is a significant size difference between the atoms, the smaller ones fill gaps between the larger atoms in the lattice, forming an interstitial alloy (such as steel). Stainless steel serves as an illustration of both types of alloys since it incorporates carbon atoms in the interstices while also having iron atoms replaced by nickel and chromium.

Deep neural networks' recent advancements rely partly on extensive labeled training data like ImageNet. Nonetheless, creating such datasets can be challenging and time-consuming. Conversely, acquiring noisy-labelled web images quickly and cost-effectively is much simpler. Therefore, exploring new ways to train deep neural networks with these imperfect labels becomes necessary. Present solutions focus on detecting and rectifying incorrect labels or adjusting the weightage of data within the loss function based on estimated noise levels; however, both methods may still lead to mistakes. Our research suggests that discarding some labels might be preferable when dealing with highly noisy data, as erroneous labels could steer the network toward poor results. To address this issue, we propose a dual-phase methodology for training with noisy labels. Initially, we pinpoint a subset of correctly-labeled images from the noisy dataset, disregarding the others. Subsequently, we employ a semi-supervised approach to train a deep neural network utilizing the entire dataset while emphasizing the most accurate labels. Our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of this strategy across various datasets, particularly at higher noise levels.

Typically, what happens is the breakdown of fats and proteins in the skin. Many parts of the body have carbonyl groups, which in the context of skin means a carbon group bonded to an oxygen atom. These groups can interact with the oxygen in the air and form compounds that react with oxygen in the skin. "It is not the same as when you get an oxygen-based injury from being out in the sun too long," said Dahl. "The carbonyl groups react with the oxygen and this creates a reactive oxygen species that reacts with the proteins and the fats. This causes the damage." "We know the body can protect itself from oxygen damage and we know that when we get older, this ability goes away," said Dahl. "The question we are asking is if we apply vitamin C to the skin can it help protect it from this oxygen damage." The researchers, who also include graduate student Brenna S. Coyle, have published their findings in the current issue of the Journal of Investigative Dermatology. They have shown vitamin C can protect skin cells from damage caused by these oxygen-related compounds. "The damage we're talking about is the kind that can lead to skin cancer," said Dahl. "The kind of cancer that leads to the formation of skin tumors and which are most commonly caused by UV damage. What we're trying to do is figure out how to protect against skin cancer." Dahl said the researchers have also found that not only does vitamin C protect the skin from the damage caused by these carbonyl compounds, it also helps repair damage that has already been done. "This may not only help prevent skin cancer, but it can also be used in the repair of damage that has already been done by these carbonyl compounds," said Dahl. "This is an important study," said Dahl. "We know that vitamin C is one of the antioxidants that protect the skin. We know this because we know that healthy skin has high levels of vitamin C and that when we get older and the levels of vitamin C in the skin go down, this is when we get more skin damage. "What we are trying to do is to figure out the mechanisms by which vitamin C prevents skin damage and then use this to develop treatments for skin cancer." University of Colorado at Boulder. Together with other Criollos, they conspired against the oppressive Spanish rule but faced treachery. As authorities closed in, fearing capture, Hidalgo instructed his sibling Mauricio, along with Ignacio Allende and Mariano Abasolo, to liberate pro-independence prisoners; approximately eighty individuals were freed. Before dawn on September 16th, Hidalgo rang the church bells and assembled his followers before him. Supported by Allende and Juan Aldama, he inspired rebellion amongst his parishioners. A week later, during the Battle of Guanajuato, the insurrection saw its initial significant confrontation. It wasn't until September 27, 1821, when the Declaration of Independence of the Mexican Empire proclaimed Mexico's freedom from Spanish dominance, putting an end to ten years of conflict. Popcorn kernels contain small amounts of water, and that water evaporates when heated, expands, and pops the popcorn. Due to variation in the water content of the kernels along with the moisture level in the popped corn itself, there can be significant variability from kernel-to-kernel (or even within a single kernel) as well as between batches or pots of popped corn. This makes it difficult for microwave ovens to pop consistently sized corns every time they are used. While an engineer could design a specific timed sequence of popping conditions optimized to lead to predictable popcorn sizes, manufacturers have done so only after extensive testing and often through trial and error. As such many different types exist on the market today. However, once these sequences were developed they became proprietary information locked up by their respective manufactures. The result is that consumers cannot easily compare one type against another nor know how each performs relative to its own parameters. Some simply use whatever comes preloaded into their machine while others may but struggle because if they want better performance than given out by default this requires additional cost.

In markets for online advertising, some advertisers pay only when users respond to ads. So publishers estimate ad response rates and multiply by advertiser bids to estimate expected revenue for each ad slot. To generate data on these estimates - which are sometimes called "demand curves" - publishers use several tools: " Sell-side platform providers collect more information about user behavior than most people know exists (or think is available). They keep records of every click that an advertiser made through the site or app they run; their algorithms can signal whether a consumer clicked because he was exposed to an ad click-through rate or if she simply found what she wanted in her search results without clicking any ads organic traffic. Eigenvector continuation is a computational method that finds the extremal eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a Hamiltonian matrix with one or more control parameters. It does this by projection onto a basis of eigenvectors. First, an initial set of eigenvalues and eigenvectors is found by diagonalization of the Hamiltonian matrix. Then, each of these eigenvalues and eigenvectors is continued as the control parameter is varied. The process continues until the extremal eigenvalues and eigenvectors have been located. The advantage of using eigenvector continuation to find the extremal eigenvalues and eigenvectors is that it can be done very quickly, especially for large matrices. It is also relatively simple to implement, and does not require any special numerical techniques or software. This makes it a useful tool for many different kinds of scientific research.

A flat tax is one of two things. 1) You charge the same exact tax to every person. So if the tax is 2000 you charge everyone 2000. 2) You charge everyone the same percentage. So everyone is taxed at say 30. The issue with a flat tax is that it hurts the poor more than it hurts the rich, as there are no exemptions or deductions. Everyone owe a flat percentage of their income, and due to the costs of the government that percentage has to be set high in order to get the money it needs to function. A fair tax does not means anything specific, but I think you are asking about a progressive tax. In a progressive tax you take into account how much harm a tax will do to someone. So the poorest will pay no taxes, and you gradually increase the amount paid in tiers going up 5 or so per tier. This is more "fair" because it does less harm. 2000 means a lot when it is 1 months pay or more, but it does not really mean much of anything if it is 1 of your salary.','The term fair tax is subjective, depending on what is viewed as "fair," but I can tell you what a flat tax is. It is generally regarded as a system of income tax where everybody, regardless of income level or possible deductions under current tax law, pays the same percentage of their income as tax. It doesn't matter if you make 20,000 or 2 million, you both would pay whatever it is, be it 10, 20, etc. Under most versions of the flat tax, there are no deductions, reinforcing the idea of it being flat and unchanging. Currently in the US, and Europe, and most of the world, taxes operate using brackets, where different levels of income are taxed at different rates. Keep in mind, income is only taxed at the bracket it lies in. If I make 100,000, at the first 10,000 is tax exempt, I pay no income on that. However, income between 80,000 and 100,000 might be taxed at 25. There are arguments for and against a flat tax, and whether it is fair. One argument for it is that since everybody pays the same percentage, and the same amount relative to income, its the most fair way of handling it. The argument against it is that affluent people have the ability to pay higher taxes without hurting themselves financially as much as the same tax would hurt a poorer person.

Instance-level video segmentation requires a solid integration of spatial and temporal information. However, current methods rely mostly on domain-specific information (online learning) to produce accurate instance-level segmentations. We propose a method that utilizes both spatial and temporal attention mechanisms to improve instance segmentation accuracy without requiring online learning. Our approach, called SPAIR (Spatial-Temporal Attention with Instance Refinement), consists of two main steps. First, we compute spatial attention maps for each frame in the video to localize object regions. The attention maps are computed using a convolutional neural network (CNN) that takes the current frame as input. The resulting maps highlight the regions of the image that are most relevant for object localization. Second, we use a temporal attention mechanism to track object regions across frames. This is done by computing a dense correspondence field between consecutive frames and using it to propagate the attention maps from one frame to the next. This allows us to maintain consistent object localization across frames, even in cases where the object moves or undergoes significant deformation. Finally, we refine the instance-level segmentations by applying an instance segmentation network to the spatially and temporally refined attention maps. Our experiments show that SPAIR is competitive with state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy while being significantly simpler in terms of implementation and faster in terms of runtime.

Different perspectives exist among non-theists regarding deities. While some dismiss the notion of God but acknowledge its importance for others, there are also those who regard God as embodying human ideals and ambitions. During the 1800s, the English atheist Charles Bradlaugh famously stated his refusal to deny the existence of God due to the ambiguity of the term itself. He was particularly skeptical towards the Christian conception of God. On another note, Stephen Jay Gould suggested separating philosophical thought into two independent realms which he referred to as "non-overlapping magisteria" (NOMA). According to him, matters concerning the divine fall outside the scope of scientific inquiry and belong exclusively to religious discourse. Science, therefore, addresses all empirically verifiable phenomena within the natural world while religion grapples with profound meanings and ethical principles. Consequently, the absence of tangible evidence connecting spiritual forces to physical occurrences positions science as the primary authority over natural processes.

In this paper, we describe a new online tool for linguistics, the Linguistic Atlas of Early Middle English (LAEME). LAEME is designed to organize and store detailed information about individual instances of linguistic behavior in the late medieval period. It can be used to answer various types of research questions at various levels of linguistic analysis. We have collected a large amount of data on morphological variation in English between 1150 and 1325, but this is only the first step in our project. In the future, we plan to add features that will allow us to map more than one language variety to the same geographical space, and add tools for storing and mapping lexical data. Introduction Linguists are increasingly adopting online tools that help them organize, structure and mine information that is too detailed to be printed in journals. The most famous of these is probably the Corpus of Historical American English (Davies 2010), which allows researchers to search more than 400 million words of text dating from 1810 to 2009. The corpus provides information about how often particular words were used during different periods, how they were used in different contexts, and how their meanings have changed over time. The Linguistic Atlas of Early Middle English (LAEME) is a new online tool for linguistics, designed to organize and store detailed information about individual instances of linguistic behavior in the late medieval period. LAEME has two main components: a database of linguistic forms, and a set of tools for mapping those forms to geographical space. The database currently contains information on morphological variation in English between 1150 and 1325, but this is only the first step in our project. In the future, we plan to add features that will allow us to map more than one language variety to the same geographical space, and add tools for storing and mapping lexical data. LAEME is part of a broader trend in linguistics towards the use of online tools. For example, the Oxford English Dictionary (OED) has recently launched the Historical Thesaurus of the OED, which allows users to search for words by meaning rather than by form (Crystal 2009). The Historical Thesaurus is based on the OED's database of more than 600,000 words, which covers the period from 1150 to the present day. Other online tools for linguistics include the Corpus of Historical American English (Davies 2010), the British National Corpus (BNC) (Leech et al. 2001), and the Corpus of Contemporary American English (COCA) (Davies 2008). The LAEME database The LAEME database is a relational database that stores information about individual instances of linguistic behavior. The database has two main types of data: forms and tokens. A form is a particular way of speaking or writing a word. For example, the word 'dog' can be written as 'dogge', 'dogue', 'doo', 'dow', 'dowe', 'dox', 'dug', 'dugges', 'dugs', 'dygge', or 'dyghes'. Each of these forms corresponds to a different entry in the database. A token is an instance of a form in a particular context. For example, the word 'dog' might be used in the sentence 'The dog barked'. In this sentence, 'dog' is a token of the form 'dog'. A single form can have multiple tokens in different contexts. For example, the form 'dog' can be used as a noun The dog barked or a verb He dogged her footsteps. The LAEME database currently contains more than 200,000 forms and 1.5 million tokens. The forms are organized into three main categories: morphology, phonology, and syntax. Morphology is the study of the ways in which words are formed from smaller units called morphemes. For example, the word 'dogs' is formed from the root 'dog' and the suffix s'. In 1872, the Central Pacific Railroad established a station near Easterby's - by now a hugely productive wheat farm - for its new Southern Pacific line. Soon there was a town of several hundred people that mushroomed to nearly 3,000 residents in 1900 and later doubled again during World War II as workers poured into the area from all over the country constructing the railroads. "The housing was nice back then," says John Goolden, who moved his family to Central Point, Oregon, across the street from Easterby Station. "It was surrounded by trees with walkways along it." Last week, a planned sale of Easterby's property produced some backlash among descendants of those early settlers. Many don't want their ancestors' legacy tarnished. Easterby Station today is less than 10 miles west of John Day Dam, but long ago horses pulled wagons up roads lined with towering eucalyptus trees. At least two houses still stand on the land where the settlement once grew. The old post office sits empty behind a chain link fence. According to the estate administrator at the Willamette National Bank, which holds title to the property, the bank has been working closely with the railroad since 2007 when current owner Don Meek bought the parcel, planning for eventual abandonment or redevelopment. As part of the agreement, any future owners must preserve "the historic nature of the buildings and structures located on the site including retaining physical integrity of the building facade andor exterior walls and gates as necessary while preserving the distinctive character of these features; the landscape plan around historic buildings and structures within the site; historical signage describing Easterby Station history as appropriate;" and "retain the easement rights allowing access by the railroad under certain conditions consistent with other easements owned or controlled by the banks and its predecessors." That includes the right-of-way across the western end of the property, although the easement could be modified if an ownership change requires such action. Meek bought the 400 acres of land for 1 million in 2008. He declined comment through his realtor, Dave Burns. At the moment, Easterby Station appears to have no immediate plans beyond restoration of its original charm. Ryan Wilkerson, spokesman for Portland-based Union Pacific (NYSE: UNP), said the company doesn't discuss pending transactions. But he did say Easterby Station is still open for business and serves as a depot for freight cars headed down the Columbia River Gorge toward the eastern edge of the state. A formal statement will follow after closing, according to Wilkerson. Ancestors of many of those early farmers relocated away from what's now Easterby Station in the years following WWII. Today about 1,500 people live between the small communities of Cashmere and Hermiston in southeast Hood County.

A group is called finite if it has a finite number of elements. The number of elements is called the order of the group. An important class is the symmetric groups SN, the groups of permutations of N letters. For example, the symmetric group on 3 letters S3 is the group consisting of all possible orderings of the three letters ABC, i.e. contains the elements ABC, ACB, ..., up to CBA, in total 6 (or 3 factorial) elements. This class is fundamental insofar as any finite group can be expressed as a subgroup of a symmetric group SN for a suitable integer N (Cayley's theorem). Parallel to the group of symmetries of the square above, S3 can also be interpreted as the group of symmetries of an equilateral triangle.

The recently proposed multi-layer sparse model has raised insightful connections between sparse representations and convolutional neural networks (CNN). In its original conception, this model was restricted to a cascade of three layers of non-overlapping sparse coding layers. While this model showed that the state-of-the-art accuracy in sparse coding can be obtained by applying a sparse coding layer after each of the three layers of non-overlapping sparse coding layers, it failed to match the state-of-the-art in sparse coding accuracy for images with the restricted number of sparse coding layers. In this paper, we propose a new sparse coding model with the multi-layer sparse model in which a sparse coding layer is applied after each of the four layers of non-overlapping sparse coding layers. The experiments on synthetic and real images show that the proposed model has superior performance to the original multi-layer sparse model. Conclusions In this paper, we propose a new sparse coding model with the multi-layer sparse model in which a sparse coding layer is applied after each of the four layers of non-overlapping sparse coding layers.

Its skin was a deep green color with yellow spots all over it. She couldn't help but smile as she watched the little creature jump from one rock to another. She slowly reached out her hand and tried to get closer to the toad, but it quickly hopped away. Megan kept trying to get closer, but each time the toad would hop away a little faster. She thought maybe if she stayed still and didn't move, the toad would come back. After a few minutes of patiently waiting, the toad returned. Megan felt a sense of accomplishment when the toad finally let her pick it up. She held it gently in her hands, stroking its tiny head with her finger. The toad seemed content to just sit there, which made Megan even happier. For the next few weeks, Megan and the toad would meet at the same spot every day. Megan would bring food for it and they would spend hours together. Eventually the toad became so comfortable with Megan that it allowed her to take it home. Megan was delighted to have a pet toad. She named him Fred and he lived happily with her for years. Whenever Megan went to the pond, Fred would follow her and keep her company. He was always there for her when she needed a friend. Megan and Fred's friendship was something that could never be replaced. To this day, whenever Megan goes to the pond she remembers her special friendship with the toad.

I awoke to the sound of my alarm, as I do every day at dawn. As I do every day, I began going through my daily checklist: clean up; get dressed; check the scanners; empty the rain collectors into the water tank; and gear up. I activated my exo-armor and run through it's systems, checking for functionality. With everything in order, I exited the outpost. As I approached my armored vehicle, I stopped to gaze over the landscape below. My eyes went from the ruins of New York City to the dried-up shoreline of the Atlantic. It seemed like only yesterday news reporters were exclaiming that we'd won the war. We'd driven off the Xantori invasion force. Headlines were talking about how "America" had saved the world, no matter how little truth they actually held. America certainly had been a major factor. We'd certainly been a major factor. We didn't, however, deliver what everyone thought was the killing blow. That title belongs to the United Europe Air Force. They were the ones who developed and fired the warhead at the alien ship. Our victory had barely lasted a week before our solar scanners detected more of the Xantori signals, coming from a wormhole near Neptune. Panic quickly overtook the world, sending it into a state of near-anarchy. With the militaries of the world exhausted and weak, we couldn't survive another attack. Luckily, the Earth Aeronautic Space Administration (EASA) announced that they had completed a fleet of ships using reverse-engineered Xantori tech. Each ship was said to have capacity of 1.5 billion people. With 10 total ships, they supposedly had enough room for everyone on Earth. With the Xantori's arrival estimated to be in 5 Earth days, time was running out. Planes and boats were being filled to the brim in a hurry to get everyone to the EASA's launching facility, built over what used to be Boston, Massachusetts. Merely 8 hours before the Xantori would reach Earth, the last airplanes landed and the last cruise ships and boats docked. In a race against the clock, people were rushed aboard the massive starships. I was nearing the loading docks myself, alongside my wife, my two sons, my daughter, and my parents. Just as we reached the loading area, however, I was pushed over by people scrambling for the ramps. I tried to catch up to my family but found myself stuck among the billions of people and soon lost track of them as they went up the ramp, unable to turn around. A loud warning alarm began to sound as the gates to the ramps closed. Shock and confusion spread among the masses. People were angrily shouting for the gates to be opened. They were all quieted by the sound of pistons and gears as the ramps began folding up toward their respective ships, closing with a loud "hisss." After staring in confusion at the ships for a moment, I realized what was going on. The ships actually had a much smaller capacity that what they told us. They knew not everyone would be able to fit. They lied to try and keep people calm. I quickly made my way back to the parking lot to avoid being potentially trampled by over a billion desperate people trying to make it to the ships. I got in my car and began driving as fast as I possibly could away from there, as the mass concentration of people would be a prime target for the Xantori ships. I stopped by an abandoned military outpost and began outfitting myself with armor, weapons, ammunition, anything I could fit into one of the abandoned armored vehicles. As I left the outpost and continued South, I heard the loud engines of the starships roaring. The massive vehicles rose up from their docks and began flying off into the sky, disappearing among the clouds. I checked the car's clock, which read 3:30pm. That meant the Xantori were due to arrive any minute now. Just as the EASA facility faded into the horizon, I noticed a strange shape moving across the sky. Right on schedule, the aliens descended from the skies. I quickly pulled the vehicle over and engaged its thermal cloaking device. I watched as their plasma weapons began scorching the landscape. Like a hunting dog picking up on an animal's scent, their ships all began heading for the EASA facility. They razed the entire facility to the ground, igniting a fire that turned the sky orange and black. I took this opportunity to continue South, eventually reaching the military installation I was formerly stationed at and began setting it up for my tenure. That was all nearly forty years ago, and still I wonder what would have been different if I hadn't been pushed. My thoughts, however, were interrupted by my scanner's alarm. I rushed back inside to see what it had picked up. Usually, this meant a false alarm. The scanner was quite old now and often picked up false positives or animals. I read the signal code, my eyes widening. I'd been transmitting an emergency broadcast on every channel I could in hope that it would eventually be received. The code was a message, hidden in an old military encryption. I quickly ran it through the decryption software and read the result aloud: THIS IS THE UCF TRANQUILITY. IF ANYONE REC........ The scanner suddenly shut off, its power supply giving out. I hurriedly tired to switch out the power supply, but it was no use. I kicked the scanner in anger and frustration, hoping it'd turn back on. I remembered my vehicle had a scanner on it and rushed outside, hoping to get it running. I picked up the signal again and tried sending a response, but the vehicle just wasn't strong enough. I tried in vain for what seemed like forever before another signal came through, announcing the Tranquility's departure from the Solar system. I stared up at the sky as rain clouds covered the sun, wondering if I'd ever get off of Earth.

It had been a little over 7 hours since the lander touched down on Martian soil. 7 hours ago, half the world watched as we, the pioneers of a new age, made history. The other half of the world remained asleep. But that's another story. In those 7 hours, we had made incredible progress. We had set up our base camp, established communications with Earth, and begun to explore our new home. Now, it was time to take the next step. We were going to Mars. The six of us suited up in our bulky space suits, grabbed our packs, and headed out into the Martian night. Our destination was a large crater a few kilometers away, and we were determined to reach it. The going was slow at first, but we quickly found our rhythm and made good time. As we walked, we couldn't help but marvel at the alien landscape around us. It was unlike anything we had ever seen before. Eventually, we reached the rim of the crater and looked down into its depths. It was vast and empty, and it felt like we were standing on the edge of the world. We descended into the crater, and the further we went, the more surreal it felt. It was like we were walking on another planet. As we reached the bottom, we saw something that we couldn't believe. There, in the center of the crater, was a huge structure. It was obviously artificial, and it was clearly not of human origin. We approached cautiously, not knowing what to expect. As we got closer, we could see that the structure was made of a material that we didn't recognize. It was smooth and featureless, and it reflected the light in strange ways. We circled the structure, trying to find a way in. But it was impossible. There were no doors, no windows, nothing. It was then that we realized that this structure was not meant for us. It was meant for someone else. Someone, or something, from Mars.

A molecule traveling in a realistic propagation environment can experience stochastic interactions with other molecules and the environment boundary. The statistical behavior of some isolated phenomena, such as dilute unbounded molecular diffusion, are well understood. However, the coupling of multiple interactions can impede closed-form analysis, such that simulations are required to determine the statistics. This paper compares the statistics of molecular reaction-diffusion simulation models from the perspective of molecular communication systems. Microscopic methods track the location and state of every molecule, whereas mesoscopic methods partition the environment into virtual containers that hold molecules. The properties of each model are described and compared with a hybrid of both models. Simulation results also assess the accuracy of Poisson and Gaussian approximations of the underlying Binomial statistics.

We were in History and we were doing what we usually did, which is to say fucking around and joking and flirting all under the guise of diligent group study. I had my circle, my group of friends, with whom I shared almost everything apart from my ' talent '. Tom sat to my right, his mouth sloped upwards in a lazy grin and his hand rested on his oversized midsection. A hazy green number two floated above his head, invisible to all the world but me. Across the table from me sat Cat, trying to twirl a bright purple pen in her fingers whilst talking about how she and her sister took the family tractor for a drunken joyride last weekend to celebrate the fact that she got her purple belt in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. The number four which hung above her deceptively innocent head was identical in colour to the pen in her hands. And Scarlett sat to my left, regularly touching my leg and shoulder and laughing hysterically at all my crude and forced innuendos and jokes. I could never see the number above her head, just a cloud of sorts with no definable colour or form. She was my mystery. But then The Kid came, and I found an even bigger one. You see, I had been able to see the numbers since the day I was born, and I knew what they meant before I even had the cognitive capacity to put it into words. They meant danger. The higher the number the more dangerous the person, and vice versa. I had noticed that the higher numbers had their own texture, I could feel them as well as see them. I struggle to put this into words as it is intangible, this ability of mine is inherent and intuitive, but I will try. My ex-convict father, who I still have the displeasure of enduring for two hours every month, had a sagging and scratchy number Six suspended above his bald and empty head, whilst the Prime Minister has an angry and rough looking number Nine bubbling above his. The Kid, however, had a tranquil and soft number ten which felt like running water sat serenely over him. He walked into the class and introduced himself to the teacher, saying that he was sorry for being late but it was his first day and he couldn't find the department. Our lovely teacher then grunted at him to join our group and continued looking at whatever website he was on. We guessed it was either a job-seeking website or porn. I should have been terrified. The man who perpetrated one of those mass shooting over in the states whom I saw on the news this morning was only a seven, and world leaders were only a nine. I had thought that I would never see a ten. But the way that number ten felt, not sharp and aggressive like the eights and nines, calmed me. In fact, The Kid's presence seemed to calm everyone. " Hey, you guys mind if I work with you? I don't know many people yet " he asked with complete comfort and a warm smile. " Sure thing " Cat answered immediately. The Kid pulled up a chair and sat between me and Scarlett and asked what we were working on. " Well, we're supposed to be creating a timeline of the reign of Elizabeth I " I told him. Throughout the lesson he was the focal point of the group, delegating jobs and specific years to research and collating the information himself. Everytime he spoke people listened. Well, everyone apart from me. I was just trying to understand why he was a ten, what made him so dangerous? When I looked around the group everyone was taken by him. Scarlett was now leaning into him instead of me, whilst Cat was listening to his stories as opposed to telling them herself for a change. And that was when I realised. That was when I understood why it was that he was the ten. They say the pen is mightier than the sword, but the tongue blows them both out of the fucking water. It went on like this for a further twenty minutes or so. I tried interjecting with a joke but nobody laughed, not even Scarlett, and Cat just told me to shut up and let him finish his story.

You are actually missing a basic principle there: The lean of the bike defines the turn radius completely as long as both tires are in static contact with the ground (e.g., not drifting). Vertical bike goes perfectly straight, and five degrees of lean defines a specific turn radius at a specific speed. You literally cannot stand a bike up while turning; it will stop turning. The principles are actually more complicated than you might imagine; it has to do with the bike "following" the front tire among other things. A quick search will give you some good resources as to why leaning a bike turns it if you're really interested. In the meantime, try something else: Countersteering. Get on the bike, take it up to speed, and without trying to lean, push the handlebar on the side you wish to turn towards. Want to go left? Push the left handlebar forward. This may seem as though it would turn the bike right, but it's an easy way to get exactly the turn you want. The handlebar will quite literally push back in a positive feedback circuit and the bike will turn left. Want to turn harder? Push harder. The bike will lean exactly as much as it needs to in response to your push and you'll be making smooth turns in no time.', "When you're turning a bike, it's leaning at an angle. What you're accomplishing by shifting your body weight further to that side is actually lowering your weight to the ground, not just out to the side. This lowers the overall centre of gravity, and vehicles with a lower center of gravity have more traction. Followup question is why does a lower center of gravity help vehicles (cars, too) turn. The answer has to do with the moment arm of the centrifugal force being applied to the tires being shorter.

Once a year, the small town of Sweetville held a jelly bean contest. A giant jar of assorted jelly beans was placed in the middle of the town square, and residents were invited to guess the number of jelly beans inside for a chance to win a year's supply of candy. This year, the contest drew a large crowd. The mayor gave a welcoming speech, and then everyone eagerly lined up to make their guesses. The atmosphere was lively and friendly, with families and friends chatting and laughing as they placed their entries. As the day went on, the guesses kept pouring in. Some people got creative, using math formulas and probability theories to try to calculate the exact number of jelly beans. Others just made wild guesses, hoping for a lucky break. As the deadline approached, the excitement reached a fever pitch. Finally, the time came to announce the winner. The mayor stood on a platform and took out a big sheet of paper with the correct number of jelly beans written on it. The room went silent as the mayor slowly read out the number. It was an odd number, 1,427. The crowd gasped in disbelief. It was the highest number of jelly beans ever in the history of the contest. The mayor shuffled through the entry forms and finally found the winner - a little girl named Jenny, who had guessed 1,425. Jenny was overjoyed as she was presented with the grand prize. Her beaming smile lit up the town square. She hugged her parents tightly and thanked them for bringing her to the contest. As the crowds began to disperse, Jenny sat down by herself on a nearby bench, surrounded by bags of jelly beans. She savoured the sweetness and remembered the excitement of the day. Even though the contest was over, Jenny knew that the joy of community and the spirit of competition would stay with her for a long time to come.

So did the endless six packs we drank together. I trusted them. I loved them. Empty bottles of whisky lined my counter tops. This was destiny. I was rough on the outside, practically dead. Cynical to any sort of delight or content surprise that drifted my way. I was the waterfall at the end of a peaceful river. Despair that swirled endlessly. That was true until I met Rachel. Instead of stopping her, I let her go. I watched her buy weapons, spar with behemoths and lay in bed tireless. I watched her track my father, my uncle and me. Ghostly laughter echoed in her mind, ethereal forms of children ran past her peripherals, tugging her focus this way and that. The basement was different. She passed over the bare floor. Her shoes clomped and her clothes swished in defiance of the silence around her while she moved toward a wall that seemed out of place. A simple button, red, glowed on the wall as it begged to be pressed simply to fulfill some sort of morbid curiosity present within all people. And so Lilith extended a slender hand, index finger extended, and pressed the button. Like a grumbling monolith of forgotten times, the wall parted down the middle. The deeper darkness behind the wall drank the ambient light in large greedy gulps. Coming to a rest the wall settled once more into its dark slumber leaving Lilith staring at a sleek chrome elevator that seemed starkly out of place. Well, first we need to define what a "high-risk" investment is. Usually this will mean one of two items: 1. A young company that has created something uniquely valuable 2. A company in financial distress Let's start with number 1: a young company. This is the type of company you'll usually see in Shark TankDragon's Den. Essentially someone thought up a product or idea, and started a business around it. SOME sources of risk here are as follows (by no means is this exhaustive): 1. Management. Usually someone at this stage of business is a first-time entrepreneur (or maybe it isn't their first time, but the other attempts did not realize success). They are going to make mistakes, mistakes cost money. 2. The Underlying Product or Service. So the entrepreneur has an idea. Okay. How big is the idea really? Is this just a gag gift? Is it the next major trend? How big is the market for this idea, and how much would they be willing to pay for it? 3. The Company's Short History. It's very hard to tell if you're improving or not if you've only got a year or two of financial records (which, in many cases, could be incorrect!). 4. Management's Expectations. Usually founders of small businesses are very optimistic about what they're going to do and how successful it will be. Everything they say needs to be taken with a grain of salt. 5. TIME This one is a big one. An investment in a small start up isn't like putting money in the bank or even investing in the stock market. You will not be able to access that money for at least a few years, and usually more. That can be very problematic. 6. Profitability. In order to succeed, your company must generate more cash than it spends. Many start ups do not generate more cash than spent for several years. They usually need a lot of capital from investors like you just to survive until they're big enough to gain a profit. If the company isn't structured very well, it could be a long time before profit is recognized. (Also some industries, like a whisky distillery, by the nature of their business take a long time to have a product ready to sell). Why invest amidst all these risks? Because you're able to get a large portion of the ownership of the company for relatively cheap so that if it DOES take off, you can make a TON of money. Now let's look at Distressed Companies. A distressed company is one that has been operating for a bit, but suddenly now finds itself near or in bankruptcy. Why on Earth would someone want to invest in that? Well, sometimes the company's underlying, normal performance is perfectly fine, but they took on too much debt, or some very unusual thing happened that caused them to get in the mess they're now in. Other times, the way they do business isn't the best, and so they're missing out on great growth opportunities. So, you can either loan them cash or invest in them so they survive, get back on their feet, and then realize a good return (both the company overall and you personally). It all comes down to something called your risk appetite. That is, how willing are you to lose for the chance to win? Obviously if you'd lose 100 maximum and gain 1,000,000 maximum, you'd be more likely to take that bet. If the reverse were the case (bettering 1,000,000 for the chance to win 100), you'd avoid that. It comes down to where you draw the line, how negotiations play out, and how the overall deal ends up going before and after.', "Step one is to have a lot of money so you can lose it when you're wrong and not be on the street. Step two is to be an'expert' in the field the company is in. That doesn't mean you have to actually understand pharmacology to invest in pharmacies but you have to understand the market landscape which would include knowing something about drugs and how regulations work etc. High-risk means high reward, so you only have to be correct once to make it big, however it also means you'll lose more often than you'll win.

I knew that something must be done, but I didn't want to endanger myself or others by making sudden moves. Mainly myself, though. After all, who knew what this thing was capable of. It looked off. Unnatural. It was probably 12 feet in height and about half as wide. Its bark almost looked yellow, like there was some vile fluid pulsing through its limbs instead of sap. Its limbs twisted and turned in ways that I had never seen on a tree of any sort. Worst of all, it had shown up today in all its unholy glory. Yesterday morning it was not there and trees don't grow 12 feet in a day. This I knew to be true. Something must be done. I slowly shifted my legs out from underneath the kitchen table and to my left. I pretended to remember something important I hadn't done and made a dash to the hallway where I caught my breath. I silently congratulated myself on the convincing ploy. That thing may be the incarnation of evil, but it could still be fooled. I was still in my bathrobe and slippers, but there was no time to change clothes. That thing was duped for now, but it could wise up at any moment. In several furtive dashes, I made it to my backdoor. If that thing could see through walls, I was fucked. I had no other choice, though. With a deep breath, I opened the door and made a sprint for my shed and swung the wooden door open. Inside, I saw my tool of choice; a red chainsaw with an 18 inch blade. I took it off the shelf, set it on the floor, and gripped the handle to start the thing with my right hand while I put my left foot on top of the machine to hold it down. Here I paused. I knew that once I started it up, I would be past the point of no return. I took a deep breath, and pulled with all my might. The chainsaw roared as if it was hungry. I let out a maniacal scream and charged around the side of my house, across the street, and into my neighbors yard. As I approached the intruder, I knew the convictions I formed at the kitchen table were true. This was no ordinary tree, although it was clearly trying to pose as one. The bed of mulch it sat in was freshly dug. It had probably crawled here from some hell hole to do evil in this world. I let loose another howl as the well crafted blade bit into its evil trunk. Saw dust spewed about and it seemed that the chainsaw howled with me as I ended the existence of this evil timber. As my blade tore through, I realized that this shrub had one last bit of evil planned. It was going to crush me under its weight as its final act of spite. It didn't plan on me being such a quick thinker, though. Letting go of the the chainsaw before it had torn through the trunk completely, I dove to my left. The tree, already committed to its hateful act, creaked and fell on the spot where I had been only a moment before. I breathed a sigh of relief. I had taken the life of evil itself. It was then that I noticed five me sitting on the curb in front of their flatbed truck. They had a strange look of being both astonished and tired, as if they had done a difficult job and were now witnessing something spectacular. I noticed the lettering on the side of the truck: BARTLETT'S EXOTIC TREE PLANTING. I wished I was at least wearing underwear.

Deep metric learning holds significant importance across numerous fields like image search and individual identification. However, these models often require extensive labeled data which can be limiting. We suggest creating synthetic labels through clustering assignments for deep metric learning and introducing unsupervised deep metric learning (UDML), enhanced by a self-supervision (SS) task. Specifically, our approach involves regularizing the training phase by forecasting image rotations. Our technique, dubbed UDML-SS, simultaneously acquires distinctive embeddings, unsupervised grouping of said embeddings, and a self-supervised auxiliary task. It uses conventional clustering algorithms (like k-means) to group embeddings iteratively, then selects training examples according to their cluster allocation for metric learning, all while optimizing the SS task concurrently. This self-supervision helps steady the training procedure and promotes the development of substantial feature representations without being affected negatively by erratic clustering results. On established metric learning tests, our method surpasses existing top-tier techniques significantly and exhibits strong performance when compared with different metric learning losses.

Music recommender systems (MRS) have experienced a boom in recent years, thanks to the emergence and success of online streaming services, which nowadays make available almost all music in the world. But the success of streaming services has also led to a new challenge: music overload. Music recommendation systems aim to alleviate this problem by helping users to find songs that suit their taste, but most of the existing approaches use binary features to model the user's tastes. The problem with this is that users may be interested in multiple genres of music, but there is no way of expressing this in the binary space. In this paper we propose a novel approach to generate the required features from the user-generated playlists on the streaming service Spotify. We first extract the features that users tend to use in their playlists. Next, we cluster users with similar tastes and group them in the same feature space. Finally, we propose a novel and simple approach to convert the resulting clusters into the required features. We evaluate the proposed approach using Spotify's public API and compare the results with those obtained from the state-of-the-art approaches. Citation: Pecorari, D., Rosso, P., Gallizioli, P., and Succi, G.: Feature generation for music recommender systems using Spotify playlists, ISPRS Ann. Photogramm. Remote Sens. Spatial Inf. Sci., XL-8, 295-300, 2019.

The acceleration of sparse matrix computations on modern many-core processors, such as the graphics processing units (GPUs), has been recognized and studied over a decade. Significant performance enhancements have been achieved for many sparse matrix computational kernels such as sparse matrix-vector products and sparse matrix-matrix products. Solving linear systems with sparse triangular structured matrices is another important sparse kernel as demanded by a variety of scientific and engineering applications such as sparse linear solvers. However, the development of efficient parallel algorithms in CUDA for solving sparse triangular linear systems remains a challenging task due to the inherently sequential nature of the computation. In this paper, we will revisit this problem by reviewing the existing level-scheduling methods and proposing algorithms with self-scheduling techniques. Numerical results have indicated that the CUDA implementations of the proposed algorithms can outperform the state-of-the-art solvers in cuSPARSE by a factor of up to 2.6 for structured model problems and general sparse matrices.

This paper studies a new mobile edge computing (MEC) setup where an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) is served by cellular ground base stations (GBSs) for computation offloading. The UAV flies between a give pair of initial and final locations, during which it needs to accomplish certain computation tasks by offloading them to some selected GBSs along its trajectory for parallel execution. Under this setup, we aim to minimize the UAV's mission completion time by optimizing its trajectory jointly with the computation offloading scheduling, subject to the maximum speed constraint of the UAV, and the computation capacity constraints at GBSs. The joint UAV trajectory and computation offloading optimization problem is, however, non-convex and thus difficult to be solved optimally. To tackle this problem, we propose an efficient algorithm to obtain a high-quality suboptimal solution. Numerical results show that the proposed design significantly reduces the UAV's mission completion time, as compared to benchmark schemes.

Hands shot up in agreement with what, in my humble opinion, was a pretty good case for Yorkshire declaring its immediate independence. But that was in the 1960s and the average age of those listening at the local schools' debating competition was probably under 15. We have all grown up a bit since then and so have the arguments and aspirations. The debate over the past decade has been about whether Yorkshire would be better off if it could take more control from Westminster and Whitehall. In the shadow of a referendum on independence for Scotland the opportunities for Yorkshire have clearly never been greater. "Whatever happens in the coming Scottish independence vote, there will be more devolution," says Peter Box, the veteran leader of Wakefield City Council and a serious player in the debate. He is also the chairman of the combined authority which was recently set up with the government's blessing to allow neighbouring councils to take full responsibility for all public investment in road and rail links across West Yorkshire. But Mr Box is firmly of the opinion that within 10 years Yorkshire will want more. "The genie is out the bottle, we want more power and I actually believe Yorkshire should be independent," he said. The fledging new political party Yorkshire First is also eyeing events in Scotland. "Five million Scots should, of course, be represented, but so should other regions, says its leader Richard Carter. "Yorkshire has a population of five million, an economy twice that of Wales, but with the powers of neither." The government appears to be leaving the door ajar as far as giving limited devolved powers to at least some sort of "Northern" political body is concerned. Over the past few months David Cameron, George Osborne and Nick Clegg have all lugged their soapboxes to Yorkshire promising billions of extra taxpayers' money will be heading "up north" accompanied by local autonomy on how it should be spent. The Labour leader Ed Miliband gave similar assurances as I trailed him around a factory floor near Leeds. It is over a decade since the last Labour government's proposals for directly-elected regional assemblies for the three northern regions of Yorkshire, the North West and the North East drowned in a sea of public apathy. "Times have changed," I was assured by James Alexander, one of the new generation of senior Labour leaders that have emerged in Yorkshire since then. "The idea got swamped by arguments over a new tier of government and how much more professional politicians would be paid," he told me in an interview for the BBC Look North. "Now we need a better way of making sure our needs are determined here in Yorkshire and not in Westminster." Despite the obvious high-level political support for more devolved powers practical details are scarce. It is more likely to be channelled through groups of existing bodies such as Local Enterprise Partnerships, city regions or local councils than any new directly elected assembly. As for my long-forgotten speech calling for independence? Well, it turned out the audience much preferred the ideas put forward by another debater. He argued Yorkshire folk ought be doing more to join the sexual revolution - well, it was the 1960s.

Various adaptations of linear discriminant analysis (LDA) have been suggested to address classification challenges within these contexts, notably an LDA ensemble based on random projections, which shows promise due to its computational efficiency and comparable results when optimally configured. This study delves into understanding this classifier's behavior via asymptotic analysis under the premise that dataset size and projection dimensions increase proportionally. Leveraging random matrix theory, we calculate asymptotic misclassification probabilities, highlighting how the ensemble serves to regularize the data sample covariance matrix.
