Lincolnshire Partnership NHS Foundation Trust was criticised by the Care Quality Commission (CQC) in March 2015. A re-inspection in April this year found it had made "positive progress" in some areas and said that "staff were committed and caring." The CQC said patients and staff reported improvements to the wards at Peter Hodgkinson Centre, Lincoln County Hospital, where staff said they felt valued. Improvements had also been made to the flow of patients through the service, and there were improvements to patient care and treatment. In addition, the CQC said patients could be assured that there was a system of checks to ensure that the service provided safe care. However, the report also highlighted a number of areas where improvements were required. The CQC said that the "culture and environment" of the service was still "challenging" and the patient's views did not always inform care and treatment. There were also some staffing issues and the CQC said there was a "lack of understanding and awareness of how patients' mental health needs should be assessed and met." The CQC has told the trust to address these issues. CQC Deputy Chief Inspector of Hospitals (and lead for mental health), Paul Lelliott, said: "We were pleased to see that a number of changes had been made and improvements achieved since our last inspection in March 2015. "The trust has worked hard to improve the quality of the service it provides for people using the services and staff we spoke with felt valued and supported in their roles. "People using the service were being supported to access care in the community and a new service had been introduced to help people move from hospital to their own homes, or other community-based accommodation. "However, we have asked the trust to take action to ensure improvements continue to be made. "In particular we want to see improvements made to the environment in which patients are cared for, better access to services in the community and an improvement in the way staff assess and meet patients' mental health needs."

Valencia was founded as a Roman colony in 138 BC. The city is situated on the banks of the Turia, on the east coast of the Iberian Peninsula, fronting the Gulf of Valencia on the Mediterranean Sea. Its historic centre is one of the largest in Spain, with approximately 169 hectares; this heritage of ancient monuments, views and cultural attractions makes Valencia one of the country's most popular tourist destinations. Major monuments include Valencia Cathedral, the Torres de Serrans, the Torres de Quart, the Llotja de la Seda (declared a World Heritage Site by UNESCO in 1996), and the Ciutat de les Arts i les Ciencies (City of Arts and Sciences), an entertainment-based cultural and architectural complex designed by Santiago Calatrava and Felix Candela. The Museu de Belles Arts de Valencia houses a large collection of paintings from the 14th to the 18th centuries, including works by Velazquez, El Greco, and Goya, as well as an important series of engravings by Piranesi. The Institut Valencia d'Art Modern (Valencian Institute of Modern Art) houses both permanent collections and temporary exhibitions of contemporary art and photography.

When discussions about free speech come up, it's common to hear the argument that while the government shouldn't control our words, we still face potential consequences from others. A popular reference used online is often the xkcd comic illustrating this concept. At surface level, this perspective appears rational; however, upon closer examination, it reveals certain weaknesses. 

The initial flaw lies in its failure to acknowledge the influence individuals possess over each other within society. While governments may respect our rights, it doesn't prevent others from infringing upon them. Take, for instance, discrimination based on race or gender – although these actions are perpetrated by private entities rather than the state, they still breach basic human rights. Applying this analogy to free speech, it becomes evident that both private actors and the state must uphold this fundamental liberty.

Another aspect worth considering is whether the right to free speech encompasses not just the ability to express oneself but also ensuring unobstructed communication with intended recipients. Imagine writing letters without knowing if they reach their destination – merely having the opportunity to create content isn't sufficient. True freedom of speech requires unhindered dissemination of ideas. To illustrate using the referenced comic, obstructing someone's message is analogous to destroying mail before it reaches its target.

Lastly, harsh backlash stemming from controversial expressions could curtail free speech through indirect retaliatory measures. As an example, physically assaulting someone due to their preference for marmite on toast undoubtedly suppresses their freedom of expression. Similarly, losing employment after posting racially insensitive comments on Reddit results in self-inflicted penaltages for exercising such rights. Consequently, these scenarios emphasize the importance of balancing free speech with responsible usage.

Training sparse neural networks with adaptive connectivity is an active research topic. Such networks require less storage and have lower computational complexity compared to their dense counterparts. The Sparse Evolutionary Training (SET) procedure uses weights magnitude to evolve efficiently the topology of a sparse network to fit the dataset, while enabling it to have quadratically less parameters than its dense counterpart. To this end, we propose a novel approach that evolves a sparse network topology based on the behavior of neurons in the network. More exactly, the cosine similarities between the activations of any two neurons are used to determine which connections are added to or removed from the network. By integrating our approach within the SET procedure, we propose 5 new algorithms to train sparse neural networks. We argue that our approach has low additional computational complexity and we draw a parallel to Hebbian learning. Experiments are performed on 8 datasets taken from various domains to demonstrate the general applicability of our approach. Even without optimizing hyperparameters for specific datasets, the experiments show that our proposed training algorithms usually outperform SET and state-of-the-art dense neural network techniques. The last but not the least, we show that the evolved connectivity patterns of the input neurons reflect their impact on the classification task.

It's a strange place to find a dying man. Gordon Aikman has motor neurone disease (MND). He was diagnosed at 29. This cruel condition is shutting down his body. There's neither a cure nor an effective treatment. But Gordon refuses to give in without a fight. He's raising money for research and campaigning for better patient care. His old gymnastics club is donating PS700. Gordon competed for and coached at Kirkcaldy. It's January 2015 - seven months after doctors gave him the devastating diagnosis. He can still walk with a crutch and he drove himself here from Edinburgh. But his days as a gymnast are behind him. "It's difficult" he says. "I've looked back at pictures of me doing handstands and cartwheels and I love exercise and sport. "And I still dream of being able to run but I can barely walk, so it's a dream I'm not going to realise again." Throughout 2015, Gordon's physical condition deteriorates. He has to give up driving. An electric wheelchair replaces his crutch. Carers help him feed, wash and dress. And there's worse to come. "The thing that I'm most scared of is losing my voice," he says. "I think that would be incredibly difficult. So, not only are you paralysed, unable to move, you're then suddenly not able to communicate and speak." As an insurance policy, Gordon banks speech samples with an Edinburgh university team who are developing a voice synthesizer. He also secures new rights, for all those who lose their speech, to access voice technology. As Gordon's body weakens, his campaign - Gordon's Fightback - is going from strength to strength. It's on course to raise PS500,000 for MND research. It has convinced the Scottish government that the NHS, rather than charity, should fund a team of specialist MND nurses and double their number to 12. Gordon's inspiring example has been widely recognised. His awards include the British Empire Medal, an honorary doctorate from Edinburgh University and the Public Campaigner of the Year title at the Scottish Politician of the Year Awards. Yet Gordon is modest about his achievements. "It's what I could do," he says. "It's what I could give back. It's how I could make a difference." Gordon Aikman's story is told in a new BBC television documentary. The Fight of Gordon's Life will be broadcast on BBC1 Scotland at 20:30 on Monday.

Benny found out he could see through walls. It was weird to realize that in the 15 years since people started popping up with powers, that one had never come around. She looked at me funny, and I started to wonder why I'd said that. When her hands started to turn a dull gray, and then to shine we both looked at each other in shock. "How'd you figure that out?" Matty asked me. I turned to him. "I dunno, it just popped into my head, sorta like the way I know that you're gon na be able to make balloons appear outta nowhere." "That would be hilarious." Johnny said. I looked over at him and my heart sank. All of a sudden I realized that in 5 years he was gon na get hit by a truck when he floated off the ground near and over pass and got caught in a strong gust of wind. The wind would blow him by the over pass, then past it and he'd fall down to five feet about the road right as a semi was passing by. "No seriously Brian. How'd you know my hands would turn to metal." I looked at Janey, and realized that her first daughter was going to die of lead poisoning and I froze. She walked over to me. "Are you okay?" I shook my head. "Maybe, like..." Benny chimed in with his usual slowness. He had a habit of talking slow when he got excited. His mind kind of over loaded and the words sort of got stuck in a traffic jam in his throat. " ..... ya know. That's his power. Like maybe Brian can know what other people's powers are." Matty snapped. "That would fucking suck if he's right about me." Johnny got a ponderous look on his face. "Let's test this out. That guy in the group over by the soda machine. He was talking to a councilor. What's his power?" I looked at him and realized immediately that he could warm things up with his hands. Not super hot, just warm. I told Johnny and he walked over and asked the kid. He came back over "Holy crap. You're right dude." Izzy spoke up then. "What about me? What can I do?" I looked at her. "You'll read people's minds. But it'll only work when you're singing and you'll be singing about what they're thinking." I was relieved that I wasn't seeing any more visions of death. Maybe that had been a fluke, or a stray thought or something. An hour later, Izzy started singing. "This is such bullshit. There's not fucking way I'm gon na have some lame ass balloon power. Brian's got ta be fuckin with me. If he weren't so cute I'd kick his ass, but it's such a hot ass and oh goddamn it. Is that bitch singing my" "KNOCK THAT SHIT OFF IZZY!" Matty's face was red. Izzy snapped out of a trancey state. Matty's face kept getting redder. Suddenly a red balloon appeared in the space between him and Izzy. The tense silence was broken by the sound of me vomiting on the floor. I ran to the bathroom. I turned on the facet on the first sink that came to hand and started drinking water and puking it into the sink. Then I started splashing it in my face. After awhile Johnny and Matty came in. "Are you o" "No. I'm not okay." Matty spoke up then. "This isn't about what Izzy was sing is it? I mean the thing about me thinking about you and..." I shook my head. "Naw. Not..... directly. In fact, I'm kind of flattered if that's what you were really thinking and Izzy wasn't just joking around. It's..." I could bear to tell them the truth so I fudged it. "Something feels weird when a person's powers kick in after I've seen what it'll be. I don't think I noticed with Janey because it was so quick. With you and Izzy though, there was a delay and then it was back to back. I just got really nauseous all of a sudden." They nodded looking a little bit relieved. Johnny said "I'll go let the girls know you're okay. I think Izzy's more worried than Janey, but they're both concerned." When he was gone Matty and I looked at each other for awhile. He finally broke the silence. "So..... just so you know. The things Izzy was singing..... she wasn't making nothing up. I mean..... if you're not into guys that's cool and all but..." I smiled weakly at him. "I've..... always been kinda..... I dunno. Like, curious seems such a cliche, but..... I dunno wan na thing about it right now. As Matty walked out of the bathroom, I could still see it if I looked for it. It's hard to describe looking at it, because it's not a physical thing. It's like, seeing a memory sorta. That's still not a good way of putting it, but I can't think of words to define it. Either way, I could still see that moment in his future. Matty living in NYC, desperate for money to pay off gambling debts and get some more coke. Matty thinking about his next fix and not getting his legs broken as he looks at a guy in an expensive suit outside of a swanky night club and started forming a balloon in his throat. There were other "future memories" behind that one. They were cloudier and harder to see, but very similar to the first one. Matty thinking of another fix, or another debt paid while a balloon appeared inside of someone's body. I wondered desperately if there was a way to change any of this. After splashing more water in my face, I looked in the mirror and then it hit me. I knew how I was going to die. 30 years from now I was sitting in a bath tub slitting my wrist because I was so tired of seeing death and not being able to stop it. All the people I'd helped figure out their powers. The parents with children who'd have dangerous abilities and would have that heads up would never be enough. I stood there staring into the mirror for I don't know how long. Matty came back in with a couple of sodas. "You been in here a long time. You feeling any better?" " ..... Y'know what? Instead of waiting for the weekend, what if I gave you an answer now?" Matty raised an eyebrow at me. I walked over to him and put my arms around him. "Yeah. I am into guys." Fate be damned. I was gon na try. Fuck death. I'll fight it with love.

Most businesses end their fiscal year at the same time as the end of the calendar year, but not all of them. Many businesses with seasonal revenue will choose to end their fiscal year after their highest revenue season. Since winter is pretty slow for farms, agriculture companies end their fiscal year at the end of the growing season. Others choose the period of time where they are the slowest, such as universities who don't do nearly as much business in the summer. A big reason for this is as the business slows down, it gives the accountants time to collect the books and reconcile the revenue and expenses at a time when the company is not very busy. Another reason is, it always looks good to investors to close your fiscal year on a high note. Quarter four should be your highest revenue quarter. Another reason (if the company doesn't fall into any of the above slots) is because December sucks for trying to get work done. It's going to be more expensive as tax firms are busier, and a lot of people take vacation at the endbeginning of the year. Scheduling your fiscal year-end in August means more accountants will be available and their services will be cheaper.,Say, to name an example, that you sell toys. Toys sell best in a period a few weeks just before Christmas and around new years when all the kids come in and want to buy whatever for the money they got from distant relatives. That means that the last three weeks of the year are distinctively the time of the year where the business demands the most from the staff. No sensible person would want to add to that a requirement to do inventory checks (some businesses close down for a day or two to do them) that all the staff partake in, and having the office staff answer the accountants questions. They are probably busy doing difficult returns and calling in extra staff all the time anyway. So, to be able to handle that their work load occurs right at the end of the calendar year, they need another fiscal year. The government will expect them to have their paperwork in order, but understands that there are better times to do it.', "Let's take an example of a farm that only grows 1 crop, tomatoes. The farmer starts preparing the field to plant the tomatoes in early spring, puts the seeds in the ground mid spring, and grows them all summer. by August the farmer's harvest is over. All the tomatoes are sold, and now he's got a few months to relax and begin planning next year's crop. So there will be expenses in the fall and winter related to maintaining the farm, repairing equipment, buying seed, fertilizer, etc. But do those expenses really reflect the cost of running the farm for the 2016 harvest? Or do those expenses reflect the cost for the 2017 harvest? So if the farmer follows a fiscal year that ends in August, all of the expenses in Sept, Oct, Nov, Dec will be shown against the next year's harvest. In the long run it probably comes out even, but it's a more accurate way of measuring the effectiveness of the business.,Two primary reasons: 1. benefit from auditors, and accountants, and tax lawyers and so on being available "off peak." 2. line up your 4th quarterEOY to your peak quarter (e.g. if you are water park you might want your 4th quarter to be the summer). Additionally, it's arbitrary anyway, so....','Many governments in the United States have fiscal years that start on July 1. This allows time after the November elections for a session of the legislature to be held and a budget to be drafted.

We suggest a method for determining the six degrees of freedom (6DOF) position of a satellite compared to a standard pose based soleright on one photograph. This issue holds significant importance in various orbital proximity tasks, including but not limited to, docking maneuvers, space debris clearance, and communication between spacecraft. The technique we've developed merges concepts from machine learning with those of geometric optimization; it involves forecasting the location of distinct markers within the given image, linking these markers to their respective three-dimensional counterparts found on an anticipated preexisting 3D representation, and subsequently computing the object's orientation via non-linear optimization techniques. Notably, our innovative solution contributes to expanding the horizons of machine learning and visual computing applications while simultaneously showcasing exceptional precision, earning us the top spot in ESA's latest Kelvins Pose Estimation Competition.

From 1869 until 1982, Seattle was known as the "Queen City." Seattle's current official nickname is the "Emerald City," the result of a contest held in 1981; the reference is to the lush evergreen forests of the area. Seattle is also referred to informally as the "Gateway to Alaska" for being the nearest major city in the contiguous US to Alaska, "Rain City" for its frequent cloudy and rainy weather, and "Jet City" from the local influence of Boeing. The city has two official slogans or mottos: "The City of Flowers," meant to encourage the planting of flowers to beautify the city, and "The City of Goodwill," adopted prior to the 1990 Goodwill Games. Seattle residents are known as Seattleites.

There are five television shows associated with Star Trek, the Original Series (TOS), The Next Generation (TNG), Deep Space Nine, Voyager, and Enterprise. I feel that Voyager is the best overall, most enjoyable series among those five. I can easily enjoy watching Voyager over and over again with enthusiasm compared to the other series. The others are all good shows compared to other media but of those shows, Voyagers rates just a little above The Next Generation for me. Which for me, means that Voyager is the best of Star Trek. I feel this way based on my experience of watching every episode of all the shows. Here are some of my main aspects that I enjoy in the show compared with the others. The strongest reason for my viewpoint is based on the long running story arc of the show. The Voyager crew is thrust into the Delta quadrant and they may never get back home. No one from home may have any contact with the screw. They are alone for the most part, how will they survive, not just one year but several decades? And most of the episodes, if not in full but in part will attempt to address that difficult problem, how can Voyager get home. Each episode throws more difficult challenges at them, it just makes for compelling entertainment. It feels like a true Trek, a true voyage out into space. The comradery between the characters is fun to watch, it is also great to see them pull together in order to survive. With Voyager, they have no choice but to band together and address the challenges that are in put in front of them. And on top of that, they better become friends. Paris becomes closer to Torres. Chakotay becomes closer to the captain and Seven Of Nine. Neelix becomes closer to Tuvok. And if they don't know each other, then the top officers have to come up with an approach to find a way for the crew to become allies in their struggle. There was already some tension between the Maquis and Star Fleet, it is even tougher because Janeway wants to run the ship using the Star Fleet way along with investigating new anomalies. I didn't feel like there was the same kind of interesting team structure with TNG or the other Star Treks. And in general on the show, there were great episodes that stand on their own. I liked, Year Of Hell, The Void, Distant Origin, One, Hope and Fear. Most of the episodes with the Doctor were great. Seven of Nine had some good stand alone episodes. Directors from TNG were tied with Voyager so it wasn't a complete departure from Star Trek, David Livingston, Jonathan Frakes, and Levar Burton all directed episodes. I know there has been criticism about Janeway as a captain but I felt there was a lot of other support from other characters. And here are some smaller points that impact my view: Chakotay felt like a better leader than my other favorite commander, Riker. He advised the captain as opposed to trying to usurp her. And was just a cool laid guy. Riker was mostly the same but he just didn't seem like someone who would be in charge. He would have been a great bartender? Both "The Doctor" as an AI holograph character and Seven of Nine as a reformed Borg were both comparable to a the Data AI. With the Doctor, it was interesting that they could give an AI a true personality. The Borg, which was a great aspect of TnG had many tie ins with Voyager. But there was nothing that tied the show, season to season like in Voyager. Selecting an appropriate subset of features plays a crucial role in recognizing speech emotions. Many research efforts focus on identifying a comprehensive feature set that encapsulates all emotional states. Nevertheless, it has been observed that distinct emotions often exhibit unique feature characteristics. Consequently, conventional approaches might struggle to differentiate certain emotions when using a universal feature set. To address this issue, our study introduces a novel 'divide and conquer' strategy. We begin by creating individual feature subsets tailored to each pair of contrasting emotions (referred to as 'emotion pairs'). Subsequently, binary classifiers are applied to these specialized subsets. Ultimately, the overall classification outcome is determined through a process involving both vote counting and competitive analysis. Our experimental findages suggest that this innovative approach outperforms traditional multiclass classification techniques.

The Count-Min Sketch is a widely recognized technique for data summarization. Its purpose is to approximate the frequency of items within a data stream through a compact and constant-sized data representation. Nevertheless, the precision of such a summary hinges upon specific attributes of the original dataset. Consequently, various counting methods have been developed; while some excel under particular circumstances, they may falter in others. Practitioners are often left wondering which variation to select when confronted with uncertain data and how to assess whether an approximation's margin of error is acceptable. In response, we offer solutions addressing these concerns by introducing novel count estimators, inclusive of an optimized estimator superior or equivalent to prior ones across diverse situations. Additionally, we present concrete error limits applicable during queries for both established and fresh estimators. These error evaluations further facilitate the identification of ideal parameters for adjusting the sketch's dimensions. Crucially, it is possible to infer the error distribution within individual counters directly from the sketch. Once this error distribution is approximated, the task of count estimation transforms into a matter of statistical estimation and inference, given a predetardable error pattern. This approach not only paves the way for devising improved and optimal estimators but also enables comprehensive examination of the performance and characteristics of current estimators.

That's how David Miliband, who heads the International Rescue Committee, recently phrased two pressing goals for Syria. On Monday, as a second round of peace talks gets under way in Geneva, both the worsening war and a grave humanitarian crisis will be on the agenda again. For much of the first round, UN envoy Lakhdar Brahimi expressed anguish over the failure of warring sides to agree, at the very least, a humanitarian ceasefire in the embattled city of Homs. Then, a few days after talks broke up, the UN announced a "humanitarian pause" had finally been reached between government and opposition forces. Suffering of Syrian Palestinians In pictures: Escaping besieged Homs Over the past three days, a temporary truce allowed more than 600 women, children and the elderly to escape the ruins of a shattered Old City which has been in rebel hands, under siege by government forces, for nearly two years. Young men who left the area were taken in for questioning by Syrian forces. Their fate is still not clear. But the joint aid convoy of the UN and the Syrian Arab Red Crescent Society (SARC) still came under mortar and gunfire when it entered the area with food and medicine to ease the suffering of starving people. More than 15 aid workers were pinned down, unable to exit, for hours. "All the devils in this crisis will always try to hinder our work," regretted SARC's head of operations Khaled Erksoussi, on a telephone line from Damascus with a voice tinged with exhaustion and anger. "We have to be stubborn and not lose hope about getting aid to the people in need," he emphasised. Badly needed food distribution has also started in the Palestinian refugee camp of Yarmouk in Damascus which has been cut off for many months. But Christopher Gunness, spokesman for the UN's Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA) said the operation has had to be suspended because of clashes close to the distribution area. Such is the sad reality of the existential battle in Syria. Everything - even daily bread and innocent children - are weapons in this war. If there are, to use Mr Erksoussi's phrase, "devils in this crisis," there are also few angels. All sides are putting civilian populations in harm's way to press for advantage on the battlefield. Videos and eyewitness accounts point to attacks by pro-government forces in the latest violence in Homs but Syrian officials put the blame on "terrorists" and infighting among rebel forces. There is still no recognition on the ground of that mantra repeated endlessly outside Syria that "there is no military solution to this crisis." That is what makes the prospects for success in the Geneva talks still so slim. Like these aid operations, negotiations will be a tortuous process of small steps forward, and big lurches backward. "Its very good that it is taking place but I am sad to report there is no progress," admitted a grim-faced Mr Brahimi at the Munich Security Conference only hours after the first round ended in Geneva. "It's not often that you hear diplomats being so honest about failure," remarked one observer in the audience. He then added, only partly in jest: " You have to admit there is a certain quality to it." When the stakes are so high, and the damage in Syria so deep, there is no purpose in pretending the reality is any different. And yet, the talks were not for naught. Two warring sides, who speak only with contempt of each other, occasionally sat in the same room that week. Much of the "talks" was talking past each other, or through Mr Brahimi. But the hope is that, over time, individuals will start listening to a starkly different narrative of the war coming from their enemy. No-one expects progress to be made any time soon on the main overarching goal in this process - the establishment of a "transitional governing body" set out in the "Geneva I" document that underpins the negotiations. Syrian government officials declare that President Bashar al-Assad is there to stay unless elections or a referendum decide otherwise. The opposition insists there can be no future for Syria that includes him. In the meantime, pressure mounts for progress on the other goal that is not formally part of this process. To use David Miliband's phrase, it is how to bring "humanity to the conduct of the war." A new global coalition of aid agencies and human rights groups is taking shape to give louder voice to demands for local ceasefires, aid corridors, and a United Nations Security Council resolution on humanitarian issues alone. In recent months, under pressure from allies and aid officials, the Syrian government has been giving more visas to aid workers and has agreed to limited access in some besieged areas. But there are still many more places and people who urgently need aid. The UN estimates about a quarter of a million Syrians are in desperate need in besieged or hard to reach areas. Syria's humanitarian crisis needs, most of all, a political solution. The two goals are inextricably linked. Peace is the ultimate prize. But, when so many are starving, even the arrival of bread counts as progress in peace talks.

When a person is arrested, we say they are "innocent until proven guilty." While this may be true in some senses, it is also a major lie. Unless there is a bond set that you can afford to pay, you stay in jail for months, if not years, awaiting trial. 1. Being in jail itself is a punishment. If you are eventually found not guilty, you may not get any kind of reparation for that unwarranted punishment. 2. The punishment can turn out to be afar harsher one then many of us realize. A news search will quickly show you mountains of evidence that people in jail are likely to be physically hurt, psychologically tortured (i.e. kept in solitary confinement) or killed. You may be sick or become sick and denied medical treatment. And if you are in jail for an extended period of months, even if nothing especially bad happens to you there, you are likely to lose your job and even your home because you cannot earn income or pay your bills. If we are going to take the legal principle of presumed innocence seriously, we need to radically change the way we treat people who are accused of crimes. EDIT: It has been pointed out several times that I have been mistaken in my understanding of "the legal principle of presumed innocence." It only applies in reference to how a trial is conducted. Otherwise, the politicalethical problem remains.

When you speak, you make your vocal chords vibrate. The chords create air vibrations, which then exit your mouth as you exhale and start expanding outwards. "Outwards" includes "along your cheek and back into your ear." Airwaves that carry your voice get inside the ear canal, bat on the eardrum, and you hear yourself speak. But that's only half the story. The same vibrations created by your vocal chords also travel through flesh and bone: jawbone, temples, etc. and also bat on your eardrums, but inside your skull. Your voice contains many-many different sound frequencies - normally from 300 Hz to 3400 Hz. Higher frequencies carry more energy in them, but they also lose that energy faster as they travel further and further. Flesh and bone are much more dense than air, and in this "body route" the high-frequency part of your voice loses almost all of its energy by the time it reaches your eardrums. The low-frequency part, however, loses less energy and therefore is "louder." So when you hear yourself speak, you actually hear your voice in its full range plus the bass of your voice. Other people only hear the portion that is conveyed through the air. Source: used to work with a sound editor who had musical education.','You hear your own voice differently because going from your mouth to ears, the sound travels through flesh and bone and gets a bit muddled.

If hypothetically, the Jewish population were dispersed throughout a country like the United States—which is relatively accepting of diverse religions—the situation could potentially improve significantly. Instead, adherence to preserving their faith via a stringent state within their sacred lands seems counterproductive, especially considering numerous Jewish individuals who don't practice religion yet still identify as Jewish. This leads me to question Israel's motivation behind establishing itself as a mandatory Jewish nation. It appears to me that the tendency among Jews to isolate themselves may contribute to this issue; however, claiming that every country in the world discriminates against them would be an exaggeration. While historical examples include Nazi Germany and certain areas in New York City and Northeastern America, instances of anti-Semitic behavior aren't rampant everywhere. Moreover, various cultures have managed to assimilate into American society while retaining aspects of their heritage. Hence, I fail to grasp the need for a government-enforced ethnically homogeneous state. My clarification: Is the establishment of a compulsory ethnic majority state truly necessary?

An alternative hypothesis is suggested when the initial one proves insufficient. The null hypothesis generally represents a neutral or constant situation. As an illustration, testing if a pen falls due to gravity could involve proposing the null hypothesis: "The pen remains stationary when released." If experiments show the pen consistently drops, we can dismiss the null hypothesis regarding gravity's lack of influence and consider the alternative explanation. This process predominantly involves using statistical methods. It's important to note that empirical data lacks absolute foundational truths, aligning with the Coherence Theory approach. Furthermore, discussions about causality encounter challenges such as the Agrippian Trilemma, making it difficult to fully grasp causation. Scientists rely on statistical evaluations to assess the probability of a variable significantly impacting a particular result. Researchers define 'significance' arbitrarily, commonly setting a p-value of 0.05 for determining statistical importance (i.e., a factor deemed probable in causing a specific observed effect). The arbitrary aspect of this analytical technique becomes evident through the occurrence of Type I and III errors, wherein the significance threshold (alpha level) may vary based on required sensitivity and precision levels.

Since the Peace of Westphalia, the Upper Rhine formed a contentious border between France and Germany. Establishing "natural borders" on the Rhine was a long-term goal of French foreign policy, but it remained difficult to achieve as both countries were too large for their respective territories to be divided easily into smaller units (southern Franconia being part of Bavaria, northern Anglia belonging to East Prussia). The Franco-Prussian War in 1870 provided an opportunity to do so after Napoleon III decided that he would grant German states more power in return for territorial concessions, including the Lower Rhine region. After his defeat by Prussians at Wagram, Napoleon abdicated, resulting in the Treaty of Paris creating two independent German states: Prussia and Imperial Germany. The treaty gave control over the area from the river Weser southwards along the River Elbe until the Oder-Neisse line through Pomerania with its border crossing point at Neustadt am Rugen. In its west bank, this zone became the Kingdom of Westphalia. Extension to the north followed from the lower course of the Weser all the way down to the Baltic Sea via Lower Saxony, where it joined the new state of East Prussia under the name of Prussian Silesia. On the south side of the river, however, the boundary continued further eastward near Hanau extending back towards Ostpreuen across the modern state of Brandenburg to the western half of the city. This portion of territory had been occupied by Prussian troops during the failed Austro-Prussian war; the latter having campaigned there since 1742 against French forces based in Bohemia in support of Austrian Emperor Joseph II. Such occupation did not end well when in 1803 Prussia captured Ostpreuen and Hammerstein from Austria's allies, the Hohenzollern rulers of Poland. Occupation therefore also meant annexation of these areas which had been considered part of Prussia prior to the treaties of 1801 and 1806, although they never formally left the kingdom following Charles VI's death. Withdrawal came only later around 1890, without any agreement or particular compensation. As a consequence, the present boundaries have been contested ever since the end of World War I. Relations improved dramatically thereafter despite mutual distrust - although some historians argue for continuous disputes due to dominant Germany remaining neutral throughout much of the interwar period while others suggest a positive trend began in 1933. Despite occasional flare ups such as in 1941 when Hitler demanded that Berlin give up certain parts of the Rhineland lest Germany face full invasion, tensions eased significantly during the 1950s and 1960s when Nazi unity faded away. However, relations returned to tense levels again after the fall of the Berlin Wall and subsequent reunification process in 1989. A sharp increase in violent anti-German demonstrations occurred shortly afterwards, followed subsequently by rightwing terrorists attacks on refugee centres seen mostly targeting immigrants in Germany. An elevator is connected to a cable, which is operated by a large motor capable of winding the cable up or down, thus raising or lowering the elevator. A substantial weight is attached to the opposite end of the cable to balance the weight of the elevator and simplify lifting operations. Upon entering an elevator and closing the door, you find yourself within a compartment situated inside a vertical tube known as the lift shaft. This shaft features hoisting cables affixed to the ceiling of the compartment. These cables glide over a pulley linked to an electrical motor positioned at the top of the shaft. Additionally, these cables connect to a hefty metal counterweight. As the elevator ascends, the counterweight descends, and vice versa. The counterweight minimizes the energy required to function the elevator by offsetting the majority of the elevator's weight. For instance, if the elevator weighs around twelve times the mass of its maximum capacity for passengers, then only the additional passenger weight necessitates power during operation, while the counterweight compensates for the remaining weight. Most elevators in multi-story buildings utilize this mechanism. Converserly, in smaller structures, the elevator is coupled to the head of a hydraulic cylinder filled with fluid, which extends when pressurized and retracts when drained back into a reservoir. To move between floors, users input their desired destination via buttons inside the elevator, prompting the system to regulate the fluid level in the piston accordingly. Once reaching the intended floor and halting, sensors near the doors signal the control unit to open them simultaneously. It is a common misconception to ascribe the stiffness and rigidity of solid matter to the repulsion of like charges under the influence of the electromagnetic force. However, these characteristics are generally explicable by the causes just mentioned as well as their influences on particle momentum. This can be explained in a number of ways including its dependence upon other forces such as gravity and electrostatic potentials. The strength of an electric field (or an electric current) depends upon that electric charge which is attracted or repelled by the field at any given moment. The magnitude of this attractive or repellent force varies with wavelength of the electric field in units called hertz. As long as the electric fields remain in equilibrium the charge "on" increases while the "off" increases. Thus for example if the electric field has a frequency of 100 Hz then the attractiondislike ratio would be 1:100. If however the electric field has an amplitude greater than 100 Hertz (Hz), then the attractiondislike ratio will be 0:0. If the electric field breaks down completely then the attractiondislike ratio will go to infinity. In the latter case the electric field would cease to exist, and neither attract nor repel anything. If there were no repelling magnetic field one could do nothing but sit still; it was simply enough to induce electrical charges into the atoms which would move away from each other. But as soon as a magnetic field exists between two charged particles (such as opposite electrons orbiting around the nucleus of a atom or protons and neutrons swirling about the nucleus of a proton), they become attracted towards one another and can even form a strong magnetic field when excited near one another. This happens because electrons have mass and therefore can push against the pressure of a magnetic field. When this happens a current develops that flows through the electrons in a path similar to the way water flows through a pipe carrying electricity. It only takes a small amount of energy to cause a large amount of charge to flow across the gap between two charged particles, so the faster you accelerate two charged objects together, the stronger the magnetic field becomes. Thus if the electric field received sufficient power then it would create an external magnetic field that attracts or repelled charged particles toward itself. This is why magnetic circuits have a resistance. Since the electric field acts like a resistor the circuit must also have a resistive component. This resistance forms part of what we call electric impedance which defines how powerful the electric field actually is. In practice most circuits use some kind of capacitor connected directly or indirectly to ground to provide buffering which allows the full alternating electric field to pass through without being reversed. This type of variable impedance makes sense since weak signals will be shunted back into the circuit while strong ones will be picked up. If the wind shifts from right to left in your direction it cannot reach you because of the high centrifugal force acting on the vortex, so instead what you see is the clouds blowing over slowly to the south. These random motions of the cloud patterns appear to happen randomly whenever the vortex moves northward suddenly because every time it gets closer to the pole it goes away. Now suppose you made a line going out straight where ever there is a vortex and positioned yourself at the end of it. You may notice that in the distance you never quite get back to the point where you started. That's because there is no perfect line everywhere and at times you might miss it entirely. Similarly when the conduction electrons of the molecules of the cloud "fall" onto the plane of the wind stream the electrons will eventually follow the direction of the peak (the axis of rotation of the stream). So although I describe all these individual movements of the air as "vortices," the fact remains that those vortices change direction constantly, which means more cyclic motion around the same axis. Unprecedented dynamic phenomena may appear in power grids due to higher and higher penetration of inverter-based resources (IBR), e.g., wind and solar photovoltaic (PV). A major challenge in dynamic modeling and analysis is that unlike synchronous generators, whose analytical models are well studied and known to system planners, inverter models are proprietary information with black box models provided to utilities. Thus, measurement based characterization of IBR is a popular approach to find frequency-domain response of an IBR. The resulting admittances are essentially small-signal currentvoltage relationship in frequency domain. Integrating admittances for grid dynamic modeling and analysis requires a new framework, namely modular small-signal analysis framework. In this visionary paper, we examine the current state-of-the-art of dynamic modeling and analysis of power grids with IBR, including inverter admittance characterization, the procedure of component assembling and aggregation, and stability assessment. We push forward a computing efficient modular modeling and analysis framework via four visions: (i) efficient and accurate admittance model characterization via model building and time-domain responses, (ii) accurate assembling of components, (iii) efficient aggregation, and (iv) stability assessment relying on network admittance matrices. Challenges of admittance-based modular analysis are demonstrated using examples and techniques to tackle those challenges are pointed out in this visionary paper.

Analog Network Coding (ANC) has been suggested in scholarly works to enhance network efficiency by leveraging the variety found within communication channels. However, when put into real-world applications, variances in these channel properties give rise to what's known as "ANC Noise," which emerges from the reception process and might hinder the benefits of ANC. To date, no research seems to address how spatial channel correlation impacts ANC Noise. Our study introduces a comprehensive approach for examining the influence of such channel attributes on ANC Noise. By considering spatial correlation between channels, along with per-node transmission limits, we create models that reflect their relative similarities or differences. Through this methodology, we explore ANC Noise behavior and its effects on network reliability measured by outage probabilities. Findings indicate that spatial correlation considerably alters both the fluctuation range of ANC Noise and the overall dependability of the network. Essentially, Liechtenstein was an integral part of the Holy Roman Empire—comprising primarily of what is now Germany along with some additional territories—before gaining independence following Napoleon Bonaparte's dismantling of the Empire. Although several powerful regions within the Empire elevated their leaders to King status, while others were assimilated into newly-formed kingdoms, Liechtenstein lacked sufficient strength for self-promotion and thus evaded such fate. Ultimately, most parts of Germany unified to create the contemporary nation, yet Liechtenstein successfully resisted amalgamation, remaining a present-day country governed by a Prince. For clarity, the term 'Prince' corresponds to 'Fürst,' differing from the modern English interpretation implying kinship to royalty. During the era when European monarchies prevailed, there existed a hierarchy of rulers: Emperors being supreme, followed by Kings, Archdukes, Grand Dukes, Princes, and Dukes. The Prince of Liechtenstein belonged to a specific class of Princes called a Fürst, who oversaw a Principality under the authority of the Holy Roman Emperor. Upon the dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire, Liechtenstein remarkably maintained autonomy, eventually becoming a remnant of past times as a small, independent microstate.

This study examines molecular communication within one-dimensional channels characterized by flow-induced diffusion, wherein a receiver with perfect absorption properties is employed. It's crucial to comprehend the distribution governing the variance between the initial hitting times of multiple molecules when encoding data using a restricted number of molecules and utilizing their arrival timing or sequence at the receiver. In this paper, several variants of two-stream architectures for temporal action proposal generation in long, untrimmed videos are presented. Inspired by the recent advances in the field of human action recognition and control [21], we propose simultaneous computations that involve a direct estimation of joint motion parameters given incomplete models about their instantaneous states while taking into account constraints imposed on each component model because it does not contain all relevant information needed to reach an optimal solution. Our approach allows us to consider actions from multiple viewpoints simultaneously without requiring additional processing steps or knowledge regarding which viewpoint corresponds with some specific part of the video sequence; instead, it directly incorporates these assumptions implicitly when choosing among possible candidates based upon available evidence collected during training. The performance of our framework is analyzed using synthetic data sets obtained through ImageNet benchmarking task input datasets as well as real world experiments involving thousands of hours of video sequences captured at different locations over various seasons and environments across Europe (including Paris), USA (New York City) and Japan (Tokyo).

There are three causes of mouth breathing: Obstructive mouth breathing happens when a person can't breath through their nose at all, or can't get enough air through their nose to meet the demand. It's often caused by thick nasal passages andor birth defects that narrow them. People with this type tend not be able to hold their breath during exercise as well. They may also have sleep apnea, an even worse condition in which breathing repeatedly stops while people asleep - sometimes for several minutes per night. This makes it difficult for people who suffer from both conditions to wake up refreshed, since they don't have time between breaths to fall back into deep sleep. A bad diet rich in carbs like bread will make you more likely to snore loudly too (stock image) People whose mouths breathe heavily out of habit might find themselves using less oxygen than usual because only about half their lungs' capacity is getting used. OXYGENATION The other two main types of mouth breathing involve abnormal anatomy; these include deviated septum, where one side of your upper palate has been pushed forward so much that there isn't room inside your nose anymore - meaning airflow gets blocked. Many mouth breathers actually start life doing fine but gradually change over years due to changing postures, growth spurts, colds etc. If infants aren't fitted correctly for CPAP masks after surgery then they're far more prone to develop obstructive mouth breathing later on in childhood. Then we come to chronic sinusitis; symptoms such as runny noses, eye irritation, headaches plus mucous drainage coming down face and neck drains could indicate this is what's going wrong. Chronic inflammation around those tiny tubes connecting our nostrils with our brains leaves us unable to use tissues normally to control how hard we push air past the inflamed membranes lining the inside of each tube. This results in congestion and blockages, leading to temporary suffocation every now again if the tissue becomes swollen beyond its elasticity limit. MOUTH BREATHING AND SINUSITIS Nasal infections cause swelling of the soft tissues inside the throat and nose called turbinates. These swellings restrict airflow causing pressure build-up behind the eyes and cheeks, restricting normal tear flow, and triggering body reflexes to open the mouth and suck in fresh air to compensate. Together they form a vicious circle, making the problem harder to diagnose as patients complain of a lack of smell rather than difficulty swallowing. Left untreated high levels of bacteria trigger episodes of acute rhinitis whenever they clear suddenly thanks to antibiotics. Once they've returned the cycle begins anew unless treated properly afterwards. However, studies show that most patients suffering from chronic sinus problems do take medication designed to reduce olfactory dysfunction yet continue to experience milder forms despite taking drugs. Mouth breathing habits increase susceptibility to catching common respiratory illnesses including flu 'Our findings support recommendations promoting awareness and treatment of OSA [obstructive sleep apnoea] based upon severity,' says study author Dr Michael P Smith from Brigham and Women's Hospital in Massachusetts. This paper examines the problem of rate allocation for multicasting over slow Rayleigh fading channels using network coding. In the proposed model, the network is treated as a collection of Rayleigh fading multiple access channels. In this model, rate allocation scheme that is based solely on the statistics of the channels is presented. The rate allocation scheme is aimed at minimizing the outage probability. An upper bound is presented for the probability of outage in the fading multiple access channel. A suboptimal solution based on this bound is given. A distributed primal-dual gradient algorithm is derived to solve the rate allocation problem.

It found that in many countries, including the UK, the use of physical punishment was declining - although the decline had been quicker in many of the 47 countries that have already outlawed smacking. It also found that public attitudes had shifted, with the use of physical punishment becoming less and less acceptable and a high proportion of parents doubting its usefulness. But it said physical punishment was still common in Scotland and the UK, despite its negative effects being known and the fact that it "constitutes a clear violation of children's human rights." Among the key findings of the report were: The report concluded: "The evidence for harmful effects of physical punishment is strong and consistent, and the declines in the use of physical punishment in countries where it is prohibited make a compelling case for the introduction of such legislation. "The current laws across the UK allowing physical punishment of children in the home and in private foster care should be challenged from both a human rights and a child wellbeing perspective. "The international human rights consensus on physical punishment is clear: repeated examinations of UK laws have stated in unequivocal terms the imperative of legal reform to protect all children against all forms of physical punishment in all settings." Earlier this year, a United Nations report called on the UK to "put an end to corporal punishment in all settings" and encourage non-violent forms of discipline instead. Parents in England and Wales are currently allowed to use "reasonable chastisement," although criminal charges can result from any punishment that leaves a mark such as bruising, swelling, cuts or scratches. In Scotland, it is illegal to hit children on the head, shake them or punish them with a belt, cane of other implement. Both the Scottish and UK governments have said they do not wish to criminalise parents who "lightly" smack their children. A bid to outlaw smacking in Wales was rejected by the Welsh Assembly last month. The researchers said that this position "contradicts the evidence base that physical punishment carries a serious risk of escalation into injurious abuse."

Mr Turnbull, who was communications minister under Mr Abbott, is the fourth prime minister since 2013. After taking the oath of office, Mr Turnbull attended his first Question Time in parliament as prime minister. Mr Abbott on Tuesday said his removal was "tough" but promised not to undermine the new government. In his first public comments since his removal by the Liberal party late on Monday, Mr Abbott said it had been "a tough day, but when you join the game, you accept the rules." He said he was proud of what his government had achieved, while also taking swipes at party members who had leaked to the media and carried out "a sour, bitter character assassination." He did not say if he would remain on the backbench or eventually resign from politics. Mr Abbott's removal followed weeks of tumbling polls ratings and speculation about a challenge to his leadership. In a move led by Mr Turnbull and his deputy and Foreign Minister Julie Bishop, Mr Abbott was voted out by the Liberal party by 54 votes to 44. In his first Question Time session in parliament, Mr Turnbull paid tribute to Mr Abbott, and said these are "the most exciting times to be an Australian." "The future is one of great opportunities and that requires confidence and leadership and it will be lost if we embrace the politics of fear and scaremongering." He said policies would "change in the light of changed conditions," but did not signal any immediate amendments to contentious issues including same sex marriage and climate policy. Opposition Labor leader Bill Shorten said Mr Abbott had been "a formidable fighter" in office, and praised his "generous and personal" nature. Mr Turnbull is not expected to announce a new cabinet line-up until the end of the week. But following his fierce criticism of Mr Abbott's economic leadership, there has been speculation that Joe Hockey might lose the Treasury portfolio. Ms Bishop, who has retained her role as deputy, said that Mr Abbott had "done a fantastic job in winning the 2013 election" but that "a number of people felt that he hadn't met their expectations." After surviving another leadership challenge in February, Mr Abbott had asked for six months to turn the Liberal Party's electoral hopes around, she said. "Now seven months later the majority have decided they wanted a change of leader and that he had lost their confidence." But she said Mr Abbot was "obviously very hurt." Mr Turnbull said on Monday night the government would serve a full term, meaning a general election is likely in mid-2016. The first real test of how the public has taken the news will be on Saturday in a by-election for the seat of Canning in Western Australia. The seat is held by the Liberal Party. Opinion polling done before Monday night's ballot suggested the Liberals would retain the seat but at a reduced majority.

"Old Style" (OS) and "New Style" (NS) are sometimes added to dates to identify which system is used in the British Empire and other countries that did not immediately change. Because the Calendar Act of 1750 altered the start of the year, and also aligned the British calendar with the Gregorian calendar, there is some confusion as to what these terms mean. They can indicate that the start of the Julian year has been adjusted to start on 1 January (NS) even though contemporary documents use a different start of year (OS); or to indicate that a date conforms to the Julian calendar (OS), formerly in use in many countries, rather than the Gregorian calendar (NS).

I was eating on the bench. I had just stolen a ham sandwich out of the open backpack of a passing man. My first meal in days. I had washed my grubby hands in the nearby river and was just about to start eating when a pigeon landed right beside the bench. It preened its feathers a bit and strutted closer to me. It cocked its head, as pigeons do. I was fine as long as it didn't steal my snack. "Hey, pal, can you spare a few crumbs?" The pigeon had spoke to me. I must be delusional after not eating for three days. I took a bite. "Seriously, man, can I have some of your bread?" The pigeon walked closer. "Go away, bird vermin." I pulled my sandwich closer to me. "Come on, I'm not trying to be rude, it's just that nobody's given up their crumbs to me for three days." The bird's ribs were showing under its light coat of feathers. The pigeon was in the same state as me. It had to be a hallucination. Besides, if I gave it bread, the bread wouldn't disappear. "Okay, fine." I ripped off half of one of my bread slices. It had mayonnaise clinging to its soft, porous structure. "Thanks a million, man." The pigeon spoke this as he gulped down the delicious bread. Horrified, I asked: "You're real?" "Of course, mate. Would a fake pigeon need to eat?" I chuckled. "You're in in the same state as me, bird. Would you like to sit on the bench with me? You can have more bread." "That would be nice, pal." The pigeon flapped its wings and flew up on the bench. I handed him some bread. "Looks more beautiful than it is, eh mate?" The pigeon gestured to the park with his wing. "Tell me about it." I had lived here for three years after being unable to pay my rent. This bench had been my home through sun and rain, warm and cold. "People wander through here every day, noticing the beautiful scenery at the park, but they never once feed the pigeons. I can tell you that firsthand." "They never feed the homeless men either." I let out a raspy laugh which led to a cough. Some of the crumbs in my mouth spilled onto my beard. "Yeah, life is rough for all of us, pal." He swallowed the last chunk of bread. I smiled, knowing it was the truth. I had the feeling that the pigeon would be my first friend in years.

The sky was dark, with ash filling the air. Bullets and spells whirled past the heads of soldiers and civilians alike. Thousands of men, women, and children alike perished on a minutely basis. The worlds of Althmir and Earth have never been the same since the Rift occurred. It started years ago, in the year 3,072 U. Althmir was a planet that had perfected its civilization; it created a blissful utopia for all of its inhabitants. There was not a day with strife, not a soul was starving, and death was just a mere legend. Children were eager to learn and play, whilst still retaining kindness for one another. Bigotry had faded among adults, with people of every sort lacking judgement for each other. All the issues their ancestors thousands of years in the past had faced were gone. But what is the source for this flawless society, you may ask? Magic. Unlike our world, Althmir lacked significant progress in scientific, mathematical, and philosophical study. Rather, it was a world dedicated to magic. Studies occurred, yes, but they were focused to getting in tune with one's soul, learning to harness their inner power. Day and night intellectuals of the past worked to fine tune their spells and tomes, to try to find the solution to all of their problems. For generations they struggled with these answers, until one day, a magical prodigy was born. This prodigy, who has been given the name Alek Braxton, was born into a family that was peculiar in society. The Braxtons, rather than having tried to learn traditional magic, took a liking to dark magic, a far more powerful and more secretive sort of magic. They were regarded as kind people, but everyone knew their secret, however due to the obscurity of dark magic, no harsh judgement was received beyond the raise of an eyebrow. This study of dark magic heavily attributed to Alek's ability. From the moment he was born, individuals were aware of Alek's abilities. Upon being conceived, the child had turned the one who delivered him into a toad, equipped with a smile upon his face. He continued to showcase his unique abilities throughout his life, being happy and eager to practice spells, his parents growing more and more excited to teach him their ways of dark magic. Once he reached the age of which he was capable of actually being taught how to use and control such abilities, he was immediately schooled in dark magic, with traditional magic sprinkled in to allow him to better fit into society. His parents also had taught him to care deeply about others, something we will see become crucial soon. Day after day he excitedly learned, becoming more and more gifted in magic, better learning to control his powers. Eventually, at the mere age of 10, Alek surpassed his parents in his powers. He also began to take more of an interest in traditional magic, and after reading various scholarly tomes, learned to harness both dark and traditional magic on an equivalent level. However, due to this, he began to become more distant. Alek became extremely introverted, and utterly refused to talk to other people, including his family. In the extremely rare exchanges he did have, he only made slight noises and grunts, in a way to ask for food and drink when he was deep in study or meditation. But, in spite of his being against socialization, he became extremely powerful, and by adulthood he was one of, if not the most talented sorcerer on Althmir. Upon reaching this age, he decided he would abandon his family and become a hermit, further dedicating his life to magical study. This left his family grieving, as they missed their young, once happy and eager boy. But, amazingly, despite him despising social interactions and not caring for his parents' grief for him, he cared deeply about Althmirian society as a whole, thanks to his parents' teachings. This, in combination with his magical study, led to him eventually discovering and creating powerful spells and enchantments that would completely remove any problems Althmirian society had, which were much similar to those in our world. But this was not without cost. Shortly after accomplishing this, Alek had decided to go for a long walk through the woodlands. It was then that he discovered a strange appearance in the midst of the densely packed flora. It was a tear, not of any describable color, that floated in mid air. As Alek approached it, it shot energy at him of the same color. He took cautious steps back, deciding he would magically analyze this. He began to ponder of what spell he should use, when it hit him. This..... tear, was composed of raw magical energy. It was a representation of the world's magic, somehow compacted in a form he could see. Alek realized that it likely appeared due to his usage of a large dosage of magic, something that no being has ever had before. In terms we can understand, he had created his world's equivalent to a tear in the fabric of spacetime. Alek then realized that more and more of these would appear. Unless the source of this raw magical power was eliminated, they likely would end up destroying his world. Thus, he only knew of one solution: His sacrifice. Alek proceeded to jump into the rift, his being dissolving into magical energy. He had become one with the Althmirian universe, as well as one with magic. While his body faded, his consciousness did not, and from the magic he became, he received an abundance of information, including things about the future, past, other worlds, and things no mortal could comprehend. From this, he also realized that his existence is based purely within a Reddit post in another, more scientific and philosophical universe. He also realized that I, the narrator, was telling all of you this, which angered Alek. While he cared deeply for his world, as we know, he did not like to deal with other individuals, and to have one such individual breach his privacy and the secrecy of his accomplishments only to reveal it to a relatively large gathering of people on a subreddit provided no shortage of agitation for him. This agitation caused him to get incomprehensibly angry, with each word I type only adding to his rage. His near-omnipotent and near-omniscient magical ability, while failing to give him complete access over our world, did grant him almost full leverage over his. So much so that, in what was mere seconds to him but years to the Althmirians, caused him to appear to mortals in the year 3,072 U, the U of which stands for'Utopia.' The mortal beings saw Alek as a God, and proceeded to bow in His name. Alek took advantage of this and, in a fit of rage, commanded the beings to attack another world that he grant them access to via a Rift. This world was Earth. Thus began a war that was waged between the two worlds. On our planet, every nation united in an attempt to protect their world from the Althmirian invaders. They used all sorts of weaponry, even nuclear weaponry, which decimated parts of both planets. Millions, no, billions have died due to this, and it is all my fault. Outside, I can hear it. I hear Alek yelling my name. The Althmirians are closer to my location, their magic proving stronger than the weaponry of the Earthlings. He's commanding me to cease this, to delete this Reddit post. He claims it will all be over once this is done. But, I do not believe him. I know he is reading this, and I know it is too late now. I am the narrator over both of our worlds, but unfortunately I am confined to one of them. This world is far too damaged to save, with the last remnants of humanity fading. I must keep typing, no matter what may occur. I must ensure this post survives, as it is all that will remain of us. While Alek could easily guide his soldiers on how to access my account and delete this, it won't do much. It may remove this post from my universe, but I have a bit of knowledge that transcends his near-omniscience, knowledge that will allow people to read this and know of my mistakes, and to allow them to only view it as fiction, to perceive it as a bit of fun a writer had one evening. This knowledge is of what will happen to this post. You see, after this post is sent, it will not just be sent to my universe, but to an alternate Earth. One that is beyond Alek's knowledge. It is capable of transcending his near-omniscience, for in that Earth, we are but a smaller universe, a pocket one, so to speak, that is but a bubble in what is a bubble that is so incomprehensibly large to us as well as to the residents of that Earth. And, that Earth is within another bubble that is in another bubble, and so on so forth. I would go more into detail about this, however my time is drawing short. I can hear the spells disintegrating my house, and now I must allow this tale to come to an end. I can only hope that my world's history is never forgotten, for that is a fate worse than humanity's extinction. "Why do we do this to one another?..... Why do we hurt the one's we love?" She whispered lovingly in my ear as the steak knife plunged deeper into my gut. It had been an odd year leading up to our latest anniversary, Claire wasn't her usual talkative self, she was distant with an almost harrowed look on her face, like she was in mourning. I was worried obviously, had been for some time, ever since my retirement she seemed to lack something, that spark, that energy, which I loved her for. I thought it was our son moving out to go to college, maybe she felt like she lacked a sense of purpose in her life, not uncommon for housewives of a certain age living deep in suburbia. "I don't know" I grunted attempting to remain conscious. "Not surprising, you never knew anything, Paul. You were too stupid! Do you think I wanted you to find out like this? I wanted you to find me for yourself, to know me, I wanted it to be so special." She twisted the knife. Twenty five years on the police force, twenty years a detective and seventeen married to the love of my life, the only blotch on my perfect record, my perfect life was the Hobbs End Butcher. Always three steps ahead of the department, the FBI, me. The profilers said his knowledge of police procedure, likely meant he was ex law enforcement, or current, but they never liked to err such suspicions in front of us. His brutal killing of men, much taller and imposing than he was, likely linked back to something primal, oedipal. the killing of an abusive father figure perhaps? Maybe that's why he singled me out, maybe I reminded him of whoever it was he was really trying to hurt. "I thought I knew you" "No you don't, Iv'e always had to try to show you myself, but you never saw me" When I found the first note meticulously wrapped in a red ribbon next to a bloodied unrecognisable corpse of a local gangbanger, I knew it couldn't be good. I'd seen combat, I'd killed men, it's what made me so good at my job, when you see someone breathe their last breath because of you, it's not something you can just forget about. I was good at spotting that desensitization in others, that latent guilt, the same kind I felt. But when killers start toying with you, there is no guilt, there's only pride in a good days work and I could never understand that, never will. That's why I couldn't catch him. "Why, why do this? Why now?" "You retired, like a coward retreating to a comfortable life, I couldn't live like this anymore. You needed to see the real me, like you used too. Before you gave up." The notes had been getting progressively personal, somehow he knew how to get under my skin, I feared for my family, their safety. Months even years would pass between killings sometimes but the tell tale note would always be there mocking me for my complacency and lack of clairvoyance. I grew tired eventually, I'd see the note with its spine chilling message and shrug it off, the good looking men in sunglasses and black suits had taken over the case almost fully due to my incompetence in catching that ghost. All I cared about was going home to Claire, making up for lost time, I thought she'd be happy when I retired. "But I never gave up." "What?" Her grip on the knife loosening. "I couldn't, I tried but couldn't, I hid it from you, at first to protect you, but then because I wasn't sure if I really knew you." I wanted to understand why she was upset with me, but the latest murders drove me to look into the case again instead, the same all too familiar brick wall forming around every corner. I hid it from her as best I could I didn't want her to think I was falling back into bad habits, besides she seemed to be having enough problems herself without me adding to them. But there was something about the latest murder, the note, there was something familiar about it, something less mocking but more loving. "We've grown old together, shared so much with one another, it's time we stop playing these games." My suspicions arose when I caught a glimpse of her writing my anniversary card, almost the same words, surely a coincidence? But pieces began to fall in place like they never had done before and the closer we got to our anniversary the happier she seemed as if a great weight was about to be lifted from her shoulders. I hoped for divorce papers, perhaps a surprise second honeymoon to reignite the spark, anything else. "You knew?" "Of course I knew, I love you, you couldn't hide from me forever." I brushed her face tenderly, tears of joy welling up in her eyes. Sharing a last moment before the grim reality of the situation dawned. "Actually I think I do know why we hurt the one's we love" I reach down calmly attempting to identify the all too familiar feel of cold steel. "Why?" "Because they hurt us first" She hears the metal clink too late. I got home late from the precinct, attempting to find something, anything in the case files to dispel my fears, nothing. This paper analyzes the effects of approximate multiplication when performing inferences on deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs). However, it is not clear how to implement approximation in inference engines because there seems to be no way to construct an optimal approximating solution using existing algorithms. In this paper we propose two loss functions that extract information about which parts should be used as inputs and outputs in order to minimize weights during training while minimizing both memory usage and computation time at run time especially if a GPU architecture was adopted instead of CPU one since GPUs have much larger local caches than CPUs do making cache misses less costly compared with traditional single precision floating point arithmetic operations where branch prediction may fail due lack of pipeline depth or speculative branches executed out of order by offloaded units within compute shaders. We find that these new structured loss functions provide efficient solutions even under worst case scenarios such as vanishing gradient algorithm, batch normalization etc., leading us demonstrate significant speedups over vanilla implementations as well known techniques like MSAAMSHAA without sacrificing accuracy

The term "public" suggests the utmost degree of accessibility, indicating that the public domain ought to be available for everyone. Nevertheless, its accessibility has been limited at times. During the Enlightenptaent era, philosophers often distinguished between their idea of "public" and "people". For example, Condorcet differentiated "opinion" from the general population; Marmontel referred to "the views of intellectuals" versus "the view of the masses", while d'Alembert spoke about a "genuinely informed public" as opposed to "a deafening crowd without direction". Evolution sculpts both the body plans and nervous systems of agents together over time. In contrast, in AI and robotics, a robot's body plan is usually designed by hand, and control policies are then optimized for that fixed design. The task of simultaneously co-optimizing the morphology and controller of an embodied robot has remained a challenge. In psychology, the theory of embodied cognition posits that behavior arises from a close coupling between body plan and sensorimotor control, which suggests why co-optimizing these two subsystems is so difficult: most evolutionary changes to morphology tend to adversely impact sensorimotor control, leading to an overall decrease in behavioral performance. Here, we further examine this hypothesis and demonstrate a technique for "morphological innovation protection" , which temporarily reduces selection pressure on recently morphologically-changed individuals, thus enabling evolution some time to "readapt" to the new morphology with subsequent control policy mutations. We show the potential for this method to avoid local optima and converge to similar highly fit morphologies across widely varying initial conditions, while sustaining fitness improvements further into optimization. While this technique is admittedly only the first of many steps that must be taken to achieve scalable optimization of embodied machines, we hope that theoretical insight into the cause of evolutionary stagnation in current methods will help to enable the automation of robot design and behavioral training - while simultaneously providing a testbed to investigate the theory of embodied cognition.
