In this paper, we present the submitted system for the second DIHARD Speech Diarization Challenge from the DKU-LENOVO team. Our diarization system includes multiple modules, namely voice activity detection (VAD), segmentation, speaker embedding extraction, similarity scoring, clustering, resegmentation and overlap detection. For each module, we explore different techniques to enhance performance. Our final submission employs the ResNet-LSTM based VAD, the Deep ResNet based speaker embedding, the LSTM based similarity scoring and spectral clustering. Variational Bayes (VB) diarization is applied in the resegmentation stage and overlap detection also brings slight improvement. Our proposed system achieves 18.84 DER in Track1 and 27.90 DER in Track2. Although our systems have reduced the DERs by 27.5 and 31.7 relatively against the official baselines, we believe that the diarization task is still very difficult. Index Terms: DIHARD, VAD, speaker embedding, similarity scoring, clustering, resegmentation, overlap detection

Think of entropy as chaos. Disorder. If I took a pack of cards, there's only one way the pack can be entirely in order, so the entropy is low. If I shuffle it a little bit, the entropy increases, and it increases more the more I shuffle it - that is, there are lots of possible ways for the cards to be arranged, so the entropy is high. This is also why your room seems to get messier; a chaotic room is entropically favoured over a tidy, ordered room. It's why your headphones always seem to tangle themselves in your pocket - they can only be tidy one way, and massively tangled in potentially billions of ways. The second law of thermodynamics states that the entropy of a system will spontaneously increase. Spontaneously here means'without someone giving it a helping hand'. Your room can return to a lower entropic state, if you put energy into tidying it. You can untangle your headphones, but this takes energy. A slightly more advanced example is that solids have a lower entropy than liquid, as the atoms are all stuck in place, as opposed to liquids where the atoms can flow around one another, like balls in a ball pit. Obviously, gases have a higher entropy still. TL,DR: Entropy is disorder.,Have you ever built a house of cards? Just as you are about to take a picture, your little brother comes in and knocks it over. The structure that took you hours to build is destroyed in a matter of seconds. But why can't the reverse happen? Why can't I heat up the floor a smidge, set a dictionary on the floor, yell at it, and have the dictionary fly up into the air? That's entropy. When calculating income taxes, each tax rate applies solely to the portion of your income within that specific bracket. For instance, if your earnings are $8,926, you will be charged 10% on $8,925 and 15% on the remaining $1. Consequently, there is no opportunity to obtain a greater net income than someone who belongs to a higher tax bracket. To illustrate this concept with simplified tax brackets: if you earn up to $50,000, the tax rate is 10%, while earning above $50,000 incurs a 20% tax rate. Therefore, an individual earning $20,000 takes home $18,000 after taxes ($2,000 paid), whereas one earning $50,000 takes home $45,000 ($5,000 paid). Similarly, a person earning $60,000 takes home $53,000, which includes $5,000 paid on the first $50,000 at a 10% rate and $2,000 paid on the additional $10,000 at a 20% rate. I hope this explanation clarifies how progressive tax rates work. It's important to understand that increasing your income does not necessarily result in a heavier tax burden due to the tiered nature of these tax brackets.

Imagine you have a big balloon filled with water. The balloon is shaped like a sphere (a round ball). The formula says that the volume of a sphere is equal to four thirds (43) times pi (which is like a special number that never changes) times the radius (r) of the sphere cubed (3). So if you know the size of the radius of the sphere, you can use this formula to figure out how much space it takes up and how much water the balloon can hold!

Chloroplasts have their own ribosomes, which they use to synthesize a small fraction of their proteins. Chloroplast ribosomes are about two-thirds the size of cytoplasmic ribosomes (around 17 nm vs 25 nm). They take mRNAs transcribed from the chloroplast DNA and translate them into protein. While similar to bacterial ribosomes, chloroplast translation is more complex than in bacteria, so chloroplast ribosomes include some chloroplast-unique features. Small subunit ribosomal RNAs in several Chlorophyta and euglenid chloroplasts lack motifs for shine-dalgarno sequence recognition, which is considered essential for translation initiation in most chloroplasts and prokaryotes. Such loss is also rarely observed in other plastids and prokaryotes.

Evaporation isn't exclusive to boiling points; particles transition from liquid to gas states across various temperatures due to their equilibrium vapor pressure relative to their surroundings. When the atmosphere's vapor pressure falls short of equilibrium, substances tend to transfer from objects to the surrounding environment quicker than vice versa. Conversely, if the atmosphere exceeds equilibrium, materials accumulate in the environment rather than departing from objects. Equalization between evaporation and condensation rates occurs when both forces balance each other out. Should humidity remain under 100%, moisture dissipates from surfaces like spills faster than replenishment, leading to eventual disappearance. Enclosing a spill within an impermeable container traps the evaporating water until reaching a point where it condenses at the same pace as evaporation, halting further reduction in size. In contrast, without confinement, fresh, drier air replaces the saturated air, enabling continued absorption of moisture. Essentially, every substance possesses an equilibrium vapor pressure based on temperature, representing the quantity likely to transform into gas before returning to its original state. This explains how we detect scents from non-boiling items such as plastics, metals, and leathers. Moreover, since water vapor weighs less than air, it ascends towards ceilings and contributes to cloud formation while facilitating airflow for continuous intake of arid air. Additionally, factors such as surface composition and placement influence evaporation—surfaces might absorb water unnoticed, or exposure to sunlight could slightly raise temperatures, accelerating evaporation despite not reaching boiling levels.

We study conditional risk minimization (CRM), i.e. the problem of learning a hypothesis of minimal risk for prediction at the next step of sequentially arriving dependent data. Despite it being a fundamental problem, successful learning in the CRM sense has so far only been demonstrated using theoretical algorithms that cannot be used for real problems as they would require storing all incoming data. In this work, we introduce MACRO, a meta-algorithm for CRM that does not suffer from this shortcoming, but nevertheless offers learning guarantees. Instead of storing all data it maintains and iteratively updates a set of learning subroutines. With suitable approximations, MACRO applied to real data, yielding improved prediction performance compared to traditional non-conditional learning.

Adding salt to ice reduces its freezing point, causing the ice to absorb energy and become even colder as it attempts to melt. Since heat flows from warmer objects to cooler ones upon contact, placing salted ice against skin results in the skin losing heat. For every unit of salt added, the freezing point decreases further; for instance, using 20% salt might lower the freezing point to approximately -20°C. During phase changes like melting or solidifying, substances either consume or release energy. Hence, while ice transforms into water, it becomes colder, drawing more heat from whatever it touches. Conversely, when water turns into ice, it emits heat, briefly resulting in slightly warmer ice just below the new, reduced freezing point. Combining these factors, applying salted ice to your skin causes the ice to grow colder due to melting efforts, absorbing heat from your skin in the process. It should also be noted that exposure to such conditions could lead to frostbite, necessitating immediate medical care if experienced. Ice is typically kept at -18°C inside a freezer, but once salt is introduced, the required temperature for melting falls, potentially reaching levels like -5°C initially and becoming colder with increased salt concentration. Around -1rightfrozen burns may occur under extreme circumstances.

The first attempts to use standard-frequency single-phase AC were made in Hungary as far back as 1923, by the Hungarian Kalman Kando on the line between Budapest-Nyugati and Alag, using 16 kV at 50 Hz. The locomotives carried a four-pole rotating phase converter feeding a single traction motor of the polyphase induction type at 600 to 1,100 V. The number of poles on the 2,500 hp motor could be changed using slip rings to run at one of four synchronous speeds. The tests were a success so, from 1932 until the 1960s, trains on the Budapest-Hegyeshalom line (towards Vienna) regularly used the same system. A few decades after the Second World War, the 16 kV was changed to the Russian and later French 25 kV system.

Deep-learning based salient object detection methods achieve great progress. However, the variable scale and unknown category of salient objects are great challenges all the time. These are closely related to the utilization of multi-level and multi-scale features. In this paper, we propose the aggregate interaction modules to integrate the features from adjacent levels, in which less noise is introduced because of only using small up-down-sampling rates. To obtain more efficient multi-scale features from the integrated features, the self-interaction modules are embedded in each decoder unit. Besides, the class imbalance issue caused by the scale variation weakens the effect of the binary cross entropy loss and results in the spatial inconsistency of the predictions. Therefore, we exploit the consistency-enhanced loss to highlight the fore-back-ground difference and preserve the intra-class consistency. Experimental results on five benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method without any post-processing performs favorably against 23 state-of-the-art approaches. My sources include collectors all over the world, dealers, auctions, flea markets, and just about any place I can think of. The accumulation, as I like to call it, includes all kinds of material related to the Indian matchbox industry. Within this rapidly growing accumulation, I often come across labels and subjects that I get curious about and that is how my collection takes a thematic approach. My recent exhibition, titled "Matchbox Labels And The Stories They Tell," features some prominent trends and themes spanning the entire history of the matchbox industry. I exhibited 5,000 labels from my collection of 25,000. AE Matcheswala was an early matchbox label which started using sulphur. It set up its factories in Mumbai in western Maharashtra and Khambhat (also known as Cambay) in Gujarat state, and continued to trade in matchboxes until after World War Two. The company exported its matchboxes to Arab countries. Ambarnath, written in Hindi on this label, was the location of the first Wimco factory in western Maharashtra state. Very few Wimco labels used Indian languages and they did not last long. This rather drab label featuring the dhow is not one of their common brands. This label promoted the Swadeshi (self-reliance) movement during the partition of India's Bengal region in 1905. A number of Indian labels started during the independence struggle after calls were made to boycott British goods. Most firms used Indian languages to add nationalist fervour to their brands. Labels from the 1920s and 30s tell the story of India's struggle for freedom. Some labels even celebrated important personalities associated with the freedom movement. It's believed that this matchbox was commissioned by the royal family of Bhavnagar in western Gujarat state for their personal use during British rule. Little is known about such matchboxes because records were not kept at the time and little research is possible today. Many Bollywood films were promoted on matchboxes in the 1950s. Some labels even featured Pakistani films. Actors and film posters continue to be featured on matchboxes today.

The standard approach to providing interpretability to deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) consists of visualizing either their feature maps, or the image regions that contribute the most to the prediction. In this paper, we introduce an alternative strategy to interpret the results of a CNN. To this end, we leverage a Bag of visual Word representation within the network and associate a visual and semantic meaning to the corresponding codebook elements via the use of a generative adversarial network. The reason behind the prediction for a new sample can then be interpreted by looking at the visual representation of the most highly activated codeword. We then propose to exploit our interpretable BoW networks for adversarial example detection. To this end, we build upon the intuition that, while adversarial samples look very similar to real images, to produce incorrect predictions, they should activate codewords with a significantly different visual representation. We therefore cast the adversarial example detection problem as that of comparing the input image with the most highly activated visual codeword. As evidenced by our experiments, this allows us to outperform the state-of-the-art adversarial example detection methods on standard benchmarks, independently of the attack strategy.

When a molten metal is mixed with another substance, there are two mechanisms that can cause an alloy to form, called atom exchange and the interstitial mechanism. The relative size of each element in the mix plays a primary role in determining which mechanism will occur. When the atoms are relatively similar in size, the atom exchange method usually happens, where some of the atoms composing the metallic crystals are substituted with atoms of the other constituent. This is called a substitutional alloy. Examples of substitutional alloys include bronze and brass, in which some of the copper atoms are substituted with either tin or zinc atoms. With the interstitial mechanism, one atom is usually much smaller than the other, so cannot successfully replace an atom in the crystals of the base metal. The smaller atoms become trapped in the spaces between the atoms in the crystal matrix, called the interstices. This is referred to as an interstitial alloy. Steel is an example of an interstitial alloy, because the very small carbon atoms fit into interstices of the iron matrix. Stainless steel is an example of a combination of interstitial and substitutional alloys, because the carbon atoms fit into the interstices, but some of the iron atoms are replaced with nickel and chromium atoms.

Traditionally, understanding the decision-making process of deep convolutional neural networks (DCNs) involves examining their feature maps or identifying which parts of an image influence the output most. By incorporating a Bag of Visual Words model into the network, each element in the codebook is given both a visual and semantic significance through a generative adversarial network. Interpreting why a specific outcome was predicted becomes possible by analyzing the visual depiction of the codeword with the highest activation level when processing a fresh instance. Furthermore, we suggest using these understandable Bag of Visual Words models to detect adversarial examples. Our hypothesis is based on the notion that adversarial instances will resemble genuine images but differ enough to trigger distinctly visualized codewords. Consequently, we frame the challenge of spotting adversarial examples as contrasting the image against its most active visual codeword. Our experimental findings confirm that this technique surpasses current leading approaches for detecting adversarial examples across various types of attacks.

I was walking home from work late one night when I heard footsteps behind me. I was afraid to turn around, but I knew I had to face my fear. I turned around and saw a man with a knife. He lunged at me and I screamed. I ran as fast as I could, but he was faster. He caught up to me and stabbed me. I fell to the ground and died.

Have you ever wondered what it feels like to die? How about what a particular manner of death feels like? I used to. Then I found out, firsthand, exactly what drowning feels like. It sucks. Not the death by having one's lungs fill with water, the rapids, though that is certainly unpleasant. No, I'm referring to river rapids. The water was like a thousand grasping hands, caressing me as they pulled me under. It was pleasant until my chest started burning with pain. Asphyxiation. Lack of air slowly sapped the strength from my body until I couldn't hold my mouth closed. The watery hands forced their way down my throat, now strangling me. I closed my eyes, and decided that a watery grave wasn't so bad. I had always wanted a burial at sea. This river would be my pallbearer, and carry my body to its final resting place. I let myself fall asleep for the last time. I woke up. I didn't know where, or how long I had been out. At the time, I wasn't sure if I was relieved or disappointed. What seemed like moments before I had made peace with death, and now it seemed I had cheated it. There was a certain irony to it. I thought things over. It didn't seem likely that I would have survived. With a shrug, I decided not to look a gift horse in the mouth, then found my way to the nearest road and hitchhiked back home. A month later, I fell off a bridge. Over a river. Full of rocks. Some people just have no luck in this world, and I was not among them. I simply happened to be exceptionally drunk at the time. The tumble over the railing left me falling headfirst, and my trajectory ended at a large stone. There was a crack, and I felt my skull and spine cracking just before everything went black. Against all odds, I found myself aware again, and sober. The bridge passed quickly overhead, and began moving out of sight. I was being swept downstream by the river. A brief sense of deja vu crossed my mind as my watery friends enveloped me in a welcoming embrace. Apparently they had missed me. This time, I decided, I wouldn't resist. I opened my mouth and inhaled. The icy cold water set my lungs ablaze as I became unable to breath. I blacked out, then regained consciousness on the banks. It was at this point that I began to think that something was off. I rubbed my hand along my head and back. No blood, no broken bones, no nothing. I could have sworn I had heard and felt them break. Even with no medical training, I was certain that a fall, headfirst onto solid rock, from that height, should have been instantly fatal, or at least have left me paralyzed. Also, where the hell did my alcohol buzz go? A sharp impact to the head and an impromptu cold bath shouldn't have cleared my head that well. And this was made two escapes from certain drowning. On a hunch, I pulled out my pocket knife, took a deep breath, and slashed my throat. Not my brightest idea; even if my theory proved right, it was still very painful. Blood trickled down my windpipe. Between the blood obstructing my airflow and the leakage through the slit in my neck, each gasp was an uphill battle. Eventually, darkness encroached on the edges of my vision and the world faded away. Then, like every other time, I came back. I grasped at my neck, and found it whole, if still coated in my own blood. Immortality. Depending on who you asked, it was either a curse or a gift, and now I had it. For the next year or so, my life continued as normal, though I was certainly a lot less afraid of things. Then the questions began to surface again. Would death by neurotoxin feel different from death by hemotoxin? What was Seppuku really like? It started out innocently enough, mostly with thrill seeking and moderate risk activities. I tried fugu, a Japanese dish made from a particular pufferfish that possesses a very potent neurotoxin known as Tetrodotoxin, or TTX for short. Normally, I wouldn't try any food that requires a license to prepare, lest the poison not be properly removed and the eater be killed, but I didn't exactly have to worry about dying. I took to skydiving, high elevation rock climbing, parkour, and many more extreme sports. "Adrenaline junky" didn't even begin to describe me. One night, I decided to try something. Countless empty bottles later, and I had successfully drunk myself to death. When I woke up, I was perfectly sober, not even a trace of a hangover. My body must have purged the toxins when I revived. Well, now I have a way to sober up fast. From there, it got more serious. I leaped from a building or two, hung myself, overdosed on several types of over the counter medication (you wouldn't believe the lethal dosages on some of those things; I made myself pretty sick once or twice from not taking enough to kill me.) I even attempted self-immolation once. I was curious to see whether the heat would cause a particular organ to fail first, the smoke would asphyxiate me before heat managed to finish the job, or the shock would get things over with quickly. "All of the above," turned out to be the correct answer. Electrocution was a bit of a rush, though painful. Seppuku hurt like nothing else, but it felt good to go out like a Samurai once. I also stabbed myself in the torso several more times until I had pinpointed every organ and just how it would feel to get impaled through that one. Before you ask, I never attempted autoerotic asphyxiation. Even I have standards. I did swim with the fishes several more times, though. Nothing ever feels quite like your first time. After a while, that got boring. I once set myself on fire, then jumped off a building, just to see if the fire or the fall would get me first. The rush of air extinguished the flames on my way down, so I had to try again with a more potent fuel. I went on a trip to Australia, and made a point of encountering every creature the continent had to offer. Swimming with box jellies was not my smartest move; it took me dying several deaths to extricate myself from the infested waters. General advice for those that follow; do not mess with the wildlife. Very few animals failed to finish me off, including one or two that I wouldn't have expected. Just to be safe, steer clear of the flora as well. By this point, I had a high pain tolerance and a certain degree of non-sexual masochism. Don't ask how, but I managed to get my hands on some particularly nasty poisons, toxins, and chemicals. You name it, I've probably died by it. Shady connections go a long way. Unfortunately, all of this became rather expensive. Fortunately, I had become an urban legend. Blurred videos depicting a man getting up after falling from the tallest building in a city. All I had to do was slowly bring myself into the public eye, then capitalize on my fame with literal death-defying stunts. The sponsorship deals let me do all manner of fun and interesting stuff. Firing squad, electric chair, tesla coil, fireworks. I even got a repeat trip to Australia paid for, and had a camera crew follow me, recording my run-ins with the local flora and fauna. After a while, I decided to make use of my newfound resources. I started planning elaborate executions for myself. I jumped from a high scaffold with nitroglycerine strapped to my body, detonating me on impact. Even being blown to bits couldn't kill me, it seemed; my scattered pieces just coalesced and put themselves back together like a grotesque jigsaw puzzle. Today, I attempt something more ridiculous than anything ever before. I am going to go up in a glider laced with nitroglycerine. Turbulence will detonate the sensitive explosives sooner or later, but nobody will know when. If I start losing altitude before they do, I will eject, more nitroglycerine strapped to my body. As I fall, a cord attached to me will pull a switch, detonating the plane behind me. In essence, a Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) assault involves numerous devices simultaneously bombarding a target server with multiple requests. Such attacks typically employ 'botnets', decentralized networks consisting of unsuspecting computers infected by malicious software. These compromised machines, referred to as 'zombies' or 'bots,' receive instructions from an orchestrator known as a 'herder.' Their combined efforts result in massive traffic directed towards a specific website. The strength of a botnet can be gauged via its PPS or RPS rate – pings per second or requests per second, respectively. Contrastingly, a traditional Denial of Service (DoS) attack emanates from fewer sources, often just one device. Though simpler to mitigate than a DDoS strike due to the limited number of involved IP addresses, smaller websites without robust protection measures can still fall victim to such incursions. Importantly, not every instance of DDoS activity is intended harmfully. For example, the phenomenon of Reddit users flooding certain websites has occurred when Reddit's immense popularity causes unintentional disruptaion.

Policy gradient methods in reinforcement learning aim at optimizing policies by effectively sampling from the environment. Nonetheless, although current sampling techniques typically focus only on the agent's policy, there may be alternative metrics within these frameworks that can enhance the sampling process prior to updating the policy. Along those lines, we suggest implementing SAUNA, which involves rejecting transitions during gradient updates if they fail to satisfy a certain condition or accepting them if they comply. The condition applied here is the variance explained (VeX), representing the difference between a model'right outputs and real-world observations. Utilizing VeX allows us to appraise the influence individual transitions have on the learning process, thus enhancing the efficacy of policy gradient algorithms. Throughout our research, we address several points: (i) Introducing and examining VeX as a filter for cleaning policy gradients; (ii) Testing our approach using various established benchmark settings, particularly focusing on continuous control tasks, demonstrating improved outcomes when employing SAUNA; (iii) Investigating the reasons behind VeX's effectiveness in choosing beneficial samples for learning; (iv) Demonstrating how VeX acts as an adaptable mechanism for balancing exploration and exploitation strategies.

Considering a short frame length, which is typical in Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency and massive Machine Type Communications, a trade-off exists between improving the performance of frame synchronization (FS) and improving the performance of information throughput. In this paper, we consider the case of continuous transmission over AWGN channels where the synchronization sequence is superimposed to the data symbols, as opposed to being added as a frame header. The advantage of this superposition is that the synchronization length is as long as the frame length. On the other hand, its power has to be traded-off not to degrade the code performance. We first provide the analysis of FS error probability using an approximation of the probability distribution of the overall received signal. Numerical evaluations show the tightness of our analytic results. Then we optimize the fraction of power allocated to the superimposed synchronization sequence in order to maximize the probability of receiving a frame without synchronization errors nor decoding errors. Comparison of the theoretical model predictions to a practical setup show very close optimal power allocation policies.

Researchers at MIT have created a rechargeable lithium-ion battery in the form of a 460-foot-long fiber. The batteries can be manufactured to arbitrarily long lengths. They can be 3D-printed into new shapes or formed with machines such as roll forming and bending equipment. The researchers improved on existing methods for manufacturing these types of materials, which typically leave large portions of waste because they are difficult to make thinner than 100 microns (0.0039 inches). This is an order-of-magnitude smaller than most metal structures that are being used today. In this instance, two different metals were combined inside one battery chamber at room temperature - LiNiCoMnOz and CuCl. On top of that layer, another was added: FeS2, which acts like an anode and oxidizes by releasing oxygen during charging. A separate cathode containing graphite acted based off its ability to store electrons. "If you don't add any other material it's just pure carbon dioxide coming out of it so there's no energy retention capability whatsoever," said Chris Mooney, professor of electrical engineering and director of the Center for Advanced Energy Battery Research and Development, according to EurekAlert! After these layers were stacked together, they were heated up to 500 degrees Celsius (932 degrees Fahrenheit) using steam pressure. In addition to adding more structure, heat increases chemical reaction rates between current collectors and electrodes within cells. Once cooled down to room temperature, some regions in the cell became smoother while others retained their roughness. It depends upon how much carbon we saw crystallizing through those areas that's what caused the differences in surface finish, according to Mooney. Heat treatment also increased conductivity, meaning less resistance would need to go through when electricity flows from one end to the next within the device. That reduced size will translate directly onto devices since smaller means cheaper, lighter weight and quicker charge times. Since the power supply does not require to be attached to anything, sliding over objects becomes easier too. However, Mooney didn't say whether these fibers can actually carry enough electricity to fully replace traditional batteries; he simply wanted to show how well electric vehicles could benefit from the technology before making the claims themselves. If a tree grows all its life in the open and the conditions of soil and site remain unchanged, it will make its most rapid growth in youth, and gradually decline. The annual rings of growth are for many years quite wide, but later they become narrower and narrower. Since each succeeding ring is laid down on the outside of the wood previously formed, it follows that unless a tree materially increases its production of wood from year to year, the rings must necessarily become thinner as the trunk gets wider. As a tree reaches maturity its crown becomes more open and the annual wood production is lessened, thereby reducing still more the width of the growth rings. In the case of forest-grown trees so much depends upon the competition of the trees in their struggle for light and nourishment that periods of rapid and slow growth may alternate. Some trees, such as southern oaks, maintain the same width of ring for hundreds of years. Upon the whole, however, as a tree gets larger in diameter the width of the growth rings decreases.

Scientists have confirmed that flamingos expend less energy standing on one leg than in a two-legged stance, according to a recent study. The study, published in the journal Biology Letters, found that standing on one leg allowed flamingos to minimize the amount of energy needed to maintain their balance. The researchers used infrared cameras to measure the amount of heat radiated by the birds, which allowed them to calculate the amount of energy used. Lead author of the study, Dr. Matthew Anderson of St. Joseph's University in Philadelphia, said that the findings were surprising. "We found that the flamingos only used about 50 of the energy when standing on one leg compared to two," he said. The researchers suggest that this energy-sparing technique enables flamingos to conserve energy, which is important for survival during periods of migration and breeding. Flamingos are known to stand on one leg for extended periods of time, sometimes up to six hours a day. The study also found that flamingos stood on one leg more often when they were in water, likely because maintaining balance is more difficult in water than on land. The researchers hope that their findings will lead to a better understanding of how birds conserve energy and maintain balance, and could potentially inspire new ways to design structures or devices that require balance and stability. Overall, the study sheds new light on the remarkable abilities of flamingos, which have long fascinated scientists and bird enthusiasts alike. From their bright pink feathers to their unique behaviors, these birds are truly one of nature's most fascinating creatures.

My parents were getting divorced and it felt like my world was shattered. All I had was advice from a little blue fish. But that didn't stop my mother from trying to intervene. She warned me about tattoos taking away whatever they give and that they aren't worth it. But that didn't stop me. I was an adult now. I could do what I wanted. Her opinion no longer mattered; so I took the plunge. I walked into the store called Inklings. It sounded perfect for a first timer like me. The artist was so nice although his tattoos scared me at first. He had the Toostie Pop Owl in the middle of his neck. When I asked him about it he said "it helps me solve problems." I closed my eyes and white-knuckled the armrest doing my best not to cry out. Just when I thought I couldn't handle anymore there was a break. The outline had been finished and now he asked if I was ready for the colour a process that was even more painful. I looked at myself in the mirror and those timeless words stared back at me. My mind bellowed just keep swimming. And I did. It took another hour but there it was forever on my shoulder. A reminder whenever I needed it. My mother was not impressed, she said I would regret it. I dove deeper hoping to experience that rush of clarity again. The further I went, the better I felt. I was at peace. My lungs should be desperate for oxygen, but they aren't. I was baffled. I haven't been swimming since the tattoo; they said to avoid soaking it for at least two weeks. I was extra good and waited a full month. I stopped to ponder this but the thought left as soon as it entered. The waves carried it far away from me. I continued my descent as the waves brought a new thought to the surface of my mind. Just keep swimming. Just keep swimming. Just keep swimming.

There is a tube (Eustachian tube) connecting the inside of your ear and your nose. Its purpose is to drain excess fluid and to relieve pressure in the ear. Normally the tube is held closed. When you swallow, yawn, or stretch your muscles, the tube is temporarily opened allowing pressure to equalize. An example of a time this is necessary is on an airplane when your ears pop due to the pressure change, and you need to swallow or chew gum to fix it. Normally your hear noises around you by the sound traveling through air into your ear and hitting the eardrum. While the tube is held open, it messes up your hearing because you're getting extra sounds coming up through your nose. As well, the movement of the eardrum is affected by this extra opening. The result is that it's hard to hear noises around you. But for noises coming from within (your own voice, breathing, etc.) it's a different story. Noises from within do not travel through the air; they travel through your bones going straight to your inner ear. His laughter had rung out from atop the mountain, producing an echoing chorus of chortles that tickled the ears from every angle. But Sir Night wasn't laughing anymore. The legendary beast stood before him, and as the sound of laughter continued to reverberate around him, his feelings of regret and the trembling of the sword in his hands increased exponentially. The very instant that he let out the slightest chuckle, that he did what he was explicitly told not to do, he sealed his fate. The Laughing Crow is truly a remarkable beast. In the midst of terror, Sir Night thought back to when he sought the wisdom and permission of the council of elders. They alone among those within the district of Lynnsong presided over the hunt for the creature. Only they were to have knowledge of the creature and its whereabouts, lest some amateur knight try to slay the monster and kill hundreds in the process. It was only with the counsel's blessing and guidance that he, and countless martyrs before him, could take up the task of conquering the beast. Whatever you do, you must not laugh. If you laugh, you will bring about his true form and your death. But that was impossible. And he realized that no one who laughed had lived to tell otherwise. While there was nothing humorous about the once small crow, the second he and the crow made eye contact, his body betrayed him. In that instant, he was not able to fight the laughter nor prevent it. And he hadn't the slightest idea why. The Laughing Crow had grown in size by nearly 100 times, and a seething, violent rage seemed to ooze from it, permeating the atmosphere and sending a shiver up Sir Night's spine. It spread its wings and let out a terrible, rupturing cry, blocking out any sunlight and remaining laughter. Sir Night closed his eyes, bracing himself for what was about to happen. Standing there, eyes shut tight and body quaking, he heard the beast moving towards him. In my last moments, there's nothing but darkness. Just the cry of the beast who will conquer me. True, terrible terror. I've never felt anything like this before. How could anyone conquer something like this? That's...insanity. At the realization of his own helplessness and the absurdity of his own demise, he lost control of his mental capacities. In the face of utter despair, he began to laugh, and he couldn't stop. Suddenly, the sounds of the The Laughing Crow's cry came to a halt. Sir Night could no longer hear the beast approaching him, but he remained there with his eyes closed for several minutes, not daring to move an inch. Eventually, he opened his eyes. Where The Laughing Crow had stood, murderous and hateful, was the small black crow he first met on the mountain top. While he was both amazed and confused, what he felt most was how undeserving he was of his own victory. Sir Night failed to understand exactly how he had come to conquer the creature, and after doing away with the crow, one thing became abundantly clear to him. As a knight, I will never be truly victorious..... until I'm able to laugh in the face of fear. Note: Constructive criticism is always welcome!

Cymbospondylus youngorum may have been the first giant animal that ever lived on Earth. The new type of ichthyosaur was discovered in the Augusta Mountains of Nevada with a skull almost twice the size and weight of its closest relatives. The study, led by researchers from North Carolina State University and the Smithsonian Institution, is published today (November 25) in Nature Ecology Evolution. It documents an "enormous" ichthyosaur species that could be up to 22 meters long including tail. "Our discovery suggests that many more gigantic ancient marine reptiles existed than previously thought," said Jason Beal, professor of integrative biology at NC State and co-author of the paper. "This means these animals had much greater ecological flexibility than we realized." All vertebrates fish, amphibians, birds, mammals, etc. are descended from ichthyosaurs, which were incredibly diverse during the Triassic Period between 225 million years ago and 201 million years ago. However, no members of this group survived into the Jurassic period when dinosaurs evolved on land. Cymbospondylus youngorum is a member of a newly defined genus called Cymbospondylus, meaning "swinging swimmer," because it swung around as it swam like bony plates do in modern sea turtles or gastropods such as snails. This trait helped keep the creature's head above water while swimming through the deep ocean. Beal and his colleagues studied a jawbone fossil they found in the Augusta Mountains in southern Nevada. They determined that C. youngorum lived about 231 million years ago, which would make it one of the most ancient known ichthyosaurs. Their research revealed that the jawbone belonged to an adult male measuring 9 feet, 8 inches tall and weighing more than 2 tons, making him among the largest known ichthyosaurs. By comparison, the second-largest ichthyosaur measured only 7.2 feet long and weighed nearly 3 tons; the third-largest, at 5.7 feet long and roughly 1 ton, was probably female. C. youngorum is also notable for having a total skull length (from snout tip to tip of the tail) that is 10 percent larger than the nearest living relative. Finally, the skull has two large inner ear openings slightly farther apart on either side of its face than any other recent ichthyosaur fossils. Even though scientists cannot confirm whether C. youngorum could actually swim, their examination of the bones suggest that it might not have needed to move quickly to survive. In fact, the only way the new taxon could have reproduced sexually would be if it ate something small enough to pass through its digestive tract and then reproduce asexually. Researchers plan to continue exploring rock formations in southwestern Nevada where the specimen was found. They hope further discoveries will clarify some outstanding questions about ichthyosaurs, including why so few became huge.

The rising popularity of social media has radically changed the way news content is propagated, including interactive attempts with new dimensions. To date, traditional news media such as newspapers, television and radio have already adapted their activities to the online news media by utilizing social media, blogs, websites etc. This paper provides some insight into the social media presence of worldwide popular news media outlets. Despite the fact that these large news media propagate content via social media environments to a large extent and very little is known about the news item producers, providers and consumers in the news media community in social media.To better understand these interactions, this work aims to analyze news items in two large social media, Twitter and Facebook. Towards that end, we collected all published posts on Twitter and Facebook from 48 news media to perform descriptive and predictive analyses using the dataset of 152K tweets and 80K Facebook posts. We explored a set of news media that originate content by themselves in social media, those who distribute their news items to other news media and those who consume news content from other news media andor share replicas. We propose a predictive model to increase news media popularity among readers based on the number of posts, number of followers and number of interactions performed within the news media community. The results manifested that, news media should disperse their own content and they should publish first in social media in order to become a popular news media and receive more attractions to their news items from news readers.

Now-a-days Health Care industry is well equipped with Medical Equipments to provide accurate and timely reports of investigation and examination results. Medical Equipments available in market are made for specific tests suited for a particular laboratory leading to a wide variety of devices. The result viewing experience on console of these devices is not only cumborsome for medical staff but inefficient. Therefore, Medical Equipment Interfaces act as backbone of any Hospital Management Information System assisting in better management and delivery of test results. It also acts as a mode to collect data for further research and analysis. These equipments communicate via a fixed data format but compatibility among these formats is a major issue being faced in modern and legacy medical equipments. In this paper, we present a case study of designing and implementing a cloud based Generic Medical Equipment Interface (GMEI) along with the state of the art in such systems. This solution removes the burden of reentry of patient details into the Electronic Health Record (EHR) and thrives for accelerating EMR initiative in the country.

Certain nouns possess two distinct diminutive variations that convey different meanings; for instance, 'bloem' translates to 'flower,' whereas its diminutive versions are 'bloempje' and 'bloemetje', both signifying "small flower" yet differing as 'bloempje' implies a literal small flower and 'bloemetje' suggests a bouquet. There are instances where nouns appear exclusively in diminutive form like 'zeepaardje' (seahorper), whilst others such as 'meisje' (originally derived from 'meid') have developed standalone definitions apart from their original ones - 'meisje' means girl even though it is a diminutive version of 'meid'. Diminutives may occasionally be used on uncountable nouns to denote a singular serving, exemplified by 'biertje' denoting a conical ice cream or 'kleertjes' which only exist in plural, referring to clothing.

The receiver of your handset converts your voice to electrical signals and transmits them over the telephone wires to another person's handset, where they are then converted back to audio signals. This is the basis on which the telephone system is built. (For mobile phones, there is transmission between the phone and a local tower through radio waves, but the rest of the connection is essentially the same.) The main technical difficulty, of course, is routing the call to the correct destination. In the past, your call would go to a local exchange, you would tell the operator there what person you want to talk to (or provide their phone number), and then they would literally connect the wires on the switchboard so that your phone line has a direct connection to the line of the person you're calling. The principal used at exchanges is the same, but is now computerized, removing the need for the operator as well as the physical moving of wires. The desire for automation required that you be able to send information back and forth without the intervention of a human operator. When you dial a number, your handset sends electrical signals that will be interpreted as those numbers to the exchange. That's also how a busy signal or a dial tone is sent; it's just a complex electric circuit. You may have heard of "pulse" and "touch-tone" dialing. Landline handsets usually have options for either one, so they can support older networks, but mobile phones always use touch-tone. In the more modern system, instead of sending special electrical pulses, each number has an assigned tone that is sent, instead. (The sound of the tone is, of course, still sent as electricity.) The use of special tones makes it easier to transmit a wide range of information. If your phone plays particular tones when dialing particular numbers on the pad, you're hearing the tones that will be sent to the exchange. On a landline, instead of dialing, you can actually just play the sound of the appropriate number into the horn and it will work just as well.

Essentially, your cells exist within a watery environment where they are linked together via various proteins. This surrounding liquid contains numerous substances either dissolved or suspended. Your cell requires specific components found in this mixture, commonly referred to as the "interstitial fluid". For these nutrients to reach the interior of the cell, several pathways may be taken. Some nutrients travel inward without any effort due to diffusion - a spontaneous occurrence facilitated by the partially permeable nature of the cell membrane. Other nutrients traverse specialized protein channels present in the membrane. However, nutrients tend to move towards areas with lower concentrations. In addition, certain proteins function as 'pumps', using energy to transport nutrients across the membrane against their concentration gradient. Similarly, nutrients transition from your bloodstream to the interstitial fluid via capillaries, which are thin-walled microscopic blood vessels spread throughout your tissues. These capillaries don't serve individual cells; rather, each one caters to dozens or even hundreds of cells based on the location within the body. Consequently, you find a higher density of capillaries in facial regions compared to extremities such as feet. Edit correction: It should be termed "interstitial fluid", instead of "intercellular solution".

One example of omnidirectional antennas is the very common vertical antenna or whip antenna consisting of a metal rod (often, but not always, a quarter of a wavelength long). A dipole antenna is similar but consists of two such conductors extending in opposite directions, with a total length that is often, but not always, a half of a wavelength long. Dipoles are typically oriented horizontally in which case they are weakly directional: signals are reasonably well radiated toward or received from all directions with the exception of the direction along the conductor itself; this region is called the antenna blind cone or null.

In our study, we compared this network to the open-source online annotated genome annotation project called GEO (Global Entropy Ecosystem) that captures both coding as well as noncoding information in the human genome. The data sets are quite huge: there were approximately 2 million genes included in the annotations for GEO and about 100 thousand genes were uploaded into GEO using a custom pipeline (Figure 2), indicating that GEO's contribution is not just limited to coding information but also includes some non-coding information such as gene maps or protein sequences (Cheung et al., 2013). As an example, among those represented genes, more than half are known to be involved in gene regulation (Zhang, 2012; Karowal et al., 2014a). At least one large part of these genes have been previously linked with neurodevelopment disorders including schizophrenia Cheung et al., 2013) and epilepsy Karowal et al., 2014b. Our comparison showed that high quality code that spans many different proteins was encoded over 30 of genes annotated in GEO. Among these codes, most of them encode proteins important for visual function. However, only 1 out of 213 genes encoding a neuronal ion channel has been related to any other central nervous system disorder, suggesting that many more similar genes may remain untyped (Figures 3A-C). Despite the diversity of genes, they reveal strong shared gene networks across species and taxa, which indicates under what conditions these genes might interact to produce visual effects. A common step between different types of neurons seems to be their activation. Although neurons show differences in size, shape and composition within the brain, it remains unclear whether these differences impact neuronal connections or a set of early experiences, which could possibly affect development later on in life (Kita et al., 2015). We found that the results revealed by the work published above suggest that interconnectivity patterns in the fly neural networks are comparable to those in humans. On top of this, we discovered that the fly brain contains highly interconnected networks involving both spatially and temporally separated parts. This shows that brains widely divergent from each other display similar characteristics, even though the physical structure and inner workings differ considerably. It implies that many complex functions occur at smaller scale, which means that the overall computational complexity of the fly brain is comparable to that of humans. These insights provide valuable insight into how the brain works in general. While previous studies have shown the importance of coding information in certain types of interactions and processes, none of the current research focused solely on the linkages between coding information between genes and developmental events. For instance, in a recent review article, Izumi (2015) described how the phenotype of animals greatly depends upon the interaction between genetic expression and phenotypic outcome. However, although much more effort needs to go into this area due to the relatively low number of genes, she did mention that "the link between individual genes and behavioural traits is becoming clearer." Unfortunately, the relevance of coding information alone cannot explain why phenotypes vary so much across individuals, nor can it provide the basis for new hypotheses regarding developmental mechanisms (Izumi, 2015). One of the main reasons behind this discrepancy is the lack of reliable genomic tools for studying developmental processes through the genetic linkage: since most developmental events take place inside the cell nucleus, genomic analysis of genomes tends to focus on vast tracts of DNA rather than a small subset of genes expressed at specific times (Izumi et al., 2015). Expecting to uncover some relevant links between coding information and developmental states requires a wide repertoire of molecular methods based on whole genome sequencing as well as various approaches based on SNP genotyping. While the latter approach provides valuable insights of gene function at lower levels of evolution, it also comes with its own limitations: SNPs generally do not change the allele frequency distributions of genes but influence their spatial distribution instead. Therefore, depending on which loci are selected during sequence inference, it will rarely lead to changes in the allele frequencies (e.g. exonic regions) of the targeted genes without influencing the presenceabsence of others. Thus, while studies focusing on rare variants are promising, this population would still likely not contain all relevant genes (see the Methods section). A superconducting optoelectronic neuron will produce a small current pulse upon reaching threshold. We present an amplifier chain that converts this small current pulse to a voltage pulse sufficient to produce light from a semiconductor diode. This light is the signal used to communicate between neurons in the network. The amplifier chain comprises a thresholding Josephson junction, a relaxation oscillator Josephson junction, a superconducting thin-film current-gated current amplifier, and a superconducting thin-film current-gated voltage amplifier. We analyze the performance of the elements in the amplifier chain in the time domain to calculate the energy consumption per photon created for several values of light-emitting diode capacitance and efficiency. The speed of the amplification sequence allows neuronal firing up to at least 20 MHz with power density low enough to be cooled easily with standard 4 He cryogenic systems operating at 4.2 K.

Sweating is an issue while cycling due to physical activity; however, a bicycle helmet is designed to allow ample airflow around the head, facilitating proper evaporation of sweat. Unlike skateboards, where falls are frequent, bicycles generally do not experience high-speed accidents on solid surfaces, hence their helmets are constructed to cushion impact through controlled deformation rather than relying on rigidity like those made for lower-impact sports such as skateboarding. Additionally, child bike helmets may feature sturdier shells given their propensity for slower speeds and higher likelihood of collisions. 

Regarding the structure of bike helmets, numerous large openings serve multiple purposes – reducing weight and material cost, enhancing breathability, and potentially cutting down on aerodynamic drag. However, these benefits come with trade-offs; increased ventilation might lead to discomfort in colder climates, prompting some cyclists to block off airways during winter rides. Conversely, specialized helmets for activities like triathlons minimize vents to reduce wind resistance. Although each type of helmet caters to different needs based on sport and environmental conditions, all share the essential function of protecting the wearer’s head from injury.

The primary concern I have with the decision is that it might allow companies to exclude specific groups, such as LGBTQ+ individuals, from accessing certain products or services. For instance, if establishments like bakeries were permitted to deny service to gay people under this ruling, it could potentially result in many bakeries adopting such policies, thereby restricting access to these goods or services for the LGBTQ+ community. Anti-discrimination laws exist precisely to prevent scenarios like this. In reality, how probable is it that this will occur? My guess is that there are far more inclusive businesses displaying signs saying "We welcome everyone," compared to those refusing service to LGBTQ+ people. Whenever a single establishment declares it won't serve gay people, it becomes a major topic of discussion online, suggesting that it's quite rare. Moreover, excluding gay people from a business isn't sound strategy – at its core, turning away an entire group based on their sexual orientation makes no sense whatsoever, especially since you'll end up losing a significant portion of your clientele. Some may argue that bigoted individuals would preferentially frequent businesses that discriminate against LGBTQ+ people, but provided there are alternative non-discriminatory businesses available, I don't think that poses any real problem. Even if all similar service providers decided to bar entry to LGBTQ+ individuals, wouldn't this simply pave the way for new businesses offering non-discriminatory services to emerge? This situation should naturally encourage competition amongst businesses to cater to diverse audiences without prejudice.

Traditional slot filling in natural language understanding (NLU) predicts a one-hot vector for each word. This form of label representation lacks semantic correlation modelling, which leads to severe data sparsity problem, especially when adapting an NLU model to a new domain. To address this issue, a novel label embedding based slot filling framework is proposed in this paper. Here, distributed label embedding is constructed for each slot using prior knowledge. Three encoding methods are investigated to incorporate different kinds of prior knowledge about slots: atomic concepts, slot descriptions, and slot exemplars . The proposed label embeddings tend to share text patterns and reuses data with different slot labels. This makes it useful for adaptive NLU with limited data. Also, since label embedding is independent of NLU model, it is compatible with almost all deep learning based slot filling models. The proposed approaches are evaluated on three datasets. Experiments on single domain and domain adaptation tasks show that label embedding achieves significant performance improvement over traditional one-hot label representation as well as advanced zero-shot approaches.

Some may prove resilient against standard laundry procedures owing to their robust nature or resistance towards cleaning agents. Consequently, odor persistence primarily relies on proximity and duration of exposure to the source.

Collective bargaining involves a legal process wherein a group of employees collaborates to discuss or modify their working conditions with their employer. It's challenging to persuade an employer to increase wages individually, but when workers band together and threaten a collective strike, there's a higher likelihood of achieving better compensation. Scott Walker believed that such practices resulted in significant financial losses for the state due to demands made by state employees seeking higher salaries through union negotiations. Consequently, he played a key role in altering legislation to hinder these activities. Those benefiting from these changes express dissatisfaction about the amendments. A crucial point to note here is that private sector unions aim to secure a greater portion of the profits they contribute to generating. In contrast, public sector jobs rely on taxpayer funds rather than producing profits. The objective of public sector union negotiations is to obtain a larger share of tax revenues instead of profits. By utilizing unions as leverage, public employees shift decision-making authority over tax allocations away from voters to unelected representatives. Walker restricted the influence of public sector unions in collective bargaining, which is a simplified explanation but should provide clarity.

Motivated by the problem of partisan gerrymandering, we introduce an electoral system for a representative democracy called democratic cellular voting designed to make modern packing and cracking strategies irrelevant by providing an incentive guarantee. Our method is based on local considerations in each cell taking into account both the number of voters within that cell (controlled by the parameter ) as well as their relative positions with respect to other cells. In particular, when any two adjacent cells have more than one voter they are merged together creating a single larger cell. We prove that our proposed mechanism exhibits efficient randomness under standard statistical complexity theoretic assumptions using the tools from discrete geometry known as chromatic numbers. The work closest to ours is [9] which introduced another flexible design for direct elections but did not provide formal guarantees about its efficiency. Moreover, their procedure does not allow for packings and cracking while our algorithm allows these manipulations without compromising efficiency. Our Contributions In this paper, we present a simple yet elegant mathematical model relating the size of potential partitions created during the election process with the parameters affecting it namely i) the total amount of resources available per unit time per candidate and ii) the influenceexposure such candidates can possess over their respective constituencies (i.e., the fraction of active citizens who would be willing to vote according to them). Since brute force enumeration techniques, like [7, 8], require exponential effort even for moderately sized problems, we develop an algorithmic approach based on combinatorial optimization theory: We take advantage of the existence of several connected components of similar characteristics within only our small world networks, obtaining a collection of feasible solutions that span most scenarios and allowing us significantly reduce computational cost compared to exhaustive search methods. A second contribution lies in identifying a set of conditions ensuring provable bounds on the complexity of certain stages in the overall election workflow; these results allow us to conclude tight upper and lower bounds regarding expected runtime. Furthermore, utilizing theoretical machinery developed previously [4] along with additional analysis steps we informally show that our algorithms exhibit almost optimal behaviour up to logarithmic factors. Finally, although approximate solutions may be easy to implement in practice, there exist instances where achieving maximal accuracy appears impractical due to increased overheads or prohibitive execution times; similarly, exact computations incur high costs especially if performed throughout all iterations required. As a result, appealingly, we demonstrate how best performing approximations can quickly alleviate the need for exhaustive searches, thereby saving significant amounts of computation time as well as resulting in improved performance metrics. A principal obstacle encountered with gradient-based optimization techniques in model-free reinforcement learning lies in crafting a strategy that maximizes sample efficiency while minimizing variance. Our study implements the Kronecker-factored curvature approximation method (KFAC) alongside a novel gradient estimator known as RELAX, which utilizes control variates optimization. This integration aims to enhance the sample efficiency when applying this gradient estimation procedure within reinforcement learning contexts. One of the basic principles of physics is that things move in "straight lines" at "constant speed" unless there's a force acting on them. Our best theory of gravity at this point says it should act as if everything were moving through space like water flowing downriver, and according to our observations, things do seem to be doing just thatbut only for very large objects (like galaxies), not atoms or molecules or even smaller bits of matter. Pinpointing where this boundary lies has become one of theoretical particle physicists' holy grails; so far they've found no obvious signpost that would show up if you could look closer than about 100 picometers into an object with 1 nm resolution. But now we might have an answer thanks to work by researchers from Harvard University who set out to see what happens when you try to examine individual protons using light. The results suggest that this limit may actually exist after all. It had previously been thought that proton-proton collisions inside atomic accelerators can't really provide enough energy density to get close measurements because most particles are too diffuse. This means their motion will quickly average themselves out over larger distances before being able to be detected. However, recent experiments performed at SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory showed actual protons undergo a similar type of diffusion process - only much faster. Which suggested maybe more energetic events such as those seen within atom smashers aren't necessary anymore: They're good enough already. And indeed, the team figured something else was going on here. This new research shows how these diffusing protons interact with other nearby protons via optical photons emitted during electron scattering, which creates information known as angular momentum distributions. These then produce a pattern called Bragg diffraction patterns, made up of peaks and valleys. So clearly some sort of physical interaction between the two protons must take place. What's still missing though is evidence showing this behavior occurs under realistic conditions.

Consequently, the heart accelerates due to reduced vagal activity.

Examples of energy transformation include generating electric energy from heat energy via a steam turbine, or lifting an object against gravity using electrical energy driving a crane motor. Lifting against gravity performs mechanical work on the object and stores gravitational potential energy in the object. If the object falls to the ground, gravity does mechanical work on the object which transforms the potential energy in the gravitational field to the kinetic energy released as heat on impact with the ground. Our Sun transforms nuclear potential energy to other forms of energy; its total mass does not decrease due to that in itself (since it still contains the same total energy even if in different forms), but its mass does decrease when the energy escapes out to its surroundings, largely as radiant energy.

On the other hand, as a visitor or non-citizen, I don't need to pay sales tax since I won't be using public services such as roads or emergency response teams. Stores at airports are aware that travelers will leave the country, hence sales tax is waived when making purchases. This system ensures fairness by exempting tourists from taxes they wouldn't benefit from. It's important to note that duty-free items tend to be pricier than regular retail stores. Nonetheless, requesting duty-free status might result in lower prices compared to larger shops located away from airports.

Crude oil, true to its name, is unrefined and consists of diverse carbon compounds, ranging from smaller lighter molecules such as butane and propane to larger chains containing numerous carbon atoms. These chains store varying amounts of energy based on their structure. While burning crude oil releases this energy, the heterogeneous mixture also generates multiple combustion byproducts that could clog or damage engines, especially due to heavier petroleum waxes and oils. Consequently, utilizing crude oil directly isn't feasible, prompting us to refine it into valuable commodities.

In the oil refinery sector, a term known as 'crack spread' estimates the quantity of gasoline and fuel oil produced from crude oil barrels using a basic ratio, e.g., a 3-2-1 spread implies three barrels of crude yield two barrels of gasoline and one barrel of heavy fuel oil. However, actual production processes may differ significantly, enabling more extensive creation of oil derivatives from the same initial input. Refinement necessitates intricate procedures involving substantial energy consumption. Impurities like sulfur, nitroeneous compounds, salts, and residues need removal before heating the oil in vertical columns, resulting in stratification according to density - with gasoline residing atop while denser materials settle below. Further processing ensures precise carbon chain compositions; additionally, specific chemicals enhance gasoline performance within automotive engines. Extensive quality control measures via laboratory analyses guarantee product standards throughout the entire operation. Overall, transforming crude oil into marketable fuels involves complex and resource-intensive methodologies.

We study the problem of leader selection in leader-follower multi-agent systems that are subject to stochastic disturbances. This problem arises in applications such as vehicle formation control, distributed clock synchronization, and space mission coordination with unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). In each scenario, a group of agents must synchronize their actions so as to avoid collisions while moving toward an objective location or maintaining positions relative to one another. The goal is for all agents within the group to follow in lockstep without drift in order to achieve overall system stability. In this paper we consider two different scenarios: 1) A model predictive controller approach; 2) An observercontroller architecture based on output feedback linearization. For both approaches we present conditions under which agent groups can be stabilized and provide design guidelines regarding how many followers there should be per agent. When designing the formulae presented here it is important to note that these constitute worst case bounds because they assume the most pessimistic condition among all possible realizations of uncertainty in initial state measurements. We also show that our results give insight into why previous work did not guarantee stabilization due to insufficient follower numbers. Some open problems remain including extension beyond nonlinear uncertain models and continuous time dynamics. Numerical simulations verify the analytic predictions.

A quantum effect called superabsorption allows a collection of molecules to absorb light more efficiently than if each molecule were acting individually. Researchers have used this phenomenon to create a new type of optical device that could improve the sensitivity of solar cells, cameras, and other devices. The system, described today in Nature, consists of two microscopic silicon wires arranged so that they face each other and are spaced only nanometers apart. The researchers found that when light hit one wire, it would appear to be absorbed by the other wire. The effect could be observed even if the wires were separated by a distance five times larger than the light's wavelength. The phenomenon is the result of quantum effects that cause light to "tunnel" through the space between the wires. When the light reaches the second wire, it appears as if it was emitted there. This is similar to the way that an electron in one quantum state can tunnel into a different quantum state - an effect that is widely used in many kinds of devices, such as the tunnel diodes used in transistor radios. The effect has been observed in the lab before, but this is the first time it has been seen in a silicon-based device. The finding may enable researchers to integrate the effect into silicon-based systems, which are important in a wide range of optical applications. It's been known for some time that when you have a system in which two resonators are very close to each other, there can be a coupling effect, called vacuum Rabi splitting, which enhances the interaction between the light and the matter. The team, led by David Kim, a postdoc in the laboratory of Xiang Zhang, a professor of mechanical engineering at the University of California, Berkeley, found a new way to create the coupling effect. They turned the usual arrangement upside down by placing the resonators on top of each other, separated by a nanoscale gap. This allowed the coupling between the resonators to be much stronger than in the usual configuration. The new device could be used to enhance the efficiency of solar cells, in which the photovoltaic material absorbs only a fraction of the incident light. The material is generally chosen to absorb a particular wavelength of light, but it is ineffective at absorbing light at other wavelengths. If an optical antenna could be used to couple these "forbidden" wavelengths to the material, it would increase the overall efficiency of the device. The system could also be used to create an optical modulator, which could alter the amplitude, phase, or frequency of a light beam, potentially allowing a system to be used as a type of optical transistor. One application for this technology would be to speed up the data transmission in computer chips. Optical modulators have previously been made using a different type of superabsorption effect called electromagnetically induced transparency. However, these devices can only operate at very low temperatures. The new device works at room temperature, making it suitable for many applications.

The utilization of the unlicensed band through LTE-U presents an opportunity to address the limited availability of wireless spectrum. Nevertheless, ensuring harmonious operation alongside existing WiFi networks remains a critical obstacle in implementing LTE-U technology. This study examines the issue of shared use of the unlicensed spectrum between WiFi and LTE-U systems. A novel approach employing ruin theory is introduced, facilitating equitable distribution of excessive spectral resources within the unlicensed band to LTE-U users while preserving the functionality of WiFi services. By leveraging the principle of ruin probability, we achieve balanced resource allocation via duty cycles in LTE-U operations, thereby safeguarding the interests of WiFi systems and upholding their operational standards. Our simulations indicate that our method, grounded in ruin theory, surpasses traditional equal duty cycle division strategies in terms of offering greater fairness towards WiFi systems.

Typically utilized by public sector or academic institution staff members, there exist significant distinctions between 401(k) and 401(a) retirement plans. While individuals under a 401(k) select from various investment alternatives presented by the employer, those enrolled in a permanent plan may encounter limited discretion over their investment selections as the employer maintains greater influence over both the quantity and nature of the assets. Participation in a 401(a) scheme is compulsory according to the predetermined rates established by the employer, whereas contributing to a 401(k) is voluntary and based on personal preference regarding the desired retirement savings amount. In this paper, we provide details of a robotic system that can automate the task of picking and stowing objects from and to a rack in an e-commerce fulfillment warehouse. The system includes a robotic arm with sensory and gripper hardware for picking items from a rack, an item conveyor for transporting picked items to a packing station, and a vision-based sorting system for identifying objects at the conveyor. The robotic arm is mounted on a linear stage that can move along the length of the rack. The gripper is equipped with suction cups and pressure sensors to enable it to pick up a variety of different objects. The item conveyor is used to transport picked items to a packing station. The vision-based sorting system uses a camera to identify objects at the conveyor and sort them into bins. The system has been designed to be scalable and modular. It can be configured to work with different types of racks and objects, and can be expanded to include additional robotic arms and conveyors as needed.

Once upon a time, there was a young girl named Sarah who struggled with spelling. She had always struggled with spelling, but she never thought it would lead to something as strange as what happened to her one day. Sarah was trying to write a letter to her friend, but as usual, she found herself struggling to spell many of the words correctly. She was so focused on trying to spell the words that she didn't notice anything unusual happening around her. Suddenly, she heard a loud noise, and when she looked up, she saw that a strange figure had appeared in her room. He had pointy ears, a red suit, and a pitchfork. Sarah was terrified, and she quickly realized that she had accidentally summoned a demon named Stan. Stan looked at Sarah and asked, "Who are you, and why did you summon me?" Sarah was too terrified to speak, but before she could try to reply, Stan looked down at the letter she had been writing and laughed. "Ah, I see what happened. You summoned me because of your poor spelling. Well, I'm here now, so what can I do for you?" Sarah didn't know what to do. She had always heard that demons were dangerous creatures and that summoning them was never a good idea. She tried to ask Stan to leave, but he refused. "I can't leave until you tell me what you want me to do. That's the deal," he said. Sarah thought for a moment and then decided to take a chance. She told Stan that she needed help with her spelling and asked if he could teach her. Stan laughed again and said, "Well, I suppose I can help you with that. After all, it's not every day that someone summons me for such a harmless reason." Over the next few weeks, Stan worked with Sarah to improve her spelling. He helped her learn new words, showed her spelling tricks, and even helped her with grammar. Sarah was surprised at how helpful Stan was, and she soon started to look forward to their lessons. Eventually, Sarah became much better at spelling, and she didn't need Stan's help anymore. She thanked him for his assistance and told him that she was glad she had accidentally summoned him. Stan laughed and said, "Who knows? Maybe we'll meet again someday if you need my help." Sarah smiled and waved goodbye to Stan as he disappeared. She couldn't believe how lucky she was to have summoned such a helpful demon. From that day on, she never underestimated the power of spelling.
