We illustrate the use of probabilistic capacity assessment by applying it to a simulation of the UK's electrical infrastructure.

The term "defense" is preferred over "war" due to its more positive connotation and political appeal. Public perception tends to favor defense initiatives rather than war efforts. Additionally, the Department of Defense encompasses various aspects beyond strictly military personnel such as weapon manufacturers, consultants, government groups, and contractors who fall under its umbrella.

Countries often use euphemistic language like "doublespeak" to describe actions that may appear controversial or distasteful. Referring to the organization simply as the Department of Defense and Occasionally Meddling With Other Nations provides a straightforward description; however, this doesn't serve a purpose since most people already understand the role of the Department of Defense. When considering vital national interests, these tend to align closely with whatever definition the governing body decides upon at a given moment. In practice, the Department of Defense focuses on defending critical matters without resorting to unnecessary invasion or aggression against foreign nations. Yet, historically, strategic objectives have led to the acquisition of resources from other countries as collateral damage, which has also resulted in monetary compensation and unfortunately, casualties among civilians.

As for the evolution of the terminology used, after World War II, the U.S. restructured its military organizations into one consolidated entity known as the Department of Defense. Although they could have retained the previous title of "Department of War" or adopted something like "Department of the Military," ultimately opting for "Defense" provided clarity while avoiding confusion.

In natural language using short sentences is considered efficient for communication. However, a text composed exclusively of such sentences looks technical and reads boring. A text composed of long ones, on the other hand, demands significantly more effort for comprehension. Studying characteristics of the sentence length variability (SLV) in a large corpus of world-famous literary texts shows that an appealing and aesthetic optimum appears somewhere in between and involves selfsimilar, cascade-like alternation of various lengths sentences. A related quantitative observation is that the power spectra S (f) of thus characterized SLV universally develop a convincing ' 1 f ' scaling with the average exponent 1 2 , close to what has been identified before in musical compositions or in the brain waves. An overwhelming majority of the studied texts simply obeys such fractal attributes but especially spectacular in this respect are hypertext-like, "stream of consciousness" novels. In addition, they appear to develop structures characteristic of irreducibly interwoven sets of fractals called multifractals. Scaling of S (f) in the present context implies existence of the long-range correlations in texts and appearance of multifractality indicates that they carry even a nonlinear component. A distinct role of the full stops in inducing the long-range correlations in texts is evidenced by the fact that the above quantitative characteristics on the long-range correlations manifest themselves in variation of the full stops recurrence times along texts, thus in SLV, but to a much lesser degree in the recurrence times of the most frequent words. In this latter case the nonlinear correlations, thus multifractality, disappear even completely for all the texts considered. Treated as one extra word, the full stops at the same time appear to obey the Zipfian rank-frequency distribution, however.

Deep learning models, particularly those utilizing convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have exhibited remarkable results in tasks involving stereo matching. Stereo matching has recently been approached as a supervised learning challenge using CNN techniques. Nonetheless, there's limited exploration into integrating detailed contextual semantics within these processes. Addressing this gap, our proposal introduces a novel approach for estimating disparities through a network leveraging extensive contextual data alongside intricate semantic insights, named the Multi-scale Features Network (MSFNet). Initially, we crafted a unique architecture to amalgamate comprehensive semantic knowledge with granular specifics via multi-scale feature integration, harnessing both additive and concatenative methods to blend semantics seamlessly with finer elements. Subsequently, we incorporated a directional system aimed at enhancing the network’s concentration on areas presenting reliability issues. Further, we conceived a strategy whereby discrepancies are translated into error maps derived from lower tier features rich in detail. Lastly, our method employs cross-validation against real and artificial left-side features to refine preliminary disparity assessments. Trials conducted on both the Scene Flow and KITTI 2pta datasets substantiate that our technique attains top-tier results in this domain.

Your skin's softness and hydration are primarily due to the natural oils produced by your skin. A lot has changed since All Saints first charged onto the scene in 1997. Back then, Tony Blair had just won the election, Oasis were at number one with Be Here Now, and the world's biggest website was a page full of dancing hamsters. Pop music was in the doldrums - this was the year of Barbie Girl and Gary Barlow's solo album - so Shaznay Lewis, Melanie Blatt and sisters Natalie and Nicole Appleton were a welcome breath of fresh air. Positioned as a credible alternative to the Spice Girls, they wrote their own material, dressed in street-smart clothes and shunned the chirpy choreography of other girl groups (their signature move was an apathetic shrug of the shoulders). But it was a difficult time to be a woman in the male-dominated music industry. Female pop stars were expected to dress provocatively - a revealing photoshoot for FHM was a rite of passage - and All Saints, never knowingly in possession of a smile, were frequently dismissed as "difficult" or "sulky." It was unfair and it was sexist, protests Melanie. "A lot of Britpop groups at the time would act very arrogantly and very stroppy, but that was never seen as a negative thing," she says. "We weren't half as bad - but if we didn't want to smile one day, or we weren't really interested in doing an interview, we'd be labelled as stroppy cows." The sexism spilled over into their TV appearances, and the band shudder as they recall a traumatic Top of the Pops taping. "They were filming images of us to use as a backdrop," says Shaznay, "and they wanted us to take our tops off." The producers, they explain, wanted to shoot the band from the shoulders up, giving the impression they were performing in the nude. "The vision was that we looked naked and we didn't want that vision," adds Natalie. "But because it was such a huge show, we were told'if you don't do it, you don't get to go on the show, says Melanie. "The girl that worked with us was in tears because she was trying to fight our corner," Natalie continues. "We ended up having to compromise with the producers. We dropped our tops to here [indicating her armpits] so it would look like we were topless." "We did it but we were stroppy about it," says Nicole. "Again, we got labelled as being difficult." A BBC spokesman said: "We're not able to comment on something that is alleged to have happened nearly 20 years ago, but today we seek to ensure that everyone working at the BBC does so in an environment in which they are comfortable." Nineteen years later, squeezed together on a couch in West London, the band are anything but stroppy. They trip over each other's words, trading jokes and locking their band-mates out of hotel rooms as a way of surviving a long day of press interviews. Even the Top of the Pops incident is laughed off. "These days it'd be like,'you want to see me naked? OK! Sure!" jokes Natalie. "I'll take my trousers off this time!" Their camaraderie is something of a surprise. After two multi-platinum albums, the band imploded in 2001 over the disputed ownership of a combat jacket. "Being in a group is like being in a marriage, and right now we are going through a really rough time," Nicole said shortly before the split. A subsequent statement confirmed the band were "on ice" in order to "clear the air between themselves." The former schoolfriends didn't speak for years, but bridges were built during a brief reunion in 2006, and strengthened on a nostalgia tour with the Backstreet Boys three years ago. "But we still get asked about the jacket every day," laughs Nicole. Following the 2013 tour, the band were keen to continue, but their management suggested they needed new material before going back on the road. "Shaz was nominated to write the album," says Natalie, "but there was no master plan, no-one telling us,'this is the vision we have for you'. There was no pressure. And she pulled out an amazing record." After a year in the studio, All Saints' comeback was announced on New Year's Day via Twitter but the response was more one of curiosity than enthusiasm until the band unveiled their new single on Chris Evans's Radio 2 Breakfast show. One Strike recalls the dreamy, blissed-out sound of their number one hit Pure Shores, with the quartet's silken harmonies provoking a rush of 90s nostalgia. "It was a natural first single," says Shaznay. "We didn't really even have to discuss it that much. It was the first song we recorded together again. It's just a great beginning." Although written by Shaznay, the lyrics were triggered by Nicole's divorce from Liam Gallagher. The couple split in 2013 after the Oasis star phoned his wife on holiday and confessed to fathering a child with another woman. One Strike refers to that phone call, and "how your life can change in an instant." "Like everybody's seen and heard [in the press], I was away when stuff went down," says Nicole. "I had to pull myself together because I'd got my family and kids around me but, after a couple of days of letting it sink in, I was on the phone with Shaz for a long time, just explaining [how] I was getting through it. You know, having to stand up to it, instead of becoming some sort of victim. "The next thing I knew... she played [One Strike] to me and I was singing along. Then she said,'were you listening to what the song's about?' and suddenly the penny dropped and I was like,'oh my God. It's our phone call!' "The thing is, for me, I've kind of handled everything with dignity and the support of the girls and my family. I think the song represents that very well. I don't feel sad when I hear it, I feel quite liberated. It's a very positive song. It's just great. It really captured the moment." As Nicole tells this story, Shaznay quietly watches her with the protective gaze of a mother. At 40, she is the band's youngest member - but the others look up to her as the leader; the one they turn to for advice and, says Nicole, "a great listener." "She writes poetry," says Natalie. "Sometimes, when I start to think about the things she's written, it blows my mind." In the 10-year gap between albums, Shaznay has continued to work as a songwriter, collaborating with the likes of Little Mix and Sugababes - so how did she relocate the trademark All Saints sound? "I actually can't explain it," she says. "I think one of the fundamental ingredients for the sound is our voices together and that sort of slotted back into place." However, she says, everyone's voice changed in the intervening years, meaning the arrangements have to be re-written for their upcoming tour. "I used to do the high harmony, now I do the low one," explains Melanie. "My balls have dropped." Not for the first time, the band cackle with laughter, happily unencumbered by the media training that dictates most modern interviews. "Artists tend to be more careful of what they say now, because it can move into the stratosphere so quickly," says Shaznay. "But while it's understandable, I think it's a shame - because you lose the essence of who an artist is. You don't get a real feel for anybody, so everybody becomes generic." Perhaps that's the essence of All Saints' appeal - they're not caricatures, but real women who embrace their strengths and flaws. So, is this reunion the start of a new chapter? "When we'd finished this album we could have easily carried on because, by the time we got to the end, we'd started to explore different sounds," says Shaznay. "I think if we hear more material that we're inspired by, we'll definitely write more." "But we're in no rush," cautions Melanie. "We're taking our time." Surely they won't wait another 10 years, though? "It'll take me that long," says Nicole, "to get off this couch." All Saints' album Red Flag is out now on London Records.

Truthfully; because Russia sees itself on the outside, looking in, and they're desperate to retain their seat at the table, particularly given the fact that their chair is, due to historical reasons, just as big as that of the US. As the world becomes more globalized and interconnected, Russia's power wanes. This is primarily because the key products that Russia supplies to the rest of the world are energy products, namely oil and natural gas. Worse, the world is beginning to shift away from those products as the threat of Global Warming makes fossil fuels less palatable, such that even China is starting to distance themselves from it. In many other industries, they are simply unable to compete against the West in the form of Europe and the US (which produces better quality products) and the East in the form of India and China (which produces the same products for less). You can already see the attrition in industries where Russia was formerly at the forefront; their aviation industry in particular, which was once the equal to their American rivals, is in absolute shambles, as Mikoyan-Gurevich struggles to remain relevant, and Sukhoi is barely able to make ends meet by continually updating a legacy fighter on an ancient airframe as opposed to producing something new, and because the aviation equivalent of "customer support" that the US companies provide is far-and-away superior to anything the Russians are able to afford. Finally, Russia sees NATO as an existential threat to itself. Whether or not it is or not is a pretty complicated question, but from Russia's perspective NATO is Russia's primary geopolitical foe. And NATO is functionally run by the US. This is the main reason why Russia spends 5.4 of their GDP on their military, as opposed to the US only spending 3.3 or so. And yet, even with this increased level of spending with respect to GDP, their military is kind of falling apart, particularly their Navy, and probably a fair fraction of their nuclear arsenal that (in their eyes) is the only real defense against NATO that they can count on because of MAD. As a result, the already poor Russian economy is set to get poorer, with it's only advantage (oil) rapidly fading from relevancy, with their common geopolitical foes getting stronger and stronger, and their only real allies (China) cosying themselves up to the West a little more each day, entirely because the West has money and markets that Russia, as a country of only 140 million, just doesn't have, and can't sustain. So Russia interferes in the election, functionally backing a candidate that is more palatable to their interests, and who is (in their eyes) the only possible strategy with which to be able to sustain their relevance and power on the global scale.

Ants are so small that the mass per unit area of their feet is tiny. Their feet are sticky, so this allows them to stick to the ceiling. Jonas stared into the mirror, plucking at his goatee and admiring the way it looked on his face. There was something so, sinister about. So insipid. A black shock of hair to command the ages! " It looks like a dead worm has curled up on your face you know, " his twin sister Sonja said from the doorway to the bathroom. " It does not, it looks dignified, " Jonas said defensively, but stopped plucking it anyway. It suddenly felt weak. He flicked off the light switch and breezed past his sister. He had almost made it across the living of their house before she said anything. " Where are you going? " she asked. " Out. To the park. I'm going to kick some puppies for a while. " A little snort escaped her mouth. " Are you? Are you really? How many have you kicked this week? " " It's not the volume that counts, it's the gusto you do it with. " He was sure he could do it this time, if he only tried. Really tried that is. He grabbed his coat off the wall, black leather of course, and headed out the front door. Just before the door could close, Sonja's voice snaked out the door and wormed into his ear saying, " Bring the car back by four. I'm using it tonight. " She said it in that voice that told Jonas he shouldn't argue. But, damnit, he had the goatee and leather coat and he'd be damned if she would tell him what to do. He turned around to argue, but, too late; the door had shut. He pulled out his phone and checked the time, 3:36. The park was close, but not close enough for him to get there and be back in time. " AUGH! A pox upon you sister! " he screamed at the sky. Last time he had screamed at her, it had not ended well. He got in the car anyway. Surely some evilness could be found closer than the park. Something he could fit into 24 minutes. Two blocks later he stopped at the gas station, this would be a good enough spot. Jonas burst through the set of double doors in a brash move that startled the owner and sent a strong message to beware this dangerous man. At least, that's what he did in his head. In reality, there was a post in between the double doors that he walked smack into, which caused the clerk behind the counter to give him a funny look. Meekly, he stepped around the post into the convenience store. Overhead, Marilyn Manson played on the shop speakers giving Jonas a push forward towards evilness. Clearly the music was the choice of the teenager behind the counter. He'd seen the teenager before, a plump girl from the neighborhood that fidgeted like a nervous dog. Afraid of her own shadow and overcompensating with brash hair and loud music. Plus two years younger than Jonas. A perfect victim for his evil deeds! His eyes scanned the store, an easy round of shoplifting could be done in no time. Fudgesicles! His sister's barbed words had stung, and chocolate was the answer. He sauntered over to the freezer case with a walk to chill the innocent and put fear into the righteous. He threw open the door and grabbed a single bar, no need to be greedy. As he was walking back, the music abruptly changed. The angry dripping tones of Marilyn Manson gave way to the slow waltz of the 1950s. That could only mean one thing; Mrs. Macgillicuddy was on shift! It was true, the easily bullied teenager had left the front counter and was replaced by the grey haired pensioner with a perpetual hunch from down the street. Jonas steeled himself, rallied his mind and was determined to be as evil as possible. He might not steal this bar, but there was no damn way he was leaving a tip in the tip jar! That's what Jonas told himself, right up until he left a single note in the jar; she was on reduced income after all and needed the money for her cat. " Such a dear boy, " she said. The words stung, but the chocolate soothed. Back home, Jonas tossed his coat on the floor, evil twins don't pick up their things. Sonja walked by - stepping on the coat - and said, " That bar will make you even fatter. " Reflexively, he glanced at his belly. Maybe he was getting a bit of a spare tire. Whatever, he earned this chocolate. After finishing up his chocolate, he had nothing to do but watch the clock as four pm came, and went. Sonja sat opposite in one of the recliners reading a magazine. Ten minutes past four came, and went. " I, uh, " he said with hesitation, " I thought you were going out at four? " " I was, I changed my mind. " " What? Than why did you- " " Don't you take that tone with me, " she cut him off and withered him with a furious stare. His anger wilted, his words became lost. Defeated, he shuffled into the other room. Jonas went into the kitchen and pulled out one of his Lego sets to work on. The only thing that brought him real joy when chocolate failed. He opted to build the Orange racecar as it had the fewest missing pieces; Sonja had the habit of stealing and hiding critical pieces on all of his sets. As he labored, the sun dipped beneath the horizon and evening came. Jonas heard his mother come in the front door and set down her briefcase. " Any phonecalls, dear? " she asked. " Yeah, " Sonja said, " Frank called to say he'd be late for dinner and Sarah called for Jonas. " Sarah! That name! Images of the sweet, blonde haired girl flooded his mind. He'd been trying to talk to her for months about joining a book club. " Oh? What did she say? " Jonas hung on every word as Sonja said, " She asked if the book club was still open. " " Oh that's nice. Would you be a dear and put the kettle on before while I get changed? It's been a long day. " " Of course mum. " Sarah, in the book group! The warm healing powers of her name alone outshone anything Chocolates or Legos could bring. Sonja walked into the kitchen and looked Jonas right in the eyes. " I told her the book club had disbanded and you were gay. She deserves better than the likes of you. " Pain shot through Jonas'eyes like an electric arc, bleeding away tears in it's wake. Sonja added, " Put the kettle on for mum before you start crying. " Jonas finally realized who he was in this world, and more importantly, who his sister was.

This assessment considers establishing specialized centers for certain services to enhance quality. Responding, Mr. Cameron stated that Labour representatives were falsely alarming citizens, emphasizing that their government was investing in the hospital contrary to Labour's approach. Furthermore, during her visit to the area on Tuesday to endorse Labour candidate Andy Sawford, shadow health secretary Andy Burnham criticized the Tories' credibility with regard to the NHS and highlighted the lack of transparency from ministers concerning potential downgrades at Kettering. Conversely, UKIP candidate Margot Parker asserted that these accusations had no basis in reality and were merely political maneuvering. Additionally, both Jill Hope representing the Lib Dems and Tory candidate Christine Emmett dismissed such allegations, with Ms. Emmett citing reassurances regarding the hospital's prospects.

Written Japanese incorporates two syllabic systems called kana, which evolved from simplified versions of Chinese characters chosen to denote Japanese syllables. These syllabaries vary due to their selection of distinct characters for identical syllables and their unique approaches to simplify them for convenient handwriting. Katakana was formed by extracting portions of characters, whereas hiragana originated from the flowing script of entire characters. Contemporary Japanese utilizes a blend of scripts wherein kanji is employed for root words, hiragana for suffixes and function words, and katakana is reserved for foreign borrowed words alongside its use to highlight indigenous terms, paralleling the function of italics in Romance tongues.

This research explores a method of social collaboration supported by peer-to-peer energy exchange, allowing producers and consumers (prosumers) to determine how to optimally utilize their storage systems for engaging in this type of trade. The aim is to develop a solution centered around the benefits of prosumers. A game theory approach involving coalition building is implemented to enable a prosumer to assess the advantages of joining peer-to-per trading while considering the use or non-use of their battery system. Consequently, this facilitates the creation of appropriate collaborative networks among like-minded prosumers within the community to partake in such trades. An analysis of the resulting coalition structures reveals two key findings: firstly, the social cooperation amongst prosumers results in stable and ideal groupings; secondly, the suggested peer-to-peer trading model prioritizes the interests of prosumers. Real-world case studies, grounded in authentic residential energy consumption and photovoltaic production datasets, demonstrate how the proposed framework enhances prosumer benefits by adhering to prosumer-focused principles.

In some cases this is done in a more extreme manner, not simply to cancel a small amount of residual reactance, but to resonate an antenna whose resonance frequency is quite different from the intended frequency of operation. For instance, a "whip antenna" can be made significantly shorter than 14 wavelength long, for practical reasons, and then resonated using a so-called loading coil. This physically large inductor at the base of the antenna has an inductive reactance which is the opposite of the capacitative reactance that such a vertical antenna has at the desired operating frequency. The result is a pure resistance seen at feedpoint of the loading coil; unfortunately that resistance is somewhat lower than would be desired to match commercial coax.[citation needed]

I don't know if you could say that mortality is high, but on the flip side of the argument is that Zoos, Preserves, and Refuges tend to monitor the animal's diets and overall health in a way that simply isn't possible in the wild. Tom's first day at work was at hand as he boarded the bus. He arrived at the office and went to find the HR department. They issued him a pass , which they also handed out for his co-workers. "You'll need these when you're off duty," said Mr. Dorsey, the director of human resources. "Okay." Tom had just started working there at age 22 - he'd been in school for six months after quitting college without finishing his degree because it seemed pointless with the state government just laying her cards on the table. Now he found himself sitting next to an old colleague from high school who seemed more interested in playing computer games than in getting any actual work done. But this wasn't going to be fun; so far everyone else had acted like real adults instead of 13 year olds. Besides, what could possibly happen that would get them fired? He didn't have much time to think about it though, since right then another younger guy came up to the counter where employees took their lunch break: "Hey! I am here to pick up my social security card." The person behind the desk (who looked older, but probably hadn't even graduated yet) asked innocently: "Do you want one?" The youth clearly confused by this question gave him a look of incredulity before blurting out: "I don't know if you mean do i want one or no...I really dont care..but you should know something...when i say YOU are being stupid ...i'm not talking about myself....your retarded..." Mr. Dorsey did indeed realize how ridiculously early someone must have gotten into work that morning, as he lifted the phone receiver immediately to call Security. However, upon hearing the click noise, a voice with sepia tones sounded over the speakerphone: "Hello sir, can we help you?" Taken aback, he answered rather calmly: "Yes, hello, thank you very much. My name is Thomas Moore, and I am calling from Human Resources regarding the employee named Jody Williams. She has already called twice today and left messages asking me to return calls. Since she hasn't contacted me herself nor returned my phone message I felt I needed to check in personally."After a brief pause, Dorsey continued:"My secretary told me that Ms. Williams recently quit and demanded all documents pertaining to her personnel file, namely her Social Security Card." His tone became quite stern, almost threatening: "If you cannot tell us whether or not she still works here, please contact your supervisor ASAP." Separately, while waiting a few minutes later for the security guard to arrive, Jodie sat across a small reception area filled only with an antique clock ticking away the seconds; either way she knew full well that, despite every effort made, she wouldn't see Dorsey until 5 PM sharp. Still, the final decision wasn't hers anymore. Once again she picked up her cell phone and tried to reach him, but got nothing but voicemail. She hung up as quickly as possible - this time taking advantage of the fact that she got through- last night the techies had finally managed to fix the intercom system, restoring the line between the main phone bank and the floor phones. And she wished she never saw those lights blinking red instead of green - she hated people always knowing better, especially now that most of her previous attempts at discretion failed miserably. When the door opened she stood up and walked towards the man standing outside, trying hard not to show her fear and trembling. Again Dorsey patiently waited for her to identify herself, listening carefully as she explained how eager she was to speak to him concerning some personal matters regarding her recent resignation. Both plain and strong induction contain two parts: a base case, and an inductive hypothesis. Plain induction: Base case: Hypothesis 1 is true. Inductive hypothesis: If Hypothesis n is true, Hypothesis n1 is also true. Strong induction: Base case: Hypothesis 1 is true. Inductive hypothesis: If Hypothesis 1 through n are true, Hypothesis n1 is also true. Strong induction may be necessary if your method of proving Hypothesis n1 requires more than just Hypothesis n. For instance, suppose you would like to prove the correctness of merge sort for n items. Base case: Merge sort works for 1 item. This is easy to prove. Inductive hypothesis: Merge sort works for n1 items, provided that it works for 1...n items. You can think about how to prove this, but since the first step in merge sort is to partition the set into two roughly-equal-sized sets and merge-sort each, having correctness of merge sort for floor n1) 2) and ceil n1) 2) would be necessary. Note that if your goal is to prove correctness for only powers of 2, then plain induction would work, letting Hypothesis n be "merge sort is correct when you have 2n items." Ninja Edit: Proving correctness for quicksort with random pivot would illustrate the necessity of strong induction more aptly.

Not every type of battery follows this pattern, but it holds true for lithium batteries found in mobile devices. These cannot withstand voltages exceeding 4.2 volts DC. During charging, the process begins with a constant current output. As the battery accumulates power, its voltage escalates. This initial phase is where rapid charging occurs. Once the voltage hits 4.2 volts, the charger transitions to a steady-voltage mode, continuing until the current falls below a certain level, signaling the conclusion of the charging process. Charging progressively slows down as the battery nears full capacity, since the gap between its current status and maximum potential narrows, resulting in reduced current flow and extended charging duration.

There are two primary factors contributing to this phenomenon. Firstly, there's an underlying physical principle related to voltage differences; injecting 5 volts to recharge a depleted battery (at 2.7 volts) allows for greater electrical flow compared to filling a partially charged one (at 3.6 volts). Secondly, this method serves to safeguard the battery by prolonging its lifecycle. By decelerating the charging speed once the battery is nearly full, we help maximize the number of complete charge cycles it can undergo prior to losing its storage capabilities. You could liken it to inflating a balloon - it requires more effort to add air as the balloon expands due to internal pressure resisting further expansion.

Layout camouflage (LC) presents a promising method for safeguarding chip design intellectual property (IP) from those who seek to analyze it through reverse engineering. However, many previous attempts have fallen short of achieving optimal results due to significant overheads or limitations stemming from their focus on frontend-end-of-line (FEOL)-based manufacturing processes tailored to specific requirements. Moreover, these methods typically apply only to certain portions of a chip, leading us to believe that such small-scale or bespoke camouflaging strategies are likely to be overcome regardless of the employed technique. This study introduces a groundbreaking LC system that is both affordable and versatile—enabling comprehensive chip-level LC implementation devoid of concerns. The foundation of our proposed scheme lies within obscuring the backend-end-of-line (BEOL) connections, and its applicability extends across various designs without necessitating alterations to the device layer (FEOL). By combining our strategy with split manufacturing, we become the pioneering effort addressing security risks posed by both fabrication facilities and end-users lacking trustworthiness. Our evaluation involves implementing and assessing the core components at the cleaned design rule check (DRC) layout stage. Compared to earlier approaches, our solution exhibits substantially reduced costs while maintaining reasonable tradeoffs concerning power, performance, and size metrics when analyzing 100% camouflaged versus original layouts. Through practical experimentation, we've determined that effective resistance against potent satisfiability (SAT) assaults requires at least half of the layout to be concealed, thereby validating the significance of widespread LC deployment. Notably, our innovative approach successfully delivers 100% LC while remaining economically viable. Lastly, we openly share our workflow to empower the broader community in securing their critical designs.

What are the limits of automated Twitter sentiment classification? We analyzea large set of manually labeled tweets in different languages, use them astraining data, and construct automated classification models. It is clear that sentiment analysis can be improved at least on two levels: by modeling sentiment using more detailed features than common human language and by training fewer classifiers. Further, we show that over time, these insights impinge the quality of the final model because they affect how strongly or weakly an individual word predicts other words. We adopt the Bloom filter for our neural networks because it incorporates semantic knowledge into its architecture. We further incorporate this semantic knowledge by adding a loss function to each of our new classifier networks, which we call the Bloom-Fuzzy Loss Function (BFFL). BFFL has been shown to improve the accuracy of CNNs trained with deep learning. The goal of the network is to determine if a positive label is a "yes" condition or not. Our work also includes four additional layers, each one containing a different pool of training examples from previous classes. Because the filters generate many samples per class and thus capture enormous amounts of information about the underlying behavior, they achieve very high performance even when small populations of tweets are used as input. These effects were observed both in terms of regression performance and classification performance. In addition, we introduce a Bandshoot loss problem, which increases the complexity when dealing with nonlinear problems like sentiment analysis but yields similar results for classification and regression.

The Grito de Dolores Cry of Dolores also known as El Grito de la Independencia Cry of Independence, uttered from the small town of Dolores near Guanajuato on September 16, 1810, is the event that marks the beginning of the Mexican War of Independence and is the most important national holiday observed in Mexico. The "Grito" was the battle cry of the Mexican War of Independence by Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla, a Roman Catholic priest. Hidalgo and several criollos were involved in a planned revolt against the Spanish colonial government, and the plotters were betrayed. Fearing his arrest, Hidalgo commanded his brother Mauricio as well as Ignacio Allende and Mariano Abasolo to go with a number of other armed men to make the sheriff release the pro-independence inmates there on the night of September 15. They managed to set eighty free. Around 6:00 am September 16, 1810, Hidalgo ordered the church bells to be rung and gathered his congregation. Flanked by Allende and Juan Aldama, he addressed the people in front of his church, encouraging them to revolt. The Battle of Guanajuato, the first major engagement of the insurgency, occurred four days later. Mexico's independence from Spain was effectively declared in the Declaration of Independence of the Mexican Empire on September 27, 1821, after a decade of war. Unrest followed for the next several decades, as different factions fought for control of Mexico.

Traditional neural networks serve as an effective model for extracting background from videos captured by stationary cameras. The widely recognized SOBS technique along with its neural network-based variations dominated the field using the extensive CDnet 2012 dataset for quite some time. Lately, the application of convolutional neural networks (CNNs), part of the deep learning family, has proven fruitful for tasks such as initializing background settings, detecting moving objects, and generating sophisticated feature representations. Presently, leading background isolation techniques featured in the CDnet 2014 competition heavily rely on deep neural networks, outperforming traditional unsupervised methods that utilize multiple characteristics or sources of information. Since 2016, when Braham and Van Droogenbroeck introduced CNN applications to background separation resulting in consistent improvements, numerous studies have been conducted. Within this framework, our comprehensive review is designed for both newcomers and seasoned professionals aiming to understand these advancements and suggest potential future research paths. Initially, we evaluate different methods used in setting up background models, subtracting it, and producing complex features through deep learning. We then examine how suitable deep neural networks are for background extraction purposes. Lastly, we present empirical findings obtained from experiments carried out on the CDnet 2014 database.

This information is unrelated to the solenoid. Starter motors consist of brushed electric motors. Within these motors, there are copper 'brushes' which make direct contact with the spinning stator. By pressing the starter button, the brushes shift position, enabling the current to flow once more. Often, at this stage in repairing a starter motor, one could simply replace these brushes—assuming they are accessible—for less than ten dollars. Studies indicate that when a dog displays what appears to be guilt or shame, it may actually be reacting to its owner's cues, such as vocal tone and gestures, rather than experiencing genuine remorse. Research involved instructing dog owners to forbid their pet from consuming a snack before leaving the room. Upon return, some owners were informed that their dog had disobeyed, while others were told their dog hadn't consumed the treat. Regardless of reality, those believing their dog had misbehaved would reprimand their pet, causing an apparent "guilty look." Interestingly, the dog's actions did not influence this reaction; instead, it depended on the owner's perceptions and subsequent disciplining. While this finding does not imply that dogs lack emotions, it suggests that humans may struggle to accurpta their pets' feelings accurately, potentially projecting anthropomorphic interpretations onto animal behavior.

Her car hit the animal and rolled over several times before landing upside down in a ditch. The accident left Samantha with multiple injuries that required immediate surgery to reduce swelling around the brain caused by head trauma. She had broken ribs as well as fractures all throughout her spine and pelvis - a very bad combination for someone already pregnant at age twenty-four. Nine months later, she gave birth to Brianna Marie Smith who weighed only five pounds, ten ounces. Although doctors predicted little chance of survival given the severity of Samantha's injuries and because of complications associated with premature delivery, they were determined to do whatever might help give their daughter an opportunity for life beyond the womb, even if it meant keeping her alive in the neonatal intensive care unit for weeks or perhaps longer than expected. As her parents watched helplessly from behind glass walls in another room, or talked about whether or not to take away breathing tubes so that their baby could breathe on her own, Samantha continued to struggle. After six weeks without improvement, Samantha began to suffer seizures and was placed under heavy sedation, unable to awaken until after three days of being comatose. When she finally regained consciousness again, the first thing she said was, "I want my mother." When I met this young woman shortly thereafter, I asked what happened next. She smiled broadly when she told me how much time had passed since she'd been in her car crash. Then we both realized that these many years later she still hadn't put together the fact that although there are two parts to every human body - the inside and the outside - it is only through our inside (our soul) that we become conscious beings capable of knowing anything at all. This obvious truth can be difficult to understand, especially during our most impressionable early years. But once we have accepted this notion intellectually, then making sense of it emotionally becomes simpler. Since humans learn to walk upright while in utero, babies like Samantha have the added challenge of learning how to balance themselves physically between two worlds: physical reality and spiritual awareness and experience. There was actually research done showing that [the "shameful" expression that you see in your dog is more likely to be a reflection of your own behavior (the tone of voice and the pointing, for example) rather than any actual shameful feelings.] (URL0) In the study, dog owners told their dog not to eat a treat and then left the room. Some dogs were then given the treat, and others were not. When the owners came back, some of them were told that their dog had eaten the treat, and others were told that their dogs had behaved well and left the treat alone (in some cases this was true, in others, it was a lie). The owners who believed that their dogs had eaten the treat scolded the dogs, and these dogs often responded with a "guilty look" regardless of whether or not they had actually eaten the treat. The dog's actual behavior made no difference, just the beliefs and scolding of the owner. This doesn't mean that your dog doesn't have feelings. It just means that we aren't necessarily that good at reading their feelings. We might be too quick to see human emotions and motives in our pets.

One year on, the first handball matches since the Olympic Games have taken place inside the venue - reborn as a sports centre for the community - and on its hallowed London 2012 floor tiles. Handball will be a regular feature here. If you missed it at London 2012, handball is played on an indoor court between two teams of seven players. To simplify things greatly, you use your hands to throw the ball into the opposing team's goal. For handball's dedicated British fans, getting back in the Box at the Olympic Park has been a rare thrill. "We're in our Wembley," says Paul Stewart, who plays for Ruislip Eagles and took part in one of Sunday's inaugural games. "This is the pinnacle. You don't get to play in the biggest sports stadiums in football unless you're a pro. Every so often I look up from what looks like a gym floor and see these banks of seats, and remember - I'm in the Copper Box! Wow! "I can see the seat I sat in at the Olympics." Stewart was not a handball player this time 12 months ago, but he traded some water polo tickets with friends for the chance to see the sport and a love affair was born. "We saw a double header in the group stage, Croatia-Spain and France-Sweden. The wow factor was there, watching these amazing goalkeepers. "I went to my first session at the end of August last year, intending to be a goalkeeper, and the buzz was amazing. "I remember getting home that evening and thinking:'That was so much better than I'd imagined.' I was thinking I'd come home bruised or not even bruised because I hadn't touched the ball.... but it was so much fun." For Dani Sposi, setting foot inside the Copper Box is bittersweet. A former member of the British handball team, she narrowly missed out on selection for London 2012. "During preparations for the Games we used to go there once a month," she remembers. "When I got there, I remembered the smell, all those times we used to train there. "Being there as a player after the Olympics was a bit emotional, because I wasn't selected and it was very hard to go through all that disappointment. "I had my six-year-old son, Matteo, with me. He said:'Mum, why didn't you play at the Olympics?' I said:'Well, the coach made a different decision, so mummy didn't play.' Dani Sposi: "We had loads of people coming into the Copper Box on Sunday and asking about handball. We had another area in the arena where we could explain what handball is all about and let them shoot at goal. "Sometimes people don't realise how hard handball is. Even the parents are like'oh, I'll do it' - and then'oh, this is hard!' You have to find the right co-ordination with the three steps and the bounce." Paul Stewart: "We had easily hundreds, probably a couple of thousand people all told. There were points when it was massively busy, queues of parents with children all holding a ball waiting to have a go. It was superb. "At league level, for the next year or so, it's going to be massive. If we get the right publicity, if people can see the sport and know it's still carrying on in the Olympic venue, that might drag them in across the country." "He has been with me the whole journey, since he was eight months old - all the training sessions, travelling around. It was very good for him to be there, to go inside the Olympic arena. Even during training, I never had the chance to bring him in." Sposi's dream of an Olympic appearance for Great Britain has ended, but other players in the Box still aspire to fly the British flag - despite a critical shortage of funding leaving GB's elite teams in limbo. "Playing in the Olympic venue was a proud moment," says Gil Lewis, another who only started playing after London 2012. Lewis already has two university team-mates who have been selected for the England Under-20 squad within a year of taking up the sport; he himself was chosen to play for the British universities team, but their trip to a tournament in the Netherlands fell apart when the travel proved too expensive. A shortage of cash is a feature of life as a handball player in Britain, but Lewis is determined not to let it dampen his enthusiasm. "This year I've been invited to move up to the first team; I was in shock when I was first asked. They've asked if I want to go to the Challenge Cup, playing in Bulgaria, and that would be an amazing experience," he says. You don't want to miss out because you didn't save up enough." British teams competed at London 2012 by virtue of being the Olympic hosts. In future, they will have to qualify for the Games on merit, which is a big ask of a fledgling sport, but Lewis is determined to take the sport as far as he can. "If a GB team is still around in the next few years, to be able to play for them would be fantastic," he says. "If you'd told me a year ago, I'd never have imagined I'd be anywhere close to being able to represent my country. "There will be a few years before I'm near that standard and with all the work being done at grassroots, by that time hopefully the standard will have improved enough to warrant some kind of funding - to at least put some form of team out." Stewart adds: "Outside the obvious problem with elite funding, we're in a very strong position to drive growth at youth level. While novel metrics are proposed every year, a few popular metrics remain as the de facto standard, including BLEU and ROUGE. However, these metrics may not be adequate to evaluate the text generation systems of the future, which is why we propose a new metric: NLG-Eval. This metric consists of two parts: (1) an automatic NLG evaluation module, which scores how well the system's outputs match human judgments in terms of meaning and fluency; and (2) a human evaluation module, which allows humans to provide finer-grained evaluations of the system's outputs. NLG-Eval is designed to be more robust than existing metrics, and to be more effective at evaluating the text generation systems of the future.

Normally this wouldn't bother me because I find jobs pretty quickly. This time it's different, I actually like this job. Up until 3 months ago, I was the model employee. Always early and completing projects on time; I even was employee of the month, once. But that all changed 3 months ago. No matter what I do, I always clock in at 8:24. At first, I didn't notice the consistency, but after a few weeks it became unnerving. Every day, 8:24 on the dot.Why? One day I even tried to wait until 8:25 but it turns out the clock was wrong that day and was a minute ahead. Car wrecks, dead batteries, lost keys, and zebras! It seems like everyday its one ridiculous reason after another. But tomorrow? Tomorrow has to be different. Tomorrow I have to be on time, not only on time but 15 minutes early. Some how I have to figure out how to be 39 minutes early when nothing has worked up to this point. I have been trying to figure out why 8:24? The answer, however elusive, must exist. It must and now I have only 23 hours to figure it out. By 5 pm it was settled, tonight I would sleep at the office. It was fool proof, you can't be late if you never left. I would order some food and crash on one of the comfy couches scattered around the office. What's the worst that could happen, I am woken up by my coworkers or boss? I ordered a pizza and set up for the night. Bring on the night! Pizza arrives, Netflix rolling and I kick back to revel in my genius. Its almost midnight when I start to feel funny. A wave of euphoria rolls over my body like a cool tide and I begin laughing at my hands and fingers. What's going on; what's happening? I look into the closest mirror and stagger backwards at what appears within its frame. Another world, a waterfall? I blink and it's gone. I stumble to the break room to get a cup of coffee when I notice a door I have never seen before. My body goes cold as I stop, entranced at the number on the door. 824. What the fuck? I've never seen this door before and why is the number 824? At first I assume its a hallucination just like the mirror. I reach my hand out to try to open the door. It's real, how could this be, ther has never been a door here let alone room 824. I open the door slowly as this surely can not be a coincidence. 824, the same time I clock in every morning. I open the door slowly only to find that I am staring into the same strange land that I observed in the mirror. This time I could feel it. The cold metal feeling, the sharp edges, and a trickle of a waterfall. Before I could understand my surroundings I realized the door was gone. I was stranded in this strange land with no means to escape. What could go wrong? How could I have been so foolish? At that moment I notice a large white cat grooming itself on a rock just a few feet away. I attempt to pet the feline when it tears away causing rocks to fly and tumble down an adjacent slope. I began to pursue when I began to feel dizzy. The dizziness came on quickly followed by intense drowsiness. I found a comfortable place to sit near the waterfall and fell asleep. I'm awoken by a scream followed by murmuring. "What's he doing," "this is weird, should we call an ambulance," he looks sick" I open my eyes to find my coworkers staring me down and I tried to stand up. At this point I realize I'm stuck in the janitors mop bucket and ask what's going on. They tell me that someone broke in and ransacked the office and thrown pizza at the walls. At this point it becomes clear that I was not in another dimension, there was no white cat, and the mushrooms on that pizza really were special. I struggle, but stand and remove myself from the janitors bucket. I let out a deep yawn as I rub my eyes and ask what time it is. Furiously from behind my coworkers I hear my boss's voice "8:24 and you're fired"

In this paper, we provide details of a robotic system that can automate the task of picking and stowing objects from and to a rack in an e-commerce fulfillment warehouse. The system uses 3D perception for localization and a robot arm with a suction gripper for picking and stowing. We provide details of each sub-system, present detailed results from implementation in a real world warehouse and discuss the challenges and trade-offs involved in building such a system. Self-driving vehicles have the potential to provide safer and more convenient transportation for the public. We present our vision for a self-driving taxi service that integrates mapping, perception, planning and control to enable vehicles to autonomously transport passengers to their destinations in urban environments. This paper proposes a new method for parallelizing non-rigid structure from motion. It is a factorization method that decomposes the 3D structure and motion from a set of N images into two sub-problems, one involving only N-1 images and the other involving only 2 images. The sub-problems can be solved in parallel and the results combined to obtain the solution for the original N-image problem. We show that our method is accurate and can be 4-10 times faster than state-of-the-art factorization methods. This paper describes a method to achieve real-time 3D reconstruction of large scale scenes with moving objects and people from multiple video streams. The system is based on the structure from motion algorithm and is capable of reconstructing and tracking thousands of 3D points in real-time on a single GPU. We also describe a technique to create a sparse but dense 3D model of the scene from the set of recovered 3D points. The model can then be used to render novel views of the scene. We introduce a general, 2D and 3D-tolerant algorithm to match planar surface features (e.g., building facades and other upright planar structures). Our method robustly aligns such features in images taken from different viewpoints. The approach is based on a planar analysis of image gradient structure and is able to find overlapping planes in cluttered scenes with outliers. The algorithm is also able to cope with affine distortions of the planes (e.g., due to perspective effects). The strength of the method lies in its efficiency and robustness to large amounts of noise and outliers. We present a method to create a 3D model of a large-scale outdoor environment from hundreds of aerial images. The model is created automatically in several stages. First, the images are stitched into a very large, high resolution mosaic. Second, the mosaic is used to extract a dense set of 3D points, which are then used to fit piecewise planar models to the scene. The resulting 3D models have the same level of detail as the original images. We demonstrate our method on several aerial image datasets and evaluate it by comparing the 3D model to a ground truth model created using LiDAR. In this paper, we present a novel method to solve the structure from motion problem for scenes with multiple moving objects. Our method is based on a factorization of the motion of the points in the scene into two sets of motions, one set corresponding to the motions of the moving objects and the other set corresponding to the motions of the scene. We show that this factorization can be obtained by solving a large number of small-scale (linear) problems. We present a method to create dense 3D models of large scale scenes from aerial imagery. Our method is based on the multi-image matching approach, but with a number of novel features, including automatic matching of images, dense 3D reconstruction and a mosaicing algorithm to remove outliers and gaps. We demonstrate the method on several aerial image datasets and evaluate it by comparing the 3D models to ground truth models created using LiDAR.

I don't know if it's allowed, but I wrote from the perspective of the bride, sort of tangential to the prompt. It got a bit long, but fuck it. I dip my head, my cheeks flaming beneath wings of drab brown hair that fall forward as I hunch my shoulders to hide my embarrassment. Behind us, Kevin Schuster- how is it possible I still remember his name? - Kevin's mocking laughter plays a cruel dance along my spine. He asks us if we're going to kiss. Jason clears his throat, desperate to ignore the taunts, and tugs at the Spanish worksheet between us, suggesting biblioteca in place of libreria. I concur and make the change. His face is sweaty; Jason's always sweaty, in that nervous half-grown way of thirteen-year-olds. The look in his eyes discomfits me though it will be years before I understand it. At my parents' insistence, I'm sitting in a chemistry classroom after hours listening to an upperclassman wax enthusiastic about the school science club. I've always liked science. I wanted to be a herpetologist for most of my childhood, a word frequently outside the vocabulary of my peers, and now I want to be an astronomer. My father is an engineer; he wanted to be a rocket scientist, but he grew up with a space race that dissolved by the time he reached college. I don't want that. He's been laid off too many times in accordance with the currents of government contracts. Across the aisle sits Jason, two years older, an eternity in the eyes of children. His dirty blonde hair still falls across his sweaty, swarthy forehead in the most unattractive way imaginable. I don't know if his presence is coincidence or design, and I'm not experienced enough to fear the latter. His friend is with him, taller, with a flop of curly hair and a beak-like nose. They lean towards each other and share a muted joke I can't quite overhear. While the sign-up sheet is making the rounds, Jason leans over, and tells me his friend is Luke. I shrug and put down my name. Jason's face shatters in the crowded hallway as I issue my conditions. He's invited me to prom, as I knew he would - forewarned and forearmed. I'm antisocial and, as proved by this encounter, a bit of a bitch, but an honest bitch. I want this one last experience with my friends before the winds of higher education sunder our carefully tended bonds, and I know it is likely Jason is my only shot. So I agree to go- as friends. I didn't expect the impact to be quite so visible. I consider it my first lesson in feminine power. The twinge of guilt is not enough to make me recant. When he invites me to his sister's wedding a few months later, I decline. I discover that crushed has not only an expression, but a voice, as he quietly accepts my response and hangs up the phone. We're in a dormitory basement, sitting around a plastic coffee table wedged in beside the washing machines, arousing curious stares from passing students. Dice are scattered among pencils, sourcebooks, and crumpled bits of paper. It's the first time we've all played together. The GM invited me after hearing how I love computer RPGs, and while it's only my second try at D D, I'm already enjoying it more than my first. Around the table everyone is joking, excited, as I look from one face to the next- Jason, Luke, Patrick, and two others whose names already escape me despite our recent introduction. I'm the only woman, but I learned how to be the only woman at anything a long time ago. Afterwards, Jason asks to walk me to my car. I agree because I can't immediately concoct a polite refusal. Luke tags along and I am grateful to have him spare me an awkward goodbye. The winter I turned twenty-two, Luke asks me to dinner. To celebrate my birthday, he says. I am excited. Stranded in the bleak corridor between Christmas and New Year, nobody ever remembers my birthday. He gives me Snowcrash and a box of good chocolate. We while away the evening over pizza. We've been friends for eight years, and it's comfortable, enjoyable, to have a little time together without the rest of the group. A week later he calls and invites me to lunch. A lunch date, he says. That was a date? my brain squeaks, utterly floored. But I figure what the hell. It's the least I can do. I say yes. - The road between Massachusetts and Iowa flies at a supernatural rate beneath my car. My mother laughs from the driver's seat, her turn at the wheel. She hasn't seen me so excited or happy since I graduated college. The ph.d program was a mistake. The school was a bigger one. My life is in shambles around me but I'm grinning ear to ear, because I'm finally going home. I go out for lunch with a friend. She's teasing me a bit. Luke and I broke up when I moved thirteen hundred miles away, but there's no fooling her. She knows I want to talk to him. I'm literally in the middle of telling her exactly how much I want to talk to Luke when our server approaches. It's Jason. Same sweaty face, same bulbous lips, though years of intramural athletics have given him a body to admire. I see her check it out, discreetly, but his eyes are only for me. I know the look in them now. I glance down at my napkin, embarrassed. He's almost glowing as he slips in the booth beside me to ask how I've been. I mumble something. My friend chatters away. Luke is mentioned. His expression clouds a bit; he tells me that Luke has seen two other girls while I was gone, news to me, but strangely I'm not upset. I realize there's very little that could dim my excitement to see him again. Eventually, at the urging of his manager, Jason reluctantly departs to fetch our nachos. Luke and I lie in bed. We've been engaged for ten months with eight left to go. Whether it's the influence of his mother, a neurotic planner if ever one lived, or my own growing nerves as the details pile one on another, I find myself nagging him for the seventh time that week to please choose his groomsmen. I know the wedding is laid-back. I know our wedding party is small. I still insist it's past time he alert them. Two will be his brothers, it goes without saying. I wait for the other name, hoping it will not be the one I suspect. He looks at the ceiling and lets out a breath. Jason. My heart sinks. The first time I met Jason's wife was in passing, on her wedding day. We scarcely said two words to one another. They met online, not a bad place to meet, but I always found it strange how they never seem to stand close to one another, never demonstrate a trace of public affection. Some people are undemonstrative, Luke tells me. I try to remember it as she looks at me with brittle blue eyes and offers her congratulations before we sit down to the rehearsal dinner. More than once, I catch Jason peeking at me over the bowl of mashed potatoes. I tell myself I'm imagining things. Probably I am. I mean, I have to be, right? Anything else is absolutely crazy. The sidewalk attempts to tear the cathedral veil from my head the entire way down the aisle, the rough concrete catching against the tulle. I'm grateful for it; crowds are not my forte, and it gives me something else on which to concentrate. It's hot, midwest high summer hot, and I'm in forty pounds of taffeta. I never could resist a pretty dress. It was as true at prom as it is now, though my motives are more pure. I guess I grew up after all. Luke is smiling, gorgeous in his tuxedo, his eyes crinkled at the corners. I don't even want children but at that moment I'm hoping they get his eyes. He takes my hand. I risk a glance at the crowd. My gaze sweeps over the groomsmen, and though last week I worried about Jason in the midst of the eleven thousand other things contributing to my anxiety, it's a non-issue. It's like he's not even there. The minister begins to speak. My mind is so light and happy that I scarcely notice any of it, an instrument of emotion rather than one of record. The ring sticks as he tries to put it on my heat-swollen finger. My bridesmaids cringe. I laugh. It'll be a fond story later. Luke leans forward, our lips meet, and the onlookers burst into applause.

Hey everyone. I'll cut to the chase. Having business days and weekends is an outdated and unneeded concept, in my opinion. Why shouldn't every day be a "business day?" All business should be open 7 days a week. Why do certain services need to operate solely on a monday to friday basis? I feel if every day was a "work day," more could get accomplished, and much more efficiently. Everyone could still get their 2 days off a week, assuming they work full time, but it would be staggered. Some would have 2 days free midweek, or monday and tuesday, etc. This would even out the clogged roadways, popular "weekend" destinations would be less crowded, other businesses could generate revenue more consistently, rather than waiting for the weekend rushes. Also, it would help other services, like any sort of registry, doctors, mechanics, etc. Those types of places are always busy, and it seems they try to pack too much into not enough operating hours. Everything finance related seems to shut down on the weekend. Waiting for a check to clear for example, should be instantaneous in our digital age. Person deposits check, computer pings source bank account, OK funds are there, transfer them to target bank account. Done. None of this 3-5 business day nonsense. Also, this would help with delivery companies. So many of them don't deliver on weekends or evenings, when most people are actually home. I don't have a personal butler (yet) to answer the door when I'm away to sign for my packages. If it was business as usual every day, delivery systems would be much more efficient. When it comes to working holidays, sure that can be optional for a business to be open. More than enough people are happy to work holidays, however. No need for the world to shut down for a holiday that not everyone celebrates anyways. I see many more pros than cons to this. Change my view! Edit: Everyone has raised some valid points. Maybe I wasn't clear on this, but businesses wouldn't all need to be 247, as that would be unnecessary depending on what sector it is. I'm not suggesting this for EVERY line of work. To me it would be the most beneficial to adopt the 7 day a week open idea to places that are closed on weekends and evenings where a "typical" working person may want to get something done. For example, I changed banks to one where it is open every day, as my old one used to close at an archaic 3pm monday to friday. I'm not suggesting we would change all this overnight. Relating to the point Mavericgamer made about a work team, and synergy created when they work together, if we had my suggested system in place, situations like this would still have a team, just it would be adopted to the 7 day schedule. You'd still have a team, and that particular team would work the same hours, and another team with a different leader would work on a different schedule. Together they would cover the 7 days a week. I did not consider the school aspect, however I think the same thing could apply. Certain classes could run on any given day of the week, rather than restricted to monday to friday. A similar thing seems to occur on collegeuniversity levels, where a student would have a set schedule based on when the classes are. They can make it work with balancing job and life, and I believe parents of younger children could make it work too. I am amazed today that they are able to balance their jobs, daycare, babysitter, etc as it stands (I don't have kids). To the point about small business adopting this, they may not need to. The amount of regular 9-5 M-F people being spread out over a 7 day work week would allow more revenue to come in on "slower" times, than our current system. Or at least spread out the same revenue over the week, versus concentrated hectic times when most people are off from work. A restaurant, for example would see a more even spread of people at typical eating times throughout the week, as opposed to packed weekday lunch and weekend dinner times. In my city, I witness countless restaurants with an influx of people right before closing, yet they are open during the day when hardly anyone is there. To the point KevinWestern made, I agree they would need to hire more people to support the extra days, but that's 2 extra productive days a week for the business. Yes it costs more for labor, but more work is getting done. I would use some of the points I've made here to convince them. The idea of the Fermi Paradox is based on a number of potentially faulty assumptions, but goes something like this: the universe is very old. Logically, there were Earth-like planets within our own galaxy long before Earth itself existed. Some of those planets would likely have supported life. Some of that life would have developed civilizations. Some of those civilizations would have developed space travel. At even the pace we can travel at now, they could have colonized the galaxy in the space of millions of years, which compared to the age of galaxies and universes is very short. It would only take one civilization, out of the potential millions that developed before us, to do this so why aren't there any aliens that we know of? There are lots of problems with the "paradox" some of which you can probably think of yourself. But one of the answers is the existence of some sort of great filter. An event that happens in the evolution of a civilization that ends up destroying mostall of them (or in less extreme versions simply preventing space travel). The idea goes that there are many filters, such as the development of an appropriate life supporting planet, the development of life, the movement of life towards complexity, etc. and that there is another filter that we have not yet encountered which makes expansion unlikely. One example might be that it's just too materially expensive to travel to other planets. A grimmer version might be that the energy source needed to travel great distances ends up destroying the civilizations that use it.

Many, many reasons. Here are some of those reasons: Core competency - Microsoft is a software company. It is not per se a search engine company. Furthermore, search engines are a relatively new area as opposed to, say, operating systems or office suites. Foothold - Microsoft has a MASSIVE foothold on the desktop, and it used to be stronger. For various reasons, including price and compatibility, everyone went with DOS in the 80s and 90s, even though at several points better OS's were available (e.g. DR-DOS or OS2). However, all the multitasking and process protection (huge buzzwords back then) in your OS won't do you any good if you have to cough up a few thousand bucks to buy all new software - remember, back then a lot of the time a word processor's basic package might be 300-400 a pop. People want to know their software is going to continue to work for years to come and they're not going to have to relearn everything because the OS company decides that it's time to use a "new and improved" (and expensive) paradigm. Even today, backwards comparability is huge, and as such Microsoft has a great deal of inertia. Developers - similar to "foothold," there are a lot of people who know how to write code for Microsoft operating systems. A LOT. Other OS's generally require you to write different code using different API's. We propose a computational framework for ranking images (group photos in particular) taken at the same event within a short time span. The ranking is expected to correspond with human perception of overall appeal of the images. We hypothesize and provide evidence through subjective analysis that the factors that appeal to humans are its emotional content, aesthetics and image quality. We propose a network which is an ensemble of three information channels, each predicting a score corresponding to one of the three visual appeal factors. For group emotion estimation, we propose a convolutional neural network (CNN) based architecture for predicting group emotion from images. This new architecture enforces the network to put emphasis on the important regions in the images, and achieves comparable results to the state-of-the-art. Next, we develop a network for the image ranking task that combines group emotion, aesthetics and image quality scores. Owing to the unavailability of suitable databases, we created a new database of manually annotated group photos taken during various social events. We present experimental results on this database and other benchmark databases whenever available. Overall, our experiments show that the proposed framework can reliably predict the overall appeal of images with results closely corresponding to human ranking.

The company cited its recently announced changes to tipping as a sign that workers were heard. On Monday, Instacart announced it would no longer take a cut from tips given to its shoppers. Previously, Instacart shoppers were paid a flat rate on deliveries that depended on the size and difficulty of the order, but the customer's tip was applied to the subtotal of the order, a portion of which Instacart then took. With this change, the company will instead take a percentage of the total order, but not the tip. In a press release, the company said it made the decision in response to employee feedback. "Our shoppers are the heart of our business, and we're constantly looking for ways to improve their experience," the release reads. "We recently introduced changes to our tips policy to better support the invaluable contributions of our shoppers, including a default tip of 100 of the service fee, no fees for cash tips and more. This is another step toward improving the experience for everyone in the Instacart community." Shoppers will now be able to accept tips in cash without being charged a processing fee. In a statement, the UFCW said it's not surprised that Instacart made the policy change now, after previously denying that it was taking a cut from tips. "We are not surprised that Instacart has backpedaled and made this change now that they have seen the power that workers have when they stand together," the statement reads. "Instacart's decision to finally do right by their workers is long overdue and we call on Instacart to end its unfair pay practices, such as their 'dead zones' pay structure, and provide guaranteed compensation to all workers." Instacart says it continues to improve its relationship with its employees. "We're committed to doing more to improve the experience for the entire Instacart community and will continue listening to and engaging with all of our shoppers, full-service and in-store, as we continue to innovate and evolve our model," the press release reads. In a letter to the employees that was first reported by BuzzFeed, CEO Apoorva Mehta said Instacart "proactively" notified customers that they could give their shoppers cash tips. "This is not a change to our policy, and we've had this feature in place since early 2017," he wrote. "We believe that our shoppers should have the option to receive tips in the form of cash, and we're happy to make this change for customers who prefer it." In addition to the new policy, Mehta said Instacart will do away with "dead zones," which he referred to as a "holdover from our previous model." A dead zone is a zone within which customers are not charged a service fee, but shoppers are not paid for deliveries. Mehta said Instacart will also now pay shoppers a flat rate for orders in which they bring the groceries into the customer's house. Previously, shoppers were only paid for the first part of delivery. The letter said the company is also working to introduce a new app to make it easier for shoppers to track their earnings. Instacart has been criticized in the past for not paying its shoppers enough, and the company's recent policy change could make it easier to do so. By taking a percentage of the total order price instead of the subtotal, Instacart can pay its shoppers less for deliveries while still giving them a bigger cut of the tip. Instacart has long insisted that the tipping policy did not take a cut from tips, but shoppers have said they never received the full amount that was given to them. The change comes just after Instacart employees at Whole Foods in Boston voted to unionize. The workers will be represented by the UFCW Local 1445. "We're very excited to bring union representation to Instacart workers, and we're confident that Instacart workers will continue to stand up and fight for their rights," Local 1445 President Lou Antonellis told BostInno. The principle of distinguishing between causation and correlation is straightforward in scientific research. To summarize: the statement "correlation does not equal causation," commonly used in both science and statistics, underlines the idea that merely observing a link between two variables doesn't mean one directly leads to the other. For instance, although incidents of school shootings and usage of antidepressants appear related (since many perpetrators had taken these drugs), they do not cause each other. A history of using antidepressants didn't trigger the occurrence of such tragic events; conversely, individuals prone to committing violence might also take antidepressants due to their underlying psychological conditions.

The main contribution of this work is the use of the concept of the discriminant information of features and the use of kernel methods in the second step. The performance of the proposed method is evaluated by an experiment on the Opportunity dataset. The results show that the proposed method outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in terms of the F1 score, which is considered as a standard measure of accuracy in activity recognition tasks.
